paragraphs.text: EUSEBIUS ON THE TITLES OF THE PSALMS. AN INTERPRETATION OF SOME POINTS IN SUMMARY. There are one hundred and fifty psalms, fifty being a sacred number: in days it makes Pentecost, and in years it makes what the Hebrews call the Jobel. Among the Hebrews the psaltery is called the nabla. Of all musical instruments it alone is fully upright. It gets no help toward its sound from its lowest parts, but has the resounding bronze above. "Psalms," then, are pieces played on the instrument alone, without voice. A "song" is performed by the melodious voice. A "song of a psalm" is when a voice is brought in to sound together with the instrument. A "psalm of a song" is the reverse, when the sound of the strings goes first. By the rule of allegory, a psalm is the harmonious movement of the body toward good work, even if contemplation does not altogether follow. A song is the grasp of truth without action, when the soul is enlightened about God and his oracles. A "song of a psalm" is when action leads the way to knowledge, as in: "If you desire wisdom, keep the commandments, and the Lord will supply it to you." A "psalm of a song" is action guided by knowledge about how and when one ought to act. That is why the titles with "psalm" come first, for the saint does not begin from contemplation but by faith runs through everything in his actions. Toward the end there are many songs, and where there are "ascents" there is no psalm anywhere, either by itself or in combination. They are all songs on their own, for the ascent looks only to contemplation. The diapsalma is not found in Aquila or in the Hebrew; instead of it [?] ARGUMENT OF EUSEBIUS, SON OF PAMPHILUS. The division of the book of Psalms would be as follows, according to the accurate copies and the Hebrew itself. The psalms are not all David's, as one might suppose. Some belong to other prophets, who prophesied as they sang. That is why the whole scripture of the Psalms among the Hebrews is not titled "of David" but is called, without further specification, the Book of Psalms. The children of the Hebrews divide the whole book of Psalms into five parts: the first, from 1 to 40; the second, from 41 to 72; the third, from 73 to 88; the fourth, from 89 to [?]; the fifth, from 106 to the end. There are 12 untitled psalms and 138 [?] titled ones. Of the

titled ones the divisions are as follows: of David, [?]; of the sons of Korah, 11; of Asaph, 12; [?]; of the Israelite, one; of Solomon, 2; of Moses, one; anonymous, 17; those headed "Alleluia," 15. The anonymous ones are those that have titles but do not show whose they are. (1) Reg. 1: omission.

EUSEBIUS ON THE PSALMS. The psalm seems to have taken its name from the psaltery. The psaltery is a musical instrument that differs in shape from the kithara, and the song played on it is called a psalm. A song is a musical utterance voiced with melody and without an instrument. A "psalm of a song" is when the song goes first and the same melody is then played on the psaltery; a "song of a psalm" is the reverse. So it is in the histories of the Kingdoms and of Chronicles. After Saul's death King David brought up the ark of the covenant of the Lord, which had been in the house of Obed-edom for twenty years since it had been brought back from the people of Ashdod, and having

installed it in Jerusalem, he chose by lot from the tribe of Levi four psalm-singers as leaders of the songs. They were to play and sing before the ark to the Lord, and to raise a joyful voice in thanksgiving and praise with tuned instruments and songs, with lyres and harps, drums and cymbals, psaltery and horn. These were Asaph, Heman, Ethan and Jeduthun. A number of singers was assigned to them: two hundred and eighty-eight singers, seventy-two to each, 32 from Ham, 25 from Shem and 15 from Japheth. Standing before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, they played and sang to the Lord, one on the lyre, another with cymbals, another on the kithara, another on the psaltery. In their midst stood blessed David, himself the leader of the leaders of songs, holding the psaltery in his hand. Each sang and played, hymning God in the Holy Spirit in due order. Whenever the Spirit leapt upon one of the leaders of the psalm-singers, the others stood by in silence and responded (1) to the singer in harmony, "Alleluia." In the Hebrew book of Psalms they were all written down without numbers, and in different ways. Some are joined together and others divided. For instance, the first and second are joined in the Hebrew. Again, the ninth, which is one psalm with us, is divided into two in the Hebrew. It should be noted that the psalms are not arranged in the chronological order of the history. They are much rearranged, as the book of Kingdoms and the order itself show. When much idolatry had taken hold of the Jewish nation, they say, the people forgot their ancestral scriptures, so that they did not even keep the book of the law of Moses or preserve any memory of their fathers' piety. So it was that they killed the prophets who exposed their impieties. It is no wonder, then, that in such a state of the times some of the psalms contained in the book were lost and handed over to oblivion for long periods. Later on, they say, either Ezra or some other prophets took pains to collect them, and with them he [?] (sic) the book of Psalms. He did not find them all at once but at different times, and he placed first those that were found first. So David's psalms are not all placed in sequence. In between are found psalms of the sons of Korah, of Asaph, of Solomon and of Moses, of Heman, Ethan and Jeduthun, and then David's again, arranged in a mixture throughout the book, not according to when they were spoken but according to when they were found. As a result, psalms that were later in time but were found first were taken up first, and earlier ones found afterward were put in second place. You would find that the same thing happened with the prophets. Everything has been stored up in the book of Psalms as in a great common treasury. You should also note

that the book of Psalms contains new teaching after the legislation of Moses, and that it is the second teaching scripture after that legislation. For David came after the death of Moses and Joshua, and after the judges, and was counted worthy to be called the father of the Saviour. He was the first to give the Hebrews the new manner of psalmody. Through it he abolishes (1) what Moses had legislated about sacrifices and introduces a new manner of worshipping God through hymns and shouts of joy. Throughout his whole work he also teaches very many other things that go beyond the law of Moses. Eusebius of Caesarea, on the diapsalma. The diapsalma was written by the five leaders who performed the psalms. King David chose them from the tribe of Levi, and their names are Asaph, the sons of Korah, Heman, Ethan and Jeduthun. A number of songs was assigned to them, seventy-two to each. They stood before the sanctuary of the Lord, praising the Master of all, one holding cymbals, another the psaltery, another the lyre, another the horn, another the kithara, and David stood in their midst. So they led the songs with such instruments in their hands. Each one, moved by the Holy Spirit, hymned God, and all responded to the singer with the Alleluia. Whenever the grace of the Holy Spirit departed for a short while and the instruments were no longer played, it is likely that at that moment the diapsalma also

Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly. By nature we all long to be blessed, and we define blessedness as the end of the good. Yet many go astray and think they can pursue it in the pleasures of the body, admiring wealth and honours and the luxuries of the present life. So the word fittingly began its hymnody to God where it had to, by sketching the man who is truly blessed and has been counted worthy of the good end found with God. Here, because those who did right in times long past were rare, it blesses one particular person, but our Saviour makes more people blessed and pronounces his beatitudes in the plural. First of all, however, the one blessed would be he himself. So one may also apply the present psalm to him, since he became the husband of his bride, the Church. The Hebrew wording seems to indicate this, for in it "blessed is the man" is said with the addition of the article. Nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of the pestilent. The first are the ungodly, those who have knowledge falsely so called. They hold nothing firm but are carried along by unexamined reasonings wherever they please. Second are all who sin after coming to know the truth. Third are the pestilent, who are not only sick themselves but also pass on destructive

teaching to others, whether in knowledge or in practice or in both. These have settled down in evil, while the second stand in sins and the first walk in error. The one who is free of all these is blessed. But his will is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he will meditate day and night. There is a great difference between those who are forced to do good by fear of punishment and those who choose the good itself by their own free choice. That is why he says, "His will is in the law of the Lord." By "law" he does not altogether mean the shadowy and figurative law, but much more the spiritual meaning hidden within it. The law of the Lord could also be the law implanted by nature in all people, through which the saints before the law of Moses are said to have done right. Of them the Apostle says: "For when Gentiles who do not have the law" (the written law, clearly) "do by nature what the law requires, they, though not having the law, are a law to themselves." Or the law of the Lord could be the gospel word proclaimed by our Lord and Saviour himself to all the nations. And he will be like the tree planted by the channels of waters, which will yield its fruit in its season. Whoever devotes himself to the divine law throughout his life, at every hour of night and day, and is watered by the spiritual streams that flow from it, is very aptly compared to a plant rooted beside waters. He is therefore truly blessed, for since he is richly watered with the divine teachings, he yields his fruit ripe. Further, the Son of God is a tree of life, according to Solomon, who said of Wisdom: "She is a tree of life to all who lay hold of her, and to those who lean on her as on the Lord, secure (sic)." So the blessed man is fittingly likened to the Son of God, who stands by the channels of waters. He is attested and proclaimed by the teachers and prophets of divine Scripture, who in the divinely inspired Scripture are also called outflows of waters. To him, then, the blessed man is likened, watered by the channels of spiritual streams from divine Scripture and bearing good fruit. And his leaf will not fall, and all that he does will prosper. As another says, his leaves are distinct from the perfect fruit. They are the affairs of mortal life, the things that belong to human life, by which the perfect fruit is covered and guarded so that it does not fall. They belong to one who takes care [?] to live strictly even in these things. Therefore in all that he does he will be prospered by God. In another sense: the blessed man is constantly watered with the spiritual waters of inspired teaching and receives fitting cultivation in the present life, and so he will yield his fruit in his own season. His season is the age

to come, since he does not belong to the present age but is a stranger to it. Therefore in that season of his own he will render to God the fruits of his cultivation here. In yet another sense, the blessed man, once transplanted from mortal life, will have the promise of being in the paradise of God, like the tree planted by the channels of waters. Not so the ungodly, not so; but they are like the dust that the wind drives away from the face of the earth. The blessed man is such as the word has described, but he is rare and found among few. The ungodly are many, and they are set against the blessed man as people who have nothing. They have gained fruit that is temporary, scattered and perishing, and so they have become like the dust that the wind drives away from the face of the earth. Therefore the ungodly will not rise in the judgment, nor sinners in the council of the righteous. You should take "in the council of the righteous" as applying to both clauses, so that the sense is this: since the ungodly, unlike the righteous, brought forth nothing fruitful or living, and no fruit worthy of God, at the time of judgment neither will sinners rise in the council of the righteous. In place of "council" Aquila and Theodotion translated "assembly," and Symmachus "gathering." So we should take "council" here to mean the assembly of the saints, as was also said at the beginning. In a second sense, the assembly of the ungodly is meant, as in "in the counsel of the ungodly." They will rise, however, to punishment and retribution: "For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether good or evil." Note that David was the first to teach clearly the resurrection, the judgment that will follow the resurrection, and the promise of the life to come, whereas Moses handed down nothing of the kind. For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the ungodly will perish. Note as a general rule that what is good is known by the Lord, but nothing bad ever is. For the way of the righteous is good. He did not say, "The Lord knows the way of the ungodly," that is, of those who are perishing; but rather, "And the Lord knew those who are his." The way of the righteous is he who said, "I am the way"; and there is also, "See which is the good way." Upon these

PSALM 2, OF DAVID. Exposition of Psalm 2. Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things? The psalm sets out a prophecy of Christ's coming that names him. It foretells that he will be plotted against by the Jews but will rule over all the nations, and that through him all who trust in him will be blessed. The first psalm blessed one particular person, saved as a rare case, but the present psalm calls whole multitudes together to blessedness. It also contains the calling of all the nations and calls the kingdoms of the earth to salvation. In due sequence it clearly foretells that all these things will be provided for humankind through Christ. For once we had learned about

the two ways, we had next to be taught about the Saviour. Through him all people have escaped the way of the ungodly and gained the way of salvation by faith in him. The word shows this when it says, "Blessed are all who trust in him." The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ. The Christ of God has come to dwell among humankind as Saviour. He is the Saviour and light of all the nations, the teacher of piety, the guide to self-control, the author of righteousness, and the source of all virtue and of the true knowledge of God. Why then, he asks, are the nations in uproar at the coming of such great goods? He came to fulfil the law of Moses, as he himself teaches when he says, "I did not come to abolish the law but to fulfil it," and through him the oracles of the prophets reached their fulfilment. Why, then, did the peoples of the Jewish nation, who study these things and are eager to have them always on their lips, devise vain things about him? And the rulers of the nations throughout the whole world, and the kings of the earth in successive ages: what terrible thing had they suffered, or what could they say against him that deserved accusation? Why did they join together at once in this evil agreement, to prepare a single plot and plan a single ungodly purpose against God, the Master and King of all, and against his Christ? The Lord and God of all sent the Saviour to humankind. The kings and rulers of the earth who make war on him, drive out his teaching and persecute his Church from age to age have failed to notice that they are directing their impiety not only at Christ but also at the one who sent him. Here, then, the word clearly prophesies that Christ, named as such, will be plotted against by men. Further on it also calls him Son of God, and teaches that the Father will give him all the nations and the ends of the earth as his inheritance. These things can be shown to have been fulfilled in our Saviour alone. Among the Jews there were also other anointed ones, that is, priests and kings of the nation, so you should examine in which of them these prophecies came true. Was any other plotted against? Was any other called Son of God? Did any other rule over all the nations? Was any other known as Christ throughout the whole world? No one could claim it. Only our Saviour Jesus Christ has filled the whole world with his own name, filling the whole world with Christians named after him, and in him alone has each of these sayings been fulfilled.
The diapsalma is found in the Seventy but not in Theodotion or Symmachus, even though they often use this word just as the Seventy do. Therefore it is likely, if the person also

…has changed [?], that the musical rhythm was preserved (1); and for this reason Theodotion and Symmachus did not add the diapsalma. “Let us burst their bonds apart, and cast away their yoke from us. He who dwells in the heavens will laugh them to scorn, and the Lord will deride them.” We take these words to be a reply to the first verses, those before the diapsalma. “Let us burst their bonds apart, and cast away their yoke from us.” The nations are bound tight by the cords of their own sins and are not free; they are fettered by their own evils. Christ speaks either to the angels who minister to him, or to the Father and the Holy Spirit, or, thirdly, to the apostles and servants of the Gospel, urging them to tear apart and burst those bonds: “Let us burst their bonds apart.” The peoples are bodily under the yoke of the law, which he teaches them to despise as containing statutes that were not good and ordinances that were not good. Brought through Christ to the spiritual law, which has good statutes and good ordinances, they lay aside the heavy yoke of the letter that kills, as the Saviour says to the fellow workers just mentioned: “Let us cast away their yoke from us.” The words “from us” can mean this: Let us do it of our own accord, without waiting for the entreaty of those who are weighed down. “From us” can also be understood in this way: “I too was born among the peoples who devise vain things and was brought up among them, and having been circumcised I am under their yoke. So let us cast away their yoke,” that is, from me and from those who, along with me, practise the law that does not save as though it did save. Or: Regarding it as a burden laid on us too, let us cast away their yoke. For one must dare to say that this is in Christ because of his love for those weighed down by the yoke. The same is found in all the compassionate, who count the sins of others as their own. This, then, concerns people both from the nations and from the people. But “He who dwells in the heavens will laugh them to scorn” should be joined to “The kings of the earth stood up”: God who dwells in the heavens will laugh them to scorn, since their minds are earthly. For they have not understood the dispensation and the wisdom of the…

(1) For τετηρεῖσθαι read τετηρῆσθαι. Ed.

…of his, since nations and peoples, kings and rulers, both visible and invisible, had gathered together, the Holy Spirit commands us to burst the bonds of idolatry and to cast off from our own soul the heavy yoke of sin. By these we were formerly enslaved and subject to other rulers. Once freed from them, we may take up the light yoke of the Saviour, to which he summons us, saying: “Come to me, all you who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke, and see that it is kind.” These words were spoken to the nations given to Christ by the Father. The passage anticipates those who would come to Christ's teaching and exhorts them no longer to bear the old yoke on their shoulders, nor to remain in the cords of their former sins. Some had once been their masters and harsh rulers: the wicked demons who long ago tyrannized the nations and whom they called gods. These held a heavy yoke over them, made their souls bow down and be crushed toward the earth, and bound them with the bonds of impiety. The passage bids them flee the domination of all these and take refuge with the Redeemer and Saviour, who has received them as an inheritance from his own Father. “Let us do these things,” he says, “we who have been made worthy of Christ's inheritance, knowing that ‘He who dwells in the heavens will laugh them to scorn’” (that is, the nations and the peoples who rose up against his Christ) “‘and the Lord will deride them.’” This was proclaimed prophetically long ago. The nation of the Jews suffered it when they were besieged immediately after the plot against the Saviour. And over the ages the enemies of the Church of Christ have suffered it too, always fought by a hidden hand, that of the Lord who dwells in the heavens, against whom they wage war. “Then he will speak to them in his wrath, and in his fury he will throw them into confusion.” But at the time of judgment, too, all the enemies of the saving word will experience God's wrath and be thrown into confusion by his fury. He whom they nailed to the cross and handed over to death dwells in the heavens and encompasses all things, so he will laugh them to scorn. And his Father, who is warred against along with Christ, will deride them and exact from them the penalty they deserve, if words of threat are words spoken in wrath. “But I have been established king by him on Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming the decree of the Lord.” “These men,” he says, “who came together against the Lord and against his Christ, will suffer these things, and such will be their end. But then, after so great a plot and so many sufferings, I have been established king by the Father himself, and I proclaim to you the Father's decree.” This would be the gospel proclamation. But if the holy mountain of God is the heavenly one, of which Paul says, “You have come to Mount Zion,” and again, “But the Jerusalem above

is free,” here he says [?] … is some interval of time. [?] the Lord [said to] him: “Today I have begotten you”? Clearly he was speaking of the temporal birth according to the dispensation. For concerning the birth that has no beginning David himself says: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” He is begotten “today,” not because he receives the beginning of his existence in being begotten, but because, through the dispensation in the flesh, he enters into adoption. Likewise, one who has received from him authority to become a child of God is ennobled when he becomes a child by being reborn through baptism, having been something else before he was a child. The Hebrew, however, was said to have, properly, the word “I bore,” which is also how Aquila rendered it. But the Apostle, being learned in the law, used the Septuagint in the Epistle to the Hebrews. He shows that these things have been fulfilled in our Saviour Jesus Christ and in no other. For no one could say that “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” was manifested and fulfilled in any other of God's prophets of old. Neither Moses ruled over all the nations, nor David, nor Solomon, nor any other of the prophets or kings who have lived since the beginning of time. The plain evidence of the facts bears witness to our Saviour alone, since the voice of his apostles went out into all the earth, and their words reached the ends of the inhabited world. “You will shepherd them with a rod of iron; you will shatter them like a potter's vessels.” Having received authority over all, you will shepherd those earlier ones who raged against you and devised vain things, and also the kings of the earth and the rulers who stood up and gathered together against you. You will not shepherd them with the shepherd's rod used for tame sheep, the rod of words and saving teachings. With such a rational rod the sheep of Christ are shepherded in his folds, that is, in the churches and in the spiritual pastures of the holy Scriptures. You will shepherd them with a rod of iron,

(1) [?] Read αὐτή, that is, the Church on earth. Ed.

with which, it is said, he will shatter them and smash their conceit like an earthenware jar. He says that the rod of iron is the rule of the Romans, which became more powerful after the appearance of our Saviour. From that time on, the many rulers among the nations and the ethnarchies of the various regions were abolished, and the kingdom of the Romans ruled alone. Daniel's prophecy also called this kingdom iron. In the case of the image it says, “the legs and the feet of iron,” and it sets out the interpretation with the words: “A fourth kingdom will be strong as iron; for just as iron crushes and subdues…” And in the prophet's vision it says: “And behold, a fourth beast, terrible, and its teeth were of iron, devouring and crushing, and it trampled the rest with its feet.” So the present passage also declares that this kingdom is meant, when it says: “You will shepherd them with a rod of iron; you will shatter them like a potter's vessels.” For Christ, having received from the Father by an unseen and invisible power the nations of the whole world as his inheritance, will shepherd those who have come to know him and have come into his fold. He leads them in and out to good pastures, so that his flock (for it was a rational flock) says: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing. In a place of green grass, there he has made me dwell; beside the water of rest he has nourished me; he has restored my soul.” But those among the nations who are unruly and exalt themselves against his sheep he brings into subjection with the rod of iron, subduing and shattering them through the Roman dominion. That is how it comes about that the rage and onslaughts of the insatiable nations against the Church of God are beaten back by the Roman threat. The rulers and populace of the cities would not have permitted the teaching of Christ, which overturns their polytheistic error, to take root in their midst, had not fear of Rome hung over them, and had not the decrees that crushed them and did not allow them to lift their heads bridled and shattered their rage. By another power, divine and ineffable, Christ shepherds his own sheep gently, never departing from them, according to the promise he made: “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst”; and again: “Behold, I am with you all the days until the end of the age.” But those who rise up against his flock in the persecutions that come from time to time he himself pursues in turn, punishing them with a rod of iron by an unseen and invisible power. He also shatters their arrogance and their swelling boastfulness like earthenware vessels, so that countless numbers of them, driven by his God-sent scourges, have already given glory to God and confessed their impieties. “You will shatter them like a potter's vessels”: he shatters them not to destroy and consume them, but to remould them. This is the potter's purpose when he shatters his own vessels, when the vessel still

keeps the potter's shaping sound and intact, not yet having been fired. Blessed Jeremiah the prophet also bears witness to this, speaking as from God: “Shall I not be able to deal with you as the potter does, house of Israel, says the Lord?” That is, he is able in the same way to remould those who have fallen apart and to restore them again to their original state. “And now, kings, understand; be instructed, all you who judge the earth. Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling. Lay hold of instruction, lest the Lord become angry.” That is, the instruction of the gospel legislation. From here the passage moves on and sets out teaching for the rulers and kings who are to be shepherded under the rod of iron. It says: “You men, now that you have recognized and understood how great is the power of him who has received the nations from the Father as an inheritance, and what kind of rod of iron is raised against you, stop making war on him. Rather, gain understanding and give yourselves over to rational instruction.” “When his wrath quickly blazes up, blessed are all who trust in him.” Blessed Paul showed that God's wrath and fury are not passions when he said: “But by your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath.” By this he indicates that the punishment for sins is called fury and wrath. “Those who trust in him,” he says, that is, in Christ, who is prophesied throughout the whole psalm, will a little later be found blessed, for the whole present life is short. But the

He has to mark the occasion so that the narrative from the Books of Kingdoms may fit what is said, and so that we may learn that, after sinning in the matter of Uriah's wife, he brought forth such fruit of repentance that he could sing again in the divine Spirit. For Absalom's revolt against his father follows the story of Uriah. From these things others too may be moved to turn from their former evils and change for the better, and they may learn what genuine conversion to God is. Besides, it is characteristic of the righteous to be afflicted. That is why the Saviour says: “In the world you have affliction”; and “Narrow and hard is the way that leads to life.” “Lord, why have those who afflict me multiplied? Many rise up against me; many say to my

soul: There is no salvation for him in his God. But you, Lord, are my helper, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head.” Those who have chosen to live according to God must expect every kind of persecution. For according to the Apostle, “All who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted.” But in everything we ought to endure hardships steadfastly, since our contest is not against a few or against small foes, but against many great ones, and not only enemies among humans, but invisible ones as well. In the literal sense, David was warred against from his youth by Saul and afterwards by countless others, and finally he was driven from the kingdom by his son and fled. He said these things at the time of his flight. It is the mark of enemies to trample on their adversaries' misfortunes and rise up against them. So when David had sinned in the matter of Uriah, many enemies rose up against him, gloating over his misfortune. [?] Long ago and from afar, through envy, the head of one who is great in body is raised high above the heads of lesser people, which lie lower down. In the same way, when the soul of the blessed man rose up and advanced in greatness, as souls may, his head is lifted up. God works with it and draws up to himself into heaven the one who offers himself to follow toward the highest things. For God grants far more than a person chooses; the benefactor outdoes in his giving the one who does good as far as he is able. For this reason Paul ascribes the cause of every good thing to God and says: “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.” God, then, and virtue magnify the soul of the saint and wholly exalt (1) it. But vice, and the power hostile to humankind that works with it, contract and narrow the soul that does not follow God. So it becomes small and stunted, and as vice spreads over it, such a soul is reckoned as nothing, according to Isaiah: for sinners have been reckoned as nothing. Just as dust is the smallest of bodies, so souls that are wholly wicked, greatly diminished, are like the dust that the wind blows away. By the head of the soul we must understand the faculty of thought, for nothing superior to it can even be conceived, since in the body too the head is the more honourable part. This intellectual faculty, then, figuratively called the head of the soul, is raised up in some people. It looks upward and rises above not only the earth but all bodies, so that it reaches as far as God. We should note that the speaker praises God's relation to him in three ways, in the order of the first thing said, the next, and the last. First he says that God is his helper, then his glory, then the one who lifts up his head. He is a helper to us too, and the name indicates one who takes hold of us, to rescue us from the many who afflict us, rise up against us, and despair of the salvation of the one who says these things.

(1) [?] ἐπαίρει.

Next after “helper” comes “glory.” For God first takes hold of a person, then glorifies him, and next lifts up the head of the one glorified. For if someone has been raised together with Christ and sets his mind on things above, not on things on earth, his head will be lifted up by the Lord, who is the Word. The Word is the glory of the one who has received him, the glory that he who does not receive glory from men has sought from the only one. You will understand how David's head was lifted up if you consider that throughout the whole inhabited world and among all the nations the name of David has been celebrated because of Christ, the Son of God, who was born of his seed according to the flesh. While he lived among men and reigned over Israel alone, and especially after Absalom's revolt against him, he had not been glorified and exalted in the way he was through the saving appearance of God that came forth from his seed according to the flesh. “With my voice I cried to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain.” The preceding psalm also mentioned this mountain, where it said: “But I have been established king by him on Zion, his holy mountain.” The speaker there was Christ. So now David says that he will hear him from his holy mountain. And who would hear him but the Lord who was established king on Zion, his holy mountain? For he believed that through him alone he would obtain forgiveness, and that he is his glory and the one who lifts up his head. So, having emphatically foretold that his head will be glorified and lifted up, he teaches where this came to him from, saying: “With my voice I cried to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain.” “I lay down and slept; I awoke, for the Lord will help me.” In these words he foretells future things as though they were past. In the second psalm it was said: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things? They stood up and gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ,” and these things were understood in a future sense. So now too “I lay down and slept” is said prophetically, in place of “I will lie down and sleep and will awake, because you, Lord, are my helper, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head.” In this he indicates the time at which these things will come to him. For after he has fallen asleep, he says, he will awake, because the Lord will help him. By sleep he means death, after which, he prophesies, these things will happen to him. He refers to the time of the Saviour's coming, after which the prophecy reached its fulfilment. Then Christ, the Son of Man, descended even to Hades and showed himself the Saviour of those there who were awaiting his arrival, so that, together with his resurrection from the dead, many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose with him. It is likely that the soul of David was among them. Taking courage in the power of the resurrection of the

Saviour, through which he too, having fallen asleep, would awake, he says: “I will not be afraid of tens of thousands of people who surround me and set upon me.” For he foresaw that myriads of opposing powers would want to hinder the return of the saints to life, because they envied their salvation. “Of these,” he says, “I will take no account, trusting in my defender, the conqueror of death.” For he shattered doors of bronze and crushed bars of iron, opened the gates of death that had been shut from all ages, and provided a way of resurrection for his own who were there, and David was one of them. That is why he said in another psalm: “You have made known to me the ways of life; you will fill me with gladness with your presence.” “Arise, Lord, save me, my God. For you have struck all who are hostile to me without cause; you have shattered the teeth of sinners. Salvation is the Lord's, and your blessing is upon your people.” He trusted in the foreknowledge of the salvation that would come to him after his sleep, that is, after death, through saving grace and benefaction, and he knew that it would come in no other way than together with the resurrection of the Saviour himself. So he fittingly prays that the Lord's resurrection be hastened, so that through it he too may obtain salvation. Therefore he says: “Arise, Lord, save me, my God.” Knowing that the Saviour is the conqueror of all who plot against the human race, the wicked demons and opposing powers, he says: “For you have struck all who are hostile to me without cause.” The Hebrew (1) does not have “without cause” but “jaw.” The Seventy rendered it “without cause,” either following ancient copies that read differently, as some of the Hebrews say, or to avoid the lowliness of the expression. As though showing God asleep, at the time when he handed us over to the opposing powers to be tested, he rouses him. Perhaps also, when he handed over the Saviour for us all, the Father was asleep, as far as he was concerned [?]. But he arises and saves him by striking his enemies, either the Jews or the spiritual beings who are hostile without reason. For the saint is at peace with those who hate him, since he loves his enemies. Speaking in more human terms, one who is not hostile without cause wants to defend himself; but, more piously, his enmity comes from telling the truth. For Paul said: “Have I become your enemy by telling you the truth (2)?” Something similar is found in the Psalms: “Do I not hate those who hate you, Lord?” But we must understand this not as an enmity that plots harm, but as one that restrains, when wickedness is spreading to many. For one must bring what help one can and heal, either oneself or through another; or, as a last resort, pray that the evil disposition be punished, that is, uprooted from the person who has it. This is what “Pray for those who mistreat you” and “Love your enemies” teach. But the one who does not love genuinely [?], and concerning his faring well

…cooperates. And what is said in the seventh psalm, "If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil, then let me fall empty before my enemies," clearly teaches us to hate no one. How, then, is it said, "Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord?" Or rather, who is so godless as to hate the one he believes to be God? It is clear, then, that those who hate Jesus and curse him hate God. For he says, "Whoever receives me receives the one who sent me"; and "Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also." So whoever hates the Son also hates the Father. And everyone who sins hates God, for he hates wisdom and righteousness, and these are Christ. And why should this surprise us, when the sinner hates even himself? For according to Solomon, "Whoever rejects discipline hates himself." So anyone who hates those who hate God will hate everyone except a few [?] of the most devout, and he will hate himself as well when he sins. Therefore we should not think of the things that hate God as living beings. They are evils that attach themselves to rational beings, such as injustice. The unjust man, insofar as he is unjust, hates God, because the injustice in him does this. And we must hate these things, since they are first and foremost our enemies. Just as righteousness and self-control come from perfection, so does this kind of hatred. So everyone who is hostile to anyone is hostile without cause, which is what we set out to show. "They hated me without cause" is of the same kind. But because of those who said earlier to his soul, "There is no salvation for him in his God," he now says, "You have broken the teeth of sinners." That is, you have taken away their words and their blasphemies against me. You have also crushed the men themselves who uttered such things against me, ungodly men who gloat over evil, and you have put their voices to shame. And you have granted this not only to me after I slept and rose again, but also to all who will be called your people. Note that in place of "Salvation" the Hebrew word uses the name of Jesus. Indeed, the conclusion of the whole psalm contains two teachings: that the Lord's power is a saving power, and that he will grant the blessing to his own people, who have been saved through him. This blessing is entirely spiritual, according to the Apostle, who said, "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ." Hence at the Savior's birth the angel said to Joseph, "And you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people." These are the people whom the word also called blessed. This, then, is what one might say by way of spiritual contemplation of the passage. But one could also say that these words were fulfilled literally. David foretold them prophetically at the time of his

distress, when his son was pursuing him, and they came to fulfillment not long afterward. In the clash of battle Absalom fell, and those who took his side fell with him, and David's prediction prevailed: "For you have struck all who are hostile to me without cause; you have broken the teeth of sinners. Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people." These things, then, were said prophetically, as though the people had already been saved and had come under David's rule.

EXPOSITION OF PSALM 4. "For the end, among psalms, a song of David." "For the end, in hymns, a psalm of David." The end of every art and science is that the one who pursues it should reach its goal. In the same way, the end of every rational nature is to be made alive in Christ. Paul says this in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, speaking of each "in his own order." He seems [?] to describe [the end] of all, as … of each one made alive according to his worth after torments [?]. Or else, even without these, Christ makes alive in himself all who die in Adam and reigns over those he has made alive. This is what the title "For the end" was calling those with understanding to see. For everyone who competes, the end is victory. There are many partial victories, and an end [?]. At one point Paul says, "In all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us"; and at another, "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith; from now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord will award to me." So the psalms titled "For the end, of David" proclaim the end and the victory of Christ, who is called David. In place of "for the end," Aquila has "to the one who makes victory." For he will win victory for everyone who has been conquered. Whoever is conquered by Christ has conquered wickedness and wiped it out by being made subject to Christ. For he does not conquer people against their will. He wins them by persuasion, since he is the Word of God. Theodotion titled such hymns or psalms "for victory," and Symmachus called them "victory songs." It is reasonable to understand them in this way even when they are not titled "of David" but perhaps "for the end, of Asaph" or "of the sons of Korah," since all the saints have taken on the image of Christ. Where the Seventy and Aquila (sic) have "among psalms," Symmachus put it more clearly as "with psalteries," teaching [?] … that the song was spoken … the psalteries, several [?] … instruments on which is sung the "For the end," or "the victory song," or "to the one who makes victory." Theodotion's "for victory, in hymns" also seems to point to this. This song, then, or melody, or psalm, with the subject described, presents that subject in a more general way in the prophet David and in a more mystical way in Christ, who takes on the person [?] "in psalms, a melody of" [?] … "A victory song with psalteries, of David." Theodotion: "For victory, in hymns, [?] of"

of the saints and makes their afflictions and their relief his own. For it is the voice of the saints that says, "Afflicted in every way, but not crushed." He also turns back those who are heavy of heart, who love vain things and seek falsehood. The word "melody," as distinct from "song," seems also to point to the artistry of the mystical rhythm. By a correct anagogical reading, it points to a way of life lived for the glory of God, together with sound doctrines and words that benefit others as well. "When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me; in affliction you gave me room." The previous psalm was spoken when David was fleeing from his son Absalom. The present one seems to have been spoken next, after the victory over Absalom. After that victory he dedicates the present psalm as a victory hymn to God, who gave the victory. Through it we too are taught not to forget God's kindnesses to us. Fittingly, then, in the previous psalm he said, "Lord, why have those who afflict me multiplied?" but in this one, "In affliction you gave me room." He says this about the disaster with Absalom. In that disaster he called on God and found that God listened. He had been in affliction for the sake of the people and the ark of God, and he was granted relief and room to breathe. The war came to an end, and the deepest peace took hold of him and of all the people. Or else he says these things about his fall in the matter of Uriah's wife, his son's rebellion, and all the other evils that befell his house. For over these things he humbled himself. He gave himself up to repentance and confession and punished himself in a measure equal to his fall. He appeased God with works of righteousness and the good fruits of every kind of good deed, and he obtained a good promise. Because of that promise he said prophetically in the previous psalm, "But you, Lord, are my protector, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head," along with everything else that the previous psalm set out. Accordingly, he now says in the present words, "When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me; in affliction you gave me room. Have pity on me and hear my prayer." Having been heard the first time he called on the Lord, he is not puffed up, nor does he grow careless. At once he prays again about the time to come, asking always to have God listening to him. He begs to be heard out of compassion, not as something owed to him. For even if he had some fruit of righteousness, he said that he did not put his confidence in that, but in God's mercy and compassion. "Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?" He called "heavy of heart" those whose minds have grown dull and who are slow to obey the divine word, those whose conscience is weighed down by wicked thoughts. He strikes them with his words and says, "How long will you remain in your sins, when you ought to hurry

to repentance and to the confession that is dear to God?" As a matter of history, David seems to be saying these things to those who were troubled and thrown into confusion by trials and hardships, and who did everything except take refuge in God. "Why," he says, "must you stir up trouble and be troubled in times of hardship? Why give yourselves over to vanity, you men heavy of heart? Why pursue falsehood and abandon the truth? Learn from this instead that God and Lord oversees and provides for all things. He never abandons anyone who is holy to him, but always does wonders for him. So be eager to become holy yourselves. Know well and for certain that the Lord will hear you too when you cry to him, just as he heard me. And once the Lord has heard you, you need no longer worry, since his help keeps you safe." According to Aquila and Symmachus, the sons of men would be the glory of the divine Word. Aquila has "How long, my glorious ones?" and Symmachus has "How long, my glory?" This is because of the intellectual and rational soul in them, which was made according to the image of God. The word reproaches them for turning themselves toward what is worse, and calls them heavy of heart and sons of men, when they ought to be sons of God, as it is written: "I said, you are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High." "And know that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful." The prophet is teaching us about Christ, who is the true holy one, as is said in the fifteenth psalm. The apostles also bore witness, saying that it was spoken as a prophecy about Christ: "You will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor let your holy one see corruption." It is also possible that we are being taught about every holy person. To believe that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful is not the same as to know it. In the same way, believing the truth is not the same as knowing the truth, and believing God is not the same as knowing God. The apostles believed the truth, but when they believed, they had not necessarily come to know it. The proof of this is the Gospel, where it says, "If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free." For he is saying that it is those who believe the truth who will come to know the truth. According to the prophets, one must believe before understanding and speaking. Isaiah says, "If you do not believe, you will not understand," and David says, "I believed, therefore I spoke." The Psalms record that knowing God differs from believing him in the words "Be still and know that I am God." He is not saying "Be still and know that I am God" to unbelievers. So the word, in summoning us to knowledge, also suggests what knowledge we must

acquire: that the holy ones have been made wonderful by God. They have been brought to the wonders of the unspeakable mysteries and the holy contemplations, and through the grace of God itself and his divine care they have themselves become wonderful [?]

"Be angry and do not sin. What you say in your hearts, be pierced with sorrow for it on your beds." He advises us to restrain the passion of anger whenever it is stirred up in indignation, and he urges us not to let our rage move us to action. He says this for good reason. Those who were with David went out to war against Absalom in anger, as was natural, since they were indignant at the son's rebellion against his father. For this reason he seems to say something like this to them: "You men, my allies, who are indeed my glorious ones: like sons of men you are somewhat heavy of heart. You pay attention to the vanity of mortal life and do not know God's righteous judgment on the ungodly, and so you are enraged against my ungodly son. You are moved by a just cause and angry with indignation, and so you rush into war. But I urge all of you: even if your anger is reasonable, you must not forget your own forbearance, nor let yourselves be inflamed further, so that you fall into sin. That is why I say, Be angry, but do not sin. And even if your souls are shaken (as Aquila puts it) by what Absalom has dared to do, take care that you do not add another sin to the earlier ones by persisting in anger." In the historical account, too, you would find him urging again and again that the young man be spared. "Offer a sacrifice of righteousness, and hope in the Lord." As mortal men, you may think many angry thoughts during the day. But on your beds, in quiet, when you have come to yourselves, be pierced with sorrow as you think over what you have done during the day. So, he says, do not be angry with those who wrong you, nor with the one who rose up against his father. Do not sin yourselves, even if ungodly men provoke you to angry deeds and to sins. Instead, if you want to be safe, "offer a sacrifice of righteousness, and hope in the Lord," and be troubled no longer, since righteousness has brought you close to the Lord. For he takes more delight in righteous deeds and virtuous actions than in any sacrifice. And to do this is far better than to be angry and set about avenging oneself. That is why, when my son rebelled, I myself was eager for this alone: to appease God through righteousness. Hence "When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me" and "in affliction you gave me room," because I offered a sacrifice of righteousness and put my hope in him. "Many say, Who will show us good things?" But others, he says, think differently. This is especially true of the sons of men who are heavy of heart and love the vanity of life. They do not know what is truly good, nor do they hope or believe that they will see it, and so they say, "Who will show us good things?" For they do not see [?]

these things, because the light of your face does not shine on them. That is why they suppose that only earthly and perishable things are good, and they busy themselves with these and chase after them. If anyone speaks to them about more divine and heavenly things, they usually ask, "And who is going to show us these?" That is what those people are like. But we, upon whom the light of your face has been stamped, O Lord, know who will show these things to us and give them to us, since by your light we have come to know them. "You have put gladness into my heart. They have multiplied from the fruit of their grain and wine and oil." In many places in the Scriptures, grain and wine are promised to the saints among their blessings, and on the other hand their loss is threatened against sinners. So it is worth drawing two groups away from a bare literal understanding. The first are the simpler believers. The second are those who, because the promise seems so small, wish to worship another God whom they have invented. We should take pains to refer the variety of bodily foods to those realities by which each soul, partaking of them as it deserves, is made holy, thrives, and is strengthened to carry out the tasks that fall to it. I think they also refer to the age to come. And so that we do not seem to make pronouncements on such great matters without testimony, Paul will be enough for us. He teaches this most clearly in the Epistle to the Philippians as follows: "Therefore let no one judge you in matters of food or drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or sabbaths; these are a shadow of the things to come." "In peace I will lie down and sleep at once, for you alone, Lord, have made me dwell in hope." This seems to point to the soul's rest and refreshment, free from harm, which will come in harmony with the divine word after its contemplation of the noblest things. For perhaps it is like the body: after eating and drinking we need the refreshment of sleep. In the same way the soul, which cannot always keep up its contemplation, at the proper time gazes intently on things as far as its own power is sufficient [?]. Then we think that rest is meant by the words "In peace I will lie down and

Those many people, he says, travel the broad and spacious road on which the many walk. They have no hope of anyone who will show them what is truly good. They grow rich in wine and oil and grain and think that they are enjoying these as good things. But to me, who have been counted worthy of the light of your face, Lord, you have given gladness of heart. This is not gladness of the flesh or the body, nor the kind that wine, grain, and oil provide for bodies, but gladness of the mind. For I have learned from the Savior and from your promises that even if griefs, afflictions, trials, and hardships never cease for me in this present life, there will still come for me Col. 2:16–17.

the time [?] of release from the body. Then I will fall asleep in peace and be released from the body. And I am fully and firmly convinced that the fulfillment of gladness will be mine when that falling asleep, the sleep of death, overtakes me. For then you yourself, Lord, will take me up with this good hope and settle me in the heavenly dwellings. Note here too the breaks at the diapsalmata. They mark either a change of thought or perhaps a change in the melody as it shifts, or in the rhythm. Asterius the Arian interpreted the psalm as follows: Why is the psalm titled "For the end, in hymns"? Because David began well and also ended his life well. Or else because he began badly, since he committed adultery, but ended his life well, since he repented. Therefore at the beginning there is reproach, and at the end there are hymns. "A psalm of David" is the act of repentance. And since where sin increased, righteousness abounded all the more, he said, "When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me." For here David calls his repentance his righteousness. God saw that his soul had been cleansed and accepted his prayer. Or else it is because in the previous psalm he lamented the persecution he suffered from Absalom, and his prayer, acting as intercessor, destroyed the tyrant. So when he was asked how he had defeated Absalom, he answered with the opening words of this psalm. "For just as God raised him up against me when I sinned," he says, "so when I repented he granted me victory over him." Why was David heard at the very moment he called? Because when Nathan rebuked him, he immediately turned to repentance, and for that reason he was immediately heard when he prayed. For God, who does all that he wills, responds at once, and while one is still speaking God will say, "Behold

Then, having told those around him how quickly he was heard, he turns his words to God and gives thanks to the one who heard him: "In affliction you gave me room." A swift calm, he says, broke up the waves of affliction. I was wasting away with hunger, and you enriched me with the fruit of grain and wine and oil, so that not only I but all who were under me enjoyed it. That is why he said a little further on, "They have multiplied from the fruit of their grain and wine and oil." Their company has become gladness of heart for me. We learn this from the history itself. When Absalom made war on him and he fled into the deserts and the mountains, he was gripped by hunger and need, as one is in a time of persecution. But God relieved his need. For first Ziba, of the house of Saul, brought him two hundred loaves, and wine, and cakes of figs, and raisins; then after him Barzillai the Gileadite, and

he himself brought him ten beds, so that he would not have to sleep on the ground, and double-sided rugs, now called quilted rugs, and jars of wine, and wheat and barley and flour and beans and lentils, and honey and butter, and sheep, and suckling calves. Giving thanks for these things, then, he says: "In distress you made room for me." But what? When you say "I was heard," did you stretch out a long speech? Did you write out a broad tablet of nouns and verbs? Not at all, says David; for God, who is satisfied even with a mere groan, has no need of many words. This alone I said as I prayed: "Have pity on me, and hear my prayer." The thief on the cross might also say this to the Lord; for when he spoke and called on him in his distress, "Remember me, Lord, when you come in your kingdom," he was heard, and instead of the cross he came to dwell in paradise and became a citizen of heaven. He too will cry out to the Jews: "Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?" Behold the creation suffering with its Creator. If you did not believe when you saw Lazarus, four days dead, running from the tomb, now at least worship the power of the Crucified: the earthquake raised the dead, and you sleep on in unbelief. Why heavy of heart? On the one hand, because you were not pierced to compunction by the wonders; on the other, because out of folly you are heavily angry against Christ. Scripture is witness, when it says: "A stone is heavy and sand hard to bear, but the anger of a fool is heavier than both"; for it is not soothed by admonition, and when it sees wonders it grows angry. "Why do you love vanity," preferring Barabbas to Christ, the murderer to the giver of life, the kingdom of Caesar to the kingdom of heaven, sin heavier than the sand of the seashore to righteousness, temporal things to eternal ones, corruption to incorruption? But besides this, "you also seek falsehood," buying false witnesses against the truth who say: "We found this man perverting the nation and forbidding us to pay tribute to Caesar." "He stirs up the people by his teaching." "If this man were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you." And what evil did he do? That he healed the sick, that he drove out demons, that he raised the dead, that from five loaves he fed as many thousands in the desert, not counting women and children? The food was still in their throats and the lie was in their mouths. David too said to those who had gone into exile with Absalom: Why were you led away with the unruly son? Why do you anoint the son against the father? Why did you follow the vain counsel of Ahithophel? If he who speaks evil of father or mother is worthy of death, how many times over does the son who whets a sword against his father deserve to die? "Why then do you love vanity and seek falsehood?" By "falsehood" he here means every vain thing, which is quick to fall and to change. "But the sons of men are vain, the sons of men are false in the balances, so as to do wrong."

"For the end": a hymn of thanksgiving is sung on behalf of the soul, or the Church, that is being led into the divine inheritance prepared for the servants of God. For there is an inheritance for those who serve the Lord; and [?] this is not corruptible, nor does it consist in perceptible wealth. Its heirs are said to be brought into an inheritance imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven. To this the Savior calls the worthy: "Come, at my right hand [?], you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you." Having taken [?] of this inheritance, the one who speaks the present psalm sends up a prayer to God who prepared it, that he may be deemed worthy to be shown an heir of it according to the new covenant, just as the title, "for her who inherits," also indicates concerning his own soul. "Give ear to my words, O Lord; understand my cry." Now the words announced through the mouth [?] are heard and received by the ears; but the [?] … through words, even if they claim with their lips to know and confess the God who is over all [?] … yet in their heart, that is, in their mind, there was not even a single true notion about God. Such, then, was all life before the coming of our Savior. (1) The one who denies God is most truly and most fittingly called a fool. For if the beginning of wisdom is the fear of God, fearlessness [?] and the rejection of it would be the opposite of wisdom. "For to you will I pray, O Lord; in the morning you will hear my voice; in the morning I will stand before you, and you will look upon me [?]." By these words she who inherits is taught to dedicate the first-fruits of the day's actions to God [?] … worship; which she would not do unless [?] … even from her bed, having ignorance [?]. "For you are not a God who wills lawlessness; the evildoer shall not dwell beside you, nor shall the lawless abide before your eyes." As one deemed worthy of the promised good things, she who inherits [?] … shows the lawless to herself [?]. For the lawless [?] … once sojourned with you,

[?] "You have hated, O Lord, all who work lawlessness; you will destroy all who speak falsehood [?]. The Lord abhors a man of blood and deceit." Not those who once worked it, but those who are still working it now, as persisting in wickedness: these God hates. But beyond all these, he hands over to destruc- (1) [?] on Psalm 17.

-tion those who not only reason out falsehoods through deception but also speak them and serve them to others, as the godless heretics do. And on top of all these, "the Lord abhors the man of blood," and he places the deceitful man under the same punishment as him. Abhorrence expresses an extreme aversion of the one who abhors toward what is abhorrent, as at a great outrage. "Lord, lead me in your righteousness; because of my enemies, make my way straight before you." Christ is the righteousness; for he became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption. "For there is no truth in their mouth; their heart is vain." Vain too is the heart of the wise men outside, of whom it is said: "The Lord knows the reasonings of the wise, that they are vain"; their throat breathed out dead doctrines, since they did not teach the life-giving Word of God but the false and dead one. "Judge them, O God": those who plot against my hopes of the inheritance; for these embitter you. Judge them: for while you are eager to save, they make war by their plots. He wishes them too, having already been judged here, to be benefited, having come out of the mass of their impieties. "And let all who hope in you be glad; they will rejoice forever, and you will dwell among them." Indeed, at the Savior's coming those who awaited his incarnation were glad; it was hoped for by the prophets and by those who understood their words. For God the Word came to dwell here, having become flesh by taking on flesh, so as to dwell in those who believed in him, according to the saying, "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us." These will also rejoice forever, seeing the glory of the incarnate Word, as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth; and they also say: "Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, we know him so no longer," since they have the contemplation of his glory, according to which he is the Only-begotten from the Father. "And those who love your name will boast in you, for you will bless the righteous." Since there is a [?] kind of boasting, of which Paul says, "Let no one boast in men," and the prophet, "Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom," and so on, the boasting of him who says, "But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ," and, "Let him who boasts boast in the Lord," is not of that kind. Such are those of whom the passage speaks, who have loved his name; for they boasted as those who honored him by free choice, not out of fear. The cause of their boasting is obtaining the heavenly blessings, of which the Apostle says: "Blessed be God, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places." And the goal of these good things, of the hoped-for inheritance,

is the crown of righteousness, which those will obtain who can say with Paul: "Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness." God was pleased to use this as a weapon to guard against every assault of enemies coming against his own. [?] Psalm of David 6. "For the end, in hymns, concerning the eighth." The eighth is the day of our Savior's resurrection, the saving Lord's Day, on which we believe there is cleansing from all sins; on it every infant was circumcised in symbol, but in truth every soul born in God is cleansed through regeneration. And this day is so much better than the seventh that on it the law concerning the Sabbath is set aside, if the infant's eighth day should fall on it; for a man is circumcised on the Sabbath. "Lord, do not rebuke me in your wrath, nor chasten me in your anger. Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak; heal me, Lord, for my bones are troubled." For every sin arises from weakness, as the soul always gives way to passion; therefore he takes refuge with the Savior and physician, the Son of God. For when he comes to be in the rational soul, as the Word of God he takes away its irrationality; as Wisdom he releases it from folly, as Righteousness from injustice, and as Truth he frees it from falsehood. He indicates the vigorous powers of the soul, by which it is accustomed to resist the passions manfully, when he says that his bones are troubled; and to make this clear he added: "And my soul is greatly troubled." The healing of the soul's weakness is the power that comes from God; having obtained it, one says: "I can do all things in Christ who strengthens me." That the bones are not wholly bodily is shown by the verse, "All my bones shall say: Lord, who is like you?" and by, "Our bones were scattered beside

"And you, O Lord, how long?" He shows that his repentance was drawn out over a long time. For the wise physician of souls does not hear the petitioner immediately, at his first turning, so that he may come into an abiding habit of the good, having shown a firm repentance; and after sufficient perseverance in confession he says [?]: "At an acceptable time I heard you." For to those who call on him not out of sin he will say: "While you are still speaking, behold

"For in death there is no one who remembers you, and in Hades who will confess to you? I am weary with my groaning; every night I will wash my bed, with my tears I will drench my couch." Being wise, David knew well that the present life is the time for healing, after which no one can set things right; and he does everything, wishing to be healed

[?] before being overtaken by the common end. Therefore he says: Instead of the one night on which I sinned, I make confession every night, trying to wash myself clean, and the bed on which I sinned, with tears of repentance. For I know that even if forgiveness is granted [?], I shall have no end of tears. The phrase "Who will confess to you?" stands for "no one"; for here it does not signify rarity. "My eye was troubled by wrath; I have grown old among all my enemies." The remembrance of your wrath and anger, he says, has troubled my mind; which is what the Savior taught when he said: "The lamp of the body is the eye." For it is not possible for one of the body's two eyes to be the lamp; nor is a bodily eye troubled by the wrath of God. In place of achievements he recounts his own sufferings, among them the affliction and humiliation which he endured for a very long time in the midst of his own enemies. "Depart from me, all you who work lawlessness, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping. The Lord has heard my supplication; the Lord has accepted my prayer. Let all my enemies be ashamed and troubled; let them be turned back and be put to shame very speedily." Having obtained a hearing from God, he turns his prayer to him again, and asks that his enemies withdraw and be put to shame, having failed in the very plots through which God provided salvation for him. He also asks that they be greatly troubled; which will surely await them at the time of God's righteous judgment.

"O Lord my God, in you I have hoped; save me from all who pursue me, and deliver me, lest like a lion he seize my soul, while there is none to redeem or to save." Not on men, nor on the counsels of men, nor on a multitude of soldiers have I hung my hopes. Therefore deliver me, since so many enemies are continually pressing upon me: not only now Absalom and Ahithophel and those with them, but also long ago, when I was young, Saul and very many others, and the demons who through them wage secret war against me. Of their ruler it is said: "Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour"; it is from him above all that I ask to be delivered. "O Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is injustice in my hands, if I have repaid with evil those who repaid me, then let me fall empty before my enemies." How much boldness he shows in not bearing grudges! For this is the outstanding achievement of

David, as gentleness is Moses' (for he was gentle above all the men on the earth), and faith is Abraham's (for Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness), and endurance is Job's, and chastity Joseph's, and wisdom Solomon's. The steadfastness of the saints is not attested in the same things; rather, each excels in some remarkable contest [?]. So David, who at all times bore no grudges [?], sets this before God, asking to receive the same from him. For he knew by the divine Spirit the Savior's future promise: "If you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your trespasses." Therefore, after sufficient repentance, he obtained forgiveness. "Then let the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it, and trample my life into the ground, and lay my glory in the dust." Insisting, he says: If I have not achieved this, may I not be freed from sin before death, nor recover my own glory, but may I be overtaken in my very sins, so that, as when I sinned, the hostile one may trample my soul forever, until the death of returning to dust. But if I have achieved it, may I be redeemed and receive the like, and not remain in the dust into which I fell through sin, abiding in carnal sin. The life of one who still bears the image of the earthy is trampled into the ground by the enemy; and even if such a one seems at times to be glorified, his glory has been laid in the dust, as is the case with those who act for glory, and for the praise of men, or for their approval. "Arise, O Lord, in your wrath; be exalted in the borders of your enemies. Awake, O Lord my God, by the command which you gave, and an assembly of peoples will surround you." He calls on him to rise up like a general, with indignation, against the camp of the ruler of the invisible enemies, saying: What you commanded us men to do, to struggle against the invisible powers, do yourself. For when these have been overthrown by you, I too will be saved, and not I alone: the Church of the nations will also surround you, once all the error of the demons has been driven away. And standing in her midst as in the midst of a chorus, you will send up a fitting hymn to the Father, just as you said: "I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the church I will sing your praise." "And for its sake return on high. The Lord will judge the peoples. Judge me, O Lord, according to your righteousness, and according to my innocence that is in me." Since God will bring every work into judgment, and all must stand before the judgment seat of Christ, David, having rightly learned that he is to judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in uprightness, says: Be judge of me too, O Lord, not according to my other deeds, but according to my simplicity and righteous-

"Let the wickedness of sinners come to an end, and you will guide the righteous, O God who tests hearts and reins." It is a wise and great thing to ask that wickedness come to an end, and that the righteous be steered so as no longer to be tossed by storms. Having spoken of God's righteous judgment, he declares him alone to be a just judge, as the only one who sees hearts; for he renders to each according to his works. For man looks on the outward appearance, but God discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart; no judgment is hidden before him. Having shown God to be such, he says with a confident conscience: "My help is from God, who saves the upright in heart." For he hopes for good things because of the one who tests hearts and reins, since he has nothing crooked in his heart. "If you do not turn, he will polish his sword; he has bent his bow and made it ready." Perhaps these things are said covertly about the devil; for to these [?] applies "he has travailed with injustice," and what follows. "Behold, he travailed with injustice, conceived trouble, and brought forth lawlessness. He dug a pit and hollowed it out, and he will fall into the hole he made. His trouble will return upon his own head, and his injustice will come down upon his own crown." These things were fulfilled literally in Ahithophel. For when he was outdone by Hushai, being a wise man he despaired of Absalom's cause, and fearing the punishment to come from David, he went home and hanged himself, suffering what he had plotted for David to suffer, and wiping off onto his own head the wickedness he had planned against him. And in general, everyone, through the evils he has done, carries the verdict against himself on the day of judgment. "I will give thanks to the Lord according to his righteousness; I will sing to the name of the Lord Most High." As one who plotted against no one and dug no pit, but overlooked those who wronged him, while the ungodly perish in the judgment, he says, "I will give thanks to the Lord according to his righteousness," setting forth his own just claims as in a court of law; "and I will sing to the name of the Lord Most High," trusting that he will be deemed worthy of the chorus of those saved by him.

PSALM OF DAVID 8. "For the end, concerning the winepresses." The things prophesied here about the consummation of the ages produced the title "for the end." And "concerning the winepresses" refers to the churches established throughout the whole earth, which by allegory are called winepresses. Once there was a single people, namely Israel, for whom the temple among them was styled a tower, and the altar before the temple a winepress vat, according to the word of Isaiah. But the multitude of winepresses now indicates the many altars distributed among the individual churches. Therefore also in Psalm 83, which is entitled in the same

way, many altars and dwellings and courts are foretold, as in: "How lovely are your dwellings, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord"; after which he adds: "Your altars, O Lord of hosts." "O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth! For your majesty is exalted above the heavens. Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babes you have perfected praise because of your enemies, to destroy the enemy and avenger." It was not wonderful in all the earth of old; it became so after the Savior's coming, when an assembly of peoples also surrounded him, in agreement with the present verse, "Out of the mouth of infants," and so on. For he teaches that the young and new assembly after his ascension on high was made up of infant souls, through the regeneration in Christ which was established everywhere in the world after his ascension. Therefore also, when the children cried out to him, "Hosanna in the highest, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord," he says to those who were indignant: "Have you never read, 'Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babes you have perfected praise'?" And perhaps "because of your enemies" is also said on account of the chief priests and Pharisees. The enemy and avenger is the lion mentioned in the preceding psalm. The greatest wonder, then, is that so great an enemy and lion, the ruler of this age, has been brought down through infants and nursing babes; after which God is marveled at everywhere and among all. Being an enemy, he lies in wait to trip people up into sin, and afterward he punishes those who have sinned. And he makes clear how the name of the Lord, of old known to no one, became wonderful in all the earth, by saying next: "For your majesty is exalted above the heavens." And the third clause, added in "Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babes you have perfected praise," would agree with "An assembly of peoples will surround you."
