For it teaches that the young and new assembly of those surrounding God after his ascension on high was made up of infant souls and nursing babes; this is what it calls the peoples regenerated in Christ. For having ascended on high after his descent to [?] heaven (1), the Lord who is presented through the prophecy perfected for himself on earth the assembly of the peoples, forming it out of infants and nursing babes. "For I will behold the heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have founded. What is man, that you remember him, or the son of man, that you visit him?" Even if, he says, heaven and the things in it, which you established to stand through the whole age, are wonderful works, he established [?] … ibid. 14 [?]

for he established them forever, as he says elsewhere, and he set an ordinance, and it will not pass away. Yet to you they are not great things to bring into being, but the work of a slight power, corresponding to fingers; for this is what he called the lesser powers of God. These things, then, remain firmly established. But when I consider man, who passes away one by one, I am amazed that you both remember him and care for him. That would not have been so if he were some small and perishable creature; but he is so honored that from the mouth of infants and nursing babies praise has been perfected for him. So even if he is small in body, yet in his soul, which is made according to the image, he has been honored, so that through this your name has become wonderful in all the earth. The divine Spirit marvels and, in its wonder, offers a prayer, saying: "I see [?] the heavens, which encompass the whole world; I see also the moon and the stars, and I recognize that all these are by nature great and wonderful parts of the whole creation. Yet, although they are such, I know that they are the least of your works." They are, at any rate, the works of your fingers—not of your hands, nor of some great power, but, as one might say, of your fingertips. In this figurative way the powers of God are named, by which he formed the created things that are perceived and seen. "You made him a little lower than the angels; with glory and honor you crowned him." And indeed God crowned man with glory and honor in other ways too: by saying of man alone, "Let us make man according to our image and likeness"; by appearing in various ways to holy men and imparting to them the Holy Spirit and heavenly power, so that they could know the future, drive out diseases and raise the dead; and, greatest of all, by honoring him with the coming of the Only-begotten. "With glory and honor you crowned him, and set him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things under his feet, sheep and all oxen, and also the beasts of the plain, the birds of the sky, and the fish of the sea, that pass along the paths of the seas." For to the rational nature, as made like God, he granted rule and power over all things. Man, having received the divine image, was appointed ruler of the things on earth, just as God is king of all. But if it is said universally, "And you set him over the works of your hands," and it says elsewhere, "And the heavens are the works of your hands," it is clear that he set him over the heavens as well. And perhaps this mysteriously signifies the dwelling in heaven of those who are transferred there from earth, when they are to inherit the kingdom of heaven, as has been promised. As Paul says: "Heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ." So too the words "He subjected all things under his feet" must be understood, for now, of living creatures; but since an angelic life also

is laid up for men in heaven, man, once set there over the works of his hands, will be a beholder of the heavens and of what is in them. The blessed Paul, however, took this too as referring to the Savior, to be fulfilled in the age to come. That is why the Father says to him: "Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet."

PSALM OF DAVID 9. For the end, concerning the hidden things of the Son. Many were the things he did in secret: his birth in the flesh from a Virgin through the Holy Spirit, his extraordinary and wonder-working powers, his very death, his descent into Hades, and his return to life from the dead. All these things he did in secret, for he hid them even from the rulers of this world. It is concerning these hidden things that the Prophet says: "I will give thanks to you, O Lord, with my whole heart; I will tell of all your wonders." He himself says something similar in the Gospels: "I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you hid these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to infants." In the psalm too, then, he gives thanks for the hidden things. And after the thanksgiving he offered for our salvation, he promises to teach us about the wonders of the Father, exulting in the vision of the Father. As Son, he also had knowledge of the name of the Godhead of the ineffable and unnameable Father. "These things above all," he says, "I will do once I have conquered death, the enemy of life," of which it is said: "The last enemy to be destroyed is death." For it will be turned back, that is, to its original state, when it did not exist. For God did not make death; but through the envy of the devil death entered the world. When this has come about, all the rest as well, the enemies and foes of your word, being weakened

"And he will judge the world in righteousness; he will judge peoples in uprightness." Since those in the world are not alike in their works, God's judgment would not be righteousness if he punished sinners in the same way as he glorifies the righteous. "He will judge peoples in uprightness." By "the inhabited world" he means the Church, which is inhabited by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, in keeping with the words: "I and the Father will come to him and make our dwelling with him." By "peoples" he means the rest, outside the Church, or those of the circumcision. For as many as sinned under the law will be judged by the law, while those who sinned without the law perish without the law. "And the Lord became a refuge for the poor, a helper in times of need, in affliction. And let those who know your name hope in you, for you have not forsaken those who seek you, O Lord." To what sort of poor man has the judge become a refuge, if not to the one who

in his first life traveled the narrow and afflicted way, and to the poor man who is called blessed—that is, poor in spirit? Having learned this, let those who know your name, and who know that in the time of righteous judgment you will not forsake those who seek you now, hope in you from now on, enduring all things for the sake of the rewards. "We will rejoice in your salvation. The nations are caught in the destruction they made; in the very snare they hid their foot was caught. The Lord is known as one who executes judgments; in the works of his own hands the sinner was caught. A song of the interlude." Having plotted against the godly, they impaled themselves on destruction. Then too God will be known as one who exercises just judgment. "A song of the interlude" is said because a change has taken place, either of the melody (according to the Hebrew term) or of the tune, or else of the very thought of what has been said, as the speakers turn the discourse to another sense. "Let sinners be turned back into Hades, all the nations that forget God." For even if they are insensible now, the time of judgment will come. But the man of God, even if he seems to be despised by God when he suffers incurable harm at the hands of sinners, is nevertheless not given over to oblivion. For the poor in spirit "will not be forgotten forever"; he will have fruit and a good end because of his ... in present things

"Arise, O Lord, let not man prevail; let the nations be judged before you. Appoint, O Lord, a lawgiver over them; let the nations know that they are men." He rouses God, as though his forbearance and the riches of his kindness and long-suffering were causing him to delay, and working ruin for ungodly men. Having prayed that the nations be judged before God, he now accordingly asks that, before the coming judgment, a lawgiver be given to the nations, so that they may learn that they are men and not irrational animals; for law is not given to irrational creatures. He would not be speaking of Moses, who came from among men long ago, nor of the law laid down for the Jews alone; nor is another to be expected, since the law of the New Covenant has gone through the whole inhabited world. For Christ is the lawgiver, and the preaching of the Gospel has prevailed over the nations. Of him the Father says through the prophet: "Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my chosen one in whom my soul is well pleased. He will bring forth judgment to the nations. He will not quarrel or cry out, nor will his voice be heard. A bruised reed he will not break, and smoldering flax he will not quench; but he will bring forth judgment unto truth. He will shine out and will not be crushed until he establishes judgment on the earth, and in his name the nations will hope (1)." But the Hebrew and all the other translators rendered it: "And in his law the nations will hope."

ACCORDING TO THE HEBREWS. "Why, O Lord, do you stand far off, and overlook us in times of need, in affliction? While the ungodly man is arrogant, the poor is set on fire; they are caught in the schemes they devise." Or, since God is the one who catches the wise in their craftiness, according to the Apostle, is he asking that this very thing happen now? For when the many see such men prospering amid their many ungodly deeds and meeting with nothing painful, they count them blessed and worthy of praise. And both they themselves are greatly harmed and so are those who become emulators of their wickedness. "For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who does wrong is blessed. The sinner has provoked the Lord; in the greatness of his anger he will not seek him. God is not before him; his ways are defiled at all times. Your judgments are removed from his sight; he will lord it over all his enemies." He goes through the present condition of the ungodly, wishing to show that the coming judgment is necessary. For "provoked" Aquila rendered "ridiculed"; for they truly do ridicule the words about God's judgment. Whoever persists in sins is hindered from seeking God, as he gathers up for himself a multitude of wrath. Therefore he does not seek, cutting himself off even from the natural notions of God and keeping the ways of his life impure; for this reason he never takes God's judgments to mind, especially since he is permitted to lord it over his enemies. "His mouth is full of cursing and bitterness and deceit; under his tongue are toil and trouble." Full of cursing is the mouth of the heterodox, who speak evil of the Creator, and of revilers; full of bitterness, that of the hot-tempered; full of deceit, that of the deceitful. "He lies in ambush with the rich in secret places, to kill the innocent." And he does these things deceiving himself, as though God did not see. "For he said in his heart: God has forgotten; he has turned away his face so as never to see." The ungodly man does all these things against God's poor, deceiving himself and supposing in his reasonings that there is no God who oversees. "Arise, O Lord my God, let your hand be lifted up; do not forget your poor forever. You see, for you observe toil and anger, to deliver them into your hands. To you the poor man has been left; you have been the helper of the orphan. Break the arm of the sinner and the evil man; his sin will be sought and not be found." Thus he now rouses the forbearance of God to the judgment of the ungodly. The hand being lifted up signified judicial power. For as long as it does not punish the ungodly, it seems to be itself punished [?]; but when it renders to each what is just, it is said to be lifted up. (1) Tetimoreisthai: for tetimoresthai, as also elsewhere. Ed.

and no one will escape it. That is why he says: "To deliver him into your hand." Therefore your poor man, having heard your words, which say: "Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath. Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord."

FOR THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID 10. Since this psalm too is inscribed "of David, for the end"—and according to Aquila, "for the victor," and according to Symmachus, "a victory song of David"—you will say that David too, after the misfortune that befell him, uttered the

"In the Lord I have put my trust; how will you say to my soul, Flee to the mountains like a sparrow?" This is the voice of the perfect man, who is able to say with the Apostle: "Who will separate us from the love of God?" It is not the voice of the imperfect man, who flees from place to place and escapes his pursuers, as a sparrow escapes those who hunt it; such a one, even if he does escape, would say: "Our soul was rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters." "For what you had prepared they have torn down; but the righteous man, what has he done? The Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord, his throne is in heaven. His eyes look upon the poor; his eyelids examine the sons of men. The Lord examines the righteous and the ungodly." God, who alone is righteous and judge, seeing his own people warred against, what did he do? Dwelling in heaven and holding an unshakable kingdom, he overlooks nothing on earth. To the poor he grants the oversight of his beneficent powers, which he calls eyes; and likewise, as eyelids, his judicial providence, which discerns all things. For the sake of justice he will judge the righteous too, in case they have also erred in anything. "He will rain snares upon sinners; fire and brimstone and a stormy wind are the portion of their cup." In many places the cup signifies grievous punishments, as in Isaiah: "Awake, awake, Jerusalem, you who drank the cup of falling (1), the cup of wrath." And God says to Jeremiah: "Take the cup of unmixed wine from my hand, and you shall make all the nations to whom I send you drink it." Such is the cup set before us here, whose contents are fire and brimstone and a stormy wind; for such were the things brought upon Sodom. The fire signifies the threat of burning, the brimstone the fuel that stirs the fire up still more, and the stormy wind the whirling onset of temptation. For it is said in Isaiah: "As a storm would pass through the desert, coming near: fearful and harsh is the vision announced to me." But there is also for the godly a cup that intoxicates, as the best of all, of which perhaps this too was said: "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup." And through good works one may flee the one and choose the other. (1) Eisptoseos: perhaps ekptoseos. LXX: ptoseos.

"For the Lord is righteous and has loved righteous deeds; his face has beheld uprightness." As righteous, he looks upon the poor and disciplines sinners; and he is righteous by essence, not by participation. Yet, though he is such, he loves the righteous deeds found in the many righteous, accepting the intention of each. But each judgment too has a certain righteousness; and the judgments of God are many, as it is written: "The judgments of the Lord are true, justified altogether." So the righteousnesses are many too. He also beholds uprightness, the disposition in keeping with right reason; for he rejoices over those who have it, even when he sees them reproached. Perhaps, just as there are many righteousnesses in his judgments, so also there are many uprightnesses. And because he accepts uprightness, his face beholds it. For God shows himself present in the works of his providence and in the outcomes of his judgments. PSALM OF DAVID 11. For the end, concerning the eighth. The title is the same as that of Psalm 6. We said there that the eighth day even overrides the law of Moses, if it brings an infant to circumcision on the Sabbath, since the eighth day of circumcision then falls on it. We said that the Lord's Day too has a similar power, being the day of the Lord's resurrection, and being the eighth counting from the first, yet by nature the first; for it is purifying of all

"Save me, O Lord, for the godly man has come to an end, for truths have dwindled from among the sons of men. Each one has spoken vain things to his neighbor; with deceitful lips, with a double heart they have spoken." He denounces the whole generation of his time; for further on he will say: "You, O Lord, will guard us and preserve us from this generation and forever." For such was that earlier generation, of which the Savior too said: "The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it," and "the queen of the South," and so on; and again: "So will it be with this evil generation." "It is not unjustly that I accuse it," says the Prophet, "but because no one in it is godly, no one true. Since, then, I find no one to be the cause of my salvation, you yourself, O Lord, become that for me." He exposes the unbelief of the Jews, of whom Moses too says: "Sons in whom there is no faith." That they spoke vain things when plotting against the Savior and approaching him deceitfully, the scripture of the Gospels clearly teaches. "May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips, the boastful tongue." That is, those who said: "We will magnify our tongue; our lips are our own; who is lord over us?" For it belonged to God, not to man, to overcome

their wickedness and to quench words that blasphemed Jesus. Just as Pharaoh said, "I do not know the Lord," so they too say, "Who is lord over us?"—thinking themselves masters able to quench the Savior's teaching by their own words, as though they were answerable to no one. These were the lips of the Pharisees and Sadducees, who approached the Savior hypocritically and called him Rabbi, while secretly plotting against him. And the elders and chief priests of the people were boastful, daring to interrogate the Savior and say to him: "By what authority do you do these things, and who gave you this authority?" "Because of the misery of the poor and the groaning of the needy, now I will arise, says the Lord. I will set him in safety; I will speak boldly in it." Or it may be taken thus: "The poor, who have become poor in spirit for my sake, groan continually, humbled as they are, attending to my word and keeping an unwavering faith. For their sake I will arise, and, as befits my resurrection, I will establish salvation for all men; and in this, as in a great achievement, I will speak boldly." "The words of the Lord are pure words, silver refined by fire, tested for the earth, purified seven times." Silver that has been refined many times is unmixed with any other matter; so the words of the Lord are pure of falsehood. "You, O Lord, will guard us and preserve us from this generation and forever." When you guard your poor, and when you wall them about [?] together with the coming generation, which is called eternal, then the lawless, being outside your grace that will be poured out on all men, will walk around in a circle, becoming spectators of those who are saved; and [?] this will be when the lowly among men are exalted. "The ungodly walk around in a circle; according to your exaltation you have greatly cared for the sons of men." Since the circle is opposed to the straight line, as crookedness is to straightness, and the ungodly walk in a circle, it follows that the godly walk a straight path. Because of the end ... [?] he contended manfully; and the end is the fruit of his labors, which procures eternal life and the kingdom of heaven. So he offered up the song to God "for the end"; but at the beginning, as one still contending, he utters his first words: "How long, O Lord, will you forget me forever? How long will you turn your face away from me?" God forgets those who forget him through sin; and he turns his face away from those who do anything shameful, judging them unworthy of his watchful care. Therefore, pricked by his conscience and fearing God's judgment, he adds:

"How long shall I take counsel in my soul, with sorrow in my heart day and night? How long will my enemy be exalted over me? Look upon me, hear me, O Lord my God. Enlighten my eyes, lest I sleep in death, lest my enemy say: I have prevailed against him." The enemy is exalted over the one who sins, since he is humbled by sin; and the opposite happens when he acts righteously. As one who does not wish to be heard without having earned it, he puts "look upon me" first, asking God to see his good deeds. Or else it is because God does not hear unless one is righteous ... [?] The face of God is full of light, being a power that provides for doing good; whoever shares in it will be enlightened, as one who enjoys the rays of the sun. But when it is turned away, the soul, no longer enlightened, is darkened, and the inner eyes, which are the reasonings of the mind, cease to function. And if the soul persists in sin and the darkness prevails still more, because the face of God remains turned away, it becomes thereafter, so to speak, the soul of a wickedness that offends incurably; and unless it keeps watch, it might be said to have sinned unto death.

FOR THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID 13. Since these things, spoken prophetically, were to come to pass at the consummation of the ages, "for the end" is written at the head; but "psalm" (1) is not said, because it accuses all men. "The fool said in his heart: There is no God. They are corrupt and have become abominable in their practices; there is none who does good." Of the godless, some held that there is no God at all, but that it is an empty name; others fashioned gods that do not exist, thrusting aside the one who does; still others said that he exists but does not provide for the things on earth. All these were turned to godlessness by thinking in this way, even if they did not dare to say so because of the natural notions all men have about God. That is why they said it in their heart and not with their mouth; for with their mouth they even seemed to speak of many gods. But they were refuted by what they did, for the tree is known by its fruit. For since they refrained from no licentiousness and corrupted their life in every way, even if they professed countless gods, it was plain that they thought nothing sound about God. Truly foolish, then, was the life of men before the Savior's coming (2). If the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, then wisdom is opposed to not fearing him and rejecting him. "All have turned aside, together they have become worthless; there is none who does good, not even one." The words before us seem to me to contain a hidden accusation of the Jewish nation itself as well. For if, having stooped down [?], the whole life of men

[?] the Lord [looked down] from heaven, and when he had surveyed everyone on earth, he found that all had turned aside and become worthless, so that no one at all could be found among human beings, not even one, who had not become worthless or turned aside. It follows that the Jewish nation, and the one called Israel itself, is included among all of them. Indeed, the words before us clearly declared that all turned aside and together became worthless, so that there is no one who does good, not even one. The full extent of the disease that had arisen among human beings had to be made plain before the Savior's coming, so that his arrival might appear necessary to all. For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified freely by his grace. Isaiah too gives the same sense in agreement, where he says, addressing the synagogue of the Jews: "See, for your sins you were sold, and for your lawless deeds I sent your mother away, because I came, and there was no one; I called, and there was no one to answer." The words "because I came" would be like "The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men"; and "there was no one, and there was no one to answer" would be like "All turned aside and became worth-

"Will not all who work lawlessness come to know, who eat up my people as they eat bread?" It seems to me that he is prophesying the change that would take place in the nations, from a bestial life and from ignorance of God to a gentle and God-fearing way of life. One can see this with one's own eyes and bear witness to the truth of the prophecy. So you will read the passage as a question, with the text asking and saying: Even if all turned aside before the coming of Christ and became worthless, will not all who work lawlessness come to know in the time after this? Here we supply "the Lord," and again take what follows as shared with it. For will not even those who once ate up God's people like bread and never called on the Lord come to know him? Isaiah agrees, prophesying about the same people and saying: "Those to whom nothing was announced about him will see, and those who have not heard will understand." "There they were afraid with fear, where there was no fear. For God is in the righteous generation." Who are these but those who work lawlessness and who formerly did not call on the Lord? For a time will come when they will recognize him, and then they will also take up the fear of God and a good dread. That it is good to take up the fear of the Lord is clear from the saying, "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom." So those who are meant will be afraid with fear "there," that is, "then." And whom will they

fear but the Lord? And "there": where, but in the generation that is to be established? That is why he adds, "For God is in the righteous generation." "You put to shame the counsel of the poor, but the Lord is his hope." In other judgments concerning contracts and partnerships one must not look at persons; in the same way, in matters of counsel one should not consider office and wealth, but a mind that is well ordered and has a good conscience. We should take care to understand the passage, if possible, as referring to the Jews, who were eager to put the Savior's counsel to shame because they thought him a poor man and did not recognize the wealth of his Godhead. At any rate they constantly oppose his teaching and slander his miracles, as though they had come about not by divine power but from some other source. "Who will give out of Zion the salvation of Israel? When the Lord turns back the captivity of his people, Jacob will rejoice and Israel will be glad." Since all had turned aside and together become worthless, it was time to turn the discourse to prayer and to say, by way of intercession, "Who will give out of Zion the salvation of Israel?" For what is needed now is the one who grants forgiveness of sins, the cause of eternal salvation. This salvation, which came according to the flesh from the seed of David, has been given out of Zion: "For the deliverer will come from Zion and will turn away ungodliness from Jacob." You will apply to this also the words "Out of Zion the splendor of his beauty." One can also understand that the salvation came from the heavenly Zion, since Christ is said to hold the kingdom there. That is why our goal and the hope of the upward calling is the kingdom of heaven. Then, next, he presents the freedom from evils that is to be secured for all people through the salvation. And see how, while some are redeemed, he says that others rejoice: when the captivity of the Lord's people is set free, he says, "Jacob will rejoice, and Israel will be glad." So, since the souls long held captive by demonic error are to obtain freedom through God's salvation, and people from all the nations are to turn to the Lord, the righteous and the prophets who have long been at rest with God, who are themselves the true Israel and the true Jacob, will rejoice and be glad, because their prophecies about us are being fulfilled and because they share in the joy of our salvation. That is why Simeon, having said of the Savior that he would be "a light for revelation to the nations," added, "and the glory of your people Israel."
FOR THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID. 14. "Lord, who will sojourn in your tent? And who will dwell on your holy mountain?" Proceeding from the nearer matters, he describes the

perfect person. Sojourning is a temporary way of life in hope of something better. That is why David says, "I am a sojourner and a stranger, as all my fathers were." For Abraham was a sojourner who did not own even a foot's breadth of land, and only with difficulty bought a tomb. This is a symbol: one who lives in the flesh ought to be a sojourner, but on passing out of it ought to rest in one's own proper places. And he calls blessed the one who, sojourning among foreigners, does not cling to the things on earth as though they were his own. The tent of God is the flesh he has given to the human soul to dwell in. Who, then, treating it as belonging to another, will hand it back fruitful to the one who gave it, so that it may become a tent of God, who dwells in the saints? Then he moves on to something greater: "And who will dwell on your holy mountain?" Not in the earthly Zion, as the Jews suppose, but in the one of which Paul says, "You have come to the mountain of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem." So whoever has passed beyond this flesh and put to death his members that are on earth, and has achieved holiness, will dwell in the holy city. Longing for it, David said, "I will pass through into the place of the wonderful tent, to the house of God," and, "How beloved are your tents, Lord of hosts!" The word "who" shows how rare this is, as in "Who has known the mind of the Lord?" and "Who will announce to you the eternal place?" and "Who then is the wise and faithful steward?" Or perhaps, having questioned God, he received an answer: "Lord, who will sojourn in your tent? Or who will dwell on your holy mountain?" Perhaps, too, the one who is transferred to heaven sojourns there as one arriving from a stay abroad, for heaven is the tent of God. But consider whether the one who keeps to the way of life under the law, which was a tutor leading to Christ, sojourns in the Lord's tent, busying himself [?] with the tent of witness, while the one who has reached Christ and the teaching of the gospel dwells on God's holy mountain, of which it is prophesied, "The mountain of the Lord will be manifest." Consider again whether God's holy mountain is the Word of God, and his tent the man whom he assumed. One must first know Christ according to the flesh, and then dwell on God's holy mountain, having beheld his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, and say, "Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him so." For it is to such a person that it is said, "Go up on a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion." In another sense, the mountain of God is the one that will be inhabited only by holy souls who are perfect in righteousness: heaven itself, and the kingdom of heaven proclaimed by the Savior. This is the heavenly Jerusalem; this is Mount Zion and the city of the living God, according to

the holy Apostle, who says, "You have come to Mount Zion and the city of God [?], the heavenly Jerusalem." You will understand the tent as the one above, set up on the mountain, from the passage that says, "But Christ, having come as high priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tent, not made with hands, that is, not of this creation." When David came to think of these things, he cried out, "Lord, who will sojourn in your tent?" For truly rare and hard to find, perhaps one in ten thousand, is the one worthy of that ascent and of sojourning in heaven. The tent spoken of, the one in heaven, would be the dwelling of God himself. But a human being who is to be transferred from his stay on earth, as from captivity, to the heavenly dwelling will be there like a stranger and sojourner, since he has migrated from elsewhere and set out from another country. That is why it is said, "Who will sojourn in your tent?" Blessed is the one who comes to be on that mountain and is settled there, for the text teaches that this abode will be lasting and everlasting for those who are worthy. "He who walks blameless and does righteousness." A single action does not make the earnest person perfect; rather, one must continue through the whole of life in the activities of virtue, so that we may become blameless and irreproachable along the way itself. This way would be the saving knowledge that he himself set forth when he said, "I am the way." For in addition to the first achievement one must also take care for works and deeds done in righteousness,

"Speaking truth in his heart, who did not deceive with his tongue." So after achieving what has been mentioned, one must not exalt oneself over any of the less perfect, lest, suffering a kind of shipwreck, one lose one's own good things. "In his sight the evildoer is held in contempt, but he honors those who fear the Lord. He swears to his neighbor and does not break his word." Here he says that in one matter it is reasonable on occasion to swear, and having sworn, not to break the oath. And what matter is that, if not the pledging of genuine companionship and friendship? The oath of such a man is a blameless word, by which his "Yes, yes" and "No, no" are confirmed. "He did not lend his money at interest, and did not take gifts against the innocent." Since it sometimes happens that, after all the achievements listed, someone stumbles and falls sick with bribery and usury, he treats this disease as well. For the one who does this for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, and out of love and kindness toward his neighbor,

gives, but not in order to receive a return from people; rather he stores it up for himself as in a treasury and keeps it for the repayment that God will make in the future. "And did not take gifts against the innocent." He might perhaps accept an honor that brings no grief or harm to those who give it; but if ever he were to accept gifts when there is some underlying cause that harms another, he would utterly overturn everything said before.

A PILLAR INSCRIPTION. OF DAVID. 15. The psalm is headed "to David," or "of David" according to the other translators. I have called it a psalm in accordance with common usage, for strictly speaking one would not call it a psalm, since the heading does not mean to indicate this. Rather, it is a pillar inscription containing a wonderful prophecy, worthy of being recorded forever, as though engraved on a pillar. "Keep me, Lord, for in you I have hoped. I said to the Lord, You are my God, for you have no need of my goods." That the contents of the prophecy were uttered through David would be clear to everyone. But when one asks to whom the words should be referred, a trustworthy teacher for us would be the apostle Peter, who in the Acts of the Apostles cited what is in this psalm. Having gone through the psalm's words before the people and taught that they were spoken about the Savior, he goes on to say: "Brothers, I may speak to you with confidence about the patriarch David, that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. Being therefore a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn to him with an oath that from the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up the Christ to sit on his throne, he foresaw and spoke of the resurrection of the Christ, that he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. This Jesus God raised up, and of this we are all witnesses." Since this has been said, it would be superfluous to inquire any further to whom the prophecy should be referred, once we have been taught by so great a witness. According to the Seventy, the prophecy is called a pillar inscription because it contains the Savior's victory over death, achieved through his resurrection from the dead. Among those who compete in stadiums, the greatest and most extraordinary feats are honored with a pillar, and trophies won in wars against enemies are inscribed on pillars to be remembered for a long time. In the same way the Savior's great trophy, which he raised after overthrowing the one who has the power of death, was inscribed in their writings long beforehand, from the times of the prophets; that is why it is called a pillar inscription. "For you have no need of my goods": not so that he may grant what is deserved in return for what we have offered him. But others say that the psalm is spoken as from the person of the Savior

but spoken in his human capacity, as we find many such things in the holy Gospels. Such is the saying, "Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; yet not as I will, but as you will," and, "I am going to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God." So too we find him praying continually and bending his knees. In the same way, then, in this psalm he asks to be kept, and is kept by himself. He asks as a man, but grants the request as God, with his own Father evidently approving and working with him. "For you have no need of my goods." Symmachus translated this differently: "I have no good apart from you." Every abundance of good things, he means, comes to me through your grace. Both readings hold to piety. For we enjoy good things from God, and he has no need of our righteous conduct, though for our benefit he gives laws about it. "To the saints who are in his land he has made all his wills wonderful in them." "You are the body of Christ, and members in part." Making the sufferings of his Church his own, he can speak these words as from its person: "To the saints who are in his land he has made all his wills wonderful in them. Their weaknesses were multiplied." Others say that "his land" is the Church, where the wills of God become wonderful. And the wills of God are the various kinds of virtue, as is shown from the saying, "I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will do all my wills": this is how the wills of God are interpreted. God is made wonderful in his saints, since those who are wise in God's way have something more than other people in practicing virtue. For the courage of the witnesses of the truth, prophets and apostles, is not the same as that of others who show courage; nor is the chastity of those who keep the chastity that Joseph and Susanna had the same as the chastity of others. So it is with the other virtues too: God makes the virtues of the saints wonderful, so that they incomparably surpass those who are counted earnest by human standards. Since the wills of God are thus wonderful in the saints, their weaknesses (the saints', I mean) are multiplied, as they see how far they fall short of God's strength and greatness. Yet even if these weaknesses of theirs are multiplied, they do not linger or remain with them, but depart at once. For as soon as they became aware of them, they found them hastening to be no more, because they are strong in being empowered by Christ [?] first: "In God we shall do valiantly." I think that these words indicate the former condition of all who were once idolaters, in [?]

being godless and idolaters, they did not run aground on just one error. For their polytheism, idolatry and weakness were manifold. But since from among those very people some changed through the saving grace and became saints of God, it is said, "To the saints who are in his land he has made all my wills wonderful in them." And since there is joined to this, "Their idols were multiplied," or "their labors," or "their weaknesses": all these belonged to those who later became saints, before their change from worse to better. But afterward they hastened, not neglecting or delaying, but quickly showing repentance after the grace that came to them, through which all the Savior's wills were made wonderful in them. Hence, granting them forgiveness of former sins, he says, "I will not gather their assemblies from blood," or, according to Aquila, "I will not pour their libations of blood." For formerly, he says, they made libations of blood: the Jews when they offered sacrifices to God according to the law, and the Greeks when they worshiped demons. But I, having handed on new sacrifices to them, will no longer receive their libations of blood; nor will I pour these out as a high priest who receives them from their hands and pours them. Rather, having handed on to them new mysteries and new sacrifices, bloodless, smokeless and spiritual, I will teach them to use these. "Nor will I remember their names with my lips": that is, their old names. For formerly those from the nations bore names that matched their deeds, being called profane and unclean, idolaters, polytheists and godless. But now I will no longer remember those names, and will give them others in their place, calling them pious and God-fearing, saints, called and chosen, and Christians. "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup; you are the one who restores my inheritance to me." It is fitting to recall what was said in the second psalm. For there, too, the Father spoke to him in human fashion: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession." And in the holy Gospels he himself said to his own Father about the holy apostles, "Father, those whom you gave me were yours, and you gave them to me, and none of them was lost except the son of perdition." But just as here he speaks in human fashion, asking to receive, so elsewhere he shows that he himself is master of all: "For my sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life"; and again, "I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them too, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock, one shepherd." In the present passage, however,

…psalm. He speaks in human fashion: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup.” He calls the kingdom of the nations his inheritance, and he calls the death he endured for us his cup. He spoke the same way in the holy Gospels: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” It is as if he had said more plainly: “The Lord is the portion of my Church, which is my inheritance. The same Lord has also become the portion of my cup, that is, of my death…”

“You are the one who restores my inheritance to me.” For long ago, he says, I had a different inheritance and different measured lots. “When the Most High divided the nations, his people Jacob became the Lord’s portion, and Israel the measured lot of his inheritance.” But at that time the portion, the inheritance and the lot was the former people. When that people fell away and was cast off because of their impieties, a different portion, other measuring lines and other lots were given to me in place of the former ones, “among the best.” For this second one, he says, is the best, and it pleases me. “I set the Lord before me always, for he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken.” The saint, who always reckons that the Lord is before his eyes, is not shaken but stands firm. The Lord is at the right hand of the righteous. But of Judas he says, “Let the devil stand at his right hand.” A PRAYER OF DAVID, PSALM 16. “Hear my righteousness, O Lord; attend to my supplication. Give ear to my prayer, which does not come from deceitful lips.” In his prayer he begs God to listen, not to his voice or his words, but to the virtue within him. That virtue cries out, as it were, through deeds of righteousness and presses its plea on the divine hearing. No one who knew himself guilty of wrongdoing would readily raise such a cry. The words “Attend to my supplication” would be spoken by someone who has been tested, who sends up to God in prayer petitions that are fitting for God. Such a person does not call on God for small and ordinary requests, or for mortal and human things. This is what the Savior taught when he said, “Ask for the great things, and the small will be added to you.” Third, he begs God to give ear to the very words of his prayer and, so to speak, to judge his voice itself, since it does not come from deceitful lips. For we often utter solemn things and use words from the divine Scriptures with lips that have not been purified. Some people have freely used abuse against others, or slander, lies, deceit, perjury, obscene talk or other improper language, and then suddenly change and call upon God in prayer. Only the saint purifies his tongue, his lips, his very voice and even his ordinary words, because he knows the saying: “For every idle word you will give account on the day of judgment.” God gives ear to a prayer that is offered not from deceitful lips but from a purified tongue, one accustomed to meditate on the divine oracles. Therefore, concerning

righteousness he said “hear”; concerning supplication, “attend”; and concerning the voice uttered by the lips, “give ear.” So in these words he asked for three things, and he put the more important one ahead of the other two. “You have tested my heart; you have visited me by night. You have tried me by fire, and no unrighteousness was found in me.” How far the meaning of these words goes beyond human weakness! For who will boast of having a pure heart, and who will boldly claim to be clean of sins? So it would befit Christ alone to say these words. Perhaps in this passage he has called the descent into Hades and the realm of death “night.” For although it was night, the time of trials, the dark and lightless place of death, he was tested there and was found worthy of the Father’s visitation through the resurrection, and he received it. Like gold thrown into the fire, he remained bright and pure. For he alone of all people since the beginning of the world committed no sin, nor, as Isaiah says, was deceit found in his mouth. “So that my mouth may not speak the works of men, I have kept hard ways because of the words of your lips.” But Symmachus, who says, “I kept myself from the ways of the transgressor,” brought out a different meaning. In his version the one who offers the prayer shuns every transgressor and all the ways of such people, because all deeds of wickedness are harsh and hard. “Make my steps perfect in your paths, so that my steps may not be shaken.” In these words too the Savior has given us a model. He teaches us never to be puffed up [?] or to think highly of ourselves. We should instead be thoroughly convinced that we always need help from God, so that our steps may not be shaken and so that he may fit our feet to his paths. “Show the wonder of your mercies, you who save those who hope in you.” He is said to save those who hope in him, not those of the seed of Israel or those who live by the law of Moses. It is as if he had found a new way and appeared as the savior of those who have put their hope in him. For, as the Apostle says, faith, hope and love remain. These three are woven together, as though tied tight by a single bond. That is why he joins faith to hope, saying, “Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen.” These spring from love for God, and through them love for God is strengthened in turn. “Guard me, O Lord, as the apple of the eye, from those who resist your right hand. In the shelter of your wings you will shelter me from the face of the ungodly who have afflicted me.” Let every righteous person pray and ask God to be found worthy of his protection. He should confess that he cannot be his own guard because of the great number of those

who stand against him. Let him also beg to be guarded like the apple of an eye, since he sees that enemies who resist the right hand of God, adversaries of every kind, are plotting against the eye of his soul and wish to blind it. Even though many ungodly people afflict him, that is, make him wretched and shoot arrows at him, let him take refuge under God’s wings and ask to receive shelter beneath them. The Savior too sent up these words to the Father on behalf of his Church, which is his body. By “wings” you should understand the powers of his providence. “My enemies have surrounded my soul; they have shut up their fat; their mouth has spoken arrogance. Casting me out, they have now encircled me; they have set their eyes to bend down to the ground. They have seized me like a lion ready for its prey, and like a young lion lurking in hiding places.” In place of “Casting me out, they encircled me,” Symmachus translated, “Calling me blessed, they immediately encircled me.” And they set their eyes against me, he says, to make me turn aside. For they were eager to shake me and move me from my firm position and from my progress toward God. In this they imitated our adversary the devil, who prowls like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. They seized me as well, like a lion ready for its prey and like a young lion lurking in hiding places. For they did not carry out their plot against me openly but lay in wait in secret. “Arise, O Lord, get ahead of them and trip them up. Deliver my soul from the ungodly, your sword from the enemies of your hand. O Lord, divide them from the few from the earth in their life; and their belly was filled with your hidden things. They were sated with sons, and they left what remained to their infants.” In this, too, may I be helped. But deliver your sword as well, he says, from the hand of the enemies. For there is a danger that the enemies may snatch from my hand your sword, which I have trusted and used against them, take it away from me and use it against me. This sword would be the word of God, which is active and sharper than any two-edged sword. It is given to the soul as a sword for defense against the enemies. And this often happens: when the enemies of God have discarded and twisted the words and readings of the divine Scriptures, [?] they use them to overthrow innocent souls. Therefore he prays that God’s sword may be delivered from God’s enemies, and “from the few from the earth.” For this Aquila rendered: “from the dead [?]”

“…out of the depths [?]”; and Symmachus: “from the dead, from those who have sunk down [?].” For he prays to be delivered also from those who are already counted among the dead, because they are wholly deprived of the life that is lived according to God. In place of “divide them,” Aquila translated “their part is in life,” and Symmachus “their portion is among the living.” Through this he teaches that the portion, the lot and the whole wealth of the ungodly, who are often called the enemies of God, lie in the present life and in this mortal existence. In this life their belly has been filled with every kind of food, enjoyment and luxury. He also says, “with your hidden things,” for which Symmachus translated “and with your stored-up things.” For whatever is precious in this mortal existence and mortal life, among the things considered stored up and hidden away, they have possessed. They have worked gold and silver and every metal of the earth. They have searched out precious and costly stones of every kind, and they have been filled with all these things. They have also had their fill of children, sons and daughters. That is why he adds, “They were sated with sons.” Not only were they sated with these things themselves; after being filled first, they also left inheritances and successions to their descendants after them. Another commentator says: “Even though it is easy for you, O Master, to send them to death, I nevertheless beg that they be scattered while they are still alive, that their evil alliance be broken up, and that they receive a share of the punishments you have stored up.” For so God himself says in the great song of Moses: “Behold, are not all these things gathered up with me and sealed in my treasuries? On the day of vengeance I will repay, at the time when their foot slips.” Symmachus also translated this verse as follows: “Sons will be sated, and they will leave their remnants to their infants.” I know, he says, that you will bring your just punishment not only on them but also on their sons [?], on the descendants who imitated the wickedness of their forebears. “They will be sated” means “they will have their fill of evils.” “But I will appear before your face in righteousness; I shall be satisfied when your glory is shown to me.” They will pay such penalties, but I will delight in the good things that come from just providence, having experienced your kindness to the full. Trusting in the righteousness and virtue I have gained, I will appear boldly before your face. This is my hope, and this is my great lot. One day I shall be filled with it and satisfied with every delight, when your glory is seen in the kingdom of heaven.

…on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul, and he said.” Symmachus has: “A victory song of the servant of the Lord, David.” We needed to learn from the psalm that David dedicated this hymn as a victory song for his victories over his enemies and foes. He dedicated it to the cause of every victory, who also makes people victors and is therefore called the Giver of victory. We also needed to learn that this hymn, or song, is called a victory song of David. It is titled “For the end” for one of three reasons. It may be because it was spoken around the last years of his life, after all the deeds recorded in the history. It may be because it contains prophecies of what will happen at the consummation of the age. Or, third, it may be because it directs the reader to the end of the words contained in this hymn, where we find the calling of the nations and the prophecy about Christ. The title is phrased in this way because Saul is included along with all the enemies. In another sense, God delivered him from the hand of Saul, since “hand” is often taken to mean “action.” So it was fitting that the one who delivered David from all his enemies did him an even greater kindness and delivered him also from this “hand” of Saul, that is, from his way of acting, so that he would not suffer the same fate as Saul. “I will love you, O Lord, my strength. The Lord is my firmament, my refuge and my deliverer. My God is my helper, and I will hope in him; he is my protector, the horn of my salvation and my defender.” . . . . . In another sense he calls God his strength because he confesses human weakness and admits that he could have done nothing without God. Paul too said, “I can do all things in Christ who strengthens me.” Aquila and Symmachus translated “rock” instead of “firmament,” and the great Apostle also said, “And the rock was Christ.” David built his house upon this rock and so became like the wise man who built his house upon the rock. That is why he prevailed over all the enemies who assailed him like rain, winds and rivers. He put his hope not in bodyguards or an army but in God. He had God as his helper, his full armor and his horn, so that he too could say, “Through you we will gore our enemies with the horn.” “The pangs of death surrounded me, and torrents of lawlessness troubled me. The pangs of Hades encircled me; the snares of death caught me first. In my affliction I called upon the Lord and cried out to my God. He heard my voice from his holy temple, and my cry before him will enter his ears.” Through these words he teaches how, when he was troubled by the torrents of lawlessness and was suffering the other things just mentioned, and felt himself in danger, he fled to the harbor of his salvation. That is why

he says: “In my affliction I called upon the Lord and cried out to my God.” Then he teaches that he did not miss his goal when he trusted in this way, for hope does not put us to shame. So he adds: “He heard my voice from his holy temple, and my cry before him will enter his ears.” What temple of God should we understand David to mean here, when the house in Jerusalem had not yet been built? Surely he means the heavenly city of God, the Jerusalem above, of which the temple built on earth was an image. “And the earth was shaken and trembled, and the foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken, because God was angry with them.” He is prophesying very clearly the descent of the Lord, who came down from heaven because of death, the torrents of lawlessness, the pangs of Hades and the snares of death. He first describes what happened at his descent, saying, “And the earth was shaken and trembled.” For this Aquila says, “And the earth was moved and quaked.” The event confirms the word. For when the Son of God came to dwell on earth in his incarnate presence, all who inhabit the earth were moved and shaken. Every ear, Greek and barbarian alike, was filled with the report about him. The so-called foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken, or, as Symmachus has it, overturned, because he was angry with them. The mountains were the heights raised up against the knowledge of God: opposing powers that for a long age had led all the people of the earth astray through the superstition of many gods. So the foundations of these mountains, that is, their depths and their schemes, perceived the power of the Lord and were troubled, because he was angry with them. What this anger does to the mountains just described, he teaches next, saying: “Smoke went up in his anger.” When a log is burned by fire and then put out, it gives off smoke. In the same way the opposing powers, which were once compared to fire, burned up and consumed human souls. But when their fire was put out by the anger of the Lord, the smoke rising from them showed the signs of its extinction [?]. Then he goes on: “And fire will blaze from his face; coals were kindled by him.” For the Son of God did these things invisibly against the opposing powers, putting out their fire with another fire that was stronger and mightier. That is why Moses says, “Our God is a consuming fire,” and the Psalms say, “Fire will go before him and burn up his enemies all around,” and again, “God will come openly, our God, and he will not keep silent. Fire will burn before him,

and all around him a mighty storm.” The Savior himself also revealed this fire when he said, “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I wish, if it is already kindled?” All these things happened because he bowed the heavens and came down. He did not bow just one heaven but every heaven there is. For these words reveal the lowering of his height and the self-emptying of his divinity. He describes his descent most vividly with “He bowed the heavens,” portraying his coming down in more bodily terms. “And thick darkness was under his feet. He mounted upon the cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds.” By the mist and the thick darkness he shows how hidden and secret was his dispensation as a man. Then he goes back to where he came from. He ascended into the heavens and flew with the cherub, although he had not come down with it, for he bowed the heavens and came down by himself, without the cherub. But of his return it is said, “And he mounted upon the cherubim and flew,” with the body he had taken up. When the divine powers saw him ascending in this way, they gathered around him and escorted him on his way up, crying out: “Lift up your gates, you rulers, and be lifted up, you everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall come in.” These things were fulfilled at the time described in the Scripture of the Acts of the Apostles: “And when he had said these things, he was lifted up as they watched, and a cloud took him out of their sight. And as they were gazing into heaven while he went…” Then he teaches about the Savior’s unseen and hidden presence among people, which he still keeps even now after the ascension: “And he made darkness his hiding place; around him was his tent, dark water in the clouds of the air.” For how he is with us is not evident to everyone, according to his own words: “Behold, I am with you always, until the end of the age.” By his tent he means nothing other than his holy Church, in which he promised to dwell when he said, “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst.” And since the prophecies about him were also spoken obscurely and in a hidden way, it is fitting that the next words are “dark water in the clouds of the air.” “At the brightness before him the clouds passed by, hail and coals of fire.” The divine Spirit is accustomed to call the prophets clouds, and the rain they bring, that is, the prophetic words. Isaiah teaches this when he speaks allegorically of the people as a vineyard, as has been said, and of clouds that will no longer bring rain upon it. “And the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High uttered his voice.” He teaches in the

[?] the passage [describes] the things that the Savior accomplished by his power after his ascension, and it showed his going up clearly in the words before us, where it says: “And he thundered from heaven.” For how could he who had earlier bowed the heavens and come down thunder from heaven, unless he had certainly gone up again? This was shown by the words: “And he rode upon cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds.” So it has been shown that he came down, then went up with the cherub, then thunders from heaven and next does what is recorded against his enemies. First, “from the brightness before him his clouds passed through, hail and coals of fire.” For as was said of Egypt at the seventh plague: “The Lord sent thunder and hail, and fire ran,” it says, “over the earth; and the Lord rained upon the land of Egypt. There was hail, and fire flaming in the hail. And the hail struck in all the land of Egypt.” All these things happened so that the people of God could gain freedom from their slavery under the Egyptians. In the same way here, the Lord who flew up upon the cherub was freeing the churches drawn from the nations and the souls of men from subjection to godless idolatry and the evil demons. So he let loose hail and coals of fire against the spiritual Egyptians. I think that the powers sent to punish the ungodly are called hail and coals of fire. Punishing and chastising powers, then, invisibly serving the will of the Lord against the demons that work the error of many gods, drove them all out. That is why nearly all their oracles have failed and their soothsaying has been abolished. Their temples have been left deserted, and their votive offerings have been plundered by an unseen and invisible power. The Lord accomplished all these things after his ascent into heaven [?]. “And he sent out arrows and scattered them, and multiplied lightnings and threw them into confusion. And the springs of the waters were seen, and the foundations of the world were laid bare, at your rebuke, O Lord, at the blast of the breath of your wrath.” By the foundations of the world you should understand the powers of the wisdom of God, through which the whole creation was founded long ago, and after this [?] the world was established, which shall not be moved. But you may also wish to understand the world as the Church of God. Then its foundation is, first of all, the unbreakable and solid rock on which it has been built, according to the words: “On the rock I will build my Church, and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it.” And the rock was Christ. Or, as the Apostle puts it when he teaches about him: “For no one can lay any other foundation than the one that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.” And after him, the foundations of the Church are the words of the prophets and apostles, as the Apostle said: “Built upon

the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the cornerstone.” If you take it this way, you will not stray from the truth. These foundations of the world, then, were uncovered when the enemies of God were removed out of the way. For a long time they had darkened the eyes of our soul, so that we could not see divine things. But they were scattered by the arrows the Lord let fly, and they fled at the rebuke of the Lord and at the blast of the breath of his wrath. So it was fitting that we, set free from them and given our sight back, saw the springs of the waters and gazed upon the foundations of the world. And this has happened in our own time in many regions. “He sent from on high and took me; he drew me out of many waters.” For he had been swallowed up and taken like a captive, and the God and Father of all sent his own Son and took him. Where he took him from, he teaches next, saying: “out of many waters.” Indeed he also says in the sixty-eighth psalm: “Save me, O God, for the waters have come in even to my soul; I am stuck in the mire of the deep, and there is no foothold.” In keeping with this, then, he gives thanks in the present passage and says: “He drew me out of many waters.” What the waters are he adds more clearly: “From my mighty enemies and from those who hate me, for they were too strong for me. They came upon me first in the day of my affliction.” And the Holy Spirit announces this as good news: that he took him up out of the many waters, and that he was set free from the enemies who had long held him in their power. “And the Lord became my support, and he brought me out into a broad place; he will deliver me, because he desired me. And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness.” He says: The Lord has already heard my confession, my prayers and my supplications, and has become my support. For I was about to be overthrown and to suffer a great fall, if after my sin I had fallen into complete apostasy. But he himself stood by me and became my prop and support when he sent his prophet Nathan, brought my sin home to me, and set me upright again. He also brought me out into a broad place, or “into spaciousness,” as Symmachus has it. For when I was hemmed in and all but despairing [?] … Ps. 68:2, 5.

[?] of his righteous judgment, he will not remember my sin and what I dared to do in the day of my misery, but will repay me according to my righteousness. For he will weigh my other deeds, those done in virtue and righteousness, against my sin as on a scale and balance, and will find that they far outweigh the sin I committed. Therefore he will repay me not according to my sin (for he has already repaid me for that, punishing me in this present life through the misfortunes that overtook me). Rather, he will repay me in the day of his righteous judgment according to my other deeds, those done in righteousness, and will give my recompense according to the cleanness of my hands; for I have washed off the filth that once clung to them. “And I shall be blameless with him, and I shall keep myself from my iniquity. And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness, and according to the cleanness of my hands he will repay me.” He goes on next to list what his righteousness was and how he cleansed his hands. “For I have kept the ways of the Lord, and have not acted impiously against my God. For all his judgments are before me, and he did not remove his ordinances from me. And I shall be blameless with him, and shall keep myself from my iniquity.” He says: Since, then, I provided these things for myself after my sin and gathered so many remedies for myself, it is fitting that I take up the same statement a second time and say that, because of what has been said, “the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness, and according to the cleanness of my hands before his eyes.” Instead of “before his eyes,” Symmachus rendered “right in front of his eyes.” For I was not eager to show off my cleanness to human eyes, or to please the many; I made every effort to be pure right in front of the eyes of the Judge himself. “With the holy you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent; with the elect you will be elect, and with the crooked you will be perverse. For you will save a humble people, and you will humble the eyes of the proud.” Perhaps by “a humble people” (or “poor,” as Aquila has it, or “meek,” as Symmachus has it) he is prophetically hinting at the company of the apostles. By “the proud” he means those who were once exalted: the high priests, teachers and rulers of the people of the circumcision. They once turned proud eyes against our Savior, and God humbled them, while in every way he saved his own humble, poor and meek people, the people of our Savior's apostles and disciples. “For you will light my lamp, O Lord; my God, you will lighten my darkness. For in you I shall be delivered from trial, and in my God I shall leap over a wall.” Looking for the lamp of David, I found in the hundred and thirty-first psalm the words: “There I will make a horn spring up for David; I have prepared a lamp for my

[?] then I shall obtain the salvation that comes from you. Or: I shall leap over and vault across all the strongholds of the enemies, the fences and the wall which they are eager to throw around me to shut me in. “My God, his way is blameless; the words of the Lord are tried by fire; he is a shield to all who hope in him. For who is God except the Lord? Or who is God except our God?” He declares that God's governance and the ordering of his providence are blameless, that is, beyond reproach. His words too are tried by fire, that is, tested and proven. When you examine them, you cannot find anything foreign mixed into them. That is the case with the writings of the wise of this age, which sometimes have some semblance [of truth] but are full of every kind of godlessness and impiety. What, then, do the fire-tried words of the Lord teach? That he is a shield to all who hope in him; that there is no other God but our Lord alone, and no other mighty one but our God. And for this reason he is rightly a shield to all who hope in him, since no one else can be found who is able to stand against one so great and so mighty. “It is God who girds me with strength and has made my way blameless, who makes my feet like the feet of deer and sets me upon my heights.” He says: He does not protect and shield us while we stay idle and do nothing. We too contribute to our own salvation by struggling and fighting the enemies. So he arms me as well with his own powers and strengthens my mortal, human strength by his grace, so that, like a man with his loins girded, I may stand against the enemy in the strength he supplies me. And just as it was said, “God, his way is blameless,” so too, wishing me to be in his image and likeness, he has made my way blameless as well. Through teachings and exhortations and every kind of instruction he shapes my way, that is, my life and conduct, so that it is blameless. Instead of “blameless,” Aquila rendered “perfect.” And further,

in addition to this, he made my feet like the feet of deer. There is much said about deer in the sacred writings. Anyone who examines at leisure the passages cited would find that their meaning refers to the holy men of God, who destroy every creeping and venomous creature. For that is the nature of the deer: it kills snakes and destroys every reptile. The animal also lives in the mountains and is a swift runner, just as the saints of God look to the things above and not to those on earth, and pursue the heights out of longing for the kingdom of heaven. So David too gives the credit for his likeness to the saints to the grace of God, saying next: “and sets me upon my heights.” Other [powers] may try their hardest to drag us down and pull us into the depths and valleys of wickedness. But our God, like the president of the games teaching us to be good runners, urges us on to the heights that suit us, and the grace is his. For it is not our own power that sets us upon our heights. By nature the human soul's dwelling is in heaven, and the heights there are not foreign to it but its own. That is why he says: “setting me upon my heights.” “He trains my hands for war, and you made my arms a bow of bronze. And you gave me the shield of salvation, and your right hand upheld me.” Besides all this, you have given me the shield of salvation by sending down your Son to fight for me with his own shield. Consider carefully what this salvation of God is that is prophesied throughout all Scripture. Simeon also spoke of it in the Gospel: “Now, Master, you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation.” “And your right hand upheld me.” Perhaps the right hand of God may be the only-begotten Word, by whom he established the heaven. “And your discipline set me upright to the end, and your discipline itself will teach me.” Symmachus rendered: “And my obedience will make me grow,” and Aquila: “And [?] of your meekness multiplied me.” “You enlarged my steps beneath me.” You enlarged beneath me the steps by which I pass from vice to virtue, from things perceived by the senses to things grasped by the mind, and from the present age to the age to come. At first they seem narrow and laborious to someone walking the hard-pressed way. But when I had risen above them by making progress, I saw that they had been widened. For one who has passed beyond the stages of progress, because he has reached the end, no longer feels the narrowness, the toil and sweat that progress involves, since he has come into a spacious place. “And my footsteps did not weaken.” If I had gone on toiling forever, my footsteps, that is, the legs of the inner man, would have weakened. But since after the labors for virtue

rest follows, my footsteps do not weaken but are strengthened, so that one may say: “And you set my feet in a spacious place.” Moreover, whoever follows Jesus follows in his footsteps. By treading the very path that Jesus wore smooth, he gains strong footsteps of his own, so that he can say in deed: “My footsteps did not weaken in the straits of affliction.” “I will pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I will not turn back until they are finished. I will crush them, and they shall not be able to stand; they shall fall beneath my feet.” And how many enemies and foes he overcame with God's help! [?] He says: This too came to me from your grace, that my feet were not hemmed in, and that I was not caught in the nets of the enemies or in the snares they laid in my path. For you yourself, my God, removed all these and made my path level. You will understand “they shall fall beneath my feet” in a manner worthy of the prophetic Spirit if you remember the Savior's promise to the apostles, in which he said to them: “Behold, I give you authority to tread upon snakes and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy.” “And you girded me with strength for war; you tripped up beneath me all who rose up against me.” He says: You gave me courage and strength. Having said above, “It is God who girds me with strength,” here he teaches the outcome of the work as well, saying: “And you girded me with strength for war; and you made my enemies turn their backs to me.” [?] Those who are only now being freed from enmity through repentance do not yet have the boldness that comes from virtue, and so they would be made by the Father the back of Jesus; for in this way, coming behind him, they will be able to follow him. Perhaps this too might be said: the earnest man, who has boldness toward God, stands before the Lord; but the worthless man, cast behind because of his own wickedness, will be made the back of the Lord. For since the worthless themselves were the first to turn their backs to him and not their faces, he too will turn away from them and have them at his back. And if every righteous man should say these words, you will explain that the wicked powers harm those who see them when they come face to face, since they are always hideous; but once thrown behind one's back, they will not be able to do any work upon it, according to the words: “The sinners worked upon my back.” “The Lord lives, and blessed be my God, and let the God of my salvation be exalted. It is God who grants me vengeance and has subdued peoples under me, my deliverer from wrathful enemies.” For although he humbled himself, bowing the heavens and coming down, yet he is exalted, according to the words: “God highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name.” “It is God who grants me vengeance and subjects peoples under me, my deliverer from my wrathful ene- (1) “Back … will have”: perhaps νῶτον should be read for νῶτος. Ed.

-mies; you will exalt me above those who rise up against me, and you will deliver me from an unjust man.” It is said that he will bring vengeance and punishments on the disobedient and contrary people; or, as Symmachus has it, “God who provided me with punishments.” But to the other order, of which it was said above, “You will make me head of the nations; a people whom I did not know served me,” he grants that they be subject to him. That is why he adds, as Symmachus has it: “And subjecting peoples to me.” He says: He also became my deliverer from my wrathful enemies and from those who rise up against me [?], and he himself delivered me from an unjust man. In these words he clearly points to certain enemies and adversaries of his, and besides them to another man, truly full of every injustice. Through them the passage prophetically signifies the rulers of the Jewish nation and the traitor Judas, who became worse than any unjust man, because, though the Savior had judged him worthy of such great things, he repaid him with the opposite. “Therefore I will give thanks to you among the nations, O Lord, and sing to your name; he magnifies the salvation of his king, and shows mercy to his anointed, to David and to his seed, forever.” He passes over to the other order, the right-hand order, as one might call it; and one can grasp this from the facts themselves and see it with one's own eyes. After the coming of our Savior, David, as though he were still alive even now and living among men, sings to the God of all among all the nations through his own writings, songs and hymns. In the same way, the one born of his seed, to whose person the present words refer, having likewise prevailed over those who plotted against him, might say: “And you will exalt me above those who rise up against me.” Those, then, he leaves behind. But he imparts his own grace and truth to all the nations. And still, even now, he himself is present everywhere on earth and stands in the midst of those who have put their hope in him, and through his own Church he gives thanks to the Father. That is why he says: “Therefore I will give thanks to you among the nations, O Lord, and sing to your name.”

FOR THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID. 18. The present psalm too is one of those that lead us on to a good end. But it is also recorded as a song of thanksgiving, sung as a victory song by those who have overcome their enemies. That is why Symmachus has: “A victory song of David.” And because it is dedicated to God who grants victories, Aquila has: “For the Giver of victory, a melody.” “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands.” This contains teaching that sets forth the mighty works of God. The incorporeal, unbegotten and divine substance is hidden and invisible, because eyes of flesh cannot grasp it. For this reason those whose soul's eyes are maimed have fallen away from [the knowledge of] what truly exists [?]. With godless mouths they declare that there is no God, and that nothing exists higher than the things seen in bodies,
