but that the whole world came into being by spontaneous and irrational chance, at random and to no purpose, from no cause at all. So this passage, through the psalm, must set forth its teaching about God by way of proof, together with his power as creator of all things, and it works through some such reasoning as this. The nature of mortals is small and weak; human reasonings are timid and our ideas unsteady. So we fall immeasurably short of glorifying God as he deserves. One should never suppose that human voices, or a tongue and lips of flesh, could ever give an account worthy of God. But if we must listen to a teaching that is effective, supremely great and fitting for God himself, then let anyone whose soul has strong senses exert and rouse himself to hear a proclamation that worthily voices the boundlessly great power of God. The heavens themselves, which encompass the universe, utter this proclamation as they hymn their own Creator, God, the Maker of all things, with songs and praises. These are the highest heavens of all, lying above the firmament beneath them and embracing the whole of creation, both the creation perceived by the senses and the spiritual creation. They utter the glory of God not in the Greek language, nor in any other tongue, but in very deed. Through their own order and their well-proportioned, harmonious and all-wise station, they teach the boundlessly great power of the one who causes them to move in this way. For “from the greatness and beauty of created things their Maker is perceived by analogy”; and “his invisible attributes, since the creation of the world, are clearly seen and understood through the things he has made, both his eternal power and his divinity.” Whoever thinks, then, that the heavens came into being by themselves, without some creative Word and apart from divine power, and attributes to their own bodies the cause of their great size, of their shape, and of their steady and orderly motion, is foolish and impious. Therefore those who have a sensible mind should agree that they all but hear the voice of the heavens themselves crying out in deed, as they send up fitting glory to their own Maker and Creator, God. In the same way the firmament, which Moses presents as made on the second day of the creation of the world, is different from the heavens just named. This firmament, then, proclaims to all and cries aloud, teaching that it did not come to be what it is by chance, but that it too is the work of God, the Maker of all things. That is why it is said: “And the firmament proclaims the work of his hands.” Moses knows that a heaven was made before the firmament was formed, earlier even than the day, for he says: “In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth.” Next, after the making of the first heaven, he introduces the power and coming into being of light, teaches that the light was called day, and says that there was morning and evening, one day. Then, beginning the second day, [he describes the making of] the firmament

[?] …introduces the making. But Scripture also knows of more than one heaven. That is why it says, “Praise the Lord from the heavens”; and again, “Praise him, you heavens of heavens, and you waters above the heavens”; and elsewhere it is said, “The heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord.” The firmament, too, is called heaven. The Savior promises the kingdom of the heavens, and in the prayer he teaches us to say, “Our Father who art in the heavens”; and again, “The powers of the heavens will be shaken.” “Day to day pours forth speech, and night to night proclaims knowledge.” Day teaches, and night teaches, those willing to be instructed. They teach how great is the wisdom, the ineffable and incomprehensible power, of God, who measured out for them the intervals of time. Suppose no one had ordered hours, times and seasons for them, and they had come into being by some chance occurrence, through a motion without foresight or reason. Then surely the days would not have kept equal intervals throughout all ages. Their seasons would have been confused, and the nights likewise would have run on at random, however things happened to fall. For disorder is the sister of irrationality, and confusion follows on chance. On the other hand, reason leads all good order, and wisdom leads harmony and concord. Their alternations and yieldings to one another are like this: at times the days lengthen while the nights give way, and at times the nights recover, as their hours increase, the debt they had lent in advance. These all but speak, and talk with a great voice, bearing witness to the all-wise ordering of the God of the universe and proclaiming to men the knowledge of God. In this way the voices of the days and nights cry out by their very works to those able to heed them, so that their teaching escapes no one’s hearing. Indeed, the whole inhabited world of men is filled with their rhythmic, alternating dance. That is why it is said: “There are no speeches nor words in which their voices are not heard. Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” Clearly this means the voices of the days and nights, of the heavens that tell the glory of God, and of the firmament that proclaims the work of his hands. Having come to this point, I am moved to wonder how the holy apostle, in the Epistle to the Romans, applied the words “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” to the disciples, evangelists and apostles of our Savior. But when I paid attention to the apostle’s wording, I found that he had made the citation with great precision, by way of a fitting adaptation. For he did not do as he does elsewhere. At times he said, “Isaiah cries out concerning Israel”; at other times, “As Isaiah said before”; and again, “As [?]…”; and again:

“For Scripture says.” He did not speak in this way with “Their sound has gone out into all the earth,” adding a formula like those set out above. If he had said anything of that sort, introducing it as prophecy, someone might perhaps have taken him to be forcing the saying in the psalm. As it is, he evidently used the citation from the psalm as plain speech. So one could say that he used the testimony by adaptation, and did so fittingly, usefully and gracefully. “In the sun he has set his tabernacle, and he is like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber. He will rejoice like a giant to run his course. His going out is from the end of heaven, and his circuit reaches to the end of heaven, and there is none who will be hidden from his heat.” Besides what has been said, the sun stands as a teacher of the glorification of God, keeping the inviolable law of a master and great king. For it never dares to turn aside from the course appointed for it, nor does it overstep the bounds of the heavenly ordering. It goes forth at dawn, as though coming out of an inaccessible and untrodden bridal chamber, adorned like a bridegroom and resplendent with the bloom of light. Once it has passed the eastern horizon, it rides across the whole world, completing its own course without weariness. It circles round and round like some giant, mighty in strength and invincible. It starts, as if from the starting post, at the very edge of the eastern horizon and runs through the whole world in a single day and night, so that no one is left without feeling its heat. It does these things in service to the bidding of him who made it and set it in the firmament. That is why it is said, “In the sun he has set his tabernacle.” Although this is said clearly, the other translators rendered it more plainly still. Aquila says, “For the sun he has set a tabernacle in them”; Symmachus, “For the sun he has appointed a tent in them”; Theodotion, “For the sun he has set a tabernacle in them”; and the fifth edition rendered it similarly. For God has set the sun’s tabernacle and dwelling in the heavens mentioned before and in the firmament already spoken of, as Moses said: “And God made the two great lights, the great light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night, and the stars. And he set them in the firmament of heaven to shine upon the earth.” Through these things the sun shows, all but crying aloud, that it is not its own master and is not free, and it acknowledges the Master of itself and of all things. “The law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is sure, making infants wise. The ordinances of the Lord are right, gladdening the heart; the commandment of the Lord is radiant, enlightening the eyes. The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever and ever; the judgments of the Lord are true, justified

altogether. They are more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. For indeed your servant keeps them; in keeping them there is great reward.” The law of God has included all these things for the conversion of the soul. First it contains testimonies, ordinances and commandments. Then it attached fear to all of these, like a staff that turns people back, and over them all, like a crowning flourish, it placed the judgments of God. To each of these it joined a distinctive property. To the law, the general name that covers everything, it joined the conversion of the soul. In what follows it shows how the soul is converted. It speaks of a sure testimony, by which the infant in Christ is made wise. Then come the ordinances of the Lord, and it adds as their property that they are right and yield gladness as fruit to those who share in them. Besides these comes the commandment of the Lord, whose property it also set forth, calling it radiant and enlightening the eyes of the soul. To the fear of the Lord it joined purity, and to purity, enduring and eternal life. Over all, and after all, it added the judgment of God, and joined to it truth and righteousness. “Who will understand transgressions? Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others.” Instead of “spare your servant from those of others,” Aquila rendered, “And also keep your servant from the arrogant.” He sends up this prayer too, and does so out of real necessity, that he may be rescued from arrogance. For an arrogant thought often attends those who do well, as the soul is puffed up and grows slack over the good things it knows it has. Then the evil of arrogance [?] throws it down in another way, and it falls. That is why the Apostle says, “lest, being puffed up, he fall into the condemnation of the devil.” He had needed to say beforehand, “For indeed your servant keeps them,” calling himself a keeper of God’s commandments. So now he entreats to be rescued from arrogance, and adds: “If they do not gain dominion over me, then I shall be blameless, and then I shall be cleansed from great sin.” His meaning is this: “For the present, I have called myself a keeper of God’s precepts. But I am not yet aware of being cleansed from my hidden faults, and I still struggle and take care to be rescued from arrogance. So I rightly say this, as one who has not yet attained perfection. I shall know for certain that I am blameless, and shall be cleansed from great sin, only when my hidden faults no longer have dominion over me, and neither an arrogant thought nor evil demons enslave me.” By “great sin” he means sin carried into effect. “For if I am not cleansed from my hidden faults, they persist, and

these transgressions pass over into wicked action, and I become liable to great sin.” “And the words of my mouth will be for good pleasure.” When you have granted me these things, the words of my mouth will be for good pleasure: the words I brought forth in praying to you, hymning you and giving thanks to you. Words “for good pleasure” are words worthy of acceptance. “And the meditation of my heart is before you always.” The meditation of my mind, carried on in reasonings and thoughts, is before you always, since it is free of all blame. Yet the blamelessness of my meditation has come from nowhere but from you, who cleansed me from my hidden faults. “O Lord, my helper and my redeemer.” With you helping, O Master, I fall to none of those who wage spiritual war against me. And if through my own inattention it happens that I am captured by the adversaries, you redeem me from those who have seized me. So you are found to be at once helper and redeemer.

FOR THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID. 19. “May the Lord hear you in the day of affliction; may the name of the God of Jacob defend you. May he send you help from the sanctuary, and support you out of Zion. May he remember all your sacrifice, and may your burnt offering be made rich. Interlude.” According to the title, the psalm is ascribed to David. But consider whether, as regards the history, it may have been a prayer that supported David’s supplications. He was entreating and imploring in prayer to gain God as his Savior while he was drawn up in battle against foes and enemies. As he did these things, a choir of holy angels was likely praying all these words along with him, or else God-loving men, the very priests and ministers of God. They would be saying, “May the Lord hear you in the day of affliction,” and what follows, and also, “And may the name of the God of Jacob stand by you.” For this invocation and title by itself is enough to defend against every adversary. It would be fitting for holy powers and choirs of sacred angels to pray these things along with, and on behalf of, not only David. They would do so for anyone who, like him, sends up to God through prayers spiritual and pure sacrifices. “May the Lord grant you according to your heart, and fulfill all your counsel. We will rejoice in your salvation, and in the name of our God we will be magnified. May the Lord fulfill all your petitions. Now I know that the Lord has saved his Christ.” After the interlude, those who are praying prophesy that God will give him all that he asked in his mind, the God to whom he offered the spiritual sacrifices. They prophesy too that God will bring his counsel to fulfillment, since what he had resolved was not foreign to God. “And we shall share with you in the enjoyment of the good things,” they say, “rejoicing in your salvation. For we have learned from the Holy Spirit that the offspring to come from you will be the salvation of all people, and because of that we too will be magnified in the name of our God. May your petitions also be granted, for they are worthy of God.”

“He will hear him from his holy heaven; in mighty deeds is the salvation of his right hand.” His right hand, and all his saving and favorable deeds, are shown in mighty acts. For he will bestow his benefits on people with powers and signs and wonders. “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will call on the name of the Lord our God. They were bound fast and fell, but we rose and were set upright. O Lord, save the king, and hear us on whatever day we call upon you.” Experience of events will prove which is stronger. The enemies, trusting in horses and chariots, will be bound fast and will fall, like Pharaoh, who was drowned in the Red Sea. But we are armed with the name of the Lord our God, and with our prayers we contend alongside you who send up the sacrifices. So we will rise and be set upright, while you carry off the victories over the enemies. “These things will come about,” they say, “even now, and also at the time when the salvation just spoken of appears. For then above all, every opposing power, the hidden and invisible enemies of God, will be routed by that very salvation and will fall. And all who receive the salvation will rise up from their ancient fall.” That is why Simeon said of him: “Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising of many.” Clearly he means the fall of his foes and enemies, and the rising of those who had fallen long ago but were raised up through him. “These things will happen then. But now, Lord, save King David for us, at every present moment and on whatever day we call upon you.” As another writer says, these things also fit Hezekiah. And you will understand them also according to the anagogical

FOR THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID. 20. For what is said here is directed to an auspicious end, and it signifies the destruction of God’s enemies. Hence Symmachus has “A victory song,” and Aquila, “A melody for the victor.” “O Lord, in your power the king will be glad.” I think these words too are spoken by those who prayed for David in the preceding psalm. Now the king himself [?] has learned from the oracles given to him about the salvation that would come forth from his seed, and about the power in that salvation. At these things he will be glad and exult greatly. Taking courage from them, and prevailing through them over his enemies, he dedicates the prizes of victory to you, the God who gives victory. He rejoices and exults beyond measure, since you preserve him from the plotting of his enemies. Yet he does not exult so much in his own salvation as in the fact that his salvation comes from you. For he desired the salvation that comes from you, and in his prayers to God he sent up supplication about it with his lips. So he will not fall from his hope,

nor be deprived of his request. Instead, as he prayed, he will [?] obtain his desire. “And in your salvation he will exult greatly.” For God gladdens him with joy, he says, when he sets him face to face as a beholder of his glory. That is why Symmachus says, “You will make him joyful with gladness from your presence.” At the time of judgment David will stand in the midst of the saved and behold the face of the great King, his head crowned with the precious stone and adorned with glory and majesty. Then he will be filled with divine joy and heavenly gladness. “You have given him his heart’s desire, and have not withheld from him the request of his lips. Interlude. For you went before him with blessings of goodness; you set on his head a crown of precious stone. He asked you for life, and you gave him length of days forever and ever. Great is his glory in your salvation; glory and majesty you will lay upon him. For you will give him blessing.” Having declared the promises mentioned above to David, the word goes on to teach the reason why he will obtain such great things. And what was the reason, if not his hope in the Lord? Through it he obtains mercy, and so he will not fall from the hope he has from God the Most High, nor be shaken from this firm standing. For hope does not put to shame. “May your hand be found by all your enemies; may your right hand find all who hate you. You will make them like a fiery oven at the time of your presence. The Lord in his wrath will throw them into confusion, and fire will devour them.” These things are said to God by those who send up the prayer. They say: “Those who have made themselves your enemies, O God, never cease waging war on the souls dedicated to you and on all the saints who belong to you. Even so, they will not escape your inescapable hand and your invincible power. For the time being your enemies are exalted, to the extent that they have been allowed to train your own people like athletes. But they are exalted only for a little while. Before long your hand will overtake them, and your right hand will hunt them down as they flee.” And what will it do when it has overtaken them? “You will make them like a fiery oven at the time of your presence.” At the time when your face shines forth, when you will show your own kingdom, they will have gathered the fire of wickedness for themselves. You will make them kindle their own punishment against themselves, so that they become a fiery oven to themselves. It is just what happens to people whose bodies are feverish with illness: no one heats them from outside, but they bring the fire on themselves from within. So then, he says, you will make your enemies and those who hate you like a fiery oven. That is why it will be said to them: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled.” “Their fruit you will destroy from the earth, and their seed

from among the sons of men.” Countless impious and godless men have had descendants, yet the sons of wicked fathers have often shown themselves pious and God-loving. So the seed of the godless and the fruit of the impious are their words, their teachings and their godless doctrines, which they have put forth among people and which last after their death. Because God is good, he hands these over to plunder and obliteration, so that nothing of the impious remains, and none of their seed either. “For they turned evils against you; they devised counsels [?] which they cannot establish. For you will make them turn their back [?]; with your remnants you will prepare their face.” Again he sets out the reason why they will suffer these things, saying, “For they turned evils against you.” Instead of “they turned,” Symmachus has, “For they conspired against you for evil.” [?] …they were waging war [?] against men. But they plotted against those men for no reasonable cause, nor because of any wrong they had done, but solely because of their piety toward you. So one might rightly say that they plotted against you, God, and that all the schemes they devised against your holy ones were contrived against you, God. Therefore the things foretold will overtake them, and they will not be able to escape your hands. They schemed and did everything with a godless mind, plotting against you, God. But you turned them back and made them fugitives, so that they turned their backs as they were driven by [?]… FOR THE END, ON BEHALF OF THE HELP AT DAWN. A PSALM OF DAVID. 21. [?] The title of the psalm assigns the whole subject of its contents to the time of our Savior’s resurrection from the dead. For it is entitled “On behalf of the help at dawn.” The evangelists in turn will show us what the help at dawn involved. Luke writes as follows: “On the first day of the week, at early dawn, women came to the tomb, bringing the spices they had prepared. They found the stone rolled away from the tomb, but when they went in, they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. And while they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them [?]…”

“Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here [?], but he has been raised. Remember how he spoke to you while he was still in Galilee.” The other evangelists have said the same. Do you see how the help at dawn was fulfilled at the time of our Savior’s resurrection? That is why the Holy Spirit links the whole plan of the saving passion to his resurrection. He directs the prophecy to that very end through the title, which says: “For the end, on behalf of the help at dawn [?]. A psalm of David.” And how could the prophecy not be [?]…, the prophecy that contains our Savior’s resurrection and the [?]… of his Church?

[?] …and the calling of all the nations, and the foreknowledge of the generation and of the people that is to be born. At these things, as at great blessings, the Holy Spirit rejoices and composes the psalm. “O God, my God, attend to me; why have you forsaken me? Far from my salvation are the words of my transgressions.” The words “attend to me” do not appear in the Hebrew. Only the Seventy added them to the first line, and so our Saviour, speaking aloud, rightly left them out. Notice too that nowhere in all this did the other translators mention transgressions. It would not have been fitting to attach transgressions to the person of our Saviour, who committed no sin, and in whose mouth no deceit was found. Instead, he went on lamenting over those among the people who were doing things that deserved weeping and mourning, and over his apostle Judas, who slipped and fell away from his own rank, and he cried: “Far from my salvation are the words of my lamentations.” He means: the words of my lamentations, which I have constantly made on behalf of the people, have turned out to be far from my salvation, since the people gained nothing from the salvation I procured for them. But we do not want to seem to have used the other translators here as a clever device for refuting those who have interpreted the psalm differently. So we will use the translation of the Seventy, since those interpreters also paid attention to this reading when they said that the psalm does not fit the Lord. Then let them hear John crying out: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.” Let them hear the divine Paul saying: “Him who knew no sin he made sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.” And again: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us.” He is the fountain of righteousness, yet he took up our sin. He is an ocean of blessing, yet he accepted the curse that lay upon us, and he endured the cross, despising the shame. In the same way he also spoke words on our behalf. He willingly submitted to the chastisement appointed for us, for “the chastisement of our peace was upon him,” says the prophet. How much more, then, did he speak words for our sake and in our place, crying: “Far from my salvation are the words of my transgressions.” [?], he says, with reference to the offences of our nature. “O my God, I will cry to you by day, and you will not hear; and by night, and it will not be counted as folly in me.” The Saviour says these things as a confession made on our behalf. He means: but when I cry out like this, I know that you will hear. The words should be read with a pause. And by night I will cry out, and it will not be counted as folly in me, when my circumstances are grim. Many people are so darkened in their troubles that they do not even know what they ought to say when they cry out to God. But I know why this night-like condition surrounds me.

“But you dwell in the holy place, you, the praise of Israel.” [?] …to them, and always [?] …to them, and always hearing them. In this, then, also praise [?] …and you are accustomed to become the praise of Israel [?] …of every holy one. If God dwells in all the saints, how much more in his own Only-begotten [?] …he will hear him all the more. [?] “In you our fathers hoped; they hoped, and you delivered them. They cried to you and were saved; they hoped in you and were not put to shame.” He means: so I know clearly that all our fathers, who put their confidence in your help, were not cheated of their hope, and when they called on you for aid they enjoyed your providence. “But I am a worm and not a man, a reproach of men and despised by the people.” The worm is the lowliest of all animals. It arises from the decay of bodies, and it consumes and corrupts whatever it touches. The prophet Isaiah mentions it when he says: “Fear not, worm Jacob, few in number, Israel. I have helped you, says God who redeems you, the Holy One of Israel. Behold, I have made you like the threshing wheels of a wagon, new and saw-toothed, and you will thresh mountains and grind hills small and make them like dust. You will winnow them, the wind will carry them off, and the storm will scatter them. But you will rejoice in the Lord.” Through [?] the prophecy called him a worm and few in number, and then joined something great to this [?] when it said: “You will thresh mountains, and grind hills small, and make them like dust, and winnow them.” So in the present words, when the Saviour says, “But I am a worm and not a man,” he shows how lowly, weak, contemptible and cast off he was in his passion, and also how he would destroy the opposing powers. For he was going to submit to death and enter the very region of the dead, and there, like a worm, hand the hostile powers over to corruption. Or you could say in another way that he is called a worm and not a man because, unlike human beings, his flesh did not come into being through the union of male and female. In a third way, he is pointing to his own death and his lifeless corpse. That is why he adds: “But I am a worm and not a man, a reproach of men and despised by the people.” A corpse is not a man. If he had been wholly dead, it would have been enough to say, “But I am not a man.” But since he possessed a power that destroys death, he rightly called himself a worm and not a man. And our Saviour and Lord truly became a reproach to all, since he took up the shameful cross for our sake. That is why another prophecy also says, speaking in his person: “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell upon me.” Other people, then, held him in reproach according to the [?] comparison [?] …so says the Arian; for there is one will of the Father and the Son, but according to the man [?]…

…at the time of the passion. Another group among them treated him as an object of contempt. Who were they? The people of the circumcision. That is why he goes on to say, “and despised by the people.” For these people mocked and jeered at him, saying: “Aha, you who destroy the temple and build it in three days! He saved others; let him save himself. If he is the King of Israel, let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe”

He goes on to speak about the same people in the next words: “All who saw me sneered at me; they spoke with their lips and shook their heads: ‘He hoped in the Lord; let him deliver him; let him save him, since he delights in him.’” These words were fulfilled at the time of the saving passion, as Matthew relates: “Those who passed by blasphemed him, shaking their heads and saying, ‘Aha, you who destroy the temple and build it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down now from the cross.’ In the same way the chief priests, mocking him along with the Pharisees and the scribes, said: ‘He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is the King of Israel, let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him. He trusts in God; let God deliver him, if he wants him. For he said, “I am the Son of God.”’” “For you are the one who drew me out of the womb, my hope from my mother’s breasts. On you I was cast from the womb; from my mother’s belly you are my God. Do not stand far from me.” He shows that his birth did not take place according to nature. He was not formed like all other human beings, or like the other animals, which come from male and female. His birth had something more than our common nature. “For trouble is near, and there is no one to help. Many bullocks surrounded me; fat bulls encompassed me.” You would not be wrong to say that the fat bulls stand for the rulers of the Jewish nation: the chief priests, scribes and elders. Scripture mentions them in the sixty-seventh psalm, where it says: “Rebuke the beasts of the reed, the herd of bulls among the heifers of the peoples.” There it calls the peoples heifers and the leaders of the peoples bulls. In the present psalm, instead of “Many bullocks surrounded me,” Aquila (1) [?] renders: “Fat bulls, the fattened ones, encompassed me and hemmed me in.” According to Aquila it reads: “The mighty ones of Bashan crowned me.” Here the text hints at Pilate’s company of soldiers, which it calls Bashan. They plaited a crown of thorns and put it on him in place of a diadem. “They opened their mouth against me like a lion ravening and roaring,” crying: “Away with him, away with him, crucify him! His

(1) Read: Symmachus.

blood be on us and on our children.” Aquila says: “Like a lion seizing and roaring,” and Symmachus: “Like a lion hunting, roaring.” For those who thirsted for blood and drew the Saviour’s blood down on their own children were no different from a roaring lion. “For many dogs surrounded me; a congregation of evildoers encompassed me.” After the Jews he mentions the soldiers from the Gentiles, since the Jews handed him over to them. So the prophecy kept the order in which the events took place. It rightly called the Jews bulls and the soldiers dogs. The Jews were under the yoke of the law, even though they openly broke the law, while the soldiers were unclean according to the law. This is also what the Lord called the Canaanite woman: “It is not right,” he said, “to take the children’s bread and give it to the dogs.” Yet after the passion, those who had once been dogs passed by faith into the rank of sons. And those who had once received the care given to sons were given the name of dogs, because they had raged like dogs against their Master. It is about them that the blessed Paul cries out: “Beware of the dogs; beware of the evil workers; beware of the mutilation.” The prophetic word, after calling them dogs, said: “A congregation of evildoers encompassed me; they pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones.” This is plain and clear even to the most contentious. For in the holy Gospels we hear the Lord himself saying to his holy disciples: “See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself.” He also showed Thomas the marks of the nails and the wound from the spear. And at that time “they counted all my bones.” That is, they stretched him out so tightly as they nailed him that anyone who wished could easily make out how many bones he had. “But they observed and looked upon me,” meaning that they jeered and laughed. “They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots.” The account in the holy Gospels teaches this too, more clearly. “You who fear God, praise him; all the seed of Jacob, glorify him; let all the seed of Israel fear him.” The whole Jewish nation was divided into three orders. First came the common multitude of the nation, which was called Israel. Next came the priestly order, which was the house of Aaron. Third came the servants of the priests, which was the house of Levi. Another psalm lists these three and then introduces a fourth order besides them, those who fear the Lord. These were the people turning to God from the Gentiles. For it said: “House of Israel, bless the Lord,” and likewise the house of Aaron and the house of Levi, and finally those who fear the Lord. In that psalm, those from Israel were placed before those who fear the Lord. But here, after the resurrection of the Saviour,

[?] iii, 2. Luke xxiv[?], 59[?]. Ps. cxxxiv, 19.

those who fear the Lord are placed before Israel. He had said: “I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the church I will sing your praise.” So the hymn had to be given first to the members of his Church, and these were the Gentiles saved through him. He refers to them when he says: “You who fear the Lord, praise him.” He is very precise here. To his own brothers and disciples, as the stronger and more capable, he promises to declare the Father’s name. But to his Church and the multitude of the people he no longer hands on the Father’s name, because they could not take it in. Instead he teaches them a hymn. Then he commands the seed of Jacob to glorify him, putting the Jewish order second, after the people from the Gentiles. He very precisely calls them not Jacob but the seed of Jacob and of Israel, because they were descended from the patriarch. They were not worthy to be called Jacob because they shared their father’s zeal or resembled him. They bore this title only because they were his seed. “For he has not despised or been angered at the prayer of the poor man, nor turned his face away from me, and when I cried to him he heard me.” “The poor shall eat and be filled, and those who seek him shall praise the Lord; their hearts shall live for ever and ever.” Here he says “they shall eat,” but further on, “All the fat ones of the earth ate and worshipped.” When they ate, they became fat. Before they ate, they were called poor, and he promises that they will enjoy the food he will provide. For he says, “The poor shall eat.” These are the people whom he places first in the Beatitudes, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” To them he also promised what follows: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled.” He means: when the poor eat and are filled, or “are satisfied,” as Symmachus has it, then they will praise the Lord as they seek him. And when they have eaten the food he gave them and have sought him, they will reap the great fruit described next: “For their hearts shall live for ever and ever.” For the bread of life that he provides for them will be the cause of their immortality and eternal life, as he himself taught when he said: “I am the bread of life that comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.” And again: “If anyone eats of my bread, he will live for ever,” and so on. Do you see how well this agrees with the psalm, which says, “The poor shall eat and be filled,” and “their hearts shall live for ever and ever”? “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the

nations shall worship before him. For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he rules over the nations.” When the light of salvation has shone on them, they will remember that they did after all have a Lord, the one who is truly the Master of all. For those whom they had taken for lords were [?]. Remembering their own Master, they will flee to him for refuge. Long ago they turned away from him through some plot of their enemies, but now they will recognize him as their Lord and turn back to him. In case anyone should think this is said about the Jewish nation, the text adds precisely that it will be fulfilled for all the nations throughout the whole world. Then what will they do once they have turned? “All the families of the nations shall worship before him.” Instead of this, Symmachus and Aquila said, very precisely, “all the kindreds of the nations.” For what nation does not have kindreds that have turned to the God of all? What city, what country, what household does not have some who are set apart and chosen for God? And how were the kindreds of the nations to put aside their forgetfulness and remember the God of all? How were all the ends of the earth to turn to him? He goes on to say: “For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he rules over the nations.” The demons and the devil, who once held power, have been overthrown, and the kingdom of the God who is over all now prevails alone. So the text follows an orderly sequence. First it says “they shall remember,” second “they shall turn,” and third “they shall worship.” And all this will come about “because the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he rules over the nations.” “All the fat ones of the earth ate and worshipped; before him shall fall down all who go down into the earth. And my soul lives for him, and my seed shall serve him.” On every day of our Saviour’s resurrection, the day called the Lord’s day, you can see this with your own eyes. Those who share in the holy food and the saving body, after they have eaten, worship the giver and provider of the life-giving food. You can marvel at how the words are fulfilled in deeds, exactly as they are written. Instead of “the fat ones of the earth,” Symmachus translated “the sleek ones of the earth.” These words signify those whose souls are well nourished and strong from the heavenly food. These, then, ate and worshipped. And since every knee must bow to him, in heaven, on earth and under the earth, he rightly goes on to say: “Before him shall fall down all who go down into the earth.” Instead of this, Aquila rendered: “Before his face shall bow all who go down into the dust.” These words clearly depict the posture of those who bend the knee in the Church of God, where people are accustomed to worship by bending their knees and pressing their foreheads to the ground in this

way. Next it says: “And my soul lives for him, and my seed shall serve him.” Symmachus rendered this more clearly by joining it to what came before: “Before him shall kneel all who go down into the dust, whose soul [?], and their seed shall serve him.” He means that all of them will kneel, bend the knee and worship: those who hope that their soul will live, and whose seed will serve him. Someone might prefer to hear the words “And my soul lives for him” (in the Seventy’s translation) and “My seed shall serve him” as spoken in the person of the Saviour. In that case he would say that the Saviour, who speaks this whole psalm, is speaking about every soul devoted to him and about his own seed. And what would you call his seed, if not the sons born to him through the birth of the Holy Spirit? They will serve his Father and share in eternal and blessed life. “The coming generation shall be announced to the Lord, and they shall announce his righteousness to a people that is to be born, which the Lord has made.” The Saviour had already spoken of his seed when he said, “And my seed shall serve him.” Now he makes clear what this seed is, calling it a coming generation and a people that is to be born. Living things that are born take the beginning of their existence from seeds. In the same way, he shows that the people to be born and the coming generation, which is new and fresh, will have their beginning from nowhere else than from his own spiritual seeds. While he was present on earth, he sowed these seeds through his apostles: the Spirit of adoption. Instead of “The coming generation shall be announced to the Lord,” Symmachus very wonderfully has: “It shall be written in a book for the Lord” (1). The coming generation was to be announced, but a book of prophecy about the coming generation and the people to be born would also be dedicated to the Lord.

PSALM 22, OF DAVID. “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing. In a place of green pasture, there he has made me dwell; beside the water of rest he has nourished me; he has restored my soul. He has led me.” Sheep are in a middle condition. On one side are the perfect, who have made progress; on the other are those who wallow in the depths of wickedness and are therefore compared to reptiles and wild beasts. The perfect person would be one whose soul is stamped with the ways of virtue, in keeping with the image and likeness of God. Such a person calls the Lord his King, not his shepherd. But one who has fallen from this state, and through his own freely chosen perversion has changed into a bestial condition, might be called a horse mad after mares, or a ravening wolf. Scripture usually calls such people snakes, offspring of vipers, swine, dogs and foxes. But those who turn from such a fall to a better state, while they are still, so to speak, at the beginning and in the doorway of the knowledge of God, might rightly be called God’s sheep. But when they have advanced to the

…more perfectly, are called men. But while they are still sheep, led under the shepherd David whom Ezekiel made known, that is, under our Savior and Christ, who is of the seed of David, they are taught to say: “The Lord is my shepherd, and I shall lack nothing.” And these same people, partaking of the spiritual and new food and pasture found in the holy Gospels, will say: “In a place of green pasture, there he has made me dwell.” The one who is being brought into Christ drinks water. He is not yet able to share in the wine of the true vine, because he is still a sheep. For the present he is fed on the saving water, of which the Savior cried out, saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink”; and again: “Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him, out of his belly will flow rivers of living water”; and again: “Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst for ever.” Such a person might say: “Beside the water of rest he has reared me.” And having laid down the whole burden of his old sins through the washing of regeneration and the renewal of the Holy Spirit, he might also say: “Beside the water of rest he has reared me.” For that water is truly a water of rest. Through it a person throws off the heavy and wearisome load of sins that weighs down the soul, scours away every filth, spot and stain, and is released from many-stranded bonds. Conscious of all this, he will say: “Beside the water of rest he has reared me.” Then, like one whose soul had long been fainting, who has recovered himself through the green pasture given to him and the saving water, and has run back as it were from death, he will say: “He has restored my soul.” All these things will belong to the one who is shepherded by the Lord through the David made known by the prophet. “He has led me in paths of righteousness for his name's sake.” He does these things, he says, so that his name may not be blasphemed, as it would be if his sheep perished or were badly led. “For even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, for you are with me.” For sin is far from everyone who is with God. By “shadow of death” he means the common death, the release of the soul from the body, in contrast to the death of the soul, of which it is said: “The soul that sins, it shall die”; and: “There is a sin unto death.” For the destruction of the soul is not a shadow of death but true death. So since they have learned that whoever believes in the Son of God shall never die, but has passed from death to life, they speak very precisely when they say that what comes upon them is not death but only a shadow of death. By this they mean the dangers to which human beings are exposed, and bodily death, which is nothing other than the separation of the soul from the body. “Your rod and your staff, these have comforted me.” These things, then, comfort the one who is struck and chastised, for he is convinced that God scourges every son whom he receives.

“You have prepared a table before me in the face of those who afflict me. You have anointed my head with oil, and your cup, which makes one drunk, is like the very best.” For they know both the spiritual oil with which they were anointed [?] on the head, and a drunkenness that strengthens rather than dissolves, and the mystical food set before us by him who became both shepherd and bridegroom. In these good things, he says, we take our delight, while our foes are grieved and wasted with vexation, because those who were formerly slaves, he says, have met with so great a change: “You have anointed my head with oil.” “And your mercy will pursue me all the days of my life, and my dwelling in the house of the Lord will be for length of days.” Trusting in your mercy and your grace, I know that I shall not fall from the hope I have in you, since I am trained by your mercy all the days of my life. This mercy of yours, and your grace itself, has counted me worthy to gain your house and your Church as my dwelling place. There, spending my days as in the house of God, a sacred and holy temple, I shall attain length of the days that are with you, and eternal life. For to dwell in your house, never to leave it or turn away from it, but always to spend my time within the sacred precincts: these things, I believe, will be for me the causes of length of days, the days that subsist from your light. Instead of “for length of days,”

PSALM OF DAVID 23. In some copies I found: “For the first day of the week.” “The earth is the Lord's, and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it. He founded it upon the seas, and prepared it upon the rivers.” For if a divine Word did not preside over the earth, he says, and if the wisdom of God had not founded it in this way, it would long ago have been carried down somewhere by its natural weight and have gone off into the depths. But the wonder-working and marvel-making power of the Lord of all was stronger than the earth. It willed that so great a mass, and so great a fullness of the earth, the whole world and those who dwell in it, should be borne aloft, suspended above the backs of the waters. That is why it is said: “He founded it upon the seas.” For the heavy and lifeless earth did not establish itself upon the depths. It was the Creator of all, the Son of God, who by divine craftsmanship (2) willed the solid and heavy element of earth to ride upon the backs of the sea and to stand above the watery nature, and who founded it in this way. By another line of reasoning, too, he shows that the earth did not come into being of itself, and that it was not by chance, at random and without reason, that (2) Another reading: “by mighty work.”

such a shape was put around it. That is why he adds: “And he prepared it upon the rivers.” For if the earth were entirely smooth and even all over, like the sphere of the Greeks, it would never have been able to receive the formation of rivers. Nor would it have been fit for farming, since the rains falling on it would run off in every direction. Conversely, if it were a single flat slab spread out and stretched into plains, even then no rivers would have formed on it, neither those that flow from ever-flowing springs nor those gathered from the winter rains. They would long ago have flooded the whole of it and made it fit neither for seeds, nor for plants, nor for farming. It would not even have been of use to its inhabitants, since everything would be flooded and swept away by the inundation of the waters. So it would have been if some creative Word and the wisdom of God had not skilfully given it such a shape. But as it is, it was so constructed as to be formed into mountains and glens, hills and ravines, so that rivers make their courses unhindered, mountains, groves and plants are allotted to the animals, and lands and plains are set apart for human beings to live in and to farm. Who then would not confess that these things belong to a truly wise providence? Foreseeing what was to come, before the fullness of the earth and before the things in it came to be, providence shaped the earth in this way, moulding it into a fitting form, so that it might be suitable for all. In a more mystical sense, the earth has become the Lord's. “Who shall ascend to the mountain of the Lord? Or who shall stand in his holy place?” The mountain must be taken to mean the final good and God the Word, to which a person ascends who longs to reach its summit by progress. Such a person is rare, and that is why it is said: “Who shall ascend to the mountain of the Lord? Or who shall stand in his holy place? One who is innocent in hands and pure in heart, who has not taken up his soul in vain, and has not sworn deceitfully to his neighbor. He shall receive blessing from the Lord, and mercy from God his Savior. This is the generation of those who seek him, who seek the face of the God of Jacob. Interlude. Lift up your gates, you rulers, and be lifted up, you everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall come in. Who is this King of glory? The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle.” Perhaps through this question and answer they are teaching all people the lordship of our Lord Jesus Christ, if indeed one supposes that these powers were not ignorant of it [?]. Some say that the second question and answer were not spoken to powers still higher up, but to the same ones. And the interlude placed before “Lift up your gates, you rulers” seems to mark a change of melody, since it also marks a change in the sense itself. And in saying that he will come in, he quietly hinted at his going out as well. Then, since he was not going to enter his kingdom alone, the text bids all the gates be thrown open because of those

who are to inherit the kingdom of heaven with the Son of God. For he opened many and various gates for entering the heavens, since there are also many dwelling places with the Father. Consider whether these words might not resolve the question raised by the psalm that says: “God has gone up with a shout, the Lord with the sound of a trumpet.” For here the Holy Spirit supplies both the shout and the sound of the trumpet. At the ascension of the Son of God into heaven, it is likely that the angels who had ministered to him in his dispensation toward humanity ran ahead of him, prepared the heavenly gates for him, and sent forth voices and angelic cries, the ones recorded in this psalm. These he called a shout and the sound of a trumpet, when he said: “God has gone up with a shout, the Lord with the sound of a trumpet.”

OF DAVID 24. This is not entitled a psalm, or a song, or anything of that kind, and its contents are not referred “to the end.” Rather, they are words that David composed in the Holy Spirit, which is why the other translators prefix the title “Of David.” We may therefore reasonably say that it contains teaching about confession to God. David himself used it first, and then handed it on to us too, instructing us how those who have fallen sick must heal their own souls through confession. “To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul. My God, in you I have trusted; let me not be put to shame, nor let my enemies mock me. For none of those who wait for you shall be put to shame.” He says this as one who has lifted his own soul on high, moved it away and raised it above the affairs of this world, and set it up above, close to God, in its disposition, by turning away from mortal and human things and turning genuinely toward him. Then he says: I have done this not out of confidence in myself, but trusting in you, my God, and with great boldness. Whoever has despised all things perceived by the senses and seen by the eyes, and has lifted his soul to the bodiless and invisible God, dares to call upon God as one who has become his own possession. That is why he says: “My God, in you I have trusted.” This much, he says, is my part. For the rest I need prayer and help from you, God, so that I may not fall away from my goal, nor be broken off like someone falling from a high summit. That is why I beg and entreat not to be put to shame, nor to be mocked by my enemies. This will be granted me by the help of you, my God. For the first things depended on my own choice: to lead and carry my own soul wherever I wish. But the second need your support and help. “Let those who act lawlessly without cause be put to shame.” All that is needed is to persevere in one's purpose, and not to change or desert the faith. For those who are easily swayed and carried about by every wind may at some point suffer shame,

[?] but not so those who have learned to say: “I waited patiently for the Lord.” Instead of “those who act lawlessly,” the other translators and the fifth edition have rendered “those who apostatize.” They clearly declare that transgressors, those who do not abide by their former purpose, will be put to shame. For when they find the fruit of their apostasy empty, having apostatized from God for nothing, they will be put to shame. “Make your ways known to me, O Lord, and teach me your paths. Guide me in your truth and teach me, for you are God my Savior, and I have waited for you all the day long.” The ways of the Lord are the workings of his providence, by which he steers the whole universe. The divine Apostle was teaching about these when he said: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how inscrutable his ways!” In the same way, his paths would be the particular workings by which he governs all things. Through these, travelling as it were through the things of heaven and earth with his providential power, he shows his own paths and journeys to those who are able to understand. That is why Symmachus renders: “and teach me your journeys.” And as you teach me these things, set me firmly on your truth, so that I may not go astray by holding false opinions, and mistake one thing for another in the contemplation of nature. This is what has happened to those who did not have you, God, as their teacher, but made guesses about things by mortal and human reasoning, and have been flung far from the truth. [?] Having been taught by you that you are not only my Creator and Maker and God, but also my Savior, I have rightly waited for you all the day long, that is, all my life [?], having learned that none of those who wait for you shall be put to shame. “Remember your compassions, O Lord, and your mercies, for they are from of old. Do not remember the sins of my youth and of my ignorance.” I do not think these words suit David so much as those who are being taught to confess their former sins. For we do not find that David sinned in his youth, or in his childhood, or that he ever lived in ignorance. Perhaps, then, this teaching has been handed down like a medicine, as from a physician to the sick: to those who came to the knowledge of God in the prime of life after wallowing in youthful sins. Having learned it, they might confess the wrongs they committed in ignorance, uncovering them to God and laying bare to him, as it were, the old wounds of their soul, and asking to obtain healing and treatment through his mercy [?] “for the sake of your goodness, O Lord. Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he will give a law to sinners in the way. He will guide the meek in judgment; he will teach the meek his ways.” Good

and upright, he says, is the Lord: he disposes all things well, loves the straight way, and brings what is crooked into straightness. That is why he does not turn away from sinners or overlook them, leaving them to be destroyed by their own sins. Rather, as a loving and good Savior, he cares for the sick more than for the healthy. He gives them a law, showing them ways of repentance and setting before them laws suited to their salvation. For there is a way of salvation shown to sinners, the way of conversion, repentance and confession, which is different from the one given to the perfect. In giving his law, God shows one way to those who sin, another to those turning back from sin, another again to those making progress in virtue, and yet another to those who are more perfect. So to sinners he shows a way, but the meek he will guide in judgment, that is, with discernment, caring for them as for better people. That is why he also counts them worthy of a beatitude, as in the words: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.” These he also teaches his ways. Instead of “his ways,” Aquila and Symmachus said “his own way.” For the Savior himself walked this way, as it is said: “Learn from me, for I am meek and lowly in heart.” Leading them along this way, then, he becomes their guide and leads them by the hand. Thus, as a wise lawgiver, he shows one way to sinners and another to the meek. “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth to those who seek out his covenant and his testimonies.” Many, he says, are the ways of the Lord, yet in all of them his mercy runs ahead, and truth hastens along with mercy. For he has mercy on all that exists and abhors nothing that he has made, since he did not make anything that he hated. In every way of God's governance and providence, then, his mercy runs ahead, and truth follows after mercy. And to those who seek out and devote themselves to the search, he who said, “Seek and you will find, knock and it will be opened to you,” hands on the truth about the things they are seeking. His covenant, in a general and universal sense, is the name given to the whole of the divinely inspired Scripture handed down to human beings. His testimonies are either the things testified about him prophetically in divine Scripture, or the things he solemnly charged those who are being instructed in divine matters. “Who is the man who fears the Lord? He will give him a law in the way that he has chosen. His soul will lodge among good things, and his seed will inherit the land.” Let everyone who fears the Lord hear, he says, whichever single way he may choose to travel, what awaits him. For now he will suffer hardship, as is to be expected, while he is trained in the contests of godliness. But there will come a time when his soul will lodge among good things. And what good things are these, if not those of which it is said: “What eye has not seen,” and so on?

As for the seed that he sowed in the earth during the time he lived on earth, it will inherit many, since it becomes a cause of salvation for many. What would you call his seed, if not his teaching, his words and his writings, or the men begotten by him according to God and made his disciples? Through them, even after he has gone to his rest among good things, countless others will attain the inheritance with God, since they have received good seed and benefited from its godly fruit. “The Lord is the strength of those who fear him, and his covenant is to make it known to them.” Aquila rendered this “the secret of the Lord,” Symmachus “the converse of the Lord,” and Theodotion and the fifth edition “the mystery of the Lord.” From this the one who fears the Lord, mentioned above, has advanced to such great blessedness: the converse of the Lord, his secret and his mystery have become known to him, together with the mysteries contained in his covenant, that is, in divine Scripture. “My eyes are ever toward the Lord, for he will pluck my feet out of the snare. Look upon me and have mercy on me, for I am alone and poor. The afflictions of my heart have multiplied; bring me out of my distresses.” He asks this not as if salvation were owed to him because of his good deeds. For I know, he says, that even when I have done everything in my power, I still need your mercy. Therefore look upon me and have mercy on me. For I know myself to be poor and helpless, and not sufficient for my own salvation. It is characteristic of all who love God to afflict themselves in tribulations, in hardships, in straits and in persecutions. Yet they are not ignorant of the end of these things, and so they entreat God that they may reach it, saying: “Bring me out of my distresses.” Their hope is that, having passed through the hardships of life, its misfortunes and trials, they may one day be able to say: “We went through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment.” “See my humiliation and my toil, and forgive all my sins. See my enemies, how they have multiplied, and have hated me with an unjust hatred. Guard my soul and rescue me; let me not be put to shame, for I have hoped in you.” Some things I strive to do myself, he says, and others I ask to receive from you. I punish myself, and, as if paying the penalty for the wrongs I committed before, I chastise myself, humbling myself in toils and labors. But you, O God, like the judge of the games, as you watch my contest and my labors, grant me the remission of my sins, and forgive whatever I have ever done in my sins. And as you see how many my enemies are who have plotted against me, and how they have hated me with an unjust hatred, become the guardian of my soul,

and deliver me from the plotting of my enemies. Having done so much and prayed so much, I ask not to be put to shame. For having made you my hope, I know for certain and am persuaded that hope does not put to shame. The innocent [?] and the upright clung to me, because I waited for you. Redeem Israel, O God, out of all its afflictions. Besides my other achievements, this too was a great one for me, and dear to you, O God: I became for many a pattern of endurance, of a dignified life, and of repentance and confession. That is why innocent and upright men joined me, clinging to me and asking to share my life, for no other reason than that I endured steadfastly and bore everything, having set you, my hope, before me as my shield. To all this he adds: Redeem Israel, O God, out of all its afflictions. Either he, the one making confession, is calling himself Israel because of the achievements he has just described, for such a man is Israel in soul. Or else he has been taught not to guard himself alone, nor to be zealous for himself alone, nor to entreat God for himself alone. Having succeeded and set his own affairs in good order, he now sends up his supplications on behalf of the whole people of God. Just as above he asked to be delivered from his own afflictions, so now he entreats that the whole people of God, who are called Israel in a spiritual sense, may be delivered as well.

A PSALM OF DAVID, 25. Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my innocence, and hoping in the Lord I shall not be shaken. If someone were to refer the present words specifically to David, he might say that David is making an intercession to God about his own life. The holy Apostle said: First of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions and thanksgivings must be made, and so divided these into four kinds. It is therefore fitting for us to pay close attention to what is found in the book of Psalms, noting which psalms contain supplications, which prayers, which intercessions, and above all which thanksgivings. We should also note how each differs from the others, and gather from the whole book of Psalms the distinctive marks of each kind. Supplications, for example, are found in the psalms that contain entreaties and petitions, among which confessions are also included. Such is the twenty-fourth psalm, which is neither an ode, nor a psalm, nor a hymn, nor anything of the kind, but is simply inscribed "Of David." Prayers are those whose superscription bears the title "prayer," such as the sixteenth, the eighty-fifth, the eighty-ninth, the hundred and first, and the hundred and forty-first. Thanksgivings are those like the hundred and second, in which it is said: Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his benefits, and so on.

The psalm now before us contains an intercession. In it is written: Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my innocence, and so on. You may say, then, since David did indeed begin in this way [?], that men dear to God each had certain outstanding excellences among the achievements of their lives, in which each of them was especially distinguished. For example, Joseph excelled in chastity, Job in enduring terrible things, and Solomon in wisdom and understanding. Abraham is said to have been justified by faith, and others again are attested for other contests of virtue [?]. Like these, David too is recorded as having acquired an outstanding virtue, which was forbearance. Through it he bore with Saul, who had done countless things against him, and the record shows that David endured them all meekly and with forbearance. Since this, then, was David's outstanding virtue (I mean meekness, humility and forbearance), he gathered all these together and called them innocence. As one who had succeeded especially in this respect, he says in his intercession to God: Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my innocence. But having declared something great about himself, as though boasting of his outstanding achievement of innocence or simplicity, he checks himself and necessarily adds: And hoping in the Lord I shall not grow weak. So he necessarily [?] bound himself to hope in the Lord, and he accuses himself as one who could be shaken, turned aside and made weak. Yet, trusting in his hope in God, he was confidently assured that he would suffer nothing. For he knew that hope does not put to shame, as the Apostle says. Test me, O Lord, and try me; refine my kidneys and my heart with fire. For your mercy is before my eyes, and I have been well-pleasing in your truth. He did not say "Test me, O Lord, and try me; refine my kidneys and my heart with fire" out of boastfulness or pride. He said it as a prayer, asking God to purify him through the fire if he needed purification. So he asks that the virtue he spoke of earlier, the one in which he had shown himself outstanding, be tested and tried. He trusts not in himself but in the mercy of God. "In this way," he says, "always keeping you, O God, and your mercy before my eyes, I disciplined my whole life and all my actions, so as to be well-pleasing in your truth. For I walked and conducted myself not with hypocrisy but in truth, striving to please God alone." I have not sat with the council of vanity, and I will not go in with lawbreakers. I have hated the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the ungodly. "If anywhere," he says, "men came together who were not serious, and who sat together not about serious matters but held their meetings about vain and needless things, I fled from them, so as not to become entangled in their vanity. [?] And if they met so as

even to dare to do something against the divine law, I fled from them all the more, refusing to enter into error along with them. And if ever I saw people assembling, not for vanity nor yet for lawless deeds, but for wicked and ungodly doctrines, convened supposedly as a church, I considered them still more deserving of hatred than those already mentioned. I knew of yet another class besides these, that of the ungodly, who do not know God and wallow in idolatry and error. I withdrew from them, so that I did not even wish to sit with them or spend much time with them, lest some share of their ungodliness be passed on to me. That is why I say: And I will not sit with the ungodly." I will wash my hands among the innocent, and I will go around your altar, O Lord, to hear the voice of praise and to recount all your wonders. Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house, and the place where your glory dwells. "Going around your altar, I sent up hymns instead of sacrifice. I made my voice audible to those nearby, so that all could hear my voice praising you, O God, and recounting all your wonders. For in my hymns to you I included the wonderful deeds you displayed to our forefathers. And I did not only go around your altar; I loved your whole house, O Lord, and above all its beauty, which is seen in godly doctrines and words and in the divinely inspired readings." The beauty of the house of God may also be the good order of those who assemble there: their blameless life, the decorum of the congregation, and the concord of those gathered. But because of the greatness of their love for God, even the very ground is dear to God-loving souls, and this is something other than the beauty of God's house we have described. So he fittingly adds: And the place where your glory dwells. But I have walked in my innocence; redeem me, O Lord, and have mercy on me. My foot has stood in uprightness; in the assemblies I will bless you, O Lord. With the measure we measure it will be measured back to us, and with the judgment we judge we shall be judged. For this reason he constantly puts forward his innocence, that is, his refusal to remember wrongs and his forbearance toward those who had sinned against him. He does so in order that he himself might obtain a like pardon from God for the fault he had fallen into. Having made this entreaty, he is inspired by the holy and prophetic Spirit and goes on to say: My foot has stood in uprightness; in the assemblies I will bless you, O Lord. For he prophesies that, even if his feet were at some time tossed, shaken and unsteady, he will not fall because of it. He will stand in uprightness, since he is destined to bless God in the churches. In this way he foretold that he would be remembered throughout all the churches of God. And so even to this day, throughout

the whole world, David blesses the Lord in the churches of Christ. The Lord is my light and my Savior; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life; of whom shall I be afraid? And what does the prophetic Spirit teach by this? It teaches how one who is devoted to God ought to give thanks to him, and what he ought to ask of God. The passage contains a thanksgiving. Fittingly, then, it bears no title such as psalm or ode or anything similar. The Lord is my light and my Savior; whom shall I fear? The man whose soul wallows in night and darkness does not know where he is being carried or how he is stumbling. He will fear countless evils, as one who draws them wholly upon himself. So, suspecting every fear, he cowers and denies his confession of God. But the man whose eyes of the soul have been enlightened by the Lord's radiance first of all sees how great his own champion and Savior is. Then, having learned by experience that the Master and Lord of all has become his shield, his invincible armor and his protector, he becomes fearless. Since the eyes of his soul are steady and enlightened, he sees that all his enemies, whether men ignorant of God or the invisible and wicked powers, are without so great a Savior and helper, and he looks on them as already fallen. Therefore, confident in his own champion, he laughs at all their plotting. That is why he says: "If so great a helper were not with me, enlightening my soul and protecting my life, I would rightly have feared the principalities and powers, the world-rulers of this darkness, and the spiritual forces of wickedness, together with those through whom they work and who rise up against God's athletes. For these could have thrown my soul into confusion had it not been enlightened. But since the Master of all himself, the Son of God, is my light, and he is also my Savior, I may rightly say: Whom shall I fear? For I shall pay heed [?] to none of all these enemies, nor shall I be afraid of any of them, since I trust in the protector of my life." Here again you will notice that "my Savior" in the Hebrew contains the name of our Savior Jesus Christ in the very Hebrew letters, in which one might [read] Jesus

The one who says these things teaches what kind of Savior he had experienced, such that he could laugh at his enemies' plotting. Therefore he says: When evildoers drew near to me to eat my flesh, my oppressors and my enemies, they themselves grew weak and fell. "They pressed upon me like untamed beasts, all but wanting to swallow me up and chew my very flesh." Hence Symmachus has: When evildoers drew near to me to

devour my flesh. "But those who had planned these things against me, and had already come close to my flesh, somehow suffered the very things they had meant to do to me." For they themselves, he says, grew weak and fell, "though I had done nothing against them. Clearly my light and my Savior made war on them with ineffable and divine power and threw them down. He did this so that I might be delivered from their plotting and suffer no harm, and so that they too might benefit. Their wickedness was weakened, and they gained by not adding to their own depravity through harming me." In some copies the title reads: A Psalm of David before he was anointed. One thing I have asked of the Lord, and this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the delight of the Lord and to visit his temple. The beauty, comeliness and delight of the Lord are beheld in the house of God, that is, in his Church, through the divinely inspired and sacred teachings. In them is the true beauty of the word and the true comeliness, and in them God himself takes delight and makes his dwelling. You would not be wrong to call comeliness also the chaste and dignified life and the whole virtuous conduct of those who live [?]

For he hid me in a tent; in the day of evils he sheltered me in the hidden part of his tent. He lifted me up on a rock. "My Savior gave me all these things when evildoers drew near to me to eat my flesh. For they grew weak and fell, while I, by his right hand, was hidden, living in a tent. I spent my days in the wilderness and did not then have the house of God or his temple. But he also sheltered me in the day of evils," that is, in the time of persecutions and trials, "and not just anywhere, but in the hidden part of his tent." You will understand this saying from what Moses records about the tabernacle and its innermost parts, which no one might enter and which they called the Holy of Holies. These were the hidden parts of the tabernacle. "In the same way, then, in the time of trials my Lord and Savior himself sheltered and hid me in the innermost part of his tent. He did not actually put me in some particular place, but in a sanctified state of soul, set apart from the common life of the many. And these things," he says, "happened to me until the time of the day of evils was over." This agrees with what is said elsewhere: Go, my people, enter your chambers, shut your door, hide yourself for a little while, until the wrath of the Lord has passed. "But he did not want me to be hidden altogether, or to lie concealed in the hidden part of his tent and benefit myself alone. He judged that a different state of things would also be useful, and so at the end of the day of evils he lifted

me up on a rock." And the rock, says the Apostle, was Christ. "For by his word, his wisdom and his saving power he lifted me up, the same one who earlier hid me in his tent and sheltered me in the hidden part of his tent in the day of evils. He brought me through the evils and the time of my enemies and the foes who oppressed me, and set me in a calm and peaceful harbor. He brought into the open the one who had long been hidden, raised me aloft and set me on high, to be seen by all and glorified by all, established and founded on his unbreakable and most secure rock." And now he has lifted up my head above my enemies. You will understand this if you note how the Apostle said: As long as it is called Today. In the same way you will say that here too the "now" signifies time that endures. For the man of God, having won the prize of victory over his enemies, always rises above their heads. So too David himself is exalted and lifted up to this very day, sung throughout the whole world and celebrated among all the nations. And his head has truly been lifted up above those who were once his enemies, the invisible powers. But the man of God, exalted in this way, does not give himself over [?] to idleness or inactivity; instead he brings greater zeal to the worship of God. Therefore he adds: I went around and offered in his tent a sacrifice of jubilation. These were the sacrifices sent up through the voice, through words about God, and through hymns and thanksgiving. In the preceding psalm, the one being instructed in divine things was taught to speak of the future: I will wash my hands among the innocent, and I will go around your altar, O Lord. Here, however, as one who has already made progress and obtained the fulfilment of the promise he prayed for, he goes on to say: I went around and offered in his tent a sacrifice of jubilation. And earlier it was said: To hear the voice of praise, but here: I will sing and make music to the Lord. Hear, O Lord, my voice with which I cried; have mercy on me and hear me. My heart said to you: My face has sought you; your face, O Lord, I will seek. In place of My heart said to you, My face has sought you, Symmachus gave a clearer rendering: My heart spoke to you; my face sought you. For the face of the soul longed for the vision proper to it. Moses too once asked to obtain this, saying to God: See, I have found favor before you; show yourself to me, so that I may see you and know you. He asked this so that with unveiled face he might behold the glory of the Lord as in a mirror. Therefore he says: Your face, O Lord, I will seek; do not turn your face away from me. For if the highest perfection and the final

progress in God would be the progress that leads to God's face, so that one stands before him and enjoys the radiance of his divinity... But he knows that God often turns himself away from those who cannot take in his face and are not [?] his sons, and shows them his back. So indeed he said to Moses: You shall see my back, but my face shall not be seen by you. So that the one spoken of in these words may not suffer this, he supplicates and entreats, saying: Do not turn your face away from me; do not turn aside in anger from your servant.
