Be my helper; do not cast me off, and do not forsake me, O God my Savior. For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord has taken me up. "Do not turn away from me, your servant, because I have dared to ask such things. For a man clothed in flesh is not permitted to be counted worthy of such things. That is why you said to Moses: No one shall see my face and live. For mortal life cannot bear the sight of your face. So rather be my helper, that I may obtain what I have asked." Do not cast me off: in place of this Symmachus rendered "Do not throw me away," and Aquila "Do not leave me." Then he adds: And do not forsake me, O God my Savior. "For when you take hold of me and stretch out your right hand, there is hope of obtaining every good thing. No other helper is at hand for me. Among human ties none could be dearer than father and mother, yet these very people have left me, because I withdrew from them all in order to devote myself to you alone, O God. For this I also give thanks: bereft of all and forsaken, I was taken up by you." Give me a law in your way, and guide me on a straight path because of my enemies. Do not hand me over to the will of those who oppress me, for unjust witnesses have risen up against me, and injustice has lied to itself. The divine Apostle often taught about himself, saying: For I am in no way inferior to the super-apostles. Yet to such words he added: Not that I have already obtained this or am already made perfect, but I press on to see if I may lay hold of it. And again elsewhere: I pummel my body and bring it into subjection, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified. Compared with other people, he was aware that he had advanced and attained such perfection as is possible among men. But in truth he knew that he fell short in many things, and for this reason he confessed that he was not perfect. It seems to me that the one who spoke the words before us had the same thought in mind. For what had passed, he rendered fitting thanks to God; but as a man, he was wary of the slipperiness of human weakness. So, regarding the time to come, he begged God to be his lawgiver himself. "For the ordinances of Moses," he says, "are not enough for me. That law was not laid down for the righteous, but for the lawless and disobedient, the ungodly and sinners and the like." For these

[?] for Moses gave laws, issuing ordinances to suit their hardness of heart. “But I,” he says, “have not placed myself under the law of Moses. That is why I did not promise a sacrifice made by slaughtering animals, but a sacrifice of shouting for joy, a newer way than the ordinances of Moses. So I ask to receive a new law from you.” Show me your way yourself, then; or, in Aquila’s version, “enlighten me.” “Do not only show me the way and give me laws, O Lord, but also guide me on a straight path, so that I do not strike my foot against a stone, because of my enemies. Do not hand me over to the will of those who afflict me. For I ask you to lead me along a level and peaceful road for the whole span of my life. Those against me are not only enemies, but also unjust accusers and false witnesses, who do everything that enemies do.” Injustice truly lies to itself when it does not rest on the facts and does not prevail against those it bears false witness against. I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. Perhaps he is also referring back to his earlier request, and by “the good things of the Lord” he means the Lord’s face, which he mentioned above when he said: “Your face, O Lord, I will seek. Do not turn your face away from me.” That is why Aquila renders it, “I believed that I would see in the good of the Lord,” and Symmachus, “I believed that I would see the goodness of the Lord.” But he will see the face of the Lord and the good things of the Lord not in this earthly place, nor in the region of mortals, but in the land of the living, which the Savior also promised when he said: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.”

OF DAVID. 27. To you, O Lord, I will cry; my God, do not be silent toward me, lest you be silent toward me and I become like those who go down into the pit. We have not forgotten what we said earlier about the psalms inscribed “To David” or “Of David” without any further addition, and now we will add to it the tradition that has come down to us. The Hebrews say that when psalms have a title of this kind, one must go back to the psalms above them and find the psalm placed at the head of those that follow, which are either entirely untitled or inscribed “To David.” Once we learn the superscription from that psalm, we should apply it to the meaning of the psalms joined after it as well. Now the psalm before us, which is the 27th, has this superscription, and so do the 26th, the 25th and the 24th. But the 23rd psalm was “To David,” and likewise the 24th. It follows, then, according to the Hebrew tradition, that all the psalms that come after it should also be taken as [?], so that by this reasoning the psalm before us should be regarded as a psalm that contains a prayer. He himself shows this as he goes on, saying: Hear the voice of my supplication when I

pray to you. Let us consider what meaning the words of this prayer contain. He says that he cries out to the Lord and calls upon him as his own God. “For you,” he says, “have deigned to be called my God, according to the promise [?] to the saints when you said: ‘And I will be their God, and they shall be my people.’ Accept my prayer.” And do not be silent toward me, lest you be silent toward me and I become like those who go down into the pit. He said this in anguish, afraid that he might somehow be made like those who, when this mortal life has ended, go down into the pit of death. In the preceding psalm he had said, “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.” Even so, as a man still clothed in flesh, he was in anguish at how frail and changeable life is. The Apostle too was anxious that after preaching to others he himself might be disqualified. The divine Scriptures usually call the dwelling place of souls in what is called Hades “the pit.” David himself shows this not long after, in the 29th psalm, where he says: “O Lord my God, I cried to you, and you healed me; O Lord, you brought up my soul from Hades; you saved me from those who go down into the pit.” Do you see how in these words he has joined Hades and the pit as the same thing? In the psalm before us he sends up cries to God, begging not to become like those who go down into the pit. In the twenty-ninth he shows that his prayer has been granted, saying: “Lord, I cried to you, and you healed me; you saved me from those who go down into the pit.” The dwelling place of souls in Hades is fittingly called a pit. A pit is a cistern that receives the waters carried down into it from above and on high. In the same way the region of death, called Hades, receives the souls carried down into it from above, from human life, and so it is fittingly called a pit. He begs, then, not to be dragged down into the pit just described. “And this,” he says, “will happen if I become like the rest of mankind, whom you do not hear, which is a sign that you have turned away.” [?] Instead of “Do not be silent toward me,” Symmachus says, “Do not keep silent from me, lest, when you are quiet and far from me, I become like those who go down into the pit.” Because they did not understand the works of the Lord and the works of his hands, you will tear them down and will not build them up. By “the works of the Lord” you might understand the existence of all created things, through which God, the maker of all, brought everything from non-being into being. By “the works of his hands” you might understand his governance of what has come into being, through which he exercises providence and orders all things, steering them with his providential powers as though with his own hands. Blessed be God, for he has heard the voice of my supplication. The Lord is my helper and my protector; in him my heart hoped,

and I was helped. And my flesh has flourished again, and willingly I will give thanks to him. God, who does not lie, keeps his own promises, in which he has pledged: “While you are still speaking I will say, ‘Here I am.’” He stands near those who call on him with a pure heart and is not far from the one who prays for what was done [what was said before], and so he has given ear to the supplications spoken above. Then, through the prophetic Spirit, he gives the soul of the one who prayed something like a sign that it has been heard. The soul perceives this, turns its words of supplication into thanksgiving, and confesses that it has recognized the kindness done to it. That is why it says: Blessed be the Lord, for he has heard the voice of my supplication. The Lord is my helper and my protector; in him my heart hoped, and I was helped. For it felt the right hand of God stretched out to it and taking hold of it, so that it would not be dragged down into the pit described above. Out of overflowing joy the prophet says that not only his soul but also his flesh rejoiced and was renewed, because of the good hope promised to the body as well at the resurrection of the dead. That is why he adds: And my flesh has flourished again. To this he joins: And willingly I will give thanks to him, which seems to me similar to “I will sacrifice to you freely.” Instead of “and my flesh has flourished again,” Symmachus says, “my heart blossomed”; Aquila, “my heart exulted”; Theodotion, “and my heart flourished again”; and the fifth edition, “my heart was strengthened.” Again, instead of “willingly I will give thanks to him,” Symmachus renders, “and with my songs I will praise him,” and Aquila, “and from my song I will give thanks to him.” The Lord is the strength of his people, and he is the protector of the salvation of his Christ. In these words, then, the prophecy has clearly mentioned Christ and those he saves, and it has fittingly portrayed them all through the one person of David. “For as he saved that man when he prayed,” it says, “so he will be the strength of all his own people too.” Save your people and bless your inheritance; shepherd them and lift them up forever. What Christ’s inheritance is, the second psalm shows: “Ask of me,” it says, “and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.” You would not be wrong to say that the God-loving men among the former people, the prophets and the righteous, also became part of Christ’s inheritance and shared in his salvation. For it is not right to count the crowds, and those who have entered the Church of God unworthily, as his people. Only those who live in a way that pleases him are his people, and of them he could say: “And I will be their God, and they shall be my people.” And shepherd them and lift them up forever. He shepherds them here by laying down his life for them, as he says in the Gospels: “The good shepherd

lays down his life for the sheep”; and again, “My sheep hear my voice”; and again, “I will be with you until the end of the age.” And at the proper time he will lift them on high and count them worthy of the heavenly kingdom.

A PSALM OF DAVID. 28. At the departure from the tabernacle. Bring to the Lord, you sons of God, bring to the Lord sons of rams. Bring to the Lord glory and honor. Bring to the Lord glory to his name. Worship the Lord in his holy court. I think these words mean the same as what is said about the calling of the nations in the ninety-fifth psalm: “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth. Sing to the Lord, bless his name; proclaim the good news of his salvation from day to day. Declare his glory among the nations, his wonders among all the peoples. For the Lord is great and greatly to be praised; he is to be feared above all gods.” After this comes: “Bring to the Lord glory to his name. Take up sacrifices and enter his courts. Worship the Lord in his holy court.” In these verses the word first announces in advance the grace of the gospel poured out on all the nations throughout the whole world, and mentions the new song, that is, the New Covenant. Then it commands that glory and honor be brought to the Lord, and so on. It gives this command not to the Jews but to the families of the nations, or, in the version of the other translators and the exact Hebrew, to the kindreds of the peoples. In the ninety-fifth psalm these things were clearly prophesied about the nations. In the psalm before us the word commands the sons of rams to offer the same things to the Lord, and I think they are no different from the families of the nations or the kindreds of the peoples. For it is not the rams themselves who are commanded to offer what is required, but the sons of the rams. I say this according to the Hebrew reading, which does not contain “Bring to the Lord, you sons of God.” For this reason that phrase is also marked with an obelus in the Septuagint, because it is found neither in the Hebrew nor in the other translators. But if we must also consider the Septuagint version, I say that the word commands the sons to bring to the Lord not rams but sons of rams, along with glory and honor and what is said next. Comparing this with the ninety-fifth psalm, I would say it is a prophecy about the conversion of the nations. Nor would we be wrong to declare that those here called sons of God are the disciples, apostles and evangelists of our Savior,

through whom the calling of the nations was evidently accomplished. The word before us commands them, first of all, to bring to the Lord sons of rams, and not rams. For in the forty-fourth psalm it was said to the Church gathered from the nations: “Instead of your fathers, your sons have been born.” The word urged her to forget her fathers, saying: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, and the king will desire your beauty, for he is your Lord.” These words were spoken to no one but the Church of Christ alone. In them the divine Spirit exhorts her to forget her former people and her father’s house, because of the error of many gods and the superstition of her fathers. Then, since he had urged her to forget her fathers, he must add: “Instead of your fathers, your sons have been born.” He calls these sons of rams because of [their former] lack of reason. Then he adds: Bring to the Lord glory and honor. You will understand this from our Savior’s charge to his disciples, in which he urges them: “Let your works shine before men, so that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father in heaven.” Third, in addition to these, the psalm before us, in agreement with the ninety-fifth, commands us to bring to the Lord glory to his name. We offer him glory through sound doctrines. We also offer him honor when we obey the command that says: “Honor the Lord from your righteous labors, and give him the first fruits of your fruits of righteousness.” And we confer glory on his name when our works shine before men, so that they see them and glorify our Father in heaven. How his name is glorified among the nations is also shown by the word spoken through the prophet to the Jewish nation: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord Almighty, and I will not accept a sacrifice from your hands. For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name has been glorified among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice; for my name is great among the nations, but you profane it.” In addition to all this, those described above, the sons of God or the sons of rams, are commanded to worship the Lord in his holy court. For he does not want them to worship him outside the court, nor privately and in seclusion, but by gathering together in his Church. Instead of “in his holy court,” Aquila renders “in sanctified [?] splendor,” and Symmachus “in holy splendor.” The word wants us to offer our worship with fitting adornment and with the righteousness that is dear to God, having become wholly given to holiness and seemliness.

The voice of the Lord is upon the waters; the God of glory has thundered; the Lord is upon many waters. For when the sky was clear on the summit of Carmel, he heard the sound of many waters. Indeed, if anyone gathers together what is written about waters in the Old Testament, he will see it: “The Spirit of God was moving over the water”; and “Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls, and birds that fly”; and the events of the flood, how when everything else was submerged, Noah alone and those with him were saved in the ark; and what happened in Egypt, at the Red Sea, and at the Jordan, how the children of Israel crossed over with dry feet. The voice of the Lord is in strength. For the one who can do all things in Christ who strengthens him hears the commandments of the Lord and does them. The voice of the Lord, then, is not in the weak and slack soul, but in the vigorous soul that works the good with strength. The voice of the Lord is in magnificence. “The voice of the Lord,” he says, “is shown not only through the waters we have mentioned, but also through his strength and his magnificence.” This can be perceived with the eyes by one who views the whole boundless world at once [?] and then looks at its parts one by one: their indescribable magnitudes, their inexpressible beauties, and the manifold wisdom seen in them. These things show the power and strength of the one who constituted all things. That is why the prophetic writings drew their teaching about God from his mighty works. So it is said in Jeremiah: “The Lord who made the earth by his strength,” and so on. The voice of the Lord breaking cedars; the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon, and will grind them small like the calf of Lebanon (sic), and the beloved is like a son of unicorns. Or it may be read this way: by “the calf of Lebanon” he seems to mean Jerusalem, and by “the beloved” the son of unicorns of old. For they were descended from holy fathers who were called unicorns, because they used God alone as their horn, so that they took pride in him and said: “In you we will gore our enemies.” Their sons are the leaders of those of the circumcision, who are called here Sarion according to the other versions, a name that means “rulers.” These he broke with his threat together with Jerusalem, which he called a calf and Lebanon. The prophet Ezekiel clearly shows this when he says: “Thus says [the Lord]: The great eagle, with great wings, long in span, full of talons, which has the [?] to enter Lebanon, took the choicest parts of the cedar, the tender tips, and carried them to the land of the Chaldeans.” He also explains this in what follows, saying: “When the king of Babylon comes against Jerusalem, and

[?] of it.” For he called these the choicest parts and the tender tips. By its calf he means the altar on which they offered calves and sacrifices. All of these were broken along with Sarion, that is, the rulers. “In the same way,” he says, “he will also break the ungodly among the other nations, who exalt themselves like the cedars of Lebanon.” The voice of the Lord shaking the wilderness; the Lord will shake the wilderness of Kadesh. For truly the whole inhabited world of men, which before was a wilderness empty of the knowledge of God and of piety, was shaken by the preaching of the gospel, so that it was changed from vice to virtue and from ignorance to divine knowledge. So the wilderness became an inhabited world. The voice of the Lord preparing deer, and he will lay bare the forests; and in his temple everyone speaks of glory. “For the Lord,” he says, “prepared deer.” The deer is an animal that loves the wilderness, kills snakes, bears horns and is clean according to the law, and he sent them out into the wilderness described above. They ran through it, trampled underfoot the snakes that were in it, and drove all the venomous beasts of the wilderness far away. When these had been driven out, the forests were laid bare. And in his temple everyone speaks of glory. This is said with great precision: “And in his temple everyone speaks of glory.” For it is no longer the Jews, or the people of the circumcision, but everyone from all the nations who has turned to God. The Lord will give strength to his people; the Lord will bless his people with peace.

OF THE DEDICATION OF THE HOUSE OF DAVID. 29. Someone might object that the psalm makes no mention of building a house or a temple, and that nothing in it could fit the dedication of a house, so as to make one think the present psalm was spoken for the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. But since its title is “Of a song of the dedication of the house,” consider whether by “house” he is here hinting at his own soul. The divine Spirit had once dwelt in it as in a temple, but at a certain time left it deserted [?] and withdrew, because of the wrong he committed in the matter of Uriah and his wife. Because of this deed he went down even to death, having committed a sin unto death. In effect he was then brought down into the pit and into Hades, and truly went down into corruption. For this reason he gave himself up to lamentation and put on sackcloth instead of his royal robes. But he showed a remarkable repentance, chastising and punishing himself and persevering long in confession, and so he received a promise that his sin would be forgiven through the Christ who would come forth from his seed and would descend even to Hades. So it was fitting that he turned from his dejection, and from confessing what he had dared to do, and sent up thanksgiving to God, saying:

"Lord, you brought up my soul from Hades; you saved me from those who go down into the pit." That his mourning has been turned into gladness is also shown by the words: "You turned my lament into joy for me; you tore off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness." Since, then, the house has been shown to be David's soul, the words before us would fit the dedication of such a house. "I will exalt you, O Lord, for you have upheld me, and have not let my enemies rejoice over me. O Lord my God, I cried to you, and you healed me. O Lord, you brought up my soul from Hades; you saved me from those who go down into the pit." David says these things in the psalm before us. But in the twenty-seventh psalm the same David cried out: "To you, O Lord, I will cry; my God, do not be silent toward me, lest you be silent toward me and I become like those who go down into the pit." There he was praying for these things. Here he gives thanks as one who had earlier been brought down and fallen into the pit, but has been brought up again and rescued from it, and has not suffered the same fate as those who went down into it and never came up. For in the first place it is blessed not to sin. But since the weakness of human nature is subject to these things, the second-best course, as one might say, is to rally again (sic), to recover after the illness, and to regain one's natural health. "Sing to the Lord, you his holy ones, and give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness. For wrath is in his anger, and life in his will." He calls them to rejoice with him in his repentance and to confess, that is, to give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness. This means rekindling the memory and never forgetting the good things the Lord supplies to human beings. Above all it is fitting to give thanks more fervently, remembering God's love for humanity, which is so great that he never wishes any evil for anyone. And if someone, through his own wickedness, should ever need to be corrected, he prepares for himself a wrath of anger; but God's will is never to wish death for a human being, but life. That is why it is said elsewhere: "As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner so much as his repentance." So here too it is said: "Life is in his will"; for wrath is not in his will. Anger and wrath are prepared for sinners against God's choice and against his will. The Apostle shows this when he says: "Or do you despise the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is leading you to repentance? But by your hardness and your unrepentant heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will repay each according to his works."

"But I said in my prosperity: I shall never be shaken." He justifies the Lord's judgment, confessing how his fall came about. One who stands firm in the standing that God grants ought to remember the word that says, "Let anyone who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall," and ought to give thanks to God for his standing. But he did not reason rightly. He thought that he stood among the finest things by his own virtue, and declared himself unchangeable and immutable. "Lord, by your will you gave strength to my beauty." Since he had not reasoned rightly in what he said before, he came to realize that his standing, his prosperity and the beauty he then had did not come from himself, nor were they his by his own doing. So, having learned his own weakness by experience, he confesses: "But you turned away your face, and I was troubled." "You did nothing more," he means; "you neither pushed me nor threw me down. You simply left me alone, because of my boasting, bereft of your help. You turned away your face, and at once I was exposed and became troubled, falling under my own sins and my own enemies. To you, O Lord, I will cry, and to my God I will make supplication. What profit is there in my blood, in my going down to corruption?" According to Symmachus: "When I was in distress I said: To you, Lord, [I will call?], and I will beseech you, my Master. What gain is there in my blood, when I am brought down to corruption? Will dust confess to you, or declare your truth?" "These and similar things I plead, sending up cries from below, from the deepest pit, asking to learn from you, God, as from a teacher. What profit comes to me or to others from my blood? Or what more will people gain from my going to corruption? In the blood of another there will be great and abundant profit for the whole world, when your Lamb who takes away the sin of the world comes like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer. By his blood redemption and freedom from evils will come to all who are to be saved through him. And his descent to those who had perished and were in death will be the cause of salvation for many. For much dust and much earth, the fleshly and earthy people of old, will confess to you; and they, changed for the better, will declare your truth. Will there, then, be some such good for the world in my blood as well? Will anyone profit if I am dragged down by Death? Or will dust, the man taken from the dust and made from it, be changed from the earthy, become spiritual, and declare your truth? No, nothing of the kind will come from me. Therefore I beg not to be made like those who go down into

"The Lord heard and had mercy on me; the Lord became my helper. You turned my lament into joy for me; you tore off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness." "When I prayed this," he says, "the Lord heard. He is not far from those who call on him purely and faithfully; of him it is said, 'The Lord is near to all who call on him in truth.' Having heard, he had mercy on me, and he showed his compassion toward me in deed, for he became my helper." Having said this as if speaking to us, and having taught us what happened to him, he turns his thanksgiving back to God himself and recounts God's kindnesses toward him. "For you had mercy on me," he says, "and became my helper. In this way you turned my former tears, my laments and my mourning into laughter, joy and exultation. You made true the beatitude spoken long afterward about those who weep and mourn: 'Blessed are those who weep, for they will laugh; and blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.' You stripped me of the tokens of mourning, the sackcloth in which I afflicted and punished myself, and you girded me with a belt of gladness. You granted me all this so that I might not remain dust and earth that does not confess you, but so that my glory might sing to you. In my going down to corruption there was no profit, either for me or for others. I was being deprived of the life that comes from you, and others gained no salvation at all through me. But when you turn my lament into joy for me, tear off my sackcloth and gird me with gladness, no small profit comes of it. For having recovered my former glory, I will sing to you with it, and I will sing to you not with a bad conscience but with a free and pure mind." That is why he says: "So that my glory may sing to you, and I may not be pierced with sorrow." "And so I will continue through all ages, confessing to you and constantly recounting your kindnesses toward me." "The Lord became my helper." Note that "became" does not always mean coming into being; sometimes it means a relation to someone. So whenever such an expression is used of the Savior, it signifies a relation to something and not coming into being. "You turned my lament into joy for me." The word "lament" (literally "beating") signifies awareness, as the act itself shows, when the hands beat the breast. So the one who has become aware of his own sins, and has actively roused his perception with spiritual hands, will turn from wailing and take up joy, the fruit of the Spirit. "You turned" shows the change from beating one's breast and grieving to joy. And "I may not be pierced" means, he says, "I may not change my mind." The glory of the one who says these things, which sings to God, is upright conduct and sincere knowledge. "O Lord my God, I will confess to you forever"; that is, "in all things that happen,

not only in pleasant ones but also in hardships, I give thanks to you, Master." [?] FOR THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID. OF ECSTASY. Neither the Hebrew Scripture nor the other translators have "of ecstasy" in the title. [?] Perhaps, because the psalm says, "But I said in my ecstasy: I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes," someone made the addition to the title. He was referring it to the time when David, being in ecstasy, said, "I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes," and so reasonably referred back to what is said in the psalm [?]. In any case, the present title also directs readers to "the end," either because of the last parts, in which an exhortation [?] ... of what was done at the Savior's passion [?], things which were to happen at the consummation of the age. But since the passage also sketches good hopes for David, which were to come to him in the future [?], it fittingly refers the title to "the end." The whole psalm contains the supplication of David, who has made himself wholly dependent on God, and who begs not to lose his hope. "In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me never be put to shame. [In your righteousness deliver me] and rescue me. Incline your ear to me; [hasten] to rescue me." [?] Though he abounded in great wealth, and though he prided himself on his victories over his enemies, he was convinced that none of these would contribute to his safety, but only hope in the Lord. That is why he pleaded [?] ... those who strive after things like his [?] ... For "in your righteousness" Symmachus rendered "in your mercy." "Be for me a protecting God, and a house of refuge to save me. [For you are my strength and my refuge?] [?] You will bring me out of this snare which they have hidden for me, for you are my protector, Lord. Into your hands I will commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, O Lord, God of truth." [?] "As I experienced long ago, I am convinced that now too you will bring me out of every snare the enemies are preparing for me. For as long as [I am] in this mortal life [?] ... having trusted [?]." "You have hated those who pay regard to vanities [to no purpose]. But I [have hoped in the] Lord. [?]

I will exult and be glad in your mercy." "You rightly delight in lovers of the truth and welcome them; that is why it is said, 'The Lord seeks truth.' But those who cling to vanity you rightly turn away and hate, since they pursue falsehood. For vanity is what is full of falsehood. That is why you exhort, saying: 'Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?' But I turned away from vain things and hoped in you alone, my Lord. So I am convinced that I have not entrusted myself to you in vain, for the end of hope in you is joy and gladness." "For you looked upon my humiliation; you saved my soul from distress. You did not shut me up in the hands of enemies; you set my feet in a broad place." "You have looked upon my humiliation at other times too. Often my soul fell into the distress my enemies brought upon it, and I did nothing more than humble myself and afflict myself through supplications to you, God. Then you yourself, my champion and protector, did not pass me by, but accepted my humiliation, saved my soul from distress and did not shut me up in the hands of enemies. Wondrously, when I was already caught in the nets and handed over to my enemies, you snatched me away and set me free, and set my feet in a broad and open place, letting me walk freely wherever I wished." History too teaches that he was often caught by Saul, and was even shut in the cave, yet he escaped Saul's hands; and at another time he escaped the Gittites by feigning madness. "Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am afflicted; my eye is troubled with anger, my soul and my belly." "I beg," he says, "and ask to be shown mercy, because I am afflicted." In place of this Aquila says: "For I am hemmed in." "For I travel the narrow and afflicted way for your sake and for your promises. Moreover, the eye of my soul, that is, my mind itself and the reasoning faculty within me, was troubled with anger." In place of this Aquila says, "My eye was parched in provocation," and Symmachus, "My eye was clouded through provocation." "For when I provoked you," he says, "and stirred up anger against myself, daring to do things deserving anger and wrath, then confusion, clouding and drought seized the reasoning part of my soul. And my soul and my belly," he says, "were also clouded and troubled at the time of my provocation." Just as we have understood the eye of the soul by analogy with the eye of the senses, so you would not be wrong to call its belly the faculty of memory, in which, as in a stomach or belly, the soul is accustomed to store up all the nourishment that comes through words. That is why it is said somewhere: "Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name." And the Savior says: "Whoever drinks of the

water that I will give him, out of his belly will flow rivers of living water, springing up to eternal life." Here too, then, the Savior called the faculty of memory, or even the governing part of the soul itself, a "belly." "Clouded, then, in the eye of my soul and in the belly just mentioned, I gave myself over to healing and treatment, handing over my life to pain, groaning and poverty, as though being cured by successive courses of treatment." For "My strength was weakened in poverty, and my bones were troubled," Symmachus rendered more clearly: "Because of my affliction my strength and my bones have decayed." "For I afflicted myself so much," he says, "that through the excess of affliction my strength weakened and failed, and the very bones of my soul, the powers in which I once showed courage, decayed"; or according to Aquila, "and my bones were parched." These things are needed as instruction and as a model for those who wish to obtain forgiveness for their own offenses. "Among all my enemies I became a reproach, especially to my neighbors, and a dread to my acquaintances. Those who saw me outside fled from me. I was forgotten like a dead man, out of mind; I became like a broken vessel." If we refer these words to the time of our Savior's passion, they would fit his own lips. Then his enemies, seeing him hanging there, mocked and reproached him, as is written in the Gospels; his acquaintances, his disciples and his friends were seized with fear and withdrew, abandoning him; and the leader of the company of his disciples denied him three times. Then too he was forgotten like a dead man, out of mind, and was even thought to have become like a broken vessel. Yet these words, referred to the one who makes confession in the psalm, also show how extreme his affliction was. He wore himself down so much that his life failed in pain and his years in groaning, his strength weakened in poverty, and the bones of his soul were troubled. For this his enemies laughed at him, as though he were beating himself for nothing and in vain. He became a reproach not only among his enemies but also among his neighbors, who knew him best because they lived closest. Seeing him wearing himself down in confession to God, they laughed at him and reproached him. His relatives and friends were afraid of him, as though he were mad and out of his mind. So they withdrew and fled from him, despairing of his recovery, and forgot him as if he were already dead, and treated him like a broken vessel. He says he suffered all this while afflicting himself in confession and repentance. "These people," he says, "behaved toward me in this way. But I did not conduct myself like this without reason. I heard the slander of many who lived around me, and they gathered together and plotted to take my soul. For the

invisible and unseen enemies, when I fell into sin, joined forces to plunder my soul. So I, aware of their plot, gave myself over to such severe punishment, in the hope that God, seeing my deep humiliation, might have mercy on me and rescue me from my enemies' plot." "But I hoped in you, O Lord; I said: You are my God; my lots are in your hands." "While my enemies were plotting these things against me," he says, "I hoped in you, Lord, and I said that you alone are helper enough for me. For you are my God; my lots are in your hands." In place of "my lots," the Hebrew reading and the other translators have "my times." "For even if my enemies are now especially strong, as though their time against me had come, my times are kept in your hands; and in those times I know that my own lots are kept with you. So I rightly beg and plead to be rescued now from my enemies and from those who pursue me." "Make your face shine upon your servant; save me in your mercy. Lord, let me not be put to shame, for I have called upon you." When the sun rises, the darkness is dispelled; when it goes below the earth, night takes over everything, and wild beasts and evildoers come out of their lairs. In the same way, when God turns away, the enemies of the soul rise up and overrun it; but when he shines forth the light of his divinity, which Scripture usually calls the face of God, all who do the deeds that darkness loves turn and flee, and everything opposed to God is dissolved. So the one who has just made his confession pleads, saying: "Make your face shine upon your servant." And again: "I ask to be saved," he says, "not because of my deeds but because of your mercy." And again: "Since I have called upon you," he says, "let me not be put to shame, for I have hoped in you." For shame befits the ungodly, who do not know you, God. That is why he says: "Let the ungodly be put to shame and brought down to Hades"; or according to Aquila and Symmachus, "Let them be silent in Hades." For now they talk a great deal in their daring; but when they are brought down to the place that suits them, they will cease their boasting. Then the lips that now speak so much against the righteous with arrogance will become mute, and all contempt shown toward the righteous will be avenged. "How great is the abundance of your goodness, Lord, which you have stored up for those who fear you! You have worked it for those who hope in you, before the sons of men. You will hide them in the secret place of your face from the troubling of men. You will shelter them in a tent from the contradiction of tongues." "I pleaded for these things," he says, "that you would make your face shine upon your servant, and that I might be saved by your mercy and not be put to shame, since I have called upon you, being convinced

[?] …since your goodness is great and beyond words, and full of great riches. That is why the Apostle also says: "Or do you despise the riches of his goodness and forbearance and patience?" But for now you do not make your goodness plain to all. You hide it and store it up, keeping it for those who fear you. For you also brought it about for this very purpose, I mean to bestow it on those who hope in you. And you will indeed bestow it in due time before the eyes of the sons of men, so that all may see your goodness given to the worthy at the time when good things are repaid. That is why in this life too, in times of trial, you count the souls devoted to you worthy of your shelter and hide them, rescuing them from the turmoil of men. As in a shelter, you cover them under your hand from the contradiction of tongues, so that they suffer no harm either from those who fight against them with words or from those who devise schemes against them by deeds [?]

Blessed be the Lord, for he has made his mercy wonderful in a besieged city. Having addressed his plea to God at such length in confession, he brings the discourse to a happy end by blessing God, "for he has made his mercy wonderful in a besieged city." Symmachus translated this as: "Blessed be the Lord, who has shown his mercy to me as in a fenced city." "For through me," he says, "God was glorified. When countless enemies rose against me and tried to besiege my soul as if it were a great city, my guardian threw a fence around me and showed his mercy to be wonderful, saving me like a city surrounded by a strong wall. Such have you been to me, my Lord, at the time when I humbled myself in the distraction that came upon me, when my eye was troubled with anger, and my soul and my belly too. I was not crushed, but I humbled myself as one cast away from before your eyes because of my sin. These things I said in confession. But you, the loving and good God, did not cast off your servant. In keeping with the promise that says, 'When you turn back and groan, then you will be saved,' you heard me while I was saying these things, and so you made your mercy wonderful [?] in a city.

OF DAVID, OF UNDERSTANDING. 31. Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. David had afflicted himself greatly over the offence he had committed and had uttered the words of the thirtieth psalm, anxious and in anguish [?] over God's judgement on the things of which he was conscious in himself. Then, through the Holy Spirit and his prophetic power, he recognized the forgiveness of sins that was to come to all people through saving grace, and that the idolaters from the nations

and the godless, though pierced through with countless evils, would one day obtain complete forgiveness of sins all at once through the washing of rebirth. So in these words he declares them thrice-blessed. "I," he says, "who have wasted away with laments and constant tears because of my sin, and have fallen into every kind of misfortune on its account, call those people enviable and blessed who received forgiveness of their sins without toil, through God's love for humanity. For he treats them with such generosity that he not only forgives their sins but also covers them, leaving not even a trace of them." Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not reckon sin, and in whose mouth there is no deceit. What was said before was said in general terms, about all who would obtain forgiveness of sins through grace. What is added here shows how forgiveness is given, through the words "to whom the Lord will not reckon sin." It shows that a sin, once committed, cannot become uncommitted. But the Lord, who has authority at the reckoning of accounts, can either reckon the deed against the sinner or not reckon it, pardoning it and granting forgiveness. Each of those who come to the pardon given through baptism will obtain forgiveness through confession of the Savior, that is, through faith in the God of all, and through sincere confession. So the text very precisely adds the phrase "and in whose mouth there is no deceit," or "in whose spirit there is no deceit," for the reading is found both ways. For blessed is the one who makes his confession with a pure spirit and offers the words spoken at the washing of rebirth. But if deceit should be found in his mouth, or in his spirit and soul, he has deceived himself and so does not obtain forgiveness. He will even increase his own evils, storing up more wrath against himself on the day of wrath. Because I kept silent, my bones grew old through my crying out all day long, and so on. "Those whom I recognized by the Spirit and called blessed are blessed indeed. But I, having toiled much in cries and confessions to God, grew weary and fell silent." For this Symmachus translated "Because I fell utterly silent," and Theodotion "Because I grew weary." In place of "through my crying out," Symmachus gave "through my lamenting every day." His bones grew old, crushed by the great affliction he underwent in his confession, by which he also wore down the powers of the soul, which are called bones. That is why Aquila has: "Because I was mute, my bones were worn away in my roaring," and Symmachus: "Because I kept silent, my bones grew old from lamenting every day." He wore himself out and exhausted himself not for a month only but every day. I made my sin known, and I did not cover my iniquity. I said, I will declare against myself

my iniquity to the Lord; and you forgave the impiety of my heart. Pause. Others rendered this not as "the impiety of my heart" but as "the impiety of my sin." Symmachus translated it more precisely, saying: "so that you might take away my sin." "I did this and this," he says, "so that this and this might happen to me." According to Symmachus, he said these things not as one who had already obtained forgiveness but as one doing everything in order to obtain it. Such an interpretation makes sense. If he was calling others blessed whose iniquities were forgiven, as though he himself had not yet obtained forgiveness, how could he say here, "and you forgave the impiety of my sin"? So I say that Symmachus' version, "so that you might take away the impiety of my sin," is the more precise. For this every holy one will pray to you at a fitting time. Yet in a flood of many waters they will not come near him. "Therefore every holy one, taking an example from what I have done, will pray to you most eagerly and confidently, if ever the time should call him to come to a prayer like mine. And when he prays after my example, you will hear him too and grant him the salvation that comes from you, so that he suffers no harm even if countless flooding waters rush against him. For he has built his house upon the rock and hung his hopes on you, the great Savior, so he will remain unshaken and steadfast. Because of your protection it will not be able even to approach him or come near him." [?] Symmachus' translation presents this sense [?] when it says: "For this every holy one will pray," meaning, "Therefore every holy one will pray to you, finding the right time, so that many flooding waters may not come near him." But if it is read as in the Seventy, "For this every holy one will pray," we shall say that "this" plainly means the forgiveness granted to me. "Because of your mercy and the love for humanity you showed me, every holy one will be hopeful of obtaining the same from you, if ever, as a man clothed in flesh, he should fall into some such sin, and a time should come that requires a confession like mine and

I will give you understanding and instruct you in this way in which you shall go; I will fix my eyes upon you. What was said through the prophet, "While you are still speaking, I will say, 'Here I am,'" was fulfilled in David too. While he was praying and sending up his petition, the divine Spirit counts him worthy of an answer and urges him to take courage. "For I," he says, "will give you understanding and instruct you." For this Aquila says: "I will make you knowing and enlighten you in this way in which you will go," and Symmachus: "I will give you understanding and show you the way you will travel." For he promises to show him the one who said, "I am the way." This [?] was the Word of God, who leads those who travel to

the thrice-blessed goal, his own Father. Instead of "I will fix my eyes upon you," Symmachus says, "I will take counsel concerning you with my eye." For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer. So it is fitting that he counts the one who had prayed so earnestly worthy of his own eye: his mind enlightened by the illuminating rays sent from the divine eye, he will see the way promised to him. That is why the eyes of the Lord are not on all but on the righteous alone, for he turns his eyes away from the ungodly. Be glad in the Lord and rejoice, you righteous, and boast, all you upright in heart. Having concluded the answer to the one who prayed and promised him what was said above, the text passes on to the human race as a whole, for in the abundance of his love for humanity he wants all to be saved. And David himself, having gone through his own confession and been granted a favourable answer and promise, out of overflowing joy secures the same benefit for the rest of humanity too. Be glad in the Lord and rejoice, you righteous, and boast, all you upright in heart. He gave fitting counsel to the rank of sinners on the left, offering himself as an example to those turning back from their sins. In the same way, through these words he brings the righteous the good news proper and suited to them. He urges them to rejoice in nothing worldly, but to take pride in the Lord and rejoice in him alone, glad and exulting in so great a good. For, as the Apostle says, "Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord." So here too it is fitting that he seals the conclusion of the whole discourse with the words: "And boast in him, all you upright in heart." That is, do not take pride in yourselves, but in the Lord himself, who has become the cause of all your virtue.

A PSALM OF DAVID. 32. In the Hebrew reading and in the other translators, the psalm has no title. But it follows closely on the one before it. Having said at the end of that psalm, "Be glad in the Lord and rejoice, you righteous," he began this one with almost the very same words: "Rejoice, you righteous, in the Lord." And it seems to me that what is said here is addressed prophetically to the people described in the previous psalm, in the words "Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered." For "Rejoice, you righteous, in the Lord" is proclaimed to those who have obtained forgiveness of their sins through saving grace. Do not trust in yourselves or in anything worldly, but in the Lord. Take pride in him, boast in him, and rejoice, you blessed ones whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered. "For praise of God," he says, "befits all the upright." And according to

Aquila: "For the upright, hymn-singing is comely." For a hymn is not comely in the mouth of a sinner, so it is fitting that praise of God becomes those who have pure minds and pure lips. Give thanks to the Lord with the lyre; sing to him with a ten-stringed harp. These things were written according to the first tradition of the law. The one who keeps his inner and outer senses pure and blameless sings to God on a ten-stringed harp. Sing to him a new song. The old song was practised by the former people, using the old lyre and the old harp, lifeless instruments, as through symbols and images. But the new song, more magnificent and more worthy of God, is sent up to God through a living lyre and through the ten-stringed harp just explained. Sing well with a shout of joy. This shout is mystical, which is why it is said somewhere: "Blessed is the people that knows the shout of joy." And the one who said, "I went around and offered in his tent a sacrifice of shouting," declares that in place of oxen and calves and blood sacrifices he has offered sacrifices of shouting.

For the word of the Lord is upright, and all his works are done in faithfulness. He loves mercy and judgement; the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord. Let our grasp of what exists come to us through faith, and the conduct of practical life through mercy and judgement. These are what the upright word of the Lord loves, since it has made us able to judge and to tell good from its opposite. So he wants us to do nothing without judgement, and not to be carried along irrationally by the impulses that arise from them [?]. Instead we should deliberate with judgement about what must be done, and above all be merciful: forgiving toward those who sin, and compassionate and kind toward those in need of mercy. By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the breath of his mouth all their host. So by the Father [?] all the host above the heavens was made firm. That is, they have their vigour, stability and steadfastness in holiness, and in every virtue befitting the holy powers, from the help of the Spirit. Here, then, "the breath of his mouth" is written. Elsewhere we will also find "the word of his mouth," so that the Saviour and his Holy Spirit may be understood. Both worked together in creating the heavens and the powers in them. That is why it is said: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the breath of his mouth all their host." For nothing is made holy except by the presence of the Spirit. In the case of the angels, the creating Word, the maker of all things, gave them their entry into being, while the Holy Spirit brought them their sanctification along with it, for the angels were not created as infants. Let all the earth fear the Lord; and let all who dwell in the

world be shaken by him. Having set out God's mighty works and all but shown before our eyes how great the Lord who made such things is, he quite consistently urges us to fear him. He brings the good news that people should no longer pay heed to idols or worship demons, but should worship the maker of such great things. For "be shaken," Symmachus gave "be in reverent awe." You will understand how all who dwell in the world were to be shaken by him if you consider how, through the preaching of the gospel and the saving teaching, churches of God were established throughout the whole world. Every ear was filled with the word, and all people were moved by such great power, turning from their former error about idols and coming to remember true piety. For he spoke, and they came into being; he commanded, and

The Lord scatters the counsels of nations; he sets aside the reasonings of peoples, and sets aside the counsels of rulers. The prophetic Spirit foresaw that persecutions would be kindled against those who were leaving their former superstition, turning away from the error of many gods and turning to the Lord of all. So it was bound to urge those who had come to know the maker of all not to dread the terrors and threats of the nations that remained in unbelief. "Even if they plot countless things against you," he says, "they will be able to accomplish nothing against you. For the maker and Lord of all himself, in whom you have taken refuge, will with a single nod scatter the plots of the nations against you and the schemes of the unbelieving peoples against you. And if rulers and kings should ever be inflamed against you, he will set aside their counsels too, and his counsel alone will prevail forever." Moreover, the reasonings of his wisdom will not be set aside as human reasonings are; his judgements endure from generation to generation. For he keeps his reasonings for those who are worthy of him. Since some worthy people are found in every generation and succession of humanity, it is fitting that he preserves his reasonings for them and extends them from generation to generation. These things were foretold prophetically long ago, and we have received the fulfilment of the words in actual events. All that the rulers of this age contrived against his Church, the persecutions they raised against us and the counsels they devised against us, cannot be adequately told. Nor can it be told how all these were scattered by the power of God, and how this was fulfilled in deeds not only in our own time but in every generation, beginning from the time of the Saviour's divine appearing. Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people he chose as his inheritance. For of old Israel was his portion and inheritance, but since it rejected him, grace has passed over to the nations. From heaven the Lord looked down;

he saw all the sons of men. From his prepared dwelling place he looked upon all who dwell on the earth. He who fashioned their hearts one by one, who understands all their works. So that we may know how the nation called blessed came into being, and where the people he chose as his inheritance got its formation, he goes on to teach that the Lord himself visited all the sons of men who dwell on the earth and formed the nation and people just mentioned out of all of them, using no other ministers. For "from his prepared dwelling place," Aquila translated "from the foundation of his seat," and Symmachus "he looked from the seat of his dwelling." And his Word ministered salvation to those being saved: for he sent his word and healed them, and rescued them from their corruption. Why the Lord looked from heaven, and why he counted all the sons of men worthy of his oversight, he shows next, saying: "He who fashioned their hearts one by one." For this Symmachus says: "He who fashions each of their hearts one by one." If he had made the human mind like that of the irrational animals, there would have been no need for him to look upon the sons of men, for the general providence that cares for all things alike would have been enough. But as it is, the human soul is an exceptional substance, since it is attested of man alone that God said, "Let us make man according to our image and likeness," and "the Lord made man; according to the image of God he made him." So it is fitting that, caring for his own image, he looked from heaven and saw all the sons of men. The present text shows this when it says, "He who fashions their hearts one by one." "One by one" is said in the sense of "set apart from the other animals." By "hearts" he meant their thoughts, and he showed that each person, set apart, holds his own mind like a locked storeroom, so that no one can grasp another's thoughts. No one among men knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him. That is why it was said of our Saviour alone, to show his divinity: "For he himself knew what was in man," and again: "Knowing their thoughts." The present passage shows this too, for "He who fashioned their hearts one by one" is followed by "who understands all their works." He alone understands from what choice people's works are carried out. No one else can understand with what intention and what impulse each person does what he does. A king is not saved by a great army, and a giant will not be saved by the greatness of his strength. A horse is a false hope for safety; for all its great power it will not save. Behold, the eyes of the Lord are on those who fear him, those who hope [?] … 20. ⁵ Genesis 1:26, 27. ⁶ 2 Corinthians 2:11.

…who hope in his mercy, to deliver their souls from death and to keep them alive in famine. These verses keep to the sense of what was said before. The word first summoned everyone on earth to the fear of God by saying, “Let all the earth fear the Lord.” Then it encouraged them not to be anxious or afraid of the persecutions that would rise against them, and in the verses before these it added, “The Lord scatters the counsels of the nations,” and what follows. Keeping to the same sense, it says through the present verses as well: Take courage, all of you to whom the word is addressed. If you come to his fear, you will have his eyes, his power of clear sight, watching over you and rescuing you from all your enemies and all who plot against you. For behold, the eyes of the Lord are on those who fear him, those who hope in his mercy, to deliver their souls from death. Apart from these eyes of God there is no other hope of salvation. There is none for a king who trusts in military power, none for a giant who prides himself on his great power and strength, and none for a horse that trusts in the swiftness of its feet. All these deceive, fail and mislead those who have put their hope in them. But you who call on the Lord and have taken up his fear, take courage. Do not fear the counsels of the nations, which the Lord scatters, or the thoughts of peoples, which the Lord sets aside, or the counsels of rulers, which he himself overturns. Do not be dismayed by a king who trusts in the size of his army, or by a giant puffed up with the strength and might of his body. Instead, with the eyes of his providence as your great safeguard, hope in him alone and in his mercy, so that he may deliver their souls from death. The death of the soul would be the denial of God, complete apostasy, and the sins that lead to death. So even if the bodies of those who hope in the Lord are sometimes handed over to the death common to all because of their testimony to him, his eyes still care for the better part and have delivered their souls from death. And they do not only do this; they also take care to keep them alive in famine. In times of persecution, teaching and the reading of the divinely inspired Scriptures are often forbidden, and there are few people to distribute spiritual food to human souls. Even so, the eyes of the Lord nourish the souls of these people too through the outpouring of the divine Spirit. They make them taught by God, so that they are nourished by an ineffable power even without human teaching.

On Psalm 33, of David. When he changed his face before Abimelech, and he sent him away, and he departed. Some have supposed that the title of this psalm refers to the story in which David, fleeing from Saul, is recorded as having come to Achish king of Gath. At that time he pretended to be mad and drummed on the doors of the city,

and staggered about, and fell, and his spittle ran down onto his beard. So Achish said to his servants, “Why have you brought an epileptic man to me?” These interpreters heard that he changed his face, but in my view they overlooked what follows: “before Abimelech.” Achish was king of the foreigners who lived in Gath, but Abimelech is mentioned as a priest of God, and David is recorded as having come to him as well, before he went to Achish. For Scripture says: “And David comes to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest, and Ahimelech was astonished at meeting him and said to him, ‘Why are you alone, with no one with you?’ And David said to the priest, ‘The king gave me an order today and said to me, “Let no one know the matter on which I am sending you and about which I have given you orders.” And I have given instructions to the young men at the place called “Faithfulness of God.” Now then, if you have any loaves at hand, give me whatever is there.’ The priest answered David and said, ‘I have no common bread at hand, only holy bread. If the young men have kept themselves from women, you may eat.’ David answered the priest and said to him, ‘Indeed we have kept away from women yesterday and the day before. When I set out on the journey, the young men were purified. And this journey is a common one; that is why it will be sanctified today because of my vessels.’ So Ahimelech the priest gave him the loaves of the presentation, because there was no bread there except the loaves of the presence, which had been removed from before the Lord so that hot bread could be set out on the day they were taken away.” This is what the account about Ahimelech contains. Next it is added that David rose and fled that day, and that after leaving Ahimelech he came to Achish king of Gath. Now someone will say that, since the story about Ahimelech does not record that David changed his face, the name Abimelech stands here by mistake instead of Achish. For it is clearly said of Achish that David “changed his face,” when his spittle ran down and he drummed. I consider it bold and rash, however, to dare to declare that divine Scripture has erred and contains so great a mistake as to put a priest of God in place of a foreigner. This is especially so since the Hebrew reading and all the other translators have Ahimelech. Assuming the title is true, then, it follows that we should ask how and when David changed his face before Abimelech, and he sent him away, and he departed. It seems to me that the solution to the question can be found by comparing the other translators. Aquila and the fifth edition translated it this way: “Of David, when he changed his taste before Abimelech, and he drove him out, and he departed.” For perhaps it is because of the

loaves of the presentation, which he received from Abimelech and ate with the young men who were with him, that he is said to have changed his taste before Abimelech. He tasted consecrated food, the priestly loaves that no one was allowed to eat except the priests, and so he changed his taste. Symmachus, by saying “Of David, when he transformed his manner before Abimelech,” has suggested another sense. He says that David's manner was changed before Abimelech because, when asked the reason for his journey, David lied and deceived the priest. Using deceit was foreign to David's character, so according to Symmachus, by using it on that occasion he changed his manner. From what has been said, you will also be able to fit the translation of the Seventy to the story of Abimelech. It says that David changed his face before Abimelech because he did not tell him the true reason for his flight, but deceived him and said one thing in place of another. As a result he even received the sword of Goliath from him and became the cause of his destruction. For when Saul later learned what had been done, he sent men and killed Abimelech himself and all the priests of the Lord, and struck Nob, the city of the priests. All this happened because David changed his manner, or his face, before Abimelech. The Scripture of the Kingdoms has “Ahimelech,” but since a letter has been interchanged, there is no need to be disturbed. Because the letter the Hebrews call beth looks like kaph, the name was rendered in different ways. The two letters are almost one and the same, and only a very small stroke tells them apart. The Saviour also mentions this story about David in the Gospels, saying: “Have you not read what David did when he and those with him were hungry, how he entered the house of God and ate the loaves of the presentation, which it was not lawful to eat, either for him or for those with him, but only for the priests?” This is said in the Gospel according to Matthew. But in the Gospel according to Mark the Saviour is recorded as saying: “Have you never read what David did when he was in need and was hungry, he and those with him, how he entered the house of God in the time of Abiathar the high priest and ate the loaves of the presentation?” Who would not be puzzled as to why the Saviour mentions Abiathar here and not Abimelech? One might answer that Abimelech had two names, so that he was the same person as Abiathar. Indeed, the Scripture of the Kingdoms mentions a son of his called Abiathar, who alone escaped when the priests were killed and joined David. Someone else might say that the history mentions Abimelech as a priest, but that here the Saviour says Abiathar was

high priest at that time. For David entered, he says, the house of God in the time of Abiathar the high priest. And the written history clearly says that Ahimelech and the priests of God were killed by Saul, but it does not record that a high priest was killed. Let this be what we have to say about the title of the psalm. I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall be in my mouth continually. David gives thanks for having been found worthy of priestly food and says: Not only [?], but I will go on confessing my thanks and blessing him all my life, and my mouth will never leave off praising him. For instead of sacrifices and whole burnt offerings I have been taught to bring him the sacrifice of the lips. As I flee, no helper is with me, and I have no refuge or safety. I take the Lord alone as the guard of my soul, and my soul takes courage in him, not in my own righteous deeds. So it is fitting that my soul shall boast in the Lord; let the meek hear and be glad. Let all who are meek, humble and gentle out of reverence for God take me as their example. Let them take courage and be filled with gladness, expecting the same things I do and making the Lord himself their hope. He also went away having received from Abimelech the sword of Goliath the foreigner. So he says: “But I will not boast even in this, but in the Lord, through whom I gained this sword.” For the priest had said to him: “Here is the sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you struck down in the valley of Elah, and it is wrapped in a cloak. If you will take it, take it for yourself, for there is no other besides it.” So when David heard this, he said: In the Lord my soul shall be praised. That spear brought David great glory. He was only a boy and did not even know how to carry weapons of war, but he defeated Goliath by faith in God. For this reason that sword alone had been laid up in the sanctuary as a votive offering, which the priest indicated when he said, “And there is no other.” It was not permitted to lay up weapons of war in the tabernacle of God. That sword alone was laid up as a memorial of David's victory over the foreigner, deposited as a thank offering to God, who had granted him the victory. Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together. Those who adorn the image of God in themselves through their deeds and a virtuous life glorify and exalt him. I sought the Lord, and he heard me. For “he heard me” answers “I sought.” This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him and saved him out of all his troubles. Again, as before, he offers himself as a model for teaching others. He calls himself poor because of the humility and modesty of his soul, and he teaches about himself as though speaking of someone else, saying:

This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him. “But do not think,” he says, “that I alone have obtained this. I am thought to be king and ruler of the whole nation, but I am poor in soul because of the fear of God. Know for certain that the same Lord is present to those who are poor like me, by which I mean those who fear him, and will hear them.” O taste and see that the Lord is good; blessed is the man who hopes in him. The one who is truly a man through hoping in God perfectly and without fail is blessed. One could quite reasonably apply this phrase to Aquila's translation, since according to Aquila the title said: “Of David, when he changed his taste before Abimelech.” He partook of the loaves of the presentation and changed his taste, and then through the tasting he perceived divine power supplied to him. For this reason, in keeping with the saying “What I received without guile I share without grudging,” he urges others to hurry to the same taste and to pray to be fed with the bread of life. The loaves of the presentation prescribed through Moses were a symbol and image of that bread. Therefore David, understanding what the bread of the presentation was an image of, urges people to hurry not to the bodily bread but to the bread understood through it. We on earth partake of the bread that came down from heaven, of the Word who emptied and made himself small. But those in the kingdom of heaven partake of him full and complete, being fed by his divinity and enjoying the contemplations of wisdom. It is right for us to hope that we too will one day share in these, which is why it is said: Blessed is the man who hopes in him. Fear the Lord, all you his saints, for those who fear him lack nothing. David presents all these things as maxims for the benefit of others, having first enjoyed them himself when he sought the Lord and was heard by him. So he urges his saints to keep the fear of the Lord before their eyes, for it is by this fear that they are made saints. That is why another psalm says, “The fear of the Lord is pure,” meaning “purifying.” That is also why the divine law says: “You shall be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy.” The sign of fearing the Lord would be to be clean of all filth and shameful action and to keep oneself holy in both body and spirit. Those who fear the Lord and have been sanctified through his fear will lack nothing, since they have found great wealth and a good treasure in the fear of the Lord itself.

Of David, Psalm 34. Judge, O Lord, those who wrong me; fight against those who fight against me. Take hold of weapon and shield, and rise up to help me. Draw the sword, and close the way against those who

pursue me. Much is said about the sword in Ezekiel as well: “Sword,” he says, “sword, awake, and devour the limbs of the wounded.” And again: “If a land sins against me, I will send a sword upon it.” Because he is good, he sends all these things against the wickedness in human beings, for the benefit of those who are in its grip. For he saves even through wars [?], like a physician who cuts and cauterizes the diseased parts of the body to heal the whole. To these words he adds next: Say to my soul, “I am your salvation.” He believes and is fully convinced that what God says does not go forth idly but is certainly carried out in deed. In this he renounced his own salvation and gave up his own life, and prayed that the Lord's salvation might be granted to his soul, so that he too could say, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” For he himself is our salvation, which is exactly what the meaning of the name Jesus signifies. Let those who seek my soul be put to shame and confounded. “When you have done this, Lord,” he says, “and have heard my prayer, they will be put to shame and confounded, as men who made their attempt in vain, and so they also failed to get what they were striving for.” Let those who plot evil against me be turned back and put to shame. They will no longer stand before my face, but will turn their backs and yield the victory to me. As they flee and retreat, they will be scattered. For let them be like dust before the wind, and let the angel of the Lord afflict them, not allowing them to regroup or to come back. Let that same angel keep afflicting them, that is, punishing them. Let their way be darkness and slippery ground, and let the angel of the Lord pursue them. By “way” he means the wretched life of the ungodly, along which they made their journey. For without cause they hid the destruction of their snare for me. Symmachus rendered this as: “For groundlessly they hid the destruction of their nets for me.” “They had suffered nothing from me beforehand, yet they plotted against me without cause and for no reason, hiding a snare and preparing destruction for me. They may very well have seemed to make war on me through human beings, whether through Saul or through others, but I knew who caused Saul's jealousy and who incited the rest of my enemies. For there were others who hid their snares and tried to destroy my soul, and who also reproached my soul in vain.” Symmachus rendered this as: “Groundlessly they dug under my soul.” They did everything they could to drive his soul out of the gentleness and forbearance that were in it, so that he would be filled with anger and wrath, resort to retaliation, and do something evil to Saul. This, then, concerns the many enemies. About their leader he adds: Let a snare he does not know come upon him, and let the trap he hid catch him, and in the snare he shall

fall into it. Although David spoke these things as a prayer, they foretold things to come and prophesied what would happen. In the same way, earlier verses were spoken prophetically: “Let them be put to shame and confounded” means “They will be put to shame and confounded.” Again, “Let them be turned back and put to shame, and let them become like dust” means “They will be turned back and put to shame and will become like dust.” For he was foretelling what would happen to his enemies. Someone may think this saying was spoken about Saul, since he suffered these things not long afterwards. But we remember what was said at the beginning of the psalm, so we will take these words too as referring to one of the spiritual enemies, the one more powerful in wickedness, namely the devil. All my bones shall say, “Lord, who is like you? You rescue the poor from the hand of those stronger than he, the poor and needy from those who plunder him.” The bones of the soul are its powers of understanding, as was said earlier. When these are enlightened by his presence, they will say: Lord, who is like you? “For if you had not stood by the poor man and thought him worthy of your help, who would he be, and what would he amount to, alone against so many and such great enemies?” You can also understand the passage from the bare history. Keep in mind that David's flight drove him into such poverty that he needed bread and basic food, and was forced to dare to eat the loaves of the presentation. He did not come to this out of a love of luxury, or because he was puffed up with his own righteousness, or because he despised the law in any other way, but because he had gone a long time without food. That is why the Saviour says, “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry?” He was poor and in flight with a few men, but those hunting him were powerful. Saul was king of the whole nation, and the rulers with him and the commanders of the foreign enemies were stronger than David. As he escaped from their hands, he did not fail to recognize his helper. So much for the history. But if you think of the hidden and invisible enemies of the righteous man's soul, you will see that in the battle against these spiritual enemies, who are always trying to plunder his soul, we need no other helper and Saviour than his Christ. You should also consider whether the poor man is different from the needy man, and whether the difference is one of substance or only of concept. The same person can be poor because he has become poor by losing the wealth he had, and needy because he gains what he needs to live by toil. Unjust witnesses rose up; they asked me things I did not know. Those who are witnesses not of righteousness but of unrighteousness rose up, stirred themselves up, and question me captiously [?] about things I do not know. For the good man knows nothing of base things; that is, he has not been mingled with anything wicked. As evidence: “He who keeps a commandment will not know an evil word.” And here
