…for the [?] means that he has not done, and has not been mixed up in, any evil word. It would be false to suppose that one who keeps the divine commandment does not know what an evil word is. Since he can tell evil from good, he has turned away from every other word and come to keep the commandment. What he means, then, is this: "Though I had no experience, knowledge or notion of evil things, they provoked me and questioned me about them," as the Egyptian woman did with Joseph, and the elders with Susanna. "They repaid me evil for good, and childlessness to my soul." I was eager to fulfil my duties toward everyone blamelessly and wished, if possible, to live at peace with all people. In return for these good things they repaid me with evil, showing themselves enemies and ill-disposed in everything. As far as it lay with them, they tried to destroy my soul's fruitfulness in good things. If, then, I had been persuaded by their questions and become the kind of person they wanted to make me, my soul would have been made childless, no longer receiving the divine seed of the Bridegroom. And if a teacher's disciples are called his children, then the teacher's soul truly is made childless when it falls into errors. By its own stumbling it destroys those born of it through discipleship. Instead of "childlessness to my soul," Symmachus rendered "things overturned against my soul." The present verses are joined to what was said earlier in the thirty-third psalm, and that psalm recalled the story of Abimelech, before whom David changed his countenance, as has been explained. So perhaps the present passage can also be referred to those events. For Saul learned from Doeg that David had come to Abimelech, had received loaves and had escaped. He then killed all the priests of the Lord, along with Abimelech himself and his whole family. David, then, could have said these things with reference to Saul, so that the whole psalm is referred to that time when Doeg bore false witness against Abimelech before Saul. Perhaps the Holy Spirit, depicting the sufferings of the priests, uttered the present words: "Judge, O Lord, those who wrong me," and what follows. But the words spoken in the singular about one person, "Let a snare come upon him which he does not know, and let the net which he hid catch him, and he will fall into that very snare," can be applied to Doeg. And the words "Unjust witnesses rose up; they asked me things I did not know; they repaid me evil for good, and childlessness to my soul" might be spoken in the person of Abimelech. It is also likely that David himself said these things, for the psalm bears his name. With an apostle's disposition he would say: "Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?" and "When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it." Besides these, one might call "unjust witnesses" all those who slandered David before Saul. At one time the Ziphites

came and said, "Look, David is hiding among us." At other times, it is likely, others who wanted to please the king bore much false witness against him and said things against him that he neither knew nor had in mind. But "They repaid me evil for good" can be referred to Saul himself. Saul had often been treated well by David, yet he repaid him with the opposite, devising terrible things against his life and producing childlessness in his soul. Childlessness of soul occurs when the seeds that a soul sows in others, whether through kindnesses or through teaching, bear no fruit. So although David brought forth many good things toward Saul, Saul produced childlessness for him by not yielding fruits worthy of what had been sown in him. "But I, when they troubled me, put on sackcloth, and humbled my soul with fasting, and my prayer will return to my bosom." In addition to what has been explained, consider whether the present words might also fit the person of our Saviour, as uttered prophetically in his own person. See whether the sense does not run smoothly in this way too, with nothing to hinder it. Let our Saviour, according to his humanity, be speaking to his own Father from the beginning of the psalm up to "and shut up the way against those who pursue me." In the twenty-first psalm, which he clearly speaks, it is also said: "Attend to my help." Moreover, the Gospels record that he devoted himself to prayer. Indeed, what is written here was fulfilled in deeds after the outrage the Jews dared against him. Not long afterwards a soldier's sword and a Roman war overtook them, and not without God's judgment. For it was God who was making war on them through the army of their enemies. The Saviour himself sets this forth in the parable about those who refused the invitation to the wedding and murdered the messengers. There he says that the king sent his troops and burned their city. In this way, then, the present words were fulfilled. Because they wronged the Son of God, they were judged, and his blood was avenged. And because they had made themselves enemies of Christ, God made war on them and pursued them with weapon, shield and sword. For divine justice did not pursue them invisibly, but through enemies among men. It is remarkable that it says, "Pour out the sword." War no longer overtook them partially, as it had in former times, but a sword of war was poured out upon them. That is why it is said, "But wrath has come upon them to the end," and elsewhere, "Pour out your wrath upon them." Anyone who has read through the Histories of Flavius Josephus has learned from them how the Jews were shut up under siege and perished by famine and civil strife. Who among such readers will not marvel at the voice that says here, "And shut up the way against those who pursue me"? After this, it would befit the Saviour alone to say to his own Father, according to

his humanity: "Say to my soul, 'I am your salvation,'" and what follows, up to "and let the angel of the Lord afflict them." These things too were fulfilled when they were driven from their own mother city and scattered among all the nations. Then it says: "Let their way be darkness and a slippery place." Their way, on which they walked of old, was bodily worship, and it has become darkness and a slippery place for them. It also says, "the angel of the Lord pursuing them." These, then, are the wages of what they dared against him. But do not hear these words as though the Saviour were cursing his own enemies, for he instructed his own disciples, "Pray for those who mistreat you and wrong you." Hear them instead as spoken prophetically, foretelling what would happen to them. He next teaches why he foretells that these things will happen to them: "For without cause they hid for me the destruction of their snare; in vain they reproached my soul." These words concern the crowd that gathered against him. What follows, however, is no longer said of many but of one, and it can be applied to Judas. He concealed his plot against him, feigned friendship and betrayed the Teacher with a kiss. So of him one might say: "Let a snare come upon him which he does not know, and let the net which he hid catch him, and he will fall into that very snare." So much for these words. He knew well to what a good end the plot against him would lead, and he sets this forth too: "But my soul will rejoice in the Lord; it will delight in his salvation. All my bones will say, 'Lord, who is like you? You rescue the poor from those who plunder him.'" In the twenty-first psalm, which is clearly spoken in the person of the Saviour, it was said: "I was poured out like water, and all my bones were scattered." There the word signifies the scattering and flight of his apostles, which they suffered at the time of his passion. Then was fulfilled the saying "I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered." For the bones of his body were his first disciples. At that time they were scattered, having stumbled because of him, as he himself made plain when he said, "All of you will fall away because of me this night." But after the resurrection they saw him and were filled with joy and gladness. In the present passage too it is said of the same people: "All my bones will say, 'Lord, who is like you?'" The words joined to these also fit the person of our Saviour very well: "Unjust witnesses rose up; they asked me things I did not know. They repaid me evil for good, and childlessness to my soul." You will find similar words in the hundred and eighth psalm, where it is said: "And they fought against me without cause; instead of loving me they slandered me. They set against me evil for good, and hatred for my

love." They brought childlessness upon him, though he did everything to gather them and regenerate them to himself. He made this plain when he said: "How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing!" In this way they repaid him evil for good, and childlessness to his soul. Having foretold these things here, he next sets forth his love for humankind and his forbearance: "But I, when they troubled me, put on sackcloth." Instead of "when they troubled me," Aquila says, quite remarkably: "And I, in their sickness, my clothing was sackcloth." Symmachus has: "As for me, in their sicknesses my garment was sackcloth." Theodotion and the fifth edition said: "But I, when they were troubled." For the Saviour suffered along with their evils and the sicknesses of their soul. He made signs of mourning and lamentation, putting on sackcloth for their sake, and he also humbled his soul with fasting. That is why he taught: "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death," and "Now my soul is troubled." He endured these things out of surpassing love for humankind, suffering and grieving on their behalf like a father over sons who are perishing. That is why he said of himself in the prophets: "A man under a blow, who knows how to bear sickness." Again: "This one bears our sins and suffers pain for us." And again: "He was wounded for our sins, and by his bruise we were healed." So [?] both in their sicknesses and when they were troubled, the Saviour saw the ruin that would overtake them and their final destruction. He put on sackcloth for them and humbled his soul with fasting. But they behaved in such a way that his prayer for them was not carried to the Father's ears. Instead, as if beaten back by the greatness of their impiety, it was dragged down and returned to him. That is why he said: "And my prayer will return to my bosom." If they had been going to be saved and turn from their impieties, the Saviour's prayer would have run straight to the Father's ears without hindrance or obstacle. As I explore every possible sense, let these things necessarily be considered for these passages. "And they rejoiced against me and gathered together; scourges were gathered against me, and I did not know. They were split apart, and were not pierced with remorse." These words must be taken in two ways, as we have already said. Either David was relating these things about himself while Saul pursued him, or the Holy Spirit is speaking prophetically about the Saviour. Instead of "They rejoiced against me," Aquila, keeping close to the Hebrew wording, says: "And in my limping they rejoiced and were collected together." Symmachus has: "While I limped they rejoiced and assembled." The fifth edition has: "And in my weakness they rejoiced." I think these readings indicate the time of the passion, in which, according to

the Apostle, "he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God." He also endured limping for our sake, willingly bearing weakness on our behalf. He made himself weak, not because another overcame him, but by surpassing power. He emptied himself and took the form of a servant, concealing and humbling himself and making himself weak to the point of death. So in his limping and weakness they gathered together, and [?] they laid scourges upon him. He made this plain through another prophet as well, who says in his person: "I gave my back to scourges, and my cheeks to blows; and I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting." These things were fulfilled at the time of his passion. Symmachus says: "And tearing at me, they did not rest." "I did not know," he says, "why they scourged me, for they had no reasonable pretext for the blows they laid on me." Instead of "They tempted me, they sneered at me with sneering," Symmachus says: "With hypocrisy, with feigned words." "They gnashed their teeth at me." You would find many illustrations of this in the Gospels. The Pharisees came to him to test him, and at other times they sneered at him. They gnashed their teeth at him, furious at the multitude of those who were becoming his disciples. "Lord, when will you look on? Restore my soul from their wickedness, my only one from lions." Instead of "When will you look on?" all the other translators agree in saying, "Lord, how long will you look on?" The Saviour marvels at the Father's long-suffering and surpassing forbearance. So he says, "How long will you look on?" Then he pleads: "Restore my soul." This would be like "Father, glorify me with the glory that I had with you before the world existed." Next he asks that his only one be rescued from lions. The twenty-first psalm is akin to the present psalm and, as has already been shown, contains things similar to these. It says: "Save me from the lion's mouth, and my only one from the hand of the dog." There too he mentioned the only one, the dog and the lion, and also unicorns: "and my lowliness from the horns of unicorns." By these I think he signifies the opposing powers that plotted against his only-begotten soul at the time of his passion. Instead of "my only one," Aquila rendered "my solitary one," and Symmachus "my solitude." But if David is saying these things, it is not hard to apply the sense to him as well. "I will give thanks to you in a large Church." The twenty-first psalm too is spoken in the person of our Saviour. After the prophecies about his passion it mentioned his Church, saying: "In the midst of

the Church I will sing your praise." There this was said after "Rescue my soul from the sword, and my only one from the hand of the dog. Save me from the lion's mouth, and my lowliness from the horns of unicorns." Joined to these words was "I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will sing your praise." In the same way, in the present passage he first says, "Restore my soul from their wickedness, my only one from lions," and then adds: "I will give thanks to you in a large Church; among a weighty people I will praise you." Instead of "weighty," Aquila rendered "bony," that is, strong, since the bones are the most powerful and strongest parts of the whole body. So the weighty people is the one founded on the rock, unshaken and unbreakable. He therefore gives thanks to the Father for his large Church. For this Church is truly large. In the twenty-first psalm he called it great: "From you comes my praise in the great Church." The Father, then, brings about praise for the Son in the great Church, and the Son gives thanks to the Father in the large Church, established throughout the whole [?]

"Let those who are my enemies without just cause not gloat over me, those who hate me without reason and wink with their eyes. For they spoke peaceably to me, but in anger they devised deceits. They opened their mouth wide against me; they said, 'Aha, aha, our eyes have seen it.'" If the happy outcome that followed our Saviour's passion had not been seen, those who contrived the plot against him might perhaps have had grounds to gloat over him, as though he had been destroyed and had achieved nothing. But his large and great Church shines throughout the whole inhabited world. He himself still stands in its midst even now, gathering his weighty and powerful people and giving thanks through them to his own Father. For "where two or three are gathered in his name, there I am in their midst." So it is fitting that those who rejoiced at evil were covered with shame and turned back. What had they suffered that deserved enmity, that they should take up such hatred against him? That is why Aquila translated "without cause." They winked with their eyes, mocking him and disparaging the teachings of my wisdom. Then: "They spoke peaceably to me," he says, "but in their heart they devised deceits and anger." These things too were fulfilled when the Pharisees, hunting for something to seize on, said to him: "Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the word of God in truth, and you care about no one, for you do not look at a person's face. Tell us, then: is it lawful to pay tax to Caesar or not?" They put these words forward deceitfully. That is why he anticipated them and hinted at this, saying: "They spoke peaceably to me, but in anger they devised deceits." On that occasion they spoke with him deceitfully. In the end, however, at the time of the passion, they shouted with their whole mouth, asking

for his blood to be upon themselves and upon their children. He sets this forth in the present words: "They opened their mouth wide against me." Then, when he was handed over to them like a sheep to the slaughter, and like an innocent lamb silent before its shearer, they saw his suffering and cried out: "Aha, aha, our eyes have seen it." "You have seen, O Lord; do not keep silent." Above he said, "When will you look on?" and in the present words he says, "You have seen, O Lord." What has he seen? He has seen how deceitfully they approached him, how they opened their mouth wide against him, and how, having done what they wished, they shouted, "Aha, aha, our eyes have seen it." "But you, Lord, who have seen these things and have borne with them patiently, do not keep silent. Take up the judgement seat of your justice and say: 'You did these things, and I kept silent'; and again, 'I have kept silent; shall I keep silent forever?'" In his humanity he pleads with his own Father: "Do not stand far from me" and "Awake and attend to my judgement, my God and my Lord, to my cause." At the time of his passion for us he uttered such words so that people might believe that he had truly and really become a human being and willingly accepted death for us. "And let them not gloat over me; let them not say in their hearts, 'Aha, aha, our soul'; nor let them say, 'We have swallowed him up.'" "For when you," he says, "proceed against what they have dared and judge according to your justice, they will not gloat, nor will they say in their hearts, 'Aha, aha, our soul has prevailed.'" Even if they once said this with their mouth, they will not say it in their hearts as well. Nor will they say, "We have swallowed him up," when they see my resurrection and my Church established throughout the whole world. For someone is swallowed up when he has once gone down into the deep and never come up again; thus it is said that once "death, having prevailed, swallowed them up." But there too those who were swallowed came back, which is why it is said: "And again God took away every tear from every face." Here too, then, even if for a time they thought they had swallowed him up, they will not say so to the end, he says. Accordingly he prophesies: "Let those who rejoice at my misfortunes be put to shame and confounded together; let those who speak boastfully against me be clothed with shame and confusion." It is easy to see how these words were fulfilled when referred to the person of our Saviour. From that time until now, those who once prided themselves on many gifts have been rejected and cast off. Meanwhile, those from all the nations who have received the one whom they killed have been freed from the error of many gods and continue to worship the God who is over all. The first group, covered with shame for what they did, have been confounded, while the second are filled every day with joy and boldness. So the oracle in Moses is fulfilled, which says to the people of the Jews:

"Let those who desire my righteousness exult and be glad, and let them say continually, 'Let the Lord be magnified,' those who desire the peace of his servant. And my tongue shall meditate on your righteousness, on your praise all the day long." The beginning of the prophecy threatened that judgment and war would come upon those who had wronged the one prophesied and made war on him; the middle part denounced their conduct; and the closing part described the shame and disgrace that overtook them. But the conclusion of the whole prophecy proclaims the good news of exultation and gladness and good things to all who desire his righteousness. You will understand his righteousness if you take it as his divinity, since he became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption. So those who have understood this, he says, may they exult and be glad; and he teaches them always to say, "Let the Lord be magnified," if indeed they embrace peace with the one prophesied, since those who took up enmity against him have paid the penalty they deserved. And this would be his peace, which he graciously gave to his disciples, saying, "My peace I give to you, my peace I leave with you." So much, then, for those who desire and love his peace and honor his righteousness. Finally, speaking of himself, he sets the seal on the end of the whole discourse, saying, "And my tongue shall meditate on your righteousness, on your praise all the day long." When these things have come to pass, he says, both for those who love me and for those who hate me, I will not cease meditating on your righteousness, and on your praise all the day long—not all the days, but one single day, unbounded and unending. For the abiding and dwelling with you is an eternal day. And I will meditate on your righteousness, singing its praise—the righteousness by which, judging justly, you counted worthy of your grace and calling not one nation, but all the nations throughout the whole inhabited world. In another sense, since we are the body of Christ and individually members of it, those who devote themselves to the divine teachings might be called his tongue, so that the present words can also be referred to them. FOR THE END. [?] OF THE LORD, TO [?]. It is inscribed neither as a psalm nor as an ode nor as anything of that kind; but it contains teaching which at the beginning convicts everyone who is without fear and without reverence, and is for that reason given over to every lawlessness, and in its conclusion shows the end of such people. So, having said at the beginning, "The transgressor says that he will sin within [?]—[?] took the psalm as referring both to [?] and to Christ, or rather to Christ; but the one [?]

himself," he says toward the end, "There all who work iniquity have fallen; they were thrust out and will not be able to stand." In the middle it contains teaching about God and the good hopes of men who love God. These words are spoken by the servant of the Lord, David; for this is what the superscription signifies. Having separated himself from the ranks of the transgressors, he [?] to supplication of God, having made himself a slave to the law and to God's ordinances. And he teaches the rest of mankind to act as he did, and not to be carried away along with the

"The transgressor says within himself that he will sin; there is no fear of God before his eyes. For he has acted deceitfully before him, so as to find out his iniquity and hate it." Symmachus interpreted these words more clearly, rendering them this way: "My heart speaks within me concerning the faithlessness of the ungodly man: the fear of God is not set before his eyes. For he thinks that his doings slip by unnoticed, until his injustice is found out, so that it is hated." Through these words David himself says, My heart and my reasoning perceived these things about the ungodly man. For he has deceived [sic] his own faculty of contemplation, by which he could have known the fear of God, having turned aside the eyes of his mind. Hence, according to the Hebrew reading, he is said to have dealt deceitfully in his own eyes, "so as to find out his iniquity and hate it." Thus, he says, he perverted himself and cast the fear of God away from his own eyes, so that his iniquity became manifest and was in turn seen and found out, and for this reason deserves hatred. Such a man has given himself over to sin without disguise, so that even the words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit. And he chose these things entirely of his own will, since he is self-determining and able to follow the good way, but did not want to; hence it is said, "He did not want to understand so as to do good; he devised iniquity upon his bed." For not even at the time of quiet, when after the day's activities people give themselves over to rest and calm and sleep, does such a man come into a state of calm; even at that time "he devised iniquity upon his bed." "Lord, your mercy is in heaven." Very fittingly, after describing the wickedness of the transgressor, he sets forth the surpassing riches of God's patience, by which he bears even with lawless and ungodly men, teaching that the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience are full of great mercy. And this mercy of God is the cause of the life and good cheer of sinners and ungodly men. So he says that the treasure of his mercy is stored up in heaven, and that his truth too is with him, filling [?] all that is above the heavens; yet it reaches even to the clouds, or, according to Symmachus, to the upper air. So too

it is said elsewhere, "In heaven your truth will be prepared." God's truth, then, is in heaven, but like rain borne through the clouds it drips down even to the earth. Hence it is said, "And your truth reaches to the clouds." From the so-called clouds God's truth pours out to men as well; for Scripture is accustomed to call the prophets or the angelic powers clouds, since through them God's truth has come down to men. Thus it is said in Isaiah, "And I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it"—that is, upon the Jewish people, figuratively called a vineyard. Further, your righteousness, he says, O Lord, is great and lofty, compared to mountains, and to mountains of God; and besides this, your judgments are incomprehensible. For just as the so-called abyss is boundless and incomprehensible to men—which is what the passage signifies that says, "Placing the deeps in storehouses"—so too your judgments, O Lord, which proceed from your righteousness, are like the great deep. Instead of "Your righteousness is like the mountains of God," Aquila translated, "Your righteousness is like strong mountains." Scripture mentions all these things fittingly, showing that because of God's mercy in heaven, and because of his truth and his righteousness, and because his judgments are incomprehensible "like a great deep," even the ungodly and godless and sinners enjoy not only life but also the other things supplied by his love for mankind. Hence it adds, "Men and beasts you will save, O Lord, as you have multiplied your mercy, O God." For because of your judgments, which are like a great deep, and because of your righteousness and your truth in heaven, men and beasts alike are saved; so greatly have you multiplied your mercy, O God, that not only those who are worthy share in the life that comes from you, but also the brutish and senseless among men. For since many find fault and accuse, asking, "Why do the ungodly prosper and enjoy God's good things?", he necessarily teaches that God is rich in mercy. But if there were only mercy and love for mankind, nothing would prevent anyone from pursuing the life of sinners; so he teaches that truth and righteousness are mingled with the mercy, since righteousness and truth will lay hold of sinners after the mercy. For if they are not benefited by God's mercy and patience, his righteousness and truth will pursue them, for they will be subjected to a just judgment. For God's judgments are indeed, indeed unspeakable; a great and boundless depth—or, as Scripture says, a great abyss—is contained in the account of his judgments. These things, then, await the ungodly. "But the sons of men will hope under the shelter of your wings. They will be drunk with the fatness of your house, and you will give them to drink from the torrent of your delight. For with you is the fountain of life; in your light we shall see light." Since your judgments are

a great deep, it is fitting that you provide not only for men but also for beasts; so greatly have you multiplied your mercy, O God. But beyond these there is also a special order, those named after the ones already mentioned, the sons of men, who, having something more than the men and beasts saved by you, are counted worthy to hope under the shelter of your wings; or, according to Symmachus, "Under the shadow of your wings they are free from care." For those who have hoped in you and are set apart from the order of those who have been censured, you, God, yourself surround and shelter with your own wings. And since these have hoped a good hope—and "hope does not put to shame"—"they will be drunk with the fatness of your house, and you will give them to drink from the torrent of your delight." The house of God is his Church; the fatness of the house is the divinely inspired readings; the drunkenness is the sober and temperate benefit gained from the readings; and the torrent of delight, from which those who have hoped under the shelter of his wings are given to drink, is the river in the Church of God, of which it is said, "The rushing streams of the river gladden the city of God," and, "The river of God is filled with water." And Christ is a torrent of delight because his appearance among men was for a time. "For with you is the fountain of life." We have come to know that Christ is life from the teaching of the Gospel, in which the Savior himself teaches, saying, "I am the light and the truth and the life"; and also, "What came into being in him was life, and the life was the light of men." Hence here too light is joined to life, in harmony with the Gospel; for after saying, "For with you is the fountain of life," it adds, "In your light we shall see light." For this life is the giver of rational light; hence it is said, "And the life was the light of men." Those who partake of these things will at the end have the sight of the light. "Extend your mercy to those who know you, and your righteousness to the upright in heart." To those who do not know him, mercy will be only for a time; but to those who know you, O Savior, extend your mercy and your righteousness, by which, judging according to desert, you will repay some according to their works and make good your promises to others. Instead of "and your righteousness to the upright in heart," Symmachus rendered, "and your compassion to the simple in heart." "Let not the foot of pride come against me, and let not the hand of sinners shake me. There the workers of iniquity fell; they were thrust out and will not be able to stand." Nor may I acquire the hand and the deeds of sinners; for these are wont to shake and dislodge from their standing with you, O God, those who will be thrust out into the outer darkness. Instead of "There they fell," Symmachus rendered, "where the workers of injustice fall." For may I not be there, he says, where those who have been shaken fall, and having fallen are thrust out, and having been thrust out will never again be able to return. Fittingly

he said these things, after describing what the end will be of those who have hoped in the shelter of God, taking up again the memory of the transgressor mentioned at the beginning, who said within himself that he would sin, and of those like him. [?] PSALM XXXVI.

OF DAVID [?]. "Do not be provoked by evildoers, nor envy those who work iniquity." Since in that psalm he brought in the transgressor urging himself on to sins, and described the life of such a man and the end of his overthrow, it follows that in the present one he exhorts us to flee the ways of transgressors and not to emulate deeds like theirs. Since being provoked is different from envying, you will say that to be stirred up and roused to jealousy is what being provoked means. Hence Aquila translated, "Do not contend among evildoers," and Symmachus, "Do not quarrel with wrongdoers." You will also understand what is said from this passage: "They provoked me to jealousy with what is no god, they angered me with their idols; and I will provoke them to jealousy with what is no nation; with a foolish nation I will anger them." So too the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, said, "Or do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?" But to envy, or emulate, is to want to have for oneself the good that one thinks one's neighbor has. And emulation is in itself neither good nor bad; for often it is the zeal of which the same Apostle says, "They are zealous for you, not rightly, but they want to shut you out." Envy, then, could never be good, for it is grief at a neighbor's prosperity; but zeal is sometimes good, as we have explained. Here, then, according to Aquila the passage exhorts us not to contend among evildoers; according to Symmachus, not to quarrel with wrongdoers; according to the fifth edition, not to be stirred up among evildoers; and according to the Seventy: "Do not be exasperated," he says, "nor stirred up when you see others doing evil; nor let the wicked who prosper rouse you to want to prosper as they do." For they, prospering and living in luxury, provoke you; but do not be provoked or exasperated. Nor envy those who work iniquity, nor call them blessed and think them well off, nor pray that you too may fare as they do. "For like grass they will quickly wither." Then he teaches the reason, saying that their end is like that of grass, which flowers for a little while and quickly withers. "For all flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass. The grass has withered, and the flower has fallen." And also, "like green herbs they will quickly fall away"; they are not even worthy to be compared to cultivated herbs. Why then is it worth envying these, who having flowered for a little while are tomorrow thrown into the oven, as the Savior taught? "Hope in the Lord, and do kindness, and dwell in the land, and you will be fed upon its wealth. Delight in the Lo-

[?] your." Having turned us away from envy of the wicked with the first words, he immediately sets beside them the right and royal road, showing how one should walk. Hence he says: Look up, O man, fixing your gaze on the helmsman of the universe and making him your hope; take courage, as one moored to a great anchor. Let your mind hold this hope; and in your actions work and do kindness, as if sowing seed for yourself toward a good harvest of fruits. Once you have acquired these two, have no more anxiety about anything. Dwell in the land free of care, and pass this temporary life as in a tent, staying only a little while. For you will be shepherded like a good sheep tended by a good shepherd. For if there is any true wealth of soul among men—that found in divine doctrines and in the teachings of the divine readings—you will enjoy it, so as to say, "The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing." For you will lack nothing, being shepherded in the wealth of the good shepherd, which has been given to men who are still shepherded on earth. Instead of "and you will be fed upon its wealth," Symmachus rendered, "and be shepherded continually," and Aquila, "and feed on faithfulness." Then, just as he described the end of evildoers and of those who work iniquity, so too for you who hope in the Lord and do kindness he enumerates all the good things that will be yours. First, you will be shepherded upon the true wealth of the good shepherd; second, you will delight in the Lord; and third, he will give you the requests of your heart. The one who will be able to delight in the Lord is he who has purified the senses of his soul, so as to be able to eat the living bread and his life-giving flesh, and to drink his saving blood. Nourished and fattened by these, enjoying the divine intoxication: "Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the requests of your heart." For even from now on you will delight in him, having resolved to give yourself to him. And he will give you also the things to come, which you await to receive. For he who has given the present things will lavishly bestow also "what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered the heart of man." Instead of "Submit to the Lord and entreat him," Aquila says, "Be silent before the Lord and wait eagerly for him," and Symmachus, "Be still before the Lord and entreat him." For one who does what has been said and hopes for what has been described should keep quiet for the present and await in silence what has been promised. "Do not be provoked by the one who prospers in his way, by a man who commits transgressions. Cease from anger and forsake wrath; do not be provoked so as to do evil. For evildoers will be destroyed, but those who wait for the Lord, they will inherit the land." He necessarily takes up the subject again. For since you have learned, he says, what wealth is stored up for you, do not be provoked by the man who commits transgressions and is thought

to prosper in the present life. Do not be exasperated, nor call such a man blessed, knowing well that wrath awaits him on the day of wrath and of the just judgment of God. Therefore do not be angry or enraged at the ungodly man who seems to prosper, nor envy him so as to want to do evil as he does; for know well and be fully persuaded that the end of evildoers is ruin. For evildoers will be destroyed, but only the long-suffering who wait for the Lord, they will inherit the land. For if there is any good land promised to the saints, those who wait for the Lord will inherit it; for along with the other good things enumerated, this inheritance too will be given them. And if there is a Jerusalem in the heavens and a heavenly Mount Zion of God, it follows that the land promised to the worthy should also be understood as heavenly. "And yet a little while, and the sinner will be no more." He explains what was said above: "For like grass they will quickly wither, and like green herbs they will quickly fall away" he explains by "Yet a little while, and the sinner will be no more; and you will seek his place and will not find it"; and "Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the requests of your heart" he renders more clearly by "But the meek will inherit the land, and will delight in abundance of peace." For he shows how one will delight in the Lord by saying that abundance of peace is with him, the abundance of peace that those who have delighted in the Lord will enjoy. Through these words Scripture clearly teaches that some other good land will be given to the meek, and refers the delight and the abundance of peace to the life to come. For he was not unaware that in this present life the righteous will die just as sinners do, so that it could be said of them too, "Yet a little while, and the righteous will be no more, and you will seek his place and will not find it"; for they too die just as sinners do. Nor would he have said of this present earth, "The meek will inherit the land," when he clearly saw that Moses, the meekest of all, had long since departed from among men and been released from this present earth. "The sinner will watch the righteous man and gnash his teeth at him." [?] both the uprisings of the ungodly against the righteous and the ends of both orders. For not content with his own offenses, he says, the sinner cannot bear to see the righteous man worshiping God; for he regards the other's life as a reproof of his own depravity. Hence he says, "He is grievous to us even to behold"; and so he watches for how he may bring him down. But the righteous man takes no notice, nor does he know of the plots secretly devised against him; while the all-seeing Lord, foreseeing the fall of the one who plans these things, laughs at his schemes. And for the time being he does no more than laugh at him as he vainly devises such things; but when he proceeds to deeds, having sharpened his swords so as to plot even to the death against the one who for God's sake [?] pover-

…to the one who has taken up poverty and want and attains the highest philosophy, then the Lord, who long ago laughed at them, turns their sword against their own heart and breaks the bows that the ungodly bent against the righteous. For he will pursue them, no longer laughing at what they plot, but bringing the fitting justice to bear against them. That these are not mere words, but true deeds borne witness to by the events themselves, the experience of what has happened has proved to us who are now setting them out. With our own eyes we have seen how sinners, in the persecutions against us, drew the sword against the righteous; how they bent their bows to bring down the poor and needy and to slaughter the upright in heart; and how they did so, bringing down and killing, by various kinds of death, the holy martyrs who showed manly courage for God. And just as we witnessed these things, so too we have seen the justice of God that pursued them, and it was such that one would not be wrong to say truly that their sword had entered their own heart and their bows had been broken. "Better is a little for the righteous." This was not only foretold but has been fulfilled in deeds, at other times as well. The righteous man in his poverty is content with little, having been taught to say in prayer, "Give us today our daily bread"; but the sinner, overflowing with wealth, thinks it the enjoyment of some good. "But I," he says, "know well, and I teach others too, that the righteous man who receives his daily bread from God is far better off than the sinners with their wealth." If you ask why, learn the reason: the one who is content with little has the Lord to uphold his soul, his life and his livelihood, and the Lord suffices him beyond all wealth; but the arms of sinners do not stay strong, nor is their wealth secure, for very soon they will be broken off like green herbs and wither like grass. "The Lord knows the ways of the blameless, and their inheritance will be forever. They will not be put to shame in an evil time, and in days of famine they will be satisfied, for the sinners will perish." For of those in the right-hand rank, I mean the righteous, God not only upholds their life but also knows exactly the days that await them in the age to come, and the inheritance prepared for them, of which we spoke above. So the brevity and pain of the present life will do them no harm at all, nor will being poor and needy for the Lord's sake. For their endurance is a training ground for their will, and by it, traveling the narrow and hard way, they will obtain what has been promised. In place of "knows," Symmachus rendered, "The Lord foreknows the days of the blameless." And something else that is great will be theirs: in an evil time they will not be put to shame, and in days of famine they will be sat-

-isfied. The evil time is the time of wrath against the ungodly, in which the one group will experience the righteous judgment of God, while those of the right-hand rank, who seek eternal life, will receive glory and honor and incorruption. And not only then: in the present time as well, the righteous will be satisfied as they enjoy divine food, while sinners will perish from famine and from lack of spiritual food. Who, having seen with his own eyes the ungodly of our day, admired for their wealth, glory and high offices, and ruling over great nations, suddenly fall from their height, would not confess that the oracle speaks the truth when it says: "But the enemies of God, as soon as they were glorified and exalted, vanished; like smoke they vanished"? Smoke is the sign of a fire that has been put out. That is why the illustration likens these men too to it: for a season they blazed like a fire, and then they were extinguished. "The sinner borrows and will not repay, but the righteous has compassion and gives." Possessing nothing, the sinner often borrows useful and saving words from the righteous, or receives benefits from God, yet he does not repay the debt. For having been benefited, he ought to offer works and deeds worthy of what he received. But he does not repay, and he remains barren of the works of righteousness. The righteous, however, rich in the wealth that is according to God, has compassion and provides for those in need. Moreover, those who bless the righteous will become his fellow heirs. For the very inheritance that the word promised to the righteous above, it also promises to those who bless the righteous, in keeping with the oracle to Abraham that said, "And I will bless those who bless you." And the words "And those who curse him will be destroyed" would be like what was said to Abraham: "And those who curse you I will curse." For just as one who throws a stone up high throws it on his own head, so the one who pelts the righteous with curses will receive the curse turned back upon himself, since a curse cannot stand against the righteous. "A man's steps are directed by the Lord." In addition to what has been said, the man of God has this as well: God makes his ways smooth, so that his life runs well and he worships God unhindered, with no one tripping him up, because of the One who directs his steps and makes his way worthy of acceptance; hence it is said, "And he will delight in his way." "When he falls he will not be dashed down, for the Lord supports his hand." And even if it should ever happen that he slips and falls, and in a time of temptation he slips, buckles and falls into some sin, still he will not be dashed down; rather, like a noble athlete who is overpowered and gives way a little, at once he himself…
"I was younger, and indeed I have grown old, and I have not seen a righteous man forsaken, nor his

seed seeking bread." But I have examined the life of the righteous from childhood to old age: there has never been a single time when the righteous man was left desolate; he always has his own Lord at his side as helper. Therefore he says, "I was younger," or, according to Symmachus, "I was young, but I have also grown old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread." And indeed, how could the seed of the righteous come to lack bread, when he himself, through the wealth supplied to him by God, "is merciful and lends all day long"? You will understand this in its deeper sense when you learn that, having received the talents from the master of the house and the mina from the Lord, he puts them to use in trade, obeying the one who said, "You ought to have put my money in the bank." "The words of the Lord are pure words, silver refined by fire, tested for the earth." So the one who is devoted to the practice of the divine words, and has gathered much spiritual wealth, knows nothing else to do but to be merciful and to lend all day long. According to Aquila, "all day long he gives and lends": to some he gives, to others he lends. Doctrines and contemplations he gives to the souls of those able to receive them; but what lies in the ethical commandments he lends, so that those who receive it may pay back the fruit of the loan through their works. So also you will hear Moses promising those who keep the divine laws, "You will lend to many nations, but you will not borrow." And it was in this way that the divine apostles lent to many nations, and Paul above all. For this reason those who were their disciples, being their seed, were never in want of bread, since they had those who supplied them with spiritual food, and by partaking of it they were filled with blessings. Hence it was said, "And his seed will be for a blessing." And even according to the bare letter, if one considers how the Savior said, "And in this age he will receive a hundredfold," and sees the word fulfilled in actual deeds through his disciples, he will see how the righteous man is merciful and lends all day long. For if all the believers were of one soul and one heart, and no one said that anything was his own, but all things were held in common, and all who owned property sold it and laid the proceeds at the feet of the apostles, and they distributed to each as anyone had need, it is clear how these were merciful and lent all day long. "Turn away from evil and do good." When you have freed yourself from all wickedness (for this is in your power, and if you will it, you can), you will still not be perfect for having done this, unless the second thing is also present in you, and that is doing good. For besides not stealing, you should also share your possessions with those in need; besides not being greedy, there is something more, namely doing good to those in need; and besides keeping away from wickedness, you should also rescue others from wickedness. When you have done these things, "dwell," it says, "forever and ever." In place of which

Symmachus rendered, "And you will be at rest forever." For this end, eternal life, awaits you. For the Lord, being a judge, loves judgment, and he will not forsake his holy ones but will keep them safe forever. "The lawless will be punished, and the seed of the ungodly will be destroyed. But the righteous will inherit the earth and dwell upon it forever and ever." In keeping with what was said before, he teaches that the lawless, who did not keep the commandment, will pay an eternal penalty; and just as the seed of the righteous was said to be for a blessing, so the seed of the ungodly will be destroyed. But the righteous will inherit the land promised to the meek, and will dwell in it forever and ever. The word announces these things many times on purpose, confirming the promises by repeating them, and wanting us to dwell on these same words and meditate on them, chewing them like spiritual food so that they may be well digested and nourish our soul. "The mouth of the righteous will meditate wisdom, and his tongue will speak judgment. The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps will not be tripped. The sinner watches the righteous and seeks to put him to death. But the Lord will not abandon him into his hands, nor condemn him when he is judged." Continuing the exhortation of his discourse, he urges us to become imitators of the righteous man by listing his riches. For besides what has been said, he has this too: God has granted him, a mere man, a great gift, the knowledge of true wisdom. For wisdom is the knowledge of things divine and human, and it is that through which all things came to be, for "he made all things in wisdom." And this is the Word, who in the beginning was with God and was God, through whom all things came to be. God therefore sent down to humankind its utterances, words and teachings, so that the righteous man might not be idle, inactive and destitute of good things, but that his mouth might at the same time have the meditation of heavenly wisdom. Partaking of it as of heavenly food, he first strengthens his own soul, and then supplies others as well. Hence it was said, "The mouth of the righteous will meditate wisdom, and his tongue will speak judgment." Knowing that "the law of God is spiritual," and delighting "in the law of God according to the inner man," he has received into his very heart the contemplation of the law and the depth of the mysteries in it; and through this discipline his steps will not be tripped, since it was said above as well that his steps are directed by the Lord. And if ever a sinner, envious of his progress, should plot his death, he will be called a fool for attempting the impossible. For his great protector will not abandon him into his hands, nor condemn him when he is judged. Symmachus has, "Nor will he condemn him when he is on trial."

"I saw the ungodly highly exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon." So he says that in the present he has come to know the end of the ungodly by experience: "I have not heard by hearsay, from others telling of things that happened long ago; I saw it myself," he says, "blasphemous and godless men admired by all, lifted up and haughty, thinking they would go on living forever. But while I was still reasoning with myself how these men, ungodly as they were, had obtained so much, I wished to look at them a second time and lifted up my eyes; and they were nowhere, but had suddenly vanished. Then, wishing to find some trace or remnant of them, I could not even find the place where they had seemed to stand." Therefore, since such is their end, you who are being taught, flee this way of the ungodly: wash away all wickedness from yourself and love the straight way. For a remnant and a good hope remain for the one who has pursued peace and friendship with God, and so has become a man of peace. According to Symmachus, he says, "Keep simplicity and look at what is upright, for there are things to come for the man of peace."

PSALM 37, OF DAVID. For remembrance. "Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath." The sixth psalm begins with the very same words, syllable for syllable, and the rest of the sixth is also akin to what is found in the present one. But in the sixth the superscription read, "For the end, in hymns, concerning the eighth, a psalm of David," whereas in the present one there is none of this, only "a psalm of David, for remembrance." Yet the addition "for remembrance" seems to send us back to the superscription of the sixth, so that the present psalm is also "for the end," "in hymns" and "concerning the eighth," since "for remembrance" would point to all of these. But since, in going through the sixth, we said what occurred to us about its superscription, we too will refer the reader to the remembrance of what was said there. It seems to me that David, having confessed the sin he had committed in many places and in various ways, set apart the present psalm specially for himself as a remembrance, so as always and continually to have it on his lips, and that he used it like a healing charm for the cure of his soul. So he sends up a supplication to God, by which he turns away the wrath that hangs over all who sin and propitiates the good Lord with words of overwhelming confession. In saying, "Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger," he does not refuse rebuke, but rebuke with anger; nor does he flee discipline, but discipline with wrath. It is as if a man under a physician's care, who was applying cautery, the knife and bitter antidotes to treat his illness, were to say, "Do not treat me with fire, nor with the knife and incisions, but with gentle and milder medicines." Such a man does not refuse

the treatment, but the painful manner of the remedies. It has often been said that when "anger" and "wrath" of God are spoken of in the divinely inspired Scriptures, they do not signify passions in God, for the Divine is foreign to every passion. Rather, the language of Scripture is accustomed to use such terms metaphorically, just as it speaks of God's eyes, ears, hands, fingers, feet and other members. These are usefully arranged with human beings in view, as Scripture comes down to the infancy of its hearers. In the same way, then, it depicts the punishments brought upon sinners by God's judgment, which are grim and painful to those who suffer them, as though they were brought on out of anger and wrath. The holy Apostle teaches this when he says: "By your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will repay each according to his works." It is as if someone were to call the punishments that the law holds over a murderer "anger" and "wrath": not that the law is truly angry and wrathful, but that the one being punished takes the penalty to be the law's wrath. Moreover, the evil demons who carry out punishments against the ungodly, and other such ministering powers of God, have been called wrath and anger. Thus it is said in the account of the ten plagues brought upon the Egyptians: "He sent upon them anger and wrath, a mission by evil angels." In the same way, what is supplied to the worthy through the right-hand and good powers has been called the right hand of God. David therefore implores that he not be rebuked by evil powers, nor disciplined by a mission of grim angels, but by saving words and beneficial teachings. And in another sense he entreats that he not be kept for the day of wrath and revelation and righteous judgment of God, but that here and now, in the present life, before his death, he may wash away his sins. And he attained his aim, for he evidently paid the penalty through what he suffered before his death, as we have learned from the history of the Kingdoms. Besides, he punished himself, subjecting himself to all kinds of afflictions in the ways he made his confession. And he speaks in yet another sense: "If I have done something for which I deserve to be rebuked in anger, yet, since I have repented, I beg to be rebuked by reason and not by anger, and to be disciplined by teaching and not by wrath." "For your arrows have been fixed in me." Job, the athlete, who endured trials of every kind, was not ignorant of where these things came from; that is why he said, "For the arrows of the Lord are in my mouth, and their fury drinks up my blood." But David, who was not struck in his body like Job but mortally wounded in his very soul, does not say like Job, "For the arrows of the Lord are in my mouth," but, "For your arrows have been fixed in me, and you have pressed your hand upon me." Job, for his part, mentions the hand of the Lord, saying, "For it is the hand of the Lord that has touched me." And the devil said to the Lord, "Stretch out your hand and touch all that he has"; and again, "Stretch out your hand and touch

his flesh and his bones." But it was a different hand and different arrows that struck Job's flesh and his bodily possessions. Here, since David was sick in his very soul, he indicates that other arrows struck him and another hand of God touched him: as we have already said, the spiritual arrows, or rather the very words of God piercing his soul and punishing his conscience. Or perhaps he also means the devil himself, and the devil's fiery arrows of passion and lust, which [?] him into desire for the wife of Uriah? Of these the Apostle also teaches when he says, "Take up the whole armor of God, so that you can quench all the fiery arrows of the evil one." Just as Job called the devil's arrows, and the sores inflicted on his body, "arrows of the Lord," since it happened by God's permission, saying, "For the arrows of the Lord are in my mouth, and their fury drinks up my blood," so it is likely that here too David spoke of "arrows of the Lord," since it was by the Lord's permission that the adversary made war on him, so that he might learn not to say, "I shall never be shaken." For since, strengthened by the grace of God, he once thought highly of himself, so that he grew presumptuous and said, "But I said in my prosperity, I shall never be shaken," for this reason he was rightly handed over to the tempter, who laid hold of his soul and did him greater harm than he did Job. But if the words of God, which remind us of his righteous judgment and teach of the wrath that hangs over sinners, are sharper than arrows, piercing the conscience, then in this sense too you might say that David, stung by these sacred and divine arrows, has good reason to beg off rebuke in anger. "For the arrows that have struck me from you," he says, "if anger and wrath were added to them, punish me sufficiently and chastise me enough; and your hand too has laid hold of me through one misfortune after another." "There is no healing in my flesh in the face of your wrath; there is no peace in my bones in the face of my sins." "For my flesh, through which I committed the sin, I have handed over to punishments, chastising myself." He showed this elsewhere too, saying, "And I humbled my soul with fasting"; and, "My flesh was changed for lack of oil"; and, "I forgot to eat my bread because of the sound of my groaning"; and other such things. In place of "wrath," Aquila and Symmachus agree in rendering, "in the face of your indignation." "For the stern rebuke from your divine Scriptures was enough for me, and the threat delivered through Nathan." In place of "in the face of my sins," Symmachus rendered, "because of my sins." There is nothing at all strange in calling one's own people "bones." For if we are members of one another, and we have all been reckoned as in one body, the

…he said these things after describing what the end of those who have hoped in the shelter of God will be, taking up again the memory of the lawless man mentioned at the beginning, who said within himself that he would sin, and of those like him: “Do not be provoked by evildoers, nor envy those who do lawlessness.” In that psalm he introduced the lawless man urging himself on into sins, and described both the life of such a man and the end of his overthrow. So, consistently, in the present one he urges us to flee the ways of the lawless and not to envy deeds like theirs. But since “being provoked” (parazēloun) is different from “envying” (zēloun), you will say that to be irritated and roused to jealousy is what “being provoked” means. Hence Aquila translated: “Do not contend [?] with evildoers,” and Symmachus: “Do not quarrel with wrongdoers.” You will also understand the expression from this passage: “They provoked me to jealousy with what is no god, they angered me with their idols; and I will provoke them to jealousy with what is no nation, with a foolish nation I will anger them.” So too the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, said: “Or are we provoking the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?” But “envying,” in the sense of wanting to have for oneself what one thinks one's neighbor has, is good. And “being zealous” is morally neutral, for often there is a zeal of which the same Apostle says: “They are zealous for you, but not rightly; they want to shut you out.” Envy, then, could never be good, for it is grief at a neighbor's prosperity; but zeal is sometimes good, as we have explained. Here, then, according to Aquila, the word urges us not to fight with evildoers; according to Symmachus, not to quarrel among wrongdoers; according to the fifth edition, not to be provoked among evildoers; and according to the Seventy: “Do not be stirred up,” it says, “nor provoked when you see others doing evil; and do not let the wicked who prosper rouse you to want to prosper as they do.” For they, prospering and living in luxury, provoke you; but do not be provoked or stirred up. Nor should you envy those who do lawlessness, nor call them blessed and think them well off, nor pray that you yourself may fare as they do. “For like grass they will quickly wither.” Then he teaches the reason, saying that their end is like that of grass, which blooms for a little while and quickly withers. “For all flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass. The grass withered, and the flower fell.” And again: “Like green herbs they will quickly fall away.” They are not even worthy to be compared with cultivated herbs. Why then should anyone envy these people, who bloom for a little while and tomorrow are thrown into the oven, as the Savior taught? “Hope in the Lord, and do what is good, and dwell in the land, and you will be fed on its wealth. Delight yourself in the Lo-

…[the light] of my eyes had departed from me, and my friends and neighbors had gone far off, they immediately leapt upon me and did violence to my soul. Like malicious men they spoke vain things to me, slipping vain thoughts into my soul within. And enchanting and deceiving me with guile, they baited me as if with good things, dragging me down into sin. “But I, like a deaf man, did not hear, and was like a mute man who does not open his mouth. And I became like a man who does not hear, and who has no reproofs in his mouth.” For to these, he says, I had nothing to say, being filled with shame. I had no word for my defense, nor anything to say to my enemies, having once been conquered by them. Not trusting in myself, nor setting before my eyes any hope other than you, I prescribed for myself the course of healing. Since, then, I hoped in you, Lord, and hope does not put to shame, for this reason you will hear me, because you delight in mercy and do not desire the death of the sinner so much as his repentance. Therefore, having hoped in you, I beg to obtain healing from you. “Lest my enemies rejoice over me”: they have not yet rejoiced completely, but they will rejoice if I do not obtain your mercy. So that my enemies may not rejoice over me, they who earlier, when my feet were shaken, boasted against me, I have fled to you, and I say: May I not be put to shame forever. For I have not been utterly overthrown, nor have I fallen such a fall as those who have become apostates from you.

FOR THE END, FOR IDITHUN, AN ODE OF DAVID. 38. What is said in the present ode bears a close resemblance to what is said in the psalm before it. But David, when he sang that one, composed it as a reminder for himself, whereas this one he now hands on also to others who have suffered as he did, teaching them to emulate and imitate him by making a like confession. Unless, perhaps, the Holy Spirit was teaching David through Idithun to say these things, for Idithun too was counted worthy of the prophetic spirit. We learn from the present words that each person ought to converse with himself, and not wait for teachers from outside, but address his own reason and mind by himself. “I said: I will guard my ways.” At the very time of temptation, he says, when the one who works sin was rising up against me, I said: “I will guard my ways, so as not to sin with my tongue.” And then too “I set a [?] for my mouth [?], and I was struck dumb and humbled, and kept silent from good things.” Symmachus translated it this way: “I said: I will guard my ways, so as not to sin through my tongue. I will guard my mouth with a muzzle while the ungodly man is still opposite me. I became speechless in silence; I kept silent, not being in a good state.” Do you see how he taught the reason why he did not dare to open his mouth, saying, “And I kept silent from good things,” or, according to

…of his flesh and of his bones. But it was a different hand and different arrows that struck Job's flesh and his bodily possessions. Here, since David had fallen sick in his very soul, the text signifies that different arrows struck him and a different hand of God touched him, as we said before: rational arrows, or rather the very words of God piercing his soul and punishing his very conscience. Or perhaps it signifies the devil himself and the devil's fiery arrows, the arrows of passion and lust that set him burning with desire for Uriah's wife? Of these the Apostle also teaches, saying: “Take up the whole armor of God, so that you may be able to quench all the fiery arrows of the evil one.” Job called the devil's arrows, and the sores inflicted on his body, arrows of the Lord, since they came about by God's permission, saying: “For the arrows of the Lord are in my body [?]; their fury drinks up my blood.” In the same way it is likely that David here too spoke of arrows of the Lord, since it was by the Lord's permission that the adversary made war on him, so that he might learn not to say: “I shall never be shaken.” For once, strengthened by the grace of God, he thought highly of himself, so that he grew arrogant and said: “But I said in my prosperity: I shall never be shaken.” For this reason he was rightly handed over to the tempter, who laid hold of his soul and harmed him more than he harmed Job. But the words of God, which remind us of his righteous judgment and teach of the wrath hanging over sinners, are sharper than arrows and pierce the conscience. So you might also say that David, stung by these holy and divine arrows, reasonably begs to be spared rebuke in anger. For the arrows from you that have struck me, he says, if they also take on wrath and anger, punish me more than enough, and I have had enough of misfortunes one after another [?]. “There is no healing in my flesh because of your wrath; there is no peace in my bones because of my sins.” For I have handed over my flesh, through which I committed the sin, to punishments, chastising myself. He showed this in other places too, saying: “And I humbled my soul with fasting”; and, “My flesh was changed for lack of oil”; and, “I forgot to eat my bread because of my groaning”; and other such things. Instead of “wrath,” Aquila and Symmachus agree in translating: “because of your indignation.” For the stern rebuke from your divine Scriptures was enough for me, and the threat delivered in person through Nathan. Instead of “because of my sins” (literally, “from the face of my sins”), Symmachus translated: “on account of my sins.” And there is nothing absurd in calling one's own people “bones.” For if we are members of one another, and we have all been reckoned as one body, [?] [References: Job [?]; Ephesians 6 [?]; Job 6 [?]]

…nothing prevented him from calling “bones” especially those individual members who are most useful. But we say that these things did not happen to the divinely inspired David alone, but to very many others as well; or rather, they still happen to this day when the saints are tested. For unexpected crises often spring up, so that uprisings by one's own people, whom we say are figuratively called “bones,” are harder to bear than war waged by enemies. And if these things are common to all, the manner of prayer would be common to all as well. For it suits everyone who is tested and suffering and longing to obtain gentleness from God. “For my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily on me. My wounds have stunk and festered.” Through these words Scripture teaches us not to hide our own evils, nor to keep our sins in the depth of the soul like some blackness and rot. “All day long I went about gloomy, for my soul was filled with the mockery of mockers.” You can also understand it this way: having indicated beforehand in the title that the psalm is “for remembrance,” he fittingly recounts and takes up again what befell him long ago. He teaches what state he was in when he fell into the slip of sin, for which reason he makes his whole confession. For I came into all these things, he says, since at a certain time “my heart was troubled, and my strength left me, and the light of my eyes, even that was not with me.” For at the time of the sin his mind suffered no small disturbance, confused and darkened by the one who works sin, so that he even fell into folly and did the works of folly. Then too his strength abandoned him, for he was no longer able to say, “I can do all things in him who strengthens me,” having been conquered by passion and lost his strength. And something else grievous happened to me, he says: “the light of my eyes” (this was the prophetic spirit, which enlightened the sight of his [soul]) “even that was not with me,” but had left me and withdrawn; since “wisdom will not enter a soul that devises evil, nor dwell in a body enslaved to sins; for the holy Spirit of instruction will flee deceit and will withdraw from foolish thoughts.” Moreover, his former friends and neighbors, who had been with him all the time, left him and stood far off, no longer able to be with him, but lamenting [?] from afar his misfortune as that of a close friend. Who were these but those who had rejoiced over his former good deeds, namely the good angels and ministers of God, who are accustomed to share in the joy of human salvation? When these had gone far from me, others who work sin came near me, did violence to me and mocked my soul. For they had long been thirsting for my blood, and had been praying for a long time to see my fall; and as if seizing their opportunity, when they saw my strength and the light abandoning me

Symmachus? For since I was not in a good state, nor had any confidence, I remembered the one who says: “You have sinned; be still.” Therefore I kept silent, not being in a good state. And not only was I struck dumb and kept silent from good things, but also “my pain was renewed.” For the pain of my soul, and the wound that arose in me from sin, lying deep within and fixed in my very conscience, was renewed, as the one who had worked the sin rose up against me and reproached me. “My heart grew hot within me.” Remembering the sin, he says, I was burning with the fire of despondency, set ablaze by my conscience itself. “I spoke with my tongue: Lord, make known to me my end.” And after my confession, I ask to learn what kind of end I shall meet. He said these things because he was weighed down, thinking this temporary and mortal life very long because of how burdensome it was. So he longed to have the time of his release made known to him, so that he might take heart once he had received the good news of his freedom from the things of this world and his release from trials. And going on in what follows he said: “I am a sojourner with you and a stranger, like all my fathers.” “Behold, you have made my days handbreadths, and my existence is as nothing before you.” Instead of this Symmachus rendered: “Behold, you have given my days as spans.” Someone else might say that human days are called “handbreadths” (palaistai) because they are full of contest and wrestling (palē) and trials. Next he says: “And my existence is as nothing before you.” Instead of this Aquila translated: “And my decline is as if it did not exist before you,” and Symmachus: “And my life is as nothing in your sight.” For the whole span of a human life, compared with the life of God and with the endless ages, is as nothing before God. That is why it is said elsewhere: “The heavens will perish, but you remain; they will all grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will roll them up, and they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will not fail.” Moreover, all human striving is vanity of vanities, and “all things are vanity, every living man,” or “every man set up,” according to Aquila, or “every man standing,” according to Symmachus. For the one who is now standing, still passing through this mortal life in the present time, would be vanity. Indeed, if no hope of immortality, of eternal life and of the kingdom of heaven, were laid up for human beings, every living man might reasonably have been thought something vain. “And now what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord?” Symmachus rendered the present words thus: “Now then, what do I wait for, Master? My hope is in you. Deliver me from all my transgressions; do not make me a reproach to the fool. I became speechless [?]; I will not [?] open my mouth, for you have done it.” After all that has been said, he says, nothing is left for me, O Lord, but to wait for you and to have my

hopes in you, for the substance of the soul comes from you. Therefore I beg and implore to be set free from the evils of this world and rescued from my iniquities. For once I fell in with a fool, of whom I also spoke above: “When the sinner stood before me, I was struck dumb and humbled, and kept silent from good things.” So, handed over to folly at once, I became a reproach. Fittingly, then, acknowledging the things in which I sinned, I was struck dumb and did not open my mouth, because you had done it. For fear of you made me dumb, striking me for the things in which I had sinned and silencing me so that I would not speak. Instead of “you made me a reproach to the fool,” Aquila says, “do not make me a reproach to one who wastes away”; Symmachus, “do not give me up as a reproach to the fool”; and the fifth edition, “do not give me up as a reproach to the fool.” This shows the entreaty of one who has sinned, imploring not to be handed over to a fool to be reproached. But if the Lord himself hands over the sinner to the fool to be reproached by him, you might say that this too happens for the benefit of the one reproached, so that through affliction he may make a fuller confession of his sins. David asked not to suffer this, since of his own accord he was doing everything that is pleasing to God. “Remove your scourges from me; for I have fainted under the strength of your hand. With rebukes for iniquity you have disciplined man, and you have made his soul melt away like a spider's web; surely every man is vain. Interlude.” In the psalm before this one he offered himself to blows meant to turn him back, like a grateful pupil to his teacher; that is why he said: “I am ready for scourges.” But since by now he had had enough of the scourges that kept tormenting him, he begs that from now on they cease, and that the scourging stop here. And he confesses next, saying: “I have fainted under the strength of your hand.” Of this hand it was also said above: “You have pressed your hand upon me.” Then he teaches that the hand did not discipline in vain, nor scourge to no purpose, but for the benefit of the one who had sinned. Therefore he says: “With rebukes for iniquity you have disciplined man.” For on account of the iniquity committed, and because of the sin committed, you rebuked the one being disciplined and brought on him both the scourges and your hand mentioned before. And by these very things you made the soul of the one being disciplined melt away, humbled and wasted for its own benefit. For when he was living in luxury he slipped into sins, as it is written: “Jacob ate and drank, and the beloved one kicked; he grew broad and fat, and departed from God who nourished him.” Therefore, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord, the flesh has been handed over to destruction; and as the flesh is punished, the soul melts away, wasting like a spider's web. That is why he says, “And you made his soul melt away like a spider's web,” and adds, “Surely every man is vain,” once again lamenting the man who toils and suffers aimlessly and in vain in this life.

“Hear my prayer, Lord, and my supplication; give ear to my tears. Do not keep silent, for I am a sojourner on the earth and a stranger, like all my fathers.” Here he confesses that he is a sojourner and a stranger. He knows of another life of refreshment, which he longs to obtain, saying: “Let me be, that I may be refreshed.” So it was not in vain that he called every man a sojourner. He sends up his supplication with weeping and tears, knowing well that “Blessed are those who weep, for they will laugh,” and “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.” And he describes his own good deeds, adding: “For I am a sojourner and a stranger, like all my fathers.” It is a rare man who can, in imitation of the God-loving fathers and the prophets of God, pass this temporary life not as a resident but as a sojourner.
