It was in this that the present speaker took pride, regarding human life as a sojourn and an exile. “Let me be, that I may be refreshed before I depart and am no more.” Instead of this Symmachus says: “Withdraw from me, that I may smile before I depart and am not.” For if, he says, I do not smile here, my tears turned into laughter by your grace, and if in this present life you do not release me from my sin and forgive what I have done, so that I may recover myself and be refreshed, then once I am released from this temporary life there is no time left for repentance. And if I do not obtain forgiveness, I shall no longer exist in the life that is with you; but, cast away, I shall be like those who go down into the pit. Therefore I implore you from here, saying: “Do not keep silent toward me, lest you keep silent toward me and I become like those who go down into the pit.”

FOR THE END. OF DAVID. 39. “I waited patiently for the Lord, and he paid heed to me.” Affliction produces endurance, and endurance proven character, and proven character hope; and hope does not put to shame. Fittingly, then, the righteous man does not merely endure, but, holding his hope firm and not despairing of the salvation that comes from God, he persists in endurance. Even if he prays and is not heard at once, still he waits in hope and perseveres in supplications and prayers. And if he should ever fall into error, as David did, he confesses that he is not ignorant of the evils he has come into. And if after this he recovers himself, aware of his error, he will give thanks, recognizing from what depth of misery he has been drawn up by the one who became the physician and savior of his soul. Therefore he will say: “He brought me up out of the pit of misery and out of the miry clay.” He will obtain this because he waited patiently for the Lord. You would not be wrong to say that the “pit of misery” is the depth of sin, and the “miry clay” the pleasures of the body made of clay, into which the soul slips and is plunged, and as it were sunk in the deep. So the one who has risen out of these, drawn up by the right hand of the Savior, then from that point on, with pure reason, the [?] of the soul

…having set his foundations firm, he will rightly say: “And he brought me up out of the pit of misery and out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and directed my steps.” He calls the firm foundation of the word a “rock,” in contrast to the mire. Standing on it, he will say: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine?” and so on. And God did not only set his feet on the rock; he also makes him walk and run on it, as he wins approval for good deeds. That is why he adds: “And he directed my steps.” Then, as one changed from worse to better, he lays aside the old song, in which he lamented the things spoken in the psalms before this one, and takes up a new song to the One who saved him and put a new song and hymn into his mouth. For he has stripped off the old self with its deeds and put on the new self, which is being renewed in the knowledge of God. After all this he becomes an example to many, so that others too, seeing his change, may take up good hopes and make the same change from worse to better. That is why he says: “Many will see and fear, and will hope in the Lord.” And what will they see? “This very thing,” he says: “that I came into the depths of evils, into the pit and the miry clay; and that, drawn up from there by God’s grace, I stood upon the rock, my steps were directed, and I was counted worthy of a new song.” When the many see these things, they will take up the fear of God, of which it is said, “The fear of God is the beginning of wisdom,” and will sketch out a like hope for themselves. “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who has not looked to vanities and false frenzies.” One who has come to know God’s grace by experience proclaims to all the benefits done to him. From what has happened to him he draws a general statement, teaching that all people can obtain the same things he did. “For I am not the only one,” he says, “who could be blessed because I was counted worthy of such things. The same road lies open to all, not to some and closed to others. So no one who sets his hope on God will fall short of the blessedness that I too was counted worthy of.” “Vanities” and “false frenzies” are all the pursuits that busy themselves with things temporary and vain, since “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.” Earlier it was also said: “Surely all things are vanity, every man living,” and again: “Surely they are disquieted in vain. He heaps up treasure and does not know for whom he will gather it.” “False frenzies” are the cares that the many pursue for empty and vain ends. There is, by contrast, a sober frenzy: the rising above the present life, on account of which the many thought God’s prophets were out of their minds. The righteous man takes pride in such ecstasy, saying: “But I said in my ecstasy, Every man is a liar.” And the Apostle, having experienced this, said: “For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you.”

“Many are the wonders you have done, O Lord my God.” Someone who has perceived the manifold wisdom of God in creatures both universal and particular, both those perceived by the senses and those contemplated by the mind, would be struck with amazement at the surpassing power of the God of all things. He would then say: “Many are the wonders you have done, O Lord my God.” And once he has also examined the principles of universal providence by which God governs all things, and found them incomprehensible, he will add: “And in your thoughts there is no one who will be likened to you.” Such was the one who said: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how inscrutable his ways!” In the present passage David uttered these words at the right moment. He had learned by experience that he had been saved in a new way, namely through obedience to the divine oracles. For in former times, through Moses, sacrifices and whole burnt offerings were commanded to be offered for sins; but now a new way of salvation is handed down, apart from sacrifices and whole burnt offerings. He also teaches that there are countless remedies for salvation, which the grace of God has given to human beings, and that no one can speak worthily of the multitude of God’s thoughts or grasp it with the mind. Symmachus renders it: “Very many are the marvels you have done, O Lord my God, and your thoughts on our behalf cannot be set out before you.” Then, where we read “I declared and I spoke; they were multiplied beyond the sand,” Symmachus again translated it this way: “If I should declare and announce them, they are more than can be recounted.” For “we know in part,” he says, “and we prophesy in part. All your wonders are beyond number and beyond comprehension. But among the things I have grasped, I found this too: that in the present time you did not want the sacrifices and offerings under Moses. In their place you prepared my ears and the obedience to your oracles, and in place of whole burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin, I brought myself to you.” That is why he says: “Behold, I come,” having been called by you and having obeyed most eagerly. “I have come, hastening to do your will; for I am persuaded that you accept this in place of every whole burnt sacrifice.” “And this is written about me in the heading of the scroll.” And what is this, if not to prefer your will to sacrifices and whole burnt offerings? “And to do your law”: not according to its obvious wording, nor keeping the commands given through Moses as the many do, but “in the midst of my belly,” or, as Symmachus has it, “I was eager for your law within my inmost parts.” For there is a belly of the soul, so named figuratively, of which it is said in the Gospels: “Rivers of living water will flow from his belly, springing up to eternal life.” “In this secret and hidden chamber of the soul,” he says, “I willed to do your law, and to carry out the commandments about sacrifices and burnt

offerings spiritually and according to their inner sense. For I knew that these things are dear to you, and far better than what was handed down to the Jews in bodily form.” “I have proclaimed the good news of righteousness in the great congregation; behold, I will not restrain my lips; O Lord, you know. I have not hidden your righteousness in my heart; I have spoken of your truth and your salvation.” By “truth” he means the truth that stands in contrast to the shadow. You may also understand it this way. Blessed David promises to proclaim in the great Church, gathered by divine grace throughout the whole world, the righteousness of God, the truth of prophecy, the admirable salvation and the measureless mercy. And the assembly of the faithful themselves could also say these words, promising to make a return for their salvation by running together to the church, moving their lips in hymnody, proclaiming God’s just judgment, recounting his ineffable care, and showing the truth of the prophetic promises. “But you, O Lord, do not remove your compassion far from me; your mercy and your truth have upheld me continually.” Even after obtaining salvation, the Church of God needs the same providential care again, because of the many kinds of attack from men and demons, which it mentions in what follows: “For evils without number have surrounded me; my iniquities have overtaken me, and I could not see. They are multiplied beyond the hairs of my head, and my heart has failed me.” Let no one think these words unsuited to the interpretation given. For the three youths too, though they had attained the height of virtue and put on the victor’s crown, prayed in the furnace and said: “We have sinned, we have transgressed, we have done wrong, and we have turned away from your commandments and have not kept your ordinances.” So did the wonderful Daniel, so the inspired Jeremiah, so the divine Isaiah, so the most wise Paul: “For Christ came into the world,” he says, “to save sinners, of whom I am the first”; and again: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle.” In the same way, then, the Church of God here, pounded by the billows of the impious, does not think highly of itself for its struggles. Instead it attributes what has happened to its sins and offences, and asks to receive help from the Saviour. Besides, the Church of God is not made up entirely of the perfect. It also contains those who live at their ease, who embrace a slack way of life and choose to be slaves to pleasures. And since it is one body, both kinds of words are uttered as though by one person. You may also understand it this way. Since no one should be called blessed before his death, the Apostle rightly does not hesitate to say, though he was an apostle, called and chosen by Christ Jesus: “I pummel my body and bring it into subjection, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified.” The same is true of

David. Though he had shown it in many things, had found God ready to hear him, and had been set free from the pit of misery and the miry clay; though he now stood in safety, with his feet planted as if on a rock; though he had been counted worthy of a new song, that is, of the true word about sacrifices, the proclamation announced as good news to the great Church of God (for this was the new song of which he said above, “And he put a new song into my mouth”); nevertheless, though he had obtained so much, he takes up the words of supplication again because human life is so frail, and he entreats and begs to be guarded by the grace and mercy of God. For by these words he called back to mind and went over the evils that had happened to him before. Indeed, the memory of old evils makes us more careful not to fall again into the same [?] … the memory of his former iniquities, and he teaches [?] that his iniquities had poured like a mist over the seeing faculty of the mind. The rest follows from what was said before: “Be pleased, O Lord, to deliver me; O Lord, make haste to help me. Let those who seek my soul to take it away be put to shame and confounded together. Let those who wish me evil be turned back and put to shame. Let those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done!’ receive their shame at once.” Even now he senses many enemies around him pressing hard upon his soul, and he sends up this prayer concerning them. For they do not stop envying even those who are already perfect and stand upon the rock. So he asks to be rescued from the things just mentioned, and that those who seek out his soul to take it away be put to shame and confounded, while he himself is fenced about by God’s right hand. Those who seek the soul of the righteous man are confounded and disgraced (for so Symmachus rendered it) when, after devising every scheme against him, they achieve nothing. Then, having been able to do nothing, they give up and go away, covered with shame. That is why, after their disgrace, their shame and their confusion, he adds: “Let those who wish me evil be turned back and confounded.” For though they had been able to do nothing, and yet [?] (1) Read ἀνεπόλει.

kept devising plots against him, expecting to get the better of him each time, they would say: “Well done, well done!” “But since they have said this so often,” he says, “by your grace let them at last be gone, carrying away their own shame.”

FOR THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID. 40. “Blessed is he who considers the poor and needy; in the evil day the Lord will deliver him. May the Lord preserve him and give him life, and make him blessed on the earth, and not hand him over to the will of his enemies. May the Lord help him on his bed of pain; you have turned all his bed in his sickness.” Going on, the text then adds: “For even the man of my peace, in whom I hoped, who ate my bread, has made great his tripping against me.” Our Saviour and Lord is recorded in the Gospel according to John as having said these words as though in his own person, in his discourse to the disciples, where he said: “Truly, truly, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his master, nor is one who is sent greater than the one who sent him. If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them. I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But this is so that the Scripture may be fulfilled: He who eats my bread has lifted up his heel against me.” No other Scripture is found that says this; only the present one, in which it is said: “He who eats my bread has made great his tripping against me.” It is time, then, to take what the psalm contains as spoken prophetically of his person. That is why it is also headed “For the end”: it directs us either to the consummation of the age, at which what was written was being fulfilled, or to the last of the events the psalm makes known. If, then, these words are referred to the Saviour, you could say that the one who is blessed is the one able to understand why he took on poverty for our sake. For “though he was rich, he became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich”; and “being in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” as the divine Apostle clearly taught. Another person, too, will consider the poor and needy when he hears him say in the Gospels: “Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was a stranger and you took me in; naked, and you clothed me; I was sick, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me.” To these words he adds: “Inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.” So in this way too, truly blessed is he who considers the one presented in this way as poor and needy. But if the words are referred to David, you could say that they are joined in sequence to the preceding psalm. For near the end of the 39th it was said in David’s person: “But I am poor and needy.” And so great a king said this, one who had gathered untold wealth to prepare the temple [?] later built by Solomon, humbling

and lowering himself, being modest in soul and truly poor in disposition. For this reason the present psalm is joined on, calling blessed the one who considers someone so poor. The word “needy” appears neither in the Hebrew nor in the other translators. In a fourth sense, one might say that the saying is a maxim, urging kindness and love for the poor. For it is fitting to be compassionate and generous toward those more commonly called poor, understanding that God, who judged that they should be poor, brought them into this condition. He did so both to train them through poverty and because he wished those with abundant means to offer the fruits of their own free choice by sharing with the needy. So the rich man is put to the test through the poor man, to see whether he is merciless, unfeeling and heartless, or kind and merciful. That is why there is so much said about the needy and the poor in the divine precepts. In a fifth sense you could find another order of poor: the one the Saviour calls blessed, in the words, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” There the Saviour called blessed those who live the philosophic life according to God and are poor through godly discipline; these were his disciples and apostles. Blessed, then, is he who considers the poor, the one who is poor and needy in this way. As the fruit of this good and thrice-blessed understanding, he will receive what is said next: “For in the evil day the Lord will deliver him,” or, according to Symmachus, “in the day of affliction.” For if some trial should arise, or he should ever fall into misfortune and hardship, then just as he considered the poor and needy, so the Lord will consider him in good time, measuring out to him the same measure with which

“May the Lord preserve him and give him life.” Indeed, he will both preserve him and make him live; or, according to Symmachus, “He will guard him and keep him safe.” And he will grant him a third thing: “he will make him blessed on the earth”; or, according to Symmachus, “He will be counted blessed on the [earth].” For while he is still on this earth he will obtain blessedness from God, and the heavenly goods promised for hereafter await him. To these words he adds: “And may he not hand him over into the hands of his enemies,” in place of which Symmachus [?] … [?] v, 5.

[?] …my heel was made great. Judas was a man of the Saviour’s peace. He too, with the other disciples, had heard the Saviour say: “My peace I give to you, my peace I leave with you.” And also: “In whom I hoped,” it says; or, according to Aquila, “I trusted,” or, according to Symmachus, “I had trusted.” For the Saviour gave him a share of the same gifts as the other apostles. The Saviour trusted him and had good hopes for him, because he too had free will. Judas was not by nature incapable of being saved. Had he willed it, he could have been taught by the Son of God like the other apostles and become a fine and good disciple. Sharing the table of the Teacher, he not only ate ordinary bread with him but was also counted worthy to partake of the food that nourishes the soul, of which the Saviour said: “I am the bread that came down from heaven and gives life to human beings.” This man, then, who had been counted worthy of so much, lifted up his heel against the Saviour as if to kick him. That is why it is said: “He has made great his tripping against me.” Where the Seventy say “tripping,” the Hebrew reading has “heel.” Aquila followed the Hebrew closely and rendered it so. Hence the evangelist John too, as a Hebrew of Hebrews, recorded that the Saviour said not “tripping” but “heel.”

On “But you upheld me because of my innocence,” or, according to Aquila and Symmachus, “because of my simplicity”: this is said because “he was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth”; and “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten.” Showing the utmost forbearance, he kept silent when he was accused, and when false witness was brought against him he made no answer. He even gave his back to the whip and his cheeks to blows, and did not turn his face away from the shame of being spat upon. That is why he says: “But you upheld me because of my innocence, and established me before you forever.” At the end of all this, the prophetic Spirit sends up a word of thanksgiving to God, saying: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. So be it, so be it”; or, according to Aquila, “assuredly, assuredly”; and according to Symmachus, “Amen, amen.” This is why our Saviour and Lord, in his own discourses, used to say “Amen I say to you” to confirm what he was saying. Aquila brought out its meaning more clearly by saying “assuredly, assuredly.” Now since the whole book of Psalms is divided into five parts, the first part ends here. It begins with Psalm 1 and ends with the one now in hand. It is time, then, to move on to the second part, which begins with Psalm 41 and ends with Psalm 71.

FOR THE END; FOR UNDERSTANDING; FOR THE SONS [OF KORAH]. The first part of the Book of Psalms contained forty psalms, all of them David's. The part now in hand contains thirty-one: eight of these belong to the sons of Korah, one to Asaph and one to Solomon, and the rest to David. The psalms of the sons of Korah come first among them, so let us examine these first, so that we may understand what is said. Through their superscriptions the sons of Korah urge us not to read what is said in a careless way. The present psalm presents the prophetic choir as deeply grieved and downcast in soul at the falling away of the people of the circumcision. It begs for redemption and for freedom from evils through saving help. And he seals this at the end of the passage, saying: Hope in God, for I will give thanks to him, the salvation of my face and my [?]

The superscription contains neither "psalm" nor "song" nor anything of the kind, and this is fitting. What follows is full of rather gloomy words, so the psalm is simply headed "for the end." It contains predictions of things that did not yet exist but would come about at some future time. For the sons of Korah lived in the wilderness in the time of Moses. Their father Korah rebelled against Moses and perished with his clan, but his children did not perish with their father, because they had not shared in his impiety. They showed repentance and very great reverence toward God, and so God accepted them so fully that they even shared in the gift of prophecy. From their line, in the time of David, there arose another Korah, who bore the same name as the earlier one, and he had sons of his own. Whether it is these sons or the earlier ones, through the psalm in hand they foretell the captivity of the people that came long afterward and the scattering of the Jewish nation among all the nations. Further on, at any rate, they say: And those who hate us plundered them. You gave us up like sheep to be eaten, and scattered us among the nations. You sold your people for nothing, and made us a reproach to our neighbors. History does not record that these things happened in David's time, and that is why the psalm is headed "for the end." And since anyone who would grasp these things needs divine understanding, the heading necessarily adds "for understanding." Instead of "for the sons of Korah," Aquila and Symmachus both translate "of the sons of Korah," which teaches us that the prophecies are theirs. They confessed that they thirsted for God himself, and that they had a longing, a yearning and a desire for the fountain that is with him, of which it is said: For with you is the fountain of life; in your light we shall see light. So they said: As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God. The deer is a horned animal; but

it is also clean according to the Law. Moreover, it kills snakes and destroys every kind of reptile, and it is also one of the animals that seek out the deserts. The prophetic choir was like this: they loved the desert and lived apart. At any rate, they are said to have made their home in deserts, in mountains and in caves. They also destroyed every hostile power and every serpent of the mind, since they too had the power to tread on snakes and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy. They were horned, so that they could say: Through you we will gore our enemies with the horn. They were also pure in soul, if anyone ever was, and so they were compared to a deer. For the Bridegroom himself is likened to a young deer in the Song of Songs, and in Job it is said: Have you watched the months of the deer, and will you send forth their birth pangs? The Lord is said to make such rational deer perfect in Psalm 28, which says: The voice of the Lord that makes the deer perfect. So these deer, when the fountain failed them because of the lawless deeds of the people and God had turned away, wept by themselves. They took their own tears as food, lamenting the destruction of the people night and day. They confessed that they did not thirst with their bodies and flesh for the pleasures that flesh loves. Rather, the soul itself longed and yearned, in Symmachus' rendering, for the journey to God. So they said: So my soul longs for you, O God; and again: My soul thirsted for God, the mighty, the living one. For they knew that the Lord lives, according to the saying, Who alone has immortality, and that he alone has life in himself, according to the words: For with you is the fountain of life. And this living water is the fountain itself, which later came (1) in answer to the prayers of the prophets. The Savior himself taught that he gives it to human beings, saying somewhere: Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him, it will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life. And again: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, out of his belly will flow rivers of living water. It was for this drink that the prophetic choir thirsted when it said: My soul thirsted for God, the mighty, the living one; and: When shall I come and appear before the face of God? They said these things because they saw that they were far from seeing God face to face. They also perceived that the face of God had turned away from the people, and that the power that had always cared for them no longer watched over them. So they lamented their life on earth, and prayed that some day they might stand before the face of God. Therefore they said: When shall I come and appear before the face of God? They used such words because they were filled with great boldness and a good conscience. For they were entirely sound in soul and cleansed of every blem- (1) Perhaps "trickled down."

-ish and stain and defilement, and so they asked to appear before the face of God. But the one who sins flees from that face, and through prayer and supplication begs to be spared it, saying: Turn your face away from my sins. Turning away from everything on earth and loathing every luxury that people enjoy, eating only bread, and only because he must, and even that with tears,

My tears have been my bread day and night. The choir of the prophets saw that the face of God had turned away from the whole people. They counted the destruction of the many as their own loss, and took up laments on behalf of all. These men of God carried their hardship so far that they fed on their own tears; all day and all night they refused even bread itself and gave themselves to weeping alone. They did this and suffered this most of all when they heard the people itself, or rather the impious among them, saying: Where is your God? Surely it was not enemies and foes who said this to them every day. It is more likely that the unbelievers within the nation blamed the prophets for worshiping God in vain and toiling for nothing, and said to them: Where is your God? Hearing this from brothers, kinsmen and acquaintances, they mourned all the more. So they say: I remembered these things, and I poured out my soul within me. That is: "I did not show my distress outwardly. I hid my pain inside, in my own soul, and was shaken within myself." The Apostle suffered something of this kind when he said: But we ourselves had the sentence of death within ourselves. So here too they say: I poured out my soul within me. Only a perfect person can say this. He means: "When those who reproach me said to me, Where is your God?, I was stung with grief and was in great pain of soul, struck by the words of the impious. Yet I kept my thoughts within myself, so that they would not pour out and I would not fall from the hope in God set before me. For I called to mind the end that awaits me, since I knew that Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. I knew for certain that after these sorrows I shall pass into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, to the house of God, with the voice of rejoicing and thanksgiving, the sound of those keeping festival. So I remembered these things, and did not fall from hope; instead I poured out my soul inwardly, within myself." And since he had set such hopes before himself, he rightly treats his own soul and says: Why are you so sorrowful, O my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I will give thanks to him, the salvation of my face and my God. For he took courage in himself and urged himself to bear his present sorrows nobly. And Symmachus says: For I shall pass [?] into the tabernacle; I shall be carried

along to the house of God, with a voice of praise and thanksgiving from a multitude keeping festival; or, in Aquila's rendering, of praise and thanksgiving from a crowd keeping festival. This shows what the end will be for those who in this present life nobly endure everything that comes upon them. For the thrice-blessed end will receive them: the wonderful tabernacle of God and his house deep within it. Into that house the worthy will be brought, carried along and lifted aloft by angelic powers. The Apostle knew this when he said: We shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord

He calls it the wonderful tabernacle of God to distinguish it from another that is not wonderful, such as the one built on earth in the time of Moses. You will understand the truly wonderful tabernacle to be the one on which the blessed servants of God fixed their hopes. This was the heavenly tabernacle, of which Moses built copies in the wilderness. The divine Apostle also taught about this wonderful tabernacle, saying: We have such a high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens, a minister of the holy places and of the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched, not man. To this he then adds: They serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things, as Moses was instructed by God when he was about to complete the tabernacle. For, See, he says, that you make everything according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain. But these things were images and symbols of the heavenly things. Christ, however, came as high priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle not made with hands, that is, not of this creation. He entered once for all into the holy places, not through the blood of goats and calves but through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption. If there is joy in heaven among the angels of God over one sinner who repents, then it is fitting that when a God-loving soul, after this present life which was enough for its training, is found worthy to enter the heavenly holy places, there arises a voice of praise from a multitude keeping festival and giving thanks for the salvation of the one being saved. Whoever has been taught these things and is persuaded that they are true rightly says to himself: Why are you so sorrowful, O my soul, and why do you trouble me? Or, in Symmachus' rendering: Why are you bowed down, O my soul, and why are you troubled within me? Wait for God, for I will continually give thanks to him for the salvation of his face; or, in Aquila's rendering, with the salvation of his face. He means: "For very soon I shall be in the tabernacle of God, carried there by holy angels because of its heavenly height and loftiness. I shall stand before the face of God and attain the sight of his salvation. Once I have been found worthy of these things, I shall in due time send up to him the thanksgiving and gratitude that I owe him."

"What has been said is what is laid up for me in hope. In the meantime, at present, many trouble me. Yet I was not so troubled that I fell away and became openly exposed to those who trouble me. Just as above I poured out my soul within me, so here too my soul was troubled within myself." In Symmachus' rendering he says: My soul melts within me when I remember you from the land of the Jordan and from Hermonim, the smallest mountain. Deep meets deep at the sound of your torrents. The sense of these words seems to me to be this. After the death of Moses, when Joshua was leading the people into the promised land, the priests stepped into the Jordan carrying the ark on their shoulders. And the Jordan, as Scripture says, was overflowing all its banks, as in the days of the wheat harvest. And the waters coming down from above stood still in a single heap, and the water that was flowing down went down into the Salt Sea. And all the sons of Israel crossed on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan. The stream below flowed away into the salt sea, while the water coming down from above was miraculously held back by the power of God and turned backward. So the streams pouring down from the springs of the Jordan above had no outlet; they arched up and became a heap [?], the waters piling up one on another because their outlet was blocked. Then deep met deep, as the waters were held back and heaped up into a crest. He means: "So when I recall the grace of the visitation that came to the people then, I rightly melt away in soul now, since God shows no such providence in our time. For they miraculously crossed the Jordan and the mountain beside it, called Hermonim, which is very small. But in my time, as I say this, nothing of the sort has been done. Instead, all your billows and your waves have passed over me"; or, in Symmachus' rendering: All your storms and your waves have gone over me. "So my soul was rightly troubled within me"; or, in Symmachus' rendering: My soul melts within me when I remember you from the land of the Jordan and from Hermonim, the smallest mountain. "For long ago, in these places, deep met deep at the sound of your torrents, as the water was held back so that it would not hinder those crossing the Jordan. But then [?] because of the providence that watched over the people of that time. Now, however, all your storms and your waves have passed over me, flooding me and drowning me, with no one to hold them back." [?] the sons of Korah, prophetically bewailing the final rejection of the Jewish nation, whose sufferings he took upon himself. By day the Lord will command his mercy, and by night his song. He says: "Even if all your storms and your waves have passed over me, I know well and am persuaded [?] that there is no time when you do not show mercy. For you are a merciful God

yes, compassionate and patient. So I treat myself with good hopes. I know that every day God commands his mercy, and I spend the nights devoted to his song. During the day I see what people do and the calamities that surround us, your billows and your waves, and I grieve within myself. But at night I am free from what troubles me by day, and I recount the mercies of the Lord. I remember how he commands his mercy every day, and I send up hymns and songs to him, keeping the nights free for this." That is why it is said: And by night his song is with me; and in Aquila's rendering: And in the night his song is with me. And not only this, but also a prayer to the God of my life. "I sing a hymn of thanksgiving, for I have been taught to give thanks in everything, and I revive myself with the good hopes to come. But because of the sorrows that oppress me in the meantime, here in the present, I send up a prayer to the God of my life, for I know that he is the source of my life." And praying to him I say: My helper (or, in the rendering of Aquila and Symmachus, My rock, on which I stand and shall not be overthrown), why have you forgotten me? "I have not forgotten you. I know your mercies and your compassion, and I know the hopes laid up for me; so I keep your song within me without ceasing. But you have forgotten me. Why? I want to learn the reason why all your billows and your waves, that is, the trials and the many afflictions, have passed over me with your permission. For the reason why you have forgotten me must be something great." In saying these things the prophetic choir (1), as I said, takes the condition of the people as its own. It seems to me that through these words it points to the final rejection and falling away of the whole nation, which came about after their unbelief toward our Savior and Lord. And to the one who asked, Why have you forgotten me?, he might answer with the words of the Gospel: How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing! Since, then, they were forgotten because of their own wickedness, the prophetic choir rightly grieves as if for its own body, for by the law of nature, when one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. So it adds, in Symmachus' rendering: Why do I walk about gloomy while the enemy oppresses me? And my adversaries reproached me as though my bones were slaughtered; or: While my bones were being crushed, those who oppress me reproached me. For when the bones of the prophets, that is, the powers of the soul, were crushed by weeping and lamentation, the enemies of God among the people rose up as though there were no one to defend them, reproaching them and saying: Where is [?]

has a title in the other translators. But it is clear that it seems to be part of the psalm before it, both from the similar words in the two and from their similar sense. I say, then, that in the present psalm too the prophetic choir sets out these words on behalf of the people. The people had been thrust away and handed over to the nations and to wicked men, yet they begged and pleaded to be vindicated and rescued from the hands of their enemies. When the people were mistreated, those who did right came to suffer with them, grieve with them and share their condition. In the same way, the right conduct of God-loving men also gives others fellowship and a share in good things. So, taking the sufferings of the people upon themselves, they offered prayers on behalf of the multitude and sent up a common supplication to God. It was fitting, then, that they uttered these words as if from one mouth: Judge me, O God, and plead my cause against an unholy nation; rescue me from the deceitful and unjust man. For you, O God, are my strength; why have you thrust me away? Why do I go about gloomy while the enemy oppresses me? Someone might say that these words are spoken by one or perhaps two who were found righteous in the whole nation of the Jews. Then let that one rare man, such as Jeremiah or someone like him, weep and send up these words, begging to be rescued from an unholy nation (by which he would mean those of the circumcision themselves) and from an unjust and deceitful man, so that he himself might never become unjust and deceitful. Let him call on God, saying: You are God my strength; why have you thrust me away and left me in the midst of such a people? These words would also suit the prophet Elijah, who spoke against the people, saying: Lord, they have killed your prophets and torn down your altars, and I alone am left, and they are seeking to take my life. And Jeremiah clearly teaches that every righteous person had vanished from the people, saying: Run through the streets of Jerusalem and through its squares, and see whether there is anyone who understands, and I will be merciful to them. Then, since the multitude of wicked men brought affliction on the righteous man, he said that this made him gloomy: Why do I go about gloomy while the enemy oppresses me? In another sense too: when enemies and foes were oppressing the nation and had gained the upper hand over it, the one devoted to God was stung in his

…their just claims, and to judge and decide for them rightly. In the same way the God-beloved speaker says to God in the present passage, "Judge for me, O God", not "Judge me"; and Symmachus also has "Judge for me." Become my judge yourself, and decide this case of mine, and plead my cause, so that once I have been vindicated I may contribute my own good deeds to the salvation of the whole multitude. "Send out your light and your truth; they have led me and brought me to your holy mountain and to your dwellings." You may also understand it this way: Once I have received the light that is with you and the truth that is with you, I shall be guided. The light will illumine me, and your truth will lead me by the hand to your holy mountain, the heavenly one, and to your dwellings there. They spoke of these in the preceding psalm as well: "For I shall pass into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, as far as the house of God, with a voice of rejoicing and thanksgiving, the sound of one keeping festival." And as one consecrated as a priest to you, O God, I shall come to the innermost places and as far as the altar, and I shall come to you, the God who gladdens my spiritual youth. "I will give thanks to you on the lyre, O God." By the lyre he means the body, through which the mind is naturally fitted to strike up music, and through whose senses, as through strings, it habitually sends up the melody that is fitting for God. Through these words the prophetic choir is clearly asking for the light of God and his truth to be sent, since at the time these words were uttered the light was not yet shining on the earth, and the truth was not in any way present among human beings. But the light that is sent must be other than the one who sends it. Of this light it is said: "That was the light that enlightens every person coming into the world." And the Savior himself teaches this in his own person, saying: "I am the light and the truth and the life." "Why are you deeply grieved, my soul, and why do you disquiet me? Hope in God, for I will give thanks to him, the salvation of my face and my God." Symmachus has: "Why do you melt away, my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Wait for God, for I will give thanks to him forever, to the salvation of my face and to my God." Wait, he says, so that you too may one day be able to say, "I waited patiently for the Lord, and he attended to me." But also hope in God, for hope does not put us to shame. Why should one be troubled, or why be deeply grieved, when such great good things are expected? "For yet a very little while, and the one who is coming will come and will not delay." The light will be sent, and the truth will arrive, and the things prophesied will be fulfilled; and the goal of the whole matter is the salvation of my face, my God himself. For when I am counted worthy to stand before God and to behold face to face the salvation of which so much is said throughout all the Scriptures, then indeed I shall give thanks to him as my God

and my Savior. He did well to join the light to the truth. What perceptible light is to the eyes of the body, truth is to the eyes of the soul when they gaze intently at the nature of things. Then they are no longer deceived; they are illumined by grasping what truly exists, and they receive knowledge of the truth. So the passage itself has explained what the intelligible light does: it brings the truth to view. Fittingly, then, when the Savior handed these things on to his disciples, he taught them: "I am the light and the truth and the life." You will apply the conclusion in the same way to each of the other interpretations as well, whether it is those in Babylon who say these things or those from the nations who had not yet believed.

FOR THE END, FOR THE SONS OF KORAH, FOR UNDERSTANDING [?]. The present words do not contain a psalm, as the heading says, nor an ode, nor a hymn, nor anything of the kind, since the sense of what they contain does not involve that kind of contemplation either. Rather, they are supplications like the earlier ones and on the same subject. I mean the falling away of the Jewish nation, addressed in the person of the prophets through the sons of Korah. Here they make things clearer, revealing more plainly the reason they lamented in the preceding psalms. In fact, they recount the sufferings that befell the people. They therefore rouse us to understanding, and by the heading they refer it to the end, because these things were to happen at the end, [?] the sons of Korah foretold them prophetically as though they had already happened. In the earlier psalms they lamented and declared their griefs to God; in the present one they also recount the sufferings themselves. "O God, we have heard with our ears." In place of "who commands the deliverances of Jacob", Symmachus has: "You are my king, O God; give command concerning the salvation of Jacob." "Through you we will gore our enemies with the horn." Those among the people who did what was right, and the prophets among them, would say this. They confess that they won deliverance for themselves not by their own power, or by bow and sword, but by the power of their horn. The Scripture of Daniel calls kingdoms horns, and the Lord himself is called the horn of the saints. That is why he says, "Through you we will gore our enemies with the horn." And elsewhere it is said: "My protector and the horn of my salvation," and so on. So he himself is the horn. Consider how it is said elsewhere: "His praise is above earth and heaven, and he will exalt the horn of his people," as though the one who exalts the horn just mentioned were someone else. See, then, whether the Word of God, the Lord himself, is not clearly the horn of the people, and the one who exalts him the Father who begot him. For since he humbled himself to the point of death, even death on a cross, therefore God highly exalted him, according to the Apostle. Trusting in this horn and king of theirs, they confess that they will overcome their enemies not by bow or sword or by their own virtue, but by the power of their king. Then, since they have gained as king and horn

the Lord himself, they fittingly say that they will not fall into the hands of their enemies but will prove stronger than their foes. They show this by saying: "You saved us from those who afflict us, and you put to shame those who hate us." Their enemies were covered with shame, while they themselves were saved not by their own power but by the power of their horn. So they fittingly add: "In God we shall be praised all day long"; or, according to Aquila, "In God we shall boast"; or, according to Symmachus, "We hymn God all day long, and we will give thanks to your name forever." The Scriptures commonly use "confession" to mean thanksgiving. So those saved by the virtue of their king fittingly say that they boast and sing hymns, praise and are praised, give thanks and confess. These things were spoken in the person of the choir of the prophets. But in what follows, the same speakers recount what befell the multitude, making it their own. "But now you have cast us off and put us to shame, and you will not go out with our forces." The multitude of the whole Jewish nation had been found guilty of every kind of impiety and lawlessness, yet it was not foreign to the prophetic body. So those who spoke the first words fittingly make their own what befell the multitude. With a diapsalma inserted between, they bring forward these words to mark how great a change there is in what follows. Our fathers told us, and we heard with our own ears, what kind of things you did in their days, and so on. But now we do not see such things with our eyes; we see their opposite. For you have cast us off, you, O God, who saved our fathers long ago. Because of our sins you have put to shame those who once took pride in you and boasted in you, leaving them deserted and without help in battle against their enemies. You did not go out with our forces, or, according to Symmachus, "with our armies." "And therefore you turned us back before our enemies"; or, according to Symmachus: "You put us last before every adversary, and those who hate us plunder for themselves. You gave us up like cattle for food, and you scattered us among the nations like winnowed chaff. You sold your people for nothing, and did not set a high price on them. You made us an insult and a mockery to those around us. You made us a byword among the nations, a shaking of the head among the tribes. All day long my disgrace is before me, and the shame of my face covers me, at the voice of the one who reproaches and blasphemes, before the face of the enemy and of the one who takes vengeance for himself." This much, in Symmachus' version, the prophetic choir recounted in its supplication to God, taking the people's sufferings upon itself. The present passage, then, has made clear why it lamented earlier. "All these things came upon us, and we did not forget you." The people once acted impiously in the wilderness and were then handed over to the destroyer. Aaron took the censer and offered incense on behalf of the people, and God was reconciled to the multitude because of

the priest's offering. In the same way the prophetic choir, and those among the people who did what was right, send up their rational sacrifice through their prayer on behalf of the people. They bring their own good deeds to God for the multitude in place of a sacrifice and fragrant incense. For it is not fitting for the multitude to say these things, nor for those handed over to their enemies because of their impieties. But just as the prophets took the sufferings of the people upon themselves and said that they themselves had suffered them, so they make their own good deeds common to all. They knew well that they were members of the whole body. And it followed that when one member suffers, all the members suffer with it, and when a member is honored, all the members rejoice with it. "We have suffered all the things we have mentioned," they say, "but none of them moved us from remembering you, and we did not deal unjustly with your covenant"; or, according to Symmachus: "Nor did we break faith with your compact, nor did our heart turn back." In place of "And you turned our paths aside from your way", Symmachus gave a clearer rendering: "Nor were our steps [?] moved." "In a place of affliction": or, according to Aquila, "You crushed us in an uninhabited place, and you covered us over with the shadow of death." We did not forget you, nor did we break our covenant with you. "If we forgot the name of our God, and if we spread out our hands to a foreign god, will not God search this out?" "We call on you as witness," he says, "as judge and examiner of our words and of the thoughts in our minds that are hidden from most people. You yourself know whether, after suffering so much, being humbled in a place of affliction and covered by the shadow of death, we have forgotten your name. You know whether we did not boast in your name, full of confidence, or whether we despaired of your help, went over to someone else, and spread out our hands to another god. Of these things too you are the judge. You also know the secrets of the heart and the very thoughts in which we are put to death every day for the sake of piety." For whoever has firmly resolved, at each temptation, to accept death for the truth has in effect already died. The Apostle said this too, since persecutions were continuous, one after another, and troubles threatened him with death. At each temptation he was prepared to contend steadfastly to the point of death, and so he rightly said that he died every day. It was in this sense that the prophets of God of old said these things in the present passage: "For in our hidden thoughts we were put to death all day long." More than that, "we were reckoned as sheep for slaughter." For once we had given ourselves up as a sacrifice on behalf of the whole people, we were sacrificed in thought and resolve, [?] us in the shadow of death.

as you yourself, O God, bear witness, for you alone know the secrets of the heart. Since we have suffered so much, we have every right to turn you toward us boldly, to rouse you as though you were asleep, and to say: "Why do you sleep, O Lord? Arise, and do not cast us off forever"; or, according to Symmachus: "Why are you like one who sleeps, O Master? Awake, and do not reject us forever." Even if you have cast us off in part because of the sins of the people, we beg you not to cast us off forever, but to accept our good deeds on behalf of the whole people. It must be noted that the passage [?] a pair of persons

"Why do you turn your face away, and forget our poverty and our affliction?" Symmachus has: "Why do you hide your face, and forget our ill-treatment and affliction?" You hide your face, O God, and turn it away so as not to see what is shameful and unseemly and unfit for your gaze. But since our good deeds just mentioned give us confidence, why do you hide your face? And when we suffer and endure so much hardship for the sake of piety toward you, why do you forget our ill-treatment, or our poverty, as the Seventy put it? For even if these good deeds are great by our measure, by yours they are all poor and small and very slight. Still, coming from us, they are great. So we beg you not to forget our poverty, but to remember also our affliction, which we have endured for your sake. And since our soul has been brought down to the dust, we beg you to pardon our weaknesses. Elsewhere too he entreats God with the same argument, saying: "Remember that we are dust; as for man, his days are like grass." But also "our belly has cleaved to the ground." It ought to have been filled with holy streams and with a spring of living water welling up to eternal life. Instead, from excessive drought, our belly has cleaved to the ground. By the belly of the soul understand its memory, or else its ruling faculty. There it gathers all its learning and contemplations. There too it receives seed and conceives, and when it has carried the child to term it gives birth to a spirit of salvation, as in the words of the one who said: "From fear of you, O Lord, we conceived in the belly, and were in labor, and brought forth a spirit of salvation." With entreaties as moving as these, the prophets of God of old and those among the people who did what was right made their petition, and they beg also to obtain redemption. And this did come to pass. While they were still speaking, God heard them and turned their lamentations into something brighter. Therefore those who lamented so much next prophesy concerning those who are to be changed, and they sing an ode concerning the Beloved. Through him the good God, hearing those who prayed, granted to the whole human race freedom from evils and the redemption of souls.

CONCERNING THE BELOVED. [PSALM] 44. "My heart has poured forth a good word; I speak my works to the king. My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe." Those who lamented so much in the preceding psalms now sing odes and songs instead of their former lamentations. They show that the Beloved of God has become the cause of their change from gloom, and they praise him throughout the whole ode. But since these things were to happen much later, they fittingly entitle the prophecy "For the end", or "A victory song", or "For the victor", because of the triumphs over spiritual enemies. They added "For those who will be changed" to the title, since the very speakers of these words have changed from gloomy words to a brighter ode. Moreover, what the whole ode contains is full of very great change. The Beloved of God emptied himself, took the form of a slave, and was found in appearance as a man. In this he seemed to undergo no ordinary change, though as God he is unchangeable and immutable. And those whom he redeemed from captivity under the devil and transferred into freedom under God truly underwent the finest change themselves. That is why the queen mentioned in the words is commanded to forget her own people and her father's house. The daughter of Tyre, a foreigner, is called to this fair change. Virgins, and certain sons who take the place of fathers, and peoples giving thanks to God, were counted worthy of the same change. Because of all these, the ode is entitled "For those who will be changed"; Aquila has "Upon the lilies" and Symmachus "For the flowers." For those who were changed breathed out fragrance and became fresh flowers of the Church, and so they were given this name. But so that these things may be understood, "For understanding" is necessarily added to the title. It is also there so that we may understand that the whole passage contains an ode concerning the Beloved, or, as Symmachus has it, "a song to the Beloved." When you reach this point, you will gather together everything said about the Beloved, as for example in Isaiah: "I will sing to my beloved a song of the Beloved concerning my vineyard. The beloved had a vineyard." By these words is signified [?] a vineyard [?] beloved, [?] and the Greeks too know, those skilled

[it is] said, "concerning the Beloved." And in the Psalms it is said: "The Lord will give a word to those who bring good news with great power. The king of the powers of the Beloved." Here too the Lord God of the universe is clearly mentioned on his own, and the Beloved again on his own. In third place come those who proclaim the good news of the Beloved, to whom it is said that a word is given from God himself above. In this way the testimony concerning our Savior is established. And in another place it is said again: "And the beloved is like a son of unicorns." Let the seal of them all be set beside these: the saving Gospel, which revealed the Beloved to human beings by the Father's voice crying from above: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Now that so much has been demonstrated about the Beloved, the present prophecy, whose title reads "An ode concerning the Beloved", should be clear and beyond dispute. That this was the Christ, and that he is distinct from the Father who anointed him, the psalm itself shows as it goes on. Let this be said about the title. What follows is again recounted by the prophetic choir, which [spoke] the first parts as well

Some have supposed that the psalm, or ode, is spoken in the person of the Father about the Word who was with him in the beginning. On this view the Father brought the Word forth, as it were, from his heart or from his very inward parts, and a good word came forth from a good heart. But to me these words seem to refer to the person of the prophet, since what follows in the passage no longer fits the interpretation that refers them to the Father. For the Father would not have said of his own tongue, "My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe," nor "Fairer in beauty than the sons of men," for his surpassing beauty does not come from comparison with human beings. And further on he says: "Therefore God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness." He did not say, "I, God, anointed you," but "anointed you," which shows that the speaker is someone else. Who, then, is this? The prophet, who received the working of the Holy Spirit that came into him

In place of "My heart has poured forth", Symmachus has "My heart was stirred by a word". He says that someone else announced the word [?] and that he himself was stirred by hearing it. When they say, "I speak my works to the king," the king they mean is no other than the Beloved himself, to whom what follows is also addressed. "To him," he says, "I will recount my works"; or, according to Aquila and Symmachus, "I will declare my just deeds." The choir of the prophets, full of great confidence because of its good works, dared to say this. And if you want to know what the prophets' works were, you can learn it from the preceding psalm, where they said: "All these things came upon us, and we did not forget you, and we did not deal unjustly with your covenant"; and again: "For

"For your sake we are being put to death all day long." It was a great work both to prophesy things to come with the tongue and to serve the King with the song of the gospel. Instead of "Pen of a swift-writing scribe," Aquila has "Reed of a quick scribe"; and Symmachus: "My tongue," he says, "is the stylus of a quick writer." Quite wonderfully he calls his own tongue neither the hand of a skilled scribe nor a scribe, but the pen of a swift-writing scribe. He shows that the prophetic tongue was the instrument of another who used it, the Holy Spirit. The Spirit is the scribe, and the tongue of the prophets was his stylus and pen. So the swift-writing scribe is one, namely the Holy Spirit; the prophet is another; and the third is the prophetic tongue, which held the place of pen and stylus, being the instrument of the Holy Spirit who used it. One should know that in the translation of the Seventy the sense is joined to "the pen of the scribe," and the whole saying is taken as a single verse, which runs thus: "My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe; fair in beauty beyond the sons of men." But the Hebrew text and the other translators close off the sense of what comes before and begin their rendering at a new point, and so we too have reasonably placed "Fair in beauty beyond the sons of men" at a new beginning. Aquila translated it this way: "With beauty you have been made beautiful beyond the sons of men"; and Symmachus: "In beauty you are fair beyond the sons of men." So the first lines of the song were spoken as a prelude. For when the prophetic choir was about to proclaim the good news of the Beloved and bring forth the song about him, it used a prelude, and ended the prelude at "My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe." From here it then begins the song addressed to the Beloved himself, and cries out to him: You are fair in beauty, you are beautiful; or, you have been made beautiful with beauty; or, you have been made fair with beauty, O Beloved, beyond the sons of men. For even though you yourself became, as fully as anyone, one of the sons of men, and were counted among those who have lived on earth, still nothing else can be compared with your beauty. Clearly this means beauty of virtue, for in that way Isaiah will not seem to contradict it when he says: "And we saw him, and he had no form or beauty; but his form was without honor, falling short beyond the sons of men." Those words foretold the cross and the passion, which were full of drunken abuse and outrage; that is why the prophet added: "A man in affliction, who knew how to bear weakness, he was dishonored and not esteemed." But the psalm, as has been said, calls beauty not that of his body but that of his virtue, which received no stain of sin. Next comes: "Grace has been poured out on your lips; therefore God has blessed you

forever." Moses found a particular grace, and Noah too found a certain grace before God, and each of the righteous had a share in grace. But in the case of the Beloved the whole of the Father's grace was poured out into him, for it was the Father who spoke in the Son. Hence she too who ministered to his coming among men was called "full of grace." For in him it pleased the whole fullness of the Godhead to dwell bodily; therefore all the saints have received from his fullness. You may also consider it this way: the first work of the Beloved is the grace poured out on his lips, in the sense already given. And in another way, "grace and truth came through Jesus Christ," since he did everything as a free gift, forgiving the sins of some, healing the diseases and infirmities of others, and granting the Holy Spirit to others. So it was fittingly said to him: "Grace has been poured out on your lips." After this, those who earlier lamented and described their own slavery under their enemies now fittingly beseech the Beloved to hasten and come to them, armed with weapons of war against the enemies pressing upon them, so that he may strike those enemies and lead them out of their captivity. Therefore they say: "Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one." That is: You are fair and beautiful, but in addition to your fairness and your beauty, take up your full armor for us, your suppliants; put the sword on your thigh, and so, taking up your power, bend your bows. Then, having struck down the enemies, prosper and reign. By the sword of the Beloved understand the power that destroys and punishes the enemies. For "the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword." Elsewhere too the prophet Ezekiel mentions a sword of God, saying: "Thus says Adonai the Lord: Say, Sword, sword, be sharpened and be enraged, that you may slaughter victims; be sharpened, that you may gleam, ready for destruction." And again: "Cry out and wail, son of man, for it has come upon my people; it is upon the leaders of Israel." And further on: "Mark out for yourself two ways for the sword of the king of Babylon to enter; they shall go out from one land," and what follows. Through these words he calls the sword of Nebuchadnezzar, which was brought upon the people, the sword of the Lord. You have it also in the Gospels: the king who made a wedding feast for his son hands over to slaughter those who refused the invitation and killed the royal servants. "And he sent his army," it says, "and burned their city." By the king's army it means the Roman force that besieged Jerusalem. Since, then, such a sword was needed against those who rose up against the Beloved, the prophecy fittingly says to him: "Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one. In your fairness and your beauty bend your bow, and prosper and rei[?]

Then he adds: "Because of truth and meekness and righteousness, and your right hand will guide you wonderfully." He explained these words in the same way as the rest. "Your arrows are sharpened, and peoples will fall beneath you, in the heart of the king's enemies." This is set in an inverted order. You should join the sense this way: "Your arrows are sharpened in the heart of the king's enemies." First he says: your sharpened arrows will be aimed at the heart of your enemies; then, peoples will fall beneath you once the enemies have been driven off by your arrows. At that time the peoples, having gained their freedom and found relief from the evils that oppressed them, will run to your feet. The arrows of the Beloved sent against the heart of the enemies you should understand as invisible and unseen blows against the rulers of this age. Wounded by these arrows, the demons once said: "Ah, what have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come before the time to torment us?" From what came before we have learned that the Beloved of God was fair and beautiful and full of grace, a blessed king and conqueror of enemies. From the present passage we are taught that besides all these things he was also God. For the Holy Spirit cries out to him, saying: "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever"; or, according to Aquila: "Your throne, O God, is forever and beyond." And since he had named him king in the foregoing, he fittingly adds: "A rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom." For there is nothing crooked or twisted in him. And so that no one, understanding it in a Jewish way, should suppose that the Beloved of God would be a mortal king like most others, he necessarily teaches that the throne of his kingdom was from eternity and will endure and remain forever and ever. That these words are not addressed to the Father but to the beloved and only-begotten Son he makes clear as he goes on, saying: "You loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore God, your God, anointed you." For who could the God anointed by God in these words be, except the one proclaimed as God in the Gospels: "And the Word was with God, and the Word was God"? This God the Word, then, loved righteousness and hated lawlessness. Aquila translated this more exactly, saying: "He loved righteousness and hated impiety." For with right judgment he loves those under him who are righteous and hates those who are the opposite. Therefore he is anointed above his fellows with a better oil, called the oil of gladness, and he is anointed by God, his own Father, with "oil of joy" according to Aquila, or "oil of exultation" according to Symmachus. His fellows are many, that is, his companions who have shared in his grace, who might also say: "We have become partakers of Christ." Some have read the present text in this way: "Therefore, O God, your God anointed you," and they use this reading, keeping close to the Hebrew

wording. For God is named Elohim in the Hebrew text, where it says: "In the beginning [?] your throne, O God, is forever and beyond." The Seventy and Symmachus said "Your throne, O God" with the nominative form; but Aquila used the vocative, keeping close to the Hebrew wording, which has Elohim. Yet the same Aquila, who said "O God" in the vocative here, did not translate the vocative again when, further on, Elohim occurs a second time, in "Therefore God anointed you"; instead he used the nominative, saying: "For this reason God, your God, anointed you." To be consistent with himself he ought to have used the vocative here too for the same word, and had he translated it so, he would have said: "Therefore, O God, your God anointed you." "Myrrh and stacte and cassia from your garments, from ivory palaces." Instead of "ivory palaces" Aquila said "from temples of tooth." Here the temples are the Churches of the Bridegroom and the souls dedicated to Christ, which have all their strength in spiritual food. Teeth are a symbol of food and of words. Hence Christ's own teeth are said to be whiter than milk in the prophecy that speaks of him: "His eyes are joyful from wine, and his teeth whiter than milk." According to the other translators, his temples or palaces are called ivory because ivory ornament comes from a dead animal; and those who are approved in the Church shine out in no other way than by putting to death their members that are on earth, as the Apostle commands. "The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a robe woven with gold, adorned in many colors." The daughters of kings, that is, of Christ and his Church, were the individual souls. But the queen herself, the mother of the daughters, stood at his right hand, clothed in a robe woven with gold, adorned in many colors. Who could she be but the whole catholic Church, gathered out of all nations from one end of the earth to the other? He built her for himself upon the rock, so that the gates of Hades should not prevail against her. More properly you might say that this signifies the heavenly Church, which is the mother of the holy men on earth. The divine Apostle taught this when he said: "But the Jerusalem above is free, which is our mother." He also calls her the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, made up of myriads of angels in festal gathering and the church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven. She, then, would be the perfect bride of Christ, and you would not be wrong to say that the Church on earth is her daughter. She is queen, since she already reigns with her bridegroom; that is why she is said to stand at the King's right hand. [?] She is his bride, receiving his seed, and continually conceiving and bearing the spirit of salvation. He also clothes her in the royal robe, the luminous robe of incorruption, which is wholly spiritual and clothes the angelic powers in heaven.

This is what the present text calls "woven with gold." But "clothed, adorned in many colors" is found neither in the Hebrew reading nor in the other translators; therefore it has been marked with an obelus. "All the glory of the king's daughter is within [?], clothed in golden fringes, adorned in many colors." You will understand, he says, how she is clothed in golden fringes when you hear Paul saying: "We know in part and we prophesy in part." For knowledge in part gives her the ornament of gold only at the edges. "But when the perfect comes," he says, "what is partial will be done away." When she who is for now being nurtured on earth like a child passes over into the heavenly Church, she will then lay aside the golden fringes, that is, the knowledge in part, and be clothed in a robe of gold. "Virgins shall be brought to the King after her; her companions shall be brought to you." The Daughter, so often named in the foregoing, does not remain on earth forever, but will be taken up in due time. Yet not all of her together will be counted worthy of this passage. Instead, a part of her, those honored in the first rank within her, will be brought to the King. These are the ones who have achieved chastity in Christ, sanctified in soul and [?] body and spirit. After the first order, those near them will be brought, for there are many dwelling places with the Father. These are the ones who hold the place nearest the virgins through a dignified and self-controlled life. He shows how they will be brought, saying: "with gladness and exultation." You will understand how this is meant if you set beside it the Apostle's words: "We shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord." For the virgins will not come or go to the King by themselves; they will be brought, with others carrying them, namely divine angels lifting them aloft and raising them on high so that they may make the journey upward with ease. They will be brought with gladness and exultation, and will be led into the King's temple, being counted worthy of the royal house of the kingdom of heaven. A temple is a house of God, so the King to whom they are led is God. They are also led by those who handed down instruction to them, the Law and the prophets. "Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you." The other translators have rendered the sense of this more clearly: Aquila says, "Instead of your fathers there shall be your sons"; Symmachus, "Instead of fathers your sons have come to be." The meaning of the saying is this: your sons, born in you and from you, will become fathers to you. For you will have as fathers those whom you yourself have borne. You will see the saying fulfilled if you observe how foreigners from the nations come to the Church of God and, being born again in her, become her sons; then, advancing in progress, they are appointed her fathers, promoted to preside over

her and counted worthy of the priestly ministry. He explains more clearly how you will have them in place of fathers, saying: "You will make them rulers over all the earth." The word says this to the Church on earth, which extends from one end of the earth to the other. Over her the Church of God herself appoints her own sons as rulers and fathers. "Therefore peoples will praise you forever and ever." The Daughter of kings mentioned before, that is, the Church on earth, perceiving the power of the Father's name, since he granted him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, after the promises spoken to her, believed the words and was filled with joy and gladness.

For the end. For the sons of Korah, concerning hidden things. Psalm 45. "Our God is our refuge and strength, a helper in the afflictions that have come upon us so heavily. Therefore we will not fear when the earth is shaken and the mountains are moved into the heart of the seas." The word sends up a hymn of thanksgiving to the one who has counted it worthy of great things: for the impiety of the demons, which once held sway, will vanish as though cast into some abyss, that impiety which imitated the height of the mountains and held power over most of the inhabited world. Then the prophetic word says that the waters were stirred by a storm and the mountains were shaken as the gospel proclamation crossed over the world. Here it called the throng of demons mountains because of the bulk of their arrogance and the loftiness of their pride; and it called the minds of men waters, because like waters they are easily carried this way and that and stirred up by the spirits of deceit. The history of the Acts teaches us this as well: how, as the holy apostles traveled about the world, the cities were filled with storm and uproar. In Ephesus Demetrius stirred up the whole city, and in Lystra and Derbe the very same thing happened. And again in Philippi and Thessalonica, in Athens and Corinth, the spirits of deceit raised these waves, and some who were driven by them shouted against the holy apostles: "These men who have turned the world upside down have come here too." Blessed Habakkuk foretold this as well: "You set your horses upon the sea, stirring up many waters." He called the holy apostles horses because they became a divine chariot; riding upon them, the Master scattered the many and various doctrines of impiety. You may also understand the confusion and turmoil of the earth in another way, when you hear the Savior say: "I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what more do I wish, if it is already kindled?" And again: "Do not think that I came to bring peace upon the earth; I did not come to bring peace,

but a sword. For I came to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, and a man's enemies will be those of his own household." It is as if he were saying more plainly: and to make each man's household his enemies. Need one say that whole cities and peoples and nations of every kind were thrown into confusion by the gospel word as their old superstition was being dissolved? But while these were being shaken and thrown into confusion, the sons of the Church and those who lead her say: "We will not fear." They claim God as their own, saying "Our God," in contrast to the gods falsely so named among the nations. If only men had been shaken, it would have been enough to say: "We will not fear when the earth is shaken." But since invisible powers and evil demons were also shaken and tossed about by the saving word, he fittingly alluded to them too, as hidden and escaping the eyes of others, when he said: "and the mountains are moved into the heart of the seas." "Their waters roared and were troubled; the mountains were shaken by his might." You will understand these mountains as the spiritual forces of wickedness, from the gospel teaching.
