For when the Savior healed the epileptic boy, he went on to tell the disciples: "Truly I say to you, if you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, 'Move from here to there,' and it will move, and nothing will be impossible for you," calling the demon just mentioned a mountain. How the mountains are moved into the heart of the seas you may learn from the Gospel according to Luke, where it is said that the demons begged the Savior not to command them to go into the abyss. Scripture is accustomed to call the abyss "seas," as is said in Job: "Have you come to the sea, and walked in the tracks of the abyss?" Moses too taught about this abyss in the account of creation, saying: "And darkness was over the abyss." But while these things are happening, "We," he says, "will not fear, while their waters roar and are muddied and the mountains are shaken by his wondrous glory," according to Symmachus. The Savior's glory was the growth of the Church and the multiplying of those who believe in him, and the overthrow of polytheistic [?]

The diapsalma marked a division between the sense of what was said before and what is about to be said. So the word, having passed on as it were to another section, again signifies in riddles the peaceful state of the Church of God, which it calls the city of God because of its God-fearing way of life. The city of God is the community of those who live according to God, and this fills the whole inhabited world. For from the rising of the sun to its setting one can find this city of God established through the Church; and since she has the heavenly word springing up within her and pouring down like rain, she is filled with every divine gladness. Aquila and Symmachus say: "The channels of the river gladden the city of God." [?]

…and the divisions, hearing Paul say: “There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of service, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who works all things in all.” The Most High has sanctified his tabernacle. According to Symmachus: “The holy place of the dwelling of the Most High.” For although the city is great and large, there is a certain choice part of it. Among those in the Church, the general multitude is large, but few are those devoted to holiness and keeping the commandment that says: “You shall be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy.” And it is in these holy ones that the dwelling of the Most High is said to be, for only in them does that voice of God find place which says: “I will dwell in them and walk among them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my [?]

God is in her midst; she shall not be shaken; God will help her at dawn, at dawn. Another again says: “I think he is hinting at the morning assemblies, in which we are accustomed to gather in the churches throughout the earth.” The oracle also rouses us in another way and urges us to early-morning prayers, so that we may offer him, as it were, the firstfruits of our life; for at these times the purified mind, being most free of disturbance, is accustomed to minister to God like a priest. Diapsalma. Nations were troubled, kingdoms bowed; he gave his voice, the earth was shaken. Here he presents the people who inhabit the earth as troubled, and the kingdoms on earth arming themselves against the Church and taking up war against the word of the gospel. Then, just as in battles, when the victorious side prevails, the opposing side is thrown into confusion and turns to flight, so now also, as the word of the gospel conquers, nations were troubled and kingdoms bowed—or, according to Symmachus, “kingdoms were overturned.” Moreover, when he gave his voice, the earth was dissolved. For when the word of the gospel was newly going out into the world, the nations, finding it strange and defending their former superstition, were stirred up together, and their kings rose up against the Church. But since God was her refuge, they were all overturned, though our Savior had given nothing more than his voice alone. For he gave his voice, and the earth was shaken. And what voice but the one that came through the preaching of the apostles [?]? Fittingly, then, we who said above, “God is our refuge and strength,” take up the same confession again, saying that such great achievements did not come from our own power, but the Lord of hosts who works these things was with us. And he was our helper, the God of Jacob. Here too they fittingly mentioned the God of Jacob, referring us back to the one who appeared to Jacob in the form of a man. For there wrestled

with him, it says, a man, who also said to him: “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name, for you have prevailed with God.” And Jacob arose and called the name of that place “Form of God,” saying: “For I have seen God face to face.” For this is the very one who appeared to Jacob in the form of a man. He is the Lord of hosts who is with us, and he is our helper, the God of Jacob; for through him we have accomplished everything described above. Come and see the works of the Lord, the wonders he has set upon the earth, removing wars to the ends of the earth. He will shatter the bow and break the weapon in pieces, and burn the shields with fire. Indeed, if one attends to the times, one can find these very things fulfilled even literally. For before the appearance of our Savior there were local lordships and petty governments by regions and by cities, and wars broke out in every corner of the earth, so that even the farmers working the land had to look after spears and swords and every kind of weapon of war. But after the saving theophany, the Roman empire, as a single monarchy, began to prevail over most nations, and the saving Gospel, beginning at the same time, ran through to all the nations. And another prophecy was also fulfilled, which proclaims somewhat as follows through Isaiah: “And they shall beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into sickles; and nation shall not take up sword against nation, and they shall no longer learn to make war.” These things, then, are also signified by the present words, and they were fulfilled literally, according to the history just given, and in the spiritual sense, according to the overthrow of the intelligible and invisible enemies. By the spears and weapons and shields of the opposing powers they meant [?] the lifeless carved idols and statues of polytheistic error, or else godless men and the impious thoughts that the invisible spirits insinuate into human minds, with which they shoot, hurling their fiery darts against souls that are unguarded and not fenced about by faith. Be at leisure and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth. Since, then, the affairs of war had ceased and the turmoil had been dissolved, and deep peace had been given to all on earth, he fittingly wants the occasion to be used for good, and the soul to take up a saving leisure. That is why he says, “Be at leisure and know”; for there is no other way to share in divine knowledge than by being free of the things that drag one in the opposite direction. Hence the king of Egypt, being hostile to such leisure, fittingly answers those who say, “We will go a three days’ journey and serve the Lord our God,” with the words: “You are at leisure, you are idlers.” Then, not wanting them to have leisure for God, he wears them out with clay and brickmaking. But to us the rulers appointed over all the earth cry out

to be at leisure, promising the knowledge of God as the fruit of leisure. And God speaks through them, saying: “Know [?] that I am God,” and also, “I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth.” For of old I was known among the Jews alone, when “God was known in Judea; his name was great in Israel.” But now I command you to keep leisure, so that you may learn and know in what way I shall be exalted among all the nations as well, being glorified by them more than by those who were formerly thought to know me. FOR THE END, ON BEHALF OF THE SONS OF KORAH, A PSALM [?]. All you nations, clap your hands; shout to God with a voice of exultation. For the Lord Most High is awesome, a great king over all the earth. It seems to me that the title is in error. For it should have been inscribed not “on behalf of the sons of Korah,” but “for the sons of Korah” or “of the sons of Korah,” as in the preceding titles; for the other translators and the Hebrew have it in the same way as the preceding ones. And since the word exhorts the nations quite plainly, with nothing veiled, the title fittingly does not urge us to understanding, nor is it “concerning the hidden things”; instead it is called simply a psalm, or a “melody” or a “song” according to the others. “For the end” is necessarily prefixed, because the prophecy was to be fulfilled in later times. Quite consistently with what was said before about the Beloved and about his heralds, the Holy Spirit commands all the nations to perform signs of gladness: to clap their hands, as at the celebration of a wedding of bridegroom and bride, and to shout to God, as for a king acclaimed for his victory over his enemies. And fittingly, after the Savior’s victory over the enemies, now that he has received the Church as his bride, the Holy Spirit summons everyone to hasten to the feast. That is why it cries out to all the nations throughout the world: “All you nations, clap your hands; shout to God with a voice of exultation.” Next it teaches the reason for the exhortation, saying: “For the Lord Most High is awesome, a great king over all the earth.” For formerly the Lord Most High himself reigned only over those in heaven and was unknown to those on earth, when demons ruled over the people of the earth. But now through the Beloved he has made his grace shine upon those on earth, and the Most High himself has become awesome to those enemies who work the error of polytheism; for he drove them all out and put them far from the flock of humankind. And when leisure had come, he was proclaimed great king of the nations over all the earth. Therefore the word exhorts his subjects to clap with their hands, that is, with works and deeds, as if uttering sounds worthy of the kingdom of the Most High; and it also commands them to shout to him with a voice of exultation,

so that they may hymn him not only with works and way of life but also with right doctrines and theology. He subjected peoples to us, and nations under our feet. He chose for us his inheritance, the beauty of Jacob, which he loved. That neither peoples were subjected to the sons of Korah nor nations came under their feet is clear to everyone. These words, therefore, are spoken as if in the person of the apostles. For they, commanded by the Savior himself to make disciples of all the nations, and inspired by his power, set out on their journey to all the nations, passed through even the barbarian tribes, and ran through the whole inhabited world. Fittingly, then, these things are said in their person to those who accepted the preaching: “Even if the Lord we preach is not grasped bodily and with eyes of flesh, learn from the deed itself who he is and how great he is. Do you not see who we heralds are—what humble and unlettered men? Nevertheless the word that comes through us has such strength that it has filled the whole world. Where, then, does such great power come from, which has subjected peoples to us and nations under our feet? By ‘peoples’ I mean the former ones who have become obedient to our teaching, and by ‘nations’ those who still remained in unbelief, who often rose up and wished to make war on us and on the word we preach, but whom the great King subjected under our feet, so that we came upon them and trod upon them.” Indeed, even against their will we established churches for our [?] in the very midst of their cities and lands. And he chose for us his [?] inheritance, which he promised to his Beloved, saying: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and [?] the ends of the earth as your possession.” This, then—clearly the Church from the nations—he chose and distributed to us his apostles. For she is chosen, having come into being by election out of all the nations, and not by succession of descent. Instead of “his inheritance,” the others have rendered “our inheritance” or “our allotment.” For just as, in the case of the former people, those with Joshua son of Nun distributed the land of promise by lot, driving out its former inhabitants, in the same way the heralds of the kingdom of God, passing through the whole world, received as their lot the peoples already mentioned, having driven out the unseen and invisible enemies. This inheritance he says is the beauty of Jacob—or according to Aquila, “the pre-eminence of Jacob”; according to Symmachus, “the glorification [?] of Jacob”; and according to the fifth edition, “the boast of Jacob.” For the Church of Christ has become the boast and glory of the ancient prophet Jacob because of Jacob’s own predictions about the nations; for it would have been a dishonor to him if his words had not proved true, but their having come to fulfillment is his glory and his boast.

The rulers of the peoples were gathered together with the God of Abraham, for the mighty ones of the earth are God’s; they were greatly exalted. Together with the others mentioned before, rulers of peoples too were gathered into one Church, becoming the people of the God of Abraham. For so Symmachus translated it, rendering it admirably: “The rulers of the peoples were assembled, the people of the God of Abraham.” For those who were formerly rulers of the peoples, idolaters given over to every superstition of error, have become peoples of the God of Abraham, having come to know the God of Abraham, calling upon him in their prayers, and holding their assembly with him. Theodotion too, who was himself one of the careful translators, translated it like Symmachus, saying: “The rulers of the peoples were gathered together, the people of the God of Abraham.” Why, then, did the Seventy say “with the God of Abraham”? Because the Hebrew writes “with” and “people” with the same letters. For it says “am Elohim,” which can mean both “with God” and “people of God.”

A SONG OF A PSALM FOR THE SONS OF KORAH. 47. Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised, in the city of our God, on his holy mountain, well-rooted, the joy of all the earth: the mountains of Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great king. The first three psalms inscribed “of the sons of Korah” contained words of calamity and grief; the fourth indicated a change to a brighter state, which is why it was a song on behalf of the Beloved; likewise the fifth was “concerning the hidden things”; and the sixth too was likewise a psalm. The one at hand, which contains a greater theology than those before it, is fittingly entitled “A song of a psalm for the sons of Korah”; for at the same time some hymned God by crying out with their voices, while others played the same song on musical instruments, bringing the harmony into accord with the melody. They send up a hymn on behalf of the Church to the one who won the victories over the enemies and redeemed his Church from bitter and harsh slavery. The psalm before this one, then, exhorted the nations to clap and to shout to God with a voice of exultation, and to sing psalms to him, because God is king of all the earth; and to sing psalms with understanding, since he has become king over the nations. But those who had been commanded to do these things needed to learn both the manner of the shout and the psalm itself, as from a teacher; that is why the present passage necessarily teaches this. So the nations that have been brought over from godlessness to the divine teaching are instructed to speak of their own Lord as God and to say: “Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised”—or “greatly to be hymned,” according to the others. You will understand how he is called great if you look up to heaven and survey the whole universe, as Isaiah said: “Lift up your eyes on high and see who has displayed all these things.” For from the greatness and beauty of created things the Maker of creation is seen by analogy—great not in bodily

size, but in incomprehensible power. He is great also in wisdom and goodness and forbearance and love for humanity, and in the other divine powers conceived of in him; that is why it is said: “And in your thoughts there is none who shall be likened to you.” He is the one who [?] certain godless demons made [?] by incantations, who established his own kingdom on earth and accomplished among human beings each of the things listed above. And he is not only great but also greatly to be hymned—not, however, by everyone or in every place, but in the city of our God and on his holy mountain. For those outside his city, being ignorant of the divine teaching, do not know how to hymn him or to speak worthily of God. That is why they have cast the revered name down onto lifeless matter, or onto kinds of irrational animals, or onto the elements—earth, water, air, fire—or onto the parts of the universe; and others have held impious opinions about God in still other ways. For this reason, being strangers to the city of God, they have fallen away from the true hymn. The city of our God is the Church, which the oracles above also indicated, where it was said: “The streams of the river gladden the city of God; the Most High has sanctified his tabernacle.” These things concern the Church on earth, of which it is said: “I will dwell in them and walk among them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.” But if there is another city better than this, whose builder and maker is he himself, see how in it too he is great and hymned and greatly to be praised, being worthily conceived of and spoken of as God within it. Where this city has been built, the [?] teaches, saying: “On his holy mountain, well-rooted”—that is, well founded and rooted—“and the joy of all the earth.” And what this mountain might be, the great Apostle teaches, saying: “We have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels in festal gathering, and to the church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven.” And that this is the true city of God, the same Apostle showed when he said: “But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.” And the mountain worthy of God is heaven itself. But since he did not deem even human beings on earth unworthy of his own kingdom—for the psalm before this one showed this, saying: “King of all

[?] For no one can lay another than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ; and he is also the joy of all the earth. The sides of the north. That is why it is also said to occupy the sides of the north. Among the ancients it was said: “From the north evils will be kindled upon all who inhabit the earth.” But since the kingdom of God, established on earth, drove out those who of old held the sides of the north, and quenched the cauldron set beneath them, and has prevailed over the evils that of old filled the north, the aforementioned mountain is fittingly said here to extend to the sides of the north. Moreover, the grace of the king was to be poured out even upon the nations that were formerly idolatrous; and since the geographers conceive of the whole earth as having two parts—one in the southern, meridional zone, which they say belongs to the inhabited world on the opposite side of the globe, and the other in the northern zone [?], which we inhabit—the present passage, signifying our own inhabited world, fittingly named it “the sides of the north.” These words cannot be taken in any other way than this: since the Church of God, having filled the sides of the north and the whole northern inhabited world, is visible to the eyes, it is said: “The mountains of Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great king.” God is known in her strongholds. Here again he gives signs of God’s presence in his aforementioned city. For just as it was said above, “God is in her midst, and she shall not be shaken; God will help her toward dawn, at dawn. Nations were troubled, kingdoms bowed; he gave his voice, the earth was shaken,” so now too he sets forth the clear evidence of God’s presence in his city, saying: “God is known in her strongholds”—when he comes to her aid. Instead of “in her strongholds,” Symmachus said: “He will be known in her palaces.” For since God is unseen and invisible, his presence is known most of all when enemies attack his city and he provides her with help. And what would you call the strongholds of the city but the churches set apart in various regions and places? For the whole godly commonwealth established throughout the inhabited world is understood as the great city of the king, while the local churches are its strongholds. In their midst is always God, who said, “Where two or three are gathered together, there I am in their midst,” and, “Behold, I am with you all the days until the end of the age.” He is known at the time when, as enemies attack, he comes to the aid of his own city and its strongholds. Next after these words is joined the assault of the enemies against the Church of God, for it says: “For behold, the kings were gathered together; they passed through together.” According to Symmachus: “For behold,” he says, “the kings drew up in battle array; they came together.” And what kings but the enemies of the godly commonwealth drew up in battle array

…with one another, and laid down written laws for making war on the Church of God? Yet the great wonder of God, who is known in her strongholds, is shown precisely when the kings gather together and take up war against his Church, stirring up persecutions and devising countless plots against her, and prevail nothing. So he adds: "They themselves saw it, and so they marveled." Having learned his power by experience, they then marveled, though they had not marveled before. Next, "they were troubled," since they had set themselves up as enemies of God; "they were shaken, and trembling took hold of them; there were pangs as of a woman in labor." From then on the thought of the judgment of the God they had been fighting came before their eyes. So Symmachus renders it: "They themselves saw and so marveled; they were troubled, they were astounded, shuddering seized them, pangs as of a woman in labor." For they were in labor, as it is said: "Behold, he has travailed with iniquity, he has conceived trouble and brought forth lawlessness. He dug a pit and hollowed it out, and he will fall into the hole he has made. His trouble will return upon his own head, and his iniquity will come down upon his crown." We have seen these things fulfilled in deed with our own eyes, though those who come after us may well refuse to believe them even when they hear them told. In our own time, all who set themselves up as enemies of God's Church, the rulers and tyrants of this age, were tormented with scourges sent by God. Some suffered a rotting of the body, so that worms swarmed out of them while they were still alive, with an unbearable stench. Others were blinded while still living, so that they came to recognize the God-sent scourge that had overtaken them. They sang a recantation, confessed the God of the Church to be great and true and the only Lord, and gave orders, with great zeal, that the city of God against which they had once made war should be renewed and rebuilt. As for the next words, "With a violent wind you will shatter the ships of Tarshish" (or in Aquila, "With a scorching wind you shatter the ships of Tarshish"; or in Symmachus, "By a violent wind you will break the ships of Tarshish"), you will see on reflection that the ships of Tarshish are said in the history recorded in Kingdoms to have once brought great wealth to Solomon. In the same way, then, the passage hints through the shattered ships of Tarshish that the wealth and power of the kings mentioned earlier would be shattered, would sink wholesale into the depths, and would vanish completely. "As we have heard, so also have we seen in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God; God has founded it forever." Those who in the past heard only the prophetic words from the sacred readings, but now see with their own eyes the outcome of the predictions in the events themselves,

say: "As we have heard, so also [?]" … [?] "Many prophets and righteous men desired to see what you see," and, "But blessed are your eyes, because they see." Such words would suit us as well, who have seen similar things in our own times. These things were indeed fulfilled in the city mentioned before, which no man but God himself has founded forever. For its foundation is shown to be eternal, and its building to be established not by men but by God himself, above all when it remains unconquered and indestructible while so many enemies besiege it. "As is your name, O God, so also is your praise to the ends of the earth; your right hand is full of righteousness." Since his right hand, which does good and provides every blessing, is full of equity and righteousness, and there is no partiality with him, the Gospel was rightly preached to all the nations. So the Apostle says: "For I am not ashamed of the Gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For in it the righteousness of God is revealed." Consistent with this, the next words are: "Let Mount Zion be glad." This mountain, on which the Church had been founded, was also indicated in what went before. The rock and the mountain, then, was Christ himself. He rejoices, then, and is filled with all gladness over the great building raised upon him and over the invincible city, and the Lord who saves them rejoices together with those who are saved. And "the daughters of Judea exult because of the judgments of God." Who might these be but the apostolic souls and the whole company of the disciples and evangelists of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who came from the Jews? They indeed rejoiced and were filled with all exultation and delight because of God's righteous judgments, since through them the saving Gospel was preached to all the nations together and to all people. "Encircle Zion and embrace her; tell of her in her towers. Set your hearts on her strength, and divide up her strongholds, so that you may tell of it to another generation. For this is our God; he will shepherd us forever." Everything said before deals with the divinity of the one who has accomplished such great things among people. The present words, however, are addressed to certain persons, telling them to take charge of the city of God mentioned before by encircling it and embracing it with their hands, so that they might surround it on every side and guard it. To whom, then, is this command given? I think it is given to the divine powers and the holy angels who guard the Church of God and the godly commonwealth within her. To these the Holy Spirit speaks, saying: "Encircle Zion and embrace her," or "wall her round," as Symmachus has it. In place of PATROL. GR. XXIII.

"Tell of her in her towers," Aquila says, "Count her towers," and Symmachus, "Number them." For the most prominent and strongest buildings of the city above all, being superior to the rest and more essential, have been entrusted by number to these guards to keep with care, so that they may hand back safe and complete the number they received. You will understand the saying from the Savior's words to these same disciples and apostles, who stand out like towers and excel the rest of the building: "But even the hairs of your head are all numbered." For he who raised them to such a height and made them towers of his Church entrusts them to greater guardians, the holy angels, so that they may suffer nothing from their enemies. That is why, in the Acts of the Apostles, when the servant girl reported that it was Peter who had knocked at the door, the other disciples, knowing that each of the Savior's disciples had been entrusted to certain angels, said: "Perhaps it is his angel?" The Savior also teaches about the little ones in the Church, saying: "For their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven." Fittingly, then, the present passage gives these very angels the command: "Number her towers." Then next: "Set your hearts on her strength, and divide up her strongholds"; or in Symmachus, "Set your hearts on her rampart; measure out her palaces." The guards of the Church are commanded to do all these things, for "The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him and will deliver them." And what strongholds does he mean, if not those mentioned above: "God is known in her strongholds when he upholds her"? We said that the city means the whole godly commonwealth throughout the inhabited world, while her strongholds are the individual local churches. It is these individual churches, then, that the present passage commands them to divide up, for it wants to set each of the angels as guard over certain churches separately. Then he adds: "So that you may tell of it to another generation." For it belonged to angels to be able to recount God's mighty deeds to different generations. "And that this is God, our God forever and ever; he will shepherd us forever." For you may be guards, like keepers of a flock, but the shepherd of the flock would be someone else. And who is he, if not the one who said, "I am the good shepherd"?

FOR THE END, FOR THE SONS OF KORAH, PSALM 48. The sons of Korah had first set out the earlier matters in due order. They had announced the second matters as good news, and on top of these they had proclaimed the calling of the nations and passed on the teaching about the Church of God. After all this they had to bear solemn witness about the end of the present life and the divine judgment seat, in which God will bring every deed into judgment, and we will all stand

before the judgment seat of God, so that each may receive what was done through the body, according to what he has done, whether good or bad. So he must call all the nations to hear what is about to be said. Just as he summoned every race of people to salvation, he likewise calls all together to the teaching about the divine judgment, saying: "Hear this, all you nations; give ear, all who inhabit the world, both earthborn and sons of men, rich and poor together." Some nations are wilder and live in tents in the deserts, while others lead a settled civic life and live on farmed land. He therefore has to make a distinction. After the general call to the nations he introduces a particular class, those who inhabit the world, and so he says: "Give ear, all who inhabit the world." Aquila and Symmachus have "who inhabit the dwelling place," by which he means the cities, villages and houses into which their inhabitants retire. Then he divides the inhabitants of the earth again, saying: "both earthborn and sons of men." For he admits to the hearing not only the free but also the class of slaves, or else both those who lead a more rustic life and those who are otherwise well-born and have been given a liberal upbringing. Or else the "earthborn" are those who have chosen to live in the desert, and the "sons of men" are the more civilized. [?] Symmachus translated it this way: "Both mankind and, besides, the sons of each man," so that [?] the first indicates the whole human race in general [?], and the second each individual. "My mouth will speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart understanding. I will incline [?] my ear to a parable; I will open my riddle on the harp." These words can also be spoken by the apostles. He calls enigmatic sayings parables. Indeed, the Lord spoke to the crowds in parables and explained them to the apostles privately at home. In this sense the choir now carries on its lips the wisdom of God, Christ (for Christ was called the power of God and the wisdom of God), and says: "My mouth will speak wisdom." For they preached him to all people. [?] With their minds sharpened, they understood all of Christ's parables even before he explained them. That is why, after these parables, the Savior said: "Have you understood all these things?" And they said to him, "Yes." Their heart, then, meditated on understandings, and they opened these to those unable to follow, with the bodily instrument serving the soul that lives in it for this purpose. He took this instead of a harp to strike up these divine hymns, each part of it being skillfully [?]

"Why should I fear in an evil day? The iniquity of my heel will surround me." If the speaker is the Lord, you will find that his heel is Judas, the last part of the body and the one nearest the ground. For the body

of the Lord is the apostles. Why then should I fear the [?] of Judas [?] … "Like sheep they are laid in Hades; death will shepherd them." Having described what the ungodly do before death, he now says what they will suffer once they are in Hades itself. They will be death's flock, shepherded by it. Or, as Symmachus has it, "like sheep [?] they placed themselves in Hades." For they did not wish to be placed under the good shepherd, and for this reason they have become death's flock. Some he will lead away into the eternal fire, others to where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth, and others into the outer darkness. In place of "And their help will grow old in Hades, away from their glory," Aquila has: "And their

stamp—I will wear away Hades from their dwelling." They wiped out in themselves what is according to the image and likeness of God, and through wicked ways they put the forms and shapes of irrational beasts and reptiles upon their soul. This stamp, which they impressed on themselves, will be worn away in the dwelling of Hades. In Symmachus: "And Hades will wear out their strength, away from its honored dwelling." For whatever strength they thought they were gaining for themselves through the wickedness that had grown into them, Hades will wear out in its dwellings. And this is the end of the ungodly. But the godly, counted worthy at that time of the morning and of a new light, of the dawn, will rule over the ungodly; or, as Aquila has it, "will prevail," or as Symmachus has it, "will subject them to themselves." For there he will rescue the soul from the ungodly who humbled the upright here, so that it is not led away with the ungodly but is in other places and other flocks. "For his soul will be blessed in his life; he will praise you when you do him good." The righteous man blesses the Lord at all times, but the sinner gives praise only at the moment when some good comes to him from God, and blesses God then.

PSALM 49, OF ASAPH. The psalms headed "of Asaph" are twelve in all, and eleven of them run in sequence, beginning from the seventy-second. The present psalm was detached from these not without reason. The psalm before this one dealt with the judgment of God, and the present one does too, so it was fittingly placed after it. Moreover, it overturns the legislation given through Moses and hands down the form of the new covenant given to the nations. The same is true of the psalms of the sons of Korah. These too are twelve, but the first eight were placed in sequence, and the remaining four were detached from them and placed after the psalms of Asaph. Perhaps this is because nearly all the psalms of Asaph, so to speak, prophesied the rejection of Israel and its scattering among all the nations, after which the grace of God passed over to all the nations. So the remaining psalms of the sons of Korah followed, foretelling the calling of all the nations. "The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and has called the earth." The other three translated: "The mighty God, having spoken, called the earth." The Seventy called rulers and judges "gods," since judging is proper to God alone. Accordingly, in the eighty-first psalm, having prophesied, "God stood in the assembly of gods; in their midst he judges gods," he added, "How long will you judge unjustly?" So too the law declares: "You shall not revile gods, and you shall not speak evil of the rulers of your people." Those who have preserved what is according to the image might reasonably be called gods. Their God gathers the whole world to judgment. He is the Lord, the Word of God made man, who spoke through the Gospel. He calls everyone, but not everyone obeyed the Gos-

pel. Those who obeyed obtain what was promised, but those who reject grace are threatened [?] with fire. He will come at his glorious appearing from the heavenly Zion, of which Paul says: "But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother"; and, "You have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem." The "splendor of his beauty" is his glorious appearing as God, and this is also what "God will come manifestly" signifies. At his first coming he was judged by men and kept silent. Though he suffered so much, he did not retaliate, nor did he reveal his divinity to everyone. But then, it says, he will come manifestly and will not keep silent. The fire goes before him and purifies his kingdom, consuming all combustible matter, so that no wood, hay or straw may appear before his face. He will reject or accept, saying to some, "Come, you who are blessed by my Father," and to others, "Depart from me." "Fire will burn before him"; "I came to cast fire on the earth." Here he calls the teaching of the Word of God fire, because fire burns up wicked habits but tests the pure. That is why "around him is a fierce storm"; for all who want to live godly lives in Christ will be persecuted, and also, as he says, "In the world you will have tribulation." "He will summon the heaven above, and the earth, to judge his people. Gather to him his holy ones, who establish his covenant with sacrifices." Alternatively, he shows that the judgment of the former people is a separate one by summoning heaven and earth. For when he gave the law through Moses, he said: "I call heaven and earth to witness against you today"; and again, in the great song: "Give heed, O heaven, and I will speak; and let the earth hear the words of my mouth." So Isaiah too says: "Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: I have begotten sons and raised them up, but they have rejected me." Now, then, he will call on the same witnesses. In the Gospels the Savior separates his flock, that is, the members of the Church, placing the sheep on the right and the goats on the left. In the same way the same Lord now separates his people. The Hebrew and the other translators have "Gather to me." For as it is said in the Gospels, "And he will send his angels, and they will gather all the nations," so now too he gives the same command to the same angels. He wants his holy ones, who are to obtain what was promised, to be set apart first, before the ungodly. "Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?" The food of God is the food of which he said: "I was hungry and you gave me something to eat; I was thirsty and you gave me something to drink." Fed by these, I will say: "Whatever you did for one of the least of these, you did for me." One can also offer a spiritual sacrifice through words about God and through thanksgiving, and whenever someone promises God what is fitting and then

carries it out in deeds. For Scripture calls promises vows [?], as in the saying: "If you make a vow, do not be slow to pay it. It is better not to vow than to vow and not pay." So, having sown for righteousness, hope to reap the fruit of life. "But to the sinner God said: Why do you recite my statutes, and take up my covenant in your mouth?" The passage moves from the class of the righteous to the class of the wicked. For that class had something more, namely knowledge of the new covenant. He calls a "sinner" not someone who is a stranger to the Scriptures but a transgressor. And he rebukes him not for breaking sabbaths, sacrifices or rules about particular foods, but for breaking the natural laws, which made God's teachings senseless to him, for by sinning he cast them away. For it is a natural law that we must not do what we do not want to suffer. The godless idolaters are also adulterers, and those who steal the truth are also thieves. So at one point he says, "You were bold in wickedness," and at another, "You plotted deceitfully. You pretended to speak sincerely, as to brothers, while secretly slandering them. You even lay in wait for those born of the same mother as you," meaning the synagogue, or else the church. While you did this, I kept silent when I became man. Or else: "You went from bad to worse, despising my kindness, forbearance and patience, so I will bear it no longer. For you supposed that I approved of your deeds, or else that I remembered none of them. But I will rebuke you and set everything before your eyes, so that you may see it and be ashamed."

FOR THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID, 50. When Nathan the prophet came to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba. "Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy." He confesses that a great wound of the soul needs great mercy. "Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin." Look again to the mystery of Christ. The power of baptism surpasses the purification of the law and accomplishes the cleansing of the soul itself. For that purification was used for the purity of the [?] soul. "Against you alone have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged." He is not saying, "I did not wrong Uriah." He is saying that he had dared to commit the greatest lawlessness against God himself, after God had made him king instead of a shepherd, given him victory over his enemies and adorned him with every kind of blessing, and that he had repaid his benefactor in such a way. "In your sight" is also made plain in the history: "For what had been done," it says, "was evil in the sight of the Lord." Or else: "I thought I was someone, sheltered by you long ago. I thought that from then on I would be unshakable, saying in my prosperity, 'I shall never be moved.' That is why you turned away the

…your face from me, and [?] the one who has been taught by your mercy: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have laboured in vain.” “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me.” These words would be like those in Job: “Cursed be the day on which I was born, and the night in which they said, ‘Behold, a male.’” For why was it cursed, except that he was conceived in iniquities? It followed that a curse should accompany sin. Jeremiah used the same words, saying: “Cursed be the day on which I was born, and the night in which my mother conceived me.” For it would have been a blessed thing if the first woman had not, after her transgression, served corruptible birth at all, but had remained in paradise, made like the divine angels. But through the envy of the devil death entered into the world, and birth through blood and flesh served death, to keep the mortal race in existence. That is why conception too, as something subject to death, was disparaged by the blessed. Symmachus has: “Into injustice I was brought forth in travail, and in sins my mother bore me.” I was travailed over and carried in the womb, he says, so that I might pass into injustice, and, having come to be in sins, might be convicted. In this sense he says: I was not conceived in my mother's iniquities, nor did she conceive me in her own iniquities; rather, I was born into injustice, clothed in mortal flesh. And I say these things since you have loved the truth. “You will sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow.” Hyssop is a symbol of freedom from passion, and washing signifies knowledge. Through freedom from passion we are cleansed, and through knowledge we are made white. “Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities.” Alternatively: one whose soul has been cleansed from an evil conscience might say to God, “Your face, Lord, I will seek; do not turn your face away from me.” But one who sees the shameful wounds of his soul being laid bare rightly says to the great Judge: “Turn your face away from my sins,” but not from me myself; rather, heal me as one who is sick. “Restore to me the joy of your salvation.” Among the Hebrews a very great difference is shown between “your salvation,” the more common expression, and “your saving one.” For “your saving one” is written among them as Ieshuach, which plainly indicates the name of our Saviour Jesus, and all the translators render it consistently in this way, whereas “your salvation” is written Oisouath (1). “A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit; a broken and humbled heart God will not despise.” Another said: The sacrifice of praise befits the healthy, but for the sick the sacrifice is that of the humbled [?]

and broken heart. And since my heart has been crushed, as Symmachus puts it, I fittingly prayed for a clean heart within me, O God, in place of the crushed one; and in place of the broken spirit, as Symmachus has it, I said: “And renew a right spirit within my [?inward parts].” A broken spirit is one that breaks itself through confession, and such too is the heart that humbles itself through repentance. When it has become such after the swelling of sin, God will accept it in place of sacrifice. “Then you will be pleased with a sacrifice of righteousness, offering and whole burnt offerings.” But someone might object: how, having just said, “For if you had desired sacrifice, I would have given it,” does he now say, “Then you will be pleased with sacrifice,” as though God would accept sacrifice after the city was rebuilt? But he did not say simply “sacrifice”; he said “of righteousness.” For when you show favour to Zion and the walls of Jerusalem are built, such a sacrifice will be offered to you. The God-fearing commonwealth would bear the image of the heavenly city of God, and for this reason the Church of God also bears its name. By its walls he means the angels who fence it about, or else those who are ordained priests and fight in its defence. Instead of “you will be pleased with,” Symmachus said “you will accept.” The offering and the whole burnt offerings must also be understood as being of righteousness, and the calves as well. For all of them are carried out in righteousness, in the bloodless and spiritual sacrifices offered in the Church of God throughout the whole world. For elsewhere too it was said to the Jews through a prophet: “I take no pleasure in you, says the Lord Almighty, and I will not accept sacrifices from your hands. For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name has been glorified among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice.” This is what is now called a sacrifice of righteousness. It is also a sacrifice of praise, as he said earlier: “Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise.”

(1) FOR THE END. OF UNDERSTANDING. OF DAVID. PSALM 51. When Doeg the Idumean came and reported to Saul, and said to him: “David has come to the house of Ahimelech.” Psalm 33 was spoken by David when he changed his countenance before Abimelech, who sent him away, and he departed. This psalm would follow that one in the order of the history. For the Scripture of the Kingdoms says: “And one of Saul's servants was there on that day.” It marks the time at which David came to the house of Abimelech and ate the loaves of the presentation, having received them from the high priest. For at that very moment Doeg the Syrian, who tended Saul's mules, arrived ahead of him, came to Saul, and said: “I have seen the son of Jesse coming to Nob, to Abimelech the son of Ahitub, the priest, and all the sons of his father; and

he inquired of God for him and gave him provisions.” And the king sent to summon Abimelech the priest and all the sons of his father, the priests of [?] who were in Nob, and they all came to the king. Then, at Saul's command, that same Doeg killed the priests of the Lord, three hundred and five men who wore the ephod, and struck Nob, the city of the priests, with the edge of the sword, from man to woman, from infant to suckling, and calf and donkey and sheep. When David learned that these things had been done in this way, he utters the present words, which contain neither song nor hymn nor anything else of the kind. For how could anyone sing songs and psalms over the calamity of so many priests? That is why nothing of the sort is inscribed. Only “For the end” and “of understanding” are said, since the final words announce good things, where he says, “But I am like a fruitful olive tree,” and so on. And the meaning of the words it contains requires understanding from God. Earlier, when he was with Abimelech and tasted the priestly food, having changed his taste (or his manner, according to the rendering of the other translators), he sent up blessing and thanksgiving to God, saying: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall be continually in my mouth,” and so on. But now, when he learned of the deed of the slanderer Doeg, and how he had slain so many priests by a devilish act, he composes the present words as if addressed to him, saying: “Why do you boast in wickedness, O mighty one? All day long your tongue has devised lawlessness and injustice.” The words before us were spoken much earlier, in the time of the history, than Psalm 50. For they were both done and spoken while Saul was still alive and before David became king. But long afterwards, after the death of Saul and toward the end of his own reign, David makes the confession in Psalm 50, which he placed first because of its connection with Psalm 49, as has indeed been shown. The psalms from 51 up to 70, twenty in number and inscribed “of David,” have taken their subject from another starting point. At any rate they seem to have been spoken while Saul was still alive, before David became king. The present one was spoken while Saul was still living: “When Doeg the Idumean came and reported to Saul that David had come to the house of Abimelech.” Psalm 53 too was spoken “when the Ziphites came and said to Saul, ‘Is not David hiding among us?’” Psalm 55 is inscribed “When the Philistines seized him in Gath,” and this too was the time before David's reign, while Saul was still alive. Psalm 56 is inscribed: “Of David, when he fled from the face of Saul into the cave.” Likewise Psalm 58: “When,” it says, “Saul sent and watched his house in order to kill him.” Psalm 59, though spoken after the death of Saul,

when David was already reigning, was nonetheless also earlier than the affair of Uriah. This is indicated by the superscription, which shows the time when it says: “When he burned Mesopotamia of Syria and Syria of Zobah, and Joab returned and struck the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand.” These events precede in time the confession in Psalm 50. Moreover, Psalm [?62] was spoken by David when he was in the wilderness of Idumea, while Saul was still alive. And see how nearly all the psalms of David in the second part of the book of Psalms, except Psalm 50, are ones spoken by him long before the time of the affair of Uriah. The first part of the same book, from the first psalm up to the fortieth, had the opposite order, for that part contained the psalms that came after the confession of Psalm 50. Thus the third psalm was spoken by David when he fled from the face of Absalom his son, and he fled from his son after the story of Uriah. In Psalm 6, too, he lamented over that same deed, saying: “I am weary with my groaning; every night I will wash my bed, I will drench my couch with my tears.” And Psalm 7, spoken “concerning the words of Cushi the son of Jemini,” would belong to the same period. For Cushi, who had been David's chief companion, joined Absalom. Moreover, Psalm 17 has been shown to have been spoken toward the end of David's life. Psalm 37 too, inscribed “For remembrance,” has the same sense as Psalm 6 and begins with the same words, saying: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor chasten me in your wrath.” As it goes on, it makes the same confession as the one in Psalm 50 [?], among other places in the words: “For my iniquities have gone over my head… My wounds have grown foul and festered because of my folly.” And if you gather them up for yourself, you will find that most of what is in the first part of the Psalms was spoken after the time of the story of Uriah, while what comes after Psalm 50 precedes the affair of Uriah in time. Why, then, were the psalms that are first in time not placed first in chronological sequence? Instead, those spoken first, while Saul was still alive, are in the second part of the Psalms, and in the first part are those that are later [?] in time. I think the book has taken this order so that the discourse should not move from better things to worse. For “For the end, do not destroy” seems to have been observed in the ordering of the psalms as well. That is why the gloomier psalms were placed first, so that the more cheerful ones might be kept for second place, and the worse might be covered over and blotted out by the better ones in the second part. It is also likely that David wished to cover his later offence by his earlier good deeds. But someone might say that

out of an excess of piety he placed his own confessions first, since “the righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech.” But now that we have exercised ourselves so much over the order that has been given, it is time to move on to the words of Psalm 51 before us. He writes the present words, then, having learned what Doeg the Syrian had done in his slanders against him. That is why he addresses him directly, saying, “Why do you boast in wickedness, O mighty one?” Or else he addresses the devil who was at work in Doeg. For he was well aware of the one who always opposed him and made war on him continually, sometimes through Saul, now through Doeg, and at other times in other ways through others. The one who is weak, feeble and slight in wickedness, because the better disposition prevails in him, will hide his face when he sins, being weaker in wickedness. Stung by his conscience, he may repent and devise a remedy for his own wickedness through confession and sincere repentance. But the one who is mighty in wickedness is puffed up by it and boasts of it, priding himself as if on some great achievement. And the present text seems to me to depict a disposition opposite to that of the one who made his confession earlier, in Psalm 50. For there, having slipped once into wickedness, he at length repented and beat his breast in confession, bewailing his own evils [?]; but the present one, being in wickedness

“And he will scrape you away from your tent, and uproot you from the land of the living for ever,” so that the righteous, seeing it, may always fear, and may laugh at him, saying: “Behold the man who did not make God his strength, but trusted in the abundance of his wealth and made himself strong in his own ruin.” These things are said as if to Doeg, who was a Syrian by race but lived in the midst of Israel, and who perhaps even came along with the crowd to the tent of God and pretended to be devout. But they are also said to everyone who is mighty in wickedness and uses his tongue instead of a sword to destroy souls. Such a person the husbandman of souls will pluck out like some bitter and destructive root, even if for a short time he seems to be planted in God's tabernacle and in his Church. Plucked out and cast far from the tabernacle of the saints, such a person will lie there as a pitiable spectacle for the benefit and correction of those who see him. Having seen with their own eyes God's severe judgement against such a person, they will be filled with anguish and will take care not to fall into the same things. Then, recalling the former boastfulness of the one mighty in wickedness, his loftiness and arrogance, and seeing also the humiliation and destruction that overtook him afterwards, they will consider him a laughingstock, seeing from what heights to what depths he has fallen. And they will accept God's judgement, confessing that it is just. Then they will also go over the causes for which he suffered these things,

the ungodly man, and so justify God's judgement. For he ought not to have been proud of his wealth, nor to have exalted himself over the vanity of the present life, but should have made God alone his hope and helper and not wavered in this hope. Instead he abandoned the good anchor of his own soul and hung his hopes on vain wealth, and so made a mockery of himself, earning nothing but laughter for his vain and foolish boasting. “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God; I have hoped in the mercy of God for ever, and for ever and ever.” From what has been said we have learned what end the one mighty in wickedness will meet. But I, says David, having been taught these things by the Holy Spirit, would never be lifted up by an abundance of passing wealth, nor by the vanity of mortal life, for “vanity of vanities, all is vanity.” Rather, fleeing the way of the one mighty in wickedness, I would sharpen my tongue and my words not for the destruction of others, but for the benefit of souls and for the service of saving words. And in my other deeds too I would so flourish and bear fruit that my soul might be compared to an evergreen and fruitful plant planted in the house of God. Therefore I say: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God”; or, as Symmachus has it: “But I am like a flourishing olive tree in the house of God.” For I did not turn away from the house of God; rather, planted within it as in God's field, and enjoying the streams of the spring in the house of God, I became fruitful and evergreen, after the example of the olive tree, which is counted among the evergreens. Note that when David said these things, he was neither in Jerusalem, which the children of the Jews supposed to be the house of God, for it had not yet been built, nor even in the tabernacle constructed by Moses, which was still among the Jews at that time. For, fleeing Saul, he was living among other peoples. Nevertheless he knew that he was planted in the house of God, understanding the house of God as the God-fearing commonwealth. And since he was fruitful, bearing not bitter fruits but sweet ones full of great kindness, he fittingly compared himself to a fruitful olive tree, an image that signifies mercy toward one's neighbours and kindness toward all. As one laden with so many good things, then, he fittingly adds: “I have hoped in the mercy of God for ever, and for ever and ever.” For the end of the one mighty in wickedness showed his uprooting and disappearance, since the root that bears bitter fruits had to be plucked out by the wise husbandman of all things. But the one who, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, hoped in the mercy of God for ever and ever, gains immortality and eternal life from the good hope, from which he will never fall away. For hope, according to the Apostle, does not put to shame. Then, having pictured for himself good hopes as the reward of good fruits,

he attributes the cause to the giver of all good things, saying: “I will confess to you for ever, because you have done it.” For it was not I, he says, who made myself like a fruitful olive tree; you made me so, for the grace comes from you. Therefore I will never cease to acknowledge my gratitude to you and to confess you. And having once hoped in the mercy of God, “I will wait for his name.” For once the good hope has been set before us, we need endurance. Therefore, he says, I will wait for your name, “because it is good before your holy ones”; or, as Symmachus has it, “because your name is good in the presence of your holy ones.” Knowing, then, that it is good and productive of good things, not for those mighty in wickedness, nor for those cast out from among the living, but for the holy, I will rightly wait for your name, confident that I shall never fall away from your mercy. So, then, I have hoped in him for ever, and for ever and

FOR THE END. FOR MAELETH. OF UNDERSTANDING. OF [DAVID]. The fool said in his heart: “There is no God.” They have become corrupt and abominable in iniquities; there is none who does good. Psalm 50 contained the confession of a disposition that repents of its sins; the psalm that follows it contained the madness of the godless disposition that is mighty in wickedness, and showed what kind of end awaited this one and what kind awaited the former. For to the one who boasted of his own evils it was said: “Therefore God will destroy you for ever; he will pluck you out and remove you from your dwelling.” But in the person of the one who had confessed, there followed: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God; I have hoped in his mercy for ever.” The present text is not a psalm, for it is not inscribed as such, nor is it a song or anything of that kind; it contains a prophecy of the saving appearance of God, which many prophets and righteous men longed to see. The present text, then, speaks over the fall of all humanity, praying as if over a common shipwreck and saying: “Who will give out of Zion the salvation of Israel? When the Lord turns back the captivity of his people, Jacob will rejoice and Israel will be glad.” For it was through the saving appearance of God that the one who confessed and declared his own sins was to obtain cleansing, and the godless disposition among humans, mighty in wickedness, could obtain healing in no other way than through the Saviour alone, who is able to heal even the incurable passions of the soul. Let this suffice concerning the sequence. Note that the present prophecy now appears for the second time in the book of Psalms: in the first part as Psalm 13, and in the second part here. For Psalm 13 is almost word for word the same as the present one from beginning to end, beginning with “The fool said in his heart: There is no God,” and ending with “Who will give out of Zion the salvation of Israel? When the

…when the Lord turns back the captivity of his people, Jacob shall rejoice and Israel shall be glad. Only a few words make the difference between the two psalms. The title of the thirteenth said, “To the end, for David.” The present one has the same wording but adds, “for Maeleth, of understanding.” Aquila translated this “on a dance,” Symmachus “by a chorus,” Theodotion “for the dancing,” and the fifth edition the same. “Of understanding” is put there of necessity, since we need understanding to grasp what the dance or chorus indicated by the title is, and why a prophecy already spoken once in the thirteenth psalm has been taken up here a second time. “To the end,” which appears in both, would indicate the time when the things prophesied were to be fulfilled. At the consummation of the age the Salvation of God appeared to people on earth and formed a chorus, gathered from all the nations in his Church, to sing hymns and doxologies to his Father. So the word fittingly urges us to understand this chorus. And notice the paradox. The title says “for the chorus” or “for the dance,” yet the psalm shows no one on earth who is good, no one who does kindness, not even one. It goes on: “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the sons of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands and seeks God. All have turned aside, together they have become worthless; there is no one who does good, not even one.” If human affairs were such that not one good person was found among the sons of men, how can the title be said to be “for the chorus”? But you will say that since all had turned aside, not even one excepted, and those on earth were corrupt and had become abominable in their iniquities, the prophet fittingly prayed in what follows: “Who will give out of Zion the salvation of Israel? When the Lord turns back the captivity of his people, Jacob shall rejoice and Israel shall be glad.” For by the foreknowledge of the prophetic spirit he perceived that through the Salvation the people's captivity would be turned back and set free from the dominion of their enemies. When this was accomplished, God's chorus would be formed out of the very people freed from captivity. So it is fitting that these words are referred “to the end,” and that the psalm is said to be “for Maeleth,” that is, “for the chorus.” It is as if it had been translated more plainly, “for those who will be freed from captivity.” This is also why it directs us to understanding. The prophecy is said to be “for David” because it was spoken by him, and so the other translators give the title “of David.” And one may say that David himself, who prophesied, “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God; I have hoped in the mercy of God,” knew that he would obtain mercy in no other way than through the prophesied Salvation. That is why in the fiftieth psalm he said, “Restore to me the joy (Ps. [?])

of your salvation,” and in the present one, “Who will give out of Zion the salvation of Israel?” For he prayed that the common good might be given to him as well. The thirteenth psalm also follows closely on the one before it, the twelfth. In the twelfth the same author prayed, “How long, O Lord, will you forget me forever? How long will you turn your face away from me?” He went on with the verses that follow and then added, “But I have hoped in your mercy. My heart shall rejoice in your salvation.” Since he had mentioned the Salvation in the twelfth, in the thirteenth he goes on to say, “Who will give out of Zion the salvation of

The title, then, which requires much understanding, was said to be “for the chorus” that was to be formed among people through the Salvation. This was accomplished in fact after the appearing of our Saviour Jesus Christ. Through him a single chorus was formed for God throughout the whole inhabited world, such as had never existed before: the catholic Church of God, founded on the unbreakable and unshakeable rock of the saving word. But the words at the beginning of the prophecy present something like a shipwreck of all people on earth. It said: “The fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God.’ They are corrupt and have become abominable in iniquity; there is no one who does good.” The same was shown in the thirteenth psalm too, especially in the Hebrew language, where both psalms have the same words and the same letters, even though our translation seems to have some words changed. Instead of “They have corrupted and become abominable in iniquity,” the thirteenth has “They are corrupt and have become abominable in their practices.” Again, instead of “There is no one who does good,” it has “There is no one who does kindness.” The change comes from the translators. Through these words the passage signifies the falling away from the common notions about God, and the impious and godless reasoning that prevailed over all humanity before the appearing of our Saviour. God had sown good seeds of the knowledge of himself in the common notions, yet such perversion took hold of every fool among humankind that he adopted a godless opinion in his own reasoning and thought that there is no God and that God does not exist in the universe. Such a man was truly godless and utterly foolish. He held that there is no providence overseeing all things, no universal mind, no being beyond the universe that is the maker of all things. The rest of humankind gave themselves over to the polytheistic error of idolatry and fell into godlessness by another kind of folly. They too corrupted the sound seeds about God that had been sown in them, and handed themselves over to the abomination of dead idols, worshipping things without honour that were truly abominations. Hence it is said, “They have corrupted and become abominable in iniquity.” Symmachus rendered this more clearly: “They were corrupted and practised abomination with injustice.” For they

practised abomination, turning things that do not exist into idols as though they did exist, with the utmost injustice. What injustice could be worse than this, by which, “claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed beasts, and of reptiles,” in the words of the holy Apostle? Then, acting in keeping with their godless and perverse practices, they fell into every kind of wicked living. Hence the next words: “There is no one who does good. God looked down from heaven upon the sons of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God. All have turned aside, together they have become worthless; there is no one who does kindness, not even [one].” The fool deceived himself, saying in his heart that there is no God, and all the rest became abominable by practising abomination. But the true word teaches that the God and Lord over all not only exists and holds all things together, but also watches over and visits not only the universal parts of the whole but also the particular ones, including the sons of men who spend their lives on earth. In his providence for the sons of men he comes down from his own greatness. As if from the highest summit of his supreme power, which is above all things, he descends to examine the people on earth, looking to see whether anyone anywhere understands how his providence governs, and whether anyone has set all the deceits of life in second place and taken up the search for him. He searched and found no such person, because all had turned aside and together had become worthless, so that he found no one doing good, not even one. So he fittingly threatens those who had corrupted them, saying next: “Will not all the workers of iniquity know, those who eat up my people as they eat bread? They did not call upon the Lord; there they feared with fear where there was no fear.” God looked down from his own dwelling, that is, from heaven, where he is said to dwell because of those there who receive his kingdom. He saw that all the sons of men had become worthless and had turned aside from the straight and right way. So, like a good shepherd who cares for his flock among humankind, he fittingly threatens those responsible for their perversion, saying: “Will not the workers of iniquity know, those who eat up my people as they eat bread?” It seems to me that these words are said about the opposing powers, the invisible enemies and foes of the human race. They made the human race food for themselves and devoured people's souls like fierce beasts, as the prophecies say: “Those who devour my people with their whole
These very ones, he says, have now done these things against the people and against my rational flock among humankind, as though they had not set God before their eyes (PATROL. [?])

Will they go on doing these things forever? Granted that for now they have not called upon God, and they work what is contrary and hostile to God. Will they not come to know, at some time, the punishment that will come upon them? Yes, there will be a time when they will fear with fear. What time would this be but the one when the Salvation shines forth? Then fear will no longer come upon my flock, but fear will seize those fierce beasts, the unseen and invisible demons, there where there will be no fear. At that time those who are worthy of good things will have no fear. But on those who now raise themselves up against my people will fall the fear of the wrath that will pursue them, which will come and scatter the bones of those who please men. In this they will be put to shame, since then the judge of all will treat them as nothing. In place of “For God has scattered the bones of those who please men,” Symmachus translated as follows: “For God will scatter the bones of those encamped around you; you will be put to shame, because God has rejected them.” Aquila keeps the same sense: “For God scattered the bones of those encamped against you; you put them to shame, because God cast them off.” The sense of the passage shows that the powers of those plotters against the people mentioned above, the invisible enemies and unseen foes, will be destroyed. The scattered bones of the enemies would be the powers of their wickedness, which the passage threatens to scatter at the time it indicates. They will also be put to shame then, when God rejects them or treats them as nothing and shows that they are nothing. The Word of God, the guardian of humankind, fittingly made these threats. He looked down from heaven upon the sons of men and searched among them whether anyone understands or seeks God, and found no one. Instead he found that all, through the plotting of their enemies, had turned aside and become worthless, so that not even one doer of good works remained. The thirteenth psalm contains the first part in the same way, but what follows is different. In the thirteenth these words are added: “For God is in the righteous generation; you have shamed the counsel of the poor, but the Lord is his hope.” Here, however: “For God has scattered the bones of those who please men; they were put to shame, because God treated them as nothing.” The thirteenth received its own interpretation in its proper place. Our account of the present passage, as it occurred to us, is set before the reader. “Who will give out of Zion the salvation of Israel? When God turns back the captivity of his people, Jacob shall rejoice and Israel shall be glad.” Through the revelation of the Holy Spirit the prophet had great visions of the destruction of the enemies of the human race, and he then added, “Who will give out of Zion the Salvation?” It is as if he said, “Who will grant that these things at last come to pass in deed?” For there is no other way [?] for freedom from evils to be secured for the

sons of men than through the appearing of the Salvation of God alone, of which all the Scriptures speak at length. So he prays: “Who will give out of Zion the salvation of Israel?” We have often said that the Christ of God, our Saviour and Lord, is foretold in this way in the prophecies, for they are accustomed to call him Salvation. They proclaimed beforehand that he would be made known to all the nations, both elsewhere and in the words: “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth. Sing to the Lord, bless his name. Proclaim the good news of his salvation from day to day. Declare his glory among the nations.” And again: “Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done marvellous things. The Lord has made known his salvation; before the nations he has revealed his righteousness.” And Isaiah says, “The Lord will reveal his holy arm before all the nations,” and so on. We have often cited before the fulfilment of these words, attested by Simeon. He took our Saviour and Lord Jesus Christ in his arms while he was still an infant, and cried out: “Now, Master, you dismiss your servant in peace, according to your name, for my eyes have seen your Salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all the nations.” These things were fulfilled in the Gospels. But the prophets of old foresaw the future by the Spirit and came to love and long for those good things. They cried out in their prayers, at one time saying, “Show us, Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation,” and at another time praying, “Who will give out of Zion the salvation of Israel?” What would happen when the Salvation appeared the passage then sets out: “When the Lord turns back the captivity of his people, Jacob shall rejoice and Israel shall be glad.” You see how it foretells that when the Salvation appeared, the captivity would be turned back. This agrees with the saving voice heard in the prophet who speaks in his person: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the poor, to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind.” The Saviour himself took this passage in his hands in the synagogue of the Jews, read it through, and set his seal on it, saying, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” So once the captivity was released, choruses were formed from then on out of those who had been captive, sending up hymns to the King who set them free. And then Jacob shall rejoice and Israel shall be glad. Then, but when? At the time of the freedom of God's people that is indicated here. So you should understand that the people set free is one group, and those who rejoice at its salvation are another. This is the meaning suggested when the passage says, “When God turns back the captivity of his people,” and so on.

For these will be glad when the Lord turns back the captivity of his people. Two orders, then, are presented here: those who did not fall into captivity, and those who did fall into it but obtained freedom through the Salvation. You will say, then, that the prophets and righteous men of old, the patriarchs, and all who remained pure of idolatrous error, are those who did not fall captive to the spiritual enemies. And you will say that those who suffered captivity are these: those of the nations who were turned to godlessness and enslaved to polytheistic error, or those of the circumcision who were sold through their own sins, and in short all those of whom it was said above, “The fool said in his heart, ‘There is no God’; they have corrupted and become abominable in iniquity.” When these are set free through the shining forth of the Salvation, the prophetic chorus that has long been at rest with God will rejoice and be glad, sharing the joy of those freed through the Salvation as of its own members. This chorus is properly called Jacob and Israel because of the realities that the names signify.

TO THE END, AMONG HYMNS, OF UNDERSTANDING, FOR DAVID, WHEN THE ZIPHITES CAME AND SAID TO SAUL: “IS NOT DAVID HIDDEN AMONG US?” PSALM 53. O God, save me by your name, and judge me by your power. The psalms in the first part of the book of Psalms were shown, from the title set over each, to have been spoken after David's fall in the matter of Uriah. In the same way, the titles over each psalm here indicate the time when they were spoken. The present one, for example, refers us at once to the first book of Kingdoms, so that we may learn from there on what occasion David sent up this hymn. The history runs as follows: “And David stayed in the wilderness of Masedek, in the narrow places; and he stayed on the mountain in the wilderness of Ziph.” Then it tells how Jonathan son of Saul came to him and said: “Do not be afraid, for the hand of Saul my father shall not find you. You will be king over Israel, and I will be second to you, and Saul my father knows this.” The two of them made a covenant before the Lord, and David stayed there, and Jonathan went to his house. After this it adds: “And the Ziphites went up from the parched land to Saul at the hill, saying, ‘Is not David hidden among us in Mesara, in the narrow places, at the new place?’” When Saul learned this, he set out in pursuit of David, and he was soon close to taking him, for it is written: “And Saul heard, and pursued David into the wilderness of Maon.
