Saul and his men went along one side of this mountain, and David was taking cover so as to get away from Saul. Saul and his men were closing in on David and

his men to seize them. And a messenger came to Saul, saying, ‘Hurry and come, for the Philistines have attacked the land.’ So Saul turned back from pursuing David and went to meet the Philistines.” This much comes from the history. After these events, when he had been saved from Saul's hand, David committed the present hymn to writing, marking the occasion and indicating what happened through the title. This is why he also urges us to understand its contents, saying, “To the end, among hymns, of understanding, for David.” Aquila has, “For the one who gives victory, in psalms, of the skilled one, of David.” Symmachus has, “A victory song on psalteries, concerning understanding, of David.” For even when he was fleeing and making for the wilderness, he took the psaltery with him in place of a protective amulet, using it and the hymns sent up through it to God. He used songs and spiritual psalms in place of sacrifice, and instead of fragrant incense he performed spiritual worship through prayers. So, when the Ziphites came and said to Saul, “Is not David hidden among us?”, David learned of it, either by revelation of the prophetic spirit or from one of those who usually carried such reports. At once he took the psaltery in his hands and through it offered God the rational sacrifice, saying the present words. In them he asks to be saved by God in no other way than through his name. That is why he says, “O God, save me by your name,” for he knew that there is a name that is above every name. In incantations against venomous reptiles there are certain words and names that show such power that they put the most fearsome reptiles to sleep and even kill them. In the same way he knew that the name above every name brings salvation to those worthy of salvation and drives away the enemy and opposing powers. He wished, then, to be saved in the name of God, but not without judgment. He wished it only if he were found worthy of salvation. So he adds, “And by your power you will judge me,” or in the other translators' words, “you will plead my cause.” For first he asks to be judged and to have his case tried against those who were driving him out or had slandered him. Then, if he proved to be the one wronged, he asks to receive vindication from the judge, who punishes wrongdoers. Having said this, he adds, “O God, hear my prayer; give ear to the words of my mouth.” It is as if he were pleading his case before the one who judges between him and those who wrong him. So that his plea may be accepted, he sends up the prayer, which he also asks to have heard, saying, “O God, hear,” and so on. What the prayer intended, and what plea it made, he sets out next:

“For strangers have risen up against me, and the mighty have sought my life, and they have not set God before them.” This was his plea. And see how he does not draw out his words at length. Since he is speaking to God, who knows all things, he only reminds him, and says nothing of the long account of what happened. Perhaps by “strangers” he was hinting at the Ziphites, who to

[?] … to Saul, slandering him? And who were "the mighty" who sought his soul, if not Saul himself and those with him, who, "not setting God before them," hounded a man who had done them no wrong, deceiving themselves into thinking that they could do something against him even against the will of God? This was the conduct of men who had not set God before them. "These things were written," says the Apostle, "for our admonition," so that we might become imitators of the saints whenever we fall into similar circumstances. For there is never a time when all who wish to live godly lives are not persecuted, and hated with an unjust hatred by those who choose the opposite way of life. And the present passage is indeed necessary for our instruction, so that we too may chant these words over ourselves like a charm, sending up such words to God whenever we fall among enemies and are plotted against by them, slandered and endangered. We may be confident that the words of the prayer will not be idle, but will bring us great benefits, just as they did for those who first prayed them. Indeed, as soon as David had prayed these words, he immediately found God listening and was granted his help. For when he was on the very point of being caught and handed over into Saul's hands, he was saved by God beyond all expectation, when a message called Saul away to other business, according to the narrative already cited. Therefore he says next: "For behold, God helps me; the Lord is the protector of my soul. He will turn the evils back upon my enemies; and in your truth destroy them." Pause. The pause marks a change of thought. For the earlier words were sent up to God as a prayer, but what he now adds he says prophetically, foretelling salvation for the one who prayed and downfall for the enemies from whom he prayed to be rescued. These things he prophesies by the Holy Spirit. What concerns himself he indicates in the words "For behold, God helps me; the Lord is the protector of my soul"; what concerns his adversaries—whether the Ziphites who had slandered him to Saul, or certain spiritual and invisible enemies who envied his progress in the ways of God and for that reason plotted against him—he indicates in the words "He will turn the evils back upon my enemies; and in your truth destroy them." According to Symmachus he says: "He will repay evils to those who wall me in; in your truth silence them." And see whether this does not agree with the narrative. For when he wished to hide among them, the Ziphites, as if stripping him bare and walling him in, denounced him to Saul, using slanderous words against him. That is why, it seems, he was alluding to them when he said: "He will repay evils to those who wall me in, and in your truth silence them." For silence would be good for them, so that they would not use such slanders against me. And it was most fitting that he named God the protector—or, according to Symmachus, the "support"—of his own soul. For since

above, "the mighty" sought his soul, intending to plot not so much against his body as against his soul, it was natural that he too should name the Lord the protector of his own soul. For he cared nothing for his body, nor for his external possessions, nor for this passing life, but only for his own soul. "I will sacrifice to you willingly; I will confess your name, O Lord, for it is good." In the first part he sent up petition and supplication to God and set out his plea of innocence; in the second, filled with the Spirit, he foretells both what would happen to himself and what would befall his enemies; and then, next and in due order, in the third part he promises to offer God sacrifices and thanksgiving for the benefits he had received. For as one who had been saved and freed from the plots of his enemies—and not only that, but who had also looked upon the destruction of his enemies—he promises to sacrifice and to confess the name of the Lord. And he foretells this, prophesying before the outcome of events. For when the Ziphites came to Saul and said, "Look, David is hiding among us," and the story concerning him and those who had slandered [?] him was only just beginning, then he foretells the end of the events, anticipating what would happen later as though it had already happened. Therefore he says: "For you have rescued [?] me from every affliction, and my eye has looked upon my enemies." These things happened later; yet by the foreknowledge of the Holy Spirit he announces them as already done, and gives thanks for them, and promises to sacrifice and to confess the Lord, saying: "I will sacrifice to you willingly." Aquila has: "With a freewill offering I will sacrifice to you." For since he was homeless, without city or hearth, spending his days in the wilderness, he found a new kind of sacrifice. And what was it? "With a freewill offering," he says, "I will sacrifice to you." For the willingness and the resolve with which I will offer the sacrifice to you are enough. For he was well aware that God rejects sacrifices made with blood and the slaughter of animals, but welcomes the rational sacrifice offered through praise, since he had already learned the words: "Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Lord." This sacrifice, then, he says, I will offer you willingly, [?] dedicating to you my will and my resolve, and offering you thanksgiving itself in place of sacrifice. Therefore he adds next: "I will confess your name, O Lord, for it is good"—here "confession" is very plainly used in the sense of thanksgiving. For because he had been rescued from every affliction and his eye had looked upon his enemies, for these things he sends up thanksgiving and promises to render the freewill sacrifices.
"Give ear, O God, to my prayer, and do not disregard my supplication." As regards the

history, the present words might seem to have been spoken by David at the time when he was on the run, fleeing from the presence of Saul and living in the wilderness. Indeed, he says further on: "Behold, I have fled far away, and lodged in the wilderness." And since Saul and his accomplices were plotting against him to the point of death, he might also have said in his own person: "I was grieved in my brooding, and troubled by the voice of the enemy and by the oppression of the sinner. For they turned lawlessness upon me, and in anger they bore a grudge against me." It is not difficult, then, to fit these words to the person of David; but not so what follows, where he adds: "For I have seen lawlessness and contradiction in the city; day and night it will go around it upon its walls, and lawlessness and toil are in its midst. And usury and deceit have not departed from its streets. For if an enemy had reproached me, I would have borne it," and so on. For which city he means, in which he beheld what he says he saw, no one could say from the history. And who was this man he addressed, saying: "But you, man of like soul, my leader and my acquaintance, who together with me made sweet the food"? For if I had suffered these things from an enemy, he says, or if someone who admitted that he hated me had done them, it would have been nothing surprising; but as it is, you—neither a hater nor an enemy, but an intimate and a friend, of like soul with me, appointed leader by me, honoured with a place at a common table, sharing equally with me in one and the same entrance and prayer in the house of God—have you dared such things against me? I do not see what reason there could be for David to say this in his own person. For Saul was not of like soul with him, nor a friend, nor, as Symmachus puts it, "of like ways." For what likeness of ways could there be between two lives so utterly different? Nor was Saul ever of like soul with David, nor are they ever recorded as having gone into the house of God in harmony. On the contrary, Saul plainly appears to have been David's enemy all along; that is why David naturally fled from him and hid, guarding himself against an open enemy. Nor, again, could one fit what is said about this city to the history of David. For in what city did he see, as he says, lawlessness and contradiction, not only by day but also by night, and toil and labour, injustice and usury never departing from its streets? For Saul's city was said to be Ramah, and his residence Gibeah, since Jerusalem had not yet come under Israel but was still held by foreigners.

And as for David's seeming to utter curses, saying, "Let death come upon them, and let them go down alive into Hades," how could this agree with the solemn praise of his celebrated virtue, of which he is recorded as saying: "If I have repaid with evil those who repaid me, then let me fall empty before my enemies"? For to pray such curses upon one's enemies would not befit the forbearing David, who always honoured and revered Saul, so much so that he did not dare to lay hands on him even when he once had

him in his power, as the history itself shows. And further on he adds: "His words were softer than oil, yet they are darts." Whom, then, could one point to as having done this to David? From all this I conclude that there is no room for referring the present words to the person of David. Rather, I think they were spoken by prophetic power and are shown to have been fulfilled in our Saviour and Lord alone, when the rulers of the Jewish nation gathered together in Jerusalem and held a council and deliberated how they might destroy him. In that council some voted for his death, while others spoke against it, as Nicodemus did when he said: "Does our law condemn a man without first hearing from him?" These things, then, the Holy Spirit foretells prophetically through the present words, saying: "For I have seen lawlessness and contradiction in the city day and night." And the Gospel scripture clearly bears witness to the prophecy, applying to the traitor Judas the words: "If an enemy had reproached me, I would have borne it; and if one who hated me had boasted against me, I would have hidden from him. But you, man of like soul," and so on. Since, then, the sequence of the words is shown to have been fulfilled in no other way than through what was done to the Saviour, and since the testimony of the Gospel's citation refers the part of the reading quoted above to the traitor, it would be consistent for us too to take the present prophecy as referring to the time of the Saviour's passion, and to show that each of the things it contains reached fulfilment at the time of the plot against our Saviour. The heading, then, here too rouses us to understand its contents, and points us to "the end," because these things were fulfilled in deed at the consummation of the age. It is also said to be "in hymns"—or, according to Aquila, "in psalms," or, according to Symmachus, "with psalteries"—since the end of the Saviour's passion was attended by hymns and psalteries and songs, on account of his resurrection and of the salvation of those redeemed through it. So much for the heading. As for the prophecy, it asks God to give ear to the speaker, and to grant him this first; then, second, to take notice of the petition and supplication sent up in the prayer and not to disregard it; and third, to look upon the condition of the one sending up the prayer, and so to deem him worthy of his hearing. Therefore he adds: "Attend to me and hear me." For the one sending up the prayer, as it were, appeals to God by presenting himself and saying to God, "Attend to me"; and he sets out his own condition in what follows, saying: "I was grieved in my brooding, and troubled by the voice of the enemy and by the oppression of the sinner." For he shows God his grief and his trouble, and what he calls his "brooding," as things worthy of his regard. Therefore, he says, attend to these things—how I was grieved, how I was troubled, how I am filled with brooding—and accepting them, hear me. The prophet says

these things by the divine Spirit, seeing as already present what the Jews were going to dare against the Son of God; and at this he remained confounded and troubled, filled with grief and helplessness, which he called "brooding." So he grieved and was troubled and brooded, helpless and at a loss over the outrages that were being dared, which he recounts a little later, saying, "I have seen lawlessness and contradiction in the city," and so on. These things came to pass in deed only later, but the prophet foresaw them by the Holy Spirit, and so he grieved and was troubled and brooded, filled with despondency over those who dared such things. Therefore he asks God to look upon his condition, saying: "Give ear, O God, to my prayer, and do not disregard my supplication; attend to me and hear me." Being in such a condition, he made his request, saying next: "Drown, O Lord, and divide their tongues." By these words he begged that their agreement against the Saviour might be scattered, and that their boasting and the swelling of their arrogance might be humbled, so that they might not be ruined [?] by adding to their evils. Since his requests were reasonable, he asked in his petition not to be disregarded; but he was also filled with grief and trouble and brooding, saying: "by the voice of the enemy and by the oppression of the sinner"—that is, of the hostile and sinful people; for those who dared such things caused oppression to the prophetic spirit. Then he adds next: "For they turned lawlessness upon me, and in anger they bore a grudge against me," making his own the outrages committed against the Saviour. These words, among others, can also be spoken in the person of the Saviour: "For they turned lawlessness upon me, and in anger they bore a grudge against me"; or, according to Symmachus: "For they charged me with impiety, and opposed me in anger." "My heart was troubled within me, and the fear of death fell upon me," and the rest. The prophet confesses that he suffered all this because he had foreseen by the prophetic spirit the city described next, filled with lawlessness and contradiction, toil and labour and injustice, and had seen the man of like soul with our Saviour, his acquaintance, treating him as enemies and foes would. For in these words he shows God his compassion and the reasonable trouble he endured, of which he spoke above—"I was grieved in my brooding, and was troubled"—and now again: "My heart was troubled within me." According to Aquila: "My heart was in labour within me"; according to Symmachus: "My heart was twisting within me." And the fear of death fell upon him too: either of the Saviour's death, at which the prophet was filled with fear, being moved by human reasoning, or of the death of the souls that were going to perish because of such outrages. And fear and trembling also fell upon the prophet out of his surpassing reverence, as he saw the Beloved of God suffering such things at the hands of the ungodly. And darkness covered him—or, according to Aquila, "giddiness"; or, according to Symmachus, "shuddering"—as one beholding things done against the Saviour that were dreadful and

truly worthy of darkness. You will understand what is said from the example of what happens to us in dreams. For often when we are dreaming and see something frightening—wild beasts chasing us, or serpents, or enemies attacking us—we are thrown into turmoil and beside ourselves, filled with trembling, anguish and sweat. In the same way, I think, the prophet's soul too, seeing the vision of events not yet present but still to come, impressed upon the eyes of his mind by the light of the prophetic spirit, was troubled and filled with fear, dread and trembling at the enormity of the evils he beheld. Then, like someone trapped in the midst of those doing these things, with no way of escape and nowhere to turn to get clear of the evils, he prays to be lifted up on high and to escape flying through the air. Therefore he adds: "And I said: Who will give me wings like a dove's? And I will fly away and be at rest." For he asked to be given wings, like an innocent dove, to escape and fly away, so that he might flee the evils. So it was about this too that he said above, "Give ear, O God, to my prayer"—that he might obtain the wings of a dove and fly; for only in this way, and in no other, could he get far away from the city of the ungodly. According to Symmachus: "And I said: Who will give me wings like a dove's, to fly and to settle? I would have made my withdrawal far off; I would have lodged in the wilderness. I would suddenly have made my escape from the rising wind." For I would have withdrawn far off, he says, if I had obtained wings, fleeing those who dared the things described, and I would have preferred the wilderness to the city mentioned. And so, being in the wilderness, I would have waited for the one who saves me from the faintheartedness that came upon me and from the storm that overtook me. "Drown, O Lord, and divide their tongues," and so on. In these words he teaches the reason why he prayed to obtain wings, so as to fly and escape, and chose to live in the wilderness rather than in the city indicated. He says: Since I beheld, by the foreknowledge of the prophetic spirit, that such and such things would be done in the city, for this reason I have resolved to flee the multitude of evils right now. For the first impiety I see in those who inhabited that city is the impiety of their tongue. For all of them sharpened their tongues, agreeing together for evil against the Son of God; therefore, unable to bear this wicked and impious agreement of theirs, I pray, saying: O Lord, drown and divide their tongues. Or, according to Symmachus: "Cause them to be drowned, Master, and make their tongue discordant." For discord would be far better than wicked concord, since it renders wickedness feebler and weaker. This, then, was their first evil. For the leaders of the nation—the teachers of the law, the chief priests and the other rulers of the people—approached him deceitfully and dared to test him,

hunting for some hold on him and contriving plots against him. Another psalm also alluded to this, speaking in his person: "Many bulls surrounded me; fat calves encircled me. They opened their mouth against me like a lion ravening and roaring." There too it was alluding to the rulers of the people; that is why it again mentioned their mouth, because of their plots and deliberations against him. And what cries the whole Jewish people raised against him before Pontius Pilate, the Gospels record. This too was set forth in Psalm 21, which says: "For many dogs surrounded me; a gathering of evildoers encircled me." And all these things were done in the city indicated; that is why the present words say: "Drown, O Lord, and divide their tongues." Then he adds: "For I have seen lawlessness and contradiction in the city; day and night it will go around it," and so on. Symmachus rendered this as follows: "For I beheld violent injustice and unjust judgment in the city, going around its walls day and night; pain and misery within it, abuses within it; harm and assault never departing from its streets." The outrages committed against the Saviour were works of lawlessness, and truly violent injustice. "For instead of loving me," he says, "they slandered me; and they repaid me evil for good, and hatred for my love." And there was contradiction and unjust judgment among them, when many witnesses came forward against him and said nothing true or consistent. And these things were done not only by day but also by night. Thus it was at night that Peter denied him, when Judas came with lanterns and torches. And it was night too when they led him away, now to Annas, now to Caiaphas, dishonouring him with every kind of insult. And when morning came, they bound him, led him away and handed him over to Pilate, and carried out the events of the passion. All of this the prophet foresaw in the spirit, and cried out: "For I have seen lawlessness and contradiction in the city, going around it day and night," according to Symmachus. These things happened in the city; but around its walls there were lawlessness and toil, or, according to Symmachus, pain and misery. By this he indicates what was done outside the city, when they led him out and brought him to the place called Golgotha. Such were the things outside, truly full of pain and misery; and again, the things within it, he says, I saw full of abuse, harm and assault. There was injustice in its midst, and usury and deceit did not depart from its streets—for which Aquila rendered "debt and assault," and Symmachus "harm and assault." For those who contrived the plot against our Saviour were filled with every evil. "For if an enemy had reproached me, I would have borne it; and if one who hated me had boasted against me, I would have hidden from him. But you, man of like soul, my leader and my acquaintance, who together with me [?]

[?] …sweet food with me; in the house of God we walked in concord.” The Prophet took on himself, in his own person, what would be dared against our Savior, and so he fittingly said that he was troubled and filled with the fear of death. For above all, he says, the whole city was filled with lawlessness and contradiction, not only by day but also by night; the parts outside the city, around its walls, were full of lawlessness and pain and misery; and beyond this the souls of all of them were full of injury and plotting. But worst of all is that one of those of like soul with me, one of those well known and familiar to me, has acted so outrageously against me that it is unbearable and not to be endured. What comes from enemies, from those who openly admit that they oppose and hate me, could be endured at some point; for it is possible to guard against enemies and hide from them, and to think the reproaches of enemies nothing strange. But when a friend of like soul, when one I had counted worthy of honor and chosen, when a disciple who shared my table, when one who often went with me into the house of God, prayed with me, enjoyed the mystical food, and shared in the secret words about the kingdom of heaven, does such things against me, it can no longer be borne. These words follow on from what was said earlier about what was dared in the city, and were prophesied specifically about the traitor Judas. Symmachus translated these same words as follows: “For it was not an enemy who insulted me, so that I might bear it; nor did one who hated me raise his heel high against me, so that I might hide from him. But it was you, O man, of like ways with me, my companion and acquaintance; we shared sweet conversation together; in the house of God we went about, living together.” “Let death come upon them, and let them go down alive into Hades; for wickedness is in their dwellings, in their midst.” We have often shown in what came before that divine Scripture is accustomed to utter predictions in the imperative mood. So here too, instead of “Death will come upon them, and they will go down alive into Hades,” the present words are spoken as commands. The Holy Spirit is prophesying what will befall those who dared the things mentioned before. Aquila, at any rate, translated more correctly, saying: “He will bring death upon them.” And who will bring death upon them, if not their own deeds? For these have become the cause of death for them. Or else it is he who judged them worthy of death for their impious acts. The death that overtakes the impious cannot be called the common death; for that one has overtaken all the righteous too, who even after the common death live with God, as the Savior taught when he said: “The God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob is not the God of the dead but of the living.” The death of souls is also made plain in Ezekiel, who says: “The soul that sins, it shall die.” Since,

then, those indicated have separated themselves from life (and our Savior was the life: “For what came into being in him was life, and the life was the light of men”), they were fittingly cut off from him and handed over to the death of the soul. This does not mean that the soul is destroyed and annihilated, passing into nonexistence, but that it goes on living, possessing an immortal substance, in the death just mentioned. That is why it is said: “And let them go down alive into Hades.” By saying “Let death come upon them” he did not indicate the annihilation of souls, but separation from the life that is according to God, and dwelling in Hades. But perhaps they also went down alive into Hades in another sense, by sinning knowingly: they knew the Savior, that he is the Christ of God, yet pretended that he was not. That is why he foretells that they too will be swallowed up like Dathan and Abiram and will go down alive into Hades. In place of “Wickedness is in their dwellings, in their midst”: since the conspiracies and joint assemblies of those who acted against the Savior were wicked, Aquila says: “For wickedness is in their gathering.” Since, then, they came together for no good purpose and formed wicked gatherings and conspiracies, he fittingly prophesied what sort of end would overtake them. “I cried to God, and the Lord saved me,” and what follows. Even though, he says, I saw by the prophetic spirit the lawlessness that was to come about in the city mentioned before, and was grieved in my meditation and troubled, nevertheless, perceiving the outcome of events, I know well that, having cried to God, I shall not be abandoned but shall obtain salvation, since the grace of the common Savior will reach even to me. The prophet says this, according to the Seventy, rendering the future as past; hence the words “I cried to God, and the Lord saved me.” But according to the other translators he prophesies these things too in the future tense. Aquila, at any rate, says: “I will call to God, and the Lord will save me,” and Theodotion: “I will cry to God, and the Lord will save me.” For since such things were to be dared against the Savior, I, who earlier said, “My heart was troubled within me, and the fear of death fell upon me; fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me,” and who suffered these things because of the sight of what had been revealed to me, cried to God. And he did not overlook me, but deigned to make plain to me the brighter things, just as he had earlier shown me the gloomy ones: I mean the resurrection of the Savior and his glory with the Father. Seeing these things too, I was saved; therefore I say: “I cried to God, and the Lord saved me.” Hence I no longer keep quiet, nor can I remain silent; I preach and bring the good news to all people, recounting it every day and every hour, and announcing to all the wonderful and marvelous things that I have seen in the holy prophetic spirit.

That is why I say: “Evening and morning and noon I will recount and announce.” And as I cry these things to all from dawn until evening, and proclaim the saving outcome in the very brightest light of midday, he who counted me worthy of this knowledge will hear my voice; he will no longer let my heart be troubled within me, nor let the fear of death lie upon me. He will remove all these things and scatter them from my soul, and will redeem it in peace from those who want to trouble it. That is why I say: “He will redeem my soul in peace from those who draw near to me; for they were with me in great numbers.” For this Symmachus rendered: “For they were very few against me.” For those who wanted to trouble my soul were only a few, whom God, who exists before the ages, will humble, my cry [?]

That, then, is the interpretation if the Prophet uttered the present words in his own person. But if they are spoken by the Savior himself through the prophetic spirit, since it was in his person that “If an enemy had reproached me, I would have borne it,” and what follows, was said, then the Savior would consistently say this as well: The one who dared such things against me was not an enemy but a friend; not one who hated me, but one who a little before loved me. But I did nothing more than cry to God, and I had him as a Father who listens. They plotted against me, but he saved me. Therefore I will not cease, evening and morning and noon, recounting to all the virtues of the Father and proclaiming the saving Gospel for all people to hear. And the Father, hearing this voice of mine, will redeem my soul in peace from those who draw near to me, that is, from those who make war on me from close at hand and not from afar. They were very few, and God, who exists before the ages, will humble them. For the opportunity they had for a short while, in which they boasted greatly and filled their city with lawlessness and contradiction, will not stay with them; before long they will be humbled, when the wrath of God overtakes them and their city, so that even the renowned temple in it is annihilated and all the worship performed in it is abolished. In this way, then, God, having heard my cry, will humble them. “For there is no exchange for them, and they did not fear God,” and what follows. God, who exists before the ages, will humble the impious already mentioned; they will be humbled and will remain so for a very long time, since there will be no one to give an exchange on their behalf. For the Son of God gave himself once for all as a ransom and exchange for sinners. Those who believed in him he redeemed and set free from all their former sins; but the others he left humbled, since they did not accept the price paid on their behalf, nor believe in the precious blood of the Redeemer and Savior of all people. That is why the word says of them:

“For there is no exchange for them.” Why there is no exchange for them he teaches next, saying: because they did not fear God. For he, being good, and wanting all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, stretched out his saving hand to share his own good things with them too. But they did not receive what was held out from the right hand of God; instead they profaned his covenant, rejecting the new law of the Gospel. That is why Symmachus has: “He stretched out his hand to those at peace with him; they transgressed the covenant,” and Aquila: “He sent out his hand among his peaceful ones.” For he held out a peaceful right hand to those who came, so that they might receive peace from him; but they transgressed his covenant, refusing the peace held out to them. Therefore, having exchanged peace for war, they were divided by the wrath of his face. Since they did not accept grace, they were fittingly handed over to wrath, scattered far away, and dispersed and sown among all the nations. In place of “And his heart drew near. His words were softer than oil, and yet they are darts,” Symmachus translated more clearly, saying: “Their mouths are smoother than butter, but the heart of each of them makes war. His words are softer than oil, yet they cut.” Notice how here too the word presents two groups. One is of many together at once, of whom he speaks in the plural: “Their mouths are smoother than butter, but the heart of each of them makes war.” The other is as of one man alone, of whom he adds specifically: “His words are softer than oil, yet they cut.” These were the two groups indicated in the earlier verses: that of the inhabitants of the city, of whom it was said, “For I saw lawlessness and contradiction in the city,” and that concerning the traitor, of whom the word said, “For if an enemy had reproached me, I would have borne it.” Here too, then, since the rulers of the Jewish nation approached the Savior with hypocrisy and flattery, at times calling him teacher, though not with a pure heart, and at times saying to him, “We know that you are true and teach the word of God in truth, and you care for no one; for you do not regard the person of men,” the word fittingly says of them here: “Their mouths are smoother than butter, but the heart of each of them makes war.” And again specifically about the traitor, since he called him Rabbi and teacher and offered tokens of affection and friendship while carrying out the betrayal, it is fittingly said of him: “His words are softer than oil, yet they cut,” or, according to the Seventy: “His words were softer than oil, and yet they are darts.” “Cast your care upon the Lord, and he will sustain you; he will never allow the righteous to be shaken,” and what follows. Those who with deceit

and hypocrisy made their words soft in public, but inwardly hurled them like more than darts, and also the one who became the betrayer of the Savior: what end they will meet has been shown. But you who hear these things, chastened by the end of those already described, and giving yourself wholly to the one who is prophesied, take courage and cast your care upon him, as one taught by the New Covenant, through which the Savior himself instructs us, saying: “Do not be anxious about what you will eat or what you will drink,” and, “Do not acquire gold or silver or copper for your belts.” Keep these commands, then, and cast your care upon the Lord, and he will sustain you, giving you your daily bread, the rational and heavenly food, and also supplying what is needed for life. For he promised this when he said: “For your heavenly Father knows what you need before you ask him.” He will sustain you, as he does every righteous person; for he has never yet abandoned any of the righteous so that he suffered a shaking that would make him totter and fall. That is why it is said next: “He will never allow the righteous to be shaken,” or, according to Symmachus: “He will never give up the righteous to be shut in.” That is why it is said elsewhere: “I was young, and now I am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring begging bread.” Having said this, he next adds concerning those who plotted against the Savior: “But you, O God, will bring them down into the well of corruption,” or, according to Symmachus: “But you, O God, will bring them down into the pit of corruption.” Countless things have been said in what came before about this pit, as in: “I waited patiently for the Lord, and he attended to me, and brought me up out of the pit of misery and out of the miry clay”; and again: “Lest you keep silent toward me, and I become like those who go down into the pit”; and again: “Lord, you brought up my soul from Hades; you saved me from those who go down into the pit.” The righteous man is kept safe so that he is not brought down into this pit; but the impious are carried down into it, hurled down by God into the place suited to them. Scripture is accustomed to call the place of death a pit of misery, miry clay, and a well of corruption; into it the souls of the impious are cast down, like waters pouring down from above into cisterns. And since in the earlier verses he indicated the murderers of our Savior, he now consistently says about the same people: “Men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days,” or, according to Symmachus: “Murderous and deceitful men shall not live out half their days,” or, according to Aquila: “Men of blood and treachery shall not live out half their days.” You will understand how these words too were fulfilled if you consider that immediately, not long after the plot against

our Savior, the whole race of those mentioned was utterly given over to destruction, when wrath overtook them in the siege that befell them during the Roman war. So in the present time and in mortal life among men, the men of blood and deceit, not even living out half their days, were given over to such destruction. What will await them after their end here was foretold in the words: “But you, O God, will bring them down into the well of corruption.” These things, then, they will suffer. “But I will hope in you”: this is said either by the prophet who prophesies these things, or by the one who is prophesied.

FOR THE END, ON BEHALF OF THE PEOPLE FAR REMOVED FROM THE HOLY PLACES. OF DAVID, FOR A PILLAR INSCRIPTION, WHEN THE FOREIGNERS SEIZED HIM IN GATH. PSALM 55. “Have mercy on me, O God, for man has trampled me; all day long he has fought and afflicted me.” The people far removed from the holy places, as far as the history is concerned, seems to be the band fleeing with David from the face of Saul; they numbered six hundred men, as the Scripture of Kingdoms testifies. Now he was among the foreigners in Gath twice. Once was when he was trapped alone inside the gates and feigned madness; it was then that he drummed on the gates of the city and his spittle ran down his beard. The other time was when he fled with six hundred men to the king of Gath, who assigned him Ziklag as a dwelling. The present inscription seems to have been spoken by David at the time when he was staying among the people of Gath with the six hundred who were fleeing with him; they received him and kept him among them as a friend, and he was even honored by the king of Gath. That is why the superscription reads: “For the end, on behalf of the people far removed from the holy places. Of David, a pillar inscription, when the foreigners seized him in Gath.” According to Aquila it reads: “To the one who gives victory, concerning the mute dove, of the removals; of David, humble, perfect, when the Philistines seized him in Gath.” According to Symmachus: “A song of victory concerning the dove, concerning the tribe driven out; of David, the humble-minded and blameless, when the Philistines held him in Gath.” The fifth edition has: “To the one who gives victory, concerning the dove that can hardly speak, of hidden things; to David, for a pillar inscription, when the foreigners seized him in Gath.” Theodotion too, like the others, rendered “concerning the dove” in place of “on behalf of the people far removed from the holy places.” Perhaps those who said “mute dove” or “dove that can hardly speak” are hinting at David himself while he was among the foreigners and could not speak the prophecies in the Holy Spirit as he used to, nor offer his hymns with boldness. That is why they called him a dove that can hardly speak, or even a mute one. In the psalm before this one, too, it was said: “Who will give me wings like a dove? Then I will fly away and be at rest. I would have withdrawn far away, I would have lodged in the wilderness,” according to Symmachus. [Footnote: (1) “To offer”: perhaps “to utter,” as also [?]]

The Holy Spirit who worked in the Prophet, who is attested to have descended upon the Savior in the form of a dove, is tender and guileless. So when David was persecuted by Saul, the Spirit was driven out with him, and though driven out did not retaliate, but was like a mute dove removed far away and thrust out by its pursuers. For this reason the other translators say “concerning the dove.” In place of “for a pillar inscription,” Aquila translated “of the humble, perfect,” and Symmachus “of the humble-minded and blameless,” showing the reason why the Prophet’s virtue was counted worthy before God of a pillar, as it were, and of eternal memory. For David’s greatest achievement was his humility and lowliness of mind, by which he displayed a perfect virtue that drew no blame upon itself. That is why he sent up to God the present words, which contain examples of surpassing and perfect humility, saying: “Have mercy on me, O God, for man has trampled me.” As far as the letter goes, he means Saul, who rose up against him and pressed the war against him not for one day but for many; therefore he adds: “All day long he has fought and afflicted me.” Then, since he perceived by the divine Spirit that Saul was not so much the cause of such great zeal against him as certain hidden, spiritual, invisible enemies, namely evil powers and spirits, who were working in Saul and rousing him to war against him, he fittingly adds: “My enemies have trampled me all day long,” or, according to Symmachus: “Those who afflict me have crushed me every day.” Who these enemies and afflicters are, who were working in Saul, he makes clear next, saying: “For many are those who fight against me from on high.” For he was well aware that his struggle was not against blood and flesh but against the principalities and powers, against the world-rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness; it was they who sharpened Saul, so that he pursued and made war, for no reason, on one who had never done him any harm. Then next he says: “By day I shall be afraid, but I will hope in you.” Symmachus made this clear, saying: “On whatever day I am afraid, I trust in you.” For even if it seems above all that a man has trampled me, since Saul has been fierce against me, yet my enemies, who fight against me from above and shoot their arrows from on high against my soul, are very many. But I have learned to despise them all because of you, my champion and protector. For trusting in you, if ever fear falls upon my soul, I beat it back, taking courage in you, my protector. “In the Lord I will praise my words; in God I have hoped; I will not fear what flesh can do to me.” In place of “In God I will praise my words,” Symmachus rendered “Through God I will hymn his word,” Aquila “In God I will hymn his words,” and the fifth edition “In God I will praise my word.” If ever, he says, fear fell upon me because of the turmoil caused by those fighting against me, I beat it back by hoping in you; and instead of incantations and amulets,

…I went through hymns. For by praising your word I was helped, so that I paid no attention to any of my pursuers. So, hoping in God and carrying his words in my mouth, I scorned every plot that came from men, not fearing what flesh would do to me. For what could flesh and blood do against God as one's helper? "If God is for us, who is against us?" says the Apostle. Saul was flesh, minding the things of the flesh. The Apostle shows this when he writes to the Corinthians: "For where there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not fleshly, and walking in a merely human way?" So David called Saul "flesh", since Saul was full of jealousy and strife and drove David out because of them, and said: "I will not fear what flesh will do to me." Then he says: "All day long they abhorred my words; all their thoughts were against me for evil." Symmachus rendered this more clearly: "All day long they were busy with words about me; every thought of theirs was against me for evil." It was as if they had nothing else to do and no one else to talk about. They gave all their leisure to talking about me and scheming against me. They planned nothing good for me, but spent all their zeal on evil and for evil. "They will dwell near and lie hidden; they will watch my heel. As they lay in wait for my soul, for nothing will you save them; in wrath you will bring down peoples, O God." The Seventy put this obscurely, and Symmachus rendered it more plainly: "They gathered secretly and watched my footsteps, waiting for my soul through injustice. Deliver me from them; in wrath bring down peoples, O God." For in this way, he says, they spent the whole day busy with me. They kept stirring up talk about me, and every thought they had was against me. So they were eager to gather together and plot, and they did not stop there. They also pried into my heel, that is, the course of my life, to see whether they could somehow trip me and throw me down. And they watched my footsteps wherever I walked, so that they might somehow seize me. These, then, are the things that those who pursued me in vain did against me. But you, Lord, my hope, deliver me from their unjust plotting. Visit them with your wrath and bring them down from their boasting and arrogance, for this will be to their benefit. In exalting themselves and puffing themselves up they were doing these things to their own destruction, for "God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble." Therefore I beg you, bring down all who rise up against me, or, as Aquila has it, "make them descend". Then they may gain a moderate mind and think humble thoughts, and so be greatly benefited. "I have declared my life to you; you have set my tears before you, as also in your promise. My enemies will turn back on whatever day I call upon you." Symmachus rendered these words too

more clearly, as follows: "You have counted my inward parts; you have set my tears before you. Will not my enemies be turned back when you count, on whatever day I call upon you?" My enemies, he says, stirred up talk about me all day long, and all their thoughts were against me. But you yourself know what reflections I gathered within myself and what thoughts I had, for you are God who knows the heart. You have counted all my inward parts, and you know my secrets and the thoughts of my soul. That is why you set my tears before you and did not turn away from them. In your promise you pledge, "While you are still speaking I will say, 'Here I am'", and so, acting in keeping with your promises, you set my tears before you. In the Seventy's translation he says, "I have declared my life to you", as one who speaks boldly and is not ashamed of his own life. And you accepted my life. You did not shake off my tears but set them before your eyes, keeping faith with your promises. So it came about that I was heard and my enemies went backward. That is why I say: "On whatever day I call upon you, my enemies will turn back." In Symmachus he says: "Will not my enemies be turned back when you count?" When you sort them out by their tribes and clean the threshing floor, separating out those worthy of you, and you make a count of those who are to stand on the right and those who go to the left, then, when you make this count, my enemies will be turned back [?]

"Behold, I have come to know that God is mine. In God I will praise a word; in the Lord I will praise a saying. In the Lord I have hoped; I will not fear what man will do to me." In Symmachus this reads: "I know that there is a God for me. I will sing hymns to God; through God I will compose a hymn of a word. In God I have trusted; I will not fear what man will do to me." He is saying: I have learned it from the facts themselves, and I have truly come to know that I did not hope in vain, but gained God as my helper. The proof of this is that you set my tears before you. Then you listened to me, and my enemies went backward. Therefore "in God I will praise a word", or in Aquila, "in God I will boast of a word", and in Symmachus, "I will sing hymns to God". And also "in the Lord I will praise a saying", or in Aquila, "in the Lord I will hymn a saying", or in Symmachus, "through the Lord I will compose a hymn of a word". Again, as I said above, "In God I have hoped; I will not fear what flesh will do to me", and now I say, "In God I have hoped; I will not fear what man will do to me." For flesh and man are one and the same, since it has been said, "But you die like men", and "For when there is jealousy and strife among you,

are you not fleshly, and walking in a merely human way?" "In me, O God, are the vows of praise that I will pay to you. For you have delivered my soul from death and my feet from slipping, so that I may be pleasing before God in the light of the living." In place of "In me, O God, are the vows of praise that I will pay to you", Symmachus rendered it more clearly: "I take upon myself, O God, what I have vowed; I will pay you praises." I have not forgotten what I vowed, he says. My vows are within me, and I keep in memory everything I promised when I made them. I will pay them like a debt, offering sacrifices of praise, as the oracle says: "Offer God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Lord." So I will pay you vows of praise, since I know that I owe much for my own salvation. For you delivered my very soul from death. As far as it lay with them, my enemies were driving it out and forcing it to fall into death. By driving me out and forcing me to live among foreign and alien nations, they were, as far as it lay with them, putting my soul to death. That is, I would have been drawn into the idolatry of the foreigners while living among them. In the days when I was staying with Achish in Gath among the foreigners, my soul would long ago have died and fallen away from the life that is with you. But your grace and your mercy did not allow this to happen. Even when I was among the foreigners you fenced me in, so that I took no harm from living with them. That is why I say: "You have delivered my soul from death", and also "my feet [?] from slipping". Who would not have been overthrown, left in the midst of so many godless and idolatrous men, like someone who steps into mud and falls on slippery ground? But here too was your mercy and your grace, delivering my feet from slipping. I will not ascribe these things to my own strength. My soul was not so firm that I could have remained unshaken while caught among so many, had you not been my helper. Therefore I confess and give thanks that you delivered my feet from slipping. Your mercy granted me these things so that I might be pleasing before you in the light of the living, or, in Symmachus, "so as to walk before God through the light of life". Even while I stayed among the foreigners I did not turn aside from the straight and royal road. I walked in a way pleasing to you, guided and enlightened by you. I shared in a light that is not the common light open to all, rational and irrational creatures, wild beasts and reptiles, dead and lifeless things alike, but a light reserved for those alone who live by you. You will understand the light of the living, by which David and all the God-loving prophets and righteous men were enlightened, if you attend to the evangelist when he says: "What came to be in him" (that is, in the Word of God, who was in the beginning with God) "was life, and the [?]

life was the light of men", and it was coming into the world. "He was in the world, and the world came into being through him, and the world did not know him." So he was in the world, and those who were counted worthy of the life that is with God were enlightened by that light. Later he also came to his own, and to all who received him he gave the power to become children of God. Such was the power of the light of the living that it made children of God those who [?]

[?] David was shown to have been among the foreigners in Gath a second time. It was while he was staying among them that he is said to have spoken the [?] psalm. So he appears to have come into the cave twice [?]. The first time was when he pretended to be mad and escaped from the hands of Achish and the foreigners in Gath. From there he got away safely to the cave of Adullam, where all his brothers and his father's whole household went down to him. Everyone who was in distress, everyone in debt and everyone bitter in soul gathered around him, and he became their leader. There were about four hundred men. The second time was when Saul came back from pursuing the foreigners and was told, "David is in the wilderness of Engedi." He took with him three thousand chosen men from all Israel and went to look for David and his men in front of Aielein [?]. He came to the sheepfolds by the road. There was a cave there, and Saul went in to relieve himself, while David and his men were sitting in the innermost part of the cave. David's men said to him: "This is the day of which the Lord said to you that he would hand your enemy over into your hands, and you shall do to him whatever seems good to you." David got up and secretly cut off the edge of Saul's cloak. Afterward David's heart struck him because he had cut off the edge of his cloak. David said to his men: "The Lord forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the Lord's anointed, and raise my hand against him; for he is the Lord's anointed." David restrained his men with these words and did not let them rise and kill Saul. So we must ask at what time David wrote the present stele inscription, and in which cave he was staying: whether in

the cave of Adullam or in the cave of Engedi. Two psalms were spoken by him in the cave. One is the present psalm, which is a stele inscription. The other is Psalm 141, entitled "Of understanding, for David, when he was in the cave, a prayer." So one may reasonably ask whether they were spoken at the same time, and whether he composed both while he was in the cave. Judging from the words found in each, I think that the stele inscription now before us was spoken in the cave of Adullam. The prayer in Psalm 141 was spoken in the cave of Engedi, when he was hiding inside the cave while Saul was relieving himself. This is how it appeared to me, judging from the words found in each. Psalm 141 appears to have been spoken while David was in great distress and struggle. At any rate he says in it: "With my voice I cried to the Lord; with my voice I made supplication to God. I will pour out my supplication before him; I will declare my affliction before him. When my spirit was failing within me, you knew my paths. In the way on which I was walking they hid a snare for me." With these words he shows the distress by which he was being tested. He shows it still more in what he adds next: "Escape has perished from me." Saul was sitting before the mouth of the cave, and David, hiding inside, had given up hope of escape. But having given up hope of escape, he took refuge in the harbor of salvation. So he goes on: "I cried to you, Lord; I said, You are my hope." And he adds: "Bring my soul out of prison." Do you see how he points to being shut up inside the cave? It is fitting, then, that he also entitles these words a prayer, indicating the occasion by the title. He says, at any rate: "Of understanding, for David, when he was in the cave, a prayer." He prayed these things when he was caught in a great struggle at the time indicated. But the stele inscription now before us was spoken by him, I think, when he was in the cave of Adullam. There he was taking in everyone: his brothers, his relatives and the other fugitives, who were perhaps being plotted against by Saul because of him. Every soul in bitterness and everyone who had been wronged also came to share David's flight. When they saw a righteous man, honored by God, being unjustly driven out by Saul, they found comfort in their own troubles. Then they too, fleeing those who had wronged them, followed David's example,

[?] being, and at ease, he uttered such words, and still more the ones that follow, where it says: "My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make music. Awake, my glory; awake, harp and lyre; I will awake at dawn. I will give thanks to you among the peoples, Lord; I will sing to you among the nations." These words express much leisure, and gladness too. The holy Apostle says, at any rate: "Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing psalms." But he could not have said these things in the cave of Engedi, when he was hemmed in by Saul sitting at the entrance. What chance was there then to take up harp and lyre, while he was hiding in the innermost part of the cave? On the other hand, when he was at leisure and at ease in the cave of Adullam with the four hundred men who were with him, it would make no sense for him to say "Escape has perished from me" and "Bring my soul out of prison." Let this be said about the difference between the two passages. Now let us turn to the exposition of the psalm in hand [?]. "For the end; do not destroy; for David, for a stele inscription", and so on. Saul was driving David out. But David ran away, fulfilling in deed the saying, "If they persecute you in this city, flee to the next." He did not want his presence to provoke his enemy and make himself the cause of bloodguilt for him. David knew better than anyone the saying, "Do not kindle the coals of a sinner." So he withdrew and gave way, even though he was loved by the whole nation. He had a great many who suffered and grieved with him, and who could have taken him into their homes and hidden him. But so as not to put others in danger as well, he fled to the desert regions and made the caves his home. I think the holy Apostle is also hinting at the memory of David when he says: "wandering in deserts and mountains, in caves and holes in the ground." The psalm placed before this one was not called a psalm but a stele inscription, which Aquila rendered "of the humble, perfect one" and Symmachus "of the humble-minded and blameless one". In the same way the present text, as a stele inscription, sets up as worthy of everlasting memory David's virtue of supreme meekness and forbearance, the humility of one who is humble and perfect, humble-minded and blameless. Moses too was praised for this virtue, and our Savior and Lord urged us to it, saying: "Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart." Such a virtue needs perseverance and must be kept for the longest time, for "the one who endures to the end will be saved." That is why it is entitled "For the end; do not destroy." Many who began well did not last to the end. But the Holy Spirit approved of David's flight, his stay in the deserts and his long-suffering life in caves, and so says to him: "For the end, do not destroy; remain like this throughout, so that you may obtain a stele inscription and everlasting memory." And at this David was not puffed up like the Cynics among those who pursue the wisdom of this age. He did not think highly of himself or swagger over the endurance of his way of life. Nor did he grow vain because

many had gathered around him as imitators and disciples of his way of life. Nor did he put his confidence in them as bodyguards and allies. Instead, showing in deed what it is to be meek and humble, perfect, truly humble-minded and blameless, he cried out to God, saying: "Have mercy on me, O God, for my soul has trusted in you, and in the shadow of your wings I will hope." He means: I know that your wings and your shelter are reserved for perfect souls. But I am small and lowly, so I will hope not in your wings but in the shadow of your wings, "until lawlessness passes by", or in Aquila, "until the plot passes by", and in Symmachus, "until the abuser passes by". But when the lawlessness has passed by, along with the plot against me and the one called the abuser, then I will hope no longer in the shadow but in your very wings, as one who has made progress and been set free from every lawless deed and sin —

"I will cry to God Most High, to God who has been my benefactor. He sent from heaven and saved me; he gave over to reproach those who trample on me. Interlude." The righteous are accustomed to send up cries and shouts to God, not with an audible voice but with the surpassing power of the soul. That is why, even when silent, they often cried out in the spirit, for "the Spirit himself intercedes" with God "with groanings too deep for words", as the Apostle says. In this way David too cried out to God. Then, as one who had often experienced his own Savior, he gratefully adds: "to God who has been my benefactor". In saying "He sent from heaven and saved me", he indicates that a Savior was sent from God. Who this is he does not show here, but he teaches it elsewhere, where he says: "He sent his word and healed them, and delivered them from their corruption." So it was the Word of God who was sent even in ancient times and became the Savior of those worthy of his salvation. David knew him well, and so he said: "He sent from heaven and saved me." So the Most High saved the man who was worthy of salvation through the Savior. And judging justly, the same God gave over to reproach those who rose up against the righteous man and trampled on him. He did this for their good, to make them better by reproaching them and turning them back to himself. "God sent his mercy and his truth, and delivered my soul from the midst of lion cubs", and so on. With these words he supplies the meaning that was missing above. We were asking whom God sent from heaven to save David, and here he shows it, saying: "God sent his mercy and his truth." What could mercy and truth, sent forth, be but the Word of God, of whom it was said, "He sent his word and healed them, and delivered them from their corruption"? The same Word is likewise also called light that is sent, in the psalm that says: "Send out your [?light]" [?]

[?] ... your light and your truth; they will lead me." But light and truth and word, sent from the Most High God, are not without being or without real existence, for something without real existence could not be sent. And just as the Word is understood as the one who brings about healing and salvation, so here he himself has been named mercy, since he serves the Father's love for humankind; and likewise truth, since he truly exists and has being in actuality. Our own word, at any rate, which exists in syllables, phrases and names and is sounded out through tongue and voice, could not properly and truly be called a word. It has another word that begets it, which one might properly call the true word; and this, they say, is the inner word. So just as the inner word in us is what might properly be called truly a word, [?] so he really exists, subsisting in his own being, and is other than the one who sends him. That is why it was said above, "He sent from heaven and saved me." And whom he sent, he teaches here, saying: "He sent forth his mercy and his truth, and rescued my soul from the midst of lions' whelps; in their midst I lay down to sleep troubled," he says. For, caught in the midst of the whelps—the foreigners in Gath, or the enemies otherwise warring against me—I slept troubled, as far as it depended on me and on human weakness. But the Most High God sent forth his aforementioned Word, his truth and his mercy, and rescued my soul, so that it suffered no harm from the turmoil of the whelps. According to the other translators, however, he says: I did not sleep troubled when caught in the midst of lions, but I was undaunted and of good courage. Aquila, at any rate, says: "In the midst of fierce lionesses I will lie down"; and Symmachus: "In the midst of lions I lay down with good courage." Who the lions were, or the whelps and lionesses, he makes clear next, saying: "Sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword." For a base and wicked man is worse than any wild beast or venomous reptile, especially one who devotes himself to slander and evil-speaking and plots against the souls of those who love God—not with weapons and spears, but with the hidden, unseen instruments of destruction that work through words. Such people use the enclosure of their teeth like a kind of armor, fencing in and shutting up the words hidden behind the teeth; and they use their tongue, and the slanders sent out from it, like arrows that are shot. And the very tongue of such people is no different from a very sharp sword that pierces and works death. Such, then, are the human lions and the so-called whelps. But I came safely through their plot thanks to the Savior sent to me from God, who rescued my soul from the midst of the whelps. Whether these things were said about Saul, or about those who slandered David to Saul, or about the foreigners in Gath, or about invisible enemies, you yourself will consider.

But you, O Lord, even if, through the surpassing love for humankind of the Father who sent you down, you came down even to my lowliness, now be exalted above the heavens; dwell in the bosom of the Father's Godhead and fill all the earth with your glory. I say this fittingly, since I have come to be free of care about every evil and have been rescued through your watchful care from the whelps and lions spoken of above. They prepared snares for my feet and, as far as they could, bowed down my soul; they even dug a pit before my face. But because of your protection they did these things against themselves, not against me, for they themselves fell first into their own pit. Therefore, since you who were sent by the Father have done these things, be exalted now, and take up again your heavenly dwellings, which are proper and familiar to your Godhead. "My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make music," and so on. In his teachings to the disciples the Savior said this about the Holy Spirit: "If you love me, keep my commandments; and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate, to be with you forever, the Spirit of truth"; and again: "I have spoken these things to you while I remain with you; but the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom my Father will send in my name, will teach you all things and remind you"; and once more: "I still have many things to tell you, but you cannot bear them now. But when he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will tell you the truth, for he will take from what is mine and declare it to you." By these words he shows that what came from him was greater than the apostles could grasp—"for you cannot bear them," he says—but that the Spirit of truth, supplied from him and sent by him to the apostles, declares all the truth to them. If, then, this has been understood, it is fitting that David too, after crying out to the God who had been sent to help him, "Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth," should next entreat the same God to send down to him the Spirit, the

Advocate, the prophetic Spirit, declaring that he himself is ready to receive him. For the temple within him had been cleansed, and the vessel of his soul, that is, his very mind, which Scripture is accustomed to call figuratively the heart. He shows this by saying: "My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready." My heart and my power of thought are ready, he says; now send down your Spirit. For when he is present and rides upon my soul, I will sing and make music as I am accustomed, offering my own ministry and service to the power of the prophetic Spirit. Having said this, he was heard at once, according to the saying, "While you are still speaking, I will say, Here I am," and he perceived the presence of the Holy Spirit. Then, as though the Spirit were standing at the doors, the Prophet turns and rouses himself to the ministry of prophecy. That is why he adds: "Awake, my glory." My glory is to prophesy. Then he says further: "Awake, harp and lyre," hinting at the soul by the harp and at the body by the lyre; or else he is taking up in his hands his familiar instruments themselves, in order to strike up what the Spirit was prompting. And to these words he adds: "I will awake at dawn." For now that I have been enlightened by the presence of the Spirit and have come into the day of divine light, I am ready to prophesy. Having said this, he gives himself up wholly to the Spirit; and the Spirit, using the prophet as an instrument, announces good things and proclaims good news to all the nations, saying: "I will give thanks to you among the peoples, Lord; I will sing to you among the nations." At present the nation of the Jews and their people drive away your prophets and give them no place at all. But there will be a time when all the nations on earth and all the peoples of humankind will share in your mercy, so that I, the prophetic Spirit, at the appointed time will fill all peoples at once, coming to dwell in them, and will give thanks to you and praise you. Then I will sing to you not among the people of the Jews but among all the nations throughout the whole inhabited world. For this reason I say: "I will give thanks to you among the peoples, Lord; I will sing to you among the nations." He next makes clear the reason why the prophetic Spirit will dwell among all the peoples throughout the whole world and among all the nations, and why the prophetic words uttered long ago will be fulfilled in deeds, saying: "For your mercy has been magnified to the heavens, and your truth to the clouds." What is astonishing is this: that heavenly things, I say, are counted worthy of mercy, and earthly things of truth. For even if the things in the heavens seem above all to be pure, and all perfect and advanced to the height of virtue, they are nevertheless such because of your mercy. For it is not from themselves or by their own power that they share in such blessedness, but from you, the giver of all good things. Or

to take it another way: "For your mercy has been magnified to the heavens"—the mercy poured out on all people. This is the mercy said above to have been sent, in the words, "God sent forth his mercy and his truth." For the mercy that was sent accomplished such things among human beings that I, the Holy Spirit, give thanks to you among all the peoples and sing to you among all the nations. Hence it was magnified to the heavens, since it drew those among humankind who made progress up to the heavens, so that the promise of the kingdom of heaven was given to them. "And your truth," he says, "to the clouds." Clouds serve the rain, ministering to the will of divine Providence. In this way the passage shows that God takes care of human beings, since his governance extends as far as the clouds, and the truth of his watchful care reaches even to the service the clouds perform. In another sense, too, Scripture is accustomed to call clouds the perfect souls among humankind, the prophetic souls, which supply the teachings from God like rain to the souls that need them. When, for example, the prophet Isaiah was threatening the nation of the Jews with desolation, he presented God as saying: "I will take away its hedge, and it will be plundered; I will break down its wall, and it will be trampled underfoot. And I will abandon my vineyard, and it will not be pruned or dug, and thorns will spring up in it as on waste ground. And I will command the clouds not to send rain upon it." Plainly in these words the divine prophets are called clouds: filled with the heavenly Spirit, they supplied spiritual rain to human souls. God's truth and his mercy, of which he spoke a little earlier—"God sent forth his mercy and his truth, and rescued my soul from the midst of the whelps"—had long ago rescued David's soul, and they were also going to visit all the nations afterward. It is fitting, then, that the Holy Spirit, announcing the good news that he will give thanks among the peoples and sing to God among all the nations, should add the reason, saying: "For your mercy has been magnified to the heavens," and so on. Then he sets the seal on all this, saying: "Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth," repeating the same teaching about God a second time. For it is fitting for you, he says, to be exalted, even if for the sake of human beings you condescend to our lowliness, calling peoples and nations by your grace. But be exalted, and take back your own throne. For even while you dwell in the heavens and abide in your own Godhead and kingdom, you will be able to fill all the earth with your glory. Moses too records this, presenting God as saying of the Jews, because of the calf they made: "Let me alone, and in my anger I will destroy them"; but adding, about the calling of the nations: "As I live, and as my name lives, all the earth shall be filled with my glory." And in Isaiah the seraphim, surrounding the Lord of Hosts, cried out: "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory."

[?] As is said, in agreement with this, in Psalm 71 as well, which speaks plainly about Christ: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, and blessed be the name of his glory, and all the earth shall be filled with his glory." The present prophecy also sets its seal on this, saying: "Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth."

FOR THE END. DO NOT DESTROY. OF DAVID, FOR AN INSCRIPTION ON A PILLAR. PSALM 57. "If you truly speak righteousness, judge uprightly, you sons of men." The present psalm too urges us not to destroy with the end in view, but that each should keep to his own end. Both this psalm and the one before it have the same title, both containing "For the end, do not destroy, of David" and "for an inscription on a pillar." The time is not indicated in the present psalm, but it is indicated in the one before it, by the addition that says: "When he fled from Saul into the cave." That the present psalm was spoken at the same time seems likely to me not only from what has been said but also from what follows. The preceding inscription spoke about the sons of men: "Sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows." So it is fitting that the present one should address the same sons of men right at the beginning, saying: "If you truly speak righteousness, judge uprightly, you sons of men." And since the preceding psalm said, "He rescued my soul from the midst of the whelps," or "from the midst of lions" according to the other translators, it is fitting that the present one should go on to say: "The Lord has shattered the lions' molars." For we needed to learn how he rescued David's soul from the midst of the whelps. Again, concerning the teeth of those who slandered him, the preceding psalm said, "Sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows," and the present one says: "God will break their teeth in their mouth." This shows the agreement between the two inscriptions. One might also put it another way: since the preceding psalm contains the calling of the nations, the present inscription has fittingly been joined to that prophecy. It proclaims to the sons of men the teaching about God's righteous judgment, and charges all the peoples to approach the teaching of the Word with a sincere purpose and a pure conscience, and not to feign godliness. Therefore, addressing all the peoples named above and all the nations, of whom it was said, "I will give thanks to you among the peoples, Lord; I will sing to you among the nations," the present psalm solemnly testifies, saying: "If you truly speak righteousness, judge uprightly, you sons of men." For if someone truly professes righteousness, it will be shown in no other way than by judging uprightly. And he judges uprightly who has decided within himself on what accords with right reason, and to do nothing crooked or perverse. Then, since the sons of men speak what is right with their lips and profess righteousness with their mouths, but are refuted by their deeds, because in their minds they plot the opposite,

he adds: "For in your heart you work iniquities on the earth"; and the proof of this, he says, is your actions: "Your hands weave together injustice." Judge uprightly, then, you sons of men, and consider within yourselves whether your deeds agree with your words. For if you speak righteousness, how is it that your hands weave together injustice? This shows that you are plotting iniquities in your heart, thinking one thing and saying another with your mouth. If, then, you truly speak righteousness, judge, you people, and do the very things you say. Do not work iniquities in your heart, and do not let your hands weave together lawlessness. "Sinners have been estranged from the womb; they went astray from birth, they spoke lies." These words too he directs at the sons of men who profess to worship God and to follow the laws of righteousness, yet do not judge rightly. So he says to them: Listen, you who speak righteousness with your mouth but work injustice with your hands, weaving many sins together at once: nothing that anyone thinks in his mind escapes the great Judge. For even if someone thinks he can hide from human eyes, let him know that he has fallen into a terrible error and is deceiving himself. He will not escape the great Judge of all, before whose judgment seat we shall all stand. And how could these people escape God's notice, when even before they came into the light they were known to him who knows all things before they come to be? So before they were born he foresaw them as already existing and as being such as they now are, and from that time they were already rejected by him. "Sinners have been estranged from the womb." And even if they now pretend above all to speak righteousness while pursuing the opposite in their deeds, it is not only now that they have shown themselves to be such before God.
