Before they came forth from the womb, or rather even before they were conceived in the vessel of the womb, he reckoned them among those who have gone astray, and he was not unaware that they would be such. Already from that time they were known as people who would speak lies, and as having "fury after the likeness of the serpent." (The Greeks, too, commonly call the soul thymos, the word for fury.) The ancient serpent, when he deceived Eve, pretended to engage in sweet and friendly conversation, to make mention of God and to show a kind of piety, saying to the woman: "Why is it that God said, You shall not eat of any tree in the paradise?" and again: "For God knew that on whatever day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil." While feigning such things and pretending to know God, he conversed with the woman, but in his heart he was working iniquities and weaving injustice together in his deeds. So it is fitting that [?] it speaks of them as having a fury and a soul like the serpent just mentioned; and God foresaw this too by his foreknowledge. For although they hear the divine words and are taught by the sacred

sayings, they will gain nothing of benefit, because they stop up their ears and do not receive the power of the divine charms. Instead they become like "a deaf asp that stops its ears, so as not to hear the voice of charmers, or of a drug prepared by a skilled man." They have been likened to the serpent because of their hypocrisy and their feigned talk about God, and to the asp because they hide deadly venom within them. If they had been compared simply to an asp, there would have been hope that they might one day be helped. For that terrible reptile sometimes, through a charm and the preparation of certain other things, casts off its venom, lays aside its fury, and as it were becomes dead to its malice. And if such bitterness in the asp is weakened and withers through the power of certain words, so that it casts off its venom, what must one say of the human soul, made in the image of God? Surely it too would change for the better far more than that reptile kind, putting off the venom of wickedness, if it offered itself to the help of the divine teachings and to the truly God-inspired charms. That is why the passage was precise in comparing such a person not simply to an asp, but to an asp that is not such by nature but makes itself deaf by choice. Hence it is said: "Like a deaf asp that stops its ears." So too a person who does not listen to the divine words is deprived of hearing not because his soul has been made deaf, but by his own will; for he willingly makes himself deaf, doing violence to his own nature. God did not make the soul deaf, or blind, or crippled, or damaged in any way at all, but sound in all its faculties, since he created human beings in his own image and likeness. Each one makes himself deaf and blind and mutilates the very substance of his own soul. Through the prophet Isaiah the people of the circumcision are convicted of doing this. That is why it is said to them: "The heart of this people has grown dull, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and they have shut their eyes and made their ears heavy, lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I should heal them." In this way the one who does not listen to the divine words has been likened to a deaf asp that makes itself deaf. That is why Symmachus renders it: "Like a deaf asp that stops its ear, so as not to hear the voice of whisperers, of anyone skilled in charms." Now, the man who exists in the present and has made himself such becomes known to the many when he does these things; but God knew he would be such even before his birth, and long before his conception in the womb. In vain, then, does a person deceive himself who professes to speak righteousness but weaves injustice together with his hands, and then hides lawlessness in his heart, as though he could escape God's notice at the divine tribunal. "God will break their teeth in their mouth," and so on. The things said before [?]

[?] …having learned, O sons of men, about the sinners, and how, foreknown by God, they were known to him even before they came among men as those who would be such, hear what end will overtake them. For although they were born with a free and self-determining nature, able to tell good from its opposite and possessing within themselves an inclination toward either, they did not use their power of judgment rightly. They did not love what is upright, even though they knew it, nor did they pursue in deeds the righteousness which they professed in word alone and with their lips. Instead, made like the ancient serpent, they became worse than a deaf asp. For this reason, listen to what awaits them too, and learn that God, the judge of all, will break their teeth, since they differ in no way from lions, and that after all this they will melt away like water flowing off. For in place of "They shall be brought to nothing like water running by," Symmachus translated, "Let them melt away like water passing off by itself." Since they put on a pretense of righteousness with their mouth, it is fitting that God will break their teeth in their mouth. And since it was not enough for them to be made like the serpent and the deaf asp mentioned before, but they were already ravaging others as well, they were compared to lions and whelps. From these David prays that his soul may be rescued, saying in the preceding psalm: "And he rescued my soul from the midst of whelps," or, "from the midst of lions." God is said to crush their molars, that is, the powers of their wickedness, which they used for the ruin of many. And once God has shattered their teeth and molars, then at last they will be brought to nothing, as though put to death, and will melt away like water passing off by itself. Such, then, will be the end of all the ungodly. This you must know, O sons of men, so that, if you truly speak righteousness, you may judge uprightly. Do not follow the way of the men just described, nor work lawlessness in your heart, nor let your hands weave injustice together. Do not make yourselves like the serpent, nor become like a deaf asp that stops its ears, nor be carried off together with the ungodly and sinners spoken of before. God anticipated them by his foreknowledge before they came into the light and knew that they would be such; yet nevertheless he allowed them to be born and to come into the light, bestowing his grace on them too, so that their choice might be made manifest.

[?] …of Jesus Christ." And again: "In whom we also were made his inheritance, having been predestined according to the foreknowledge of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we might be to the praise of his glory." Do you see how he says that they were chosen before the foundation of the world and predestined to adoption according to the purpose of him who works all things? The same apostle presents the same thought when he says: "We know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified." And he teaches similar things about himself when he says: "But when he who set me apart from my mother's womb was pleased to reveal his Son in me." Just as he foreknew that these would love him and therefore predestined them, so too with the ungodly. He foreknew that they would speak righteousness, because they knew it, yet would not pursue it in deeds, because they wove injustice together with their hands. For this reason he estranged them from the womb and counted them among those who go astray and speak lies before they came into being. And though he knew they would be such, he allowed them to come into the open, so that the distinction of righteous and God-fearing men might shine out by comparison with the worse. For all are of one nature; but some willingly chose the better things, while others traveled the opposite road, using their free choice. And the great judge of all, seated on high and presiding over each company, awards what is fitting. Therefore those who loved him he [?], showing them to be conformed to the image of his Son, as men who have shown their love for him in deed. But those of the opposite kind, as men who have estranged themselves from his grace, he casts down. He breaks their teeth, which they did not use as they should, and crushes their molars, with which they ravaged many. In the end he hands them over to be brought to nothing, to mockery and reproach, when they flow away like running and unsettled water, having brought such an end upon themselves. "He will bend his bow until they grow weak. Like melted wax they will be taken away; fire fell

upon them, and they did not see the sun. Before your thorns perceive the bramble, as living, as in wrath, he will swallow you up." Since these words are carried obscurely in the Seventy, Symmachus has rendered the sense somewhat more clearly, translating it in this way: "Let him who bends his bow be thrown into confusion like things that are shattered; like an afterbirth dissolved, may he perish, a woman's miscarriage, so that they may not see the sun. Before your thorns grow to become a bramble, while they are still alive, whole, a whirlwind will carry them off." The sense of the passage would be something like this. Since the aim is to describe what the end of the sinners will be, learn, O sons of men, that these things too await them in addition to what was said before. It was said before this that God will break their teeth in their mouth, and the Lord will crush the molars of the lions, and that they will be brought to nothing like water running by. In addition to these things, then, they will also suffer the following. He who long ago bent his own bow, shooting and slaying others with his words as with arrows, will be thrown into confusion at the time of judgment, and his arrows, with which he shot and slew many, will be shattered and vanish. Then, just as an afterbirth that comes forth from a woman has no share in life, but dissolves and perishes; or as a miscarried child that has died within the afterbirth, coming forth from her who carried it in the womb, has no share of sensation with which to enjoy light and sun, so will the ungodly and sinners described above be. For their body, dissolved like an afterbirth, will be handed over to corruption, having no hope of the resurrection with the saints. And their soul, enclosed in the body as in an afterbirth, will be like a woman's miscarriage, enjoying neither life, nor light, nor the rays of the sun, but it will pass from darkness to darkness. It will not be received into the land of the living, nor be well pleasing to the Lord in the light of the living; nor will it say: "Return, O my soul, to your rest, for the Lord has dealt well with you." Deprived of all these things, it will be handed over to darkness. Mentioning this, the Savior said: "Bind his feet and hands and cast him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth." And this will be the [end] of the ungodly… — ¹ Ms.: holoklēron.

[?] …to perceive the sense. He says, then: "He will bend his bow until they grow weak." The Lord who is going to break their teeth in their mouth and crush the molars of the lions will himself bend his bow against them, shooting and punishing them, until they grow weak. And those struck by the fiery arrow will melt away like wax melting under fire. Therefore it is said: "Like melted wax they will be taken away; fire fell." For just as wax melts and vanishes when fire falls on it, in the same way those described will be taken away by the wrath that will overtake them, so that they will not be counted worthy to behold the sun of righteousness with the eyes of the soul. Even before their thorns grow and turn into a bramble, while their thorny deeds are still young, the wrath will overtake and swallow them up. "The righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance; he will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner. And a man will say: If indeed there is fruit for the righteous, then there is a God who judges them on the earth." Symmachus has: "The righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance; he will wash his feet in the blood of the ungodly." Just as it was set down beforehand what end those will have who falsely speak righteousness but weave injustice together in their deeds, so it was necessary, in parallel, that the good end of the truly righteous man, who shows his righteousness through deeds, should be taught. What good will come to the righteous? Now, he says, in the present time, not seeing vengeance on the ungodly, he often complains, lamenting and saying: "Why do the ungodly prosper, and grow old in wealth? Their seed is according to their desire, and their children rejoice, taking up harp and lyre." And now the same man, humbled, says: "But as for me, my feet were almost shaken; my steps had nearly slipped, because I was envious of the lawless, seeing the peace of sinners." But when he sees the end of the ungodly and the vengeance upon them, then he will rejoice and be glad. He will not gloat over the destruction of the ungodly but rejoice at the righteous judgment of God. And he will wash his feet in the blood of the ungodly, not as one who is bloodthirsty and fond of war, but as one cleansed through their punishment and made better through the conversion of others. Or otherwise: he will wash his hands over the blood of the sinner, showing himself innocent, blameless and clean of his destruction. So when the ungodly pay the fitting penalty, and the righteous man, vindicated, is filled with gladness and joy, and washes his hands and his feet (according to the other translators) in the blood of the sinner in the sense explained, then with good reason every man, every voice and tongue, will declare: "If indeed there is fruit for the righteous, then there is a God who judges them on the earth." For if there is fruit for the righteous, the fruit of which it is said in the first psalm, "And he will be like the tree planted by the streams of water, which will yield its fruit

in its season. And its leaf will not wither, and all that he does will prosper," then the following holds. If there will be a reward and good fruit for the one who has practised righteousness, which he will receive at the time of God's righteous judgment, it follows that even before the judgment there is a God who watches over and judges those on earth who are still passing through mortal life. For even if his judgments are not at all visible at present, human affairs are nevertheless not unjudged or unexamined by him. If the righteous were going to perish together with the unrighteous, and there were no fruit for the righteous, one might say that God does not even watch over human affairs. But since there will be a time in which the righteous will rejoice and the sinners will meet the end foretold about them, it is reasonable that no one should even doubt. Instead, every man should confess and declare that there is a God who is overseer and watcher of what is done among men, judging all who have lived their lives on the earth. So much for this. But one should consider whether the present prophecy, being wholly consistent with and joined to those before it, describes the end of those who studied the prophecies about Christ and spoke righteousness with their mouth. Yet they [?did not] receive him when he came, nor heed his voice as he cried out to them and said, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear." They made themselves like the serpent and made their ears like those of a deaf asp that stops its ears. These same men also sharpened their teeth and their molars with their blasphemies against our Savior. With good reason, then, it might be said of them: "God will break their teeth in their mouth; the Lord has crushed the molars of the lions." These words can also be applied to all who have set up godless doctrines and impious false opinions in godless heresies, and to those who profess the wisdom of this age and have sharpened their tongues against the saving teaching. Nor should one refuse to include with these those in the Church who busy themselves with slanders and backbiting to the ruin of their neighbors. To all of these might be said: "If you truly speak righteousness, judge uprightly, O sons of men." They should know that God will bring every work into judgment, and that all must stand before the judgment seat of God, so that each may receive what was done through the body, according to what he has done, whether good

FOR AN INSCRIPTION ON A PILLAR, WHEN SAUL SENT AND WATCHED HIS HOUSE TO KILL HIM. 58. "Rescue me from my enemies, O God, and redeem me from those who rise up against me." We have already observed earlier that the psalms from the fifty-first onward were spoken before David became king, while Saul was still alive. Almost all of those in the first part of the book, apart from a few, were spoken after the sin he had committed. We also observed that, out of an excess of reverence, he placed first in the book the psalms containing confession

although they are later in time, and joined on afterward those that were earlier in time, so that the matter of his confession might be covered over by the memory of his good deeds. The present psalm also confirms this. Let it be said, as usual, that this psalm too is an inscription on a pillar, and that it notes the time at which it was spoken, namely: "When Saul sent and watched his house to kill him." The first book of Kingdoms sets out the history more fully, as follows: "And war broke out again, and David prevailed, and fought the foreigners, and struck them with a very great blow, and they fled from before him. And an evil spirit came upon Saul; and he was sleeping in the house, and a spear in [?] …composes an inscription on a pillar; therefore it is headed: "For the end, do not destroy, for David, for an inscription on a pillar, when Saul sent and watched his house to kill him." Now "For the end, for David," and "Do not destroy," and "inscription on a pillar" have now occurred for the third time in a row. But the first psalm indicated a different time, made clear by its heading, which says: "When the foreigners seized him in Gath." The second says: "When he fled from the face of Saul into the cave." And here: "When Saul sent and watched his house to kill him." The cause of Saul's plot against David was envy. For since David had won the victory over the foreigner Goliath and was praised by everyone for it, Saul was eager to kill him. This was especially so when he saw that the Lord was with David, and he understood this very well, and all Israel and Judah loved David. His jealousy was kindled still more when he saw him prevailing in war with God's cooperation and help. So Scripture says: "And Saul saw that the Lord was with David, and all Israel loved him. And he was still more afraid of David. And David became Saul's enemy all his days." And when war broke out again, and David prevailed and fought the foreigners and struck them a great blow, and they fled from before him, the spirit of envy choked Saul once more, so that he now even

wished to kill the man with his own hand. So he made an attempt on him with the spear. When he missed his stroke, he no longer acted secretly but openly sent men to David's house and set out to kill him. Caught in such a calamity, David composes the present inscription, crying out to God and saying: "Rescue me from my enemies, O God, and redeem me from those who rise up against me. Deliver me from those who work lawlessness, and save me from men of blood." By these words he prays to have God as his guardian, helper and savior, so that he may not be captured by his enemies or fall into their hands. Or else he prays that he himself may not be shown to be like them, nor become one of those who work lawlessness, nor belong to the party of the men of blood. About these it was said above as well: "Men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days; but I will hope in you." We have often shown that he recognized as enemies not only the visible ones but also the hidden and invisible ones, who were themselves at work in Saul. For an evil spirit was upon Saul, and moved by it he was inflamed with envy against David. Here too, then, he is recorded as having overcome his foes and often winning victory over the foreigners. But his hidden enemies were formidable enemies and foes indeed, and he points to them in the present words as well, saying: "For behold, they have hunted my soul; the mighty have set upon me." Judging from the history, he appears to have had no other enemy except Saul alone. For Scripture showed this when it testified that he was loved by all the people, and this was the chief cause of the jealousy against him. If, then, all loved David, and Saul alone plotted against him, burning with envy for that very reason, how does he speak here in the plural: "Rescue me from my enemies and from those who rise up against me"; and again, "For behold, they have hunted my soul; the mighty have set upon me"? Plainly, invisible and hidden enemies are pointed to by these words. The Apostle also spoke of them: "Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the principalities and the powers, against the world rulers of this darkness, and against the spirits of wickedness." It was these that inflamed Saul against David, and so he begged God to be delivered from them. Against Goliath and the other foreigners he was sufficient himself, standing his ground and attacking them all by the law of war. But against the hidden powers and invisible enemies he asked God to become his champion. That he had done Saul no wrong but was persecuted by him for nothing, the history shows, and he himself makes it clear next, saying: "Neither for my lawlessness nor for my sin; without lawlessness I ran and kept a straight course." In place of "without lawlessness I ran and kept a straight course," Symmachus says: "Though there is no

sin, they run at me to drag me off." For though there was no pretext at all, those described undertook so much against him. And see how in these words David evidently speaks with boldness, whereas in the first part of the Psalms he said: "Like a heavy burden they weighed heavily upon me. My wounds have grown foul and festered because of my folly." These and similar things he confessed in the earlier psalms. But in the present one he says: "Neither for my lawlessness nor for my sin, O Lord; without lawlessness I ran and kept a straight course." You will understand the race that David ran if you set beside it the apostolic saying: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith; henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness." "Rouse yourself to meet me, and see. And you, O Lord God of hosts, the God of Israel." He is like a good runner and an excellent contestant fighting the good fight, and on that ground he spoke boldly, saying: "Neither for my lawlessness nor for my sin; without lawlessness I ran and kept a straight course." So he rouses the judge of the contest to watch his own virtue, and asks him to see how his deeds agree with the words he has spoken. This is also shown from the history. There he appears to have suffered countless wrongs from Saul, yet to have done nothing hurtful against him. On the contrary, he often had Saul in his power and spared him at once. And when the evil spirit choked Saul, David appeared as his savior, playing on his instrument and driving out the hostile power in Saul by the power of the divine Spirit within himself. Showing God his forbearance, gentleness and endurance, then, he said: "Neither for my lawlessness," and so on, and "Rouse yourself to meet me, and see." Then, after speaking with such boldness, he is enlightened by the prophetic spirit and taught that a time will come when the Christ of God too will be persecuted and plotted against by the nation of the Jews, and will become savior and overseer of all the nations. At that time the achievements and virtues of David himself will be sung and [?] among all the nations. Knowing this by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, he prays that this time may one day come. Therefore he says next: "And you, O Lord God of hosts, the God of Israel, attend to visit all the nations." As if to say: Israel, which was formerly called your people, received many benefits and was counted worthy of many good things, yet has shown no fruit worthy of you. Always and continually it has fallen into every kind of impiety, at one time worshipping idols, at another killing your prophets, and finally laying hands on your Christ himself. But since I have learned beforehand from your Spirit marvelous things about the conversion of the nations, I rightly pray that that time may come, knowing that with you there is no partiality. Governing all things in righteousness, you know how to save even foreign and alien nations when they turn from error. You also know how to punish those who are thought to belong to your portion, if they are found unworthy of such a calling. Therefore I pray for the nations, saying: "Attend to visit all the nations"; but about the other part I say: "Do not [?]…

…pity all who work iniquity." By saying "all" without qualification, he includes Israel as well, and those in it who were once of this kind. For what advantage, he says, did Saul gain? By race he came from Israel and from the tribe of Benjamin, and he was made king of so great a nation, yet he undertook so many things rashly and for nothing against a man who had done him no wrong. So if others should ever arise who think and act as Saul did, they need not be saved merely because they are reckoned to be of your portion. Conversely, among the foreign nations, if some are found well disposed toward salvation, nothing would prevent them from receiving your visitation, as justice requires. That is why I say: "Attend to visit all the nations"; but those who work iniquity, wherever they may come from, do not pity. He has mentioned those who work iniquity above as well, saying: "Rescue me from those who work iniquity, and save me from men of blood." That is what he called those who laid godless hands on our Savior. He hinted at the same people in Psalm 54 too, saying: "For I have seen iniquity and contradiction in the city. Day and night it will surround it"; and again: "They profaned his covenant; they were divided by the wrath of his face"; and once more: "Men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days; but I will hope in you." "They will return at evening, and they will hunger like a dog, and they will go around the city." Quite consistently, having begged that there be a visitation of the nations and vengeance on those who work iniquity, he next prophesies, saying: "They will return at evening." And who are these but those who work iniquity and the men of blood? Why "at evening"? Because these things were to happen at the consummation of the age. In place of "And they will hunger like a dog," Aquila translated, "And let them make a din like a dog"; Symmachus, "And they will howl together like dogs"; Theodotion, "And they will make a noise like a dog"; and the fifth edition likewise, "And they will make a noise like dogs." By these words he plainly called "dogs" those who, late in time, in the days of our Savior's coming, were themselves going to make war on the Christ of God, just as Saul back then persecuted the innocent man. For the same Holy Spirit teaches about the same people through the prophet Isaiah, saying: "All are dumb dogs that do not know how to bark"; and in Psalm 21, which describes the passion of our Savior, it is said in the person of the Savior himself: "Many dogs surrounded me; a gathering of evildoers hemmed me in." So those who work iniquity and the men of blood, even if they now seem very powerful and hold the kingdom for the present, as Saul did for a time, nevertheless all who have done the like will return late, and at evening they will make a din and howl together. They will utter nothing articulate, nor

offer words worthy of memory from a rational mind, but will give out barks like dogs, insolent and shameless cries. Therefore they will also hunger, deprived of the bread of life, since they did not accept the saving and heavenly food, the very one who said: "I am the bread that came down from heaven and gives life to people." Hence another prophet too, hinting at this famine, cried out: "Behold, those who serve me shall eat, but you shall hunger; behold, those who serve me shall drink, but you shall thirst." Deprived of the eternal food and having refused the bread of life, they will no longer be sheep of the good shepherd, but will be compared to dogs. Then they will also be driven out of their own city, which they inhabited wickedly, and shut out of it, so that they no longer dare set foot in it, since those who lived there filled it with blood. That is why in the passage cited earlier it was said: "For I have seen iniquity and contradiction in the city." There, however, what Israel dared against the Savior in Jerusalem itself was being shown; here, by the foreknowledge of the Holy Spirit, Scripture inscribes on a pillar what happened to them afterward, which is why it is called a "pillar inscription." The outcome of events proves that the word has been fulfilled. After their plot against our Savior, the Romans came upon them and brought the prophetic words to fulfillment. By the laws of the rulers, the whole Jewish nation has since then been forbidden to set foot in those places, with inexorable punishment hanging over those who break the law. Hence even today they pass around the borders and stand at a distance, not deemed worthy to look even from afar on the ground they once held to be holy. By circling it from outside, they confirm the Scripture before us, which says: "They will return at evening, and they will hunger like a dog, and they will go around the city." And immediately after this is added the reason why they will suffer these things: "For behold," it says, "they will speak out with their mouth, and a sword is on their lips; for who has heard?" For they have suffered all these things because of the godless and impious cries they uttered against our Savior, shouting before Pilate: "Away with him, away with him, crucify him! His blood be on us and on our children." This is what the word means by saying, "Behold, they will speak out with their mouth, and a sword is on their lips." In place of "For who has heard?" Symmachus translated more clearly, saying: "They shouted as though no one were listening." For they barked such things against the Savior as though no one were watching, and as though God were not listening to their voice. They shouted as though no one heard; but you yourself, the overseer and judge of all, not only heard them barking such things, but also made them a laughingstock. And how could they not be a laughingstock, who thought they could overcome the maker of so many wondrous works by their own [?]? In Psalm 2 too it is said: "He who dwells in the heavens will laugh them to scorn, and the Lord will mock them."

"You will treat all the nations as nothing." In place of "You will treat all the nations as nothing," Symmachus translated, "You will rebuke all the nations." The word indicates a certain rebuke from God to all the nations. Since above it was said, "Attend to visit all the nations," he consistently teaches that God, in visiting them, will first rebuke all the nations and then turn them from the error of many gods and idolatry. One can see how the word was fulfilled by observing that after the coming of our Savior, the nations most infatuated with the error of many gods, which at the beginning of the preaching opposed the acceptance of the word, were brought to their senses by sieges and other calamities meant to turn them, God in this way rebuking them and speaking against them; and so, brought to their senses after this, they submitted to the saving word. That is why there follows, in the person of the Savior: "I will guard my strength toward you, for God is my helper; my God, his mercy will go before me; God will show me among my enemies" — or, according to Symmachus, "He will make me look upon those who wall me off." And elsewhere it is said: "And my eye looked upon the evildoers who rise up against me; my ear will hear." David, too, saw the fall and end of Saul and looked upon him in the catastrophe of his death. "Do not kill them, lest they forget your people." Again he speaks in the plural: "Do not kill them," he says, "and scatter them, and bring them down," although history shows that David had no enemy at the time these things were said except Saul alone. But the prophetic Spirit proclaims these things too in the person of the Savior, about those who rose up against him, of whom it was said: "And peoples devised vain things. The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ." So those who meditated in vain on the prophecies about him, together with their rulers and leaders — do not kill them, he says, but scatter them and bring them down. He prays that they be deposed from their rank, and that is what happened. There is no longer among them a king, or a high priest, or a prophet, or even scribes and Pharisees and Sadducees. Yet he does not say that they are to be killed. That is why their race has endured and the succession of their children multiplies. For they were not killed, nor wiped out from among humankind; they exist and they persist, but as people cast down and brought down from the honor they once enjoyed with God. Further, "Scatter them," he says, "in your power" — or, according to Symmachus, "Uproot them by your power." The fact itself shows this more plainly than any word, for the Jewish nation is scattered everywhere on earth

and uprooted. So if the Jews take pride in this, that they fill all the nations and live among barbarians and in the midst of Greeks, let them know that these things were prophesied about them as a curse. The present prophecy, at any rate, says of them: "Scatter them in your power, and bring them down, O Lord my protector." But it also indicates that they would not be utterly wiped out from humankind, saying: "Do not kill them, lest they forget your people." For if they had been wiped out from humankind and were no longer among the living, he says, they would not have seen my people or known my Church flourishing. But so that they may see it and behold my people, do not kill them; rather, scatter them everywhere on earth, wherever my Church is to be established. Then, seeing my people and the Church I have founded throughout the whole world, they may come to zeal for godliness, and by the example of the people turning to God from the nations, they too may at last cease from the incurable and untreatable evil of idolatry among them. So the Savior prayed these things for them as well, asking the Father that they not be destroyed but remain alive and be preserved to behold his people and the great things from it…

"The sin of their mouth, the word of their lips; and let them be caught in their pride." Here again he presents the cause of what was said before. For he necessarily teaches why he thought it right that they should suffer these things, saying: "Because of the sin of their mouth and because of the word of their lips." One may marvel at the precision of the Holy Spirit's prediction. In our Savior's time the Jews did not themselves bring about his death; it was carried out by a Roman hand, Pilate passing judgment and soldiers taking him and leading him away, while these Jews did nothing whatever of the deed. So it is fitting that the word attributes to them not the act of the killing itself but its cause. For the rulers of the Jews held a council and set every device in motion to destroy him; the false witnesses and slanderers, to please them, stood up to the Savior's face; and the whole people, with their own voices and lips, called down his blood upon themselves and upon their own children. It is fitting, then, that the present word does not mention the act of killing, which Pilate decreed and the soldiers under him carried out, but the scheming of the high priests, the testimony of the slanderers, and the voice of the multitude shouting against him. That is why he says: "The sin of their mouth, the word of their lips," as if to say more clearly: "Because of the sin of their mouth and because of the word of their lips." For on account of these things, scatter them by your power, and bring them down, O Lord my protector. According to Symmachus, he says that what was foretold will be brought upon them by the sin of their mouth and by the word of their lips. And he adds: "And let them be caught in their pride"; or, according to Symmachus, "Let them be caught along with their

pride." For being proud and boastful, they could not bear our Savior's boldness of speech. That is why they came to him with great pride and said: "Who gave you this authority? And by what authority do you do these things?" As much as to say: "Since we control the temple and rule the whole nation, who are you, and where do you come from, that you dare such things?" It is on account of these words, then, that it is said here: "And let them be caught in their pride; and for cursing and lying they will be proclaimed"; in place of which Symmachus translated: "Let them be caught with their pride, speaking cursing and falsehood." Then he adds next: "In consummation, in the wrath of consummation, and they shall not exist." In place of which Symmachus again rendered more clearly: "Make an end in [wrath], consume, so that they may not be." The prophetic Spirit proclaims these things beforehand not as a curse on those who were to suffer them, but as a prediction of what would happen, the thought conveying this sense: Because of the sin of their mouth and because of the word of their lips they will be caught in their pride, and they will be caught speaking cursing and falsehood; and they will come to consummation and to a wrath that consumes them, so that they no longer exist. According to Aquila it is said: "Make an end in anger, make an end, and they shall not exist." So too according to Symmachus: "Make an end in wrath, consume, so that they may not be." Through these words the prophecy declares that those who dared such things would no longer exist in the city mentioned before; and that the worship once zealously pursued in that city, the kingdom established in it, and all the good things they formerly had from God — the presence of prophets, that is, the appearances of angels, and the rest of his care — would at last come to an end. And these things truly did come to an end through the wrath brought upon them. That "Make an end in wrath, consume, so that they may not be" was said of these things is clear from what follows. And what was that? "And they will know that the God of Jacob rules over the ends of the earth." For if "Make an end in wrath, consume, so that they may not be" were said of the nation itself and of the men themselves, how, once brought to an end and no longer existing, could they know that God rules over the ends of the earth? And how could it have been said above, "Do not kill them"? For "Do not kill them" would seem to contradict "Make an end in wrath, consume, so that they may not be." But it does not say here, "Make an end of them," but without specifying, "Make an end in wrath, consume, so that they may not be." We are to understand and supply from outside: "so that they may not be what they were before," and "so that they may not remain in the honor they once had with God." Once this honor was taken from them, and what they formerly possessed was removed, they were left naked and brought down from the height of their pride, and scattered among all the nations; and so they came to know

by the facts themselves that the one who of old was called the God of Jacob now rules no longer over Jacob, nor over Israel, but over all the ends of the earth. He has aptly named him "God of Jacob" here too, indicating Christ. For it was he who appeared to the patriarch Jacob in the shape and form of a man, when a man wrestled with him. He also renames him, saying: "Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name; for you have prevailed with God, and you are mighty with men." That very God, then, who spoke to Jacob will rule over the ends of the earth, being properly so called among all the nations and named Master and Lord. So that those who denied him might see this with their own eyes, it was necessarily said beforehand: "Do not kill them, lest they forget my people"; and here: "And they will know that the God of Jacob rules over the ends of the earth." "They will return at evening, and they will hunger like a dog, and they will go around the city." To confirm what was said before, he repeats the word, taking up the same prophecy again. He prophesies that they will not be wiped out from humankind nor be killed, but will return — that is, they will come to their senses late, at evening; and they will hunger like a dog; or, according to Aquila, "They will make a din like a dog"; or, according to Symmachus, "They will be in an uproar like dogs, and they will go round about the city." These things were also prophesied in the earlier verses. There, however, the cause was given next, in "Behold, they will speak out with their mouth, and a sword is on their lips," and "because of the sin of their mouth and the word of their lips"; here, after "They will return at evening, and they will hunger like a dog, and they will go around the city," there is added: "They will be scattered to eat; and if they are not satisfied, they will also grumble." Symmachus translated this as follows: "Let them come back at day [?]; let them be in an uproar like dogs, wandering around the city, so as not to lodge for the night unfed." So, scattered among all the nations, they seek something to eat like hungry dogs; but finding no rational food, they faint. And if they ever take some food from the bare reading of the divine Scriptures, still, since they partake of nothing solid and do not taste the life-giving bread, they remain unsatisfied; and not being satisfied, they grumble, just as they once grumbled in the wilderness. For this is their habit. That is why the Apostle says to us: "Do not grumble, as some of them grumbled and were destroyed by the serpents." "But I will sing of your power, and in the morning I will rejoice in your mercy; for you have become my helper and my refuge in the day of my affliction. My helper, to you I will sing psalms; for you, God, are my helper, my God, my mercy." Those who rose up against me will suffer these things, then; but I will sing of your power, the power of my Father. These words are spoken in the person of the Savior by the prophetic Spirit, just as it was said elsewhere in his person: "I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the assembly I will sing your praise." "And in the morning," he says, "I will rejoice in your mercy"; which Symmachus

translated: "And I will sing the praise of your mercy at dawn." By this he prophetically indicates the worship offered at dawn, every morning of the day of resurrection, throughout the whole world in his Church. For in the words "In the midst of the assembly I will sing your praise," the place was shown in which Christ promised to sing the Father's praise; while in "And I will sing the praise of your mercy at dawn," the time is given in which his Only-Begotten, through his own people, sings the praise of the Father's mercy poured out on all the nations, rejoicing and exulting in it. "And all these things I will render to you," he says, "for you have become my helper and my refuge in the day of my affliction." For having received all these things from the Father, it is fitting that I should sing the praise of your mercy at dawn and that I myself should sing psalms to you; for you have become my helper, my God and my mercy. None of those beneath me was able to stretch out a hand to me, but only you, the Father who is above me. Therefore I confess that I depend on you, and I will sing of your power, inscribing you alone as my helper and my refuge. These would be the words of the Savior, teaching everyone to be devout toward his Father.

FOR THE END. FOR THOSE WHO WILL BE CHANGED. FOR A PILLAR INSCRIPTION. OF DAVID. FOR TEACHING. WHEN HE BURNED MESOPOTAMIA OF SYRIA AND SYRIA OF ZOBAH, AND JOAB TURNED BACK AND STRUCK TWELVE THOUSAND IN THE VALLEY OF SALT. PSALM 59. "O God, you have rejected us and torn us down; you were angry, and you had pity on us." The present word is also "for a pillar inscription," yet it was not spoken at the same time as the psalms before it. Those were spoken while Saul was still alive and before David became king: the first "when the Philistines seized him in Gath"; the second "when he fled from the face of Saul into the cave"; and the last "when Saul sent and watched his house in order to put him to death." But the psalm before us David prophesies after the death of Saul, when he was already exercising the rule of the kingdom and had spent a long time in it. The superscription indicates this when it says: "When he burned Mesopotamia of Syria and Syria of Zobah, and Joab turned back and struck twelve thousand in the Valley of Salt." You will find the history in the second book of Kingdoms, where it is written: "And David struck Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to set his hand on the river Euphrates. And David captured from him a thousand chariots, seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand foot soldiers. And David hamstrung all the chariot horses, and kept back for himself a hundred chariots of them. And Syria of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah. And David struck down twenty-two thousand men of the Syrians. And David placed a garrison in Syria of Damascus. And the Syr…

…the Lord [preserved] David in everything he did.” A little later this follows: “And David reigned over Israel, and David executed judgment and justice for all his people. And Joab son of Zeruiah was over the army.” Again, after other things, it says: “And the Ammonites sent and hired Syria of Rehob and Syria of Zobah, twenty thousand foot soldiers, and the king of Maacah with a thousand men, and Ishtob with twelve thousand men. And David heard of it and sent out the army, the mighty men. And the Ammonites came out and drew up for battle at the entrance of the gate; Syria of Zobah and Rehob and Ishtob… And Joab saw that the battle was set against him from the front, and he picked men from all the young men of Israel, and they drew up against Syria,” and so on. Right after this comes: “And the servants of Hadadezer saw that he had been defeated before Israel, and they went over to Israel and served them.” In these passages the narrative mentions the Euphrates, Zobah, Syria, Joab and the fourteen thousand. It tells how David became master of all his enemies, and how his commander-in-chief Joab fought the foreigners and brought them under his power. The pillar inscription now before us refers to the very people against whom these things were done. In Symmachus the superscription reads: “A victory song for the flowers, of the humble-minded and blameless David, for [?] succession, when he set fire to Syria of Mesopotamia and Syria of Zobah, and Joab returned and struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, nineteen [?] thousand.” The time shows that these words were spoken while David was reigning with distinction and achieving great things. This was before the story of Bathsheba, when his affairs were going well and he stood in good repute with God and with everyone, so that Scripture testifies that he executed judgment and justice in Israel. But here it is worth raising a difficulty. How can he, being in such a condition, begin the pillar inscription with the words, “O God, you have rejected us and torn us down”? After all, he was setting up trophies over his enemies and winning victories over his foes. For these he should have sung victory songs and offered thank offerings to God. Yet he does none of this. On the contrary, he laments: “O God, you have rejected us and torn us down; you were angry, and you had compassion on us.” For “and you had compassion on us” Symmachus translated “and you led us around”; the fifth edition has “and they surrounded us”; and Aquila, “in your fury you turned us away.” Then he goes on: “You have shown your people hard things; you have made us drink the wine of compunction.” These words would seem out of keeping and ill-suited to what the superscription indicates. But I think it is not without purpose that the superscription points us to the end, and

bears the heading “for those who will be changed,” and calls the words a pillar inscription. It says “for the end” because what was prophesied was to be fulfilled at the consummation of the ages. “For those who will be changed” is added of necessity, because of the change that was going to overtake the state of affairs at that time. For when these words were spoken, Israel was master of the foreigners and stronger than its enemies. Yet at some time it was destined to undergo a change and to come under its enemies. That is why the superscription says, “For the end, for those who will be changed.” Symmachus has “For the flowers,” and Aquila “Upon lilies.” For just as the lilies of the field and the grass look lovely for a short while, but soon change and perish, so the people's affairs, flourishing at that time, were soon to change. That is why the Savior said in his teaching, “Consider the lilies of the field,” and again, “If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven.” There is also the passage, “All flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass. The grass has withered and the flower has fallen, but the word of the Lord remains forever.” According to the other translators, the prophet adds to this, “Truly the people is grass; the grass has withered, the flower has fallen,” plainly indicating the nation of the Jews. These very things the Holy Spirit now testifies through David as well, announcing in advance the change and alteration that would come upon the people. That is why Aquila has “Upon lilies of testimony,” Symmachus “For the flowers, a testimony,” and the Seventy “For those who will be changed, for a pillar inscription.” This fits closely with what was said in the psalm before this one. That psalm also pointed to the rejection of the nation when it said, “They will return at evening, and go hungry like a dog, and prowl around the city,” and what follows. Right after that it spoke of the calling of the nations: “And you, O Lord God of hosts, God of Israel, attend to visit all the nations.” Here, as before, Aquila rendered the “pillar inscription” as “of the humble, perfect David,” and Symmachus as “of the humble-minded and blameless David.” For the modesty of so great a king deserved a pillar. Though he had come out on top in so many wars, subdued peoples as far as Mesopotamia and made them pay tribute, he kept his own character. It was the same character for which he had been distinguished when Saul was hunting him and he lived as a fugitive in the deserts. At that time too divine Scripture judged him worthy of everlasting pillars as humble and perfect, or humble-minded and blameless. Now, as king, he was marching against so many enemies and gathering the wealth of all of them, yet he kept the same disposition. That is why he was judged worthy of a pillar inscription, and worthy of the prophetic Spirit. Notice how at this time, under David's reign, Israel ruled as far as Mesopotamia and received tribute from the surrounding nations. God's promise to Abraham was coming true in deeds, for in it he promised to give his seed all the land from the river

of Egypt to the river Euphrates. This was fulfilled in deeds during David's reign, as the narrative quoted from the book of Kingdoms testified. But the prophet, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, foretells what was to happen in future times. He shows what these things were when he says, “For the end, for those who will be changed.” Then, going on, he adds, “O God, you have rejected us and torn us down,” and the rest. After other things he continues, “God has spoken in his holy one: I will exult and divide Shechem, and measure out the valley of tents,” and so on. By these words he signifies God's reconciliation with the foreigners. For God, he says, has spoken, and in speaking in his holy one, he includes Moab, Idumea and all the other foreigners along with Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim and Judah. “Moab,” he says, “is the cauldron of my hope.” In place of this Symmachus gave “Moab is the cauldron of my freedom from care,” and Aquila “Moab is the basin of my washing.” Then he himself makes a promise about Idumea: “Over Idumea I will stretch out my sandal,” or in Symmachus, “Upon Idumea I will tread with my sandal.” Such are the promises he makes to Moab and Idumea. Concerning the foreigners he goes on again: “Foreigners have been subjected to me,” or in Aquila, “Philistia has made itself my companion,” and in Theodotion, “Foreigners have become my friends.” These same things are said, in the same words and phrases, in Psalm 107 as well, where, also in the Seventy's version, it is foretold that the foreigners will become friends of God. For in that psalm too it is written, “Moab is the cauldron of my hope. Upon Idumea I will cast my sandal; foreigners have become my friends.” So much for what he says about the foreigners. After this the prophecy speaks again in the person of the Jewish people: “Is it not you, O God, who rejected us? And will you not go out with our forces?” This would be like what was said at the beginning: “O God, you have rejected us and torn us down.” In these words they clearly say that they themselves have been rejected and torn down and do not have God as a helper in their forces. The foreigners, on the other hand, have all in general become friends of God. In particular, Moab has become the cauldron of his hope, or the basin of his washing, or the cauldron of his freedom from care, and Idumea has been judged worthy of God's sandal. Enlightened about these things by the divine Spirit, David speaks in common, as if in the person of the whole people, and says, “O God, you have rejected us and torn us down,” or in Symmachus, “O God, you have cast us off and cut us apart.” Here he clearly indicates that they were cast off and cut off. Then he goes on, “You were angry, and you had compassion on us.” Aquila has “In your fury you turned us away,” Symmachus “You were angry and led us around,” and the fifth edition “And you led us around.” The outcome of events, rather than words, proves the truth of all this.

After the coming of our Savior they suffered all these things, when wrath came upon them to the end. They were rejected, torn down and cast off; they were cut apart and led around, scattered among all the nations. He also says, “You have shaken the earth and thrown it into confusion,” because countless evils took place in it. By this I mean their land, that is, Jerusalem, where the royal seat was, and the sanctuary, and where all the solemn rites of the law were performed. Or it means their whole country, or even their souls, figuratively called “earth.” All of these were shaken and thrown into confusion at once because of their lawless deeds. Even so, the prophet makes an entreaty, saying next, “Heal its fractures, for it has been shaken.” For the land just mentioned, moved and shaken from its own dwelling and position, suffered fractures and breaks. Therefore it goes on, “You have shown your people hard things,” and he makes them drink the wine of compunction, or in Aquila “the wine of stupor,” or in Symmachus “the wine of reeling.” One may say that the word of the divine Scriptures, which convicts them of their unbelief in the Christ of God, is wine of compunction. Their conscience is pricked and wounded by the prophecies about the Savior, by the circumstances that surround them and by the conversion of the nations. Even if they seem to pretend not to care, these things still wound their conscience, striking them and bringing them to an awareness of their unbelief in our Savior and Lord. Such is what he foretells will happen to them. But to those who would run to the Christ of God and receive the salvation he brings, he next announces good news: “You have given those who fear you a sign, to flee from the face of the bow.” In Aquila: “You have given,” he says, “those who fear you a signal, to be marked from the face of certainty”; in Symmachus: “You have given those who fear you a sign, so as to escape from the face of the arrow.” If the people described earlier had also been among those who bore this sign, they would not have been rejected or torn down, nor handed over to wrath. But since they refused to accept the saving sign, they have rightly fallen into these things. Those who fear the Lord, however, have received the sign and used it, sealing themselves on the face. (This is how Scripture usually refers to believers from the nations, as we have often shown at length.) They have found a way to flee from the face of the bow, since no spiritual and invisible enemy dares to shoot at them because of the sign placed upon them. This sign was given to those of old as well. For Moses ordered that the doorposts of the Israelites' houses be marked with the blood of the Passover lamb, to turn away the destroyer. In Ezekiel too, when the city was about to be destroyed, it is recorded that God said to the man clothed in the long robe, whoever he was, “Pass through the midst of the city,

Jerusalem, and put the marks on the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over all the lawless deeds done in their midst.” Then he said to others, “Go into the city after him and strike. Let your eyes not spare, and have no mercy on old man or young man, on infants or virgin; kill the women too, to the point of wiping them out. But do not come near anyone who bears the mark. And begin at my holy places.” Do you see how some perished, while those who bore the mark on their foreheads were saved? The people presented in this pillar inscription were of the same kind, for it says, “You have given those who fear you a sign, to flee from the face of the bow.” He does not say, “You have given it to Israel,” but “to those who fear you.” As was said before, we have often shown that prophecy customarily calls those from the nations who take refuge in God “those who fear the Lord.” Those in Egypt once escaped the plagues and the face of the destroyer by using the sign of the blood. In the same way, the sign spoken of here has been given to those who fear the Lord to drive off the enemy and foe of human souls, who habitually shoots at them and strikes them down into the error of idolatry. “That your beloved may be delivered, save with your right hand, and hear me.” Psalm 107 also contains these words and what follows them to the end. In the present psalm, what came before pointed to the rejection of Israel. But in Psalm 107 the words before “that your beloved may be delivered,” and the words that follow it, clearly foretell the calling of the nations. For in Psalm 107 the text first says, “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make music. Awake, my glory; awake, harp and lyre; I will awake at dawn.” Then it adds, “I will give you thanks among the peoples, O Lord; I will sing to you among the nations, for your mercy is great above the heavens, and your truth reaches to the clouds. Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth.” Then it adds what stands in the passage before us: “That your beloved may be delivered, save with your right hand, and hear me,” and the rest, in agreement with the present text. I have marveled greatly at the arrangement of the Holy Spirit, for he made one psalm, Psalm 107, out of two pillar inscriptions. He took the first part, which says, “My heart is ready, O God,” and so on, from David's pillar inscription in Psalm 56. That psalm too had said, “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make music,” and what follows, in agreement with Psalm 107, up to “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth.” The second part, from “That your beloved may be delivered, save with your right hand, and hear me” together with everything added to the end, he took from the pillar inscription before us. In this way the divine Spirit teaches us that one and the same meaning runs through both. In Psalm 56 he announced the good news that the Lord would be thanked among the peoples and praised in song among the nations. In the psalm before us he signifies the rejection of Israel,

just as the earlier verses taught. After the first part, which showed the rejection of the former people and the sign that would be given to those who fear him, a diapsalma is inserted. Then the Holy Spirit sends up a prayer to God, saying, “That your beloved may be delivered, save with your right hand, and hear me.” The Spirit makes this entreaty, asking that God use his right hand to deliver and save his beloved. It does not simply plead, “Save,” but asks that he first deliver and then save “with his right hand.” The Spirit knew of no other beloved of God than human beings, who were made in his image. Though they have fallen very deeply under sin, they are still called God's beloved because the substance of the soul is intellectual and rational. So the word appeals to God by reminding him of his beloved, and calls on him to deliver them from spiritual enemies and foes, and once he has delivered them, to save them by his own right hand. And what could anyone call the right hand of God but his Christ, named this way figuratively? Elsewhere he is called power and wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. So here too he might be called the right hand, since he was to bring favorable and saving things to all people. “God has spoken in his holy one,” and the rest. When the Holy Spirit has prayed that God's beloved may be delivered, God answers without delay: “I will be exalted and divide Shechem.” God spoke these words through his Word as through an interpreter, and the Holy Spirit, hearing them, teaches us to know them too. That is why it says, “God has spoken in his holy one.” The demons never failed to recognize the Holy One of God, even after he had taken the form of a servant. That is why they cried out, “We know who you are, the Holy One of God.” In Psalm 88 it is also said, “Once I have sworn by my holy one, that I will not lie to David.” For as a father swears by a beloved son, so the God of all swears by the Son. Here too, then, “God has spoken in his holy one,” or in Aquila, “God has spoken in his sanctified one.” When was this fulfilled, if not when in the last days he spoke to us in a Son? And what did he say, if not the words that follow: “I will exult and divide Shechem”? In Psalm 107 it says, “I will be exalted and divide Shechem,” and this is very fitting there, because earlier in that psalm it said, “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth.” So in answer to “Be exalted” comes “I will be exalted.” Here, however, he answers “save with your right hand” and “that your beloved may be delivered.” Rejoicing at the salvation of his beloved, he replies, “I will exult,” or in Aquila, “I will glory,” or in Symmachus, “I will glory and distribute Shechem.” This was the portion set apart long ago for Joseph as a special gift. Formerly the children of the Jews

prided themselves on it, but now the Samaritan people do. Sikima is the same as Shechem, which Jacob gave to Joseph. Jacob's well and spring are there, which the Gospel mentions when it says that the Savior stayed there and that many of the people believed in him. After his ascension the apostles also came to Samaria and did signs and wonders there. The Acts of the Apostles records that the Holy Spirit was given to those who lived in the place, and that there was great joy there. For it is written that Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed the Christ to them. The crowds with one accord paid attention to what Philip said, as they heard him and saw the signs he was doing, and there was a great sound of joy in that city. Next it says, “When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. They came down and prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Spirit.” And it adds, “Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.” These things took place in Samaria in fulfillment of the promise before us, which says, “I will be exalted and divide Shechem.” For he distributed the Holy Spirit to those in Samaria after his ascension, after he had been exalted, when “having ascended on high he led captivity captive, and gave gifts among men.” This happened after the Savior's disciples had been persecuted and driven from Jerusalem. Scripture says, “A great persecution arose against the church in Jerusalem, and all were scattered,” and again, “Those who had been scattered went about proclaiming the word.” Then it goes on to tell how they preached the gospel to the people of Samaria, and how the apostles gave them a share in the Holy Spirit. It has now been shown what is meant by “I will be exalted and divide Shechem”: all these things were fulfilled after the Savior was exalted. Someone else might give a different reason. The place once belonged to the Jews, but now, after our Savior's ascension, it has been handed over to Greeks and Samaritans, and that is why it says, “I will be exalted and divide Shechem.” The text also says, “and I will measure out the valley of tents.” The prophetic word usually calls the dwelling place of all humankind a valley. That is why it says elsewhere, “He set them in the valley of weeping.” So, he says, I will fill this dwelling place of all humankind, this valley, with my own churches. He hints at this when he says, “I will measure out [the valley] of tents.” Aquila translated it the same way: “I will measure out the valley of shelters.” Then, he says, just as Gilead became mine, and Manasseh once became mine, and Ephraim once was, when it was “the strength of my head,” or in Symmachus “the strength of my rule,” and likewise just as Judah was once “my king,”

or, according to Aquila, “Judah is my decreer.” In the same way, the land and city of the foreigners called Moab will also be his. For it will become “the cauldron of my hope,” or, according to Aquila, “the cauldron of my washing,” or, according to Symmachus, “the cauldron of my freedom from care.” He called Ephraim the strength of his head, or the might of his rule, because the kings from the tribe of Ephraim once ruled the nine and a half tribes of Israel from Samaria. Joseph had two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh. The descendants of Ephraim broke away from Jerusalem and set up their kingdom in Samaria and in Shechem, mentioned earlier, which is also called Sikima. That is why it is said: “Ephraim is the strength of my head,” or “the might of my rule.” The descendants of Manasseh held Gilead, and so it is said: “Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine.” Gilead stood for the place, and Manasseh for those who lived there. He is saying, then: just as these became mine, both the sons of Manasseh who lived in Gilead and the sons of Ephraim who ruled the people in Shechem, and just as the kings from the tribe of Judah who reigned in Jerusalem itself were mine and were kings of my portion, so one day the foreign nations too will be mine. By Moab and Idumea he means all foreigners. Through these two nations, which were forbidden to enter the assembly of God, he takes in all the others as well. For it is written: “Ammonites and Moabites shall not enter the assembly of the Lord to the third and fourth generation, and even forever.” Moab and Ammon were sons of Lot, born of his unlawful union with his own daughters and of Sodomite seed. The law of Moses makes their descendants, the Moabites and Ammonites, outcasts. But the present passage brings Moab the best of good news when it says: “Moab is the cauldron of my hope.” It also promises good things to another nation, the one descended from Esau, when it goes on to say: “Over Idumea I will stretch out my sandal.” Idumea was named after Edom, and Edom was Esau, of whom it is said: “Let no one be a fornicator or profane, like Esau.” Countless other prophecies were also spoken against the Idumeans and against Idumea. But the present passage brings them, too, the best of good news, for God says: “Over Idumea I will stretch out my sandal.” Then he goes on to speak of the remaining nations without distinction: “Foreigners have been made subject to me,” or “have become my friends.” He calls Moab the cauldron of his hope, or the cauldron of his washing, or of his freedom from care. Once Moab had been cast out, the only way it could come into the Church of God was through the washing of regeneration. Washed, as it were, in a cauldron and cleansed of its former ungodliness, it is counted worthy of grace and so gains freedom from care. These things have come to pass in fact, and anyone can see them with their own eyes by visiting the land of the Arabs and seeing the peoples multiplying there, Moabites and Ammonites

who fill the churches of God. Likewise, according to Symmachus, he says: “Upon Idumea I will tread with my sandal.” This prediction too would not be hard to see fulfilled. One need only go to the land of the Idumeans and see with one's own eyes the great number of churches of God there, and no one would hesitate to admit that a true treading has taken place in those parts. This is why it was said above: “God has spoken in his holy one: I will exult.” Since the whole human race was about to be called to salvation, God, as befits his love for humankind, rejoiced in the salvation of those being saved. In another sense, you would not be wrong to say that his sandal means the apostles, or those who to this day serve in preaching about him. God accomplished all these things when, in the last of the days, he spoke to us in his holy one. According to another interpretation, God, having spoken in his holy one, called absolutely everyone to his grace, Jews and Greeks alike, and the nations throughout the whole world. That is why he listed Shechem and Gilead (1), Manasseh and Ephraim, Judah and Moab, Idumea and all the foreigners: he counted the whole human race equally worthy of the same calling. Yet he calls those from Israel first. It was right that the first place and the firstfruits of the gospel preaching should be given to them first, because of the promises made to their fathers. For that reason the Saviour himself preached the gospel to them first, declaring: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” He also urged his apostles to preach the gospel to them first, saying: “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter a city of the Samaritans; go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” Then, after them, he commanded his disciples to preach the gospel to all the nations in his name. So here too it is prophesied that the God of all will dwell in his holy one and will speak to people in him and through him. It is also prophesied that he will receive Ephraim, Manasseh and Judah together and alike. These were once divided, when Judah reigned in Jerusalem, Ephraim in Shechem and Samaria, and Manasseh lived in Gilead. Now that there is no longer any separation or division among them, he calls them first, and then the Moabites and Ammonites, the Idumeans, and all the rest of the people living throughout the whole world. You can learn from the history of the Gospels that when the Holy One of God visited Shechem, Samaria itself and Jerusalem, Israel was united and there was no division within it. In the same way, he sent his apostles first to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. After this, using them as his sandals, he counted the whole human race worthy of his saving grace. “Who will lead me into the fortified city? Or who will guide me as far as Idumea? Is it not you, O God, who have rejected

(1) “Shechem and Gilead”: perhaps read τὰ Σίκιμα καὶ τὴν Γαλαάδ. — Editor.

us, and will you not go out with our forces?” As the Prophet reflects on the meaning of what was said before, he is utterly amazed at the wonder of the unexpected change among the foreign nations. God had said: “Over Idumea I will stretch out my sandal.” The Prophet marvels at these words: that God himself would one day put on a sandal and walk, not on Jerusalem or Samaria or any other part of Israel, but on the land of the foreign Idumeans. So he calls those whom God was going to visit blessed, and he prays that he too might one day be counted worthy to see them. That is why he says: “Who will lead me into the fortified city? Or who will guide me as far as Idumea?” He was praying to be guided there, and for the years of his life to be stretched out to the time when God would stretch out his sandal over Idumea. Then he could see the great spectacle of God dwelling among people and walking about in Idumea, with foreigners made subject to him and becoming his friends. That is why he says: “Who will guide me as far as Idumea?” By “fortified city” he means the Church of God. It is fenced around with a firm and very strong wall, which is God's saving power, and he prayed to see this too. That is why he said: “Who will lead me into the fortified city?” Notice that he did not pray to be guided as far as Jerusalem, or Gilead, or Shechem, or Ephraim, or Judah. Rather, he was astonished at how unexpected the promise was: that the descendants of Esau, the hated fornicator, would then receive such grace that God would walk among them. So he prays: “Who will guide me as far as Idumea?” It is a remarkable thing that God is said to walk about not barefoot but in sandals. The passage is hinting at the souls that serve his will. Through them he called the nations and built his city everywhere on earth. I mean his catholic Church, the community of those who live as citizens devoted to God. Of this city it is said elsewhere: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God,” and: “The streams of the river make glad the city of God.” The Prophet was thirsting to see this fortified city, and so he said: “Who will lead me into the fortified city?” Symmachus translated this as “into a walled city.” For gates and doors and bars of divine powers wall it in, so that it may never suffer a siege. This is why the Saviour said of it: “On the rock I will build my Church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.” Longing to see this walled city, the Prophet said: “Who will lead me into the fortified city?” And praying to see the salvation of the foreigners with his own eyes, he added: “Who will guide me as far as Idumea?” Having asked “Who?” a first and a second time, he acknowledges that he knows the only one able to show him these things. This was God, to whom he had said at the beginning of the present

inscription: “O God, you have rejected us and torn us down.” So here he answers that earlier cry, saying the same thing: “Is it not you, O God, who have rejected us?” He means: who else can show us your promises and the fulfilment of your words, except you yourself, who rejected us? Or, according to Symmachus: “Unless you, O God, who cast us off and did not go out with our armies?” You, Lord, rejected us and tore us down. In the past you used to go out with our forces and fight alongside them. Now that you have called the nations, you have rejected us and no longer go out with our forces. So we have no other hope of seeing your promises unless you yourself are willing. But if you will it, we too, your prophets, can be counted among the citizens of your walled city and be guided as far as the Idumea we spoke of. “Give us help out of affliction, for the salvation that comes from people is worthless. In God we shall do mighty things, and he will bring to nothing those who afflict us.” Through these words, those who have been counted worthy of the promises are taught to be sober and watchful, to prepare themselves for afflictions, and to pray to their king: “Give us help out of affliction,” since all hope that comes from people is worthless. Having prayed this, they show their eager resolve by saying: “In God we shall do mighty things, and he will bring to nothing those who afflict us.” Paul was like this when he said: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me,” and again: “Yet not I,” he says, “but the grace that is with me.” Those who have come to the grace of God from Idumea and from the foreign nations are taught to say these things. But if these words too are spoken in the person of the company of prophets, then it would be fitting for them to mourn the rejection and downfall of the former people, and to offer a prayer for the common body of all of them, saying to God the words set out here.

PSALM 60. FOR THE END; IN HYMNS; OF DAVID.

“Hear, O God, my petition; attend to my prayer.” The five successive psalms headed “For an inscription” come to an end with the 59th. Altogether there are six psalms with this heading: those just mentioned, and the 15th, which stands in the first part of the book of Psalms. The present hymn is also headed “For the end,” because of the good promises found at its close. There are five psalms in all headed “In hymns.” Two are in the first part of the book, the 4th and the 6th, but these are called “Psalms in hymns.” The three in the second part of the book are headed only “In hymns”: the 53rd, the 54th, and the present one. The “Psalms in hymns”

seem to have been sung with the musical instrument called the psaltery. They needed the one singing to act through the body, which is the soul's instrument. The plain hymns, however, were uttered by the voice alone of the one offering the hymn, without the plucking of the psaltery, because the words in them needed only contemplation in the mind. The present hymn shows this when it says: “From the ends of the earth I cried to you.” By this it means that the Prophet, seized by God, was as it were outside the condition of the body. I am aware that the other translators rendered it no differently. In these words David makes his appeal: “Hear, O God, my petition.” For since he was in need of

great and divine things, he asks to obtain them. Then, as though showing that he is worthy to be heard, he adds: “Attend to my prayer.” He was confident that his prayer was full of rich and deep thought, and so he asked God to look upon it, to consider closely the words in it, and to test what was said as worthy of his hearing.
