Next he shows what he did that made him call on God to look upon his prayer, and so he adds: “From the ends of the earth I cried to you.” Since the other translators agree in rendering it [?] “From the end of the earth I will call upon you”; Symmachus: “From the ends of the earth I call upon you”; and the fifth edition: “From the ends of the earth I shall cry to you” — who would not reasonably look for the meaning of the phrase? How could anyone pass beyond the whole inhabited world, go beyond Ocean itself, and cry out: “From the ends of the earth I cried to you”? But consider whether [?] might reasonably be called the ends of the earth. The worthless man, who rushes about the marketplaces and crowds, the council chambers and the law courts, and is wholly [?] in the [?] of [?], might reasonably be said to live in the middle of the earth. But those who “went about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted, ill-treated,” who fled the middle of the cities and spent their lives in desert places [?] … “to my prayer,” with great boldness [?] in such a way of life, he would not be lying when he says:

“From the ends of the earth I cried to you.” He also gives the reason, adding: “When my heart grew weary,” or, according to Symmachus, “When my heart was in anguish.” For every soul that loves God grows weary and is in anguish while it lives this mortal life. So, I think, it might also say: “Alas, my sojourning has been prolonged.” And: “We who are in this tent groan, being burdened.” Paul too groaned, weary that his mortal life was being drawn out, and so he lamented: “Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from the body of this death?” But he also grew weary and was in anguish out of love for humankind, when he saw the multitude of those perishing, since “wide and spacious is the road that leads to destruction.” In the same way the same apostle mourns for many, of whom he said: “I will mourn for many who sinned before and did not repent of the sin and lawlessness and ungodliness they committed.” In his deep grief and suffering for others, the same apostle cried out: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?” Likewise the prophets lamented the people of old, and so did David. So he fled the middle of the earth, and from its extremities he cried out to God. Yet he lamented, grieved in his soul, over the destruction of the many and of Saul himself. “You lifted me up on a rock, for you became my hope, a tower of strength against the enemy,” and what follows. According to the Seventy, the passage contains a thanksgiving. He means: all that I have described came to me because you yourself, O God, raised me up and exalted me. You set me on the rock that is with you, which is your Word who proceeds from you, for the rock was Christ. You exalted me in your Word and lifted me on high, so that I no longer live in the middle of the earth but at its extremities. You have already guided me so that I have come near to you. You became my hope, and because of that hope I shall not be put to shame. Many spiritual enemies and foes press upon me, seeking my soul, but you alone were enough for me in place of everything. You became a strong tower for me and walled me in with the security of the salvation that comes from you, so that I pay no attention to any of my enemies. Since I have received all these things, it is right that I send up hymns to you, for you have been the cause of every good thing for me. Instead of “You lifted me up on a rock” and what follows, Symmachus gave a different sense: “When the strong one rises up against me, you will guide me. For you became my fearlessness, a lofty tower against the enemy.” Aquila likewise gave the same sense: “On a firm rock, be raised higher than I; you will guide me,” and so on. Through these words the passage teaches us to pay no attention to anyone who rises up against us, but to belong wholly to God and trust in him alone. So the one who is supplied with good hopes, and has gained God as a tower of strength — or, according to Aquila, “a tower of might,”

or, according to Symmachus, “a strong tower” — will say: “I will dwell as a sojourner in your tent forever; I shall be sheltered in the shelter of your wings.” He means: I will not take courage in myself, but in the shelter of your wings. This is what the Word usually calls God's providential powers. The one who loves God is sheltered under them. He never leaves God's shelter but lives within it forever. Already now he enjoys God's Church and the beauty of his house, so that he can say: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house, and the place where your glory dwells,” and: “One thing I have asked of the Lord, this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the delight of the Lord and to visit his temple.” But there is also a heavenly tent, which the Lord pitched and not man, and Moses made its image at God's command. Referring to that tent, one might say: “I will dwell as a sojourner in your tent forever.” For the perfect person has received this promise. He does not look at what is seen but at what is unseen, for what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal. “For you, O God, have heard my prayers; you have given an inheritance to those who fear your name.” If this prayer had been just an ordinary prayer offered by David, there would have been no need to include it in the book of Psalms. For he very likely made countless other prayers to God, just as we too pray every day, offering different prayers at different times. But often, while he was praying, or striking up the psalms, or offering the hymns, he was filled with prophetic power. Those who had received the gift of discerning spirits rightly marked these words, not as ordinary prayers, but as prophetic sayings, and placed them among the divine books. So here too, after what was said before, a diapsalma is inserted, and the Prophet changes the tone of his words. He has perceived that the Holy Spirit has come. He has been enlightened by the Spirit and has learned that God listened to the petition he had just made. So above, in prayer, he said: “Hear, O God, my petition.” But here, after the diapsalma, he says: “For you, O God, have heard my prayers.” Do you see how he perceived that he had been heard? This is what God promised to the worthy through the prophet Isaiah, saying: “While you are still speaking, I will say: Here I am.” For while the Prophet was still speaking, the Holy Spirit came upon him and made it clear to him that he had indeed been heard. That is why he says: “For you, O God, have heard my prayers.” The other translators convey the same meaning. Aquila has: “For you, O God, heard my prayers,” and Symmachus: “For you, O God, have heard my prayers.” Then

…he adds: “You have given an inheritance to those who fear your name.” For so far you have heard me; but, enlightened by your Spirit, I have come to know that not to me alone, but to all who fear your name as well, you will give a fruit worthy of the fear of you: the inheritance which you promised them. By speaking without limit, “to those who fear your name,” he extended grace to all people. For the inheritance is promised not to Israel, nor to the nation of the Jews alone, but to all who fear his name. “To the Jew first,” says the Apostle, “and also to the Greek.” We have often shown that the Word is accustomed to call all those from the nations who draw near to God “those who fear the Lord.” To these very people, then, he says, you have given an inheritance; but what kind he did not say, and has left it to us to seek. [?] To Israel, then, the land flowing with honey and milk was promised through Moses; but what kind of inheritance he gave to those who fear him, he left to be sought. You will find it in the beatitudes of our Savior, in which it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” And again you have the promise of our Savior, in which he says: “And in this age he will receive many times as much, and in the age to come he will inherit eternal life.” It was on account of this inheritance that the fifth psalm was entitled, “To the end, concerning her who inherits”; and in the fifteenth psalm too the same inheritance was indicated, in the words: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup; you are the one who restores my inheritance to me. For indeed my inheritance is most excellent to me.” “You will add days upon days to the king; his years to the day of generation and generation. He will abide forever before God. Who will seek out his mercy and truth?” Having said first, “For you, O God, have heard my prayers,” he joined to it by hyperbaton the words, “You will add days upon days to the king.” For having heard my prayers, he says, you have added days upon days to me. In between was inserted the mention of those who fear the name of the Lord, since the prophecy promises the inheritance to them too. Now the inheritance was eternal life, which the text signifies when it says: “You will add days upon days to the king.” Great things, then, did God promise through the Spirit to King David when he prayed: that he would add days upon days, and his years to the day of generation and generation. For this is the inheritance he promised him; and this is also shown in the twentieth psalm, where it is said: “Lord, in your power the king will rejoice… You have given him the desire of his heart”; and next: “He asked you for life, and you gave him length of days forever and ever.” For since he prayed, reaching out for heavenly things and desiring the good things that are with you, you heard him, he says; and having heard him, you gave him the desire of his heart, and did not deprive him of the wish of his lips.

What his desire was, and what the request of his lips, he teaches next, saying: “He asked you for life, and you gave him length of days forever and ever.” In the present psalm, then, David prayed in much the same way, and having prayed he was heard; and being heard he obtained this promise, in which it is said: “You will add days upon days to the king; his years to the day of generation and generation”; or, according to Symmachus: “You will add days to the days of the king, his years as long as generation and generation; he will dwell forever before God; mercy and truth will fence him round.” All these things will be obtained by the one who is able to say: “From the ends of the earth I cried to you when my heart was in anguish.” For as the worthy fruit of such progress he will receive eternal life. When the text says, “His years to the day of generation and generation,” it signifies that David will be remembered not only during the time he lived, but in every generation, or in two particular generations, the text hinting at the people of the circumcision and at the Church from the nations. For as long as the first generation reads the divine writings, it keeps David in memory; and the second generation, that of the elect from all the nations, likewise never ceases to remember David, because it always has on its lips the book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David. This, then, is what the text hinted at when it said: “His years to the day of generation and generation.” Among men he will obtain this length of days; but with God himself, it says, he will never perish; obtaining an immortal life that lasts without end, “he will abide forever before God.” How human nature could endure and extend alongside the life of God, he teaches next, saying: “Who will seek out his mercy and truth?” Symmachus rendered this more clearly, saying: “Mercy and truth will fence him round”; and Aquila likewise: “Mercy and truth will preserve him.” For these will be the causes of his immortality: the mercy and truth of God. Everyone dear to God who shares in them will be preserved for eternal life, as if salted with salt. For since he is not by nature of the same substance as God, he will not live as God does, but will be held fast by the mercy of God and by his truth. “So will I sing to your name forever and ever, that I may pay my vows day by day.” When the Holy Spirit had taught these things to David’s soul, having learned what was said as from a teacher, he seals the word with faith, crying out and saying: “So will I sing to your name forever and ever.” He does not simply say, “I will sing to your name forever and ever,” but adds the word “So.” How “so”? Just as the Holy Spirit taught beforehand, saying: “Mercy and truth will fence him round.” For so, fenced round and preserved by your mercy and by your truth, I will sing to your name forever

and ever. For I am confident that I shall obtain eternal life and the immortality that is with you because of your mercy and because of your truth, and not because of my own virtues. “So then I will sing to your name forever and ever, that I may pay my vows day by day”; or according to Symmachus: “paying my vows each day.” For I shall never fail to pay what I have promised, as continual debts that also bring me salvation. These I shall go on paying even into the endless age. For I shall not be idle and inactive in that eternal life, but there too I shall go on rendering to God the activity that is fitting and owed. And this is the continual thanksgiving that is owed and fitting to him.

To the end, for Jeduthun. A psalm of David. 61.

“Will not my soul be subject to God? For from him is my salvation.” The present psalm is spoken by David, but the title reads “for Jeduthun,” the text teaching us that David composed the psalm for Jeduthun and gave it to him to meditate on and to use like a healing charm, when some misfortune had befallen him. The thirty-eighth too was entitled, “To the end, for Jeduthun, a song of David”; in it likewise David was handing on teaching to Jeduthun, on account of the same situation, I think. For here it is said: “I shall not be shaken any more. How long will you set upon a man? You are murdering, all of you”; and in the thirty-eighth: “When the sinner stood against me, I was struck dumb and humbled, and kept silent from good things, and my pain was renewed”; and again: “Deliver me from all my iniquities; you have made me a reproach to the fool.” And see how through both he shows that he had been tried in some temptation and had suffered terrible things; which is why he took up these words. In the psalm at hand, as he proceeds, he says: “But the sons of men are vain, the sons of men are false in the balances, so as to do wrong; they are of vanity together”; and in that one likewise it was said: “But all things are vanity, every living man”; and again: “But man is troubled in vain”; which would differ in nothing from: “But the sons of men are vain; they are of vanity together.” Moreover, in the thirty-eighth you would find it said: “Yet man walks about as an image. But they are troubled in vain. He stores up treasure, and does not know for whom he will gather it.” In agreement with these would be the words of the present psalm: “Do not hope in injustice, and do not long for plunder; if wealth flows in, do not set your heart on it.” And if you too, at your leisure, set side by side the expressions found in both these psalms, you would find them holding to one and the [?] of the commentaries on the psalms set below, on the sixty-first, in which there is therapeutic teaching [?]

same meaning. David, then, seems to have handed on therapeutic teaching to Jeduthun, who had fallen into some temptation, perhaps even into some slip, so that he might take hold of himself and recover from the stumble that had befallen him. In the thirty-eighth, at any rate, he taught him to exhort himself, to converse with himself and say: “I said: I will guard my ways, so as not to sin with my tongue. I set a guard on my mouth when the sinner stood before me. I was struck dumb and humbled, and kept silent from good things, and my pain was renewed,” and what follows. Among these was also: “Deliver me from all my iniquities; you have made me a reproach to the fool. I was struck dumb and did not open my mouth, because it was you who did it”; and again: “Remove your scourges from me. I have fainted under the strength of your hand.” These and similar things Jeduthun was taught in that psalm to say, and such prayers to send up to God; and in the psalm at hand David likewise teaches the same man to converse with himself and say: “Will not my soul be subject to God? For from him is my salvation.” This signifies that he had been shaken and had suffered some turmoil in his soul. Since, then, when his tempters set upon him, some weakness came over him, and he found himself not like the one who said, “But my feet were almost shaken,” but truly shaken, he is of necessity taught to say: “I shall not be shaken any more”; or according to Aquila: “I shall [?] stumble greatly”; and in the fifth edition it is said: “I shall not be shaken any more.” The sense of the present teaching would agree with the prophecy that says: “Woe to those who drag their sins as with a long rope, and their iniquities as with the strap of a heifer’s yoke”; and with: “Does not one who falls get up again, and one who turns away turn back? Why has it turned away with a shameless turning, says the Lord?” For all these teach one who has once sinned not to remain in the sin, nor to despair of himself, nor to give himself over to the current of temptation. Therefore Jeduthun is of necessity taught to sing a charm over himself and to say these words: first, to take refuge in the great Savior and physician of souls; then to subject his soul no longer to men, nor to those who terrify him, but, setting before his eyes the great Judge and God, to subject his own soul to him alone and to free it from every alien fear. Therefore he says: “Will not my soul be subject to God?” and what follows. Here again the word “salvation” is expressed in Hebrew by the same letters with which the name of our Savior Jesus is written. Anyone reading this might reasonably ask why, when there are only two psalms entitled “for Jeduthun” (or “concerning Jeduthun,” according to Aquila), they do not stand next to each other but are set far apart. The reason for this

we set out with grammatical proofs in what we said on the thirty-eighth. And who Jeduthun was we have already shown earlier in that same place, citing the account from Chronicles, by which he was shown to have been one of those chosen to praise God. For it is written: “And they left there before the ark of the covenant of the Lord Asaph and his brothers, as ministers before the ark.” And next it is said: “Heman and Jeduthun, and the rest who were chosen by name to praise the Lord, because his mercy endures forever”; and again: “With them Heman and Jeduthun, trumpets and cymbals for sounding aloud, and instruments for the songs of God; the sons of Jeduthun at the gate”; and again: “And King David and the commanders of the army set apart for the service the sons of Asaph and Heman and Jeduthun, who spoke out with the lyre and with harps and with drums.” In place of “who spoke out,” Aquila rendered “of the prophets,” and Symmachus “of those who prophesied by the lyre”; so we must consider those indicated to have been prophets. And again it is said next of Jeduthun: “The sons of Jeduthun: Gedaliah and Zeri and Jeshaiah and Sedeias and Mattithiah, six with their father Jeduthun, playing on lyres.” In place of “playing on lyres,” Aquila again rendered “prophesying with the cithara,” and Symmachus “of the one prophesying by the lyre.” So Jeduthun too was one of those who prophesied by the lyre. Hence one might reasonably say, starting from this, that it was not David who composed the psalm and gave it to Jeduthun, nor Jeduthun who fell into temptation and needed healing from David. For Scripture nowhere presents Jeduthun as blameworthy; on the contrary, it teaches rather that David fell into temptation. So one might reasonably say that Jeduthun, being a prophet, composed the words of both the psalms mentioned above and handed them to David, so that he might be helped and healed by them in what had befallen him. Symmachus too seems in some way to support this interpretation, rendering the title in this way: “A victory song through Jeduthun, an ode to David.” And might it not be that, after the fall that befell David in the matter of Uriah’s wife, when he was no longer able to prophesy as of old, and many trials and one misfortune after another rose up against him, Jeduthun composed these words by the Holy Spirit and gave them to him as healing medicines for the soul, so that he might be comforted by the teaching in them? Having thus offered two interpretations of the present text, we shall leave it to readers to choose between them. “How long will you set upon a man? You are murdering, all of you, as though he were a leaning wall and a tottering fence.” By these words he shows that David had endured not just one trial, nor received a single blow, as it were, from his adversaries, but that, as one beaten over a long time and steadfastly enduring the blows inflicted

on him, he says to those striking him: “How long will you set upon a man?” or according to Aquila: “Until when will you plot?” or according to Symmachus: “Until when will you labor in vain?” Then, exposing the intent of those plotting against him, he says: “You are murdering, all of you.” For you are murderers, he says; not like opponents facing an athlete, who carry the contest only as far as the training ground; no, you set upon me with murderous intent, and you set upon me as one without help, as a wall already leaning and a fence pushed over. For you set upon me as though there were no one fencing me round or walling me in and guarding my soul. How long, then, will you labor at this in vain, and not stop at last, knowing that I have found my guard, my protector and Savior? That is why I was bold to say: “Will not my soul be subject to God? For from him is my salvation. For he is my God and my Savior, my helper; I shall not be shaken any more. But they plotted to thrust away my honor; they ran in thirst; with their mouth they blessed, and in their heart they cursed. Interlude.” The first words the speaker, whether David or Jeduthun, addressed to himself; the second he directed at his enemies; the third, in the present words, teach us what those plotting against him intended when they devised their plot. Therefore he says: “But they plotted to thrust away my honor.” For their whole thinking and counsel, he says, was nothing other than this: they were eager to cast me down from my honor with God and to strip me of the glory I had before. Then, having plotted to take away this honor of mine, they ran in thirst, thirsting to see my destruction. In place of “in thirst,” Aquila rendered “in deception”; Symmachus, “in a lie”; the fifth edition, “in falsehood”; and yet another edition, “in deceit.” It is likely, then, that in our reading too “in falsehood” originally stood, so that the meaning was: “They ran in falsehood”; that is, my enemies and those plotting against me did not make their run and their effort against me with truth, but gave themselves wholly over to falsehood; and that a scribal error occurred in later times, so that “in thirst” came to be written instead of “in falsehood.” How the plotters ran with lies he explains next, saying: “With their mouth they blessed, and in their heart they cursed.” For to deceive me they used sweet words, to drag me down and cast me from my standing with God; that is why they seemed to bless and praise me and welcome me to my face, while the thoughts of their mind were full of curses, by which they plotted to thrust away my honor and bring me under a curse. We are taught by this that all who plot against the people of God are eager for nothing else than to strip them of their honor with God. “But be subject to God, my soul, for from him is my endurance. For he is my God and my Savior, my helper; I shall not be moved.”

At the beginning he said, “Will not my soul be subject to God?” as though still in doubt; but here, made firm by what has been said, he speaks declaratively and confidently exhorts his own soul; therefore he says to it: “But be subject to God, my soul.” And above he said, “For from him is my salvation”; but here, “For from him is my endurance.” This would be like the one who said: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me.” For I do not possess my strength from myself, but from him who strengthens me; and here, “my endurance,” he says, does not rest on my own virtue and power, but comes from his grace: “For he is my God and my Savior”; therefore, as my God and my Savior, he supplies me with endurance. Then above you have: “For he is my God and my Savior, my helper; I shall not be moved”; or according to Aquila and Symmachus, “I shall not stumble.” There is a great difference between saying “I shall not be shaken any more” and saying “I shall not stumble” and “I shall not be moved.” For the former indicated being shaken, though not any more; but here there is a complete denial of stumbling. “In God is my salvation and my glory; the God of my help, and my hope is in God.” Here too “salvation” is named Jesus in the Hebrew, and is written with the same letters. Just as the divine Apostle wrote, speaking of our Savior: “Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood”; and again: “If anyone sins, we have an advocate with God, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins”; in the same way it is said here too: In God is my salvation and my glory, and my help and my hope. So if the meaning of the Hebrew word had been set down more plainly in the translation, it would have read thus: Jesus, being my salvation in the [?] and in the bosom of the Father, is himself my glory and my guardian, and the God of my help, and my hope that is in God. For the Word of God is all these things to those who hope in him. Therefore according to Aquila it is said: “In God is my salvation and my glory; the firm one of my strength, my hope is in God.” “Hope in him, all the assembly of peoples; pour out your hearts before him. God is our helper. Interlude.” Having mentioned salvation, he realized that it would not be healing for himself alone, but would become a common good; therefore he summons everyone to it, turning away from self-love and showing love for humankind and for his neighbors. So he invites them as to a harbor of salvation, saying: “Hope in him, all the assembly of peoples”; or according to Aquila, “Be free of care in him at every time, O people.” Those who are free of care in him and hope in him ought to lay open their thoughts

and to lay bare before him, as before a physician, the passions of the soul. That is why he adds: “Pour out your hearts before him. God is our helper.” Since you have a helper, he says, hold nothing back and hide nothing in your thoughts. Throw open the storerooms of the soul and uncover the thoughts hidden inside it, as people who entrust themselves to the one who alone is good and able to heal all things. “But the sons of men are vain; the sons of men are false in the balance, so as to do wrong; they are altogether made of vanity.” In the thirty-eighth psalm it was also said: “But all things are vanity, every living man,” and again, “But they are troubled in vain,” and, “Surely man walks about as a mere image.” Here too the present words are spoken in harmony with those. Through them we are taught to hope in the Savior alone and to claim him as our helper, since all the sons of men are vain, even if they seem to be rulers and have great power in this life. Or, as Symmachus has it, they are “a vapor,” soon to be “like chaff, which the wind drives from the face of the earth.” Solomon learned from his father here when he wrote, “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity,” and other such things. The sons of men are false in two ways. In one way they speak lies and have been cast far from the truth. In the other they lead astray those who trust them with deceits and lies. So it is not right to hand ourselves over to such people. They are used to lying and there is no truth in them. Even the balances of their soul hold nothing just or evenly weighted. They are tipped to one side, and so these people do the opposite of what is just. With these unjust balances, then, they cherish vanity and turn away from the truth and from the God of truth. Therefore we should not trust them, but claim only the Savior already mentioned as our helper. “Do not hope in injustice, and do not long for plunder; if wealth flows in, do not set your heart on it.” In the thirty-eighth psalm something related was said: “But they are troubled in vain. He stores up treasure and does not know for whom he will gather it.” The one who stores up treasure on earth and gathers a great deal of money gathers in vain. He will not necessarily enjoy it himself, since he leaves this life quicker than a sneeze, and he cannot be sure what kind of heir he will have. So why is he troubled in vain? Many, indeed nearly all, have deceived themselves. They expected to leave their wealth to their sons and those dearest to them, but they did not know the future and missed their aim. Truly, then, they are troubled in vain, storing up treasure and not knowing who will gather it. Therefore we must not hope in injustice, and [?] what comes from injustice [?]; and if wealth flows in, carried along like a river, [?]. But if it is right at times to secure some good hope even through wealth, then use just wealth, which is often provided by God, and straight and even balances, and make use of it in right [?] deeds,

storing up for yourselves treasures in heaven and sowing generously, as it is said: “He scattered abroad, he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.” This alone is a good hope. Otherwise we must not hope in injustice, nor pride ourselves on money gathered by robbery and greed. Our affairs may at some time prosper, and wealth may pour in from every side without hindrance, flowing like a river, even from sources where no one would do wrong, carried along by some unexpected current. Even then, do not assume that this comes wholly from God. Do not call yourself blessed, deceived in your mind and clinging to wealth as though it were a good. Know instead that its nature is fluid: as it flows in, so it flows away, and it has nothing firm, solid or secure. He used the word “flow” remarkably well when he said, “If wealth flows in.” Symmachus has: “If wealth bears fruit, do not set your heart on it.” But where we should set our heart, and what we should cling to, has often been said: “Shall not my soul be subject to God?” and again, “But be subject to God, my soul; for he is my God and my Savior and my protector,” and, “Hope in him, all the congregation of the people.” Since we have the great wealth and the true treasure, then, let us not hope in vain, fluid and unjust wealth. Truly vain are all the sons of men who trust in it. “Once God has spoken; these two things I have heard: that power belongs to God, and to you, Lord, belongs mercy; for you will repay each one according to his works.” Having first taught this much, the text next reminds us of God's just judgment. With this before our eyes, we should give ourselves over neither to injustice nor to plunder, nor to wealth that is temporary and blind. God did not give his charge about the judgment only once, but a second time too. And I myself, he says, heard these things accurately, fixing my mind on these two commands. For God spoke once, but I heard these two things. He spoke through the prophets, and he spoke through the apostles. The one word that God laid down once, I heard both through the Old Testament and through the New. And what was this word, if not “that power belongs to God, and to you, Lord, belongs mercy,” and “that you will repay each one according to his works”? Mercy, he says, and power: power to punish and humble the rebellious, and mercy to save those who have hoped in him. “See, then, the kindness and the severity,” says the Apostle: severity toward those who fell, through his power, and kindness toward you, through his mercy. Having said this, he lifts his face upward and addresses God, saying: “For you will repay each one according to his works.” Aquila translated the passage this way: “God spoke, and a second time I heard: that strength belongs to
God, and to you, Master, belongs mercy. And you, repay each man according to his works.”

A PSALM OF DAVID, WHEN HE WAS IN THE WILDERNESS OF JUDEA. 62. “O God, my God, I rise early to seek you.” As he fled, David came to Ahimelech the priest, then to Achish the king of Gath, and from there to Mizpeh of Moab. The prophet Gad, who was with him, advised him not to stay among the foreigners. So he left that place and lived in the wilderness of Judea. Scripture tells of this when it says: “And David stayed in the wilderness of Masseneth, in the narrow places, and he stayed in the hill country in the wilderness of Ziph. And Saul sought him every day, but the Lord did not deliver him into his hands.” While in these circumstances, he composed the present psalm and indicated its occasion in the superscription. That is why it says, “A Psalm of David, when he was in the wilderness of Judea.” Having reached this point, it is reasonable to note again that the order of the psalms does not follow the sequence of historical events, but departs widely from it. For example, the history first gives the account of Saul sending messengers to David's house to put him to death, when Michal his wife let him down through the window; but the book of Psalms recalls this event in the fifty-eighth psalm. Next, the historical Scripture tells how David came to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest; but the book of Psalms recalls this event in the thirty-third psalm. Directly after this, the book of Kingdoms says: “And David departed from there, and came and escaped to the cave of Adullam”; but the book of Psalms recalls this event in the fifty-sixth. After that, the book of Kingdoms tells of Doeg, how he slandered Ahimelech the priest to Saul; and the book of Psalms marks this time in the fifty-first. When David learned of Doeg's slander, he fled and came into the wilderness of Judea, and it was then that he composed the psalm before us. After the time of this psalm, I mean the sixty-second, the book of Kingdoms records certain events, such as how the Ziphites slandered David to Saul; but the book of Psalms recalls these in the fifty-third, which is entitled, “For the end, among hymns, of understanding, for

[?] the fifty-ninth, when Joab struck the Valley of Salt and subdued twelve thousand of Moab. After these comes the fiftieth, when Nathan the prophet came to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba. Then he composed the third, when he fled from the face of his son Absalom, and after these the seventh, concerning the words of Cush the son of Jemini. Who, then, would not look for the reason for this? It is not reasonable to suppose that these were arranged in this way without some compelling grounds. Someone else might think that the numbers themselves have a certain power, so that the sense of the words in each psalm has been fitted to its number. For example, the number fifty would contain the theme of the forgiveness of sins because of the fiftieth year in the law, which the children of the Hebrews called the Jubilee. In that year debts were remitted and released, servants were set free, and various other such things were prescribed by law. For this reason, he would say, the confession of transgression, seeking pardon and forgiveness of sins, was fitted to the fiftieth psalm. In the same way he would say that in each psalm the appropriate meanings have been fitted, on certain principles, to the power of the numbers. But whoever says this does not seem to me to hit the mark. First, no numbers at all appear in the Hebrew book of Psalms; they were written down without any numbers attached. Second, the psalms are joined and divided differently. For example, the first and second at the beginning of the book are joined in the Hebrew, and again the ninth, which is a single psalm in our text, is divided into two in the Hebrew. Moreover, the whole book of Psalms is divided into five parts, as has already been said. This being so, the theory of numbers just described would have no basis. And what reason could anyone give, for instance, for fitting the sense of the present psalm, I mean the sixty-second, to this particular number, or for assigning to each of the hundred and fifty numbers its own meaning suited to this or that number? But let anyone take these things as he pleases. For my part, I think that the psalms are mostly placed one after another because of the sense of their contents. I have observed and found this to be so in many cases. That is why they have been joined together, as having a kinship and a connection with one another. So they are not set out according to their times but according to the connection of their meaning. This has already been shown earlier from many other cases, but especially from the forty-first to the fiftieth. There we demonstrated that the psalms entitled “of the sons of Korah” keep a close connection with the meaning they convey, and that the psalm of Asaph placed next after them, and again David's confession in the fiftieth joined to these, yield without any forcing the interpretation we gave. This, then, as it seems to me, would be one reason for the order of the psalms. But I can give another as well. For when widespread idolatry had gained control over the Jewish nation,

the history of the Kingdoms teaches that they forgot their ancestral scriptures, so that the book of the law of Moses could not even be found, and no memory of their fathers' piety was preserved among them. So they even killed the prophets who rebuked their impieties, and for these things they were first handed over to captivity under the Assyrians. It is no wonder, then, that in such times the contents of the book of Psalms also fell into neglect and were consigned to oblivion for long periods. Afterward, whether it was Ezra or one of the other prophets, someone made it his business to collect them, and along with the other books gathered the book of Psalms too. He did not find them all at once, but at different times, and he placed first those found first. That is why the psalms of David are not all placed in sequence. In between, those of the sons of Korah, of Asaph, of Solomon and Moses, of Ethan and Heman, and then again of David, are found arranged mixed together in the book, not according to the times when they were spoken, but according to when they were found. So it happened that psalms later in time but found first were taken up first, while those earlier in time but found afterward were placed in a later position. Let this be our answer to the question raised, on grounds of probability. Now it is time to take up the contents of the psalm before us. Like the other prophets, David wandered in deserts and mountains, in caves and holes in the earth, and was trained in the labors of patient endurance. He sang the present psalm, devoting his leisure in the wilderness to the philosophy that accords with God. Stirring up his own love for divine things, he confesses that he thirsts for the drink of immortality. So he cries out to God, saying: “O God, my God, I rise early to seek you. My soul has thirsted for you; how many times my flesh has longed for you.” In place of “how many times my flesh has longed for you,” Aquila translated, “my flesh strained toward you,” and Symmachus, “my flesh yearns for you.” So it was not only David's soul that was strained toward God, but his very flesh and body as well, which were clearly kept chaste and pure because he devoted himself to God. And the words “O God, my God, I rise early to seek you” pointed to his purity during the night. For no one in bed

and David said to God: “I rise early to seek you. My soul has thirsted for you.” A land that has not received its usual rain would be said to thirst for it. In the same way, he says, my flesh too has thirsted for you, or yearns for you, as well as my soul, as though thirsting many times over. Just as we say in natural terms that the earth itself thirsts for water, so my flesh has thirsted for you, he says. So he adds: “In a land that is desert, trackless and waterless,” or, as Symmachus has it, “As in a thirsty land, fainting, where there is no water.” By these words he may also be referring to the actual wilderness where he stayed while fleeing Saul. Living there, far away from the ark of God and from the tabernacle of the sanctuary where the worship prescribed by the law was performed, he surely longed to see these things. Just as thirsty land craves water, so, he says, my soul longs for what is pleasing and dear to you, O God, so much that it faints and wastes away unless it can share in the fountain that is with you, of which it is said, “For with you is the fountain of life.” Therefore “my soul has thirsted for you.” He goes on to explain how it thirsted, saying: “So in the sanctuary I appeared before you,” as if to say: my soul thirsted to appear before you in your sanctuary, “to see your power and your glory.” The same thing was said earlier: “My soul has thirsted for God, the mighty, the living; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” For when I have come into your holy place, of which it is said elsewhere, “Once I have sworn by my holiness,” first I myself shall be seen by you, tested to see whether I am worthy to behold you. Then, having been found worthy, I shall see your power and your glory. It is impossible to come to the contemplation of these things without first having entered the holy place and first having been found worthy of God's good things. After this, as one already proved, a person will see the power of God and his glory. And this would be the goal of all good things: to come to the contemplation of these. That is why it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” This, then, is what David's soul thirsted for, and so he said: “O God, my God, I rise early to seek you. My soul has thirsted for you.” “Because your mercy is better than lives, my lips shall praise you.” Whoever has considered the nature of mortal life, and examined how long and what sort of thing this temporary life is, turns away from these things as small and worthless. Wholly given over to the hope above, he prays to attain it, as it is supplied by God's mercy. For no one will attain heavenly things as something owed, or as a reward his own righteousness deserves. That is why it is said elsewhere, “For what do I have in heaven?” Everything is given by the mercy and love for humankind of God, who grants great things to those who have accomplished small ones. This is what the present text means when it says: “Because your mercy is better than lives.” For even if someone lives a long life in the

present age, as though he had gained many lives over many cycles of years, all this is nothing compared with the mercy of God, which is the [?] of eternal life and of the heavenly good things. Therefore, taking courage in your mercy, I will dedicate my whole present life to you, setting apart for your service my limbs and my senses like precious offerings and costly treasures. So my lips will speak of nothing else, but will be kept chaste and pure, to be devoted to your hymns and your words. This life of mine will be occupied in blessing you always, night and day. And the hands of my body, along with the deeds done through them, I will lift up in your name, raising them on high and showing them to you clean of every lawless deed, as the one said who wrote: “I want the men to pray, lifting up holy hands without anger or disputing.” In this way my lips and my hands will be set apart for you, so that my lips will be no different from fragrant incense, and my hands will fall nothing short of an effective and true sacrifice. Then I may fittingly say of my lips, “Let my prayer be set before you as incense,” and of my deeds, “The lifting up of my hands as an evening sacrifice.” So my flesh and body will be dedicated to your service, but my soul will share in a greater power. That is why I say of it: “May my soul be filled as with fat and richness.” For the soul does not offer with lips or hands, as the body does, or with any other part or member. Instead, the whole soul by itself will be offered to you, O God, beyond every [?] whole burnt offering and beyond every well-fed animal full of richness and fat, and it will be reckoned by you as more precious than calf or bull or any irrational animal. Therefore I will dedicate this to you as the richest sacrifice and the one most dear to you, I mean my own soul. In addition to these, giving thanks with my whole mouth and with lips full of joy, I will sing your praise. So I say: “And with lips of exultation my mouth shall praise you,” or, as Symmachus has it, “And with lips of good speech my mouth shall sing your praise.” “If I remembered you on my bed, in the early mornings I meditated on you, for you have become my helper. And in the shelter of your wings I will rejoice; my soul has clung close behind you, and your right hand has upheld me.” Living in the wilderness of Judea, the wonderful David does not promise to sacrifice animals, or to offer sacrifices from irrational livestock. He promises the sacrifices described above, made through words and deeds and through the soul itself. Then, beyond this, he shows how he had devoted himself to God in self-control and complete chastity. So he says, “If I remembered you on my bed, in the early mornings I meditated on you,” or, as Symmachus has it, “Remembering you on my bed, in every watch of the night I meditated on you.” For I could not otherwise, he says, rise early to seek you, or say in prayer, “O God, my God, I rise early to seek you,” unless I had kept my bed pure. [?]

[?] and my purity [was shown?] from nothing other than my meditating on your words at dawn. For this made it plain that I did nothing else through the nights but keep you, God, before my eyes. Symmachus says, “In every watch I meditated on you,” and Aquila puts it, “In the watches I speak in you.” Both seem to show that the hours of the night were spent in meditating on the divine Scriptures. For the whole span of the night is divided into several watches; so it is said in the Gospels that the Savior came to the disciples in the fourth watch. And elsewhere he himself says, “Keep awake, for you do not know in what watch your Lord is coming”; and again, “But know this, that if the master of the house had known in what watch the thief was coming.” So the man who loved God and was devoted to God, remembering God upon his bed and keeping that bed spotless, pure and undefiled, rose in every watch of the night, gave himself to prayer, and trained himself in the divine teachings. This is what he was teaching when he said, in Symmachus' version, “Remembering you upon my bed, in every watch I meditated.” For it was on you yourself, God, that I meditated in place of any book or writing, my mind stretched up toward you, meditating on and remembering all the benefits you counted me worthy of: how you have always been my helper, how you saved me out of countless trials, and how you drew me out under your own wings, that is, by the powers of your providence. As I went over these things in my memory, I was filled with joy, or I sang your praises, God, as Symmachus puts it: “And sheltered under your wings I sang praise.” Meditating on your words in every watch of the night, and then hearing the divine law that said, “You shall walk after the Lord your God,” and “cleave to him,” I disposed my soul accordingly and became obedient to the law. I held wholly to this, counting all things, or rather turning away from all things that come after God, and I was set higher and more exalted by the longing of my soul, and I was joined to you, my God, so that I could say without lying, “My soul has cleaved to you from behind.” Yet I attained such progress and advanced to such greatness of virtue not by using my own power but by your lordship; for you yourself gave me this by your mercy. Seeing my longing for you and accepting it, you deigned to stretch out your right hand, take hold of me and draw me up to yourself. That is why my soul, helped by you, has been able to cleave to you from behind: because “your right hand upheld me.” I could not otherwise have reached so great a height had your right hand not upheld me. The Apostle teaches how one cleaves to the Lord when he says, “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit,” just as “he who is joined to a prostitute is one body.” And when David says to the Lord, “My soul has cleaved to you from behind,” it was plain from this too that by holiness and purity

“I,” he says, “attended to you, my Savior, and joined my soul to you, and meditated on your words while I was in flight and spending my days in desert places. For I did not take vengeance on those who were driving me out; nor, while I gave my time to you, God, did I send up prayers against my enemies. I attended to you alone, as I said. But they did not cease to pursue their vain zeal against my soul; for in vain they sought it, since it could not be found by them because it had cleaved to you from behind.” Therefore what awaits them they themselves do not know, but the Holy Spirit declares it. Then, next after these words, he cries out prophetically: “They shall go into the lowest parts of the earth.” For since they set their minds on the things of the earth and became of those below, it is fitting that [?] will have the [hopes?] of the kingdom of heaven; but those who ran the opposite course and set their minds on things below will be brought down into what is elsewhere called the pit, and will go into the lowest parts of the earth. For as long as every human being dwells on the surface of the earth, he is said to dwell only in the regions below, according to the one who said, “For God is in heaven above, and you on earth below.” But after their departure from here, those who love God will have heaven as their dwelling, lifted up to the higher regions and caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord, and so they will be with the Lord for ever; while the ungodly and sinners will go down into the lowest parts of the earth. The Apostle had these in mind when he said, “He who descended into the lower parts of the earth is the same one who ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things.” For our Savior and Lord descended even to the lowest parts of the earth, so that he might fill all things with his saving power. The Lord also indicates this to Job when he speaks to him in these words: “Have you come to the source of the sea, and walked in the tracks of the deep? Do the gates of death open to you in fear, and did the gatekeepers of Hades cower when they saw you?” But he descended even to the regions there in order to grant freedom to the souls of the saints long held there; whereas the ungodly, brought down into the lowest parts of the earth, will be delivered into the hands of the sword. For there is a certain sword of death there, which the Savior mentions in the twenty-first psalm when he says, “Deliver my soul from the sword, and my only one from the hand of the dog; save me from the mouth of the lion, and my lowliness from the horns of the unicorns.” All these things were said about the opposing powers. And those just mentioned will not only be delivered into the hands of the sword, but will also be torn apart, dragged this way and that by certain dreadful and cunning spirits, whom the present passage calls foxes because they have burrowed down and make their dens in the lowest recesses. These foxes, then, seize the souls of the ungodly that fall down there as if they were a windfall, and tear them to pieces, dividing them up among themselves. And

such, the Holy Spirit declares, will be the end of the ungodly. But concerning the righteous man who has achieved what was said before, it goes on: “But the king shall rejoice in God; everyone who swears by him shall be praised, for the mouth of those who speak unjust things has been stopped.” The name of the king is introduced here quite unexpectedly. For David is shown to have been fleeing from Saul and living in the desert of Judea at the time he said these things, and not yet reigning anywhere; while Saul held power over the nation and was at the head of the kingdom. What king, then, will rejoice in God? Someone will say that David himself is meant here by foreknowledge of the future, since he was about to reign very soon, once Saul had died. Another says that he was already king even then, since he had been anointed king by Samuel and was already reckoned king before God; and indeed he did reign over the band of people that was with him, which the history records. Since, then, the passage has set forth the end of those who were driving him out, it is fitting that the outcome of his own labors should also be prophesied, as one who had shown great progress. So it is said, “But the king shall rejoice in God.” For as a noble athlete of God who has come through great contests and been counted worthy of prizes and divine crowns, he will enjoy gladness in the presence of the president of the games himself. His enemies met no happy end, going into the lowest parts of the earth, being delivered into the hands of the sword, and becoming portions for foxes. This was fulfilled to the letter in the history, when Saul, fleeing from the enemy, hid himself, and seeking help from God did not find it, nor was he even granted a divine answer; so that for this reason he went to the medium and meddled in things forbidden by God. Then indeed he and those with him truly became portions for foxes. And so, abandoned by God, they were delivered to the sword of the enemy and fell in battle. Just as these things, which had not yet happened, were spoken by foreknowledge as going to befall those who were driving David out, so the Holy Spirit also proclaimed the happy outcome for David himself, saying, “But the king shall rejoice in God.” For having hoped in God and joined his soul to him, so as to say, “My soul has cleaved to you from behind,” he will obtain the highest gladness in God's presence. And everyone who swears on these things, as one who swears truly, will be praised; or in Aquila's version, “He who swears by him will boast.” For whoever does not doubt, but even takes an oath that the king will never fall short of the hope promised to him, will be praised as [?] swearing truly. And these things will come about for the king and for everyone who swears concerning him, “for the mouth of those who speak unjust things has been stopped.” In another sense, when the righteous man is made perfect through the progress in virtue that has been described, the king rejoices and is glad, that is, the only-begotten Son of God, giving thanks to his own Father, who has bestowed such great gifts on human nature. And whoever has come to know this king and makes his name the name he swears by

would be worthy of all praise, as one who has learned that it is by his power that the righteous man has been made perfect and every mouth that speaks many unjust things has been stopped. For even if for a time the mouth of the ungodly was allowed to speak unjust things and to blaspheme the righteous man, and God himself, as though he gave no help to those driven out for his sake, they will not be allowed to speak such things to the end. Their ungodly mouth will be stopped, and their boasting against men who love God will cease, once the ends described above overtake them.

FOR THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID. [?] “Hear, O God, my prayer when I make my petition; deliver my soul from fear of the enemy.” This psalm too points to the end, in which those who have fought the good fight will receive from the great president of the games the prizes of the upward call and the crowns of righteousness. So the first part of the psalm introduces enemies and evildoers rising up against the righteous man, but at the close of the whole passage it seals it with good hopes, saying, “The righteous man shall rejoice in the Lord and shall hope in him; and all the upright in heart shall be praised.” It teaches that such is the end of those who have fought for godliness. For the athlete of the fear of God, who has countless enemies and foes of his soul, not only visible but also invisible, takes refuge in God alone and asks for help from him, all but saying, “If God is for us, who is against us?” So he devotes himself to prayer, calling on God and saying, “Hear, O God, my prayer when I make my petition.” But one who is not like this, and disregards God's commands, could not use such great boldness; for with the measure we measure, it is measured back to us. That is why in Proverbs the wisdom of God addresses the disobedient, saying, “Because I called and you did not listen, and I spread out my words and you paid no attention, but made my counsels void and paid no attention to my commandments, therefore I too will laugh at your destruction.” For there will come a time when you call on me, but I will not listen. If, then, we want to be heard when we petition God, let us ourselves do this too, by becoming obedient to God's commands. For then we too will be able to say to God with great boldness, “Hear, O God, my prayer when I make my petition.”

[?] benefits. So, giving thanks for what is past, he adds, “You sheltered me from the gathering of evildoers, from the multitude of those who work injustice.” For having already experienced what has come upon me before, I can never forget it; and carrying it always in my memory, I am ever thankful. Yet now too I ask to receive the same help from you. In the other translators, however, one and the same grammatical mood is kept throughout the passage, and the sense of the words is one. So Symmachus renders it: “Hear, O God, my voice as I speak to you; from the terror of the enemy you will fence about my life; you will hide me from the plotting of evildoers, from the turmoil of those who work injustice.” For in the other translators too the whole is spoken not as of things past but as of things to come.

“They sharpened their tongues like swords, they bent the bow, a bitter thing, to shoot the blameless in secret. Suddenly they will shoot at him, and they will not be afraid.” Although David came long before the saving advent in time, he was not ignorant of the teachings of the Gospel, having been taught by the divine Spirit. He knew very well the saving word that says, “Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.” So he was not anxious about the multitude of an army drawn up in battle, nor about those arrayed in full armor and with spears; these he despised, as one who had brought down the great Goliath without effort or sweat. But he was anxious about those he hinted at in the present words: “They sharpened their tongues like a sword, they bent the bow, a bitter thing.” Do you see what kind of enemy armor he describes? Earlier too it was said, “Sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword.” These words are recorded as spoken “when he fled from the face of Saul into the cave.” From the similarity of the language, then, it appears to be the same time at which the present words were also spoken, about those very men and others like them. Again, “when Saul sent and watched his house to kill him,” he uttered similar words about the same people, saying, “Behold, they will speak out with their mouth, and a sword is in their mouths.” But those things were said there; in the present passage he says that his enemies, from fear of whom he prayed to be delivered, had sharpened their tongues like a sword, or in the other translators, “like a knife”; and moreover that they bent their bow, according to the Seventy translators, “in a bitter thing,” for it was by a bitter thing that they tried to shoot down the righteous man; while according to Symmachus, “They filled their bow,” he says, “with a bitter word.” For those who slandered David to Saul were truly bitter, containing nothing sweet, such as Doeg, and the Ziphites, and those

like them. But every godless word too would be bitter, just as the divine word is kind and sweet. That is why it is said, “Taste and see that the Lord is kind.” Dreadful bows, and truly sharp swords, are those of the godless heterodox, who shoot down innocent souls and slaughter them with their own swords. The wise of this age too, putting forward their deceptive and sophistical reasoning, have destroyed many souls. We therefore need intense prayer to be delivered from all of these. Those just mentioned try above all to shoot down the simple and guileless; that is why it is said, “They bent the bow, a bitter thing, to shoot the blameless in secret.” He calls the innocent man blameless, describing the slander directed against those who have done no wrong. In place of “blameless,” Aquila translated “simple.” For such people try above all to shoot down the simple man who knows nothing of evil; so he adds, “Suddenly they will shoot at him, and they will not be afraid.” For they watch for their opportunity and fall on the blameless, that is, the simple and innocent, all at once and unexpectedly. That is why the Apostle, writing somewhere to such people, says, “I am afraid that somehow, as the serpent deceived Eve, your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.” For those just mentioned could never bring down one whose soul is fortified, they “who sharpened their tongues like a sword and bent the bow, a bitter thing, to shoot the blameless in secret”; or, “to shoot the simple in secret. Suddenly they will shoot at him, and they will not be afraid.” And notice how he says they will shoot at “him,” and not at “me,” the one saying these things, but at the simple man, that is, the guileless and innocent one, still little, one might say, one of those about whom the Savior taught, saying, “Do not despise one of the little ones in my Church”; and, “Whoever causes one of the little ones to stumble, it would be better for him to be thrown into the sea.” For there too the Savior presents as the one made to stumble not a great person but the little one in the Church, just as here it is the simple man. So the enemies do not even dare to approach the great, nor those who are wise before God; it is the simple and innocent whom they hunt above all. Therefore David, having mentioned the enemies, also showed whom they usually swarm around. “They strengthened for themselves an evil word; they talked of hiding snares.” Having said figuratively in the preceding words that the enemies of the soul sharpened their sword and bent their bows, he now shows more clearly in these words what the sword was and what the bow, saying, “They strengthened for themselves an evil word.” For they did not receive a word from God, but fashioned and composed it for themselves and then strengthened it. Such are the slanderers, and those who try to strengthen and confirm the false doctrines they have painted and fashioned for themselves. Then, seeing that the evil word they had strengthened for themselves is

rotten, they do not put it forward bare, but surround it from outside with snares, hiding by certain sophisms and fallacies the scheme they have contrived against those they plot against; for in this way they suppose they will be impossible to catch or trap. So “they said” among themselves, “Who will see them?” and “they searched out lawless deeds.” For in their searching they found nothing profitable from the divine law, but devised lawless deeds for themselves. In Symmachus' version, “They all searched out lawless deeds.” And after much searching on these matters and devising countless things by themselves, yet finding nothing true in the end, they failed, having gained nothing more from all their searching. So it is said, “They failed, searching out searchings.” Such are the enemies and foes David described, from whom he prayed that his soul might be delivered: certain searchers and seekers after lawlessness. For such people would truly be murderers of the soul; that is precisely why he called above all on God as his helper against them, counting as nothing the visible foes who are arrayed against bodies. “A man shall approach with a deep heart, and God shall be exalted. The arrow of infants,” and what follows. The foes of the soul, having fenced themselves about with evil words, hidden their snares, searched out lawless deeds, and by these means sharpened their swords and bent bows with their tongues, went about seeking the blameless, that is, the simple and innocent man, in order to destroy his soul. But God will deliver him. For the angels of the little ones in the Church always behold the face of the Father in heaven. And someone will approach them, a man, truly a perfect man who bears the one made according to the image of God. Fortified with a deep heart, he will stand in battle against them undismayed and will overthrow them all, so that God is exalted and glorified through him, and all their arrows are shown to be feeble and weak, so that their blows are reckoned as the arrows of infants and their tongues fail against themselves. For such is the man of God who stands in battle against those just mentioned with a deep heart: he receives their blows and the arrows shot by means of sophisms, but laughs at them and counts them as nothing, as though they were shot at him by feeble infants. Then, by refuting their sophisms, he will show up their tongues and their words as failing. A deep heart is one that does not hold its teachings superficially, nor prides itself on the spoken word, but has the foundations of faith rooted within itself. Consistently, then, having presented certain foes who use words, who have sharpened their tongue and bend bows with their lips, he sets against them a man of God who has a deep heart, and shows God glorified through him, and those others defeated and put to shame. “All who saw them were troubled, and every man was afraid.” It followed that, when those who are wise in their own opinion had been overthrown and the enemies of the soul

…[en]emies have been exposed by the man of God, those who are not so clever in the wisdom of this age are thrown into confusion. They belong to the party of the defeated, and are themselves godless and impious, though less skilled in wickedness than those others. So when they see that their betters have been defeated, they are thrown into confusion. That is why it is said: “All who saw them were troubled.” The man of God, however, and all his friends, who won the prizes against the enemies through that one man, feared God all the more, “and declared the works of God, and understood his deeds.” It may well have seemed that “a man and a deep heart” had brought about the overthrow of the enemies, but those with understanding recognized that God himself was the cause of the victory. That is why they proclaimed the works of God, singing hymns to the great deeds he had accomplished through men. These, then, like spectators, went on glorifying God for the victory of the victor. But the victor himself “will rejoice in the Lord and hope in him.” He will not think highly of himself or be puffed up by the victory. Instead he will be filled with divine joy and gladness, since he has become the servant and minister of God, who gives the victory. And when he rejoices, “all the upright in heart will be praised,” because they too have been shown to be victors, as it were, through the one. For the whole company and body of the saints will receive praise, since when one member is glorified, all the members are glorified with it, as the holy Apostle says.

FOR THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID. [A SONG?]. PSALM 64. “A hymn befits you, O God, in Zion, and to you a vow shall be paid in Jerusalem.” The psalm contains a prophecy of things that are to happen at the end, and that is why it is entitled “For the end.” What these things are he teaches next, saying, “To you all flesh shall come.” This means no longer the nation of the Jews alone, but all flesh, that is, every race of human beings. For this is how the Word usually refers to all people who were of old fleshly and earthly. That is why the Law too says: “All flesh had corrupted its way”; and again: “My spirit shall not remain among these men, because they are flesh.” But at that time all flesh was being accused, whereas now it is said that it will come to God. That is why Joel too, who became a prophet after David, foretells the finest things for all flesh, saying: “I will pour out my spirit on all flesh, and they shall prophesy.” Isaiah also presents the same thing, saying: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God.” And what could the salvation of God that was to be made known to all flesh be, if not the Christ of God, as we have often shown? So this salvation was foretold as something to be revealed to all people who were of old fleshly. Fittingly, then, the psalm before us signifies this very thing and seals the promise by saying, “To you all flesh shall come.” A little further on he explains the meaning more clearly, adding: “Hear us, O God our Savior, the hope

of all the ends of the earth and of those far off at sea.” And he adds, more clearly still: “And those who dwell at the ends shall be afraid at your signs.” For all who dwell at the ends to fear because of God's signs was the beginning of good things and of wisdom, since “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” For these reasons the psalm is headed “For the end.” It is the psalm of a song, and it contains a hymn of victory to the Savior of the nations. In view of all this the Holy Spirit sings to the God who is over all, saying: “A hymn befits you, O God, in Zion.” For who else should be praised in hymns for the salvation of all people than the cause of every good thing? The same Spirit teaches those who come from the nations to say to God alone, “A hymn befits you,” as people who have condemned themselves for the time when they sent up unfitting hymns to the error of many gods. Yet not every hymn befits God, but only the one sent up in Zion, that is, in his Church. For Zion in the true sense is the heavenly Jerusalem and the heavenly mountain of God. The Apostle was teaching about it when he said: “You have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels in festal gathering, and to the church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven”; and again: “But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.” This would be the true Jerusalem and the Zion properly so called, over which our Savior and Lord is also said to reign, as he himself teaches when he says in Psalm 2: “But I have been established as king on Zion, his holy mountain.” And this same city would be the kingdom of heaven proclaimed to those who receive the Gospel. Its image would be the Church on earth, which is also called by the same names: sometimes Zion, sometimes Jerusalem, and at other times daughter of Zion or daughter of Jerusalem. That, at any rate, is how the prophets addressed it in their oracles. The hymn sung in Zion, then, whether in the heavenly Zion or in the Church of God on earth, would be the only one that befits the God to whom it is sung. But all talk about God outside the Church of God, whether among the wise men of the Greeks or among the godless heterodox, would be unfitting. For some of the wise men among the Greeks fell into complete atheism, while others glorified the error of many gods. And some of the godless heretics posited a great many conflicting first principles, while others assigned the government of the universe to evil and base powers. The children of the Jews themselves also present God as having human form and human passions, because they do not understand the Scriptures, and they tell countless absurd and petty fables, so they have fallen far from the fitting hymn. Only those in the Church of God have been taught the fitting hymn by the Savior himself and speak worthily of the Father. This is what he presents in the song before us when he says: “A hymn befits you, O God, in Zion.” An unfitting hymn would be one sent up to evil demons and unclean

spirits. Also unfitting is the hymn sung to the sun and moon and stars and the other parts of the world by those who make gods of them. Still more shameful and utterly unfitting is the one composed of shameful and licentious songs about the love affairs of the gods. The only hymn that could be called beautiful and fitting is the one sent up to the God who alone is Maker, Creator and King of all things. To him it is also proper to pay vows, and to do so not outside his Church. That is why the Seventy have: “And to you a vow shall be paid in Jerusalem.” Divine Scripture regularly calls a “vow” the promise that someone makes to God, whether he undertakes to live in chastity and dedicates his life to godly philosophy, or consecrates some of his possessions, or takes on some solemn promise suited to a godly life. That is why it says somewhere: “If you vow a vow, do not delay to pay it; it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay.” It is fitting, then, first to praise the Maker and Savior of all in a worthy manner, and then to act in accordance with our talk about God by fulfilling good promises. When we have rendered him both the hymn, fittingly, and the vows, then, having fulfilled our own part, we shall have the boldness to say: “Hear prayer.” Here it precisely says “prayer” and not “vow.” The vow signified a promise, but prayer is petition and supplication. The Holy Spirit made this on our behalf, bringing a fitting supplication to God and saying: “Hear prayer.” But whose prayer is God to hear? He shows this next by foretelling the calling of the nations, which is why he says: “To you all flesh shall come.” The Holy Spirit was interceding for all flesh, so that when all flesh turns to God and calls upon him, it may find him ready to hear. That is why he did not say, “Hear my prayer,” but “Hear prayer; to you all flesh shall come.” It is as if he were saying more clearly: Since all flesh and every race of human beings is about to abandon the error of many gods and turn to you, the only true God, and to send up hymns to you, pay vows, and offer prayers and supplications, hear their prayer. “Words of the lawless have overpowered us, and you will be gracious to our impieties.” Very fittingly, after what was said about all flesh, the present passage follows, containing the confession of the “all flesh” just mentioned. Those from all the nations who were of old fleshly and have turned away from superstitious error are taught by the divine Spirit to confess the evils they were once in and to remember their own impieties. That is why he says: “Words of the lawless have overpowered us, and you will be gracious to our impieties.” Taken as spoken in the person of the “all flesh” we have described, these words would follow very consistently. But since the song of the psalm is inscribed “of David,”

one might ask when the words of the lawless overpowered David or those with him, or, as Symmachus has it, “tyrannized over” them. One might also ask what impieties so great a prophet of God and those with him had committed, since he says, “You will be gracious to our impieties.” But, as we have explained, the Holy Spirit is speaking prophetically. Having mentioned the calling of the nations and said, “To you all flesh shall come,” it then describes their confession, speaking in their person: “Words of the lawless have overpowered us,” that is, the words of the lawless have become stronger and more powerful than we are. All those who first established the deification of idols were lawless, and their words are those the poets and the wise men of this age set down in writings about the error of many gods. These, then, “tyrannized over us,” as Symmachus has it. But you did not overlook us, Master. You were gracious to our impieties, sending down to us the propitiation through which you became merciful to us, passing over our impieties. What this propitiation is the Apostle teaches when he says of the Savior: “Whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood”; and again: “He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the whole world.” “Blessed is the one whom you have chosen and taken to yourself; he shall dwell in your courts.” Those who have turned from all the nations confessed their own impieties, and since they were found worthy of the propitiation, they show progress and great benefit of soul, teaching that they have come to know who is truly blessed. Formerly they knew only mortal life and temporary existence, and no doubt they counted blessed those who enjoyed it, defining the goal of life as pleasure, riches and bodily luxury. But now that they have obtained the propitiation and cleansed away their impieties, they have come to know the one who is truly blessed. They say this is the one chosen by God and found worthy of being taken to himself by him. That is why they say: All of us who were formerly flesh have been found worthy of the calling, but we know that many are called, but few are chosen. Fittingly, then, we call the chosen one blessed, as something rare. And who is he, if not the one set apart from the many and taken up by God? How could such a one not be truly blessed, when, having obtained these two things, I mean being chosen and being taken by God to himself, he will be found worthy of yet another, greater one? For he will dwell in the courts of God. Having found this dwelling and rest at last, he will be firmly settled there, enjoying this good end. Another prophet also prayed to obtain it, saying: “My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord.” The courts of the Lord are the heavenly dwellings, of which it is said in the Gospel: “There are many dwellings

with the Father.” So the person from the nations who was formerly flesh, but has been changed and has become a man of God, calls blessed the one who is exceptional and already chosen, since he has been taken by God and received into the courts of the heavenly Jerusalem. “We shall be filled with the good things of your house; holy is your temple, wonderful in righteousness.” Those mentioned before pray that they too may obtain the heavenly good things of which the blessed one already mentioned has been found worthy, and they say: “We shall be filled with the good things of your house.” For they have come to know the heavenly house of God, in whose courts the one already chosen has been given his place. That is why they beseech that they too may one day obtain the heavenly good things. And the Church of God is also the house of God, according to the Apostle, who said: “So that you may know how one ought to behave in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth.” So they fittingly say: The blessed one has already obtained election with you, but we, who are not yet such and are still clothed as we are, love to enjoy even now, from here, the good things in your house.
