These are divine words, the teachings of wisdom, and the gifts of the Holy Spirit with which the house of God is adorned: “For to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another faith by the same Spirit; to another gifts of healing, to another kinds of tongues,” and all the other things the divine Apostle listed. With these, then, those who long for higher things prepare themselves. Then, since they have mentioned the house of God, they go on to teach what kind of house it is, saying: “Holy is your temple, wonderful in righteousness.” For this was the house of God, his holy temple. By the holy temple of God you should understand not buildings of walls and roofs, but the temple already made up of chosen souls. The saints are living stones, and the holy Apostle taught that the community of the godly is a spiritual house for a holy priesthood when he said: “You are all the house of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you. If anyone destroys the temple of God, God will destroy him; for the temple of God is holy, and that temple is you.” In saying this, he was teaching in harmony with the passage before us, which says: “Holy is your temple, wonderful in righteousness.” In temples that can be seen, people often admire the construction, achieved through lavish expense out of a love of beauty. They build them with gilded ceilings and carved work for love of beauty, and they adorn the buildings with columns and marble. In the same way the temple of God is holy, and possesses this as its first and finest good. It is also clothed with outward adornment, embellished with the manifold wisdom of God, with righteousness and the other virtues, and with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, so that it astonishes and amazes those who see it. Hence those who are found worthy to spend their time in it say with joy: “We shall be filled with the good things of your house; holy is your temple,

wonderful in righteousness.” Notice that these words were spoken in the time of David, when the visible temple had not yet been built by Solomon. The passage clearly shows that the true temple of God was not the one built of lifeless stones, but the one explained to us by the testimony of the Apostle. There is also another interpretation. Above, they called blessed the one chosen and taken up by God, who already dwells in his heavenly courts. So they too, who for the present remain among the called but pray to become chosen and to be found worthy of the same heavenly dwellings, fittingly sketch out good hopes for themselves, beseeching that they may obtain the same heavenly house and the good things in it. Then, as people who have learned what kind of house the heavenly house of God is, they explain its excellence, saying: “Holy is your temple, wonderful in righteousness.” And what heavenly temple, truly worthy of God, in which the God of all is understood to dwell, could there be other than his only-begotten Word, in whom all the fullness of the Godhead was pleased to dwell? He, then, is truly wonderful in righteousness, since he himself has become for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, sanctification and redemption. “Hear us, O God our Savior, the hope of all the ends of the earth, and of those far off at sea.” The one chosen by you and taken up into the heavenly temple is truly blessed, thrice blessed. But we hold the promises of the good things already mentioned and hang upon our hopes, and we pray to obtain them at last. That is why we entreat you, saying: “Hear us, O God our Savior.” And having heard us, count us worthy to become blessed. Take us too to yourself, choose us, and settle us in your courts, so that when we come there we may be filled with the good things of your house. And what could anyone suppose the good things of the heavenly house to be, other than what the divine Apostle described when he said: “What no eye has seen, and no ear has heard, and has not entered the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him”? Hear us, then, O God our Savior, and having heard us, count us too worthy of the good things of your house. This is what those who were formerly flesh, but have been found worthy of God's calling, are taught to say. In these words they fittingly call upon their own Savior, whom they named the propitiation above, when they said, “and you will be gracious to our lawless deeds.” Here, too, the Hebrew Scripture writes “Savior” with the same letters with which our Savior Jesus is written. They call this same Savior and propitiation “the hope of all the ends of the earth and of those far off at sea.” They show plainly that these words have nothing to do with the Jews, and that the grace of the Savior is proclaimed as good news not to them alone but to all the nations. To the nations they foretell the knowledge and understanding of God, so that they no longer hang their hopes on those they once considered their gods, but on

him alone who has become their Savior. “Preparing mountains by his strength, girded with might.” Instead of “preparing mountains,” Symmachus translated “you established mountains.” The passage goes on to add its account of God concerning the Savior already mentioned. For you, he says, are the hope of all the ends of the earth, you who have done these great works and those by your own power. First you prepared mountains by your strength, girded with might. Then you stirred up the depths of the sea and calmed the roar of its waves. Then, through these things, you troubled the nations. Through these events those who dwell at the ends gained a great deal. For they came to know you and feared because of your signs, so that they no longer set any other hope before their eyes but you. That is why it was said above: “The hope of all the ends of the earth.” In what follows, these people who dwell at the ends of the earth are foretold to fear God because of his signs, by the oracle that says: “And those who dwell at the ends shall be afraid at your signs.” What the signs were, at the sight of which those who dwell at the ends feared God and hoped in him, he taught beforehand when he said: “Preparing mountains by his strength, girded with might, who stirs up the depths of the sea, the roar of its waves. Who will withstand? The nations will be troubled.” When those who dwell at the ends saw these things, they feared because of his signs. These words signify the humbling of the evil spirits who of old exalted themselves against the knowledge of God, and the overthrow of the devil's battle line, that is, of principalities and powers, of world rulers and spiritual forces of wickedness. Of old these held sway over the nations living on earth. They churned up and agitated the sea of human life, so as to spread the belief that they were gods among all who inhabit the element of earth. But all of them have been brought down and overthrown through the saving appearance of God. Another prophet also foretells similar things, saying: “Hear, all you peoples who dwell in it, and God shall be a witness among you, the Lord from his holy house. For behold, the Lord will come down from his place and will tread upon the high places of the earth. And the mountains will be shattered beneath him, and the valleys will melt like wax before fire, because of the impiety of Jacob; all these things also because of the sin of the house of Israel.” And Psalm 17, which contains the descent of the same Lord from heaven to earth, also says: “And the earth shook and trembled, and the foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken, because the Lord was angry with them.” These words signify the descent of the Lord, that is, of God the Word. Then, at his [coming?] among human beings, they signify the overthrow, humbling and scattering of the unseen and invisible powers that of old were exalted on high and honored among all the nations.

That is why the passage before us says: “Preparing mountains in his strength, girded with power.” Girded with power, by his own strength, he has not yet destroyed those mountains completely. Instead he has prepared them for punishment, for the present setting them apart and removing them from their tyranny over human beings. He also calmed the depth of the sea by his own power. That is why it says: “Stirring up the depth of the sea, the roar of its waves.” In place of “stirring up,” Aquila translated “restraining,” Theodotion “calming,” and the fifth edition “the one who calms.” Aquila’s version reads: “Restraining the roar of the sea, the tumult of its waves, and the throng of the tribes.” Just as he prepared those mountains for the punishment that will overtake them, so he restrained the roar of the sea and the tumult of its waves. Aquila goes on to make clear what the sea is, what its roar is like, and what the tumult of its waves is, when he says: “and the throng of the tribes.” For the great throng of the nations of old, and of the tribes of people of every race, was then [?] a wave of human life. This sea of mortal life, filled with human wickedness, was in great tumult and sent out a great roar, since it had the dragon living in it. Of this dragon it is said: “The Lord God will bring the sword upon the dragon, the crooked serpent, and he will slay the dragon that is in the sea.” And elsewhere Scripture first says, “This is the sea, great and wide,” and then adds: “There is this dragon, which you formed to make sport of it.” But the hope of all the ends of the earth appeared to humanity, and all at once restrained and calmed the dragon, the sea and the roar of its waves, and quenched the throng of the tribes. After these things, the text goes on in due order: “And those who inhabit the ends will be afraid at your signs.” The signs already mentioned were enough to fill those who inhabit the ends with fear: mountains brought low, the roar of the sea restrained, the tumult of the waves no longer troubling as it used to, and the throng of the tribes itself quenched. As a result they no longer fear all those things, but only the one who conquered them all. From then on they know him and fear him, and so they receive the blessing that says: “Blessed are all who fear the Lord.” The present oracle teaches who these people might be when it says: “And those who inhabit the ends will be afraid at your signs.” Those said to inhabit the ends are not necessarily the people who live at the farthest edges of the earth. They are the people who can say with Paul: “For though we live in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh,” and: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” These people are neither sunk deep in human affairs nor entirely outside them. They stand as if on a borderland and conduct their lives at the ends of human life.

[Page 639: Eusebius of Caesarea] These [?], then, have gained much perception. They have seen the signs of our Savior, have taken up the fear of God, and so have come to the beginning of wisdom. Think of the arrogance of the rulers of each age, the uprisings against the Church of God, and the persecutions and threats of impious men. Who could see all that and not say that these are mountains lifted up and a sea that truly surges, and that the roar of the waves is the blasphemy of the impious and godless? The Savior of all the ends of the earth regularly brings all of these low in his strength, at a single stroke. So those [who see] their fall and destruction are troubled, while others benefit and take up the fear of God, confessing that the overthrow of the impious is a clear sign of the Savior’s divine power. “You will delight the goings-out of morning and evening; you visited the earth and drenched it.” Besides the signs already listed, he presents still other signs of the Savior’s power when he says: “You will delight the goings-out of morning and evening.” In place of this, Symmachus translated: “The processions of dawn and of evening, the hymn-singings.” This too is one of the greatest signs of the saving power: after humbling the things just mentioned, he established among human beings delights at the goings-out of morning and evening, or “hymn-singings” in Symmachus’ version, or “praise-makings” in Aquila’s. To establish, throughout the whole world and in the churches of God, hymns and praises and truly divine delights for God at the morning going-forth of the sun and at the evening hours was no ordinary sign of God’s power. The delights of God are the hymns sent up in his Church everywhere on earth at the morning and evening hours. That is why Scripture says somewhere: “May my praise be sweet to him”; and again: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice”; and: “Let my prayer be set as incense before you.” So these delights too are signs of the Savior. Next, he adds another very great sign to these, saying: “You visited the earth and drenched it.” A physician watches over and visits a sick person, tends the illness, and supplies everything that helps toward healing and recovery. In the same way you, our Savior, the hope of all the ends of the earth, girded with power by your strength, accomplished all these things. You brought down the opposing powers and established morning and evening delights on earth. You did this because you counted the people on earth worthy of your visitation, through which countless good things have been given to them. In this way you filled them and drenched them with your good gifts, and enriched them, as the Apostle says: “In everything you were enriched in him, in all speech and all knowledge”; or as Symmachus puts it: “With abundant fruit you will enrich it.” Next he makes clear how he drenched the earth, and how he enriched it and filled it with abundant fruit, when he says: “The river of God is filled with waters.” For you gave to those who live on earth your own river of the Holy Spirit, which from the [?]

spring gushes up [?]. With its abundant stream you flooded their rational and intellectual land, which is called “earth,” drenching it with the rains of wisdom, and “you multiplied to enrich it” with the various gifts of the Holy Spirit. And “the rushing streams of this river gladden the city of God.” The Savior also taught about this river when he said: “Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him, rivers of living water will flow from his belly, springing up to eternal life. This he said about the Spirit, which those who believed in him were going to receive.” So this river of God was filled with waters, so that one may say: “From his fullness we have all received.” The river is filled with many waters because those who drink from it are not all alike. Those who share in it belong to different ranks, and it gives each what suits them, so it is fittingly said to be filled with many waters. When the rational land receives these waters, it gives each the nourishment that suits them, and fruits worthy of so great a river. That is why it says: “You prepared their food, for such is its preparation.” Symmachus’ version reads: “You will bring its seed to maturity, for thus you established it,” meaning the earth, “and you drenched it, you multiplied to enrich it.” So by your river you will bring its seed to maturity. That is, through your own river you yourself will bring the seeds sown in it to full maturity and make them perfect, so that one yields thirty, another sixty and another a hundred. Here the human soul is called earth, as in the Savior’s parable. “Drench its furrows; multiply its produce; in its drops it will rejoice as it springs up.” The prophetic word has gone through the signs of the Savior’s power. By the Spirit’s foreknowledge it saw what was to come as though it had already happened in fact: how he overthrew the adversaries, how he visited the earth and drenched it, and how he multiplied to enrich it once the river of God was filled with waters. Having prophesied these things and seen them as though they were already before his eyes, he turns to prayer and pleads with God, saying: “Drench its furrows, and multiply its produce.” The furrows of the soul would be the thoughts deep within it, and the hidden power of its conscience, unnoticed by most people. The word of God cuts this open and turns it over like a plow and makes it smooth. It removes the thorns and the useless growth and plants its own seeds. Then it waters the soul with rational streams and drenches it. That is why it says: “Drench its furrows, and multiply its produce.” Then, in place of “In its drops it will rejoice as it springs up,” Symmachus’ version reads: “With its showers you will soften [John 7:38–39. John 1:16.]

it and its growth.” All these are signs of the one who has visited his Church. They were foretold long ago, but they came to pass in fact only through the appearing of our Savior. Through it, those counted worthy of his grace have received the seeds from heaven into their souls and yield flourishing fruit, some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. Anyone who sees the different ranks of those making progress in Christ in the Church of God will recognize the abundant harvest of what this prophecy foretells. “You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness, and your plains will be filled with fatness.” The Savior is said to have come to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense, according to the Scripture that speaks in his person: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the poor, to proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense.” So it is fitting that here too the passage signifies the day of recompense. That day is the age that will come after the end of the present one. The present oracle prophesies that this year will be adorned as with a crown by the fresh and lovely flowers of those who are to live in it as citizens, when it says: “You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness.” For that year of the age to come, since it belongs to God’s goodness, will have a blessed crown: the whole choir of the saints. The Christ of God will bless this crown and put it on, adorned with the flowers of their cultivation. But he himself will also become their crown, as Isaiah says: “And the Lord of hosts will be the crown of glory.” Then the plains of God will be filled with fatness, and then the mountains of the desert will be enriched. Moreover, “the hills” will then “gird themselves with exultation.” And besides all these, the rams of the flock will put on their own fleeces. You will understand these things if you keep in mind the differences among those who are saved. Some, whose lives fall short compared with those of their betters, are allegorically called God’s plains filled with fatness. That is why it says: “Your plains will be filled with fatness.” Others, already flowering in various virtues, have been named mountains of the Church that was once a desert. They too are richly watered from the river already described, and so they are said to be fattened. And those still higher than these, figuratively called hills, will gird themselves with exultation. These three ranks will attain blessedness in the coming year of God’s goodness. Perhaps they correspond to those who yielded a hundredfold, sixty and thirty. Those who will be set over them, their rulers and leaders, will be adorned with exceptional powers. That is why it says: “The rams of the flock have put on,” in place of “will put on.” By the rams of the flock you should understand the rulers who lead the ranks already mentioned. They have put on, or rather will put on. What they will put on he has left us to work out. But the divine Apostle teaches what their garment is when he says: “This perishable body must

put on imperishability”; and again: “Because we do not wish to put on (1), but to put on over it, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.” So the rams will put on the garment that befits them, as their perishable body is changed into imperishability and the mortal into immortality. In keeping with the image, rams too produce their garment from within, since their body bears the fleece as its fruit. But they will also put on our Lord Jesus Christ himself, clothing themselves in the exceptional garment, the light of his divinity. Moreover, “the valleys” will then “abound in grain.” The valleys could not be left out. Plains, mountains of the desert and hills were named above. But besides the ranks mentioned there are some others who are lowlier. They are not cast out of the kingdom, but compared with the others they are small and slight, and, one might say, the last of all. So the word could not omit mention of them either. It teaches that they too will bear the fruit that is due to them, when it says: “And the valleys will abound in grain,” as they bring it forth, or “food,” in Symmachus’ version. “They will cry out.” Next he explains what they will cry out, saying: “For indeed they will sing hymns.” It is as if he had said more plainly: even though they are valleys, they will still sing hymns to the one who provides good things to them as well. And as they sing hymns they will cry out, speaking boldly and with a loud voice. When they cry aloud and sing hymns, what words will they utter, if not the words at the very beginning of the psalm: “A hymn befits you, O God, in Zion”? The words “They will cry out, for indeed they will sing hymns” have to be set here, whether about the valleys or about everything mentioned before, so that we may learn that the word is not teaching these things about physical, bodily places. Yet it would also be reasonable to think that these things were said about such places, with reference to God’s physical gifts. Then, read literally, the present passage would be a hymn of thanksgiving for what is supplied to human beings year by year. For every year God, who loves humanity and gives every good thing, visits the earth and drenches it, watering it with the usual rains and filling its furrows with abundant showers. And as he multiplies its produce, he will bless it. The earth rejoices, is renewed and springs up. Then, filled with every kind of fruit, both grain and the fruit of trees, it is crowned. So one would not hesitate to say that in springtime it is crowned and its plains are filled with fatness; that the mountains of the desert flower and the hills are girded with exultation; that the rams of the flock are clothed in their own fleeces; and that the valleys themselves are often filled with grain and all but cry out by what they do and glorify God. But even if these things are fulfilled quite literally every year, the coherence of the whole passage, taken in sequence, has been shown to lead us up to spiritual contemplation. So all the things mentioned together, I mean [(1) Perhaps “to put off.”]

the plains and the mountains of the desert, the hills and the rams of the flock, and in addition the valleys as just explained, are said to send up to God a single voice and a harmonious melody. This holds both by the interpretation given and by the obvious sense. That is why you will hear of all of them: “They will cry out and sing hymns.”

FOR THE END. A SONG OF A PSALM. PSALM 65. “Shout to God, all the earth; sing to his name; give glory to his praise.” This psalm too belongs to the gospel, since it contains the calling of the nations. It was to be fulfilled not in the times when it was sung, but at the end of the ages. That is why it refers its prophecy of these things to “the end.” It is a “song of a psalm,” the reverse of the psalm before it, which was titled “A psalm of a song.” For here too the Holy Spirit sang with great joy, through the prophetic soul that received it, over the good things it was foretelling. Over these things it also commands all the nations who would receive the saving grace to do certain things, which we, to whom these things were foretold, must carry out. So it commands all the earth, that is, everyone who lives on the element of earth, not to subject themselves to the precepts of Moses and the heavy yoke of the law. They are to do only what is commanded in the present passage. First, they are to shout to God; second, to sing to his name; third, to give glory to his praise; fourth, to say to God: “How awesome are your works!” and: “In the greatness of your power your enemies will lie to you.” Let us then carry out the first command with understanding and true knowledge, shouting to God like soldiers in battle who cry aloud and raise the war cry, making themselves terrifying and fearsome to the enemy by the force of their voices. Our Savior is driving out and making war on our enemies, who long ago carried our soul captive into the error of many gods, and he arms all of us, his soldiers, against them. So we are fittingly commanded to raise the war cry through prayers to God and to help our King to victory with groanings too deep for words. This shout is raised through prayer. It is raised through theology. It is raised through sound and clear knowledge. It is also raised through the spiritual sacred service that we perform throughout the whole world in the eucharists, according to the mysteries of the New Covenant. When we celebrate the memorial of the sacrifice of the Lamb of God, we fulfill the prophecy that says: “I went around and offered in his tent a sacrifice of praise and of shouting.” That is why another oracle also blesses the people who understand these things, saying: “Blessed is the people that knows the shout.” So the prophetic Spirit rightly commands all people to do this first, saying: “Shout to God, all the earth.” Second, it commands them to sing to his name. This too we regularly do in every place. For in every church of God established among the nations, it has been handed down that these very words be chanted and sung, not only by Greeks but also by barbarians. In another sense, by way of

allegory, the human body, given to the soul as an instrument, is usually called a psaltery. Through it the inner man, skillfully playing on the limbs and senses in accordance with the law of God, could fittingly be said to sing psalms. The soul accomplished the work of knowledge, through the shout, by itself and on its own; that is why it shouts [?] to God himself. But it carries out the singing through the moral and practical activity of the body; that is why it says: “to his name.” For right conduct, seen by many people through one’s actions, brings honor to the name of God. Third, a command has been given to all of us from the nations who have come to know God, bidding us give glory. Not to God, since shouting to him was enough. Nor to his name, since we were bidden to sing to it. But to his praise. Those who praise him should praise him not in a mean or inglorious way, but with great honor and glory. For besides a firm knowledge of God in the mind, achieved through an instrument, it is fitting to fulfill the first command also through divine words that contain praises and hymns to God, with reverence and solemn honor. That is why it says: “Give glory to his praise”; or in Aquila’s version, “Give glory to his hymn”; or in Symmachus’ version, “Set his hymn in honor.” In addition, the prophetic Spirit urges all of us to gaze thoughtfully on the works of God and to consider how full of awe and amazement are the mighty works of his wisdom. “For from the greatness and beauty of created things their Maker is correspondingly perceived”; and: “Since the creation of the world his invisible attributes, his eternal power and divinity, are clearly seen, being understood through the things he has made.” When we behold these things, then, we must be utterly amazed and say to God: “How awesome are your works!” We whom you have enlightened know and grasp that your works are awesome. But your enemies wallow in darkness. Even if they sometimes want to discourse about your works and give natural explanations as best they can, they fall far short of the greatness of your power and have nothing sound or true to say. That is why we say: “In the greatness of your power your enemies will lie to you. Let all the earth worship you and sing to you; let them sing to your name. Interlude.” The first commands were given prophetically to all the earth, that is, to all the nations. But prayer was needed for these things to be carried out in practice. So after the first commands the divine Spirit rightly turns to God himself and sends up a prayer for all the earth. That is why it says: “Let all the earth worship you and sing to you; let them sing to your name.” In place of “all the earth,” Symmachus translated more clearly: “All who are on earth.” This shows more plainly that the command was given not to the Jews but to all people on earth. They needed the greatest prayer, so that by the power of God some extraordinary change might come about in them toward

…no longer to give heed to the error of many gods, but to revere and worship only the one who ought to be revered, the one and only God who is worthy of worship, and to carry out the command in which it was said: “Sing psalms to his name.” So that these things may come about, the Holy Spirit prays, saying: “Let all the earth worship you and sing psalms to you; let them sing psalms to your name.” “Come and see the works of God; he is terrible in his counsels over the sons of men.” The divine Name commands those who are called, since they stand far off, to come near, saying: “Come.” The divine Apostle showed this when he said: “And he came and preached peace to you who were far off, and peace to those who were near.” The word calls the nations throughout the whole inhabited world to the knowledge of God and to the contemplation of his works. For while they stood far from God, they neither saw him nor knew him. That is why it says: “Come and see the works of God,” the works of which it was said above: “Say to God: How terrible are your works!” Earlier it commanded them to say, “How terrible are your works!” But since those who stood far off were likely not to know what the works of God were, it fittingly says to the same people here: “Come and see the works of God.” Once you have seen them, you will learn that he is terrible in his counsels over the sons of men. Symmachus gave the sense more clearly, saying: “Come and see the deeds of God, terrible contrivances on behalf of the sons of men.” For he contrived everything for the salvation of the sons of men. Then the psalm teaches all that God is recorded to have done in the past among the ancients. What these things are, it states next: “He who turns the sea into dry land; they will pass through the river on foot.” According to Symmachus: “He changed,” it says, “the sea into dry land; they crossed the river on foot.” These things are recorded in the historical scripture, and they must be announced to the nations, who do not know them, so that they may learn that the ancient people of God was also once enslaved to the Egyptians and held under the error of Egyptian idolatry, but that God worked great and terrible things on their behalf, scourging the Egyptians with plagues sent from God and freeing his people from bitter slavery. These were the terrible works of God, and not these alone, but also what he did at the Red Sea: he changed it into dry land, saved his own people, and delivered the ungodly to the depths of destruction. “As you learn these things, my friends,” it says, “take courage, and believe that he who did such great things among the ancients will not be unable to do the like among you as well.” Therefore, “come and see the works of God,” how terrible he is “in his counsels over the sons of men.” He turned the sea into dry land, and at the river Jordan too he worked other terrible wonders, when those coming out of the wilderness into this land crossed on foot after the river had been held back. Take these very things as your examples and take courage, for the same God will also drive away your spiritual Egyptians,

the evil demons who long tyrannized your souls. And even if the sea of humanity surges, and the life of the godless and impious raises billows and dangers against you, take courage, since you have a vivid example in the sea that was once turned into dry land. In the same way your crossing from error to truth will be smooth and unhindered. And if the ancients once crossed the river Jordan by a miracle, you too may already receive good news from this, knowing that we who say these things and you who hear them “shall rejoice in him there.” “There” means in the river just mentioned. For there will come, there will indeed come a time when those set free from the Egyptian error will come, as though dressing for a banquet, to the washing of regeneration, to the mystical cleansing in the river Jordan. By these words the passage signifies the washing of regeneration, which began at the river Jordan when John the Baptist appeared in the wilderness of Judea preaching a baptism of repentance and admitted everyone, Greeks and Jews alike, to the confession of their sins. It was then too that our Savior and Lord himself came and honored that same river with his divine presence. That is why the present passage says: “There we shall rejoice in him.” It is fitting, then, that the same prophetic Spirit, announcing good news to the wilderness through Isaiah, also mentioned the Jordan, saying: “Rejoice, thirsty wilderness; let the wilderness exult and blossom like a lily, and the desolate places of the Jordan will blossom and exult. Be strong, you slack hands and feeble knees; take comfort, you who are faint of heart. Be strong; do not be afraid. See, our God has rendered judgment; he himself will come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will hear. Then the lame will leap like a deer, and the tongue of those who stammer will speak clearly; for water has burst forth in the wilderness, and a stream in a thirsty land.” The present verse expresses this same prophecy: “There we shall rejoice in him.” These things were fulfilled when our Savior appeared to humankind as God. It is fitting, then, that the present psalm addressed all the nations and said: “Come and see the works of God,” and again: “Say to God: How terrible are your works!” And having said, “There we shall rejoice in him,” it very fittingly adds: “in him who rules by his power for ever.” You will understand this too when you hear the Savior himself saying: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me; go and make disciples of all nations in my name.” This is why Aquila's version reads: “to him who holds authority by his power for ever.” In another sense, too, we shall rejoice in him once we have been found worthy of the things mentioned above. And when shall we rejoice, if not when the age to come arrives? In that age no one else will have lordship and authority but he alone who has received power

from the Father. For now, in the present age, there are many principalities, authorities and dominions, spiritual forces of wickedness and world-rulers. But then, when he has abolished every rule and authority and power, he alone will hold authority over the age, and in that age the present passage promises us joy. “His eyes look upon the nations; let those who embitter him not be exalted in themselves. Pause.” In the earlier verses the psalm hinted in a veiled way at the calling of the nations: it called the whole earth, but did not clearly name the nations. Now it speaks quite plainly of the nations and of their reconciliation with God. Of sinners it is said: “Turn your face away from my sins”; and again: “Why do you turn away your face and your right hand?”; and again: “You turned your face away, and I was troubled.” But of those who have good hopes it is said: “The eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer”; and again: “Let your eyes look on what is upright”; and again: “The light of your face has been stamped upon us, O Lord.” So great promises are given to the nations in the present passage: his eyes already look upon the nations. And notice that nowhere in this passage does it mention the Jews; throughout it announces good things to the nations. So the Savior of the nations, in his love for humankind, spread his eyes, that is, his watchful powers, over all the nations, and the rays of light sent from his eyes shine on the souls that are able to receive them. But not everyone was going to receive the grace. Some would provoke and embitter, as far as it lay with them, a love for humankind so great by refusing the gift. So the psalm fittingly adds: “Let those who embitter him not be exalted in themselves.” By these words it also signifies those among the nations who disobey the word of the gospel and will not submit to it. That is why Symmachus has: “His eyes watch over the nations; let the disobedient not exalt themselves.” In another sense it also refers to those of the circumcision who rejected the grace and scorned the Savior's call. That is why the Holy Spirit addressed them through Isaiah as well, saying: “You will hear and hear but never understand, and you will look and look but never see.” It is fitting, then, that the present passage rebukes them for being vainly puffed up about their ancestors and proud of the good name of their forefathers, and says: “Let those who embitter him not be exalted in themselves.” “Stop strutting about,” it says, “and stop puffing yourselves up for nothing, my friends, and recognize that God looks on you no more than on the other nations.” The eyes of his watchful power, which takes care of all people, look upon the nations. Why, then, are you exalted in yourselves, as if you had some special privilege, and that when you are men who are always embittering him? That the passage is hinting at them, the Spirit shows clearly through

Ezekiel, saying: “Son of man, I am sending you to the house of Israel, to those who embitter me, who have embittered me, they and their fathers, to this very day”; and next: “Perhaps they will hear, or be afraid, for it is a house of those who embitter”; and again: “And I will speak my words to them, in case they will hear, or be afraid, for it is a house of those who embitter.” And in Psalm 105 it is said: “For they embittered his spirit”; and again: “Many times he rescued them, but they embittered him by their counsel.” Moses too shows their bitterness, saying: “For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their tendril from Gomorrah; their grape is a grape of gall, their cluster is bitterness.” And in Jeremiah it is said to the same people: “How have you turned to bitterness, O foreign vine?” It is fitting, then, that here too they are called “those who embitter.” Having mentioned the nations and their salvation, the passage sets those of the circumcision beside them for contrast, saying: “His eyes look upon the nations; let those who embitter him not be exalted in themselves. Bless our God, you nations, and make the voice of his praise heard.” We observed at the very start of our discussion that the psalm concerns the gospel, and the whole fabric of the prophecy shows this. At the beginning it called the whole earth; then, after teaching more in between, it prophesies about the nations more clearly, saying: “His eyes look upon the nations.” Having taught these things, it then fittingly urges all the nations, since they have profited from learning what was said before, to bless the maker of such great wonders and terrible works, saying: “Bless our God, you nations.” “Not your gods,” it says, “the ones you wrongly believed in long ago, but ours, the one whose name we took from our fathers. Recognize that he is the true God. Now at least, if not before, you too must bless him. And when you praise him and bless him as the only true God, the common God of us all, both us and you, do not do it in silence or in a quiet voice. Do it with great boldness and courage, with ringing voices and loud cries, so that even outsiders may hear the praise you send up to God.” The Savior too showed this when he said: “What I tell you in the dark, speak in the light, and what you hear whispered in your ear, proclaim from the housetops.” The oracle that says “and make the voice of his praise heard” carries this meaning, or as Symmachus puts it: “Make the voice of his hymn heard far and wide.” The outcome of the word is a marvel to see: throughout the whole inhabited world, in the midst of cities, in villages and countryside, in all the churches of God, the peoples of Christ, gathered from all

the nations, send up their hymns and psalms with a great cry, not to their ancestral gods nor to demons who love the body [?], but only to the one whom the prophets proclaim as God, so that even those standing outside can hear the voices of those singing. In this way the oracle spoken here is fulfilled in deed: “Bless our God, you nations, and make the voice of his praise heard.” Next comes: “who set my soul in life, and did not let my feet be shaken.” Instead of “my soul,” all the other translators rendered “our soul,” and instead of “my feet,” they all likewise rendered “our feet.” “Do not send up your hymn and praises to him only for the ancient works of God,” it says, “which were set out in the preceding verses, but also for his kindnesses to us, the very ones who say these things. For he strengthened our feet, which ran far and wide to proclaim the saving Gospel to all of you nations, and he kept them steady in the currents of life by removing the obstacles in their way. And when many plotted against our soul, he himself became its savior and guardian. For these very reasons, ‘bless our God, you nations, and make the voice of his praise heard.’” These words were spoken beforehand plainly in the person of the heralds of the Gospel. Isaiah, or rather the Holy Spirit through him, admired their course and the virtue of their feet, crying out: “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of good things, who bring good news of peace!” These heralds toiled much and endured persecutions from the unbelieving nations, chains and prisons and every kind of plot, yet they stood firm. So they fittingly urge all the nations to bless the one who strengthened them, who kept their soul for life so that it would not fall into the death of sin, and who made their feet firm so that they would not be shaken, nor slip and fall. They urge them too to make the voice of his praise heard, not only for his ancient wondrous and terrible works but also for the new blessings by which he set the souls of those who say these things in life and did not let their feet be shaken. That is why Symmachus puts it in the plural: “who appointed our soul to life and did not let our feet slip.” “For you have tested us, O God; you have tried us by fire, as

These, as I said, are the voices of the Savior's apostles, disciples and evangelists, whose sound went out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world. They might also be the voices of God's holy martyrs, who, imitating our Savior's first heralds, suffered the same things as they fought their contests for godliness. So, interpreting and explaining how he set their soul in life and how he did not let their feet be shaken, they say: “For you have tested us, O God, as silver is tried by fire.” Since a man who has not been tried has not been proved, God fittingly hands his own over to trials to train them. He does not do this so that he himself may find out what kind of people they are, but so that they, having passed through the fire, may become brighter and purer. In silver there is often found a mixture of foreign matter, which stays hidden until the smelting but is exposed and separated out in the fire, and the silver that remains is pure, made better and brighter by its purification. In the same way, the men of God wash away in their trials and in the persecutions raised against them all the foreign matter that their souls have drawn in through their entanglement with the flesh. They are tried by fire and purified in such a smelting, so that they cast off every stain of sin they once acquired, being human, when they fell into certain failings. Giving thanks for this, then, they say: “For you have tested us, O God; you have tried us by fire as silver is tried.” “You did not put us to the fire like straw, or hay, or any other material that easily crumbles, but like silver, which becomes purer in the fire.” They go on to explain how they were tried by fire, saying: “You brought us into the snare.” According to Aquila they say, “You brought us into a stronghold”; according to Symmachus, “You brought us within a siege”; and according to the fifth edition, “You brought us into an enclosure.” By these words the passage refers to jails, prisons and dungeons, in which God's martyrs are shut up before their death. These are indeed like a snare, which holds the hunted prey inside it. The same speakers mention this snare elsewhere too, saying: “Our soul was rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters; the snare was broken, and we were rescued.” First, then, those who are being tried by fire are led into the snare, or the stronghold, or the enclosure, or the siege. Then they fight a second contest, which they make plain when they say: “You laid afflictions on our back.” According to Aquila they say: “You put a grinding [?] on our back”; according to Symmachus: “You put an encircling around our loins.” By these words they refer to the blows inflicted on the body, which the Apostle described more clearly when he said: “Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned; five times I received from the Jews forty lashes less one.” After the prisons, and after the blows on their backs or loins,

they say: “You made men ride over our heads.” You will understand this too when you see how, in times of persecution, godless and impious men trample on the athletes of godliness and exalt themselves over them, while the athletes are humbled and hang their heads at the blasphemies and boasts of the godless. Often, too, the persecutors have struck the heads of God's athletes with blows to the face. “But all these things,” say God's martyrs, “you brought upon us, O God. If you had not willed it, nothing of the kind would have been dared against us; these things happened because you permitted them.” That is why they say to him: “You brought us into the snare.” “For it was you who had us shut up, by allowing these things to happen. And you laid afflictions on our back. These things would never have been dared against us if you had covered us with your own hand and kept us safe. And you made godless men ride over our heads. Besides all this, we came to the utmost extremity of suffering: some of us endured death by fire, others death by water. The sword and the punishments inflicted with the sword, and the other deaths that most of us have endured, were thought nothing compared with these worse ones. So we have passed over them in silence. But since among all terrors nothing has been thought worse than death by fire and death by water, we say that we have endured these very things. Some of us were drowned in the sea and in rivers; others underwent punishment by fire. Through so many trials you tested us, O God, and through them all you tried us by fire as silver is tried. But after bringing all these things upon us, you yourself brought us out again into refreshment. It was not in our power to endure and escape such great sufferings; it was in yours, our great Savior. As you brought us into the snare, so you also brought us out into refreshment. For you did not let our sorrows last, nor stretch out our affliction without end, nor allow men to ride over our heads for long. Nor did we remain [?] in the fire when we were in it, nor were we swallowed up when we were thrown into the water; we came through this too.” That is why it is said: “We passed through fire, and we passed through the depth of the waters,” and that is why the words “through water” are used. “And having trained us in all these things and proved our patience and endurance, you brought us out into refreshment,” or, as Symmachus has it, “into a broad place.” This was fulfilled in various ways. For although the body of the godly is one, some suffered these things, others endured punishment, others were tested only by the loss of their property, and others were trained by flight and by leaving their homes. Yet before long the end of them all turned out well for everyone. God's martyrs, made perfect through death, found true refreshment, so that they could say: “Return, my soul, to your rest, for the Lord has been good to you; for he has rescued my soul from death,” and so on.

These words would be akin to those spoken in the passage at hand: “Who has set my soul in life and has not let my feet be moved”, and again: “And you brought us out into refreshment.” Those who were preserved in this life and saw the fire of persecution put out were settled in bright peace and obtained refreshment. They reached a calm harbor and enjoyed the gladness that came after the persecution. You will understand how “You set men over our heads” is meant here if you set beside it what is said in another place: “And now he has lifted up my head above my enemies. I went around and offered in his tabernacle a sacrifice of shouting.” Just as in times of persecution God raises men up over our heads, so afterward, when he has brought us out into refreshment, he lifts up our heads above our enemies. The one who said prophetically, “And now he has lifted up my head above my enemies”, was declaring this. “I will go into your house with burnt offerings.” The holy martyrs of God, after the great contests they endured, passed through fire and water and were taken up into refreshment. Then, having received the true heavenly house of God, they say: “I will go into your house with burnt offerings.” Since they passed through fire and water, they offer to their God, like a sacrifice, their own burnt offerings, those in which they bore their witness, and they speak with great boldness about the vows they had made. They had vowed to contend, and they had made this promise: to strive for godliness even to death. So, as people who have accomplished what they vowed, they say: “I will pay you my vows, which my lips uttered and my mouth spoke in my affliction.” In those very afflictions, of which they said above, “You laid afflictions on our back”, they showed a perfect and complete love for God. They made vows and gave promises to stand firm even to death, saying almost the same as Paul: “Who will separate us from the love of God? Will affliction, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger?” and: “For I am persuaded that neither death nor life, nor things present nor things to come, will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus.” These, then, are the vows he says they have paid to God, the vows which their lips uttered and their mouth spoke in their affliction. Such were their burnt offerings, truly “full of marrow”. Their souls, bearing the richness and strength of faith, could say what is said elsewhere: “Let my soul be filled as with fat and richness, and my mouth will praise you with lips of rejoicing.” Things that are well nourished, rich and fat are called “full of marrow” in this sense. Such are the souls of God's champions, “full of marrow” from divine and spiritual food, having nothing [?] and nothing weak. That is why they say: “I will offer to you burnt offerings full of marrow, with incense.”

You will understand the incense from the verse that says: “Let my prayer be set before you as incense.” These souls, then, purified by spiritual fire, have become burnt offerings; or rather, like sacrificial victims, they have offered their own bodies [?] as burnt offerings, since these were perfected through fire. Their prayers would be the incense. And since they promise to offer rams and oxen together with goats, you will notice that these words too are spoken in the person of the Savior's apostles, if you take the goats, oxen and rams to be those whom the apostles led forward. They themselves were the first to become God's witnesses. Then they made countless others their imitators and followers, and they offer these to God as their own harvest. The rams are the rulers of the churches, about whom it was said in the preceding psalm, “The rams of the flock are clothed”; the apostles appointed them as leaders of the flocks. The oxen are the souls gathered as a herd in the Church: “Is it for oxen that God cares,” it says, “or does he speak entirely for our sake?” The goats would be those newly born, born in the time of winter. This is why the other translators also call them “desert ones”, as those who escaped the time of persecution. So the apostles bring these, too, to God as newborns whom they have led forward, each taking pride in those he has led. We have interpreted these things spiritually, in a manner fitting the promise of the divinely inspired Scriptures. That is truly how the passage before us should be heard, rather than in the manner of those who suppose, following the base fables of the Jews, that God delights in burnt offerings, or in incense that the senses perceive, or in the blood of rams and oxen and goats. God himself rejects all these through the prophet, saying: “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? says the Lord. I am full of burnt offerings of rams, and I do not want the fat of lambs and the blood of bulls and goats. For who required these things from your hands?” Taken otherwise, these words would also contradict what was said earlier in Psalm 49, where it was said in the person of God: “I will not rebuke you for your sacrifices”, and: “I will take no calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks, for all the beasts of the forest are mine, the cattle on the mountains and the oxen”, and further on: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of rams?” How could what is said here about burnt offerings and rams and oxen and goats agree with that? David himself, too, said earlier in his confession: “For if you had desired sacrifice, I would have given it; you will not be pleased with burnt offerings.” And again in another place: “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you have prepared for me. In burnt offerings and sin offerings you took no pleasure.” “Come, hear, and I will tell, all you who fear God, what he has done for my soul.” The same speakers said earlier: “Come and see the

works of God, awesome in his counsels toward the sons of men”, and they said this to the nations. Now the same speakers again address the same hearers, saying: “Come and hear, and I will tell.” And who are to come? It adds next: “All you who fear God”, those whom above they sometimes called “all the earth” and sometimes “all the nations”. They point to the same people now by calling them those who fear God. We have often shown elsewhere that Scripture customarily calls the God-fearers from the nations “those who fear the Lord”. Since the apostolic preaching needs to be remembered, they necessarily promise to hand on its explanation to the nations, saying: “Come, hear, and I will tell.” They say this as if from one mouth because of their perfection, for they all became one, perfected in the Lord. The Holy Spirit utters this prophecy as if from the one apostolic choir, addressing the nations and promising to explain what God has done for their soul. Formerly they said: “Come and see the works of God, how he once turned the sea into dry land, and how they crossed the river on foot.” But now they no longer hand on ancient things. They hand on the things of the new history, recounting their own deeds and the benefits God bestowed on them. That is why they say, “what he has done for my soul”, and then they tell the story, fulfilling their promise. And what is the story? “I cried to him with my mouth,” it says, “and I exalted him under my tongue.” They have listed God's benefits to them: how they were tried by fire, how they were tested, how they entered into afflictions, how they endured, how they passed through fire and water, how they came out into refreshment. Now they must also teach that divine grace did not bestow all these things on them for nothing, but because they themselves contributed greatly toward their witness. “First,” they say, “we never ceased praying and crying out to him. And we cried out not with a shout and a loud voice, but ‘under the tongue’, keeping our cries within. For we knew that God hears even those who are silent, and that there are cries of the soul which are not uttered by the tongue but are sent up to God by an unspeakable power.” This is what the Savior taught when he said: “Go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you.” So here too they say: “I cried to him with my mouth, and I exalted him under my tongue”, or, according to Symmachus, “I called upon him with my mouth, and at once my tongue was exalted.” “But we did not only devote ourselves to prayers and petitions and supplications to God. By our very deeds we also turned away from all injustice, so that we would not even look at it, nor even think of anything unjust in our mind. For if we had harbored any such thing, we would not have been worthy to be heard.” That is why they say: “If I had regarded injustice in my heart, let the Lord not hear me.” Since, then, he had such a mind and sent up such

prayers, he rightly says: “Therefore God has heard me and attended to the voice of my supplication.” These were the reasons he brought us out into refreshment after so many trials. For all these things they send up to God the hymn of thanksgiving that is due, and they set a seal on the whole discourse by saying: “Blessed be God, who has not turned away my prayer, nor his mercy from me.” With these words, spoken as from one person, the apostolic choir sealed all that had been said before, sending up blessing, glorification and thanksgiving to God for everything already mentioned.

1. For the end; among hymns; a psalm of an ode.

“May God have pity on us and bless us; may he make his face shine upon us and have mercy on us.” The present psalm is also evangelical and keeps to the same sense as the one before it. That is why it too points “to the end” and is entitled “ode” of a “psalm”, since that one also was said to be a psalm of an ode. Perhaps neither of them states in its heading whose words they are because the persons introduced prophetically in them are so evident. In both, the heralds of the nations, namely the apostles of our Savior, are meant. In the verses before us they openly cry out, praying that the salvation of God and his way may be made known on the earth and among all the nations. Then next: “Let the peoples confess you, O God; let all the peoples confess you. Let the nations be glad and rejoice.” They repeat the words a second time to confirm what is being prophesied. The apostolic choir had said earlier, “Shout to God, all the earth”, and again, “Let all the earth worship”, and again, “Bless our God, you nations.” In the present psalm likewise it sees that the success of the gospel preaching needs much help from God, and so, as if charming itself with a prayer, it says: “May God have pity on us and bless us; may he make his face shine upon us and have mercy on us.” “We say that we ourselves are nothing, and we confess that we can do nothing, since we are lowly and unlearned, poor and the last of all men. But since God himself has willed that we become servants of the salvation of the nations, may he first have pity on us, taking pity on our weakness. Then may he add something that can give us strength.” This was to bless them, with a spiritual blessing, so that the blessing that says, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it”, might be fulfilled in them as befits his grace. These words had been spoken long ago, at the beginning, at the creation of the world, and the Jews supposed they were fulfilled only in a bodily way, through an abundance of offspring [?]. “But we know that the soul too has offspring, and that disciples are the children of their teachers, and so we ask to obtain such a blessing that we may increase and multiply in the multitude

of our disciples and in the countless thousands saved through us, so that we may say: ‘Blessed be God, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ.’” So may God first have pity on us, and then, having pitied us, bless us. This will happen only if he makes his face shine upon us, so that we too may say: “The light of your face has been signed upon us, O Lord.” [The phrase added next, “and have mercy on us”, is found neither in the Hebrew nor in the other translators, and so it has necessarily been marked with an obelus.] We pray to obtain these things so that we may be able to make his way known in all the earth. That is why it says: “That your way may be known on the earth.” What is the earth, and what is the way of God? The earth is all the people who inhabit the earth and all the nations throughout the whole inhabited world. The way of God is the godly life, whose end leads to God himself, as to a mother city of good things. The saving word itself, too, would be the way of God. That is why it goes on to add, as if explaining the sense: “Your salvation among all the nations.” “So that we may be able to make your way and your salvation (for they are the same) known in all the earth and among all the nations that inhabit the earth, have pity on us, O God, and bless us, and make your face shine upon us, so that, filled with light from your face, we may shine upon all people. For if these things are not ours, we are nothing toward accomplishing so great a task.” “Let the peoples confess you, O God; let all the peoples confess you. Let them be glad.” The heralds of the nations prayed for the first things for themselves; the words now before us they pray for those who have received the preaching through them. First they pray that room for confession may be granted to them, so that through confession they may wash away their former offenses and the impieties of idolatry. Second, they beg that, once cleansed, they may obtain the gladness and rejoicing that come from God. That is why they first say: “Let the peoples confess you, O God.” But we might not yet understand which peoples they meant, since the Jewish nation too had assemblies and peoples. So, to make us understand which peoples they had in mind, they necessarily repeat the words, making the sense clear by saying: “Let all the peoples confess you.” Or perhaps in the first words they hint at the peoples among the Jews, sending up their prayer for them first, and in the second at the peoples from the nations? To make this plain to readers, Scripture clarifies it by saying: “Let the nations be glad and rejoice.” And since “let them confess you” is said twice, consider whether the first indicated the confession of former sins, and the second thanksgiving for the good things they had received. For confession is also used in the sense of thanksgiving. This is how the Savior

gave thanks, saying: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth.” After the first and second confession, they pray a third thing for the nations that have confessed. What is it? “Let the nations be glad and rejoice.” For what reason? It teaches next: “For you will judge the peoples with uprightness.” And it says “peoples”: not some and not others, but all, as was shown earlier. Moreover, each nation, knowing that it will be guided by you to walk the way we make known to it, will rightly be filled with gladness and rejoicing. Instead of “and let them rejoice”, Aquila translated “and they will praise”, and Symmachus “and let them speak well.” “Let the peoples confess you, O God; let all the peoples confess you. The earth has yielded its fruit.” The Holy Spirit, delighting in these kind and good promises, lingers over the same words, as if relishing the common salvation of all people. That is why it repeats them a second and a third time and does not wish to depart from this saving, evangelical song. So it says again: “Let the peoples confess you, O God.” This was the greatest wonder. The Jews, who had been taught from their fathers to worship the God of the universe, were continually thrown headlong into the error of idolatry. Yet all the peoples throughout the whole world, who had wandered astray for long ages, will come to so great a change that they will not only know you, the God over all, but also gain the understanding to confess you in the twofold sense already given. “That this may come to pass at last, hasten what the prophecy foretells, so that we may become eyewitnesses of the eternal promises.” The words before us should be heard as able to be spoken also in the person of the prophets. So what comes before the pause would fit the person of the apostles, and what comes after the pause would fit the choir of the prophets, who longed to see what we see and did not see it, as the Savior's saying puts it. After this it is said: “The earth has yielded its fruit”, or, according to Symmachus, “The earth will give its produce.” For truly the natural fruit of the earth is that those entrusted with dwelling on it should know the God over all and send up to him the confessions and thanksgivings due to him. The element of earth was made for this purpose: that those who spend their lives on it should bring forth the fruits of godliness. But because of the first man's transgression it was said: “Cursed is the earth in your works. In sorrow you will eat of it all the days of your life; thorns and thistles it will bring forth for you.” This was not the natural fruit of the earth. It was a prediction of the unnatural wickedness that would grow on it. The thorns and thistles are unnatural, since they came into being because of the transgression, not only of the first man but also of those who were ungodly after him. For in the beginning, when God said, “Let the earth bring forth the herb

of grass, sowing seed according to its kind and likeness, and the fruit tree bearing fruit whose seed is in itself according to its kind on the earth”, no mention at all was made of thorns or thistles. Nor would the earth have produced them if disobedience had not followed upon man. So thorns and thistles sprang up as images of the wickedness that later came upon mankind. That is why, so that these might be destroyed, the Savior came to cast fire upon the earth. And when the saving word, like fire, destroys the thorns and thistles, the soul, renewed and freed from wickedness, yields the fruit that is proper and fitting to it. Therefore all the peoples confess, and the nations on the earth are guided. Following on from this comes: “The earth has yielded its fruit. May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us. And let all the ends of the earth fear him.” Whether it is our Savior's apostles or God's ancient prophets (for the words suit both orders), they pray to obtain God's blessing. We explained its sense above, showing how “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it” was fulfilled spiritually in them. One can see in fact how the whole earth has been filled with their successors. The churches of our Savior founded throughout the whole world, and the peoples of countless thousands in each of them, display the results of their blessing. And “our God”, in “May God, our God, bless us”, fits them well, since they possessed the knowledge of their God as an inheritance from their fathers. But next they add, without any qualification, “May God bless us”, since he is no longer God of them alone but also of all who will be saved through them. After all this they seal the conclusion of the whole prophecy, saying: “And let all the ends of the earth fear him.” For since “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom”, they necessarily pray that the fear of God may arise, as an introduction to godliness, in all people, even those who live at the farthest ends of the earth. This was indeed fulfilled after the divine appearing of our Savior, after which the sound of his apostles went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. These ends of the earth were spoken of earlier as well: “Hear us, O God our Savior, the hope of all the ends of the earth and of those far off on the sea.”

“Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered, and let those who hate him flee from before his face.” The three psalms in succession before the present one foretold the calling of the nations. Of these, the sixty-fourth was entitled “A psalm of an ode, for David”; the next, “An ode of a psalm”; and the third, “Among hymns, a psalm of an ode.” Fittingly, therefore, the present psalm too, since it is itself evangelical and contains prophecy not only about the calling of the nations but also about the Savior himself, “for the end”

…is inscribed “Of David” and “A psalm of a song,” like the psalms before it. For the words that announce good things had to be called not merely psalms, but at one and the same time psalms of songs and songs of psalms, and had to be referred “to the end,” since what they foretold was to be fulfilled long afterwards, at the consummation of the age. This psalm too is spoken by the prophetic Spirit in the person of the apostles. In the preceding psalms they prayed for themselves, calling on God as their fellow worker in the preaching of the gospel. In the same way, in the present psalms the same speakers go on to say: “Blessed be the Lord day by day; the God of our salvation will prosper our way”; and again: “Command your power, O God; strengthen, O God, what you have wrought for us.” You see how they pray to be prospered and strengthened by God so that they may finish the course of the gospel without hindrance. They also plainly mention the preaching of the gospel when they say, “The Lord will give a word to those who preach the good news with great power.” And they foretell to whom they were to preach the gospel when they say: “Ambassadors will come out of Egypt; Ethiopia will hasten to stretch out her hand to God.” Through these words they clearly proclaim good news to Egypt, hinting at the idolaters, since idolatry began in Egypt. They also say that Ethiopia will hasten to stretch out her hand to God, and by this they mean the farthest parts of the inhabited world. Next they summon all the kingdoms of the earth together, and in this way all the nations are signified. Then, so that what was prophesied in words might at last come about in deeds as well, the prophetic Spirit begins by sending up a prayer through David, saying: “Let the Lord arise, and let his enemies be scattered.” For long ago terrible enemies of God tyrannized over everyone on earth: the wicked demons who established the error of many gods throughout the whole world. And there was no one to defend against these evils, no wise man, no righteous man, no prophet; not even any of the angels or holy spirits or the divine powers in heaven. That is why he begs God himself to arise and to rouse himself from his royal throne. God's providence is said to be at rest, to be quiet and, as it were, to repose when in the riches of his kindness and patience he bears with those who sin and act impiously toward him. It is said to move and rise up when he goes forth to take vengeance on sinners. So that the enemies already mentioned might at last cease from their dominion over mankind, he entreats God to rise up and rouse himself to vengeance. Then those who had long been gathered together and had formed an evil league with one another, the league of demonic idolatry, would be dispersed and driven far apart. The enemies of God and those who hated him were certain impious and godless demons, who fill the air above the earth and work among men their wickedness of manifold error. As soon as God merely moved

and roused himself to avenge what had been done, these demons were first scattered and dispersed far from one another, and then they took to flight. After this they vanished as smoke vanishes, and they were to perish as wax melts before fire. You will understand how his enemies vanished as smoke vanishes if you consider that in former times they disguised themselves as angels of light, the devil himself and his ministers, as the Apostle says: “For Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light. It is no great thing, then, if his ministers also disguise themselves as angels of righteousness.” In those days they gave oracles everywhere, promising divinations and cures, so that the superstitious, in an excess of madness, sacrificed even their dearest ones to them. Now, however, all of them have been wiped out and left desolate, so that not even a memory of them remains. They vanished as smoke vanishes once their fire has been put out. That is why it is said elsewhere: “Smoke went up in his wrath.” For the wrath of God came upon them and quenched the fire with which they used to burn up human souls; and when that fire was quenched, smoke went up. But this smoke too, no longer fed from below and having nothing to sustain it, vanishes. Since God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all, this light sends out gleams of wisdom, knowledge and truth to his friends, so that they say: “The light of your face has been stamped upon us, O Lord.” But to the enemies already mentioned it becomes a consuming fire. That is why it is said in other places: “Fire will burn before him, and around him a mighty tempest”; and: “Fire will burn before him and will set all his enemies ablaze.” In the passage before us the enemies are said not only to vanish like smoke, but also to melt as wax melts before fire, because they have made themselves enemies of God. For God loves all things that exist and abhors nothing that he has made; he fashioned nothing out of hatred, and so he is no one's enemy. But those who remove themselves far from him and make themselves his enemies bring destruction upon themselves, as it is said: “For behold, those who remove themselves far from you will perish.” In the same way, those who do what he hates are the ones who hate God. Let this be one way of explaining the passage. But since all prophecy is evangelical, consider whether these words may refer to God the Word, who was of old resting in the bosom of the Father. For “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” And: “He was in the beginning with God.” He was the Only-begotten of God, who is in the bosom of the Father. But since he took the form of a servant, was found in fashion as a man, and humbled himself even to death, the Holy Spirit fittingly foretells his resurrection, saying: “Let God arise, and let

his enemies be scattered,” where “God” is understood as God the Word. Or else the prayer speaks of Christ when it says “Let him arise,” but is addressed to the God of the universe. In that case “O God” stands for “O God, let your Christ arise, and let his enemies be scattered.” For his enemies were gathered together at the time of his passion, when “the nations raged and the peoples plotted in vain. The kings stood by, and the rulers were gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ.” But Christ's resurrection from the dead brought about the scattering of all of them, and they vanished as smoke vanishes, and as wax melts before fire. This Christ of God they hated, and they still hate him even now: those who continually blaspheme him with godless words and abuse, who make war on his Church and slander his teaching. Otherwise you would find no one who hates the God who is over all. Not even the godless and impious, nor even the wicked demons or the unclean spirits, would say that they do. But the Christ of God they admittedly hated. First came those of whom he himself said through prophecy: “They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue, they surrounded me with words of hatred and fought against me without cause. Instead of loving me, they slandered me. They repaid me evil for good, and hatred for my love.” After them came those who still blaspheme him even now. Yet all his enemies and all who hate him have been scattered and have fled from the face of his power. They have vanished as smoke vanishes and as wax melts before fire. Indeed, no one who hated him has ever passed through life unpunished. The chief priests and scribes, the Pharisees and Sadducees, who long ago hatched the plot against him, vanished so completely that not even a memory or a name of them survives among the Jews to this day. At that time their whole nation suffered dispersion and scattering among all the nations. And in the times that followed, all who made war on his Church likewise vanished, as smoke vanishes and as wax melts before fire. Such, then, was the fate of Christ's enemies and of those who hate him. Still more was it the fate of his invisible and unseen enemies, the wicked demons and evil spirits through whom the error of many gods was worked of old. Their utter scattering came about after the resurrection from the dead. Melting like wax before fire, they cried out: “Ah, what have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come to torment us before the time?” For the invisible and unseen rays of his divinity brought torments and pains upon those who said this. What good things the company of God's friends at the right hand enjoyed at our Saviour's resurrection, the prophecy teaches next, saying: “And let the righteous rejoice, let them exult before God, let them delight in gladness.” What it means not simply to rejoice and exult, but to enjoy these things before God and in God's presence, and to revel in divine delight, cannot be worthily described in words.

“Sing to God, make music to his name; make a way for him who rides upon the west.” The prophecy dealt briefly with the enemies of God and those who hate him, but it treats the righteous at length and lingers on the remembrance of them. The Holy Spirit exhorts the righteous to sing and make music to God, since through these they will enjoy the divine gladness and the delight and exultation already mentioned. Of these two, I mean singing and making music, singing was the higher, and the lower was playing on an instrument. So he fittingly assigned the higher to God, and the work done with the instrument to God's name. “Sing,” he says, “to God, and make music to his name.” A person sings to God when his soul has been trained by sound doctrines and he sends up from a purified mind the praises of God that befit him. A person makes music to God's name when, through the movements of the body and the activity of the senses, he does such things that the name of God is glorified through him among those who see him. These are the first things the word exhorts the choir of the righteous to do; next it commands them to do something useful to others. So that God may come upon human life and walk among those on earth, it bids them make the road smooth and level for him, saying: “Make a way”; or, in Symmachus, “Pave the way”; and in Aquila, “Make straight.” That is: remove everything crooked and level everything rough, so that God's journey to mankind may be smooth and level.
