Isaiah also showed this when he said: “Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low. The crooked shall become straight, and the rough places smooth roads, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God.” Here, however, he does not command them to make a way until they have first learned how they must sing to God and how they must make music to his name. Once they have learned these things and carried them out in deeds, he wants them next to make a way, that is, to prepare human souls and make them pure and ready for the coming of the God already declared. That is why he says: “Make a way for him who rides upon the west; the Lord is his name.” Here he has called the Lord by an unusual term taken from the Hebrew: he named him Ia. That is why Symmachus translated: “His name is through Ia,” and the fifth edition: “His name is in Ia.” Through the first syllable he hinted at the name of the Saviour Jesus. He teaches that this Lord, whose name he says is through Ia or in Ia, has ridden upon the west, and this signifies his coming among men and his sojourn in the flesh. For he did not show God the Word, who is in the form of God, unveiled, flashing upon human life like lightning. Rather, he took the form of a servant and

drew in the rays of his own divinity, and so he is said to have ridden upon the west: as though he had set like the sun in the body and come to the west of mortal life (which the divine Apostle called darkness, when he said, “Against the world-rulers of this darkness”), or as though he had set in death itself. “To this Lord, then,” he says, “who rides upon the west, whose name Jesus is signified through Ia, make a way.” The prophetic Spirit gives this command to the choir of apostles and bids them carry it out with great eagerness and boldness. That is why he adds next: “And exult before him”; or, in Symmachus, “And glory before his face.” He also gives another mark of the Lord already declared, saying: “The father of orphans and judge of widows.” For if he had not deigned to become a father of orphans and an avenger and judge of widows, he would have had no concern for the lowly on earth. But in his surpassing love for humanity he deigned to ride upon the west, to become the father of the orphans in darkness, and to be judge and avenger of helpless widows and desolate souls. So he fittingly commands them to make the road that leads to the orphans who do not know the heavenly Father, and to the widowed souls bereft of their bridegroom. Taken another way, the sense could support the doctrine of Providence. It teaches that widows and orphans are left desolate and helpless in life not without God's reason and wisdom, but for his glory and to display his divine care. Children bereft of their parents have often, as orphans, received more learning and education than those brought up under fathers, and have lived long lives. They have not only had plenty to live on but have gone on to become distinguished men. Women too who have suffered the misfortune of widowhood have often lived more cheerful, untroubled and godly lives than women in marriage, because God stood by the orphans better than any father, and by the widows as their helper and avenger. That is why it is said: “The father of orphans and judge of widows.” Instead of “to him who rides upon the west,” Symmachus has: “to him who rides through the uninhabited land.” By the uninhabited land he means the country of foreign and alien nations, which Scripture elsewhere usually calls the desert. Again, instead of “judge of widows,” Aquila translated “magistrate of widows,” and Symmachus “and he who pleads the cause of widows.” It is very precise of him to call God the father of orphans but the judge of widows. Since not all widows are of the same disposition, God becomes their judge, distinguishing those who are worthy of him from those who are not. But he would not likewise be a judge of orphans, for he equally, like a father, [?]

“God is in his holy place; God settles the solitary in a house.” The word had brought the Lord already declared down to a lowly place, saying that he rides upon the west and is the father of orphans and the judge of widows. So it must now return to speaking of him as God, and it teaches

that he rides upon the west already mentioned only for a short time, for the sake of certain purposes of his plan. His dwelling and the abode that befits him are not in the west, but “in a holy place”; or, in Aquila, “in his sanctified dwelling”; or, in Symmachus, “in his holy palace.” For he has a place that befits and suits his divinity. Yet because he loves humanity, he descends from his own greatness and stoops down to the orphans and widows who dwell in the west. That is why it is said elsewhere: “For behold, the Lord, the Lord, goes forth and will come down from his place.” Let us see what he does when he comes down from there and rides upon the west. “He settles,” it says, “the solitary in a house.” Symmachus has: “He gives the solitaries a house to live in”; Aquila: “He seats the only-begotten homeward”; and the fifth edition: “He settles the single-girdled in a house.” This was his first achievement, and indeed the greatest of the achievements he has bestowed on the human race. For the first rank of those who advance in Christ is that of the monks. They are rare, and so in Aquila they are called only-begotten, as being made like the only-begotten Son of God. In the Seventy they are single-mannered: not many-mannered, not changing their manner of life now one way and now another, but achieving only one, the one that reaches the summit of virtue. The fifth edition called them single-girdled, as being solitary and girded up by themselves. Such are all who achieve the solitary and chaste life. The first of these were our Saviour's disciples, to whom it was said: “Do not get gold or silver for your belts, no bag for the road, nor sandals, nor staff.” By saying that they must not get gold or silver for their belts, he presents them as girded. So too the Apostle exhorts all of us, saying: “Stand, therefore, having girded your loins with truth.” And those who ate the Passover were commanded to have their loins girded. This, then, is the first thing that the one foretold accomplishes when he comes to dwell among those who live in the west. From the orphans and widows already mentioned he sets apart the order of the single-mannered as chosen and most precious to himself, and he settles them in a house, that is, in his Church, counting them worthy to remain and dwell in it. After them he accomplishes a second work, one that serves the common good and reaches many: “leading out the fettered with manly strength.” For by his own strength he leads out those who were formerly fettered with the chains of sins. Instead of “with manly strength,” Symmachus translated “to release,” saying: “He leads out the bound to release.” You will understand this also from the prophecy in Isaiah, spoken in the person of the Lord: “Behold, I have given you as a covenant to the race, as a light to the nations, to open the eyes of the blind, to lead the bound out of their chains, and out of

the prison house those who sit in darkness.” For those who had long been bound tight with the devil's chains and were wasting away in the demonic error of many gods, he freed from their chains and led out, granting them forgiveness of sins. He also raised together with himself those who had been prisoners in death since the beginning of time, loosing the bitter bonds of death. And he did this “with manly strength”: for he took the form of a man, and by showing a man's strength through a human body he led those already mentioned out of their chains. These were the achievements of God the Word's coming among men, and to them the psalm next adds: “Likewise those who embitter, who dwell in tombs.” Symmachus translated this more clearly, making the sense plain: “But the disobedient will dwell in the dryness of scorching heat”; and Aquila: “But those who turn away have encamped on bare rock.” For he wished to lead out even those who embitter him and to free them from their chains. But they persist in their disobedience, and by this very thing they provoke and embitter God; so they will dwell in their own tombs, so that it is said of them, “Let the dead bury their own dead.” Or they “will dwell in the dryness of scorching heat,” as people who are about to go “into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” “O God, when you went out before your people, when you marched through the wilderness. Pause.” The present passage teaches that the Word of God did not come to dwell among men only at the consummation of the ages, but was also the one who spoke through Moses before that. It says: “O God, when you went out before your people, when you marched through the wilderness, the earth shook, and the heavens indeed dropped rain.” For then too, it means, at the time when you led the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt, the whole earth was shaken, as the report of what had been done in Egypt spread to everyone. The earth was shaken then either because the report, as has been said, filled the ears of everyone on earth, or because the element itself rejoiced at God's coming upon it. Another psalm teaches this too, saying: “When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people, the mountains skipped like rams, and the hills like lambs of the flock.” So the earth shook for joy, and the heavens dropped rain. But what did they drop? Was it the food brought to the people miraculously in the wilderness, or the divine words and laws, which are food for rational souls? The earth shook and the heavens dropped rain “before the face of the God of Sinai,” that is, of the one who spoke on Mount Sinai. Symmachus translated this too more clearly, saying: “The earth was shaken, and heaven dripped before the face of this God of Sinai, and before the face of God, the God of Israel.” Might it be that the heavenly powers, like nurses and nursemaids letting milk drip from the breast for infants, likewise supplied their nourishment to those who were then infants in soul? That is why the word spoken through Moses was called a tutor by the Apostle.

"You will set apart a voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance; and it was weak, but you restored it." "Then," he says, "when you went forth before your people, when you marched through the wilderness, the earth shook and the heavens dropped rain"; but now, when you have mounted upon the west, you have worked other wonders. For you set apart a voluntary rain for your inheritance. And what was his inheritance after the former people, if not the Church from the nations? He himself teaches this in the second psalm, saying: "The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession." The Son of God is bidden by the Father [?] to ask for an inheritance: not the nation of the Jews, but all the nations and the ends of the earth. Who could this be, then, except the one who established the Church from the nations? So it was for this inheritance of his that he set apart a voluntary rain. That is why it is said of him: "He will come down like rain upon a fleece, and like drops dripping upon the earth." The voluntary rain was the gospel word, the preaching of the New Covenant handed down to the Church from the nations. And the word "voluntary" is aptly added to "rain." For the word given to the people of old through Moses was not voluntary, since it was not laid down as law according to his own will. That is why the Saviour said to them: "Moses wrote this for you because of your hardness of heart." But the gospel word was set apart by the counsel and free choice of God for "his inheritance," which "was weak," he says, "but you restored it." In Aquila's version: "When it was worn out with toil, you established it." In Symmachus's version: "Which you labored over and established." Not many words are needed to show how the Church from the nations was worn out long ago, exhausted by the labors and toils of idolatrous error. It was weak beyond measure, so that no strength at all was left in it. But the Saviour took it up and restored it, establishing it upon the unbreakable and unshakable rock of faith in him. He had indeed promised to do this when he said: "Upon the rock I will build my Church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it." Having established and restored it, he settled his living creatures in it. And whom would you call the living creatures of God, except the souls that draw from the life that is with him and are made alive? And all these things, he says, "you prepared" through your kindness and love for humankind (or "through your goodness," in the other translators' versions) "for the poor one." Here he has mystically called the human nature of our Saviour according to the flesh "poor." For he "though he was rich became poor for our sake, so that we by his poverty might become rich." He himself made his poverty plain when he said: "Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart." So for this poor one, his God and Father, in his love for humankind and his kindness, prepared

all the things mentioned before: I mean the voluntary rain, the inheritance already described, and the living creatures already mentioned. That is why all of these are followed by the words: "You prepared in your kindness for the poor one. The Lord will give the word to those who proclaim the good news with great power." The achievements of the one who has mounted upon the west [?] to happen to men. Again, the same Lord accomplishes this too, besides the rest. And how, in what way? Men who had no speech of their own and no wisdom of their own, who were wholly unlearned and uneducated, he himself will supply with a word full of unspeakable and great power. Empowered and given a mouth by the word bestowed on them, they will be appointed heralds of good things to the whole world, proclaiming to all people what was foretold. That is why, following the Lord's achievements, this is added: "The Lord will give a word to those who proclaim the good news with great power." We needed to know this as well. Above, he urged certain people to sing and make music to God and to prepare a way for the one who has mounted upon the west. Now he shows who they are by saying: "The Lord will give a word to those who proclaim the good news with great power." To these who proclaim the good news and prepare his way into the world of men, the very one they proclaim will give a divine word. For they were able to receive this much, together with great power, and this word was great for them and sufficient for the ministry of the Gospel. The Lord himself was the perfect Word of God. But they received a word, were counted worthy of a brief inspiration of his power, and filled the whole inhabited world, preaching the Gospel with great power. This is what he had promised them in his own person, saying: "But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you." In Symmachus's version: "The Lord," he says, "gave sayings to a great army proclaiming the good news." (1) This great army of our Saviour consisted of those who proclaimed the sayings given to them. First came the twelve apostles; then the seventy disciples; and besides these the five hundred others, to whom he appeared all together after the resurrection, as the divine Apostle testified when he said: "Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, though some have fallen asleep." To this he adds: "Then he appeared to all the apostles." For there were (sic) there were, after the twelve, the seventy, and the five hundred, many other heralds of the Gospel as well, both in the times of the apostles [?] (1) Drusius reads "to those proclaiming the good news."

That is why he is proclaimed Lord of the powers. And who was the Beloved of God, if not the only-begotten Son of God? The Father's voice bore witness to him, saying: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." This King of the powers of the Beloved, then, supplied his benefits to the powers in heaven, and in the same way he gives the gospel word with great power to those who proclaim the good news on earth. These people on earth were themselves his armies and his powers. That is why Symmachus's version says: "The kings of the armies were loved," or "became beloved." He bestowed another gift on them too: to divide spoils for the beauty of the house. The beauty of the house would be the distinguished ranks in the Church of God. Someone confesses that he longed for them, saying: "Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells." And again: "One thing I have asked of the Lord, and this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the delight of the Lord and to visit his temple." The holy of holies, then, would be the delight and beauty of the house of God. And these are the ranks of the Church of God that shine out in self-control, purity, righteousness, and the other virtues. For this beauty the King of the powers granted his soldiers to divide spoils. The enemies had been overthrown and put to flight. I mean the hidden and invisible powers, of whom it was said above: "Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered; let all who hate him flee from before his face." Then the soldiers of the victorious King divided their spoils among themselves. And the spoils were ourselves, the whole human race, which long ago had fallen under the power of the opposing powers. When these had been driven off, the disciples, apostles, and evangelists of our Saviour, and the rest of his army, made the souls that had been plundered long ago their own possession and distributed them among one another. Paul received as his lot the spoils from the nations, from Jerusalem and the surrounding region as far as Illyricum. Peter in turn received those of other nations, John likewise those of others, and each of the remaining apostles in the same way. From these spoils they set apart the choicest offerings for the beauty of the house of God. That is why it is said: "And for the beauty of the house to divide spoils. If you lie down among the lots, you will be the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her back with the pale sheen of gold." The word has mentioned those who proclaim the good news with great power, the house and its beauty, and also the spoils within it, and by these it hinted at the Church of God and those distinguished in it. Consistently, then, in the passage before us it makes mention of the divinely inspired

readings, as though speaking to us: "If you lie down among the lots." The lots of the Church are the Old and the New Covenant of God. He teaches that those who spend their time [?] between them will find the wings of a dove covered with silver, a dove whose back is in the pale sheen of gold. The Holy Spirit is understood to be the dove. So the words spoken in the Old and the New, as far as a surface reading goes, are covered as it were with wings, and with silvered wings, since "the oracles of the Lord are silver refined by fire, tested for the earth." But the meanings hidden in their depths are like the back of the dove described, that is, of the Holy Spirit. These are said to be "in the pale sheen of gold," since the meaning hidden in the wording, the purest sense, flashes like gold. These things are proclaimed to all of us who are gathered in the house of God, whom the word called "spoils" in the preceding verses. Instead of "If you lie down," Symmachus's version says: "If you recline among the lots." For "to lie down" here means to take one's rest. So the address urges those who devote themselves to the sacred words and promises them the benefit that comes from the divine words. The wording of the sacred readings has been purified like silver refined by fire, according to the word that says: "The oracles of the Lord are refined by fire." And again: "The oracles of the Lord are pure oracles, silver refined by fire, tested for the earth, purified sevenfold." And the spiritual meaning is shown to be choice and precious by the words "in the pale sheen of gold." "When the heavenly one sets apart kings upon it, they will be made white as snow in Selmon." Instead of "When the heavenly one sets apart" and what follows, Symmachus translated it this way: "When the one able to reign divided it, it was as though covered with snow. Selmon is a mountain of God, a mountain of rich pasture, a very high mountain, a mountain of rich pasture. Why are the high mountains so eagerly sought? The mountain that God longed to dwell in, and the Lord will dwell there to the end." The word teaches that the heavenly one, that is, the God of those who dwell in heaven, distributed the dove mentioned before to the kings upon the earth, that is, to those on earth who share in his kingdom. (These were the prophets, righteous and God-loving men, and the disciples and apostles of our Saviour, to whom the heavenly God distributed the Holy Spirit.) At that time those who were counted worthy of the gifts of the divine Spirit were made bright like snow. That is why it is said: "Why do you suppose curdled mountains?" Here the word rebukes those who think that anything else is like it. He also adds the reason why it is not fitting to compare anything else with it, saying: "The mountain in which God was pleased to dwell; for indeed the Lord will dwell there to the end." This alone is the mountain in which God was pleased to dwell, and in which the Father dwells for endless ages. That is why it is not fitting to compare anything else with it. It is true that of others it is said: "I will dwell in

them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people." But he does not dwell and walk in them as he does in this mountain. For "the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father," and "in him the whole fullness of the Godhead was pleased to dwell." He did not dwell in him at one time and depart from him at another. Rather, to an endless end the Father always dwells in the Son. And he is our peace, according to the Apostle. That is why he is also named Salmon (sic),

which means "peace." And peace is said to be the place of God, as in the verse: "His place is in holy peace." "The chariot of God is ten-thousandfold, thousands of those who flourish; the Lord is among them, in Sinai, in the holy place." The word first gave the teaching about the Holy Spirit through the dove, and then the teaching about the Son through the mountain of God. Now it goes down to the lower powers. It shows that the mountain described is indeed such that the whole fullness of the Father's Godhead dwells in it, yet it is not the Father's only possession. He also has other lower powers that minister and serve. They are numberless and many, and they differ in virtue. God, the King of all, bound them under one yoke and harnessed them as a chariot for himself, with his only-begotten Word as charioteer. Daniel the prophet also describes their multitude in his vision of God, saying: "Ten thousand times ten thousand ministered to him, and thousands of thousands stood before him." In agreement with this it is said here too: "The chariot of God is ten-thousandfold, thousands of those who flourish." In its place Symmachus translated: "The carriage of God is of ten thousands, thousands of those who resound." And what does "who resound" mean, if not surely voices full of praise and of the proclamation of God? Such are the seraphim recorded in Isaiah, crying out and saying: "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory." Among these thousands and ten thousands yoked to the chariot of God the Lord himself also dwells, in their midst, as though driving them and equipping them by the Spirit. That is why it adds: "The Lord is among them." And which Lord this is, it shows as it goes on, saying: "In Sinai, in the holy place." He means that very Lord who was seen on Sinai, the holy mountain. This was the Word of God, present, evidently, among those yoked under the chariot of God. That is why the Hebrew text has not used the [?] four-letter name here, but writes "the Lord" in ordinary letters in "The Lord is among them." It does this to show that he is other than the God signified above by the four-letter name. When "the chariot of God" was spoken of, God was indicated by the letters that are not pronounced among the Hebrews. But now he is indicated by the more ordinary characters, in which "lord" is written among men. And it marks the place precisely, "in Sinai," in order to signify the Lord who was seen on earth. Most fittingly it adds next: "You ascended on high; you led captivity captive; you received gifts among men." It hints

at his descent by saying "you ascended." For he could not have ascended unless he had first descended. "He who descended is the very one who also ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things." And what did he do when he had ascended? He led captivity captive and received gifts among men. And what captivity did he lead captive, if not the spoils mentioned before, which his [?] divided among themselves? He also received gifts among men, since the Father granted them to him according to the promise he had made to him, saying: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession." Having received these gifts "among men" from the Father, he established his Church. Next after this it is said: "For even the disobedient, to dwell." Symmachus rendered this more clearly, saying: "Still also to dwell among the disobedient." For this too, he says, he received from the Father: to dwell among those who were long disobedient and spoke against the worship of God. He received this authority as well: to dwell in the midst of the disobedient and to take gifts for himself from among the disobedient themselves. After so many lessons had been handed down through the prophecy, the Holy Spirit next blesses the giver of such good things, as for great and wondrous achievements, saying: "Blessed is the Lord God; blessed is the Lord day by day." For men are no longer led astray into glorifying evil demons, he says; rather, every day and every hour they bless the Lord already made known. And this same Lord "will prosper our way," since he himself is "the God of our salvation." The Holy Spirit says these things in the person of the chorus of the apostles, as we showed at the beginning of the discourse. These men needed God to prosper their way so that they could prepare a way for him, as was said earlier. So of necessity they say: "Blessed is the Lord day by day; the God of our salvation will prosper our way." Instead of "of our salvation," Symmachus translated "of our Saviour." In its place the Hebrew again mentions the name of our Saviour Jesus. "Our God is the God who saves, and to the Lord, the Lord, belong the ways out of death." These things too are spoken prophetically, again in the person of the apostles. Since they spoke of God in the preceding verses, consistently they say in the verse before us: "Our God is the God who saves, and to the Lord, the Lord, belong the ways out of death." Or, in Symmachus's version: "God is to us a God for salvation, and to the Lord, the Master, belong the exits into death." He alone, being the God who saves, found ways out of death. For every human being reached the entrance of death but could no longer pass through it. But the Lord indicated in the present verse, who is here again written in ordinary letters in the Hebrew book, made ways out through death and has become God named after salvation.

That is why it is said: "Our God is the God who saves." That is also why this same one, when he spoke to Job, said: "You came to the source of the sea, and you walked in the tracks of the deep. The gates of death open to you in fear, and the gatekeepers of Hades cowered when they saw you." There too he plainly describes his descent into death and his passage out from there, just as he does in the present passage. Following this, the present passage teaches the crushing of his enemies, saying: "But God will crush the heads of his enemies." You will understand this too if you set beside it the voice that says elsewhere: "You strengthened the sea by your power; you crushed the heads of the dragons upon the water. You crushed the head of the dragon." By these words too the enemies of God are made known, the enemies of whom it is said here: "But God will crush the heads of his enemies." These were dragons that swim in the sea and in a watery substance: the opposing powers hostile to God, which wallow in the salty and shifting waves of this life. Hence in Job too it was said: "You came to the source of the sea, and you walked in the tracks of the deep. The gates of death open to you in fear, and the gatekeepers of Hades cowered when they saw you." When the heads of the dragons were crushed, the gatekeepers of Hades cowered. So in fear they opened the gates of death to the one who crushes the heads of his enemies. These enemies of the Lord trampled upon the whole human race. That is why it says next: "The hairy crown of those who walk about in their trespasses." For God will crush the heads of these, he says, of those who walk over the heads of men. Instead of "crown of hair," Symmachus translated "hairy crown," and by "hairy crown" the human head is meant. So the God who made the ways out of death will crush the heads of these very enemies of his, who formerly walked over the heads of men and trampled them under their feet. Instead of "in their trespasses," Symmachus translated "in its trespasses," saying: "a hairy crown that goes about in its trespasses." For God's enemies could not have trampled the hairy crown, that is, the heads of men, unless these had been brought low by their own trespasses and sins. That is why the Saviour said to those who were not like this: "But even the hairs of your head are all numbered." Even each hair of the more honorable part of his disciples' bodies, as something necessary that contributes to the adornment of the whole, has been counted worthy of divine numbering and protection. So they will not be shaved by the razor of the enemies who walk about and trample every hairy crown that goes about in its trespasses. "The Lord said: I will bring back from Bashan; I will bring back in the depths of the sea." Here again "the Lord" is not expressed among the Hebrews by the four-letter name, but by the more ordinary letters. This is now the third time the present Scripture has made him known, presenting what one might call a second Lord. For also in the psalm that says

[?] “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand,” was written with the four letters that the Hebrews do not pronounce. But the second Lord, whom the prophet declared to be his own Lord when he said “to my Lord,” was written with other letters, the ones also used for any human master of a slave. So here too, now for the third time, the Lord who went down as far as Hades and made his way through the passages of death is named with the letters the Hebrews use in ordinary writing. That is why Symmachus rendered him as “Master.” This Lord, then, who is plainly the Word of God himself, said: “I will return from Bashan”; and again: “I will return from the depths of the sea.” In place of “I will return” and the second “I will return,” Symmachus translated as follows: “The Lord said: From Bashan I will return, and I will make them come back from the depths of the sea.” Do you see what great deeds the Lord accomplished when he went down into the depths of the sea? He crushed the heads of the dragons upon the water, and the hairs of his enemies, of those “who go on in their offenses with their hairy crowns”; and he brought back from Bashan and from the depths of the sea the souls that had long ago been sunk there. Bashan means “shame.” It was there that the Lord signified by those letters came down for our sake, despising shame for the salvation of those enslaved there. That is why it is said: “The Lord said: I will return from Bashan, I will return from the depths of the sea.” Then it continues: “That your foot may be dipped in blood.” For this Symmachus has: “That your foot may crush along with blood, and the tongue of your dogs may lap from each of your enemies.” For as he broke his enemies and shattered their heads, he filled his foot with the blood that flowed from the heads of his enemy. That is why it was said in Isaiah: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments reddened from Bozrah?” And further on: “Why are your garments red, and your clothes like those of a trodden winepress, full of what has been trampled?” Then he answers those who asked him and says: “I trampled them in my anger.” So here too, after the crushing of the dragons’ heads, it is said: “That your foot may crush with blood,” or, “That your foot may be dipped in blood, and the tongue of your dogs in it, from the enemies.” Symmachus rendered this more clearly: “And the tongue of your dogs may lap from each of your enemies.” Who would you say are the Lord’s dogs, lapping the blood of his enemies? Either those who guard his flocks, watchful guardians keeping his Church, or certain avenging powers that trample on his crushed enemies and, as it were, try to get a taste of their destruction. “Your processions were seen, O God, the processions of my God, my King, who is in the sanctuary.” These words too follow naturally from what came before.

The holy prophets of God saw beforehand the things they foretold before those things happened. That is why the text says: “Your processions were seen, O God.” And what processions were these? Was not the first his descent upon Sinai, then his ascent on high, then his descent to Bashan and his return from there, his going down as far as death and his passages out of it, and above all his return from the depths of the sea? All these were processions of the Lord here indicated, and God’s prophets saw them before they happened. For that reason they were handed down in the prophetic Scriptures. So it is fittingly said: “Your processions were seen, O God.” Then he makes it certain whose processions were seen, teaching which God is meant. That is why he adds: “the processions of my God, my King.” Not simply of God, nor simply of a king, but “of my God.” This is like “The Lord said to my Lord.” The first would be the God who is over all, while the second, the Lord who hears “Sit at my right hand,” is my Lord; hence “The Lord said to my Lord.” Here too, then, the same prophet points to the second when he says: “The processions of my God, my King, who is in the sanctuary.” It is as if he said: when I speak of processions being seen, let no one think I mean those of the God who is over all. I mean the processions of my God and my King. But “princes went before, joined with those singing psalms, in the midst of maidens playing timbrels.” These very princes who went before, or those who sang and foretold the future by the Holy Spirit, saw in advance the processions of my God and my King. They were the prophets, who came before the apostles who appeared after them. For two choirs have handed down to mankind the theology of our Savior. The choir that went first was that of the prophets; the second, which came after, was that of the apostles and disciples of the Savior. Still, the processions of the God here indicated were seen; they were seen by the apostles, who received by sight what had long before been foretold by foreknowledge. These, then, saw the processions of God with their own eyes, but certain princes went before them, those “joined with the psalm-singers.” By this the text means David himself and those with him who led the people in the same period. Joined with the singers, they went before “in the midst of maidens playing timbrels.” Such were the Jewish synagogues: immature, still young girls, who knew nothing more than how to use timbrels, bodily instruments made from the hides of dead animals. They are called timbrel-players because they knew nothing but the bodily precepts of the law. “In the churches bless God, the Lord, from the springs of Israel.” After those who foresaw the processions of the God indicated, the text goes on to address certain others who came after the first, saying: “In the churches bless God.”

And since these were different from the princes who went before, he fittingly calls their gatherings churches. The prophecy all but openly, with uncovered head, foretells the churches of our Savior. These second ones are commanded to bless God not in the midst of maidens playing timbrels but in churches. And which God? Again he adds next: “the Lord.” And he necessarily shows from what source they must draw when they hand down the theology of the Lord to the churches, saying: “the Lord from the springs of Israel.” Here again the Lord is indicated by the more common letters. The springs of Israel are the prophetic Scriptures and the legislation of Moses. He urges the second group to draw from these, as from springs, the testimonies about our Savior, and so to bless him in the churches. Then he adds: “There is Benjamin, the younger, in ecstasy.” In place of “there,” Symmachus has: “where Benjamin is the least”; and Aquila likewise: “There,” he says, “is Benjamin the small, ruling over them.” Benjamin the younger, the least or the smallest, was Paul the divine apostle, who was of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, as he himself teaches: “Circumcised on the eighth day, of the race of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews.” He is called younger, or least, or small, since he himself teaches this when he says: “Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me.” In place of “in ecstasy,” Aquila rendered “ruling over them,” Theodotion “their instructor,” and the fifth edition “instructing” or “teaching.” We need no more words to prove that the holy apostle, here named Benjamin, rules over the churches and is their instructor. But Benjamin was not alone there, that is, in the churches of God. There were also “the princes of Judah, their leaders, the princes of Zebulun and the princes of Naphtali.” By these the text signifies the rest of the apostles, some of whom were of the tribe of Judah and others of the tribes of Zebulun and Naphtali. That is why the Holy Spirit mentions their land through Isaiah the prophet, saying: “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations.” And the Savior himself, passing along the Sea of Galilee, called his disciples from there. So the text clearly taught that the churches are ruled first by Paul, the smallest, the least and the youngest of the apostles. He was once in ecstasy: when he persecuted the Church of God and ravaged it, or when he beheld the Savior in a revelation, or when he was caught up into paradise, as far as the third heaven. After Paul, it foretells that the rest of the apostles will be distinguished there in the same Church, as our princes from the tribe of Judah, the princes of Zebulun

and the princes of Naphtali. Anyone who studies the matter carefully at leisure will find the tribe of each of the apostles, since the Savior has given the promise of finding to everyone who seeks. “Command, O God, your power; strengthen, O God, this which you have wrought for us.” These words too follow from what was said before. The text had prophetically commanded the apostles to bless the Lord in the churches, and to do this starting not from any other words but from the springs of Israel. So the prophetic Spirit next sends up a prayer on their behalf, saying: “Command, O God, your power.” It is as if it said more clearly: Let your power hasten and work together with these men; and now at last let what has been prophesied go forward in deeds by your strength. And this which [?] you predetermined by your counsel, strengthen this too, so that by your power it may be accomplished in deeds. And what was this, if not what is added next: “To your temple in Jerusalem kings will bring gifts to you”? For it is this very thing, which you promised us, that he asks you to strengthen so that it may come to pass. “Kings” here means the kingdoms of the earth; in this way all the nations are signified. And the temple in Jerusalem, to which the kings will bring their gifts, can be no other than that of the kingdom of heaven, since we know of a heavenly Jerusalem. He showed it who said: “But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother”; and: “You have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.” In this heavenly city of God, then, the choicest, highest and best part is the temple of God. To this temple of yours, he says, kings will bring gifts to you. These are those who dwell in the rest of the heavenly city. They are kings because they have been counted worthy of the kingdom of heaven, and so they reign with their Lord. “For if we have died with him, we shall also live with him; and if we endure, we shall also reign with him.” These kings, then, serving under the great high priest, the Only-begotten of God, and being priests themselves, will also bring gifts into his heavenly temple, entering together with the great high priest. And so that this may come to pass, [?] “Rebuke the beasts of the reed.” Just as he prayed [?] “Command, O God, your power,” and “Strengthen, O God, this which you have wrought for us,” so now he prays that the obstacles be taken out of the way, so that the word may run its course unhindered. For by his foreknowledge he foresaw the persecutions that would rise up against the preaching of the gospel, and the spiritual beasts. He who said, “Do not deliver to the beasts the souls that confess you,” prayed to be rescued from these. You will understand what the beasts of the reed are once you learn from Job how it is said of the devil: “He lies down under all kinds of trees, beside papyrus

and reed and rush.” It does not say he rests beside a fig tree, or a vine, or an olive, or a palm, or anything like them, but beside papyrus, reed and rush. In this way it hints at souls that are feeble and waterlogged and bear no worthwhile fruit, for it was beside such that the dragon used to rest. The fearsome beasts of the reed are the opposing powers: the wicked demons and the venomous, creeping spirits. In the words before us the Holy Spirit prays that God will rebuke them, saying: “Rebuke the beasts of the reed.” He also implores God to rebuke “the congregation of bulls,” or in Symmachus, “the assembly of the mighty ones,” together with “the heifers of the peoples.” The heifers of the peoples and the bulls are those among the Jews who persecute the word. Their deeds are described in what is added next: “so that those tested with silver may be shut out.” Symmachus rendered this more clearly: “those who kick away the well-approved, like the testing of silver.” For these bulls, and the heifers already mentioned, driven by the beasts of the reed, do everything they can to shut out the saints of God from the hope promised to them. The saints of God are those tested with silver. For just as “the words of the Lord are pure words, silver refined by fire,” so too the people of God are tested like silver. That is why they say: “You have tested us, O God; you have refined us as silver is refined.” So the beasts of the reed, the congregation of bulls and the heifers of the peoples strive to shut out from the hope promised them those who have been tested with silver. Or, in Symmachus: “They kick away these very people, who are well-approved like the testing of silver.” So that those already mentioned may not stand in the way of the saints of God, it is necessarily said: “Rebuke the beasts of the reed, the congregation of bulls among the heifers of the peoples.” In another sense, you may take the bulls to be the rulers of the Jews, and their heifers to be the synagogues under them and the crowds who rose up together at the time of our Savior’s passion. This reading is confirmed by the voice in Psalm 21, spoken in the person of the Savior himself: “For many calves surrounded me; fat bulls hemmed me in. They opened their mouths against me.” By these words he hinted at the rulers of the Jewish people and the crowds under them who rose up against him. “Scatter the nations that delight in wars.” The earlier words were about the opposing powers and about the rulers of the Jewish nation. These present words are about the enemies of the Church among the other nations. The Holy Spirit saw that those of the nations who remained in unbelief would rise up against the faithful and stir up persecutions against the Church of God. So it necessarily prays about this too, saying: “Scatter the nations that delight in wars.” For when

these are scattered, the grace of the gospel will have room. That grace was going to work, and to begin, first among those who were idolaters beyond all measure. The Egyptians were the most superstitious of all human beings and of all nations. That is why he next adds: “Ambassadors will come from Egypt.” In Aquila it reads: “They will bring in haste from Egypt”; in Symmachus: “Let those from Egypt come, appearing openly.” The whole race of idolaters is indicated by those who will come from Egypt and cross over to the knowledge of God. And by what is added next, “Ethiopia will be first to stretch out her hand to God,” the ends of the inhabited world are indicated. For the text signifies that they will come from all the nations, from the rising of the sun to its setting, according to the oracle that says elsewhere: “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations will worship before him.” In Aquila: “The Ethiopian,” it says, “will make his hand run to God”; in Symmachus: “Let Ethiopia hasten to give her hand to God.” One can also say that this was fulfilled historically in the Ethiopian whom the Acts of the Apostles mention. For he very nearly came before all the other nations, since he was counted worthy before them all of the knowledge of the Savior. How ambassadors also came from Egypt historically is again shown by the Acts of the Apostles. There it is said that on the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit filled the house where the apostles were and rested on all who were present. Among them were Parthians, Medes and Elamites, and those living in Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya around Cyrene. All of these were, so to speak, ambassadors of the nations, counted worthy of the firstfruits of the Holy Spirit. But after those from Egypt, and after Ethiopia, which came first, the remaining kingdoms of the earth are called next, and with them, plainly, the nations under them. That is why it is added: “Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing psalms to the Lord.” This was fulfilled in no other way than through the teaching of our Savior alone. So there is no nation, no country, no race of people, no kingdom anywhere in the whole world where peoples gathered to God do not carry out this command. Here again he commands them to sing to God and to sing psalms to the Lord, not by (1) the four-letter name, but to the name indicated by the more common letters. And so that we may know more clearly who this Lord was, he goes on to add: “to him who has mounted upon the heaven of heaven toward the east.” This follows very consistently. Since it had been said above, “Make a way for him who rides upon the west; the Lord is his name,” in the present words he consistently says that he has mounted no longer upon the west but upon the heaven toward the (1) Read “not by.”

east. For having first learned of his descent, we also needed to be taught of his return. His descent, then, took place in the west, as he hid the lights of his divinity; his ascent to the heaven of heaven took place toward the east, through his glorious restoration into the heavens. You will understand what is said here from the example of the sun. When the sun reaches the west, it makes its unseen journey; then, arriving at the eastern horizon, it rises straight up the sky, lighting up all things and making the day bright. In the same way, the Lord indicated here went through the setting appointed for him at the time of his passion and death, passed through the region [?], and afterward is said to have ascended upon the heaven of heaven toward the east. Aquila has: “To him who has mounted in the heaven of heaven from the beginning”; and it is also rendered: “To him who rides upon the heaven of heaven from the first.” You will understand “from the first” and “from the beginning” when you hear the Savior himself say [?] “… the world was, with you.” “Behold, he will give to his voice a voice of power. Give glory to God; over Israel …” He gives a distinguishing mark of the Lord here indicated, saying: “Behold, he will give to his voice a voice of power.” From this, then, it is truly possible to characterize the excellence of God the Word, who “was in the beginning with God”: his voice is not like that of human beings but is filled with divine power. “For he will give,” it says, “to his voice a voice of power.” And above it was said: “The Lord will give a word to those who bring good news with great power.” Since his voice was filled with power, it is fitting that he also gave a word with great power to those who proclaimed the message about him. The deed itself shows the power. With a bare word he said to his disciples, “Come, follow me, and I will make you fishers of men,” and by his power he did the deed. Again, when he commanded them, saying, “Go and make disciples of all the nations in my name,” he showed his power in deed. Again, when he said, “The gospel of the kingdom must be preached in the whole world as a testimony to all the nations,” he let them see the power of his word in the very events. And when at another time he said, “On the rock I will build my Church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it,” he demonstrated its power by the fact itself. In the same way you would find divine power blended into all the other words of his teaching. This is why it is said: “Behold, he will give to his voice a voice of power.” Having taught these things, he next exhorts them, saying: “Give glory to God; over Israel is his majesty, and his power is in the clouds.” The words “Give glory to God” are addressed to all who have been called to the saving faith. But “over Israel is his majesty” signifies those from Israel who became heralds of his divinity, that is, the apostles and evangelists,

...among whom his majesty was made known, his godhead being thus called [?]. That is why it has been said elsewhere: "For your majesty has been lifted high above the heavens." The Apostle clearly teaches that not all who are descended from Israel are Israel, and that not all are children because they are the seed of Abraham; that it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God; and that a Jew is not one outwardly, nor is circumcision the outward circumcision in the flesh, but a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter. His majesty, then, is over Israel. But also "his power is in the clouds," about which Isaiah prophesies, saying: "And I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon the vineyard." By these he meant the prophets and the teachers of divine learning, who, through the supply of the Spirit, watered the souls of human beings with heavenly rain, as though they were good soil. In this way, then, "his power is in the clouds." "God is wonderful in his saints": these are others besides the prophets and apostles already named. Who might they be but those from all the nations who have been deemed worthy of purity and holiness? Among them too God is wonderful, giving them power and strength. That is why it is joined next: "The God of Israel, he will give power and strength to his people. Blessed be God." Here again it is said, of necessity, that he gives power to his holy people, so that they can say: "I can do all things in him who strengthens me." For just as a word had been given with great power to those who preach the good news, so too he had to provide strength and power to his people, so that they could stand against the schemes of the devil and say, like Paul: "Who will separate us from the love of God? Will affliction, or distress, or persecution, or famine?" and the like.

FOR THE END, CONCERNING THOSE WHO SHALL BE CHANGED. OF DAVID. [?] "Save me, O God, for the waters have come in even to my soul." There are four psalms entitled "Concerning those who shall be changed": two of David, the present one and the 59th; one of the sons of Korah, the 44th; and likewise one of Asaph, the 79th. In all of them, in place of "Concerning those who shall be changed," Aquila has rendered "Upon lilies," and Symmachus "Concerning the flowers." Now the 44th contained the prophecy about the Beloved, and the change of the Church from the nations from worse to better; the fifty-ninth signifies the rejection of the Jewish nation and the change of the foreign nations to what is most excellent; and the 79th in turn signifies the falling away of the Jewish nation and the incarnation of our Savior. Fittingly, then, the present psalm too is entitled "Concerning those who shall be changed," or "Concerning the flowers" according to Symmachus, or "Upon lilies" according to Aquila, since it too contains the change for the worse of the people of the circumcision: they had been seen in their season as lilies and flowers, but a change for the worse overtook them. Isaiah also compares them

to flowers, saying: "All flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass; the grass has withered, and the flower has fallen." By these words he likens to grass and flowers the bodily worship of the Jews, which bloomed for a short time and appeared beautiful. And so in the present psalm too, as the text proceeds, it sets forth the change and the turn for the worse of their flowering, where it says: "Let their table before them become a snare, and a recompense, and a stumbling block. Let their eyes be darkened so that they do not see," and what follows. And since these things were to come to pass in deed only long afterward, "For the end" has necessarily been placed in the title. It is not a psalm, nor a song, nor a hymn, nor anything of the kind, since what follows would not have fitted such a heading. So you might call it a prophecy spoken in the person of our Savior, recounting what befell him, and foretelling what came upon the Jews after what they had dared to do against him. At the beginning, then, the Savior sends up a prayer to the Father, saying: "Save me, O God, for the waters have come in even to my soul." And it seems to me that these words are fittingly joined to those in the preceding psalm. For in that one it was said: "The Lord said: I will bring back from Bashan, I will bring back from the depths of the sea"; and in this one: "I came into the depths of the sea, and a storm overwhelmed me." For we had to be taught how the Lord went down into Bashan, which means shame, and how he said, "I will bring back from the depths of the sea." That is why he sets forth these very things in the present psalm. Concerning the shame, he says further on: "For your sake I have borne reproach; shame has covered my face"; and again: "You know my reproach, and my shame, and my disgrace." Concerning the depth of the sea, there is: "Save me, O God, for the waters have come in even to my soul. I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no foothold. I came into the depths of the sea, and a storm overwhelmed me." For these words would follow very closely on what was said in the psalm before this one: "The Lord said: I will bring back from Bashan, I will bring back from the depths of the sea." Since in that psalm it was the Lord himself who said these things, it follows that we should consider the same one now too to be the one [speaking] the present words [?]

He, then, whom we have shown above to be none other than the Word of God, sends up a prayer to the Father, making his own the sufferings of the human being he had taken up. That is why he says: "Save me, O God, for the waters have come in even to my soul. I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no foothold. I came into the depths of the sea, and a storm overwhelmed me." Now the psalm before this one called out, saying: "Make a way for him who rides upon the west; the Lord is his name"; and then next it sets forth his sojourn

among human beings, saying: "And rejoice before him, the father of orphans and judge of widows." It also revealed the calling of his disciples and apostles in the words: "The Lord will give a word to those who preach the good news with great power." Next it taught his descent into death and his way out from there in the words: "And of the Lord, the Lord, are the ways out of death"; and in: "The Lord said: I will bring back from Bashan, I will bring back from the depths of the sea." On top of all this it revealed his return to heaven, saying: "Sing to God, who rides upon the heaven of heaven toward the east." Such, then, were the things said there. But in the present psalm he expands what was said there only in passing, showing how it had been said, "And of the Lord, the Lord, are the ways out of death," and, "The Lord said: I will bring back from Bashan, I will bring back from the depths of the sea." For he goes through these things at length here, saying: "Save me, O God, for the waters have come in even to my soul. I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no foothold. I came into the depths of the sea, and a storm overwhelmed me." Now the Word is accustomed to call temptations, persecutions and the uprisings of ungodly men "waters." Thus it is said elsewhere: "Our soul has passed through the torrent; indeed our soul has passed through the irresistible water." And the Savior himself taught this, saying: "The rain came down, the rivers came, the winds blew and beat against that house, and it did not fall, for it had been founded on the rock." So in the present psalm too, calling the temptations and the plots against him "waters," he teaches that they have come in even to his soul. In the case of Job, though he was a noble contender, it is written that God said to the tempter: "Behold, all that he has I give into your hand; only preserve his soul." But here the tempter tempts the soul itself, whatever that soul was, which he himself mentioned when he said: "No one takes my soul from me; I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up"; and again: "I lay down my soul for my sheep"; and: "Now my soul is troubled"; and: "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death." Hence he says now too: "For the waters have come in even to my soul," or according to Symmachus: "For the waters have come upon me even to my soul." Then he adds: "I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no foothold," which Symmachus rendered quite consistently: "I was plunged into boundless depths, and there is no standing." For where there was no standing for others, because all who went down there slipped and were swept away by the currents of death, there I too came, when I came into the depths of the sea; or, according to Symmachus: "I came into the depths of the waters, and a flood washed over me." And Jonah the prophet too is recorded as having prayed words similar to these from the

belly of the sea monster. He too says: "Water poured around me even to my soul; the uttermost abyss surrounded me. My head sank into the clefts of the mountains; I went down into the earth, whose bars are everlasting bolts." That is why the Savior used the example of Jonah toward those who asked him for a sign, saying: "An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah the prophet. For just as Jonah the prophet was in the belly of the sea monster three days and three nights, so too will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights." He calls "the heart of the earth" what is here called "the depths of the sea," alluding to the regions of Hades. That is why in Job too the same Lord, speaking his oracle, set forth similar things, saying: "Have you come to the spring of the sea, and walked in the tracks of the abyss? Do the gates of death open to you in fear, and did the gatekeepers of Hades cower when they saw you?" You see how here too, having said "the spring of the sea" and added "and walked in the tracks of the abyss," he makes clear what the abyss and the sea are by adding: "Do the gates of death open to you in fear, and did the gatekeepers of Hades cower when they saw you?" So in the present psalm too "the depths of the sea" hint at the regions of death, where our Savior and Lord alone went down and passed through. That is why in the psalm before this one it was said: "And of the Lord, the Lord, are the ways out of death"; and again: "The Lord said: I will bring back from Bashan, I will bring back from the depths of the sea." In place of "and a storm overwhelmed me," Aquila rendered "and a current washed over me," and Symmachus "and a flood washed over me." For it is likely that the opposing powers gathered around him when, setting foot on the sea, he crushed the heads of the dragons upon the water. That is why in the psalm before this one it was said: "And of the Lord, the Lord, are the ways out of death. But God will crush the heads of his enemies." For he would not otherwise have passed through the ways out of death than by crushing the heads of his enemies there. If anyone thinks that David says these things because he fell into many temptations, let him consider how it could have suited David to say: "They gave me gall for my food, and for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink"; or: "Let their table before them become a snare, and recompenses, and a stumbling block. Let their eyes be darkened so that they do not see, and bend their back always." And if someone gathers for himself the rest of the passages like these, he will find that they in no way suit the person of David. But the interpretation that refers them to our Savior will be confirmed with indisputable seals by the testimony of the holy Gospels, both from the example of Jonah already cited and from the words in the present psalm, "For zeal for your house has consumed me," which is attested word for word as fulfilled in

him in the Gospel according to John, where it is written: "And Jesus went up to Jerusalem, and found in the temple those who were selling sheep and oxen and doves." Then, after telling how he drove them out, saying, "Take these things away from here; do not make my Father's house a house of trade," the evangelist adds: "His disciples remembered that it is written: Zeal for your house has consumed me." Moreover, the words "They gave me gall for my food, and for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink," which stand in the present psalm, are attested as spoken in the person of our Savior, according to John, who says: "After this, Jesus, seeing that all things were now finished, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said: I thirst. A basin full of vinegar was standing there; so they filled a sponge with vinegar mixed with gall, put it on hyssop, and brought it to his mouth. When Jesus had received the vinegar with gall, he said: This Scripture too is fulfilled." And the rest of the passages, when referred to the person of our Savior, would keep the interpretation free of strain (1). "I am weary with crying out; my throat has grown hoarse; my eyes have failed from my hoping in my God." These things too were fulfilled in the Gospel according to John, where Jesus stood and cried out, saying: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink." And again it is said: "Jesus cried out and said: Whoever believes in me does not believe in me but in him who sent me. And whoever sees me sees him who sent me. I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness." And at the raising of Lazarus, lifting up his eyes to heaven, he said: "Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me." And having said this, he cried out with a loud voice: "Lazarus, come out." Moreover, at the passion itself Matthew relates: "From the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour. And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying: Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani." Then, while he was living among human beings, he cried out and urged everyone to come and hasten to his teaching; and he called back the man four days dead with a great cry. Moreover, at about the ninth hour of the passion he cried out with a loud voice; and again after this: "Having cried out with a loud voice, he gave up his spirit. And behold, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, and the earth shook, and the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised": so great were the things his great voice could accomplish. And if one were to consider how, from that time until now, throughout the whole inhabited world, he cries out in his churches, urging people to hasten to his life-giving drink and calling back those who have been made dead by sins unto death; and that by his (1) Note: "σώζοι ἀναβίαστον": perhaps read "σώζει ἀκαταβίαστον" ("keeps ... free of strain").

proclaimed passion [he calls] [?] the whole inhabited world rather than Zion, as he did then, since "their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world": he will know how it is said in the present psalm, in his own person: "I am weary with crying out; my throat has grown hoarse." For by these words he signifies how lasting his cry is. He did not cry out once and then pass on; he is always crying out and calling into the souls of all through his disciples, and he is always crying out to the Father for those who have believed in him. That is why he adds next: "My eyes have failed from my hoping in my God." In place of "have failed," Aquila says: "My eyes have been brought to an end waiting for God." He was crying out and calling because of the multitude of his enemies, which he sets forth when he says: "Those who hate me without cause have become more numerous than the hairs of my head." Now if his Church is his body, according to the Apostle, who taught, "You are the body of Christ, and members each in part," you might say that the more essential members of the body, and, so to speak, its sense organs, are the essential members of the people: the leaders as the head, the teachers as the mouth, the understanding hearers as the ears, those who see deeply into the Scriptures as the eyes, the more active as the hands, and the remaining members of the body correspondingly. It would follow from this to take the hairs as the masses of the whole people, the surplus crowd, who lend a certain adornment to the whole body but have no essential use like the other members. Far more numerous than such hairs would be those who are strangers to the faith, since they walk the broad and spacious way. That is why it is said: "Those who hate me without cause have become more numerous than the hairs of my head." Those are said to hate "without cause" who can give no reason for their hatred, like those who persecute the saving word yet can find no fault with it. In place of "those who hate me without cause," Symmachus says: "those who hate me for no reason." These, then, he says, have become more numerous than the hairs of my head. Moreover, his enemies who persecute him have grown strong. One can indeed see his enemies grow strong, exalted and very powerful at each time when they are permitted to persecute. They persecute him unjustly, and they hated him without cause. For though they have no ground for enmity and cannot give reasonable causes for which they persecute, they still persecute him unjustly. And he endured punishment for things he had not seized, and for wrongs he had not done. For if according to the laws it is fitting that penalties be exacted from those who have done wrong, and neither he nor his genuine disciples were ever convicted of lawbreaking, he rightly says: "What I did not seize, I then repaid." At the time of his passion, too, he suffered without cause and paid the penalty for wrongs he had not done. That is why he then said:

"What I did not seize, I then repaid"; or according to Aquila: "What I did not take by force, I then returned." "O God, you know my folly." Just as the divine Apostle, without reproach, called the Savior's passion "the foolishness of God," and the cross "weakness," saying, "He was crucified in weakness," and again, "But we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles; for the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men," so now too you would not be wrong to understand the "folly" spoken of here in the same way as the "foolishness" named by the Apostle. Moreover, just as "the Lord knows those who are his," since those deemed worthy of God's knowledge are a select few, so too the folly here, being worthy of God's knowledge, carried a great and deep meaning. "For my folly," he says, "did not come about against your will or apart from your knowledge." And what is this folly but what the many take for folly? For just as the foolishness was considered foolishness by the Greeks, yet was brought about according to the deep counsels of God, and what was considered foolish among men was wiser than men ("for it pleased God through the foolishness of the preaching to save those who believe"), so too the folly he underwent for our sake, when he emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and went even to death, was wiser than human wisdom. "For the word of the cross," says the Apostle, "is foolishness to those who are perishing" (and if foolishness, then folly too) "but to us who are being saved it is the power of God." This folly and foolishness, then, God did not fail to know, for it came about by his own judgment. That is why he says: "O God, you know my folly." Symmachus has spared us the trouble by rendering it: "O God, you know my inexperience"—that is, inexperience of what is found among human beings. For since he is a stranger to the wickedness found among human beings, he refers this good inexperience to the knowledge of his own Father. Another divine Scripture also mentions the Savior's folly, in agreement with the present one. It is written in Proverbs: "These things says the man to those who believe in God, and I cease. For I am the most foolish of all men, and there is no human understanding in me. God has taught me wisdom, and I have known the knowledge of the holy." Here too he says that he is the most foolish of all men and has no human understanding, yet that he has been taught spiritual wisdom by God himself and has known the knowledge of the holy. Moreover, "my offenses," he says, "were not hidden from you." For if there were any offenses in me for which they sentenced me to the cross, you surely would have been the first to know, since nothing can escape you; but there were none. That is why those who hate me hated me without cause, and those who persecute me unjustly exacted from me what I had not seized. But since false witnesses and

[?] they set up false accusers in their charge against me, "You know, O God," he says, "whether any offense has been committed by me. For if there were any offenses in me, they would not have been hidden from you." And in another sense: if he took upon himself the stamp of our sins and became a curse for us, so that it is said of him, "This man bears our sins and is in pain for us. And he was wounded because of our sins, and was made weak because of our iniquities. And the Lord handed him over to our sins," then, he says, "these offenses too I took upon myself on behalf of human beings. You knew them, O God, since they were not hidden from you. For I did not take them upon myself apart from your will, and that is why you also counted them worthy of your knowledge." "Let not those who wait for you be put to shame because of me, O Lord, Lord of hosts." Since the wise of this age slander my teaching and drive it away as full of folly and foolishness because of the shameful cross, I entreat and beg that those who believe in me may be kept unshaken by you, so that they may never be put to shame. So you yourself, O Lord, Lord of hosts, do not forsake those who are warred against for the sake of the knowledge of you which they have received from me, who always endure terrible things and hold fast even to death. And let not those who seek you, the God of Israel, be confounded for having put their confidence in me. For even if at one time they were utterly ignorant of you because they had been enslaved to wicked demons, now that they have come to know you they have forgotten everything else and continue to seek you alone. So I pray that they may not be put to shame or disgraced. This is how Symmachus rendered it: "Let not those who look for you be put to shame because of me, O Lord God of hosts; let not those who seek you be disgraced because of me, O God of Israel." Notice how "Lord, Lord of hosts" is said: the text doubles the title "Lord" and refers it to the God of the universe. "Because for your sake I have borne reproach, shame has covered my face." Other people, he says, are subjected to rebukes and reproaches for their own sins. But I, who knew no sin, have borne reproach for your sake, since you yourself, the God who loves humanity, made me sin on behalf of the human race, so that those who believe in me might become righteousness. And again, "for your sake I have borne reproach," having emptied myself in keeping with your counsel and humbled myself even to death, at the time when those who passed by blasphemed, wagging their heads and saying, "Aha, you who destroy the temple and build it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross." And likewise the chief priests, mocking along with the priests and scribes and Pharisees, said, "He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is the King of Israel, let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him. He trusts in

God; let God deliver him, if he wants him. For he said, 'I am the Son of God.'" So it is in foretelling these things that he says in the present passage, "Because for your sake I have borne reproach, shame has covered my face." For it was not because of my own sins, nor because of lawless deeds, but "for your sake" that I endured the reproach just described, and shame covered my face. Or, in Symmachus' version, "Disgrace covered his face." And I endured all these things, he says, for your sake, that is, for the sake of your will. And again, "I became estranged from my brothers, and a stranger to the sons of my mother." In these words he presents two groups. One is that of his true brothers, from whom he became estranged. The other is that of the sons of his mother, who were not, however, his brothers, and to these he became a stranger. Yet if they were sons of his mother, and so brothers, they too should have been designated in the same way as the first group. But he did not call the sons of his mother brothers, clearly because they were different from the first group, those named as his brothers. Now his disciples had become his brothers. Of them he says in another psalm as well, "I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the assembly I will sing your praise." And in the Gospel, appearing to Mary after his resurrection from the dead, he said, "Go to my brothers and tell them, 'I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.'" It was from these brothers of his, then, that he became estranged at the time of the passion indicated here, when all his disciples abandoned him and fled, and Peter himself, the chief of the apostles, denied him three times. To these he became a stranger and estranged. But to the sons of his mother, who were not also his brothers, he became a stranger. Now the Gospel mentions his brothers and his mother when he came to his hometown and was teaching in the synagogue, so that they were astonished and said, "Where did this man get this wisdom? Is this not the carpenter's son? Are not his mother and his brothers and all his sisters here with us? Where then did this man get all these things?" If, then, we took those called the sons of his mother in the passage before us to be these people, we would have to say that the holy Virgin had also become the mother of his other brothers. But James, who was called his brother, plainly did not become estranged from him or alien to faith in him. He was one of his most genuine disciples, so much so that he was the first to receive the throne of the church in Jerusalem. And his other brothers too, even if at the beginning they did not believe in him, clearly came to believe afterward. The Gospel, at any rate, records that his mother and his brothers stood outside, seeking to speak with him. And in the Acts of the Apostles it is said that the apostles were all together, devoting themselves to prayer with Mary

his mother and with his brothers. How then could he be thought a stranger to them? So there is no room for applying to them the words, "I became estranged from my brothers, and a stranger to the sons of my mother." For he was no stranger to them; on the contrary, they held him in the highest honor. So we should no longer suppose that the brothers of his mentioned earlier were sons of Mary. Those whom the psalm calls the sons of his mother, to whom he became a stranger, must be others besides these. You should understand "mother" to mean the synagogue of the Jews and the whole kinship according to the flesh of those of the circumcision, and the sons of such a mother to mean those who denied him and said, "As for this man, we do not know where he comes from." That is why, since they regarded him as a stranger, he said to them, "Why do you not understand what I say? Because you cannot hear my word." Again they regarded him as a stranger when they said, "Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?" That is why he said to them, "I have come in my Father's name, and you do not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive." In this way, then, he became a stranger and an alien to the sons of his mother. He endured all these things for the reason given next, which he necessarily sets forth when he says, "Because zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me." For since he spoke with great boldness, rebuking and driving out those who were making his Father's house a house of trade and a den of robbers, they plotted against him on this account. The evangelist shows this when he says, "The Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.
