And in the temple he found people selling sheep and oxen, and he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables. And to those who sold the doves he said, 'Take these things out of here, and do not make my Father's house a house of trade.'" And he adds, "His disciples remembered that it is written, 'Zeal for your house has consumed me.'" He also took upon himself the reproaches of those who reproached God and became their avenger. That is why he said, "And the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me." For he could not bear those who by their own deeds brought reproach upon the law of godliness, and so he directed his rebukes against the rulers of the nation. So he exhorted the crowds and his disciples, saying, "The scribes and the Pharisees sit on the seat of Moses. So do and keep whatever they tell you, but do not act according to their works. For they say and do not do." Then next, refuting them to their face, he said, "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you shut the kingdom of heaven in people's faces"; and again, "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, because you are like whitewashed tombs." It was because of rebukes like these that they contrived their plot against him. That is why he says here, "Zeal for your house has consumed me,

and the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me. And I covered my soul with fasting, and it became a reproach to me." When I saw your house filled with every kind of lawlessness, he says, becoming at one time a house of trade and at another a den of robbers, I burned with divine zeal and drove out those who were acting lawlessly inside. And when by their own wicked deeds they fastened reproach upon you, God, whose worship they professed, I again took such reproaches upon myself and was compelled to speak boldly and to apply my rebukes to them as a cure. But when I saw that they were insensible and did not turn back at my rebukes, I wept over their destruction, fasted, and afflicted myself on their behalf. Even so they reproached me, disparaging and mocking my fasting. And because I wished to show them a pattern of repentance, I not only afflicted myself with fasts but also made sackcloth my clothing, chastening and punishing my own flesh, and by the deed itself showing them the way of confession and of cleansing from former sins. But they laughed at this too and made me a byword. They gathered together and sat at their gates, made me the sole subject of their conversation, and all but babbled to one another in their mockery of me. Nor was it enough for them to disparage and mock the ascetic labors I undertook for them. They also held drinking parties and ran through songs and ditties about me, drinking hard and getting drunk in their drunken insults against me. At this I covered my soul with fasting all the more and made sackcloth my clothing, weeping over their destruction. That is why Aquila's version reads, "And I wept my soul with fasting, and it became reproaches to me. And he gave my clothing as sackcloth, and I became a byword to them. Those sitting at the gate talked about me, and the songs of those drinking strong drink." And Symmachus' reads, "And when I wept my soul with fasting, it became a reproach to me. And I made my clothing sackcloth, and I became a byword to them. Those sitting in the gate told tales of me, and those drinking strong drink sang of me." But together with these words we must also examine what the Savior says in the Gospels: "John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, 'He has a demon.' The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, 'Look, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners.'" But you will say that this happened at the beginning of the Gospel, when his disciples did not fast and he made a defense on their behalf, saying, "The sons of the bridechamber cannot fast as long as the bridegroom is with them; [?] the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast." Do you see that he too knew the proper time for fasting? If, then, you compare the time of his passion with the passage before us, you will find how

these things were fulfilled when at last the bridegroom was taken away and his disciples too fasted. At that time he foresaw that a little later he would be estranged from them; that the whole nation of the people of the circumcision would demand his blood; that Peter would deny him; and that such things would be dared against him that darkness would seize the surrounding world, the sun itself would be darkened, and the veil of the temple would be torn. He foresaw too that all the ancient sacred things of Israel would be overthrown (I mean their kingdom, their priesthood, and the Holy of Holies) and that all of these would be cast away and overthrown at once. For these reasons it would not be unlikely that he afflicted his soul with fasting and made sackcloth his clothing. At this the ungodly mocked him, babbling in the tales they told about him as a byword. For the rest of the day they gathered at the gates and led astray those passing through with their slanders against him; and at mealtime, given over to wine and drunkenness, they composed songs against him. So he covered his soul with fasting and made sackcloth his clothing for the salvation of others, [?] these things out of the surpassing greatness of his love for humankind.

"But as for me, my prayer is to you, O Lord; it is a time of favor, O God. In the abundance of your mercy hear me." They mocked and disparaged my afflictions, he says, but I persevered, offering up my prayer to you, the Lord. Notice that here too the Hebrew scripture indicates "the Lord" by the Tetragrammaton. And as I prayed to you, the Lord, I said this: "It is a time of favor, O God." Or, in Symmachus' version, "a time of reconciliation. O God, in the abundance of your mercy hear me." For even if at another time too the Father's voice bore witness, saying, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased," now above all is the time of favor. So I implore you to hear me in the abundance of your mercy and to save me in the truth of your salvation. For I do not ask for human salvation, but for the true salvation. Such is the salvation that comes from you, by which I pray to be saved from the mire, so that I may not sink in. What mire is this, if not the one I spoke of above: "I am sunk in the mire of the deep, and there is no foothold"? For the slime of the deep mentioned above is here called mire. By these words he signifies the dissolution of the body in death, of which he said elsewhere, "You will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor let your holy one see corruption." Those who were held fast by death underwent corruption, came into corruption, and remained in it; they sank in the mire. But I, even if I went down, having emptied myself even to this point, still implore, saying, "Save me from the mire, so that I may not sink in." The words that follow set out the powers at work in death itself, from which he prays to be delivered, saying, "May I be delivered from those who hate me and from the depths of the waters. Let not the tempest of water drown me, nor the deep swallow

COMMENTARY ON THE PSALMS. me up." These waters and the dragons in them were also indicated in the earlier verses, as in, "Save me, O God, for the waters have come in up to my soul. I am sunk in the mire of the deep, and there is no foothold. I came into the depths of the sea, and a tempest overwhelmed me." But in the earlier words he described his descent into these things, and in the words now before us his return from them. "May I be delivered," he says, "from the depths of the waters, and let not the tempest of water drown me, nor the deep swallow me up, nor the pit close its mouth over me." For death prevailed and swallowed up all other human souls, and the pit held them fast and shut them in with its own mouth. The pit that has a mouth may be said to be death itself, which from of old has swallowed all who fell into it, and after swallowing bites down, as though shutting its own mouth, so that none may run back. But may this not happen in my case. So I entreat you, the Father, saying, "Let not the tempest of water drown me, nor the deep swallow me up, nor the pit close its mouth over me." Or, in Symmachus' version, "nor the pit put the lid of its mouth on me." Here he mentions waters and depths and a pit. In Psalm 21 he signifies these same things but uses other names, saying, "Deliver my soul from the sword, and my only one from the hand of the dog. Save me from the mouth of the lion, and my lowliness from the horns of the unicorns." These too were said about the opposing powers in what is called Hades, as we showed when we explained those passages. "Hear me, O Lord, for your mercy is good; according to the abundance of your compassions look upon me." Here too the Savior calls upon his own Father by the name that the Hebrews do not pronounce. He is saying, in effect: since I have asked this and that, that I may not sink into the mire, that I may be delivered from the depths of the waters, and the rest that follows, grant my petition for this reason, O Lord, "for your mercy is good, and according to the abundance of your compassions look upon me. Do not turn your face away from your servant." In these words he entreats him to look upon him and not to turn his face away from him, so that, like a great judge of the games, he may assess the contest he underwent, his endurance, and his humiliation. Taking pride in these, he asks the Father not to turn his face away from him but to look upon him. Then he adds, "Because I am afflicted, hear me quickly." Or, in Aquila's version, "Because I am in straits, hear me quickly." You will understand the meaning of this too if you consider the saying, "Narrow and hard is the way that leads to life, and few are those who enter by it." He himself was the first to travel that narrow and hard way, and so he said, "Because I am in straits," and, "Because I am afflicted, hear me quickly." He had already shown his affliction and

distress in the earlier verses, when he said, "And I covered my soul with fasting, and it became reproaches to me. And I made sackcloth my clothing." Because of these things, then, he besought the Father to look and behold the struggles he endured for us. That is why he said, "Attend to my soul and redeem it." Then, pointing to his achievements, on which he besought him to look, he adds, "Because of my enemies deliver me. You know my reproach and my shame and my disgrace." For just as he said above, "You knew my folly, and my offenses were not hidden from you," so now too, he says, my reproaches are worthy to be known by you. He also made this clear in the earlier verses, when he said, "And the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me." Since, then, by your judgment and your Spirit I endured the reproaches and the passion full of shame, I say for this reason, "You know my reproach and my shame and my disgrace." You know my shame, which is not unworthy of your knowledge. And you know my disgrace, which I endured when "I gave my back to scourges and my cheeks to blows." But you do not know those who afflict me in the same way as you know me, for they are not worthy of your knowledge. So I say of them, "Opposite you are all who afflict me." They are opposite you in the sense that they have chosen what is opposed to you. They afflict me by gaining no benefit from my care, and they afflict me through their own destruction. Then he adds, "My heart expected reproach and misery." Symmachus rendered this more clearly: "Reproach has broken my heart, and I was grieved." And Aquila says, "Reproach has crushed my heart, and I was despaired of." "And I waited for someone to grieve with me, but there was none, and for someone to comfort me, and I found none. And they put gall into my food, and for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink." Symmachus' version reads, "And I waited for someone to grieve with me, and there was none, and for someone to console me, and I did not find one. And they threw gall into my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink." The Gospel teaches that his disciples abandoned him and fled at the time of the passion, yet were not without grief. For when Peter is recorded as weeping bitterly, and the rest as gathered and hiding in one house for fear of the Jews, they were not free of grief. So these words would not fit if said of the company of the apostles. They fit those who afflicted him, of whom he said, "Opposite you are all who afflict me." For I did everything for their salvation, covering my soul with fasting and wearing sackcloth as my clothing. But they did the opposite: at one time they reproached and disparaged my fasts, at another they sang against me in their drunken revels, and they did anything rather than grieve with me. I was grieved and in pain on their behalf, but they did not share my pain or suffer with me. Nor was there any comforter to be found among them to console me.

[?] Those who set their hands against me put gall into my food, even though I had given them rich nourishment; and when I was thirsty they offered me vinegar instead of drink. The gall they mixed for me was the kind the prophetic word pointed to when it said: "How have you turned to bitterness, O foreign vine?" You will understand how our Saviour is fed when you hear him say: "I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink." But if, instead of the nourishing fruits of a godly life, someone offers him bitter blasphemies and mixes godless and false doctrines into his teaching, that person puts gall into his food, and when he is thirsty gives him turned wine, wine that has turned aside from the straight road. Moses foretold such things about the Jewish people when he cried out prophetically in the great song: "For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their tendril from Gomorrah; their grape is a grape of gall, their cluster is of bitterness." So the Spirit naturally reproaches the same people through Isaiah as well, saying: "I waited for it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns"; and again: "I waited for it to do justice, but it did lawlessness; not righteousness, but a cry." By their deeds and actions, then, and by their bitter words and life, they put gall into the Saviour's food and gave him vinegar to drink in his thirst. But since the word of the prophecy also had to be fulfilled in actual events, the evangelist records what happened at the time of his passion: "After this, Jesus, knowing that all things were now accomplished, said, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, 'I thirst.' A bowl full of vinegar stood there. So they filled a sponge with vinegar mixed with gall, put it on hyssop, and held it to his mouth. When Jesus had received the vinegar with the gall, he said, 'This Scripture too is fulfilled.' And bowing his head, he gave up his spirit." Since he bowed his head and gave up his spirit after the Scripture had been fulfilled, it is fitting that in the psalm too he describes his sufferings up to this point. Then, from here on, he foretells what would befall them: "Let their table before them become a snare, and a retribution, and a stumbling block." Scripture has a sort of custom of speaking of future things as though they were past. Just now, for example, it said, "They gave gall for my food," instead of "they will give," and "for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink," instead of "they will give me to drink." Elsewhere too it is said in the same way: "They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots"; and again: "The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ." These things too, which were yet to happen, were announced beforehand as if already past. In the same way, words that seem to be spoken as commands or wishes are also to be understood as predictions in the prophetic manner, as is the case with

the passage before us. For "Let their table become" must be taken as "it will become"; and "Let their eyes be darkened" as "they will be darkened"; and what follows likewise. It makes no sense that he who commands us not to repay evil for evil, but to pray for those who mistreat us, to bless and not to curse, and even to love our enemies, should himself call down such things on others. These words, then, are spoken neither as a wish nor as a command, but prophetically, in the manner explained. In return for what they dared and did against me, such things will overtake them: their table will become for them not a place where food is set out, but a snare, a retribution and a stumbling block, because they gave gall for my food. What would you call the table of the Jewish nation but the divinely inspired Scriptures, which they are accustomed to study and recite by heart? Their contemplation and understanding contain food for rational souls, while their wording serves as a table. This table of theirs, then, the ready reading of the divine Scriptures, he foretells will become for them a snare, a retribution and a stumbling block. And it will be such for them not because it is such by nature, but because it will become such for them. That is what the words mean: "Let their table become before them a snare, and a retribution, and a stumbling block." And this is fulfilled upon them in fact. When they read the divine Scriptures they are caught in snares from them, taking the words otherwise than in their true sense, perverting the right meaning in them, and being led by them into unbelief in the Saviour. Their table also becomes a retribution for them, for in this very failure to understand what they read they receive the punishment for what they did against him. That is why Symmachus translated "and a retribution" as "and a punishment." Their table also becomes a stumbling block before them. For they stumble when they read the bare words without grasping the deeper sense within them. For instance, they hear that when Christ comes, the wolf will feed with the lamb, the leopard will lie down with the kid, and the lion and the ox will eat straw; not understanding these and similar sayings, they stumble at the Christ who has come, because these things did not happen in a literal, visible way at his coming.

[?] "...bend," instead of "you will bend"; and "Pour out your wrath upon them," instead of "you will pour out"; and "Let the fury of your wrath overtake them," instead of "it will overtake them." It is not hard to see how these things too befell the Jewish nation after its outrage against our Saviour. In earlier times, because of their idolatry, they were enslaved to enemies and foes for a short time; then they would recover their own freedom, and continue to govern themselves under their own kings, maintaining the temple and the worship in it according to the law of Moses. But after the plot against our Saviour they were deprived of everything at once. Having endured siege and slavery under the Romans, they have remained thus humbled, no longer able to lift up their heads. This is what the prophecy before us means when it says: "And bend their back continually." Notice how "continually" is said: not for a short time, as happened on other occasions, but "continually," it says. In place of this Aquila translated: "And weaken their backs perpetually," and Symmachus: "And dislocate their loins continually." This too befell them, since the wrath of God no longer visited them in measure as in former times, but was poured out upon them all at once in its entirety. Hence it adds: "Pour out your wrath upon them, and let the fury of your wrath overtake them." This is also shown in another psalm, which says: "Why, O God, have you cast us off to the end?" And the divine Apostle spoke in agreement with these words: "But wrath has come upon them to the end." First, then, their table became a snare to them; then their eyes were darkened; then their back was bent continually, as the wrath of God was poured out upon them. After this he foretells that something else will happen to them, saying: "Let their homestead be made desolate," instead of "it will be made"; "and let there be no one dwelling in their tents," instead of "there will not be." For not even this was to escape prophetic knowledge: that their homestead too would be desolate, or, as Symmachus has it, "uninhabited," or, as Aquila has it, "obliterated." By "their homestead" he means Jerusalem, which is no longer the city of God but their own homestead. That is why he says it will be desolate, and this is shown in fact. Then he adds: "And let there be no one dwelling in their tents," that is, none of its former inhabitants. The truth of this word too is set before our very eyes. If anyone were to visit those places, he would see the utter desolation of the place, and not one Jew venturing to set foot in the city, let alone live there. Not even a Jewish dwelling is left in the place, such that any of the Gentiles could live in it. Hence it is said: "And let there be no one dwelling in their tents," or, as Symmachus has it: "In their tents let there be no one dwelling." For all their tents and dwellings have been razed utterly, down to their foundations. See, then, how many things the passage has recorded: the desolation of the holy place, the obliteration of their tents, the complete humbling of the nation,

the darkening of their mind, and their failure to understand the divine Scriptures. These were fulfilled upon them at no other time than after their impiety against the Christ of God. That is why the prophecy next adds the reason, saying: "For they persecuted him whom you struck, and they added to the pain of my wounds," and what follows. All that has been foretold, it says, will befall them not because of some idolatry, but "because they persecuted him whom you struck." For you, according to the prophecy that says, "I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered," struck him for reasons you yourself know. Hence the Apostle says: "For he did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all." And to what he handed him over, Isaiah will teach, saying: "And the Lord handed him over to our sins." [?] "...knowing how to bear sickness; and the Lord [handed him over] to our sins"; and: "For he bears our sins and suffers pain for us"; and that he was wounded for no other reason than for our sins, and was made weak because of our iniquities. But they understood none of this; instead they drove him out and chased him away from themselves, asking for the murderer and denying the author of life. That is why he says here: "For they persecuted him whom you struck, and they added to the pain of my wounds." For I accepted wounds on their behalf, becoming their cleansing and a ransom for their sins; but they

added their own evils to me. At any rate, they gave "gall for my food, and for my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink," not only at the time when I suffered at their hands, but also in the times that followed, as they persisted in their blasphemies against me. That is why, in place of "they added," Aquila has "they will recount," and Symmachus "they were recounting." For it was not enough for them to have wounded him once and to have dared such things against him; boasting as if over noble deeds, they recounted to their own children what they had dared against him. Since, then, they chose this portion for themselves, persecuting him whom you struck and heaping iniquity and impiety on themselves and on their children, it is fitting that the psalm adds: "Add iniquity to their iniquity," instead of "you will add"; for there will be an increase of evils for them. Some things happen to human beings from what is in our power, and others from what follows from outside upon what is in our power. That is why it is said somewhere to God: "With the holy you will be holy, and with the crooked you will show yourself perverse." And in the law it is said in his own person: "And if you walk crookedly toward me, I too will walk toward you with crooked wrath." Since, then, they drew their iniquities upon themselves as with a long rope, you too, the righteous judge, will rightly add iniquity to their iniquity, reckoning a second against them in addition to the first. Moreover, "Let them not enter," it says, "into your righteousness." For your righteousness calls the righteous in, and receives all of them into the innermost parts of your kingdom, according to the promises; but those who have dared such things will not enter with those who will come in together into your righteousness. Nor will they be written in the book of the living; on the contrary, they will suffer the opposite of those who are written there. For even if they were the first to be counted worthy of my grace, and were once written in the book of the living for the sake of their fathers, who are alive with God, so that the promises were given to them too, yet since they have dared such things, "Let them be blotted out of the book of the living." Then, explaining what the book of the living means, he adds: "And let them not be written with the righteous." For when there is a sifting of those who have lived human lives, those worthy of life with God will be inscribed with him because of their own righteousness, while those who refused the author of life will be cast out of the book. This, then, is the end of those who dared what has been described against our Saviour. But what follows turns to a brighter theme, beginning from here with the grace of the Gospel. "I am poor and in pain; your salvation, O God, has helped me." He who said in the Gospels, "Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart," says in these words, "I am poor and in pain." He was poor because he laid aside the wealth of the eternal kingdom. That is why Paul says: "Jesus Christ, though he was rich, became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich." But he also says "in pain,"

"I have been in pain"; that is why he said above, "And they added to the pain of my wounds." For he was pained over those who were perishing, and suffered greatly for those who would not come to the salvation he was offering. That is why, as one in pain, he cried out: "O faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I bear with you?" So he says: "I am poor and in pain; your salvation, O God, has helped me." By these words he hints at the deliverance that came after his death. For if he had sunk into the mire of the deep and had come into the depths of the sea, as he showed through the words of the prophecy, and now he says, "Your salvation, O God, has helped me," he plainly shows that he obtained help after he had come into the depths of the sea and had suffered what was described earlier. That is why in the twenty-first psalm too he sent up the hymn "for the help of the morning." Then, as one who has received help, he turns his words to a brighter theme, sending up hymns to his own Father, in which he says: "I will praise the name of God with a song." To offer words with melody was a token of gladness and joy. He also says, "I will magnify him," clearly meaning his own Father. And how he will magnify him he adds next: "with praise," or, as Aquila has it, "with thanksgiving." You will understand the thanksgiving and praise by which the Son magnifies the Father if you consider the mysteries of the New Covenant, in which the Church of God throughout the whole world has received the practice of offering to God thanksgivings and rational, smokeless worship. This praise and thanksgiving is far better than the bodily sacrifices once offered under the law of Moses. That is why he adds: "And it will please the Lord more than a young calf that puts forth horns and hoofs." For if the children of the Jews pride themselves on these, let them know that my thanksgiving and my praise are much better than those things and far more highly prized by God. That is why Symmachus renders it: "And it will please the Lord more than an ox, a bull with cloven hoof and horns." Why he mentions a calf here, and not any other of the animals usually offered in sacrifice, deserves not to be passed over without examination. Of the animals the law of Moses commanded to be sacrificed, some were brought from the herd of cattle, others from the sheep, others from the birds; some were male, others female; some were voluntary, by free choice, others by obligation; some were called a sacrifice of salvation, others were for sin; some were offered for the high priest, others for the whole people, others for a ruler who had sinned. Yet among all these many differences, a calf was never offered for an ordinary ruler or for a private person. The male calf was sacrificed when [?] the whole congregation had fallen into sin, on whose behalf the priest himself, as head of the whole people and a sharer in the sin, brought the calf. You would find this if you paid attention to Leviticus, where

it is written: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel, saying: If the anointed high priest sins so as to make the people sin, he shall bring for his sin which he has sinned an unblemished calf from the herd to the Lord"; and further on: "If the whole congregation of Israel errs in ignorance, and a matter is hidden from the eyes of the congregation, and they do any one of all the commandments of the Lord which should not be done, and they offend, and the sin which they sinned in it becomes known to them, then the congregation shall bring a calf from the herd for the sin." And after this the narrative introduces a calf as a sacrifice for the high priest, where it says: "And Moses brought the calf for the sin offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the calf of the sin offering, and he slaughtered it." You see for what cases the calf was offered: when the whole congregation of Israel had sinned, and when the high priest had sinned, and not simply sinned, but had become a cause of sin for the people. For it says: "If the anointed high priest sins so as to make the people sin," for which Aquila translated: "to the offence of the people." Now at the time of the saving passion, the high priests and rulers of the Jewish nation gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ, and they themselves became the cause of the whole people's perversion. For it is written: "And the chief priests and the whole council were seeking false testimony against Jesus, so that they might put him to death"; and again later: "But the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to destroy Jesus." Those who had dared these things needed cleansing, and no other sacrifice than that of the calf, as the Scripture cited above testifies. Fittingly, then, our Saviour says in these words: "I do not offer a material calf, but the pure and bloodless sacrifice which I myself established in my own Church through the bloodless and fireless liturgy of praise; and this will please God more than the calf prescribed by Moses." That is why it is said: "I will magnify him with praise. And it will please God"—the praise, that is—"more than a young calf that puts forth horns and hoofs." The high priests and the whole nation would have obtained forgiveness and cleansing of their sins if they had made use of this sacrifice by accepting the new and saving Covenant. Then the poor man spoken of earlier sends up a prayer for those who are poor like him, about whom he teaches, saying: "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." And he says in his prayer: "Let the poor see and be glad." He prays that what was foretold may at last come to pass, so that the poor he has mentioned, namely his disciples and apostles, may see it with their own eyes. He prays that they may see "the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world."

…his praise, which is better than a young calf that puts forth horns and hoofs. And indeed, when his prayer was fulfilled long afterward, he called blessed those who had been counted worthy to see these events. That is why it is recorded in the Gospels that he said to his disciples: “But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear.” These words agreed with the saying: “Let the poor see and be glad; seek God, and your soul shall live.” Having prayed for the poor, he then addresses them directly. He brings them the good news of life, not of bodies but of souls, and he promises that they will find this life if they seek God. So he says: “Seek God, and your soul shall live.” For with him is the fountain [?] of life. He therefore commands the poor he has spoken of to put everything else second and to seek him with faith and good hope, for he promises that they will live the life of the soul. The Apostle also taught about this life when he said: “For your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, is revealed, then you too will be revealed with him in glory.” Then he adds: “For the Lord has heard the needy, and has not despised his prisoners.” Here again “has heard” is said in place of “will hear,” and “has not despised” in place of “will not despise.” Having said before, “Seek God, and your soul shall live,” he now says with confidence: Seek, because he will hear the needy. For God does not belong to those who live in luxury, nor to the puffed up and boastful, but to the lowly and needy. That is why it is said: “On whom [?]… but on the meek and lowly, the quiet one who trembles at my words?” So seek God with confidence, knowing that the Lord will hear you, the needy, and will not despise his prisoners; or, as Symmachus has it, “And he will not treat his own captives with contempt.” You will understand how these poor have become captives and prisoners when you hear Paul saying, “Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ”; in the same way the other disciples too were prisoners of Christ. Those also who live in this tent, as if in chains, groan and beg to be released from their chains. That is why they say: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” Those, then, who are weighed down by the corruptible body, who turn away from corruption and groan over this corruptible life, are God's captives and his prisoners. He will not despise their prayers or turn away from them. But those who fatten their own chains and pamper them with much luxury could rightly be called prisoners of corruption and death. [?]

…heavens.” Since churches were to be gathered for God from the poor already mentioned throughout the whole inhabited world, on land and sea, it is fittingly added: “and earth and sea and all that creep in them.” The creeping things on land and sea, here commanded to praise along with heaven and earth, are the nations. In the mortal life of humankind they had long gone about on breast and belly like reptiles. In Isaiah too the nations are allegorically called wild beasts and reptiles, where it is said: “The wolf shall feed with the lamb, the leopard shall lie down with the kid, and the lion shall eat straw like the ox. A little child shall put his hand on the hole of asps and on the nest of the young asps, and they shall do no harm.” The word interprets this immediately afterward: “And there shall be the root of Jesse, he who rises to rule the nations; in him the nations shall hope.” Since this change of the nations takes place at the coming of Christ, the reptiles just described are fittingly commanded to praise God together with heaven and the angels in heaven. That is why it is said: “Let the heavens and the earth praise him, the sea and all that creep in them.” But how can reptiles praise God unless they share in understanding and in the knowledge of God? Will the reptiles too, then, offer the sacrifice of praise? The Gospel teaches that he is hinting at human beings by these words, for it is written: “Brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Bear fruits worthy of repentance, then.” “For God will save Zion, and the cities of Judea shall be built.” He gives the reason why the heavens and earth and sea and everything in them are said to be about to praise God. The reason is this: “For God will save Zion, and the cities of Judea shall be built.” And what Zion is this, if not clearly the Church of our Savior, established throughout the whole world? Do not hesitate to call the divinely inspired Scriptures the cities of Judea, since the Jewish way of life was foreshadowed through them. As far as the Jews are concerned, these cities had been torn down. But they have been rebuilt through the new teaching in Christ, through which the true circumcision is established, along with the spiritual Sabbaths, the spiritual sacrifices, and everything that follows from these according to the interpretation of the spiritual law. In this way the cities of Judea are built, and the citizens and heirs of what was promised in the divine Scriptures will dwell in them. That is why it is said: “And they shall inherit it.” Also, “the seed of his servants shall possess it.” Who would his servants be, if not surely the disciples of our Savior? And who is the seed but the seed sown throughout the whole world, which will possess the inheritance promised in the divine Scriptures? Further, “those who love his name shall dwell in it,” clearly meaning the inheritance. To them it will be said: “Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepar…”

But if Zion is the heavenly city of God, about which the Apostle taught when he said, “But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother,” and, “You have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem,” then the cities of Judea would be [?], in keeping with the heavenly Zion, the many dwelling places with the Father. All his servants will dwell in them and inherit them: both the prophets and God-loving men of old, and those who came afterward as ministers and servants of his Gospel. Their seed too, that is, those born from them according to God, who have advanced and come to perfection in the love of God, will receive from him this prize and fitting reward: to dwell in the inheritance promised to them.

FOR THE END; [?] FOR REMEMBRANCE.

“O God, attend to my help.” The words before us are neither an ode nor a psalm nor anything of that kind. Yet they are referred to the end, since they make supplication about things to come. They are said to be “by David for remembrance,” as though they were spoken for this very purpose: that he might have them ready to recite by heart and use them as a charm in times of trouble. Two psalms are inscribed “for remembrance”: the one before us, and the thirty-seventh, which is also inscribed “for remembrance.” But that one did not refer to the end; it was “A psalm of David for remembrance.” This one, however, has the inscription “for the end.” The thirty-seventh did not foretell things to come but called past events to mind. That is why it had the same beginning as the sixth, saying: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath.” Both also had one and the same subject. For the sixth, as it proceeds, adds: “I am worn out with my groaning; every night I will wash my bed; I will drench my couch with my tears.” And the thirty-seventh teaches similar things, saying: “There is no peace in my bones because of my sins, for my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed me down. My wounds have grown foul and festered because of my folly.” With these and similar words he was recalling the memory of the offense he had committed. That is why he inscribed it “for remembrance,” going back over the past through continual confession, and why he did not inscribe it “for the end.” The present psalm, however, is said to be “for the end” because it is a supplication about things expected. The prophet anticipates them and prays, so that if enemies should ever rise up and plot against him, he might use these incantations and apply them like antidotes, as charms that turn back every evil counter-amulet. But perhaps the words are also referred prophetically to the person of the Savior. For in the psalm before this one, which clearly foretells his passion, it was said in his own person: “I am poor and

in pain; your salvation, O God, has helped me.” Likewise in the psalm before us, as it proceeds, he says: “But I am poor and needy; O God, help me.” So for this reason too it had to be inscribed “for the end.” If, then, it is spoken in the person of David, one might say this: though he reigned over a great nation and was extremely rich, he was not ignorant of the saying, “The greater you are, the more you must humble yourself, and you will find favor before the Lord.” Therefore, being modest and humble-minded, and truly making himself small as he looked to the greatness of the riches of God's goodness, he called himself poor and needy in these words. At the beginning of his speech, as though nothing could help him, neither wealth, nor kingship, nor the support of the whole nation, nor the righteousness he had gained through discipline, he sought help from God alone, saying: “O God, attend to my help; Lord, make haste to help me.” Seeing that many envied his progress in the ways of God and begrudged the salvation of his soul, he added: “Let those who seek my soul be ashamed and confounded. Let those who wish me evil be turned back and put to shame. Let those who say to me, ‘Aha, aha!’ be turned back at once in shame.” By these words he admits that he cannot suffice for himself but needs help from one stronger. If he did not obtain it, he would be left alone and shown to be weak and nothing more than a mortal man, and his enemies, who delight in misfortune, would trample on him when he fell. But if he obtained God as his helper, he himself would prevail, and shame would be poured over those who plot against his soul. In everything he did they followed at his heels and tried to catch him out, and they were in the habit of saying, “Aha, aha!” as though they were succeeding and getting what they prayed for in the things where they thought he was stumbling. But if anyone refers these words to the Savior for the reason already given, he will say this: the Savior saw those who plot against his word and teaching, who rise up against the great body of his Church and continually stir up persecutions against it. To ward off their wickedness he sent up this prayer prophetically, teaching his Church that it ought to pray this way. “Let all who seek you exult and be glad in you.” The first words were meant to overthrow his adversaries; the second, which follow, intercede on behalf of his own. If David was making a prayer fitting for a righteous man, he was praying that all who seek God, of whom he himself was one, might share in exultation and gladness while their enemies were put to shame, and that those who love God's salvation might say, “Let God be magnified.” They would say this not once, nor at just one moment, but continually, as God conquers the whole hostile race in them and through them. But if it is the Savior, in keeping with what was said before [?], praying on behalf of those from all the nations who have believed in

him, then he would be saying: “Let all who seek you exult and be glad in you.” For not the Jews alone, nor those who boast of Abraham, but universally and without limit, all who seek you, whoever they may be and of whatever race, “let them exult and be glad in you, and let them say, ‘Let God be magnified.’” And let those who love your salvation say this continually. By “your salvation” he means the Savior himself, who is called “salvation” in many places in the Scriptures. Those love him who cherish his teaching through their deeds, in pure love. “But I am poor and needy; O God, help me.” David too, though rich, was humble-minded, because he knew the greatness of God and saw himself as nothing. That is why he sought help from the Mighty One alone, saying: “O God, help me. You are my helper and my deliverer; O Lord, do not delay.” Christ too, though he was rich, became poor for our sake, as the divine Apostle taught. That is why he entrusted himself to the help of the Spirit, interceding for his people and for the Church, so that it would not suffer great harm by being warred against for long periods in times of persecution. So he says: “You are my helper and my deliverer; O Lord, do not delay.” Whether these words too are to be referred to the time of our Savior's passion, you can consider for yourself. In the preceding psalm he described the uprisings against him: how the waters came in even to his soul, how he was stuck fast in the deep mire, how he came into the depths of the sea, how those who hate me without cause were more numerous than the hairs of his head, and how he suffered everything that is said there. So it is fitting that he sends up the present petition to the Father, saying, “O God, attend to my help; Lord, make haste to help me,” and what follows. He saw the company of his apostles thrown into great confusion because of their love for him, so he uttered the second words on their behalf. He prayed that when they received his resurrection, which they were waiting and longing to see, they might be filled with exultation and gladness and say continually, “Let God be magnified,” since they were the ones who love his salvation.

“In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me never be put to shame. In your righteousness deliver me and rescue me.” Psalm 30 also contains words equivalent to these, and it begins in the same way: “In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me never be put to shame. In your righteousness deliver me. Incline your ear to me.” But that psalm was inscribed “For the end” and “A psalm of David,” whereas the present one happens to have no inscription. That one also contained confession together with supplication, while this one seems to be a prophecy uttered in the person of the Savior. That is why it does not have the usual inscription, “of David.” One might say it is proper to include it with those

placed before it, because it keeps a close connection with them. At any rate, the psalm before this one said: “O God, attend to my help. Let those who seek my soul be ashamed and confounded. Let those who wish me evil be turned back and put to shame.” And in the psalm before us, as it proceeds, the word uses the same expressions, saying: “O God, attend to my help… let them be ashamed.” The rest also keeps to the same meaning, the discourse being expanded at length through the words before us. One would not be wide of the mark in saying that these words suit the Father, because of what is said in this psalm: “For you are my endurance, O Lord; Lord, my hope from my youth.” For these very things were said in Psalm 21 in his own person, in these words: “For you are the one who drew me out of the womb,” and what follows. Again, the next thing said in the prophecy before us, “O my God, do not forsake me until I declare your arm to all the generation to come,” seems equivalent to the words of Psalm 21: “The generation to come shall be told of the Lord.” Notice carefully how that psalm said, “The generation to come shall be told of the Lord,” while the present one says, “until I declare your arm to all the generation to come.” The prophecy before us also clearly sets forth his resurrection from the dead, saying in his own person: “O God, who is like you? How many troubles, many and grievous, you have shown me! And you turned and gave me life, and brought me up again from the depths of the earth.” So whether in the person of the Savior or in the person of every righteous man, this is how the words before us should be heard. For they contain teaching that trains us, with a sound disposition, to put all things second and hang our hopes on the Lord alone, so that we say to him with a sincere heart: “In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me never be put to shame.” Those who rest their hopes on wealth and great abundance of possessions, or on worldly honors, or on closeness to rulers and their patronage, or on anything else mortal and perishable, will incur shame. “For cursed is the man who puts his hope in man and leans the flesh of his arm on him.” And the word cries aloud: “Do not trust in rulers, nor in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation.” And again: “If wealth flows in, do not set your heart on it.” Elsewhere too we are taught to say: “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me. It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man. It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in rulers.” But one who is conscious of good in himself might also say to the Lord: “In your righteousness deliver me and rescue me.” For he has taken courage with great confidence that God, judging with perfect justice, will find him deserving not of condemnation or rejection but of help and support. So he says: “In your righteousness deliver me and rescue me.” With a conscience [?]

made pure, sending up his cries of supplication to God, he also said: “Incline your ear to me and save me.” And he pleaded with God as one in real need, saying: “Be to me a protecting God and a stronghold to save me.” For God would not shield and fight for someone over some small matter. Only the perfect man could say to God: “For you are my strength and my refuge.” In place of this Aquila translated, “For you are my rock and my fortress,” and Symmachus, “For you are my rock and my refuge.” “O my God, deliver me from the hand of the sinner, and from the hand of the lawbreaker and the wrongdoer. For you are my endurance, O Lord, my hope from my youth.” The perfect man calls on God as his own possession, saying, “O my God,” since God has made a promise concerning the worthy, which says: “I will be their God, and they shall be my people.” And the one who says, “In you, O Lord, I have hoped,” who has put everything else second and cast himself on God alone, would rightly say, “O my God.” He prays to be delivered from the hand of the sinner so that he may not become like the sinner or the lawbreaker in his deeds. That is why he adds: “from the hand of the sinner, and from the hand of the lawbreaker and the wrongdoer.” He also prays that he may not fall into the power of such men. He would rightly call God his own God, not only for the reasons given earlier but also for those added next. For you, he says, are my endurance, and you are my hope from my youth. I have never stopped waiting on you, and there has never been a time when I did not set you before me as my hope. For these reasons I beg to be delivered from the hand of sinners and lawbreakers. “On you I have leaned from the womb; from my mother's belly you have been my protector.” Hoping in God from youth could also be said of David. When he was young and shepherding the sheep of his father Jesse, he went out against lions and bears to keep the sheep safe, by faith and hope in God. In this he imitated the good shepherd, of whom it is said: “As when the shepherd snatches from the lion's mouth two legs or the tip of an ear.” And while still a boy he drove the evil spirit away from Saul by the power of faith and hope in God. Likewise, anyone who has been counted worthy of God's election from a young age could say, “my hope from my youth.” Timothy was such a one, having learned the holy Scriptures from childhood. But the words “On you I have leaned from the womb; from my mother's belly you have been my protector” would fit our Savior alone. He remained untroubled and unconfused during the time he was carried in the womb. All other human beings, while being conceived and receiving the first formation of the body, live a kind of plant-like life. They use neither the senses of the body nor an attentive understanding. Their very ruling faculty and mind are submerged, and they would differ in no way from a worm. But the one who says to God, “On you I have leaned

"from the womb," he shows not only that he possessed knowledge of God, but also the very great virtue of a God-loving power, by which he was supported upon God himself. And he was such even while being conceived and carried in his mother's womb. The words "From my mother's belly you are my protector" can also apply to everyone. For if the power of God did not guard and keep what is conceived in the womb, it would never take shape or share in life, since it can neither breathe nor make use of the other senses. Yet again, in saying "You are my protector," he showed that he had something special beyond all others conceived in a mother's womb. For perhaps at the birth of other human beings certain angels are set in charge, ministering to each one's entrance into life; but at the birth of the Saviour it was the Father himself who became his protector, and that is why he was supported upon him. Thus he always had the Father as the theme of his hymn. That is why he adds: "In you is my hymn continually." For he did not cease at any time from hymning the Father, or from being hymned by him for so great an obedience. "No," he says, "my praise, or my hymn, has been in you continually. But most people, knowing none of these things, regarded me as a portent. At any rate, I became something portentous to the many, so that they held differing opinions about me: some thought that I was God without flesh and without body, seen on earth only in appearance; others that I was a mere man, having nothing more than the rest; and some subjected me to curses and slanders, while others revered and worshipped me. But my death truly became a portent to all. For that one who was God should endure the cross, and that he who had granted life to others should suffer such things, was truly a portent." That is why he says: "I became as a portent to many." "But in all these things," he says, "you have been my strong helper; for I took no other helper. All things were secondary and inferior to my power; but you alone, whom I inscribed as my hope, have been my strong helper." And according to Symmachus it is likewise said: "On you I was supported from the womb; from my mother's inward parts you watched over me. In you is my waiting continually; I became as a portent to many, but you are my strong confidence." "Let my mouth be filled with praise, that I may hymn your glory, your majesty all the day long." "Already in the past," he says, "my hymn has been in you continually; but I make my prayer for the future as well, that until the last hour of my life my mouth may be filled with your praise, and filled in such a way that no room is left free for uttering anything else or for conversing with men. And this I ask to be granted me every day, and that in all the time of my life I may not be deprived of this grace or cast away from it, even if I should have to reach the threshold of old age, and that until my very end I may do nothing else than have my mouth filled with your praise and your majes-

-ty." Instead of "all the day long," Symmachus rendered "every day": "Let my mouth be filled with your praise every day; in your splendour do not cast me off in the time of old age." "For if I must prolong my life even to old age, that is not to be refused; but I beseech you that I may never be deprived of having my mouth filled with your praise and your majesty. And if at some time my strength should fail through old age, do not forsake me even then." These things, then, it would be fitting for David to say, and for every God-loving person in their supplications to God. But in the case of the Saviour, consider how the Apostle said: "He was crucified in weakness, but he lives by the power of God." For even if he was crucified in weakness, it was not as one overcome by others; rather, he made himself weak and handed himself over into the hands of men. This he teaches when he says: "No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again." So just as he emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, so he made himself weak, so that he might be taken captive by men and might endure the cross, "becoming obedient" to the Father "unto death, even death on a cross." That is why he says: "When my strength fails, do not forsake me." Then, since he has mentioned his passion, he goes on to mention those who brought the passion about, saying: "For my enemies have spoken against me, and those who watch for my life"; or according to Symmachus, "and those who lie in wait for my life took counsel together, saying: God has forsaken him; pursue him and seize him, for there is no one to deliver him." For this is what the chief priests and those with them said at the time of the passion, wagging their heads and saying: "You who would destroy the temple and raise it in three days ... He saved others; himself he cannot save. If he is King of Israel, let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him." "O God, do not be far from me; O God, attend to my help." "My enemies, mentioned above, said: 'God has forsaken him'; but I entreat and beseech you, my own God, to be present with me always and not to stand far from me, but to attend to my help. For with you as my helper, I know that I shall see all my enemies put to shame." The words "let them be put to shame," as is usual in divine Scripture, are said here too in place of "they will be put to shame"; and "let them fail" in place of "those who slander my soul will fail"; or according to Symmachus, "those who oppose my soul." How those who contrived his death have failed, drenched in shame, we need no long words to show, since from that time every high priest among them has failed, and of the Pharisees not even the name remains, nor any memory of the dignities they held. For rulers have failed from Judah, and leaders from his loins,

now that the expectation of the nations has come, according to the prophecy that foretold this. There are no kings among them, no governors, no potentates of any kind, nor is any order left of those that once existed among them; all who slandered his soul have failed, put to shame. And in what shame those reputed to lead the Jews find themselves even now, seeing themselves accused of idolatries throughout all Scripture, while all the nations of the whole world have been turned, through the teaching of Christ, from the error handed down from their fathers! In this state they now are, seeing with confusion that they themselves have been banished from their royal metropolis, that Greeks, men of another race and another tribe, inhabit their place, and that in every province, land and city those from the nations proclaim the prophetic utterances about the Saviour. Shame and confusion have truly seized their souls, as they see the one whom they handed over to the cross only yesterday worshipped and confessed as God throughout the whole world. These things have been fulfilled in accordance with the prophecy at hand, which says: "Let those who seek evil for me be clothed with shame and confusion." These, then, will suffer such things; "But I," though I have suffered so much at their hands, "will hope continually," he says, "and will add to all your praise." Since all the translators have said "I will add" (Aquila says, "And I will add to all hymns," and Symmachus, "And I will add to the hymns"), consider whether he did not make an addition to the hymns of the Father by handing down the New Covenant in addition to the Old. For he did not abolish the first things when he introduced the second; he made an addition. And this can be found in his teachings, where he says: "It was said to the ancients, You shall not murder; but I say, do not even be angry. It was said to the ancients, You shall not commit adultery; but I say, do not even desire"; and all other such teachings, which contain an addition through the spiritual contemplation and interpretation of the law, have been handed down in his Church. Moreover, "my mouth," he says, "will declare your righteousness." For the Gospel reveals the righteousness of God, which is not restricted to the Jews alone, as was the law given through Moses. That is why the Apostle says: "For I am not ashamed of the Gospel; for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For in it the righteousness of God is revealed." Therefore it is said here: "My mouth will declare your righteousness, your salvation all the day long"; or according to Symmachus, "your salvation every day." And one may see this being fulfilled throughout the whole world, where the mouth of our Saviour, through the divine Scriptures, proclaims every day to all people the salvation procured for all through him. To this he adds: "Because I have not known letters." Having received the keys of the kingdom, and neither entering themselves

barbarians to be counted worthy of his knowledge, and to allow them to worship him in every place, and no longer in one only, so that from the rising of the sun to its setting his name is glorified among the nations. "O God, you have taught me from my youth, and until now I will declare your wonders." The Saviour alone inscribes the Father as his teacher; that is why the people of his home town said: "Where did this man get all this wisdom and these mighty works? Is not this the carpenter's son?" For they knew perfectly well that he had not studied under human teachers. Since, then, having taken the form of a slave and being found in fashion as a man, he passed through the age of childhood and endured the season of youth as we do, yet attended neither schools nor teachers during that time, but by divine power advanced in stature and wisdom and in favour with God and men, he fittingly says here: "O God, you have taught me from my youth, and until now I will declare your wonders." "And may these be kept for my disciples until the end of the age; and, as one might say, until old age and the utmost perfection, I beseech you again, O God, not to forsake me, but to be with me and to work your wonders through me, until I declare your arm to all the generation to come." "For the generation now present," he says, "is crooked and perverse, an evil and adulterous generation. Therefore to the generation to come I will declare your might and your righteousness, O God, even to the highest places, the great things you have done. You yourself, Father, will declare these things through me to all who will come after, to the generation to come, and your righteousness will be proclaimed even to the highest places." For when those on earth are saved, there will be joy in heaven, as the angels who dwell in the highest places rejoice together at the salvation of men. And do not hesitate to call the perfection of his disciples and of his Church "old age and seniority." For if the Church is his body, as the Apostle taught when he said, "Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually," then that portion of the Church which is its senior rank could fittingly be said to be perfection in virtue in the present life; after which, having as it were put off the mortal life on earth, it will be renewed, counted worthy of the heavenly dwelling, and joined to the Church of the first-

-born who are enrolled in heaven. In this way you will also understand what was said above: "Do not cast me off in the time of old age; when my strength fails, do not forsake me." For according to another interpretation he is praying on behalf of his Church, that in the time of its long continuance on earth it may not be cast off, and that even if its strength should fail then, it may not be forsaken even then. For it often happens that it fails in times of persecution, when many in the body of the Church abjure the faith through weakness of faith. And perhaps these words refer to the time of the apostasy, about which the Apostle taught, saying: "Unless the apostasy comes first, and the man of sin is revealed, the son of perdition." The Saviour pointed to this time when he said: "When the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?" And again: "Because lawlessness is multiplied, the love of many will grow cold." For then the body of the Church will be aged and weak. But so that his people may not be left desolate even then, he of necessity sends up the words before us: "O God, who will be like you? How many afflictions and evils you have shown me!" and what follows. The exact reasons for which God did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all, and made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, no one can recount except he alone. "For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him?" No one could grasp the judgment of God, nor discover the reasons for which he showed the Only-begotten many afflictions and evils. Yet he did not leave him in them, but turning back he made him alive and brought him up again from the depths of the earth. And it is said very precisely: "You showed me many afflictions and evils." For though he saw the afflictions and the so-called evils, he was not taken captive by them, nor was he defeated; rather, having proved superior to them all, he was a spectator of them, so that he more than anyone could say: "Afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair; struck down, but not forsaken." For Paul and those like him said these things having profited from their Teacher. By "the depths of the earth" he here named the region of the underworld, as the Apostle makes clear when he says: "Do not say, Who will descend into the abyss? that is, to bring Christ up from the dead." And in Job too the Lord who spoke to him said: "Have you come to the source of the sea, and walked in the tracks of the abyss? Do the gates of death open to you in fear, and did the gatekeepers of Hades cower when they saw you?" He who says here, "And from the depths of the earth you brought me up again," has clearly taught that he went down into the depths of the earth and came up again. I do not know whether anyone can take these words in any other way than by referring the prophecy to our Saviour and Lord.

The same speaker adds: "You have increased my greatness, and turning back you comforted me." How did the Father increase the greatness of his Only-begotten, if not by showing him many afflictions and evils? For just as the president of the games, by matching his own athlete against many opponents, displays his courage the more, proclaiming him victor over them all, in the same way the Father, making the greatness of the Son plain to all, surrounded him with many afflictions and evils, so that, having won the prize of victory over all, he might be proclaimed among all. That is why he says: "You have increased my greatness." "But after all these things," he says, "turning back you comforted me." How he comforted him he taught earlier, when he said: "And turning back you made me alive, and from the depths of the earth you brought me up again." For this was the comfort which the Apostle also set forth when he said: "Therefore God also highly exalted him, and granted him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth." "For I too will give thanks to you with instruments of psalmody for your truth." "You, O Father," he says, "have granted me these things: after the many afflictions and the evils mentioned, 'turning back you made me alive, and from the depths of the earth you brought me up again,' and you comforted me, increasing my greatness. And I in turn, repaying your benefits towards me, 'will give thanks to you with instruments of psalmody'; for what shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will fashion instruments fitting for you, and prepare instruments worthy of your psalmody, and through them I will sing your truth to you in psalms; and I will raise up for you such lyres that through them my lips will exult, and also 'my soul, which you redeemed,' when you brought it up from the depths of the earth and made it alive after the death it endured." And what would you call the instruments and implements pleasing to God, through which the Christ of God even now sends up psalmody and hymns and praises to the Father throughout the whole world, if not the congregations in each Church? Tuning their souls, and binding them together in one concord and harmony with the Father, the Word of God sends up a dear and sweet melody. Indeed, if one were to set side by side and compare the bodily instruments of the Jews of old, made of lifeless strings and sounding an inarticulate voice, with the hymns sent up to God in the Church of Christ by rational souls, one would find nothing alike. For better than any bodily psaltery are the multitudes throughout the whole world who hymn the God over all in one concord and harmony, through whom the Son professes to sing psalms to the Father, saying: "For I too will give thanks to you with instruments of psalmody for your truth, O God." "For no longer will I present types, nor shadows and symbols, such as were those given through

Moses, but I will set your truth before men, and I will sing to you on the lyre, O Holy One of Israel"; or according to Aquila, "I will make melody to you on the lyre, O Holy One of Israel." "Moreover, my lips will exult when I sing to you"; or according to Symmachus, "My lips will speak well of you when I make melody to you, and my soul, which you redeemed. And my tongue too will meditate on your righteousness all the day long." You would not be wrong to say that his lips and tongue, meditating on the righteousness of the Father, are those in his Church who have devoted themselves to the exercise of divine words. "And all these things I will do," he says, "when those who seek evil for me are put to shame and confounded"; or according to Symmachus, "For those who seek my harm have been put to shame, or have been [?]"; or according to Aquila, "For those who seek my hurt have been put to shame." And one can see these things too fulfilled in fact. For as the Churches of the Saviour everywhere on earth recount the righteousness of God, and as he himself fashions vessels of election, as was said before, and rational instruments for the Father, and through them continually hymns the God over all, his enemies are clothed with shame, and those who seek evil for him have been and are confounded. These are the ones who hunt for every pretext and devise insults, slanders and blasphemies against him, yet find no ground for slander either against him or against his Church. Therefore they are drenched in shame and confounded, so that they no longer dare to bring any charge deserving of reproach. And all these things are fulfilled in fact, in agreement with the prophecy which says in the words before us: "When those who seek evil for me are put to shame and confounded." "For then," he says, "when my enemies are put to shame, I will sing to you and give thanks to you, my own Father. And my tongue too will meditate on your righteousness all the day long."

PSALM 71. FOR SOLOMON. "O God, give your judgment to the king." The other translators rendered "Of Solomon." There is also another psalm of his among the Songs of Ascents, which begins: "Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have laboured in vain." In that psalm Solomon seems to have composed the song on the construction of the house which he raised in Jerusalem, since he was the first to build the temple there; the song teaches that only the buildings of God endure forever, while human ones last only for a season. And this is just what happened to his building: not long afterwards the temple he had built was destroyed by the Babylonians. But whether the prophecy at hand was spoken about Solomon himself, or is his, as the other translators have it, its words present someone else as the subject of the prophecy. That is why it is not titled a psalm, a song, a hymn, or anything of the kind. Rather, it is a prophecy foretelling that a saviour of the poor and needy would appear among men, and that he from above

[?] …that he would come down quietly and without a sound: “For he will come down like rain upon a fleece.” And that from then on righteousness would dwell among the human race at his coming. And that he would rule not over Judea alone, nor over two or three nations, but over all the nations of the whole inhabited world; that all the nations would be subject to him; and that he would be renowned among all, not for some short time but for all eternity. For what else does the present passage describe than that the one foretold would be such as no one is ever recorded to have been, either among the Jewish nation or among any other? For neither Solomon himself, nor David, nor any of those after them appeared to be such that the things signified by the prophecy could fit any of them. See, then, whether the present psalm, which proclaims his kingdom, does not follow naturally on the predictions set out in the earlier psalms concerning the Savior's passion. For we needed to be taught about this too. Many prophecies sing of the Christ foretold as coming from David. But it was likely that some would suppose that Solomon was meant by them, for he alone of David's sons reigned with the greatest glory, raised the temple to God, and is attested to have excelled in wisdom. So the present prophecy is necessarily headed “For Solomon,” or is said to be “Of Solomon” himself, so that he would no longer be thought to be the one expected from David; rather, another is hoped for from Solomon himself, one promised to him as well. If, then, we take the psalm to be spoken about Solomon himself, following the heading of the Seventy, we shall say that the Holy Spirit, having sent up the prayer to God concerning him in the first verse, where it says, “O God, give your judgment to the king,” that is, to Solomon, then speaks in what follows about the one who would be born from him. That is why it adds, “and your righteousness to the king's son,” clearly meaning Jesus, who was to come forth from his seed. The sense of the passage is this: A decree has gone forth from your Godhead, and a royal ordinance and judgment has been laid down by your Spirit, that the Savior of the world should be born according to the flesh from Solomon's line of descent. Grant, then, at last, this judgment of yours, O God, to the king, that is, to Solomon, so that the words may pass into deeds. Grant to the king himself the judgment just described, but your righteousness to the king's son, who was to come forth from his seed, so that the one born of the Spirit [?], his successor, receiving your righteousness, “may judge your people in righteousness and your poor in judgment.” So much, then, if the heading, which according to the Seventy reads “For Solomon,” is referred to the person of Solomon himself. But if, following the other translators, the prophecy is said to be Solomon's own, we shall say that Solomon himself, filled with the Spirit, presents three persons in these words: God, to whom he sends up the prayer; the king, who he was persuaded reigns over all things, namely the Son

of God; and third, the man whom he assumed, born of the seed of David [?] and of Solomon himself, who is other than the king who said in the psalm: “But I was established king by him on Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming the decree of the Lord. The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.’” For having been established, as these words clearly say, he hears from the Father: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.” Solomon himself also knows the Son of God, and calls him Wisdom in the passage of Proverbs where he says in Wisdom's own person: “I, Wisdom, have made counsel my dwelling, and I have called upon knowledge and understanding. Through me kings reign”; and further on: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, for his works. Before the age he founded me, before the mountains were set in place; before all the hills he begets me.” Wisdom, then, is the offspring of God and his only-begotten Son; and it is about him that Solomon sends up the present prayer, saying, “O God, give your judgment to the king,” clearly meaning to your only-begotten Word. Since you have judged that he should be seen on earth, so that he might reign not only over those in heaven but also over those on earth, let this judgment now at last be brought to fulfillment. And give your righteousness, O God, to the king's son. Here “the king's son” is understood as the one according to the flesh, from the seed of David, whom the pre-existent [?] Word of God formed for himself from the Holy Spirit and the holy Virgin. I think that Solomon also hints at him in Proverbs when he writes: “Who has gone up into heaven and come down? Who has gathered the winds in his bosom? Who has wrapped up water in a garment? Who has taken hold of all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is the name of his Son?” For this is how the other translators rendered it: Aquila says, “What is his name, and what is the name of his Son?” and Theodotion likewise, “What is his name, and what is the name of his Son?” Clearly the one who in these words has taken hold of the earth, who has come down and gone up into heaven, and who has done the other things that would need interpreting at leisure, could be none other than the Son of God, who taught these very things when he said: “No one has gone up into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man.” And the one here called his Son would be the one understood according to the flesh, the flesh he assumed, born from the seed of David and Solomon. But since the children of the Jews refer these words of Proverbs to the God who is over all, because they do not know the Son of God, we must show them from this passage that Scripture clearly and [?] presents him as the Son of God when it says, “What is his name, and what is the name of his Son?” Now when the word says in the psalm, “O God, give your judgment to the king,” it teaches that a judgment (krima) is something other than judging (krisis). For a judgment is what God has once resolved, what has been decided by him; judging is the weighing of those who are being judged,

and it carries with it the rendering to each according to what he deserves. That is why here he does not ask that judging be given to the king, but the judgment, that is, the decree, what the Father decided concerning his divine manifestation to human beings. The judgment, then, is given to the king, and the righteousness to the king's son. For the king himself was Righteousness, as the Apostle shows when he says: “who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption.” This righteousness of the [?], then, is given to the Son of the king, born of the seed of David according to the flesh, in whom the Word and Wisdom and Righteousness of God dwelt as in a temple.
