The reason why righteousness is given to this son of the king he teaches next, saying: “to judge your people in righteousness and your poor in judgment.” For God's poor and his people among human beings had to be judged by the king's son in righteousness, since they could not otherwise receive the king. Therefore, taking the form of a servant and being found in fashion as a man, through the Son of Man whom he assumed [?], from all the nations, according to the principle of justice, “he chose for himself a people of his own,” and those who are called his poor, whom he also pronounced blessed, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” The Apostle also teaches about righteousness in another way, saying: “For I am not ashamed of the gospel; for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For in it righteousness is revealed.” And again about the poor the same Apostle explains: “Consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to the flesh, not many well-born, not many powerful. But God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise; he chose the weak and despised things, and the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are, so that no flesh might boast before God.” “Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness.” In addition to what came before, the prophetic Spirit also prays for this: that the mountains, long hostile to the people, may put away their enmity and be at peace with it, and that the hills may announce to that same people the righteousness spoken of before. For formerly the mountains were at enmity with the people, and the hills likewise; but when the king's son made his own the people that had long been estranged from him, then the things here called mountains made peace with the people. And whom would you call the mountains and hills that are at peace with human beings, if not the choir of angels and the divine powers higher than they? These were formerly hostile to the people, when it was estranged from God; but now that it has become the possession of the king's son, they have turned from enmity and become its friends. You will understand that this is the people gathered from all the nations if you set beside these words the prophecy in

Zechariah, which says: “Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion. Behold, your king is coming, and he will dwell in your midst, says the Lord. And many nations will flee for refuge to the Lord, and they will be my people, and I will be their God. And they will know that the Lord Almighty has sent me to you.” For in these words the Lord clearly announces that he will gather a people for himself from the nations, and not from the Jewish nation. To this people, then, the powers above the world and the angelic powers, here named mountains and hills, have made peace, though they were hostile before, when it was devoted to godless idolatry. And these same powers announce righteousness to that same people: either the Christ of God, who is himself righteousness, or the saving gospel. That is why it is said: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness.” And these things will come about because the king's son already mentioned “will judge the poor of the people and save the sons of the needy.” For he first judges them worthy of salvation, and so saves them. He does not grant salvation without judgment, but after careful judgment, to his own poor and to the sons of the needy, whom the prophecy also mentions when it says: “He has sent me to bring good news to the poor, to proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind.” And what kind of poor does he mean, if not those who can say with Paul: “To this very hour we hunger and thirst, we go naked, we are beaten, and we have no home”; and those who said with Peter: “Silver and gold I have none”? Such were the poor he prepared for himself, urging them not to acquire gold or silver for their belts, nor a bag for the road, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff. Such too were those of old who “went about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted, mistreated, wandering in deserts and mountains, in caves and in the holes of the earth.” But if the word had mentioned these alone, everyone not of this kind would have been shut out. As it is, it counts a second rank as well, saying: “And he will save the sons of the needy.” The sons of the needy were the followers of the apostles and disciples of our Savior, such as the Apostle had in mind when he said: “For though you have many tutors in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I became your father”; and again: “My children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.” So he saves his own poor and the sons of the needy with righteousness and right judgment. But as for the slanderer who has chosen to make war on his people and his Church (and countless slanderers malign his Church, while others slander the life of those who excel in his Church): if you look at the end of their lives, you will see how it has been said, “And he will humble the slanderer.” For which of those who have ruled as tyrants Zech. 2:10–11.

and assailed our Savior's Church with blasphemies and slanders has not been humbled? Which of the wise of this age, having sharpened his tongue against the divinely inspired Scripture, has not received the wages of his slander? Though very many slanderers have risen [?] against his Church, and all have been humbled in their turn, he himself is foretold to endure along with the sun, lighting up the whole world, like the sun, with the rays of his teaching; “and before the moon,” or according to Aquila, “and to the face of the moon,” or according to Symmachus, “and he will endure in front of the moon.” For “before the moon” does not mean before the moon came into being, but in its presence, as though going on ahead in front of the moon. For just as the sun makes day when it is above the earth, while the moon dispels the darkness of night with its own light, in the same way the one foretold, like the moon, gives light to souls that are in darkness and night, and like the sun lights up the whole world; and he endures and remains alongside until the consummation of the age. For as far as the sun brightens the whole world, so far does he too, remaining alongside the sun and reaching out with it, give light to the souls of human beings. And likewise, like the full moon, he is said to last for generations of generations. “He will come down like rain upon a fleece, and like drops dripping upon the earth.” You will understand the coming down of God the Word if you attend to his descent and his condescension, in which, accommodating himself to human littleness, “he humbled himself, taking the form of a servant, and being found in fashion as a man.” That is why it says, “He will come down.” And the prophecy necessarily used an illustration when it said, “like rain upon a fleece.” All the other translators rendered this in agreement: Aquila saying, “And he will come down like rain upon a shearing,” Symmachus, “He will come down like dew upon a fleece,” and the remaining translators likewise. They show the descent of the Word, the one foretold, from on high, from the very heavens, to earth, and how he came down quietly and calmly, with no one perceiving it. For rain falling on a fleece comes down imperceptibly and without a sound. Since, then, the birth of our Savior according to the flesh (Perhaps read τοῖς.)

…upon a fleece, in the ways described. But after this, no longer as upon a fleece, but with great commotion and a crash heard throughout the whole world, his teaching went forth. That is why it adds next: “and like drops dripping upon the earth.” For drops, or “spatterings” according to the other translators, dripping on the earth no longer come down without a sound, but with a great noise. And this came to fulfillment when the voice of his apostles went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world

After this it says: “In his days righteousness will rise, and abundance of peace”; but according to Aquila, “In his days the righteous one will sprout, and abundance of peace”; and according to Symmachus, “In his days the righteous one will blossom.” The days of our Savior are to be understood as those from his coming until the consummation of the age. For just as we hear “in the days of David” and “in the days of Jeroboam,” so too there would be days of our Savior. But those men appeared for a little while and were soon extinguished, and so their days also came to an end. How many the days of our Savior are, the word has already shown by saying, “He will endure along with the sun and before the moon, for generations of generations.” In keeping with this, he himself promised his disciples: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age.” For this is how he was to endure along with the sun. Therefore in his days, during which he will endure along with the sun and, like the moon, give light to the souls of those in darkness, righteousness will shine out over all the earth (or according to Aquila, “the righteous one”): no longer among the Jews alone, where one or two here and there were named righteous, but throughout the whole world, where countless people are justified in Christ. The multitude of the righteous who flourish in the days of the Savior and rise like light, like their own luminary, you will recognize in the multitude of his martyrs everywhere on earth, and of those in his Church who achieve the angelic life in perfect chastity. And if it is also said that righteousness will blossom in his days, one may learn how this too is fulfilled in deed from the fact that not the Jews alone but every nation is called to the divine faith, and that slaves worship God on an equal footing with the free, the poor just as the rich, and rulers together with their subjects, with abundant righteousness of God. How abundance of peace has risen in these days of our Savior can be understood by considering the state of affairs before his coming. At that time the whole human race was divided, cut off as though from one body into countless scattered members, with the various nations long since separated from one another in various ways, making war on one another and suffering war; some ruled by tyrants, others by democracies, others by oligarchies; with local governors and tyrants nation by nation

holding power, so that the lands of neighbors were closed to contact and inaccessible to those on the borders [?] nearby; and truceless wars and irreconcilable enmities had persisted for long ages until our Savior. But from that time on, all multiplicity of rule was swept away and a single monarchy prevailed over most of the nations; and there truly came to be abundance of peace, all the nations having gained fellowship and dealings with one another. Thus the testimony before us, which fits our Savior alone, is borne out in fact. This abundance of peace, it says, will remain “until the moon is taken away”; or according to Aquila, “until the moon [?]”; or according to Symmachus, “until the moon grows old.” And when does the moon grow old? At the consummation of the age, when the prophecy will be fulfilled that says, “The sun and the moon will be darkened together”; and again, “The sun will no longer be your light by day, nor will the moon give you light by night.” So, just as above he showed that the one foretold endures along with the sun, so here too he declares that the abundance of peace that he will procure for human beings will last until the consummation. How he will come down quietly and without a sound upon the Jewish nation, how he will fill the whole world like drops dripping upon the earth, and how righteousness and abundance of peace will rise in his days, has been shown by what has been said. Next he teaches that his dominion will not be confined to some corner of the earth, but that he will be lord of all the nations. That is why it is said: “And he will have dominion from sea to sea.” For if the earth has any limits, the seas and the Ocean, boundless for human beings, surround them on every side; and this verse confesses that the one foretold is Lord of everything within all the seas everywhere. That is why it is said: “And he will have dominion from sea to sea.” You would recognize the fulfillment of the word if you observed how everywhere on earth the churches of God proclaim his Christ as Lord. And it says, very necessarily, that he will also have dominion from the river to the ends of the world. For we needed to learn where he would begin his teaching; and it signifies that his beginning would be from a river. Which river this is, the Gospel shows when it says: “Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him. But John tried to prevent him, saying, ‘I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?’ But he answered him, ‘Let it be so now, for it is fitting for us in this way to fulfill all righteousness.’” Then, after he was baptized, “the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him. And a voice was heard from heaven, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.’” For from that moment his lordship began to be made known. And remarkably, the prophet Isaiah also mentions this river when he announces good news to the wilderness in which [?] preached

[?] John the Baptist. So he cries out, saying: “Rejoice, thirsty desert; let the desert exult and blossom like a lily; and the deserts of the Jordan will blossom and exult.” Why does so great a prophet mention no other river but the Jordan itself and the desert around it? Why does he announce gladness and exultation to the desert of the Jordan, and not to Jerusalem or to the rest of Judea? So in Isaiah too we have an indication of the river that the present passage speaks of: “And from the river to the ends of the inhabited world” the one prophesied “will have dominion.” We can see with our own eyes that these predictions have been fulfilled in fact, for we see the Christ of God proclaimed as Lord in his churches to the ends of the earth.

“Before him the Ethiopians will fall down, and his enemies will lick the dust.” It follows very fittingly that after saying “He will have dominion from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the inhabited world,” he mentioned the Ethiopians, who inhabit the farthest parts of our inhabited world, both toward the east and toward the setting sun. This is why even those outside our faith seem to have spoken in keeping with nature when they said: “The Ethiopians, who are divided in two, the farthest of men, some where Hyperion sets, others where he rises.” And in another psalm it is said: “Ethiopia will be first to stretch out her hand to God”; and again in another prophet: “From the ends of the rivers of Ethiopia they will bring me their goods.” And in the present passage, in keeping with these, it is prophesied: “Before him the Ethiopians will fall down.” Through all these passages the word signifies that the ends of the earth will receive the knowledge of the one prophesied and will worship him, falling down and bending the knee. That is why Aquila has: “Before his face the Ethiopians will bow”; and Symmachus: “In front of him the Ethiopians will kneel.” By the Ethiopians who live at the ends of the earth, the nations within the inhabited world are also meant. And it is plain how everywhere on earth those who have believed in him bend the knee, fall down to the very ground, and through him send up their worship to the God who is over all. But also “his enemies,” he says, “will lick the dust,” having become like their father the serpent, who goes on his breast and belly and eats earth, according to the penalty laid on him from the beginning. In just this way you will see the enemies of the Church of Christ licking at the dust and at bodily pleasures. For if the body, in which the soul is housed, has been called dust, according to the Scripture that says, “God took dust from the earth and formed man,” then those who lick at the dust and honor the luxuries of the flesh are rightly condemned as enemies of the saving word. Such, then, are these. But that another order of those

who acknowledge the kingdom of Christ will bring him gifts is also prophesied; that is why it is said next: “Kings of Tarshish and the islands will bring gifts; kings of the Arabs and of Sheba will offer gifts.” Here too the word divides the inhabited world into two parts. It assigns one to the region toward the setting sun, which it presents first, saying, “Kings of Tarshish and the islands will bring gifts,” and by this it signifies the western sea and the islands in it. So it was that the prophet Jonah once rose to flee to Tarshish, went down to Joppa, and boarded a ship to flee to Tarshish, which they say is Tarsus. But in Ezekiel, where the name Tarshish occurs, the Seventy translated it as Carthage. The other region, toward the east, is indicated by “kings of the Arabs and of Sheba.” For the race of the Arabs is eastern, and beyond it lie the Persian lands, and the country of the Sabaeans is said to be there. In place of “kings of the Arabs and of Sheba,” Aquila and Symmachus, and the Hebrew text in agreement with them, have “kings of Sheba and Sheba.” So the name as pronounced is the same, but it differs in its letters: according to the Hebrew text, the first Sheba is written with the letter the Hebrews call sin, the second with the letter sade, and so their meanings also differ. The Saviour too mentions this name, saying: “The queen of Sheba will rise up on the day of judgment and condemn this generation, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon.” By this he plainly shows that the nation of Sheba lies at the ends of the earth. The third book of Kingdoms also records this about the same nation: “And the queen of Sheba heard the name of Solomon, and came to test him with riddles. And she came to Jerusalem with a very great force, and camels carrying spices and a great deal of gold and precious stone.” The country and the nation were called Sheba after their forefather Sheba, who is recorded as a son of Cush. So the scripture of Moses says: “The sons of Cush: Sheba and Havilah and Sabtah.” And Cush is translated “the Ethiopian.” So the nation of Sheba seems to be of Ethiopian race. There is also a second Sheba, of whom Scripture says: “The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.” Rightly, then, the psalm reads, according to the other translators: “Kings of Sheba and Sheba will offer gifts.” Still, through these words the prophecy signifies that the kingdoms of the eastern region and those toward the setting sun will bring gifts to the one prophesied, and in this way the nations under those kingdoms are meant. But might the kings also stand for the angels who preside over the nations, who are consecrated to God and offer him as gifts the churches of the nations they lead? That is why it next prophesies that all the kings will worship him. For it says not only that they will bring him the gifts already mentioned, but also that they will worship

him. Moses too taught this in the great song, speaking of Christ in this way: “Rejoice, you heavens, together with him, and let all the angels of God worship him.” These, then, are the kings: the unseen and invisible rulers of the nations, who worshiped their own Lord and brought him as gifts the souls placed under them. Therefore these words are followed by: “All the nations will serve him.” This would agree with the word that said: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.” We must be confident that this will be fulfilled when the full number of the nations has come in, and especially at the second divine appearing of our Saviour. Then indeed “all the kings will worship him, and all the nations will serve him.” And this will be the end of all things, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, when he has abolished all rule and all authority and power. For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet; the last enemy to be abolished is death.

“For he rescued the poor from the mighty, and the needy who had no helper.” In place of “For he rescued the poor from the mighty,” Symmachus has: “For he will deliver the needy who cries out.” For it prophesies these things not as having already happened, but as things that will happen. See how often he mentions the poor. First he says: “to judge your people in righteousness, and your poor with justice”; second: “He will judge the poor of the people and save the children of the needy”; now again: “For he rescued the poor from the mighty, and the needy who had no helper”; and once more: “He will spare the poor and needy, and save the souls of the needy.” I think that in all these passages he calls the apostles and disciples of our Saviour poor and needy. For his sake they took on poverty, and they attained the philosophy that drives toward the summit of virtue. That is why Isaiah foretold about them: “He has sent me to bring good news to the poor.” And the Saviour himself, speaking with them, said: “Blessed are the poor, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” “All the nations,” then, “will serve him, for he rescued the poor from the mighty, and the needy who had no helper.” The word “for,” which stands in all the translators and in the Hebrew text itself, gives a cause, and teaches how all the nations were to serve the Saviour. This will happen, he says, “because he will rescue the poor from the mighty.” It is as if he said more plainly: because he will rescue the company of his apostles, who became poor and needy for his sake, from every mighty one. For many mighty ones, visible and invisible, opposed these poor and needy men and rose up against them. But he himself, shielding them with invisible power, will rescue them from all of these, so that the ministry of the gospel preaching carried out through them would not be hindered. And he will do this by being with them, according to the promise he would make to them when he said: “Behold, I am with you all the days until the end of the age.” So indeed he spared the poor and needy, and saved the souls

of the needy. He granted all these things to his disciples and apostles, so that their voice might go out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the inhabited world. And he redeemed the souls of these poor and needy ones from usury and injustice, so that they would owe nothing to anyone. If at some time they had borrowed and fallen into debt, so that they became liable for old sins, he himself gave his precious blood as a ransom for them and redeemed their souls. This is why the divine Apostle taught: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us.” For they were debtors, bound to the legislation of Moses, but they did not fulfill what was written, and so they were under a curse for not keeping the whole law. For it was written: “Cursed is everyone who does not abide by all that is written in the book of the law, to do it.” Rightly, then, he set them free from this curse and redeemed them from usury and injustice by becoming a curse for them, giving his precious blood for them, and so making them precious to himself. That is why it is said next: “And their name is honored before him.” This is why he is recorded as saying to them: “Do not rejoice that the demons are subject to you; rather rejoice and exult that your names are written in heaven.” And why was their name honored before him, if not because he himself counted them worthy of names, calling Simon Peter, Thomas Didymus, and the sons of Zebedee Boanerges, which means “sons of thunder”? Moreover, the name they all shared was also honored before him. This is what the Gospel scripture indicated when it said: “These twelve Jesus chose, whom he also named apostles.” In place of “their name,” the Hebrew text has “their blood,” and the other translators rendered it so as well: Aquila says, “And their blood will be honored in his eyes,” and Symmachus, “And their blood will be precious before him.” By this he plainly hinted at the death of the men we have mentioned. Each of them met a different end in martyrdom, one in one way and another in another, enduring the contest of blood for the sake of bearing witness to him. So it is said of them: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones.” The passage before us, which says, “And their name is honored before him,” is like this.

“And he will live, and there will be given to him of the gold of Arabia, and they will pray for him continually.” It seems to me that “and he will live” here agrees with the saving voice that said to his disciples: “Behold, I am with you all the days until the end of the age.” To show the abiding presence of the one prophesied, and his life stretching on without end, he added: “and he will live.” For a long life was needed to accomplish what had been said. If the one prophesied is to judge

his people in righteousness and his poor with justice, to humble the false accuser, to endure as long as the sun, and to have dominion from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the inhabited world, then he rightly needed a long life. And how else would the Ethiopians, the kings of Tarshish, and the islands be subjected to him, and all the kings of the earth worship him, and all the nations serve him? For all these things he needed a lasting life. So after all this, “and he will live” is added fittingly and necessarily, and in this way the immortal and eternal life of the one prophesied is made known. Next it is said: “And there will be given to him of the gold of Arabia.” In place of “of Arabia,” the Hebrew text again has “Sheba,” and the other translators used the same word. Figuratively, one might say that this gold signifies the purest mind among human beings. But the oracle was also fulfilled historically when the magi from the east came and worshiped the Saviour while he was a child, and offered him gold and frankincense and myrrh. Perhaps “he will live” also refers to the time when Herod, plotting against the infant Jesus, “sent and killed all the children in and around Bethlehem who were two years old and under, according to the time he had learned exactly from the magi.” For then Joseph, having been warned by God, took Mary his wife and the child and withdrew into Egypt. So the present prophecy, foretelling these things, said in advance that “he will live, and there will be given to him of the gold of Arabia,” that is, the gold from Sheba; as if it said more plainly, “of choice gold.” For this Sheba and the nation of the Sabaeans are said to belong to the Arabia called Felix, and from there, it is recorded, choice gold was brought to Solomon along with other things. In another sense, too, we see with our own eyes in the churches of Christ countless treasures of pure gold dedicated in his honor. So the word rightly did not see fit to leave these out. Next it adds: “And they will pray for him continually; all day long each one will bless him.” There is no need of many words to show how all who have believed in the Christ of God offer unceasing prayers “for him,” so that they may have him always with them and as a helper to them all. And who could doubt that all day long each one blesses him? Night and day, more often than it draws breath, every soul of those who truly believe in him honors and reveres his name and blesses him, confident that the blessing returns to itself, in keeping with the oracle spoken to Christ in his own person: “Those who bless you are blessed, and those who curse you are cursed.” This is why the race of Christians grows and multiplies daily: it shares in the blessing from God, which it enjoys because it unceasingly

blesses his Christ, in keeping with the scripture before us, which says: “All day long they will bless him.” And it gives the cause of these things, saying: “There will be a support on the earth on the tops of the mountains.” By this it signifies his Church, founded and established on the unbreakable rock of his power, lifted up and raised high, as though set on the tops of mountains, that is, on the words of the prophets and apostles, on which the Church of our Saviour is built.

“His fruit will be exalted above Lebanon, and they will blossom out of the city like the grass of the earth.” You will understand how the fruit of our prophesied Saviour was exalted above Lebanon if you gather what is said about Lebanon in the prophecies. In Isaiah it is said: “Behold, the Lord of hosts throws the glorious into confusion with might”; and next: “And Lebanon will fall with its lofty ones.” It is also said in Zechariah: “Open your gates, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars.” And in the twenty-eighth psalm it is said: “He will shatter the cedars of Lebanon, and crush them small like the calf, Lebanon.” These obscure sayings are explained by the word in Ezekiel that says: “The great eagle, with great wings, broad in span, full of talons, whose purpose was to enter Lebanon, and he broke off the tender shoots of the cedar”; after which it goes on: “When the king of Babylon comes and enters Jerusalem and takes its rulers.” Here the prophecy plainly interprets the great eagle with great wings as the king of the Babylonians, and Lebanon as Jerusalem. You may also apply to Jerusalem what the other prophets say about Lebanon. Indeed, not even any of the circumcision would doubt that they must admit that what is said about Lebanon is a veiled reference to Jerusalem. “Exalted,” then, the present oracle says, “above Lebanon will be his fruit,” that is, the fruit of the prophesied Saviour. And what would his fruit be but his Church, established throughout the whole inhabited world, of which it was said, “There will be a support on the earth on the top of the mountains”? This, then, is prophesied to be exalted above Lebanon. For even if the Lebanon in question, I mean Jerusalem, once seemed to be glorious and flourishing, the fruit of our Saviour, namely the Church throughout the whole inhabited world, has been exalted far above it and has become far more beautiful, surpassing it beyond comparison. After this it presents the peoples gathered in every city and the great multitudes, saying: “And they will blossom out of the city like the grass of the earth.” “Out of the city” is said in the sense of “in each city and in every place.” But his Church has also been called the city of God because of the lawful and evangelical way of life established in it. That is why it is said: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God”; and again: “The rushing streams of the river gladden the city of God.” Since, then, the

city of God, watered by the river that floods within it, the Word, brings forth a great multitude of those gathered in the Church, it is rightly added: “And they will blossom out of the city like the grass of the earth.” His fruit, mentioned before, goes ahead of the multitude that blossoms like grass, since it is far better and higher than the grass of the earth. That is why “His fruit will be exalted above Lebanon” was placed first. After the choice fruit, that is, those who bear fruit in the Church, it counts the remaining multitudes with the words: “And they will blossom out of the city like the grass of the earth.” Then after this it says: “His name will endure forever.” Since the name of Christ abides and endures forever, it would follow that the name of Christians also lasts alongside it. This name, which is above every name, existed even before the foundation of the world; that is why it is said: “Before the sun his name abides.” And earlier it was said that he would endure as long as the sun, and before the moon, for generations of generations. We have already shown that these things cannot be applied to a mortal nature. After this it is said: “And all the nations of the earth will be blessed in him.” Set beside these words the oracle spoken to Abraham: “And in your seed all the nations of the earth will be blessed.” And see how the promise to Abraham was preserved, renewed over time through each prophet. For first it was said to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations of the earth will be blessed.” After this, Jacob, prophesying about Christ, is recorded as saying: “A ruler shall not fail from Judah until what is laid up for him comes, and he will be the expectation of the nations.” And in later times it was said again through Balaam: “A man will come out of his seed, and he will rule over many nations.” Moses too mentioned the nations in the great song, saying: “Rejoice, you nations, his people; and let all the sons of God worship him.” So here too the oracle takes up again what was prophesied to Abraham, teaching that it would be fulfilled in no other way than through Christ, when it says: “And all the nations of the earth will be blessed in him.” Then it goes on: “All the nations will call him blessed.” And how will all the nations call him blessed? By showing, through the blessedness that is in them, the grace that comes from him. “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, who alone does wonders.” The nations, blessed in the one prophesied according to the oracle that said, “And all the nations will be blessed in him,” grow with the growth that is according to God, multiply, and gain dominion over the earth. That is why the divine Apostle says: “Blessed be God, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing.” Being in this state, they bless in return the one who has become the cause of their blessing. So first they called him blessed, and then they are taught to bless him as well, by saying: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, who alone does wonders.” Observe how each part of the

[Each part of the whole bo]ok of the Psalms comes to a similar close. The last psalm of the first part was the fortieth, near the end of which it said: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, from now and forever. So be it, so be it.” The last of the second part was the psalm now before us, which likewise says at its end: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, who alone does wonders. And blessed be the name of his glory,” and what follows. The last of the third part is the eighty-eighth, which ends: “Blessed be the Lord forever. So be it, so be it.” Likewise the last of the fourth part is the hundred and fifth, which ends: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting, and all the people shall say: So be it, so be it.” The fifth part ends with “Alleluia,” and with it the whole book is brought to a close. But after the prophecy about Christ set out above, the present psalm adds: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel,” and goes on, “who alone does wonders.” What wonders? Surely the ones foretold: that he would come down like rain upon a fleece, that he would humble the slanderer, that he would endure as long as the sun, that in his days righteousness would rise, that he would rule from sea to sea, that the Ethiopians would fall down before him, that gifts would be brought to him from all the nations, that he would become a support on the earth, that his fruit would be lifted up above Lebanon, and whatever else is listed after these. For all of them we are taught to say: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, who alone does wonders. And blessed be the name of his glory forever.” The name of his glory is his divinity. If what was born of the holy Virgin was counted worthy of the name Jesus, as Gabriel said to Joseph, “And she will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins,” then it follows that by “the name of his glory” we should understand the teaching about his divinity, through which he is known as God the Word and the only-begotten God who is in the bosom of the Father. That is why the next words are: “And the whole earth shall be filled with his glory.” For long ago “he was in the world, and the world came into being through him, and the world did not know him.” And since not even the Jews, to whom he showed so many miracles, accepted the knowledge of him, he fittingly says to Moses: “Let me alone, and in my anger and wrath I will destroy them, and I will make you into a great nation”; and he adds: “As my name lives, the whole earth shall be filled with my glory.” Even if these people thrust my glory away entirely, he means, a time will come when the whole inhabited world is filled with my glory. This is just what the present oracle teaches when it says: “And the whole earth shall be filled with his glory.” Isaiah showed the same in his prophecy, where the seraphim surround the Lord of Hosts, crying out and saying: “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Hosts; the whole earth is full

of his glory.” These things were foretold long ago by divine foreknowledge, but they were [not?] fulfilled in deed before our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ shone upon the human race. For see: in our own day every demonic error has been overthrown, and the Church of Christ has filled the whole inhabited world, glorifying the God of Israel in all the earth. And since the Holy Spirit announced prophetically that these things were going to happen, a choir of angels answers, joining in prayer for their accomplishment and confirming them with the words “So be it, so be it,” or in Aquila's version, “Assuredly, assuredly,” or in Symmachus's, “Amen and amen.” After this comes: “The hymns of David the son of Jesse are ended.” For this Symmachus translated: “The prayers of David son of Jesse have been accomplished,” and Theodotion and the fifth edition: “The prayers of David son of Jesse have been summed up.” Those unfamiliar with the exact wording have not taken “The hymns of David son of Jesse are ended” as part of the whole psalm, but have read it as a note written in alongside, outside the prophecy. The other translations and the Hebrew text, however, show clearly that these words too are part of the whole psalm. King David was always praying that the birth of the Savior, foretold as coming from his seed, would shine forth; and once that birth came to pass, everything foretold [?] was going to be fulfilled. So it is fitting that after the conclusion of what has been foretold it should be added that through these predictions the prayers of David have been accomplished and fulfilled. “Have been accomplished,” or “are ended,” can also be said prophetically of time to come: each of the things listed above will happen when the prayers of David the son of Jesse are accomplished and fulfilled. It was very apt, because of the Christ of God who is being prophesied, that he named not simply “David” but added “the son of Jesse,” so that we might link with this scripture the prophecy of Isaiah, in which similar things are foretold about Christ. There it is said: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from the root, and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him,” and so on; and afterward: “And there shall be the root of Jesse, and he who rises to rule the nations; in him the nations shall hope.” You see how here too the calling of the nations is proclaimed through the root of Jesse, so that the added words “the son of Jesse” are not idle in the prophecy before us. And it is timely that here, once the kingdom of Christ and the calling of the nations have been announced, the second part of the book of Psalms closes, having begun with the forty-first and ending with the psalm now before us.

One of these has been separated from the series of the [other?] eleven and placed before the fiftieth psalm. The forty-ninth, then, is inscribed “Of Asaph”; when we discussed those passages we set out the reason that occurred to us. The first psalm of Asaph now before us presents the prophet marveling greatly at the patience of the all-good God, his forbearance toward the ungodly, and the leniency he grants to sinners. Overwhelmed by it, he accuses himself of losing heart, of nearly being shaken, and of having the foundations of his soul overturned because of the prosperity he saw among ungodly and godless men. Yet although he was troubled at first, he goes on to foretell their overthrow, saying: “You cast them down when they were lifted up. How they have suddenly become a desolation! They have failed, they have perished because of their folly,” and what follows. The second teaches in what circumstances the words of the first were spoken. It laments the final siege of Jerusalem, which the city suffered in Roman times, and describes the assault of those who besieged the place. He shows this when he says: “Why, O God, have you cast us off forever? Why is your anger kindled against the sheep of your pasture?” Then he goes on: “As in a forest of trees, they hacked down its doors together with axes; with hatchet and pick they smashed it. They set your sanctuary on fire.” And again: “We have not seen our signs; there is no longer a prophet, and he will no longer know us.” For the statement that there were no longer any prophets at the time of the siege described was a sign of their final fall. These things follow very closely on the predictions about Christ made earlier. Since they did not receive him when he came, [he] necessarily [foretells] the wrath that came upon them after what they had dared against him [?]

The third of Asaph points the reader of the earlier psalms to the end, and urges, “Do not destroy.” It is also inscribed as both a psalm and a song, because it contains the thanksgiving of those who have believed in Christ. It sets forth God's just judgment, teaching that he has fixed a time of judgment in which he will repay each one according to his works. Those who suffer hardship in this present life will not lose the hope that awaits them with God, and those who are lifted up at this present time and boast against Christ will not escape punishment in the life to come. So, speaking in the person of the apostles, disciples, and evangelists of our Savior, he proclaims: “We will give thanks to you, O God, and call upon your name.” Concerning

those who dared to act against our Savior he goes on to add: “I said to the lawless, Do not act lawlessly, and to the sinners, Do not lift up your horn. Do not lift up your horn on high; do not speak injustice against God.” Then, in the person of Christ himself, he adds: “But I will declare it forever; I will sing to the God of Jacob. And I will break all the horns of the sinners, and the horns of the righteous shall be lifted up.”

The present psalm, too, is entitled “In hymns”; and not only that, but it is also [a song?] pointing to the end. It portrays the security of the Savior's apostles and of his Church, his own abiding and dwelling in peace, and his presence in Judea; and it shows how his true city, Mount Zion, his true dwelling place, is always at peace and never falls into the hands of enemies. He indicates this when he says: “God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel. His place has been made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion.” Next he describes the fall of his enemies and of the foes of his Church, saying: “There he broke the power of the bows, the shield and the sword and the battle.” And again: “All the foolish in heart were troubled. They slept their sleep, and all the men of wealth found nothing in their hands. At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, all who rode on horses fell asleep.” To this he joins the glorious coming of the Savior, saying: “From heaven you made judgment heard; the earth was afraid and was still, when God arose to judgment, to save all the kings [?] of the [earth?].” The psalm now before us is also of Asaph, but it bears the further inscription “For Idithum,” about whom we have already spoken above. He seems to compose these words on behalf of Idithum, who, quite naturally, groaned greatly at what he had heard about the people: he was already fainting and all but despairing of himself because of the people's transgressions and what would befall the whole nation on account of them. So at the beginning he writes, as if in Idithum's person: “With my voice I cried to God, with my voice to God, and he gave heed to me.” Then he reveals the dejection that had come over him, saying: “My soul refused to be comforted; I brooded, and my spirit grew faint. I was troubled and did not speak.” And he adds: “By night I communed with my heart and searched my spirit. Will the Lord cast off forever, and will he never again be pleased? Or will he hide his mercy forever, from generation to generation? Or will God forget to be gracious, or shut up his compassion in his anger?” These were the things that grieved Idithum's soul. That is why he rightly

admitted that he had grown faint. But the divine Spirit, through the prophet Asaph, then heals his grief, saying: “What god is great like our God? You are the God who does wonders. You have made your power known among the peoples; with your arm you redeemed your people, the sons of Jacob and Joseph.” And again: “The waters saw you, O God, the waters saw you and were afraid; the depths were troubled, a great roar of waters.” And he sets the seal on it, saying: “You led your people like sheep by the hand of Moses and Aaron.” Asaph had good reason to remind Idithum of these things, so that he would no longer say, “I brooded, and my spirit grew faint,” but, trusting in the wondrous works God did long ago in the time of Moses, by which he redeemed the people, would hope that similar things would happen in time to come. The sixth is no longer a psalm, a song, or a hymn, nor does it point to the end; that is why none of these is in its inscription. Instead it rouses us to understand its contents. Why does the title contain none of the terms mentioned above? Because the whole discourse is an accusation against the Jewish nation, listing their impieties of old. The prophet does this in defense of God's just judgment. Since he is about to foretell what would happen to the nation before the coming of the Savior, he must teach that they would suffer these things for no small impieties. So he lists how often they sinned and how often the patience of God bore with them, and how in the end, when they had filled up the measure of their impieties, the wrath of God most justly overtook them. So that we may know this, he rightly inscribes it “Of understanding, for Asaph,” and goes on to recount all their transgressions.

Having summed up the multitude of the Jewish nation's impieties and engraved the charges against them as on a pillar, he consistently goes on, in the present psalm, to foretell the assault made on them in the time of Antiochus, king of Syria. Antiochus came upon Jerusalem and did not destroy the temple but profaned it, forcing the nation into idolatry. The history of these events is contained in the book entitled Maccabees, which records the multitudes who were slain and the ways in which those among them who bore witness for true piety died. That is why the prophetic Spirit offers up an intercession for the whole people, saying: “O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have made Jerusalem a watchman's hut in an orchard. They have given the dead bodies of your servants as food to the birds of heaven, the flesh of your holy ones to the beasts of the earth.” These were things the nation could take honorable pride in, which is why they are spoken with great boldness. But the words in the seventy-third were not of this kind, where it said: “Why, O God, have you cast us off forever? Why is your anger kindled against the sheep of your pasture?” In

those words he indicated the final rejection of the nation and the last fall of Jerusalem. That psalm contains no happy ending, no promise to heal what had been said; but in the present one, after the grim things, he adds at the close of the whole discourse: “Repay our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom for the reproach with which they reproached you, O Lord. But we, your people and the sheep of your pasture, will give thanks to you forever; from generation to generation we will declare your praise.” These are clearly the words of the righteous. The eighth prophecy of Asaph signifies many things at once by its title: it is “to the end,” and “for those who shall be changed,” and “a psalm”; and besides all these, it has been noted that it is also “a testimony,” the only one in the whole book so inscribed. It points to the end because it foretells the future; it is “for those who shall be changed” because of the change in the things revealed through the prophecy; and it is called “a testimony” because it bears witness to the man foretold in it, the one called the Son of Man. For it introduces a certain son of man and names him the man of God's right hand. First, then, he describes allegorically the Jewish nation's journey out of Egypt and its settlement in the land of the Palestinians, saying: “You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out nations and planted it,” and what follows. Then he reveals their coming desolation, saying: “Why have you broken down its hedge, so that all who pass along the road pluck its fruit?” And he teaches about the besiegers, saying: “A boar from the forest has ravaged it, and a solitary wild beast has fed on it.” By these words he signifies that the nation would have two besiegers. This happened in the time of the Babylonians: first the Assyrian came and carried off the ten tribes of Israel into captivity, and after him the Babylonian subdued the rest, burning Jerusalem together with the temple. The word foretells this when it says: “Burned with fire and dug up.” It happened again under the rule of the Romans: first Titus besieged them and burned the temple after what they had dared against our Savior; then Hadrian decreed that the city itself be closed to Jews. But having foretold these things about the siege of the nation, he goes on to offer a prayer concerning the saving appearance of God, saying: “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the son of man whom you made strong for yourself.” In these words he pleads that the man of God's right hand may be seen on earth. Through him, he says, we who have received him will never turn away from you, and you will give us life through him. That is why we implore you, saying: “Lord of hosts, turn us back, and show us your face”—that is, through the man just indicated—“and we shall be saved.”

Very fittingly after what has been said, the prophecy now before us is entitled “For the winepresses,” and it points to the end. By the winepresses he would mean the churches of God throughout the whole world, into which the vintage of the holy vine has been gathered. It is remarkable that it is entitled “For the [winepresses?]” [?] after the destruction of the former vine. Once that vine had been ravaged by the wild boar and its hedge torn down, the word here speaks of many winepresses, no longer of one. Isaiah too pointed to the first and single winepress when he said: “And I built a tower, and dug a wine vat in it,” that is, in the vineyard. But since there he showed the fall of the former tower, the destruction of the wine vat, and the desolation of the whole vineyard, here he fittingly announces the calling of all the nations, giving the prophecy the inscription “For the winepresses.” So he summons those who receive the good news to joy and gladness, saying: “Rejoice in God our helper; shout aloud to the God of Jacob. Take up a psalm and bring the timbrel, the pleasant harp with the lyre.” These words are for those worthy of the Gospel, who fill the winepresses with their own fruits. But about the Jewish nation he clearly adds: “But my people did not listen to my voice, and Israel did not heed me. So I sent them away according to the ways of their heart.” These words are closely connected with the preceding prophecy. As there he showed the destruction of the vine, so here he exposes the disobedience and unprofitableness of the same people; and as there he introduced the man of God's right hand and the Son of Man made strong, so here he has joined to them the prophecy concerning the winepresses, that is, the churches of God which the Son of Man established. He introduces gods, and God in the midst of the gods judging them [?]. Since in the preceding psalms he accused the whole Jewish nation, it follows that in the present one he rebukes their rulers in particular. Then, since in the psalm before this he called the Christ of God the man of his right hand and the Son of Man made strong, indicating his coming in the flesh, he here declares him to be God, so that no one should take him for a mere man like most others. He says: “God stood in the assembly of the gods.” And so that no one hearing the Christ of God called God should be troubled about the doctrine of the one sovereign rule, he fittingly gives the name of gods also to the many who are accused in what follows, all but urging us not to shrink from calling the Son of God God. For if the rulers of the nation, who are being censured, were counted worthy to be called gods, what danger could there be in [calling] the man of God's right hand and the Son of Man who was made str[ong]

[?] to confess God [?]. Then, at the end of the whole psalm, the Prophet sends up a prayer for the calling of the nations, saying: “Arise, O God, judge the earth, for you shall inherit among all the nations.” The forty-ninth psalm seems to follow on from this one, for in it too it is said: “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken.” In both, then, the God of gods is brought in, and again in both he is described as judging. In the present psalm it is said: “Arise, O God, judge the earth, for you shall inherit among all the nations.” In the forty-ninth, following on from these words very closely, the text describes how, having arisen, he judges the earth. It says: “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting.” Next it says: “God will come openly and will not keep silent. Fire will burn before him,” and so on. In these words it sets out how he is to judge. And since the psalm in hand says, “For you shall inherit among all the nations,” it is fitting that in the forty-ninth he overturns the laws of Moses about sacrifices. In their place he hands down another kind of sacrifice, a rational one, offered throughout the whole inhabited world among all the nations. That is why it is said: “For you shall inherit among all the nations.” The present psalm, being the last of Asaph's, contains a supplication and an appeal on behalf of the people, quite in keeping with what comes before. In the first of these psalms he foretold the final siege of the place. Then, going back in time, he placed second the siege under Antiochus. After that, in third place, he recalled the one earlier in time, I mean the one under the rule of the Assyrians and Babylonians. So in the present psalm, following that order, he sends up a petition and supplication about the siege that came first in time, when all the neighbors of Judea joined hands with the Assyrians against them. He indicates this when he says: “The tents of the Edomites and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagrites, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek, the Philistines with those who dwell in Tyre. For Assur too came along with them; they became a help to the sons of Lot.” After this he describes the end that will overtake them, saying: “My God, make them like a wheel, like stubble before the wind, like a fire that burns through a forest, like a flame that burns up the mountains,” and what follows. When you come to this passage you will notice that where he mentions Assur (these were the Assyrians) and the nations already named, he makes his petition against them and then foretells their overthrow. He does the same in the seventy-eighth psalm, where he foretold the events under Antiochus, who forced the Jews to adopt Greek ways and break their ancestral laws. There too he foretold the overthrow of the enemies. But he does not do so in the seventy-third, where their final rejection was revealed. These, then, are the eleven connected psalms of Asaph. The

twelfth has been placed before the fiftieth psalm, for the reason we gave when we went through those passages. But now that we have summarized these psalms, come, let us take up the first of them again and examine its meaning in detail.

A PSALM OF ASAPH. 72. “How good God is to Israel, to the upright in heart!” The third part of the book of Psalms begins with the present psalm and ends with the eighty-eighth, so that it contains seventeen psalms in all. The first eleven of these, in order, are Asaph's. Then come four of the sons of Korah, one of David, and last one of Ethan the Ezrahite. The present psalm is Asaph's. (He was a prophet who lived at the same time as David.) It is titled “Psalm” because at the end it describes the overthrow of the ungodly and the good end stored up with God for the godly. He presented these when he said: “For behold, those who remove themselves far from you will perish; you have destroyed everyone who goes whoring away from you. But for me it is good to cling to God.” The psalm begins with doctrinal teaching, in which he gives the reason why the ungodly prosper at certain times. He says the cause is this: God is good and patient. The divine Apostle also teaches this when he says: “Or do you despise the riches of his kindness and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is leading you to repentance?” Elsewhere it is said: “God is a righteous judge, good and patient, not bringing on his wrath every day.” Because he is good, he makes his sun rise on the righteous and the unrighteous, and sends rain on the evil and the good. That is why the Savior gave a definition concerning the Father, saying: “No one is good except one, God.” And if you ask about the Son, you will learn that he too is good, since he is the radiance of eternal light, the spotless mirror of the Father's working, and the image of his goodness. Such, then, is God by nature. Yet he is not known to all, but only to Israel, that is, to the clear-sighted man who knows. He points to this man by adding next, “to the upright in heart.” For whoever has nothing crooked in his soul, but applies upright reasoning to the principles of providence, is Israel. To him God is known as good, as one who bears with everyone out of the abundance of his goodness. Such, then, is God. “But I,” wanting to be a man who loves the truth, describe the sluggishness of my own soul. For in my standing and my stepping, in the feet and supports of my soul, as one might put it in a figure, I was very nearly turned aside from hope in God because of the prosperity of godless and impious men. But this I suffered only nearly. By God's grace I was not shaken, and the reasoning I spoke of did not overpower me. Otherwise I would have perished, and all my steps would have been poured out. For my steps were very nearly poured out,

but they were not poured out. You will understand how the steps of the soul are poured out if you consider this. Some people made progress in the practice of godliness and shone for a long time in self-control and purity. Later, however, they were dragged down. They began to live more slackly and slipped, or else fell from the goal entirely, as though they had suffered shipwreck of the good deeds they had long been gathering. You would not be wrong to say of such people that the feet of their soul were shaken. Indeed, they fell completely, and their steps, the progress they had made over a long time along the ways of God, flowed away and were poured out. “But these things,” he says, “I nearly suffered. I did not suffer them, thanks to God's mercy. Still, I was about to suffer them because of the envy I felt toward the lawless, when I saw their peace and their prosperity in wealth and luxury, in offices and honors. Looking at these things, I was torn apart inside, so that I very nearly fell into godless reasonings. I did not fall into them, because I was healed by right doctrines, which remind me that God is good, forbearing and patient. So, astonished at him and marveling at his abundant goodness, I said at the beginning of my words: ‘How good God is to Israel, to the upright in heart!’” In place of “How good,” Symmachus has: “Yet truly God is good to Israel, to the pure in heart.” He made clear who Israel is by adding, “to the pure in heart.” These are the true Israel. That is why the Savior also said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.” And “Israel” is interpreted as “seeing God.” “For there is no shrinking back in their death, and there is firmness in their scourge. They are not in the troubles of men, and they will not be scourged along with men. Therefore pride has taken hold of them to the end.” He goes through the things that troubled his soul as if telling a story, so that we may know that his feet were nearly shaken over no small matter, and that it was not ordinary things that almost made his steps pour out. What were these things? The ungodly, he says, who do not know God, lived such settled and pleasant lives, and enjoyed such luxury right up to their very end, that anyone would pray to have the same lot as they. Anyone would envy not only their life but even their death, for they had no reason to shun it or to count it something to pray against. So there was no shrinking back in their death. And if it ever happened that one of them met with a scourge and a blow, that is, with adversity and misfortune, or was tried by disease or loss, there was no firmness in their scourge. The blow that struck them was not firm and lasting, but brief, and it passed over the surface. Nor were they tried by the troubles of men: farming, getting their food by the work of their hands, and being ground down by poverty. On the contrary, they overflowed with wealth and lived in pleasure and luxury, suffering nothing like the rest of mankind, who are scourged every day by a hard and toilsome life. That is why they are not in the trouble of men,

and they will not be scourged along with men. Symmachus translated it this way: “For they did not think about death, for their porches were firm.” And next: “They were not in a man's misery, nor were they struck along with men.” Since they lived in such conditions, pride took hold of them. As far as human reasoning goes, being ungodly, they ought to have suffered the wages of their impieties. Instead they reveled in life while fighting against God. So, wearing themselves away, they became worse than they were, and they clothed themselves with their own injustice and impiety. In place of this Symmachus has: “They put on pride, having storehouses gained by injustice.” Beyond this: “Their injustice will come forth as from fat.” Symmachus gave the meaning of this more clearly when he said: “Their eyes bulged out from fatness.” Aquila translated it likewise: “Their eyes came out from fat.” After this: “They passed into the disposition of their heart,” he says; “they thought and spoke in wickedness.” Symmachus translated this too, as follows: “They transgressed what was plain to the heart, mocking.” For these men transgressed the very works of God that are seen by everyone's eyes, the manifest wonders of Providence. They perceived and understood them, but mocked and jeered at them out of extreme folly. Moreover, they spoke in wickedness and uttered injustice against the height. “They set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue went through the earth.” Symmachus translated this as well: “They spoke with much slander; they spoke against the height. They set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue walked about on the earth.” For they uttered blasphemous words against God, as though he neither saw nor watched over anything, or did not even exist at all. So they spoke injustice against the height and stretched their mouth all the way to heaven, though they were lowly and had their tongue on the earth. These are the reasons I confessed my own failing, and publicly set up a written charge against myself: that my feet were nearly shaken, and my steps very nearly poured out, because I envied the lawless when I saw the peace of sinners. “Therefore my people will return here, and full days will be found in them.” The godless words of the ungodly and the pride that had a hold on them were such as has been shown. But we must not overlook that these very things turned out for the good of my people. My people may well have been handed over to these ungodly men for a time, to pay the penalty for their sins. Yet the extreme folly of those men brought about their fall and became the cause of their destruction, and so it will give my people relief and room to breathe. When those men have fallen and perished because of their own impieties, my people will return here, that is, in the present life. “And full days will be found in them,” that is, in those of my people who are worthy. Full days are days filled with every good thing,

which complete the proper span of a life. In this sense it is said somewhere: “He fell asleep full of days.” My people, then, have benefited from these things. But the ungodly and godless men I spoke of were so impious that those who saw them were at a loss and said: “How does God know? Is there knowledge in the Most High?” For if there is knowledge in the Most High, and if he watches over these things and oversees those on earth, how do these men prosper while doing such things, and keep hold of their wealth forever? “And I too, seeing these things, was troubled in my thoughts, so that I said to myself: ‘Was it in vain, then, that I kept my heart righteous and washed my hands among the innocent? Was I scourged all day long, and reproved every morning?’ For if those who have done none of these things enjoy such good cheer, then my labor is in vain, and my zeal in caring for righteousness has been for nothing. In vain and to no purpose I kept my hands and my actions from unjust deeds. In vain I went on wearing myself down with fasts and hardships, scourging myself every day. In vain and to no purpose I toiled, rising at dawn, confessing my sins in my prayers to God, weeping over them and bringing forward the charges against myself in my confessions to God.” These were the thoughts that nearly shook me. In place of these words Symmachus translated as follows: “Perhaps then I too purified my soul in vain, and washed my hands in sinlessness, and was mocked every day and reproved every morning.” “If I had said, ‘I will speak this way,’ behold, I would have broken faith with the generation of your sons. And I set out to understand this; it is toil in my sight, until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand their final end.” “I only pondered these things in my own thoughts, and they put me in danger of being shaken, but I did not declare them to others. If I had decided to think this way and had put forward this godless teaching to others, I would have become a transgressor of the godly doctrines and would have broken the covenants of the generation of your children.” For all holy and God-loving men have become your children, children of God. Their generation is the succession of holy men that comes from them. “I would have counterfeited their teachings and doctrines if I had put forward my thoughts to others. And even if I had applied myself to learning the reasons why sinners stay cheerful and keep hold of their wealth forever while the righteous are brought low, even so I would not have grasped the hidden judgments concerning these things. I would only have gathered toil for myself, falling into perplexity and weariness of soul.” That is why he says: “And if I set out to understand this, it is toil in my sight.” Or, in Symmachus: “And if I reasoned how to understand this, it seemed hard labor to me.” “So, seeing that the knowledge of these things is beyond human grasp, I used a godly reasoning and decided within myself that it was better to hold back and wait for the proper time for

knowing these things. And that time was: ‘Until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand their final end.’” Or, in Symmachus: “Until I enter the holy places of God and gain understanding of their final end.” “I found this to be a good refuge for myself, where my perplexities would be resolved, namely release from this mortal life and entrance into the promises of God. In it I found healing and comfort, knowing well that when I am there I will perceive the reasons for the things I have been asking about, and will know the final end of the ungodly.” For we should not look only at the present life and their present luxury, but also look ahead to their final end. “Yet because of their deceits you have set evils for them; you cast them down when they were lifted up. How they have suddenly been made desolate! They have vanished, they have perished because of their folly, like a dream when one awakes.” “I weighed three lines of reasoning about the questions I had been asking. The first I saw to be impious and godless: the one that says, ‘Then it was in vain that I kept my heart righteous.’ The second was the attempt to understand these things, and it was full of toil and labor because of the depths of the riches of God's knowledge, and because his judgments are unsearchable and his ways inscrutable. So I settled on the third. I decided to hold back for the present, to wait, and to look ahead to the end of all things. I entrusted myself to this reasoning, since it was godly and true, and from that very faith I gained much. For by the prompting of the prophetic Spirit I came to know that because of their deceits God will cast them down before long, after they have been lifted up and exalted. Then, having been enlightened and having perceived by prophetic power the fall that will overtake them at the end, I rightly say: ‘How they have suddenly been made desolate! They have vanished, they have perished because of their folly,’ and have become like a dream when one has awakened.” As long as someone is dreaming and imagining things in his sleep, he seems to be doing something, deceived by the images of the dream. But when he wakes up and rubs the sleep from his eyes, the things he imagined are gone. So too the apparent prosperity of the ungodly in the present life, with their wealth and their pride, will end like the experience of those who dream and see visions in their sleep, then wake up and find that they hold in their hands none of the things they thought they saw and held. In place of “Yet because of their deceits you have set for them,” Symmachus put it this way: “Truly you have set them in a slippery place; you have cast them down to ruin. Suddenly they vanished; they were consumed as if they had never been, like a dream to one who has woken up.” Alongside “suddenly” and “all at once” you should place the saving words that say: “Keep awake, for you do not know on what day or hour your Lord is coming.” And again: “His master will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know.” “Lord, in your city you will treat their image with contempt.” Above he said, “Until I enter

the sanctuary of God.” Now he teaches what that sanctuary was, saying: “Lord, in your city you will treat their image with contempt.” So the divine Apostle, knowing of a heavenly city of God, rightly said: “We have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.” And again: “But the Jerusalem above is free.” This is the city of God that the present Prophet also points to when he says: “Lord, in your city you will treat their image with contempt.” “If they had kept your image,” he says, “they would rightly have been counted worthy of your city as well.” But “man, though he was in honor, did not understand; he was likened to the senseless beasts and became like them.” In keeping with his own wickedness he transformed himself into the likeness of a wild beast. He became a horse mad after females, or a ravening wolf, or a snake and brood of vipers, or something else of the kind. For this reason God throws such an image out of his city like counterfeit coin. He treats it with contempt and does not judge it worthy of the dwelling places in his city. For there are many dwelling places with the Father. That is why it is said: “Lord, in your city you will treat their image with contempt.” Asaph uttered this prophetically, as though divinely inspired, having seen the future with the enlightened eyes of his soul. Next he gives the reason he was enlightened to see the city of God, saying: “For my heart was set on fire, and my kidneys were changed.” “For I was very zealous for the Lord, like the prophet Elijah, and I was dragged this way and that in my thoughts as I saw the ungodly in good cheer. More than that, I was burning in my kidneys, in the hidden depths of my own soul. That is why I said, ‘For I envied the lawless when I saw the peace of sinners.’ For this reason I was counted worthy to be enlightened by the Spirit and to see the city of God, both those who are worthy of it and those who are not.” In place of “My heart was set on fire,” Symmachus has: “My heart was contracted, and within my kidneys I argued and disputed.” Then next it says: “And I was brought to nothing and did not know.” Symmachus translated this more clearly, saying: “I was ignorant and did not know.” And again: “I became like a beast before you.” Or, in Symmachus: “I went on like a beast before you.” “And I,” he says, “am continually with you.” In Symmachus: “And I was with you continually.” “For even though I did not understand at all before I was enlightened and learned what is said about your city and about the image of the ungodly, and even though at first I went on in folly like a senseless beast, unable to grasp the principles of your providence, still I did not abandon you, O God. I did not fall away from hope in you, but was with you continually. And I did this not by my own strength but by your grace. For you yourself, in your love for mankind, took hold of my right hand and held me together and kept me firm, so that I would not

…that my steps should not be poured out, nor my feet be shaken from standing before you. That is why I say: "You have held my right hand." For I had a good right hand, strong and fatherly (1), doing everything that is right and pleasing to you. So you took hold of it and guided me by your counsel; or, as Symmachus has it, "by your advice you guided me," ferrying me across this mortal life and leading me by the hand into the calm, safe harbor of rest with you. If you had not held my right hand, the feet of my soul would long ago have been knocked from under me, as if by a rushing torrent, and I would have fallen a terrible fall. But as it is, you yourself have held my right hand and guided me in your counsel. And in the end, after the trials I have described and the storms that threw my soul into turmoil, you brought me safely through the currents of life and received me with glory, unharmed by all these things. According to Symmachus: "Afterward," he says, "honor followed…"

"For what have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you on earth?" "Your love for humankind," he says, "your mercy and your grace have been the cause of all my blessings. For in your goodness you held my right hand and kept me safe, so that my feet were not shaken and my steps were not poured out. More than that, you received me with glory, since this is in your power as the good God. For I have nothing in heaven; these things did not come to me as something owed. And I have no one else in heaven but you alone. So I desired to gain nothing from you on earth, and I did not pray to obtain mortal and perishable things." And it was reasonable that he desired nothing from God on earth, for "I longed for the dwellings in heaven and prayed to obtain the good things there. So I wasted away my own life, wore out my life on earth, and afflicted my heart, making you alone, O God, the portion of my hope." Hence he says: "My flesh and my heart have failed; God of my heart, and God is my portion forever. For behold, those who put themselves far from you will perish; you have destroyed everyone who goes whoring away from you. But for me it is good to cling to God, to put my hope in the Lord." (1) The manuscript reads "active."

…from God. The farther they move from him, the nearer they come to destruction; and conversely, those joined to God are joined to life and put far from destruction. The end of those who put themselves far away is ruin, as it is for those who have gone whoring away from God. God does not put anyone far from himself, nor does he thrust anyone away. Each person estranges himself from God by going whoring and handing his own soul over to God's adversaries. Those who put themselves far away by their own choice bring destruction upon themselves, and once they have made themselves at home with destruction, God himself deals with them accordingly. And how was that? "You have destroyed," he says, "everyone who goes whoring away from you." A person goes whoring away from God when, having drawn near to him, he then puts himself far away. For God does not disdain to take the human soul as his bride and to sow his own seed in it. But the soul that puts itself far away and gives itself to others who want to prostitute it—evil spirits and unclean demons, or godless and impious thoughts, or foul and unclean deeds—is rightly handed over to ruin. That is why it is said: "You have destroyed everyone who goes whoring away from you." "But I knew these things, and was fully convinced of your just judgment, so I chose the opposite course from the ungodly. Though I did not understand your mysteries, and had even become like a beast before you, I was still always with you. For nothing seemed better to me than to cling to you, my God, and to choose what you yourself had decreed and commanded." For whoever clings to the Lord in this way is one spirit with him. "So nothing appeared better or nobler to me than to cling to you. That is why I say: It is good for me to cling to God." For if no one is good but God alone, where could anyone else get anything good except by clinging to him? "Already I was enjoying every good thing, cleaving and joined to God, so that I could say: My soul has clung close behind you. And for the time to come I traced out good hopes for myself. This was another good thing for me: to put my hope in the Lord. For the goal of all my hope was to proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion. For once I am counted worthy to enter your city—the one of which it was said above, 'Lord, in your city you will bring their image to nothing'—and set foot in the heavenly gates, I will announce to all the kindnesses you have done me. When I am there I will also obtain your promises, which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered the human heart." For such things God has prepared for those who [?]

The words "in the gates of the daughter of Zion" are not in the Hebrew or in the other translators, but are found only in the Seventy. So they have been marked with an obelus as superfluous.
