For the good end of all things leads to the heavenly Zion itself, which [?] was the city of God in heaven described above. The daughter of Zion is understood as the Church among us, as could easily be shown from many passages.

"Why, O God, have you cast us off to the end? Why has your anger been kindled against the sheep of your pasture?" The prophetic Spirit rouses and urges us toward understanding what is said. It does not title this, as it usually does, a psalm, or a song, or a hymn, or anything of the kind, because what it reports is so grim. It seems to contain an intercession of the kind the divine Apostle commanded when he said that all of us must offer supplications, prayers, intercessions and thanksgivings. So the text intercedes with God, prophetically describing future events as though they were past. It points to the last siege of Jerusalem, which the Romans carried out after the saving Coming. And it foretells these things before the place had even been built. For Asaph, through whom these things were prophesied, lived at the same time as David, and Solomon built the temple after David's death. The prophet foresaw two sackings of the place: the first by the Babylonians and the second by the Romans. He points to the first in Psalm [?] and Psalm 82, and to the last in the prophecy before us, which he begins with the words: "Why, O God, have you cast us off to the end? Why has your anger been kindled against the sheep of your pasture?" For the end of their utter downfall came at no other time than when our Savior and Lord passed sentence on them, saying: "Behold, your house is left to you desolate." In keeping with this, the holy Apostle, writing about them after the events had taken place, said: "But wrath has come upon them to the end." The present prophet also sets out in detail what later happened to the place in the Roman siege, where he says: "As in a thicket of trees, they cut down her doors with axes"—clearly the doors of Jerusalem—"all together; with hatchet and chisel they smashed her. They set your sanctuary on fire; they profaned the dwelling of your name to the ground." If anyone says that these things also happened in the time of the Babylonians, he must pay attention to what follows, where it says: "We have not seen our signs; there is no longer a prophet, and he will no longer know us." The sign that God watched over and cared for the Jewish nation was that he gave them prophets. Even when they were in trouble, he appointed prophets for them as physicians and saviors. So at the first siege they had Jeremiah, the great prophet of God, and Baruch. A woman named Huldah also prophesied in that same period. In the land of the Babylonians itself, Ezekiel and Daniel, distinguished and illustrious prophets, were with them. And after the return from there, in the times of Cyrus and Darius, the prophets Zechariah and Haggai were well known. How, then, could the present prophecy be applied to those times, when it says: "We have not seen our signs, and there is no longer a prophet, and he will no longer know us"? No, these things were fulfilled after the saving

Commentaries on the Psalms. …Coming and after the words he had spoken beforehand. Not long afterward the Romans came and destroyed the place. The Savior himself made this clear, foretelling the future in a parable that goes like this: "The kingdom of heaven is like a king who gave a wedding feast for his son. He sent his servants to call those who had been invited to the wedding, but they would not come. Again he sent other servants. Not only did the guests refuse to come; they even seized the servants, mistreated them and killed them." To this he adds: "When the king heard of it he was angry, and he sent his armies, destroyed those murderers and burned their city." Scripture records that the Savior said this in the temple itself while it was still standing. It was fulfilled not long afterward, when Vespasian and Titus besieged the place, and history records that no prophet arose in their time. So the passage before us describes a siege, and therefore it begins: "Why, O God, have you cast us off to the end?" From this we may admire the excellence of divinely inspired Scripture, which by divine foreknowledge anticipated what took place long ages later. "Why, O God, have you cast us off to the end?" is said because the Jewish nation often fell into impiety and wrongdoing and was handed over to the foreign nations around it. Sometimes the Moabites subdued them, sometimes the Ammonites, and at other times the Midianites. Then, when they turned back, God took them up again. Afterward, when they broke the law again, he handed them over to other enemies, and once more he won them back. He never cast them off to the end; rather, after a short time he turned them back and led them to salvation. But after the crime they dared to commit against the Savior, "wrath came upon them to the end," as the apostolic Scripture says, so that from then until now they have never again lifted up their heads. The prophecy points to this when it says: "Why, O God, have you cast us off to the end?" Through the question the text quietly hints at what was done to our Savior, after which they were cast off to the end. The Savior himself showed this when he said: "How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not! Behold, your house is left to you desolate." "How often I wanted" shows the patience granted to them over a long time, while "and you would not" points to their final rejection, when his anger was kindled against those who had once been the sheep of his pasture. Next the text offers a plea: "Remember your congregation, which you acquired from the beginning." It is very fitting that he mentions the congregation, the synagogue, and says it was God's first possession. For he also knew of the Church, which did not exist from the beginning but arose later, from all the nations, after that congregation had fallen away. He mentions the Church elsewhere too, saying: "In the midst of the Church I will sing your praise"; and again: "I have proclaimed the good news of

righteousness in the great Church"; and again: "From you comes my praise in the great Church." But the earlier congregation was not like this. It was called a synagogue from people gathering together in the same place, whereas the Church shows the special honor of being chosen. If anyone asks why the congregation that God acquired from the beginning was cast off, Christ, the Son of God, will himself explain in another prophecy, saying: "Many dogs have surrounded me; a congregation of evildoers has encircled me. They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones. They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots." These were the reasons the earlier congregation was cast off. Next he adds: "You redeemed the rod of your inheritance." He says this to move God to pity. "For you," he says, "redeemed this congregation and counted it worthy to be called your portion and the rod of your inheritance. For when the Most High divided the nations, his people Jacob became the Lord's portion, Israel the allotment of his inheritance. So remember this inheritance of yours." In place of "the rod of your inheritance," Aquila translated "the scepter of inheritance," and Symmachus "the scepter of your allotment." The text teaches that all people belong to God, but that the people he has set apart is like his royal scepter.

"Mount Zion, where you have dwelt. Lift up your hands against their arrogance to the end, for all the evil the enemy has done in your holy place." He makes clear what the rod was—or, in the other translators, what the scepter just mentioned was—by saying: "Mount Zion, where you have dwelt." For it was a royal mountain and a scepter of kingship, on which the temple and the house where God dwelt had been built. That is why Zion was called the faithful mother city, and Jerusalem the city of God, bearing the image of the heavenly city. The divine Apostle taught about that city when he said: "You have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem." Having said this, he next foretells what would happen to the place, announcing future events in advance as though they were past, as he usually does. So he says: "Those who hate you boasted in the midst of your feast"; or, as Aquila has it, "Your enemies roared in the midst of your assembly." "They set up their signs as signs, and did not know, as at the way out above." Symmachus translated this more clearly, saying: "They set up their signs conspicuously, for all to know, at the entrance above." And in place of "As in a thicket of trees, they cut down her doors with axes all together; with hatchet and chisel they smashed her," Symmachus again has: "As with tools on timber, with axes [?], they threw down her gates together with crowbars and two-pronged forks." What were the enemies' signs, which they set up conspicuously in front of the entrances, if not their instruments of war—hatchets, axes and the like, spears and weapons? Probably the standards carried in front of the camps are also meant here. And further: "They set

your sanctuary on fire," he says, "they profaned the dwelling of your name to the ground." Here he explains the meaning of what was said above. Earlier it was said, "Mount Zion, where you have dwelt"; now he makes clear how God dwelt there by saying, "the dwelling of your name." For the place was the dwelling not of God himself but of his name. At each point he presses his plea, adding: "In the midst of your feast," he says, "your sanctuary and the dwelling of your name." Such words were meant to move God and stir him to avenge these outrages, and he goes on to urge him to it, saying: "Lift up your hands against their arrogance to the end." Symmachus has: "The height of your feet has been destroyed utterly." The height of his feet was the temple of prayer. It was fitting that those who hate God boasted in the midst of his feast. For those who had formerly lived in the place raised godless hands against the Christ of God in the midst of his feast. They shouted godless and accursed cries, and on the very day of the Passover they demanded that his blood be on themselves and on their own children. So it was fitting that God's wrath pursued them in the midst of the feast, and that another prophecy was fulfilled in them as well, the one that says: "I will turn your feasts into mourning, and your festivals into

"Their kindred said in their hearts together: Let us put an end to the feasts of God in the land." "Your enemies," he says, "did all the things described above with an impious purpose. They set your sanctuary on fire, profaned the dwelling of your name, and dared all the rest. They were not plotting against human beings, nor did they set out simply to besiege a place. They were waging war against you, God, and intending to abolish your feasts." Even if they did not say this with their mouths, they reckoned it in their hearts and thoughts. At that time the enemies of God, with these thoughts in mind, tore down the place that had long been set apart for God. But the great and mighty God, in place of that one place, established churches among all the nations throughout the whole world, from the rising of the sun to its setting. "Your enemies and adversaries," he says, "set up their own signs in high and conspicuous places, right at the entrances of the temple, so that everyone passing through might see their trophies of victory. But we"—in whose person this prayer of supplication is offered—"have not seen our signs." How is it that we have not seen our signs? Only because "there is no longer a prophet, and he will no longer know us." For of old, in every period, through the generations and successions of our fathers, prophets were with them when they were besieged and carried off into captivity. This was the greatest proof and sign that they were not left uncared for. The power that watches over all things appointed the prophets as physicians for the people of that time in their worst disasters,

and these were God's signs. "But now that the things foretold are actually coming upon us, we have not seen our signs. For there is no longer a prophet, and he will no longer know us." If the prophets had been absent for a short time and then appeared again afterward, it would not have been said, "and he will no longer know us." But after the outrages they dared to commit against the Savior, the Romans came and laid the place waste from its foundations, and no prophets were present anywhere for the besieged. None have arisen in later times either, nor were any ever going to arise again. So the prophecy, having said, "There is no longer a prophet," wonderfully added, "and he will no longer know us." This could not fittingly be said of the Babylonian period, or of earlier times. For among them the succession of prophets flourished in every generation, and it lasted until John the prophet. "How long, O God, will the enemy taunt? Will the adversary provoke your name to the end?" The words "to the end" occur often in the prophecy before us. At the beginning it said, "Why, O God, have you cast us off to the end?"; then, "Lift up your hands against their arrogance to the end"; a third time, "The adversary provokes your name to the end"; and again, "Why do you turn away your hand, your right hand, from the midst of your bosom to the end?" Through these words the text points to the final siege of the place. When he asks, "How long, O God, will the enemy taunt?", he longs to learn how long these things will last, what limit of time there will be, how long (1) the adversary will provoke your name, and whether he will go on doing so to the end. Then he goes on to ask the reason for all this, and so he says: "Why do you turn away your hand, your right hand, from the midst of your bosom to the end?" The passage means this: God's bosom is full of good things. That is why it is said: "The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known." This is the ineffable treasure of the Father's divinity and the fullness of all good things, from which he gives his gifts to those who are worthy of him. Since, then, he bestows his gifts from the midst of his bosom on the worthy, stretching out his right hand to them, but turns away his

Their own prophetic writings list countless lawless deeds: adulteries, idolatries and the murder of prophets. Yet they were never abandoned to the end. The prophets stayed with them even though they did such things, and among them there were appearances of angels and the presence of the Holy Spirit. What, then, is this strange new thing? What was so great a crime of theirs that they should be thrust away to the end, and the right hand of God turned away from them to the end? In saying this he hints, without naming it, at the outrage they committed against the Christ of God. "But God, our King before the ages, has worked salvation in the midst of the earth." Having gone through what came before, he takes up again his words about providence and sets out the mighty works of God's power. He fittingly utters words of piety here, so that no one should think that what was described earlier happened because God does not watch over all things or govern them. So he says: Even if these things happened in this way, we are still convinced that you, our God, whom we also know to be our King, order all things by your royal and divine judgment for the salvation of the whole world. "For God our King before the ages has worked salvation in the midst of the earth." So even if you have allowed such things to happen in one corner of the earth because of the people who live in that place, we are still convinced that you will count the people who live throughout the whole world worthy of salvation, since you have raised up your own Christ as Savior for all people. It seems to me that with this one verse he makes a kind of answer to the questions he had raised. In return for what happened to the place he has pointed to, God, he says, has worked salvation in the midst of the earth. And here too, as usual, he foretells future things as if they were past. Next he teaches what wonders God had already worked long before, saying: "You made the sea strong by your power." Instead of "You made strong," Symmachus translated, "You scattered the sea by your strength." It seems to me that, at the level of history, these words point to the people's crossing of the Red Sea, which took place under Moses. That is why Symmachus has, "You scattered the sea by your strength," and Theodotion, "You divided the sea by your power." Then he seems to me to be hinting at the Egyptians and Pharaoh when he says: "You crushed the heads of the dragons upon the water; you shattered the heads of the dragon." By the dragon he means Pharaoh, and by its heads the rulers under him. Or else he calls the Egyptians dragons, and their captains and leaders their heads. As for "You gave him as food to the peoples, the Ethiopians," one might say that their dead bodies, cast up from the sea, became food for the birds of the sky. Instead of "to the Ethiopians," Aquila translated "to those who will go out," Theodotion "to the last," and the fifth edition "to the one who has gone out." Having mentioned those who were drowned in the Red Sea, the text next calls to mind what was done after that,

saying: "You broke open springs and torrents." For it was not Moses, he says, who struck the rock and brought springs and torrents out of it. It was you, O God, who worked these marvels through Moses. The words that follow, "You dried up the rivers of Etham," might refer to the Jordan. After Moses' death the sons of Israel crossed it on foot once it had been dried up, with Joshua leading them. The figure of speech here takes in the whole: the plural is used instead of the singular. For "Etham," Aquila translated "strong rivers," and Symmachus "ancient rivers." So much for the literal sense. But someone who takes these passages figuratively will apply them to hidden and invisible powers. He will say that these powers are the dragons named here and that the sea is their dwelling. He will say that the many-headed dragon signifies the ruler of the evil spirits himself, and that it was about him that the words were spoken: "You shattered the heads of the dragon; you gave him as food to the peoples, the Ethiopians." Following the laws of allegory, the figurative interpreter [?] will also look for certain Ethiopians (1), saying that they are people blackened in soul. He will say that they eat the dragon just mentioned, in the same way that others eat the flesh of the saving Word. In keeping with this he will also try to explain figuratively the springs broken open into torrents and the rivers dried up. But we have given the sense according to the letter, and we will move on to what follows. Having shown what wonders God, the King before the ages, has worked, the prophet adds this as well: "Yours is the day, and yours is the night." For you alone, the Almighty, have brought about so great a change in things. You changed solid rock into a flowing substance and made springs and torrents come out of it. In the opposite direction, you brought the streams of rivers to the reverse condition and dried them up. In the same way you turn day into night when you will, and turn night back into day. You also set the zones of heaven with stars, appointed courses for the sun, and laid down boundaries for everything. As if by dividing borders, you divided the whole of time and cut the seasons of the year into different sections. For although time is one, and the revolution of the universe is one and the same, you, God who can do all things, divided the whole by different turnings of the year. You joined summer to spring, marked out autumn after it, and bounded winter by spring, for you formed all these things. Since, then, you, our King from eternity and before the ages, are by nature one who works great things and marvels, and who changes the things that stand ready at your nod from one state into its opposite, we rightly beg you now too to grant our supplications and to remember this. (Instead of "this," Symmachus translated "these things.") May you bring about a change in our case as well, from the evils that have overtaken us. Instead of "You prepared light and sun," Aquila translated, "You prepared the luminary and the sun." "The enemy reproached the Lord, and a foolish people provoked your name. Do not hand over to the beasts a soul that confesses you." The works of your inexpressible power are such as have been shown. We beg you to remember them

(1) Perhaps read "some Ethiopians." — Ed.

in our case as well. For now too our enemies and foes reproach not us, who have been attacked and made subject to them, but you, our God. A foolish people that does not know you as God, but boasts in demons and the error of many gods, has provoked not us but you and your name. For this reason we pray and beg you not to hand over the souls of those who confess you, defenseless, to the cruel beasts, and not to forget them altogether. Let us not become food for beasts that by nature devour souls. Such are the opposing powers, the plotters and enemies of human souls. Instead, look upon your covenant and remember your compact, by which you were pleased to save the human race when you gave them a new covenant through your Christ. Even if some have had their minds darkened and are filled with a house of iniquities because they have not received your Christ, yet you, as God who loves humankind, do not turn away from the supplications of your poor. And who might these poor be who pray for the whole people, if not the disciples and apostles of our Savior, to whom it was said: "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for yours is the kingdom of heaven"? Isaiah also bore witness to them, speaking in the person of Christ: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the poor." So these men prayed for the whole people. Every one of them might almost have said with Paul: "I could wish that I myself were accursed for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites." The prophets of God themselves, who became poor for his sake, also made these supplications on behalf of the whole nation. "Arise, O God, plead your cause. Remember the reproaches against you from the foolish all day long. Do not forget the voice of your enemies; the arrogance of those who hate you has risen continually." It is not we who have been wronged, but you. The enemy reproached you, and a foolish people provoked your name. For this reason, arise, O God, and plead your cause. According to Symmachus: "Stand up, O God, fight your own battle, and remember the reproach against you from the fool all day long. Do not forget the voice of your adversaries, that is, of those who stand against you. How long will it rise up without ceasing?" Up to this point the text continues, calling on God to rise up and plead his cause, to remember the reproach of the foolish, and not to let the voices of his enemies and the arrogance of those who continually exalt themselves be forgotten. Yet no kinder answer is attached after this, and no promise of good things is given to those who prayed, as can be found in other psalms. That is why, at its very beginning, the text foretold rejection to the end for the people it describes, and throughout added "to the end" to its prediction of grim things. Starting from this, the divine Apostle also wrote of them: "But wrath has come upon them to the end."

"We will give thanks to you, O God, we will give thanks to you, and we will call upon your name." Instead of "For the end, Do not destroy," Symmachus translated, "A victory song concerning incorruption, a psalm of Asaph." So the text is about the incorruption laid up for the righteous, for whom the prizes of victory have also been stored up. That is why it is called a victory song. It also points us to the end, about which the Apostle says: "Then comes the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, when he abolishes every rule and every authority and power. For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be abolished is death." At that end, those who have won the good contest in the present age will receive incorruptible life. The present text also shows this at its close, saying: "And all the horns of sinners I will break, and the horns of the righteous shall be exalted." In agreement with the Apostle, the present text says that the horns will be broken and then adds, "The horns of the righteous shall be exalted." This is the conclusion of the present prophecy. That is why it is called both a psalm and a song at once. It begins in the person of the righteous, saying: "We will give thanks to you, O God, we will give thanks to you, and we will call upon your name." For the confession of thanksgiving befits them alone. It was in this way that the Savior too gave thanks in the Gospels, saying to the Father: "I give thanks to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth." First they give thanks, and then they call upon his name, so as to obtain salvation from God through this calling upon him, according to the oracle that says: "And everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved." The text can also teach confession to those who in the previous psalm lamented the fall of Jerusalem and its final siege. Those who said earlier, "Why, O God, have you rejected us to the end? Your anger has flared against the sheep of your pasture," and the rest, are now taught to confess to God and to call upon his name. Since confession takes two forms, "We will give thanks to you" is necessarily said a second time here. The first presumably signifies confession of sins, and the second the thanksgiving of those who first confessed, for the good things they have received. "I will recount your wonders. When I receive the appointed time, I will judge uprightly." The sense of these words shows that they are spoken by God. For "I will judge uprightly," and again "I established its pillars" (clearly the pillars of the earth), and then "And all the horns of sinners I will break": to whom would it be fitting to say these things, if not to God? If, then, these things are said in the person of God, how can someone else who knows God cry out as if to him,

saying: "I will recount your wonders when I receive the appointed time," and then add, "For God is judge," and again, "For there is a cup of unmixed wine in the hand of the Lord"? And how, on top of all this, can he go on to say: "But I will declare it forever, I will sing to the God of Jacob, and all the horns of sinners I will break"? Consider, then, whether in these words the only-begotten Word of God is not teaching about his own works as he sets out his account of the Father. He says: "I will recount your wonders when I receive the appointed time." Aquila has, "When I receive the appointed assemblies," and Symmachus, "When I receive the congregation." It seems to me that "When I receive the appointed assemblies" or "the congregation" is fittingly said. For he promises that when he has seized the time he will recount all the Father's wonders in the Church of the nations. The Father himself promised him this Church, saying: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession." So he says: When I receive this assembly, and when I reach this time, then I will recount all your wonders among those of the nations who are turning to you. To this he adds: "I will judge uprightly." For it is a work of justice and uprightness not to admit only the Jews, or only the race descended from Abraham according to the calling given through Moses, but to choose those who are to be saved from all the nations. That is why Peter is recorded in Acts as saying: "Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him is acceptable to him." Paul too says that the gospel is preached to the Jew first and also to the Greek: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For in it the righteousness of God is revealed." In agreement with these words he says here: "I will judge uprightly." Then he adds: "The earth melted, and all who dwell in it; I established its pillars." According to Symmachus: "The earth will be established," he says, "together with those who dwell in it; I set firm its pillars." These words agree with what was said in the previous psalm. The land was besieged and given over to fire. Of it was said: "As in a thicket of trees, they cut down her doors with axes all together; with hatchet and pick they broke her down. They set your sanctuary on fire; they profaned the dwelling place of your name to the ground." Having suffered these things, it melted, and all who lived in it suffered such things because of their impieties. But while they perished, he says, I established its pillars. Who would you say these are, if not the holy apostles and all the disciples and evangelists of our Savior? For they came out of that very land and became the pillars and foundation of the Church. That is why Paul called the leaders of the apostles pillars, saying: "James and Cephas and John, who were reputed to be pillars."

"I said to the lawless, Do not act lawlessly, and to the sinners, Do not lift up your horn." God says: I established the pillars of the holy and catholic Church, choosing them out of the land that was given up and melted together with those who lived in it. But to the rest I bore witness, charging and urging them not to act lawlessly. According to Symmachus: "I said," he says, "to those who rebel, Do not rebel; and to the lawless, Do not raise your horn." "Do not lift up your horn on high, speaking iniquity with your neck." These words can be addressed to the other group, those of the circumcision who rebelled against the Savior and exalted themselves against him. Because of them their land melted, and all who dwell in it. Yet through the preaching of the apostles he also bore witness to the nations throughout the whole world that they should not act lawlessly. He told sinners not to lift up the horn of sin, not to exalt themselves or grow insolent, and not to speak injustice against God. This is what they had done before, when they gave themselves to the error of many gods and did not … the God of the universe

"For neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains; for God is judge." And these things, he says, I declared through my apostles to all people: that they should remember the judgment of God and stop all their lawlessness, being convinced that the judge of all is not far away somewhere, but fills all things and is present everywhere. So it is fitting for us to live attentively, as people who live before his eyes. For he is not far off, as though one should think he had moved far away, either to the very east, or to the western regions, or somewhere in deserts and mountains. He is present in the midst of all and is the judge of all. The work of his judgment is to give each person what he deserves, humbling one and exalting another. He humbles the proud and those who lift their horn on high, and he exalts the humble, as it is written: "God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble." That is why he says: "For neither from the outgoings and the risings of the sun, nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains." Symmachus translated this as follows: "For not from the east, nor from the west, nor from the desert of mountains; but God judges [?]

[James 4:6]

… the judge of all mixes. You will understand this from what is said in the prophecies about a cup. It is written in Jeremiah: "The Lord, the God of Israel, said to me: Take from my hand the cup of unmixed wine, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it. They will drink and vomit and go mad before the sword that I will send among them. So I took the cup from the hand of the Lord and made all the nations drink to whom the Lord sent me: Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, its kings and its rulers, to make them a desolation, an untrodden waste and a thing to hiss at; and Pharaoh king of Egypt, his servants and his nobles." And he goes on: "And all the kings of the land of the foreigners: Ashkelon and Gaza and Ekron, Idumea and Moab and the sons of Ammon, all the kings of Tyre, all the kings of Sidon, and all the kings of the island beyond the sea." After this he adds: "The Lord Almighty, the God of Israel, said: Drink and be drunk and vomit, and fall, and you shall not rise, before the sword that I will send among you. And if they refuse to take the cup from your hand to drink, you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts: You shall surely drink." Through these words the text teaches that God brings punishments the way a physician gives a bitter antidote to those who need it, so that they may vomit and empty out the wickedness that has built up in them. It teaches that Jerusalem herself would be the first to drink this draught, and then the other nations, since all of them would receive a similar cleansing through the punishments brought upon them. The present oracle, then, in keeping with the prophetic teaching, teaches that there is a cup in the hand of the Lord. In it he gathers the fruits of each person and makes them like unmixed wine. Then he hands each person the drink he deserves, mixing it in proportion to that person's deeds according to the principle of justice. For he takes into account not only each person's bad deeds but also the good ones. He weighs them as if in due measure and makes the mixture to match each person's works. The text shows this when it says: "And he tipped it from this to that," so that a single mixture might be made of each person's wicked deeds and better ones. Instead of "He tipped it from this to that," Symmachus translated, "so as to draw from it." And all the sinners of the earth will drink the dregs. For those who have committed great sins, what is laid up is no longer a mixture but the last, muddy part. That is why Symmachus has: "But the wicked of the earth will drink and drain its dregs." "But I will declare it forever, I will sing to the God of Jacob." I said all the things mentioned above to the lawless, and I gave a charge to everyone, bearing witness. But I who said above, "I will recount your wonders when I receive the appointed time," and again, "I will judge uprightly," and once more, "I [?] …"

and the other translators also rendered it in this way, giving "in Salem." But someone schooled in the divine doctrines has been taught that "not all who are descended from Israel are Israel, nor are all who are Abraham's seed his children; for it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as seed." He has further heard the same Apostle say: "For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter; his praise is not from men but from God." And again: "For we are the circumcision, who worship by the Spirit of God and put no confidence in the flesh." And he has noted the words "Look at Israel according to the flesh," which imply that there is another, true Israel, not according to the flesh but according to the spirit. Schooled in these things, he will take the true Israel to be the one signified by the meaning of the name itself. For the name is translated "one who sees God." He will therefore declare that only the discerning man, the man of knowledge and understanding, is the true Israel. It is this man whom the present passage indicates when it says: "In Israel his name is great." The prophetic word convicts the Jew of being unworthy of the name of Israel, when it addresses them and says: "Woe, sinful nation, a people full of sins"; and: "Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom; give heed to the law of God, you people of Gomorrah." The one who says of the nations, "For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is glorified among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice," and again, "For my name is great among the nations," clearly shows that the nations can be Israel, if indeed "in Israel his name is great." To the Jews, on the other hand, it was said: "But you profane it", meaning, clearly, the name of God. And again it was said to them: "Because of you my name is continually blasphemed among the nations." If, then, the present Scripture teaches that Israel is the people among whom the name of God is glorified, it becomes plain from what has been said who ought properly to be called Israel. You will understand Judea in the same way: wherever the knowledge of God is, that is Judea. This is what the Scripture shows when it says: "God is known in Judea." But this is not found in Judea, by which I mean the country of the Palestinians, since a great deal of idolatry took place there, and the Jews themselves worshipped idols there in ancient times, so that the prophets convicted them and said: "For as many as your cities were your gods, O Judah, and as many as the streets of Jerusalem were the altars on which they sacrificed to Baal." How then can this be called the Judea that possesses the knowledge of God? And why

would you not say that the land of the Egyptians is worthy of the name, since it was said of it: "And there will be an altar to the Lord in the land of Egypt," and again: "And the Lord will be known to the Egyptians"? For if Judea is found among those to whom God is known, what prevents all who have received the knowledge of God from being said to be in Judea? In the same way, then, the Church of God throughout the whole world, in which the God over all is known, may reasonably be called Judea. Nor would you be wrong to say that Judea is the whole of the divinely inspired Jewish Scripture, since it is the possession and, as it were, the surrounding country of the true Israel, because the knowledge of God is contained in it. In this way, then, the true Judea and the true Israel are to be understood alike.

You will also understand how "his place came to be in peace, and his dwelling in Zion." If the place honored among the Jews had been kept safe from sack and war, there would be reason to let the children of the Jews think it the place indicated by the Scriptures. But it has been destroyed from its foundations, having been captured many times by enemies, while his place is said to be in peace. So a place captured many times by enemies cannot truly be thought to be the place of God. That is why he did not name Jerusalem here, so that no one might fall back on the Jewish city; instead he gave the meaning of the thing, saying: "His place came to be in Salem." Salem is translated "peace"; that is why the Seventy say: "His place came to be in peace." If, then, souls were to be found even on earth that were freed from every war and lived in well-being, tranquility and calm, these too might fittingly be called the place of God, as being able to receive the divine Spirit. That is why it was said of such people: "I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people." But if such people are rarely found on earth, while in the city of God that is called heavenly God's dwelling is filled with angels and archangels, divine powers and holy spirits, then one may fittingly say that the place of God is among them, and that this is truly the peace that is here named Salem, after the Hebrew word. That is why the Apostle, who knew this city, said: "But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother." For Salem is translated "peace," and Jerusalem "vision of peace." Its home is among the divine powers in heaven, among whom God himself walks, since they are able to receive his divinity. Next comes: "And his dwelling in Zion." Then the text continues: "There he broke the might of the bows, shield and sword and war." Here again, if these things had been done in the visible, earthly Zion, there would be no need to begrudge the Jews their wish to understand it so. But if the facts themselves show the very opposite, since Zion was laid waste by the siege of its enemies, then, in keeping with the peace already explained, we must take Zion correspondingly to be either

the Church of God, or the heavenly Zion, which the divine Apostle presented when he said: "You have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels in festal gathering, and to the church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven." For there, where no sin is at work and no enemy of souls stands opposed, the might of the bows has been broken, and shield and sword have been done away with, so that it is said of those counted worthy to dwell there: "Pain and grief and sighing have fled away."

"You shine wonderfully from the everlasting mountains; the foolish in heart were troubled." Quite consistently, after presenting the place of God, he teaches that its good things are enclosed within his place, yet he sends out rays, as it were, even to those farthest away. That is why he says: "You shine wonderfully from the everlasting mountains." And what were the everlasting mountains but Zion and Salem, which were explained above? From above, then, from the heavenly heights, as from everlasting mountains, he sends the beams of the radiance of his Godhead even to those on earth and enlightens the souls of the worthy, illuminating them with his Holy Spirit. These, then, he enlightens; but those unworthy of his light he pursues by the providence of his just judgment and throws into confusion. That is why he adds: "All the foolish in heart were troubled." For since they were truly foolish in heart, or, as Symmachus has it, "arrogant in heart," they did not receive the radiance of God's light, and therefore they were troubled. These same people, "having slept their sleep, found nothing in their hands, being men of wealth." For they dreamed for a short while in the illusion of mortal life and thought highly of themselves because of their wealth; they believed they were somebody, as they reveled in the pleasures their wealth provided. But when they woke from sleep, on departing from this present life, they found that they had nothing and held nothing in their hands. That is why it is said somewhere: "Do not be afraid when a man becomes rich, and when the glory of his house is increased; for when he dies he will not take it all with him, nor will his glory go down with him." Fittingly, then, those who are truly foolish in heart "were troubled at the rebuke of the God of Jacob," or, as Symmachus has it, "at his indignation." For at that time, coming under the sentence of God's just judgment, they will fittingly be troubled, since they dozed while mounted on their horses, that is, on their licentious bodies, when they ought to have stayed awake and kept sober, remembering the divine command that says: "Keep awake, for you know neither the day nor the hour." But they dozed and slept their sleep, given over to dreams and fantasies, and used their own bodies as horses mad with lust. All these, then, who are called at one point "foolish in heart," at another "men of wealth," and now "those mounted on horses," dozed for a while during their mortal life, or, as Symmachus has it, were stupefied,

carried away by a stupor and drunkenness of soul; then they slept their sleep, given over to vain fantasies; and finally, when they were awakened, they were troubled at the rebuke of the God of Jacob. This was our Savior, the Word of God, who is recorded as having appeared to Jacob as God, and who has received from the Father the judgment of all.

"You are terrible, and who will withstand you? From then on is your wrath." He is said to be terrible to those who refused to receive the beams of the divine light. That is why earlier the psalmist addressed God himself, saying: "You shine wonderfully from the everlasting mountains," while now he says to the same one: "You are terrible, and who will withstand you?" So the same one is both the giver of light and terrible: to those on the right he supplies light, while to those on the left he is terrible, and to them he will say: "Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels." Then he goes on: "From then on is your wrath." From when, if not from the time when those mounted on horses dozed, and the foolish in heart slept their sleep? For from then on they stored up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath, so that it is said to them: "Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled." For each person, from the moment he sins, stores up wrath for himself, wrath being understood as the punishment reserved for wrongdoers.

Next it is said: "From heaven you made judgment heard." Note carefully that it does not say "you made," but "you made heard." For before the time of judgment arrives, he has caused the words about judgment to be heard, through the divine readings, by those who live out their mortal life before the judgment. Now, then, he has made the coming judgment audible from heaven; but when the time of God's just judgment comes, "the earth," it says, "feared and was still when God arose to judgment, to save all the meek of the earth." Through these words the text clearly shows the purpose of the judgment: it is to save the meek of the earth. For of the ungodly it is said: "The ungodly will not rise in the judgment, nor sinners in the council of the righteous; for the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the ungodly will perish." When God, then, arises to judgment to save all the meek of the earth, the earth will fear and be still. For the meek will obtain salvation, while the others will be handed over to wrath; and the rest of the earth, and those who have attained [?] condition, will cease from their turmoil, having taken on the fear of God.

"For the thought of man will confess to you, and the remnant of thought will keep festival for you." This too, he says, will take place when God arises to judgment to save all the meek of the earth. And what does "The thought of man will confess to you" mean? Every tongue, and every reasoning and thought of men, will confess to God at the time of judgment, when the hidden things of men will be made manifest. "And the remnant of thought," it says, "will keep festival for you." And what could the remnant of thought be, if not the reasoning that has been cleansed of every evil

thought, being like those of whom it is said: "A remnant has come to be, chosen by grace"? In this way, then, it is called "the remnant of thought," and so it will keep festival at that time, since in due season it will have received the promises of the heavenly kingdom.

"Make vows and pay your vows to the Lord your God, all you who are around him; to the one who is terrible and takes away the spirits of rulers, who is terrible among the kings of the earth." Having completed his account of God's judgment, he now turns to exhortation and commands all of us to make vows and to pay our vows to the Lord our God. Since there is still time in the present life, he urges that this must be done. He is accustomed to call promises "vows"; that is why it is said: "If you make a vow, do not delay to pay it; it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay." Let each of us, then, pay his own resolve and his own promise as a vow, remembering the one who said: "Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Lord; and call on me in the day of affliction, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me." So now, he says, make vows and pay them. For a time will come when "all who are around him will bring gifts." For at the time of his kingdom, "the kings of Tarshish and the islands will bring gifts, the kings of the Arabs and of Sheba will offer gifts, and all the kings of the earth will worship him." Then, at any rate, when he sits on the throne of his glory, all will worship him with gifts, that is, with the fruits that each one brings. Therefore, while there is still time, he urges us from now on to make vows and pay them, so that, having stored up our own treasures, we may bring them to him in due season and become worthy to be among those who surround his throne. For all who are around him will bring him gifts, while he is terrible to those who do not draw near to him or bring him gifts. That is why it is added: "To the one who is terrible and takes away the spirits of rulers, who is terrible among the kings of the earth." For the words "My spirit shall not remain upon the sons of men" will also be said of those who were once called rulers and leaders, and who were counted worthy of the Holy Spirit but did not live worthily of the grace. From them the spirit is taken away, so that, deprived of it, they may be handed over to the punishment they deserve. Symmachus has: "To the lawgiver, who takes away the spirit of leaders, and is terrible to the kings of the earth."

FOR THE END, [?] A PSALM OF [?]

"With my voice I cried to the Lord, with my voice to God, and he gave heed to me." The psalm is said to be of Asaph, but it is attributed to the person of Jeduthun, on whose behalf its contents were composed. Hence Symmachus translated "Through Jeduthun," and Aquila "For Jeduthun." Here [?], having composed the words before us, handed them to Jeduthun to practice, like a teacher to a pupil, or like a physician giving a healing

remedy to someone in need of treatment, so that the patient might use it and benefit. In the earlier psalms David wrote on behalf of the same man, sometimes an ode, sometimes a psalm. That is why Psalm 38 was headed: "For the end, for Jeduthun, an ode of David." That this man is said to have lived at the same time as David and Asaph is shown by the book of Chronicles, as we demonstrated earlier. It seems to me that Jeduthun needed teaching on the doctrine of Providence, because he saw in human life many godless and impious people exalted and boasting, reveling in wealth and abundance, while the righteous, by contrast, were humbled and oppressed by the impious. It is likely, then, that he was vexed at these things and raised certain questions with David himself and with Asaph, of the sort that others among the ancients raised, such as the one who said: "Why do the ungodly prosper, and grow old in wealth? Their offspring are as they desire, and their children play, taking up the psaltery and the lyre. And they say to the Lord: Depart from me; I do not wish to know your ways." Since Jeduthun was, it seems, raising such difficulties, David at times and Asaph at others, like teachers and physicians, gave him teachings to cure such an opinion. So in Psalm 38 David taught him to say such things as these: "I said, I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue. I set a guard on my mouth when the sinner stood against me; I was struck dumb and humbled and kept silent," and what follows, which we set out and explained in their proper places. Again in Psalm 61 the same David taught the same man, saying: "Shall not my soul be subject to God? For from him comes my salvation. For he is my God and my Savior, my helper; I shall not be shaken any more. How long will you set upon a man? All of you are murderers." What meaning these words have has also been explained, according to the grace that was given. In keeping with these, Asaph too, through the words before us, hands on to the same man the teaching that he should not be troubled by the trials of life, nor by what he had learned from earlier prophecies about the uprising of the ungodly and the humbling of God's people. Instead, in such straits, he should take refuge in God himself as in a harbor of salvation, devote himself to supplications to him, and say the things that Asaph, as his teacher, handed on to him through the present psalm. And indeed, having received this lesson, Jeduthun healed his own soul, chanting it over himself like a charm and saying: "With my voice I cried to the Lord, with my voice to God, and he gave heed to me." For, he says, I made myself such as to be worthy of God's attention, and so he gave heed to me; and I uttered such words and cries as to be worthy of God's hearing. That is why Symmachus has: "With my voice to God; and when I cried out to God, he lent me his ears." For through these words Jeduthun was taught not to think that God stands somewhere far away from

…calling upon him. For if, as soon as he sent up his voice, he perceived that God had heard him, he was taught by the facts themselves that the Divine is present everywhere, and that the eyes of Providence watch over those

But also in the day of my affliction, he says, I sought out God with my hands by night before him, and I was not deceived. That the afflictions of the righteous are many (since an untested man is unproved), the divine words teach in every way. But that in their afflictions they became better than themselves, giving proof of their own endurance, and yet were not so confounded as to grow dizzy and be thrown into confusion, is taught by the one who said, "In affliction you have enlarged me," and by the divine Apostle, who says: "Afflicted, but not crushed; struck down, but not destroyed; persecuted, but not forsaken." So here too he says: In the day of my affliction I sought out God. For I did not look to those who afflicted me, nor to those who exalted themselves; rather, turning the eye of my soul toward God at the very time of affliction, I sought him out. And I sought him with my hands, having been taught to lift up holy hands, according to the word that says: "I want the men to pray, lifting up holy hands." And I did this not only by day but also by night, lifting up my hands before him, and seeking him both through prayer and through words addressed to him. Therefore, doing these things, I was not deceived; for when I sought him he was found by me; therefore he attended to me and lent me his ear. Instead of "with my hands by night before him, and I was not deceived," Symmachus rendered it in this way: "My hand was stretched out by night continually." This, then, I had as my greatest and only consolation. Otherwise, I would not bear any man who wished to comfort and care for me in the time of my affliction. Therefore he adds: My soul refused to be comforted; or, according to Symmachus, "My soul would not be persuaded to be consoled." I did not heed the men who tried to console and comfort me in other ways; but I remembered God and was gladdened, for the remembrance of God was enough to give me gladness. But also, he says, I mused, and my spirit grew faint; instead of which Symmachus rendered, "I talked within myself and was fainting." When, he says, I talked with myself, I fainted; and when I mused by myself, then my spirit grew faint; but when I remembered God, I was filled with gladness. And seeking him with my hands by night, I was not deceived; for I found him as though standing near me and hearing my voice. My eyes anticipated the watches; I was troubled and did not speak. The thoughts that afflicted me, he says, were of this kind. For since I saw the casting off of the people, which the prophetic words spoken earlier had foretold, I was troubled, as was natural, and I pondered within myself whether the evil would be incurable for them. For that they would be cast off for a certain time, and

that they would suffer this to the end, I believed on the strength of the prophecy that says: "Why, O God, have you cast us off to the end? Has your wrath been kindled against the sheep of your pasture?" And I was perplexed within myself as I thought over these things: "Will the Lord cast off forever, or will he not be well pleased again?" and what follows. Reckoning these things, I was troubled. Yet I brought to mind the ancient days and the years of old, gathering from the ancient Scriptures how often, when they had sinned, he cast them off and then brought them back, and how, when they were ungodly, he handed them over to their enemies and then recovered them again. Why, then, did he in former times call them back even after terrible offenses, not casting them off to the end nor cutting off his mercy, while now he will do none of these things, but will forget his own love for humankind? Will he who is long-suffering, abounding in mercy and full of compassion forget to have pity? These things I reasoned within myself by night, and I searched my spirit, investigating and testing my own thoughts and examining my spirit, to see whether it might suggest something to heal my perplexities. Instead of "My eyes anticipated the watches," Symmachus says: "My eyes held back from looking up." For gathering my thoughts into myself, I shut my eyes, so that I would not be drawn away from the matter at hand by attending to the things of sense. So, shutting the eyes of the body, I was perplexed within myself, not uttering anything aloud, nor speaking to another, but pondering by myself. Therefore, instead of "I was troubled and did not speak" and what follows, Symmachus has: "I was perplexed and did not speak. I reckoned the former days; I recalled the years of old. But [?] by night I talked with my heart, and my spirit was like a man pondering." Being thus wakeful and keeping vigil through the nights, I considered the things said earlier, where it was said: "As in a thicket of trees, they hewed down her doors together with axes; with hatchet and chisel they broke her down. They profaned to the ground the dwelling-place of your name. They said in their heart, their kindreds together: Come, let us make the feasts of God cease from the earth. We have not seen our signs; there is no longer a prophet, and he will no longer know us." Over these things, then, I was perplexed, wondering whether there would be any healing for those who had suffered these evils. And it is likely that Jeduthun, having heard Asaph's prophecy and reckoned these things within himself, brought his difficulty to the prophet as to a teacher and put a question to him, and, as if setting forth a proposition, said: "What then, O prophet? Since you have prophesied these things, I wish to know and to learn: Will the Lord cast off forever, and will he not be well pleased again? Or will he cut off his mercy to the end, from generation to generation? Or will God forget to have pity, or will he shut up his compassions in his wrath?" And in answer to these propositions

Asaph gave his teaching, writing the psalm on behalf of Jeduthun himself and teaching him to say: "With my voice I cried to the Lord, with my voice to God, and he attended to me." He was instructing him not to pry into the counsels of God, but to devote himself to prayer and to give his mind to that alone, revering and praising God's judgments. For his judgments are unsearchable, and his ways untraceable

And I said, Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High. Instead of this, Aquila says: "And I said, It is my sickness; this is a change of the right hand of the Most High"; Symmachus: "My wounding is a repetition of the right hand of the Most High"; and the Fifth Edition says: "And I said, My birth-pangs are a change of the right hand of the Most High." In addition to my earlier perplexities, he says, I also considered this within myself: that such thoughts, by which I was just now perplexed, are my sickness, or are birth-pangs, or are my wounds. For it was from weakness of soul that we put forth such words, and from a wound of the soul. For I uttered such things because I was wounded and suffered with them as for my own limbs, and also because I was in labor as for my own flesh and blood. And I suffered these things because I saw a change come about in the right hand of the Most High. For of old it worked many wonders and bestowed extraordinary benefits on the people; but now a change has come about in the right hand of the Most High. Therefore birth-pangs seized me; I confess that my soul was wounded by sickness and weakness of understanding. And I saw the change of the right hand of God as I remembered his ancient works. Therefore he says: I remembered the works of the Lord, from the beginning of your wonders. And I will meditate on all your works, and I will muse on your doings. For these, Symmachus rendered thus: "I recalled the designs of the Lord, going over your ancient marvels; and I meditated on all your deeds, and I recounted your devices," bringing these back to memory. Then, hearing now that "you have cast off to the end, and your wrath has been kindled against the sheep of your pasture," I reasonably concluded that it is a change of the right hand of the Most High. For these are signs of a reversal and change in God's ancient care for the people. O God, your way is in the holy place; what god is great like our God? You are the God who works wonders. He has perceived the change of the right hand of the Most High, and what kind of things it accomplished: instead of benefiting one nation, it became the benefactor of all nations; for he made his power known no longer to one people, but to all the nations and all the peoples. Therefore, struck with amazement and wonder, I say: O God, your way is in the holy place. For to comprehend your way is beyond mortal nature, so that one might fittingly say: "O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how untraceable his ways!" It is no longer fitting, then, to pry

into things or to search out what may not be spoken; for "who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?" Therefore, having considered these things in due season, he is overwhelmed by the depth of God's wisdom and says: O God, your way is in the holy place; what god is great like our God? You are the God who works wonders. What kind of wonders he means, he explains next, saying: You made known your power among the peoples; instead of which Symmachus rendered: "You made your strength known among the nations." For just as once of old you redeemed your people with your arm, the sons of Jacob and Joseph, when you set them free from the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage, so now too, when the change of the right hand of the Most High has come about, you made known your power among the peoples, and your strength among the nations. The waters saw you, O God, the waters saw you and were afraid, and the depths were troubled. Having said, quite consistently, "You made known your power among the peoples" (or, according to Symmachus, "You made your strength known among the nations"), he now presents the power of the New Covenant, prophetically foretelling things to come. Therefore he says: The waters saw you, O God, the waters saw you and were afraid. For just as once of old, during the journey of the sons of Israel out of Egypt, the sea saw and fled, and the Jordan turned back, so too at the coming of Emmanuel, that is, God with us, when he came to the river Jordan, the waters saw him and were astounded. Moreover, the multitudes of the peoples gathered in the Churches of God, which are likened to waters according to the prophetic word that says, "The voice of many nations, like the sound of many waters," saw with the eyes of the soul the God who had come to dwell among men, and took on a saving fear, of which it is said: "The fear of God is the beginning of wisdom." For as long as these waters were blind, they did not see God, nor did they fear him; but now they have greatly benefited from the sight and knowledge of the Word who came to dwell among them. And again, according to the history, when the Savior made the disciples get into the boat and go ahead to the other side, and then in the fourth watch of the night came to them walking on the sea, then too the waters saw him and were afraid. And also, when he rebuked the winds and the sea and there was a great calm, the depths were troubled, and there was a great roar of water. These things were fulfilled in agreement with the prophecy according to the letter. But according to the sense, the waters (I mean the church multitudes gathered from all the nations) made a beginning of wisdom, taking on the divine fear according to "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom"; while the depths, which are different from the waters, were troubled, so as to raise a roar and an uproar. You might say that the depths are the ranks of the unbelieving nations that rose up against the Church from time to time and stirred up persecutions against her.

The first, then, the waters, feared God, while the depths just described were troubled; and besides those mentioned there is a third rank, that of the clouds, which gave voice. Who were the clouds, if not those that were commanded not to rain on the former vineyard, according to the oracle that says, "And I will command the clouds not to rain upon it" (clearly meaning the people of the circumcision)? And the clouds full of water that do not rain on the old vineyard, who might they be but the Savior's disciples and apostles and evangelists, who distributed the heavenly rain throughout the whole inhabited world and gave voice, so that their sound went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world? Therefore it is said: The clouds gave voice; for indeed your arrows pass through. And what are the arrows, if not the saving and chosen ones that wound the souls of those who are being saved, by which the bride of Christ, the Church, confesses that she has been wounded, saying: "For I am wounded with love"? And the Savior himself was named an arrow, according to the prophet who said: "He made me as a chosen arrow, and in his quiver he hid me." But the Father's arrow was his only-begotten Word, while the Son's arrows were the apostles and his divine and fiery oracles. Therefore it is said in the psalm about the beloved: "Your arrows are sharpened; peoples shall fall beneath you." So here too it is said: For indeed your arrows pass through. For the arrows of Christ run about everywhere, passing through as they preach; therefore the clouds gave voice. But also, he says, The voice of your thunder was in the wheel. Here by thunder he hints at the gospel proclamation. For just as the voice of thunder is a heavenly cry that surpasses all human power, so too the gospel proclamation, being heavenly, held no merely human strength. For it did not set out from mortal counsel, but filled the whole world with divine power. Therefore the Savior also named his apostles Boanerges, which is interpreted "sons of thunder." Accordingly, here too, consistently with what precedes, it is said: The voice of your thunder in the wheel. By the wheel he signifies the whole of life; for in Ezekiel too the whole life of men is called a wheel within a wheel. The world, indeed, is a wheel, being spherical and moving in a circle. But here the wheel is the life of men, which turns without ceasing; therefore it is also called a wheel within the wheel. According to Aquila: "The voice of your thunder in the wheel"; according to Symmachus: "The sound of your thunder in the wheel"; according to Theodotion: "The voice of your thunder in the wheel." And see how in all the translators it is named a wheel; for the Hebrew word too reads bagelgel, which means "in the wheel"; and it is named in the same way in Ezekiel. When you come to that passage, you will note that divine Scripture too knows the vault that encompasses all things as a wheel. Hence they say that the world is spherical. For in Ezra too, Zerubbabel

carried off the prize before the king by saying: "Great is the heaven, and great is the sun, for it turns in the circle of the heaven and returns to its own place in one day." These things, then, belong to the contemplation of nature. But the present verses foretell the power of the gospel theophany: how through it the multitudes of the nations came to know God, while the depths were troubled; how the clouds already mentioned gave voice; how his arrows passed through; how the voice of his thunder came to be in the wheel; and, on top of all these, how his lightnings shone upon the world. What might you call his lightnings, if not the radiant gifts of the Holy Spirit that flash throughout the whole world? "For there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit. To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another faith," and the rest. These, being God's choicest gifts, flash forth and illuminate the Church

Your way is in the sea, and your paths in many waters, and your footprints will not be known. Consistently with what has been explained, the earth was shaken and quaked. For instead of "and trembled," all the translators have "and quaked." And the earth quaked in the sense in which it is said in the Gospels: "And when the Savior entered Jerusalem, the whole city was shaken, saying: Who is this?" For just as the inhabitants of the city were indicated by the place, so too here the oracle says that the inhabitants of the earth were stirred and shaken. For every ear has been moved by the gospel proclamation, which has been preached as a testimony to all the nations. And consistently the earth was shaken and quaked, or was stirred, because of what was said before. For if his lightnings shone upon the world, if the voice of his thunder resounded in the wheel, if his arrows pass through all, if the clouds gave their voice, it followed from all of these that the earth was stirred and shaken. And how his way came to be in the sea, and his paths in many waters, and how his footprints are not known, you will learn if you attend to his promise to the disciples, which says: "Go and make disciples of all the nations in my name"; and, "Behold, I am with you all the days, until the end of the age." For, being invisibly present with his disciples everywhere on earth, he journeyed in the sea of life and in the many waters of the nations; and he did this by an invisible and unseen power. Therefore it is said: And your footprints will not be known. These things, then, were fulfilled at the saving theophany. And these things, he says, came about in this way at his coming among men, in accordance with the change of the right hand of the Most High, just as of old too with the former people, when he led them out of the land of Egypt and brought them through the sea. For then too, displaying his mighty deeds, he made a way and paths in many waters, so that, as he went ahead of them, all Israel followed him

on the passage through the sea, while his own journey was unknown and incomprehensible to men; when also he led his people like sheep by the hand of Moses and Aaron. Another interpreter, then, will refer all the present verses to the exodus from Egypt, saying that "The waters saw you, O God, the waters saw you and were afraid; the depths were troubled, a great roar of water" was fulfilled at that time, and he will refer the whole passage accordingly to the history of what was done then. But I could not find how the statements that follow were fulfilled according to the letter. For the law of Moses does not record that any clouds at that time gave voice in a bodily way, nor that perceptible arrows passed through, nor that his lightnings shone upon the whole world during the time they were in the wilderness. So I have set forth the interpretation of these passages that occurred to me. Which of the interpretations given one ought to choose, the reader will know by divine (1) judgment.

OF UNDERSTANDING. FOR ASAPH. PSALM 77. Attend, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth. The text, urging us toward an understanding of its contents, gave itself the title "Of Understanding"; for we need understanding in our hunt for the meaning before us. First, then, one might reasonably ask whose person it is that says at the beginning: "Attend, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth." For it is not fitting for either Asaph or David to say these things, since they were not lawgivers; nor was it fitting for either Asaph or David to say "your ear to the words of my mouth," for they did not offer words of their own, but served the will of the divine Spirit. Therefore it is entitled "Of Understanding," so that we may understand who it is that says these things, who his people are, and what the law is; for it seems to be different from the law of Moses. These questions are resolved by the Gospel, in which it is said: "All these things Jesus spoke to the crowds in parables, and without a parable he did not speak to them, so that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled, saying: I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden since the foundation of the world." Through what prophet were these things spoken, if not through Asaph, the author of the present psalm? Some, not understanding this, added in the Gospel the words "through Isaiah the prophet"; but in the accurate copies, without the addition "through Isaiah," it says simply this: "So that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled, saying: I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden since the foundation of the world." These words are indeed found in the present psalm, not in the prophecy of Isaiah. Accordingly, on the evidence of the Gospel citation, it must be the Savior, and no one else, who here says in his own person: "Attend, my people, to my law." And so that we might understand him, he gave it the heading "Of Understanding," so that neither psalm nor song nor anything of the kind

(1) Perhaps "his own."

[?] …to think that the words are [?], but rather Christ's teaching to his own people, that is, to his Church, as he gives instructions about the transgressions of the Jewish nation. You will see that his people is a different one from the people accused in what follows if you set beside these words the prophecy of Zechariah, in which it is said: "Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; proclaim it, daughter of Jerusalem. For behold, I am coming, and I will dwell in your midst, says the Lord. And many nations will flee for refuge to the Lord, and they will be my people, and I will be their God. And you will know that the Lord Almighty has sent me to you." Notice how in these words the Lord acknowledges that he has been sent by another, the Lord Almighty, and promises to gather a people for himself out of all the nations. So it is this same Word of God who addressed the people from the nations, saying: "Give heed, my people, to my law." He teaches that his law is the Gospel. Isaiah also prophesied about it, saying: "For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, and he will judge between the nations." Jeremiah too called it a new covenant, saying: "Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers." And Isaiah again cried out about the Savior, saying: "Behold my servant, whom I have chosen, my chosen one, in whom my soul has delighted. He will bring forth judgment to the nations. He will not quarrel or cry out, and his voice will not be heard outside. A bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, but he will bring forth judgment in truth. He will shine forth and not be crushed until he has established judgment on the earth; and in his name the nations will hope." For in place of "and in his name the nations will hope," the Hebrew has "and in his law," and all the other translators have likewise agreed in rendering it "and in his law." So in the present words Christ urges his own people from the nations to give heed to his law. He wants them to give heed and not to listen carelessly, but to study his law attentively and understand it. And he also bids them to incline their ear to the words of his mouth and give heed to his law, since he gave his teachings in parables. That is why he adds: "I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter riddles from of old." The scripture of the holy Gospels teaches the same thing where it says: "Jesus spoke all these things to the crowds in parables, and without a parable he did not speak to them, so that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: I will open my mouth in parables; I will pour forth things hidden since the foundation." For in place of "I will utter riddles from of old," Matthew, who was a Hebrew, used his own rendering and said, "I will pour forth things hidden since the foun-

-dation." Aquila rendered this as "I will rain down riddles from the very beginning," and Symmachus as "I will make ancient riddles gush forth." Since the Word of God was about to bring charges against the former people and set out the reasons why it was cast off, he had to bid his own Church to give heed to what was said and to understand the charges laid out against the people of old. That way it would not fall into the same sins. Instead, by learning from the account of them what kind of end overtook them, it would come to its senses through their example. After saying, "I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter riddles from of old," he brings forward the charges against the former people. He uses those events as a parable, that is, as an example for our admonition. In another sense too, the present passage lists the transgressions of the Jewish nation, since earlier it was said: "O God, why have you cast us off forever? Why has your wrath been kindled against the sheep of your pasture?" along with everything else that was said about the siege that overtook them. In the present words he sets out the causes of these things. And in the psalm before this one it was said: "Will the Lord cast off forever, and will he never again be pleased? Or will he cut off his mercy forever, from generation to generation? Or will God forget to have pity, or in his wrath will he shut up his compassion?" Since such questions had been raised, it was fitting for him to list here the causes of the wrath that came upon the Jewish nation to the end. The Savior himself in the Gospels also addressed the same people in words much like these, saying: "How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing! Behold, your house is left to you desolate."

"All that we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us." The first words were spoken as if by a single person, and the words themselves have shown whose person it was. But here he includes others too. He comes down from his divinity and speaks in a more human way, as if in the person of the man he assumed, who came from the seed of David according to the flesh. The Gospel records this man's birth, saying: "The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham." So he includes the disciples and apostles, who were of the same race as he was according to the flesh, and goes through the subject in the plural, saying: "All that we have heard and known."
