When he was summoning his own people, setting his own law before them, and urging them to incline their ear to his words, he delivered the command as a single person, with royal authority. But now, when he summarizes the narrative of the ancient readings, he makes the speech a shared one. He recalls things done long ago and goes back over what the historical Scripture reveals, as though it were known to everyone. That is why he says: "All that we have heard and known." Not everyone hears and knows, however, but only those who understand the words. That is why Philip said to the eunuch: "Do you understand what you are reading?" Nor did the fathers tell these things to everyone. We, at any rate, who came to the divine word from the nations, cannot name as teachers of the divine lessons

our fathers according to the flesh. But the Savior speaks these words in his own person and in the person of his apostles, disciples and evangelists, who were descended according to the flesh from the same fathers, saying: "All that we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us." They received these things from their fathers and announce them to us from the nations, since we did not know them. They teach us what happened to the people of old. These things were heard in succession by children from their fathers, then passed from them to later generations, and from these were handed down again in memory to their children's children. That is why it is said: "It was not hidden from their children to another generation, declaring the praises of the Lord, and his mighty acts, and the wonders that he did." Many things have been handed down to us by the fathers which God did to benefit them. But one was more necessary than all the rest: the testimony, and the law in the testimony, which he gave them in writing. He commanded them to meditate on it and to hand on the study of it to their children and the descendants who would follow in succession. That is why he says: "And he raised up a testimony in Jacob and established a law in Israel." The "testimony" was the name for the tent of testimony. In it lay the ark of the covenant with the law inside the ark, the cherubim and the mercy seat, the lampstand, the table, and the bread of the presence. Moses was commanded to make these, and he built them according to the pattern shown to him on the mountain. That law and that testimony were given long ago to Jacob and to Israel. But since those who received them transgressed, he rightly prepared for himself another people and another testimony: the body of Christ, which is the temple of God the Word who dwells in it. He himself taught this when he said: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." Besides these, he also hands down another law to his own people, the law of the Gospel. That is why at the beginning of this passage he said: "Give heed, my people, to my law." The old law and the old solemn testimony, however, he appointed for the former people (Symmachus rendered it this way: "And he established a solemn testimony for Jacob"). He commanded them to make these things known to their sons and descendants, so that no generation would miss them and the teaching of the law would endure even to those born afterward. That is why it is said: "So that another generation might know, sons yet to be born, and they will arise and declare them to their sons." The result and the purpose of studying the law was this: "That they might set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, and seek out his commandments; that they might not become like their fathers, a crooked and embittering generation, a generation that did not set its heart aright, and whose spirit was not faithful to God." And what was the earlier generation of the fathers if not the one in the time of Moses himself? It was because of that generation

that Moses broke the tablets of the law after he received them. Moses himself called them a crooked and perverse generation, addressing them directly and saying: "Blemished children, crooked and perverse generation, is this how you repay the Lord? Are you so foolish a people, and not wise?" But so that those who came later would not turn out like their fathers, he gave them the law in writing, along with the solemn testimony. In it he accuses the fathers, but he charged and solemnly warned the children not to become like their fathers or like the former generation, which did not set its heart aright, and whose spirit was not faithful to God. For that generation was not bad by nature, nor

evil in its makeup. By its own choice it refused to obey God and embittered him, and through its perversity it became crooked. That is why Symmachus renders: "A generation without purpose in its heart, and unsteadfast toward God in its spirit."

"The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting with bows, turned back in the day of battle." The good and loving Lord showed the first forefathers of the Jewish nation, through Moses, works greater than any words can describe. But they became stiff-necked and truly "a foolish people and not wise," "a crooked and perverse generation." Once the first generation had been shown to be like this, he gave a law to those who came after. In it he laid down and solemnly declared what they were to do and what they were not to do. He urged them not to imitate their fathers, or the crooked and embittering generation that did not set its heart aright and whose spirit was not faithful to God. But they became worse than their fathers. They gained nothing from the written law handed down to them and plunged into the depths of wickedness. The first of these were the sons of Ephraim. They had been given a special honor: their tribe and their territory were preferred above the whole nation, and they were the first to receive the ark of God and the tent of testimony that Moses had built in the wilderness. Shiloh, where the tent and the sanctuary stood before Jerusalem, belonged to the tribe of Ephraim. Yet though they were the first to receive this honor, they became idolaters. The history of what they did can be gathered from the book of Judges. The present psalm also convicts them further on, when it says of them: "He rejected the tent of Joseph and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim"; and again: "And he rejected the tent of Shiloh, the tabernacle where he had dwelt among men." It also gives the reason: "They were turned into a crooked bow. And they provoked him to anger on their hills and moved him to jealousy with their carved images." So it is fitting that the present passage too says: "The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back in the day of battle." He shows more clearly how they turned back when he says: "And they became a crooked bow." For they ought to have shot

at the enemies of God and fought them. Instead, by worshiping idols, they took up war against God. That is why he adds: "They did not keep the covenant of God, and they refused to walk in his law." By "the sons of Ephraim" he also figuratively refers to the rest of the whole nation, meaning those who were like them in their ways even if they did not belong to the same tribe. Indeed, those who in later times broke away from Jerusalem and worshiped idols in Samaria were sons of Ephraim. So, having called the transgressors of the whole nation sons of Abraham [?], he rightly condemns them all together, saying: "And they forgot his benefits and his wonders that he had shown them, the wonders he did before their fathers in the land of Egypt, in the plain of Tanis." They forgot everything that had been shown to their fathers and took up arms against God. They refused to walk in his law, although both the ability and the will lay within their power. But though they had the ability, they refused to use their choice rightly. They turned their backs on God and forgot his wonders of old. What wonders were these, if not the ones done in Egypt itself, and not in all of Egypt, but in the plain of Tanis? Moses did not reveal this in his own Scripture. But Asaph, being a prophet, teaches through these words that the wonders worked in Egypt through Moses were performed in the plain of Tanis. He says it again further on: "How he set his signs in Egypt and his wonders in the plain of Tanis." And why in the plain of Tanis? Because there above all the power of demons held sway. At that time the demons who had their seat in Tanis were very powerful. The prophet Isaiah shows this in his vision about Egypt, when he says: "The rulers of Tanis will be fools; the wise counselors of the king, their counsel will be made foolish. How will you say to the king, 'We are sons of wise men, sons of the kings of old'? Where are your wise men? Let them tell you and declare to you what the Lord has planned against Egypt. The rulers of Tanis have failed, and the rulers of Memphis have perished." These were probably evil demons who promised a kind of wisdom through oracles and divinations, and by this means became counselors to those who ruled the various districts of Egypt. Or perhaps those who practiced Egyptian sorcery and opposed Moses with their magic arts were the rulers of Tanis and the wise counselors of the king? So the present passage rightly teaches that what was done in Egypt through Moses took place in the plain of Tanis.

"He split the sea and led them through; he made the waters stand like a wineskin." He summed up in a single phrase what was done in Egypt itself, saying: "the wonders he did in the land of Egypt," and adding something we did not know: "in the plain of Tanis." What these wonders were, the Scripture of Moses relates at length. The present psalm summarizes them

later on, when it says: "He turned their rivers into blood, and their streams of rain, so that they could not drink. He sent the dog-fly among them, and it devoured them," and what follows. These things were done to the Egyptians in the plain of Tanis. For now the passage passes over them and puts first the benefits to the people: how they crossed the sea when the waters were divided into many parts. This is shown by the passage that says: "To him who divided the Red Sea into parts and led Israel through the midst of it." The children of the Hebrews say that the sea was divided into twelve sections, matching the number of the twelve tribes of the people, so that each tribe crossed separately along the path assigned to it. As the waters stood apart and dry land appeared between them, the waters naturally gathered together. Pressed against one another, they arched upward and rose into the air itself, curved and suspended, enclosed by the air as if in a wineskin. That is why it is said: "He made the waters stand like a wineskin." After so great a wonder, "he led them," it says, "with a cloud by day." The cloud overshadowed them and gave them shelter, so that they would not be worn down by the scorching heat of the sun. Matching the cloud by day, a pillar of fire went before them at night and made it as bright as day for them. That is why it is said: "And all the night with a light of fire." After this it says: "He split a rock in the wilderness and gave them drink as from a great deep." Notice how here too he called the abundance of water a "deep." In place of "he split a rock," Aquila rendered "he cleft rocks in the wilderness," following the Hebrew text. This shows that it was not one rock that poured out water for them, but many. That is why the divine Apostle points this out, saying: "For they drank from a spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ." The rock followed them everywhere, as it were, and was present at every stage of the journey, at every resting place and in every location. If you look carefully, you will find this in the Scripture of Moses as well. In Exodus it is said: "And they encamped at Rephidim, and there was no water for the people to drink. And the people reviled Moses." And further on: "The Lord said to Moses: Go on ahead of the people, and take with you some of the elders of the people, and the rod with which you struck the sea, and go. Behold, I am standing there before you on the rock at Horeb. And you shall strike the rock, and water will come out of it, and the people will drink. And Moses did so." That is in Exodus. In Numbers it is said: "And the sons of Israel, the whole congregation, came into the wilderness of Zin, and there was no water for the congregation, and they gathered against Moses and Aaron. And the people reviled Moses." And further on: "The Lord spoke

to Moses, saying: Take the rod and assemble the congregation, you and Aaron your brother, and speak to the rock before their eyes, and it will give its waters. And you will bring water out of the rock for them and give drink to the congregation and their cattle." Since the rock evidently supplied water in different places, it is fitting that the present passage says about the first: "He split a rock in the wilderness and gave them drink as from a great deep"; and about the other it adds next: "And he brought water out of a rock and made waters flow down like rivers." Yet even though so much was provided for them, they still went on sinning, and they sinned not against themselves but against him. They committed their sin against God himself, acting impiously by speaking against him. That is why he adds: "They embittered the Most High in a waterless place." Aquila has "to [?] the Most High in a trackless place," and Symmachus, "to quarrel with the Most High in thirst in a trackless place." Moses taught why they embittered the Most High in a waterless place. After he had provided them with water from the rock, he relates: "And he called the name of that place Testing and Reviling, because of the reviling of the sons of Israel and because they tested the Lord, saying: Is God among us or not?"

"And they tested God in their hearts by asking for food for their souls. And they spoke against God." Moses also teaches how they spoke against God, when he says: "And the whole congregation of the sons of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron and said to them: If only we had died, struck down by the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the pots and ate our fill of bread! For you have brought us out to kill this whole congregation with hunger." After this Moses said to the people: "What are we? Your grumbling is not against us but against God. Come before God, for he has heard your grumbling." And after this: "The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: I have heard the grumbling of the sons of Israel," and so on. The present passage recalls these events when it says: "And they tested God in their hearts by asking for food for their souls. And they spoke against God and said: Can God prepare a table in the wilderness? Since he struck a rock and waters gushed out and torrents overflowed, can he also give bread or prepare a table for his people?" These words are not recorded in the history, but it is noted here that this is what they were thinking. For it says: "They tested God in their hearts," and "They spoke against God." And how did they speak against him, if not by thinking these things? They did not utter them with their lips but turned them over in their souls, and the One who knows hearts knew them and heard them. That is why it is said: "The Lord heard and held back." In place of this Aquila rendered "and did not delay," that is, he did not put it off, and Symmachus, "and was enraged." Then it says: "And a fire was kindled in Jacob, and wrath went up against Israel." And in Moses it is also written:

"And the people were grumbling [?] before the Lord. And the Lord heard, and his anger was kindled; and fire from the Lord blazed up among them and devoured part of the camp. And the people cried out to Moses, and Moses prayed to the Lord, and the fire died down. And the name of that place was called Burning, because fire from the Lord had blazed up among them." That is why the passage before us says: "And fire was kindled in Jacob, and wrath came up against Israel, because they did not believe in God, nor hope in his salvation. And he commanded the clouds from above, and opened the doors of heaven. And he rained manna upon them to eat, and gave them the bread of heaven. Man ate the bread of angels." The words "He commanded the clouds from above" seem to me to hint that an order was given to the angelic powers who at that time ministered in those wonders, and through whom the manna was supplied to the people. We also learn from this that the angelic powers are called clouds, as in the prophet who says, "And I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it"; so that the clouds are to be understood as the angels, just as here too. And it was fitting that the plagues against the Egyptians should be carried out through evil powers, as the passage says, "He sent upon them wrath and anger, affliction, a sending by evil angels," while the kinder works were done through propitious angels on the right hand. Hence it is said, "And he commanded the clouds from above, and opened the doors of heaven." By the doors of heaven being opened, understand the heavenly deeds. For everything God did by way of wonder was divine and heavenly; these things were shut off from human beings when they were not happening, but when they happened by wonder, it was as though he had opened certain heavenly doors to them. In place of "Man ate the bread of angels," Aquila translated, "A man ate the bread of the mighty," and Symmachus, "And he provided them with heavenly wheat; man ate the bread of the great." And observe that the Hebrew wording does not contain "bread of angels," but either, according to Aquila, "bread of the mighty"; or, according to Symmachus, "bread [?]"; or, according to Theodotion, "bread of the mighty"; or, according to the fifth edition, "bread of the mighty." No one translated "of angels." For the Hebrew does not read that way either, lest anyone should suppose that the angelic powers also make use of food perceived by the senses. Our Savior and Lord too, in the Gospels, rebukes those who supposed that the manna supplied to the people in the desert was the food of angels. That is why he said, "Truly, truly I tell you, it was not Moses who gave you the true bread from heaven"; and again, "Your fathers ate the manna in the desert, and they died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that whoever eats of it may not die." So if, he says, it had been heavenly bread, such as the an-

-gels might be expected to use, those who partook of the bread in the desert would not have died; but as it was, since it was not heavenly, and was not truly the bread of angels, for that reason they died. But this is truly heavenly bread, and whoever partakes of it will never die. And who this was he teaches when he says, "For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world"; and he presents himself, saying, "I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me will never hunger, and whoever believes in me will never thirst"; and again, "I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of my bread, he will live forever." So the angelic powers too reap eternal life from partaking of the Word. For only the only-begotten Word of God is the nourisher of every rational being. That is why the Hebrew reading in the passage before us rightly does not contain "Man ate the bread of angels." "He sent them provisions to the full. He removed the south wind from heaven, and by his power brought on the southwest wind. And he rained flesh upon them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the seas; and they fell in the midst of their camp, round about their tents. And they ate and were filled to excess, and he brought them what they craved; they were not deprived of what they craved. While the food was still in their mouths, the wrath of God came up against them; and he slew among the greater number of them, and fettered the chosen ones of Israel." That he provided not only bread for them but also relish, the Scripture of Moses also teaches, saying in Exodus: "And Moses and Aaron said to the whole congregation of the children of Israel, 'In the evening you shall know that the Lord brought you out of the land of Egypt, and in the morning you shall see the glory of the Lord, because he has heard all your grumbling, when the Lord gives you meat to eat in the evening, and bread in the morning to the full.'" And it adds next: "And evening came, and quail came up and covered the camp; and in the morning, when the dew lifted round about the camp, behold, on the face of the desert there was something fine like dust, white like frost upon the ground." But after this it is said in Numbers: "And the mixed multitude among them craved with a craving, and the children of Israel sat down and wept, and said, 'Who will feed us meat? We remember the fish we used to eat in Egypt for free, and the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions. But now our soul is dried up.'" Then it adds next: "And Moses went out into the camp, he and the elders of Israel. And a wind went out from the Lord and brought quail over from the sea, and cast them upon the camp, a day's journey on this side and round about the camp, about two cubits above the ground. And the people rose up all that day and all that night, and each gathered what was enough; the one who gathered much had nothing over, and the one who gathered little

had no lack; the one who gathered little gathered ten cors. And he spread the meat out to dry in drying places round about the camp; the meat was there before it gave out (1). And the Lord was angry. And the name of that place was called Graves of Craving, because there they buried the people who craved." Fittingly, then, the passage before us teaches these things, saying, "He sent them provisions to the full," and what follows. It teaches that the birds, driven by winds, were borne down into the camp. And according to Symmachus it says: "Who raised the east wind from heaven, and by his might brought on the south wind, winged birds like the sand of the seas. And he cast them within their camp round about the tents. And having eaten, they were filled to excess; and he brought them what they craved; they did not turn away from their craving. While their food was still between their teeth, the wrath of God came upon them, and slew the fattest of them, and brought the young men of Israel to their knees." And they suffered this with good reason. For he provided these things too in a wondrous way, as a demonstration of his power; but they, eating meat insatiably, were destroyed by a choleric disease, paying no heed to the marvel of the wonder and not glorifying the worker of wonders, but becoming wholly given over to the flesh; and so they drew destruction upon themselves. "In all this they sinned still more, and did not believe in his wonders. And their days came to an end in vanity, and their years in haste." Since the passage serves to expose and accuse the wickedness of the Jews, it also makes a list of their offenses, showing that the effects of God's wrath did not overtake them without cause. And indeed it teaches that even after all that has been mentioned, adding to their evils, they sinned still more; and they sinned because they did not believe in his wonders. For though they saw such things with their own eyes, they were overcome by craving (2). Then: "And their days came to an end in vanity." For when they had become spectators of God's mighty works, they ought to have devoted themselves wholly to him; but they, like irrational cattle, attended to the vanity of their bodies, growing old [?] in unreason and folly, and gaining nothing more from what was supplied to them toward the knowledge of God and the salvation of the soul. So in this way their days came to an end in vanity; and not only that, but their years too came to an end in haste—for "came to an end" must be understood as applying to both. In place of this Aquila has: "And he finished their days like a vapor, and hastened their years." For the one who spends his days in vanity also runs through his years in haste; but the one who completes his days in light and in good works—his days do not fail but become full, and his years are complete and prolonged. So for those who grew old in unbelief after such wonders, time ran past them vainly and in haste. Indeed, then, from the wonders and the benefits [toward them] (1) And he dried... the meat was before it gave out. Drying places round about the camp. The meat was still in

they gained nothing further to their profit, but through the wrath that overtook them they became better. That is why it adds next: "When he slew them, they sought him, and they turned and rose early to seek God." For when they were scourged and punished, they came to sense the one striking them, like irrational cattle, not being brought to their senses by right reason. To such people the word would say: "Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding. With bit and bridle you must curb the jaws of those who do not come near you. Many are the scourges of sinners, but mercy will surround those who hope in the Lord." "And they loved him with their mouth, and with their tongue they lied to him. But their heart was not right with him, nor were they faithful to his covenant." When they were enjoying the wonders they did not believe; but when they were scourged and slain, they turned to God. Yet they did not do even this sincerely, but with pretense and dissembling they appeared to praise him as far as their lips, though they did not do it with a pure mind; so that the oracle applies to them too which said, "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. In vain do they worship me." And they pushed so far into wickedness; but he, like a good father, taking greater pity on them, made atonement for their sins and did not hand them over to utter destruction. Rather, he turned away from them the destroying demon and the avenging angel who serves wrath, called his anger, propitiating his own Father on their behalf. That is why it is said: "But he is compassionate, and will make atonement for their sins, and will not destroy them. And he will abound in turning away his anger, and will not kindle all his wrath." For at that time he still bore with them patiently, not yet [?] them completely. According to Symmachus: "He," it says, "is merciful, atoning for sins and not destroying. And for a long time he turned away his wrath, and did not rouse all his anger." On top of this he accuses them of something else, saying: "And he remembered that they are flesh, a breath that goes and does not return." For since the one who is joined to the Lord is one spirit, and the one who is joined to the flesh becomes one body, it rightly says that they had become fleshy and carnal because of their love of pleasure and love of the body, and so had become flesh. That is why it says, "He remembered that they are flesh." How they were flesh it makes clear by saying next: "a breath that goes and does not return." For such is the spirit of the flesh: earthy, mortal and perishing. Such too were those at the time of the flood, of whom it had been said: "My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh"—as though the divine Spirit breathed into human beings in the beginning were one thing, and the spirit of the flesh another. The spirit of the flesh, at any rate, would be such as is found in the irrational animals, which is

"a breath that goes and does not return." The Apostle calls it by its proper name, "the mind of the flesh," where he says: "For the mind of the flesh is hostile to God; for it does not submit to the law of God, nor indeed can it; but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace." So those under accusation had become flesh through their love of the body, so that the saying could most justly have been spoken about them too: "Man, though in honor, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless cattle, and became like them." "How often they provoked him in the desert, and angered him in the waterless land! And they turned back and tempted God, and provoked the Holy One of Israel. They did not remember his hand, the day when he redeemed them from the hand of the oppressor; how he set his signs in Egypt and his wonders in the plain of Tanis. He turned their rivers into blood, and their rainwaters, so that they could not drink. He sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them, and the frog, and it destroyed them. And he gave their fruit to the blight, and their labors to the locust. He killed their vines with hail, and their sycamores with frost. And he handed over their cattle to the hail, and their possessions to the fire." After all that has been mentioned they continued to embitter him, that is, making God bitter toward themselves, although he is by nature kind and good and sweet, but is thought bitter by those who deserve punishment. These, then, angered him in the desert, drawing his wrath upon themselves. And again they turned back and tempted God, and provoked the Holy One of Israel. And they did all this because they did not keep in memory the wondrous mighty works shown to them long before, at the time when, redeeming them from the hand of Pharaoh their oppressor, he set them free from the dominion of the Egyptians, punishing their enemies in various ways in the plain of Tanis. There the river was first changed into blood—blood for the Egyptians, that is, but not for those being helped. Hence their rainwaters too—or, according to Aquila, their torrents, or, according to Symmachus, their streams—were changed into blood. For every body of water suffered the same as the river. But those under accusation made no mention of these things, nor did they give their mind to the plague of the dog-fly against the Egyptians, nor to the scourge of the frogs, nor to that of the blight (1); nor even to how, on their account, the Egyptians were punished by being handed over to locust and hail, frost and fire. Though they had experienced these things in deed, they became forgetful of them all. That is why, according to Symmachus, it says: "They did not remember his hand, the day on which he rescued them from the oppressor; he who did his signs and his wonders in Egypt, in the plain of Tanis; who changed their rivers into blood, and their streams, so that they could not drink; who sent the dog-fly upon them to de- (1) MS: erisythēs.

-vour them, and the frog to destroy them; who gave their produce to the sucking insect, and their toils to the locust; who killed their vines with hail, and their sycamores with the worm; who handed over their cattle to pestilence, and their possessions to the birds of prey." In place of "to the blight," Symmachus likewise translated "to the sucking insect," and Aquila "to the caterpillar"; and again, in place of "with frost," Symmachus rendered "with the worm," and Aquila "with ice." These things, passed over in silence by Moses, the present oracle has taught. The blight and the sucking insect seem to be the same as what Moses calls the gnat. For while the Scripture of Moses records ten plagues, the present passage recorded the blood, the frogs, the dog-fly, the locust, the hail, the death of the cattle, and the death of the firstborn; but it did not mention the gnats, nor the boils, nor the darkness; instead of these it spoke of blight and frost, in place of which the other translators have sucking insect or caterpillar, or worm or ice.

"He sent upon them the wrath of his anger, anger and wrath and affliction, a sending by evil angels. He made a path for his wrath; he did not spare their souls from death, and he shut up their cattle to death. And he struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, the firstfruits of all their labor in the tents of Ham." In addition to what has been said, God also did these things against the Egyptians for the salvation of the people: "He sent upon them the wrath of his anger, anger and wrath and affliction." Since wrath and anger are named in many places, the present passage interprets the sense of such an expression by adding next: "a sending by evil angels"; or, according to Symmachus, "a dispatch of harmful angels." For the dispatch of harmful angels was regarded, from the human point of view, as the anger and wrath of God. We must not suppose that the passion of wrath belongs to God; rather, the punishments that befall the ungodly by God's just judgment, through the sending of angels appointed for this, are called wrath and anger. Nevertheless, when the dispatch of harmful angels came upon the Egyptians, he himself made a path for his wrath; or, according to Symmachus, "he laid out a track for his wrath." And I think that by these words it hints at the mystical worship handed down to the people at the time of the wrath that came upon the Egyptians. For at that time they were ordered to celebrate the feast of the Passover, sacrificing a lamb as a symbol of the Lamb of God who was to be sacrificed for mankind, and smearing the doorposts of their houses with its blood, so that when the destroyer saw this he would draw back from his attack on those who had done so. At any rate, it is written: "And the Lord will pass through to strike the Egyptians; and he will see the blood on the lintel and on both doorposts. And the Lord will pass over the door, and will not let the destroyer enter your houses to strike." So for these he made a path to (1) MS: erisybē.

escape his wrath; but the Egyptians he did not spare, but handed their souls over to death, since they deserved such a punishment; for, given over to impieties and to the polytheistic superstition of Egypt, their souls were already steeped in another death. That is why the present passage teaches that it was not common death that came upon them, but the death of souls. For the destroyer to whom they were handed over took their souls as soon as their bodies were dissolved, leading them away to destruction. That is why it is written again: "he did not spare their souls from death." Then it makes this clear, saying next: "And he struck every firstborn in Egypt, the firstfruits of their labors." In place of "the firstfruits of their labors in the tents of Ham," Symmachus translated "the foremost of their strength." For the firstborn were indeed the foremost of their parents' strength. With the first plagues, then, as though calling them to repentance through his forbearance and patience, he inflicted the punishments on them sparingly. But in the end he did not spare their souls from death, and he also shut up their cattle to death, since every firstborn in the land of Egypt was destroyed, both of cattle and of men. And with great precision it says, in the case of human beings, that their souls were handed over to death; for the destroyer was a demon, who takes their souls even after death. But in the case of the cattle it no longer mentioned souls, but only common, bodily death; for cattle do not have a soul that survives the dissolution of the body, as human souls do. Moses and the present passage have described the same history in different ways: the one said that a destroyer carried out the death of the firstborn, while the present passage says that these things happened through evil angels. And there Moses says that the doorposts were smeared with blood, and that this became a safeguard for those who escaped the destroyer; but here it is said that God made a path to escape his wrath. These things, it says, were accomplished in the tents of Ham—or "in the dwellings of Ham," according to Symmachus, or "in the shelters of Ham," according to Aquila. From this we learn that Egypt was the tents of Ham. For Noah had three sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth; Ham became the father of Canaan, and Canaan the father of Mizraim, who was Egypt, from whom all the Egyptians descend; so it is fitting that the land of the Egyptians is called the tents of Mizraim's forefather. This Ham was the first to settle Egypt. "And he led his people out like sheep," and what follows. After the tenth plague against the Egyptians, it teaches how they made their journey out of Egypt, saying: "And he led his people out like sheep, and brought them up like a flock in the desert. And he guided them in hope [?], and they were not afraid." According to Aquila: "And he guided them into confidence, and they were not terrified"; and according to Symmachus, "He led [?]

[...] led them without fear and undismayed, and the sea covered their enemies. These events came before the time spent in the wilderness. The passage, however, does not keep to the order in which things were done. As in a hymn or song, it puts later things first and earlier things later. So it first narrates what happened in the wilderness, how they sinned there and how often they provoked God, and only afterwards recalls the earlier events, so that it may close its account not on grievous things but on God's benefits. That is why, right after what God did in Egypt and the crossing of the Red Sea, it adds: "And he brought them to the mountain of his sanctuary, this mountain which his right hand had acquired." Here it passes over the events in the wilderness in silence, because it has already narrated them. And what mountain is this but Zion, on which Jerusalem was built later, after the times of Asaph and [David?]? Then it takes up the narrative again in what follows, saying: "And he drove out nations before them, and allotted them an inheritance by a measuring line, and made the tribes of Israel dwell in their tents." It has mentioned the entry into the land of promise and how they took possession of Mount Zion, which David acquired long afterwards when he drove out the Jebusite by the sword. Now it takes up the history again in brief: how after the death of Moses, with Joshua son of Nun leading them, they crossed into the land of promise; how they defeated the foreign peoples in war, took the country and drove them out; and how they measured the land with a line and divided it by lot. Then it accuses them once more, teaching that they added further evils to the sins they had committed in the wilderness. After acquiring the land they again tempted and provoked God Most High there. They did not keep his testimonies, which had been handed down to them through Moses, but turned away and broke faith as their fathers had, and were turned into a crooked bow. They ought to have shot their arrows at the enemies of God and at the hostile powers ranged against them. Instead they fell into idolatry and shot at God with blasphemous and lawless words. So they became a crooked bow, as the oracle indicated at the beginning when it said: "The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting with bows, turned back in the day of battle." How they were turned into a crooked bow it explains next: "And they provoked him to anger on their hills, and with their carved images they moved him to jealousy. God heard and disregarded them, and utterly despised [...]"

[...] of their impious voice. So it adds: "God heard and disregarded them." Aquila has "and without postponement," meaning that he no longer granted them any delay or deferral. Symmachus has "And he utterly rejected Israel." God heard in the same way as was said of the people of Sodom: "The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah cries out to me." For the impious deeds of the ungodly themselves cry out and shout. Hearing them, God rejected the tent of Shiloh, the tabernacle where he had dwelt among men. Shiloh was where the tabernacle first stood and where Eli and Samuel served as priests, as the Scripture of the Kingdoms shows. Because of their impieties, then, he rejected this first dwelling at Shiloh. That is why Symmachus says: "And he cast off the dwelling of Shiloh, the dwelling established among men." The First Book of Kingdoms relates how the ark was handed over to men because of the people's impieties; how the enemy seized it and carried it off to their own land; how the sons of Israel were routed; how the sons of Eli, who were priests, fell; and how their father died at the news about his sons. That is why it says here: "And he rejected the tent of Shiloh, the tabernacle where he dwelt among men, and he delivered their strength into captivity." Where it says "their strength," Aquila translated "their might." What would you say was their might, strength and beauty, handed over into captivity and into the hands of the oppressor, if not the ark? The present passage hints at it when it says: "And he delivered their strength into captivity, and their beauty into the hands of the enemy." These he delivered into the enemy's hands, but the people he crushed with the sword. That is why Symmachus says: "And he gave up his people to the sword, and disregarded his inheritance." And once God had disregarded them, what followed took place. What was that? "Fire devoured their young men, and their virgins were not mourned." Aquila has "were not remembered"; Symmachus has "were not praised." According to the rendering of the others, because of the disaster that had overtaken them at that time, brides were no longer given to their husbands with the usual hymns and praises. According to the edition of the Seventy, however, the virgins were led away as captives and had no one to mourn them when they died, since their kinsfolk were not with them. Moreover, "their priests fell by the sword" (these were the sons of Eli), "and their widows will not be wept for." In the First Book of Kingdoms one can find how, when Eli's sons fell in battle, their wives, left as widows, suffered a terrible death. That is why Symmachus says: "And their widows did not weep." They did not survive long enough to weep, but perished together with their newborn children, according to the history, which says:

"And it came to pass in those days that the Philistines gathered for war against Israel." Then, when the people had gone out to battle, it says: "The men of Israel were defeated, and there was a very great slaughter; thirty thousand of the ranks of Israel fell. The ark of God was taken, and both sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, died. And a Benjaminite ran from the battle line and came to Shiloh that same day, with his clothes torn and earth on his head. And behold, Eli was sitting on his seat beside the gate, watching the road, for his heart was trembling for the ark of God." Next it says: "Now Eli was ninety-eight [?] years old, and his eyes were fixed, and he could not see. And the man came up and said: I am the one who has come from the camp; I fled from the battle line today. And he said: What has happened, my son? And the young man answered: The men of Israel have fled before the Philistines, and there has been a great slaughter among the people. Both your sons are dead, and the ark of God has been taken. And when he mentioned the ark of God, Eli fell backward from his seat beside the gate, and his back was broken, and he died, for the man was old and heavy. His daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, was with child and near her time. She heard the report that the ark of God had been taken and that her father-in-law and her husband were dead. And she wept and gave birth, for her pains came upon her, and in her labour she was dying. And the women standing by her said to her: Do not be afraid, for you have borne a son. But she did not answer, and her heart did not take it in." After this it adds: "And the Philistines took the ark of God and brought it to Azotus. And the Philistines took the ark of the Lord and brought it into the house of Dagon." The present passage abridges the account of all these things and adds: "And the Lord awoke like one asleep, like a mighty man reeling from wine." After the ark had been taken by the Philistines, and after the things described above had been done to the people, God showed his care and went after the Philistines, punishing them by an invisible power. That is why it says: "And the Lord awoke like one asleep, like a mighty man reeling from wine." Symmachus has "like a mighty man shouting [?] from wine"; Aquila has "like a mighty man reeling from wine." Then, having roused himself, he strikes his enemies, that is, those who had taken the ark of the covenant. He strikes them in their hinder parts and gives

them an everlasting reproach. The history in the First Book of Kingdoms teaches how he struck them in the hinder parts. It runs as follows: "And the hand of the Lord was heavy upon the people of Azotus, and he tormented them and struck them in their seats, Azotus and its territory." And again: "And the ark of the Lord," it says, "passed over to Gath. And after it had passed over, the hand of the Lord was upon the city with very great force. And he struck the men of the city, from the least to the greatest, and struck them in their seats. And they sent the ark of God off to Ashkelon, and the people of Ashkelon cried out, saying: Why have you brought the ark of God round to us, to kill us?" And it goes on: "For there was a very heavy confusion of death throughout the whole city when the ark of God came there. Both the living and those who died were struck in their seats, and the cry of the city went up to heaven." Because of these things it says in the present psalm: "And he struck his enemies in the hinder parts; he gave them an everlasting reproach." For it was a reproach to them to be struck in their seats, as men who were licentious in those parts. So he punished his enemies, but his own people he dealt with in another way. That is why it says: "And he rejected the tent of Joseph." What is this but Shiloh? Shiloh belonged to the inheritance of Ephraim, and Ephraim was the son of Joseph. So it adds: "And he rejected the tent of Joseph, and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim," although he had chosen it first and had honoured the tent of Joseph first. That is why Shiloh too was reduced to utter desolation. Through these words, by the example of Shiloh, the passage teaches those in Jerusalem, who had received the tabernacle and the ark, not to be proud. They would suffer the same as their predecessors if they did not prove worthy of God, and this did come to pass in later times. "And he chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which he loved. And he built his sanctuary like that of the unicorns; in the earth he founded it forever." He exchanged one tribe for another, the tribe of Benjamin for the tribe of Joseph. He chose one place in place of another, preferring Jerusalem to Shiloh. He also loved one mountain in place of another, namely Zion instead of the mountain at Shiloh. Then it says: "And he built his sanctuary like that of the unicorns." Aquila has "And he built his sanctuary like the high places"; Symmachus has "And he built his sanctuary like the heights." So he built his sanctuary like the high places and like the heights. The passage directs us to a deep and hidden sense. It teaches that the earthly sanctuary, established in Jerusalem and on Mount Zion, bore a likeness to the things on high. It was built like the heights, made after the image and likeness of the lofty things in heaven. The Apostle shows this too when he says: "But the Jerusalem above is free," and, "You have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem." That is why Aquila says, "And he built his sanctuary like the high places," Symmachus says, "And he built his sanctuary like the heights," and the Seventy say, "Like that of the unicorns he built his sanctuary." We understand

the unicorns to be those in heaven who are enrolled under the one horn. The Apostle pointed to them when he said: "And to myriads of angels in festal gathering, and to the church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven." "But also in the earth," it says, "he founded it forever." Symmachus has "Like the earth, which he founded forever." For in this way he built the sanctuary of the visible, earthly Jerusalem on the earth. Just as, according to Scripture, the earth is enclosed in the midst of the waters, so Jerusalem stood in the midst of foreign nations. That is why the prophecies say: "This is Jerusalem; I have set her in the midst of the nations." After this, "He chose," it says, "David his servant." Of him it is said: "I have found David my servant, a man after my own heart." God chose him not only to be the first king from the tribe of Judah, but also to be judged worthy that the Christ of God should come forth from his seed. He chose him in preference to his brothers, who were many. "And he took him from the flocks of sheep; from following the ewes with young." For he who raises the poor from the earth and lifts the needy from the dunghill also chose David, who was lowly and cast aside, so much so that he was not even counted among his brothers or reckoned as a man. David was being trained beforehand in shepherding, and through his care for the ewes giving birth he was learning to look after those who need care. From there God took him from shepherding irrational sheep, brought him forward and appointed him to shepherd Jacob his servant and Israel his inheritance. For since he had proved himself in shepherding irrational flocks, God set him over a more rational flock. How he shepherded his flocks he himself shows when he says to Saul: "Your servant was keeping his father's sheep. Whenever a lion or a bear came and took a sheep from the flock, I went out after it, struck it, and tore the sheep from its mouth. And if it rose up against me, I seized it by the throat, struck it and killed it. Your servant has struck down both the lion and the bear. And this uncircumcised foreigner will be like one of them, for he has reviled the army of the living God." And

[...] he guided them. Aquila has "And with the understanding of his palms he led them"; Symmachus has "And according to the purity of his hands he guided them." David, then, shepherded the human and rational flock. He did so not in human wisdom or by his own understanding, but in innocence and simplicity, entrusting all his care to God. His own understanding, however, he displayed through his hands, that is, through his deeds, his life and the rest of his conduct. Here the subject of the present psalm comes to an end. It contains an accusation of the wickedness of the Jewish people and a teaching about God's patience, prompted by the perplexed words in the earlier psalms. To these a kind of defence of God's righteous judgment has necessarily been added. All these things the Christ of God teaches us who come from the nations, correcting us by the ancient examples, as was said at the beginning of the discourse.

"O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have made Jerusalem a watchman's hut in an orchard."

The history makes it clear that Asaph lived before the temple in Jerusalem was built, and flourished at the same time as David. So in these words too he prophetically foretells what was to happen long afterwards. In Psalm 73 he foretold the final capture of the city and the final destruction of the temple, which took place under the Romans after the inhabitants' outrage against our Saviour, as has already been shown. In the present psalm, by contrast, he signifies that nations came into God's inheritance, defiled the temple in it, and made the city itself a watchman's hut in an orchard. He does not say that the place was given over to fire, or that it suffered anything like what he described in the psalm mentioned earlier. He further adds in the present psalm that those who defiled the place killed many holy men and servants of God. They did not allow their dead bodies to receive natural burial, but made them food for the birds of the sky. You would not find these things done in the final siege of the place. At that time there were no holy men among them, since all the inhabitants of the city had become unholy and impious because of what they had dared against our Saviour and his apostles. Nor would you find what is described here happening in the Babylonian captivity, since history does not report that holy and God-loving men were killed by the Babylonians then either. When, then, were these things fulfilled? No other time can be named than that of Antiochus, in which the book of Maccabees shows the things foretold here carried out in deed. This is what is written in it: "And Antiochus returned after he had struck Egypt, in the one hundred and forty-third [?] year, and went up against Israel with a great host. And he entered the sanctuary in arrogance and took the golden censer, the lampstand for the light and all its utensils, the table for the presentation bread, the libation cups, the bowls, the golden ladles, the

curtain, the crowns and the ornament on the front of the temple. He stripped it all off, and he took the hidden treasures that he found. Taking everything, he turned back and went away to his own land. And he carried out a great massacre, and there was great mourning over Israel. And the king wrote to his whole kingdom that all should be one people, and that each should abandon his own customs. And all the nations accepted the king's command, and many even of the sons of Israel were pleased with his worship; they sacrificed to idols and profaned the Sabbath." After this it says: "And he built an abomination of desolation upon the altar, and in the cities of Judah round about they built altars. At the doors of the houses and in the streets they burned incense to them. And the books of the psalm [?] that they found they tore up and burned with fire." And it adds: "Yet many in Israel stood firm among them, resolved not to eat unclean things. They chose to die rather than be defiled by food, and they died. And very great wrath came upon Israel." These things were fulfilled long afterwards, after the Assyrian and Median empires, after the Persian, and after the death of Alexander of Macedon. Yet the divine Spirit, through the prophet before us, foretells these very things, saying: "O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have made Jerusalem a watchman's hut in an orchard. They have given the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of the sky, the flesh of your holy ones to the beasts of the earth. They have poured out their blood like water all around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them. We have become a reproach to our neighbours, an object of scorn and derision to those around us." Where it says "a watchman's hut in an orchard," Aquila rendered "a heap of stones" and Symmachus "thickets." "How long, O Lord? Will you be angry forever? Will your jealousy burn like fire?" It seems to me that the prophet Asaph, after the accusation of the Jewish nation that he made in the preceding psalm, follows it with the present words in order to make amends, as it were, and to heal what was censured earlier. So he lists the deaths of those among the Jews themselves who bore witness for the sake of piety. God's enemies gave their corpses as food to the birds of the sky, and the flesh of God's holy ones to the beasts of the earth. Fittingly, then, after these things he seeks to appease God, as though the death of his holy ones had been offered to him as a sacrifice. That is why he says: "How long, O Lord? Will you be angry forever?" He is referring back to the earlier psalm, where it was said: "Why, O God, have you rejected us forever?" He wants the final falling away and casting off of the people to be held back, and God's wrath to cease, through the remembrance of the blood of his holy ones. You may understand the words "How long, O Lord" in both ways

…will you be angry forever?" and, in the words that follow, "Will your jealousy burn like fire?" For the "How long" applies to this too. "Jealousy" is said by comparison with men who, out of excessive affection, are jealous over their own wives if they pay attention to other men; so in the case of God too, Scripture is accustomed to call "jealousy" his punishment of those who transgress their covenants with him. The Prophet therefore makes supplication, either in his own person or as on behalf of those who survived in the times of Antiochus, after foretelling what would happen under Antiochus, king of Syria, under whom the holy ones of God endured death for the sake of piety. He asks that the wrath against the people should cease, and that God should punish its enemies. Therefore he says: "Pour out your wrath on the nations that do not know you, and on the kingdoms that have not called upon your name. For they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his place." I think it fitting that Jacob is mentioned here, because of the godliness of that ancient forefather. For as though reminding God of the God-loving man and his virtue, he entreats him through the memory of that man and seeks to appease him in the present troubles. In the psalm before this one, when he mentioned Joseph, he said that it was not Joseph but his tent that was rejected: "And he rejected the tent of Joseph, and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim." The text there signifies the place at Shiloh, since Shiloh lay in the allotment of the tribe of Joseph. Here, however, he mentions Jacob and his place: by Jacob he indicates the descendants of the God-loving man, and by his place he signifies Jerusalem, which came to be desolate in the times of Antiochus. Then he goes on to add: "Do not remember our ancient iniquities." Those who pray about ancient sins would evidently not be guilty of more recent offenses. Instead of "Let your compassion quickly overtake us, for we have become very poor," Symmachus rendered: "Hasten, let your mercies go before us, for we have become very weak." Just as an athlete who has undergone many contests and endured many bouts grows anxious that he may somehow faint and fall, in the same way these people too beg to be overtaken and to receive help. Therefore he says: "Let your compassion quickly overtake us, for we have become very poor. Help us, O God our Savior, for the glory of your name; Lord, deliver us, and be merciful to our sins for your name's sake." The Prophet utters these words in the person of those persecuted under King Antiochus. He prophetically left the prayer in writing for those who would be persecuted, so that they might know at once what words they ought to use in their prayers to God. Yet what is said does not stop with them alone. It would also suit all who have suffered similar things, since in the persecutions of our own day too, count-

less people have endured things like those described above. They too might fittingly use the present words, in which we are taught to say: "For the glory of your name, Lord, deliver us." For even if we are not worthy of help, at least do not let the name of your glory be blasphemed among the nations, as though it had not been able to deliver us. "And be merciful," he says, "to our sins for your name's sake." Above it was said, "Do not remember our ancient iniquities"; but there he spoke of iniquities. Iniquities, that is lawless deeds, were those we committed long ago, before obedience to the divine law, and they are rightly called ancient. For the lawless deeds we committed before we knew God were ancient. But now, when we send up our prayer, we are conscious no longer of lawlessness but of sins. Yet we ask that these too be forgiven, because of your name, which has been called upon us. For sparing your own name, which adorns us, be merciful to our sins, lest our enemies, having us in their power, blaspheme your name, saying: "Where is their God?" May they not be allowed to say this "Where?" Rather, may you yourself, our Savior, become manifest and avenge the shed blood of your servants. We are taught to say these things in our prayers in times of persecution, putting forward the blood of the holy martyrs in place of sacrifices and whole burnt offerings, and sending up such supplications. And before us, those in the Jewish nation who suffered similar things at the time mentioned were taught to say the same. At that time noble martyrs appeared among them, whom the scripture called the Maccabees records. Among them was a certain Eleazar, a distinguished man, advanced in years, who for the sake of piety toward God preferred a glorious death to life itself. There was also a mother of seven sons, a wonderful woman who contended in martyrdom beyond all description; and her seven sons, undergoing various tortures, displayed an extraordinary strength of endurance. There were very many other holy ones among them too, whose deaths and shed blood the text recalls in the prayer, saying: "And let the vengeance for the shed blood of your servants be known among the nations before our eyes." [?] (1) Variant reading: "imprisonments."

…body of this death?" Such were also the prophets of God, and all who do not indulge their bodies or give themselves to luxury and pleasure. On the contrary, they press down their life with fasting and toil and the other hardships of the ascetic life. They groaned to God from the depths of their hearts, not for themselves alone but for the whole people. Therefore it is said: "Let the groaning of the prisoners come before you." Who those are who are taught to say these words he shows next, saying: "Preserve the sons of those who have been put to death." For we have not been found worthy to contend to the point of death, or to pour out our own blood for God. But since we are the sons of those who suffered these things, and take pride in the virtue of our fathers, we ask to receive mercy for their sake. Therefore we say: "Preserve the sons of those who have been put to death. Repay our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom the reproach with which they reproached you, Lord. But we, your people and the sheep of your pasture, will give thanks to you forever; from generation to generation we will declare your praise." Preserve us, if not for our own sake, then for the sake of our fathers. But to our neighbors, that is, to those who rise up against us and stir up war against us, pay back what is due, multiplying the punishment owed them for what they have done. They were not content with the evils they did to us, but now they assail even you, the Lord over all, with blasphemous and reproachful words. To them, he says, render the punishment they deserve, which will be for their benefit, as they are turned back and corrected by it. But save us, the sons of those who have been put to death. Even if we have not become like our fathers, we are nonetheless your people and the sheep of your pasture. Therefore we will give thanks to you forever, that is, we will offer thanks and send up fitting hymns and doxologies to you, God, the giver of all good things, for the benefits we have received. And from generation to generation we will declare your praise to our children and our children's children, and to their successors who will come after them, handing down the saving lessons of praise like a good inheritance.

FOR THE END, CONCERNING THOSE WHO WILL BE CHANGED; A TESTIMONY, OF ASAPH [?]. "Shepherd of Israel, give heed, you who lead Joseph like a sheep." There are four psalms with the title "Concerning those who will be changed": two of David, the 59th and the 68th; one of the sons of Korah, the 44th; and likewise one of Asaph, the one now before us. The 59th indicated the falling away of the Jewish nation and the calling of the Gentiles. It said at the beginning, "O God, you have rejected us and destroyed us; you have been angry," and so on. Then, further on, it added: "Moab is the cauldron of my hope. Over Idumea I will stretch out my shoe; foreigners have become my friends," or "have been subjected to me." Likewise the 68th, which has the title "Concerning those who will be changed," presents the sufferings of the Savior and the rejection of Israel, saying: "Let their table before them become a snare, a retribution and a stumbling block. Let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see,

and bend their back continually. Pour out your wrath upon them, and let the fury of your wrath overtake them. Let their homestead be made desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in their tents. For they persecuted the one whom you struck, and added to the pain of my wounds." These, then, are the psalms of David. Of the sons of Korah, the 44th, which has the title "Concerning those who will be changed," sent up a song concerning the Beloved. After foretelling his coming, it added the calling of the Church from the Gentiles, hinting at it in this way: "Hear, O daughter, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father's house. And the king will desire your beauty, for he is your Lord, and the daughter of Tyre will worship him with gifts." In the same way, then, the present psalm, which also has the title "Concerning those who will be changed" and is directed "to the end," foretells the coming of Christ, the captivity of the Jewish nation, and the burning of Jerusalem that it suffered at the hands of the Babylonians. First it recounts the exodus of the Jews from Egypt and their settlement in the land of Palestine. Then it adds the siege that later came upon them from the Assyrians and Babylonians. Besides this it sets out a supplication for the appearing of Christ. These things will be shown in detail in the interpretation of the prophecies. At the beginning the psalm calls upon the one who shepherds Israel. This was the Word of God, as we have often demonstrated. We showed that it was not the God beyond all things who is recorded as having appeared to Abraham in the form of a man, as having spoken to Moses, and as having gone before the people in the wilderness. It was none other than the one who said in the Gospels: "Before Abraham came to be, I am"; and, "Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day; he saw it and was glad." It is he, then, whom the psalm now calls upon, saying, "Shepherd of Israel, give heed," and so on. It implores him to make his face shine for the common salvation of all, and asks that his coming may happen quickly, saying: "Stir up your might and come to save us." And after saying a third time, "Make your face shine, and we shall be saved," it presents the manner of his appearing, adding next: "Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the son of man whom you made strong for yourself." For it asks the incorporeal Word of God to bestow his beneficent power on all through the man of his right hand and through the Son of Man. In this way, then, it made mention of the saving appearance of God. The falling away of Israel it foretells at this point, saying: "Why have you broken down its hedge?" (that is, the hedge of the vine which he brought out of Egypt) "so that all who pass along the way pluck its fruit? A boar from the forest has ravaged it, and a solitary

wild beast has fed on it. It is burned with fire and dug up." After recounting these things about the vine, he foretold the desolation of the Jewish nation. Fittingly, then, the title also calls what is said a "testimony"; for he solemnly testified that these things would come to pass. Hence Symmachus and Aquila also have "testimony." Instead of "concerning those who will be changed," Symmachus rendered "concerning the flowers," and Aquila "concerning the lilies." The text compares to flowers and lilies the brief, passing prosperity that the Jewish nation once enjoyed. The Prophet, then, sends up a supplication to the Word of God, who of old watched over Israel and cared for it. Calling upon him, he says: "Shepherd of Israel, give heed." He entreats him in this way by reminding him of how he cared for them long ago. "Give heed," he says, "to your nurslings and your sheep, you who once shepherded them. For if at another time you took upon yourself the shepherd's care of human beings, and led your people who lived among men, remember these very people, and do not overlook those whom you thought worthy of such great providence. Give heed, then," he says, "and consider what your flock has suffered: how a boar from the forest has ravaged them, and a solitary wild beast has fed on it, and how it has been burned with fire and dug up at the rebuke of your face." In the Holy Spirit the Prophet teaches the Jewish nation to rehearse and declare these things, anticipating the times and the events. Then, when the things foretold arrived and were fulfilled in deed, they would have ready to hand the knowledge of how to make supplication to God. Who the one who shepherds Israel is, he himself shows, saying: "I am the good shepherd; I know my own, and my own know me"; and again: "I am the good shepherd, and I lay down my life for the sheep." He was also the one who led Joseph like a sheep. By "Joseph" the psalm means either the tribe, or the whole Jewish nation, named metaphorically after the single tribe of Joseph; or rather the man himself, the forefather of the tribe. For he was with Joseph when he was plotted against by his brothers, sold to the Ishmaelites, and brought down to Egypt; when he served Potiphar and turned away from his licentious mistress; and when he was shut up in prison. In all these events, at any rate, the scripture of Moses remarks: "And the Lord was with Joseph." Hence Theodotion seems to me to have rendered it more properly, saying: "You who guide Joseph like a sheep." In the same way you might also say that Israel himself was shepherded, the first to bear this name. He was Jacob, the son of Isaac. For he too went down alone to Mesopotamia, with his hope in God, and found as his shepherd the Word of God who was with him, the one who had appeared to him. Fittingly, then, the text, in entreating God, does not wish to mention the multitude

of the ungodly. Instead it mentions one or two of the God-loving men of old, imploring that through the virtue and godliness of the forefathers their descendants may obtain mercy. This same one who was once the shepherd of the holy men was also the one riding upon the cherubim. And which cherubim, if not those seen by Ezekiel, whose images and symbols Moses made of gold above the ark at God's command? Ezekiel mentions the cherubim in this way: "And I looked, and behold, above the firmament that was over the head of the cherubim there was something like sapphire stone, the likeness of a throne upon it." And a little later he says: "And the glory of the Lord went out from the court of the house and mounted upon the cherubim. And the cherubim lifted their wings and rose up from the earth before me as they went out, and the wheels beside them. And they stood at the entrance of the gate of the house that faces [?], and the glory of the God of Israel was over them, above." Do you see how the chariot of God is described in these words? Of this chariot it is said elsewhere: "The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, thousands of those who flourish." The chariot was the cherubim, with something like the likeness of a throne above their heads, and upon it the glory of the Lord. What the glory of the Lord was is made clear at the beginning of the book, where it is said: "Above the cherubim was something like the appearance of sapphire stone, the likeness of a throne upon it; and upon the likeness of the throne, high above, a likeness as of the form of a man. And I saw something like the gleam of electrum from the appearance of the loins upward; and from the appearance of the loins downward something like the appearance of fire, and its brightness all around." And he adds: "This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the Lord." Do you see how the text, in explaining the glory of God that rides upon the throne, [?] the form of a man? What could this form of a man be, which is said to be not God himself but the glory of God, except the only-begotten Word of God? Scripture sometimes calls him the glory of God the Father, and sometimes the form of a man, because of the man he assumed. What concerns his divinity is likened to electrum, which is more precious than any material. What is from the loins downward is likened in one place to the appearance of fire and in another to the brightness of light. For created things and human beings on earth need his different powers: those who have done what deserves light need his illuminating activity, and those who have done what deserves fire need his burning and punishing power. Moses was commanded to make images and symbols of the heavenly things, so he made the cherubim of gold. These were set upon the ark, with the mercy seat, made of gold, between them. The mercy seat lay between the cherubim and rested upon them like a charioteer. So the golden mercy seat was an image and type of the one seen above the cherubim in the prophet Ezekiel, whom we show to be the Word of God. This is why the divine Apostle calls him a mercy seat, saying: "whom God put forward as a mercy seat through faith, by his blood." These things that Moses made of gold as types, I mean the cherubim and the mercy seat, went before the people in the wilderness, ahead of Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh. For when the twelve tribes were on the march, three tribes, Judah, Issachar and Zebulun, encamped in front of the ark. Likewise three tribes, Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh, followed the ark, coming behind the cherubim. Therefore it is said here: "Appear, you who are seated Ezek. 10:18. Ezek. 1:26. Rom. 3:25.

upon the cherubim, before Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh." Hence Aquila's version reads: "You who sit on the cherubim, appear before the face of Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh." "For you," he says, "who go on ahead before the face and in the sight of Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh, appear." Here the Prophet calls upon the Word of God, basing his invocation on what was familiar to the people, and not on the vision of God seen by the prophet Ezekiel. Through his prayer he entreats the one he calls upon: "For if at one time," he says, "you consented to go before human beings and to lead the tribes just mentioned, appear now also to these same people, who are storm-tossed and perishing. You yourself, who then shepherded and led the people, stir up your might and come to save us." In these words he implores him to come among human beings, to take back again those who had turned away and fallen away, and to make them turn back to him once more. Therefore he says: "O God, restore us, and make your face shine, and we shall be saved. Lord God of hosts, how long will you be angry at the prayer of your servants?" The one called here Lord and God of hosts was the very one who shepherds the true Israel, who led Joseph like a sheep, who sits upon the cherubim, and who goes before Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh. He is called Lord and God of hosts, just as elsewhere he is called commander of the host of the Lord and Angel of great counsel. Appearing in the form of a man to Joshua, the successor of Moses, he declared who he was, saying: "I am the commander of the host of the Lord." And in Isaiah it is said: "A child has been born to us, and a son has been given to us, whose government is upon his shoulder, and his name is called Angel of great counsel." According to the other translators: "Mighty God, potentate, prince of peace, father of the age." This, then, is what the forsaken and desolate people is taught by the prophetic Spirit: to send up a prayer and say to him, "Lord God of hosts, how long will you be angry at the prayer of your servant?" Where it says "your servant," all the other translators rendered "your people." They are also taught to eat the bread of tears for what they have dared to do, so that by weeping over their own evils and mourning, they may obtain comfort, in keeping with the beatitude that says: "Blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh; blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted." In Symmachus' version he says: "You fed us the bread of tears, and gave us tears to drink by measure." For even if we have fully deserved weeping and tears, so as to be fed on laments and groans instead of bread and to be given tears and wailing to drink, still let these very things be measured out to us, so that they are not drawn out for us without end. Let them cease at some point and change into a brighter

[?] “For you made us a cause of strife to our neighbours, and our enemies mocked us” — they who in the past dared none of these things against us, when we had you as our protector. Therefore we pray, and we call on the God of hosts, begging him to turn us back. This will happen if you appear and show us your face. For when that happens we shall be saved, and we too shall say: “The light of your face, Lord, has been stamped upon us.” “You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out nations and planted it. You made a way before it, and planted its roots, and it filled the land.” At the start of his supplication the prophet called on the one who shepherds Israel. But Israel was something different from the vine spoken of here. Israel is always shepherded by the Lord, while the present vine suffered a great decline toward the worse. Through the God-beloved man, the Israel of old, he urges God to look upon that man's descendants, who are faring badly. Every discerning soul that is always shepherded by the good shepherd may also be Israel. The soul that preserves the image of the one who said in the Gospels, “I am the true vine,” may also be called God's vine. But the vine transplanted out of Egypt is the soul that has suffered corruption. The Jewish people became such a soul: they practised idolatry in Egypt for a long time and bore little fruit, as Moses testifies in the great song, where he writes this about them: “For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their tendril from Gomorrah. Their grape is a grape of gall, their cluster a cluster of bitterness. Their wine is the rage of dragons, and the incurable rage of asps.” Yet even in this state God visited them and transplanted them. He uprooted them from their entanglement with Egypt and transplanted them into another land, a rich place, as Isaiah teaches when he says: “My beloved had a vineyard on a hill, in a rich place. And I put a hedge around it, and fenced it, and planted a vine of Sorek. And I built a tower in the middle of it, and dug a winepress in it.” So he brought the vine just mentioned into a rich place, far better than the land of Egypt, and planted it there. Then, like an excellent farmer, after the first transplanting he made a way before it. He cleared away every [?] growth and cut out all foreign matter, so that nothing would stand in its way and hinder it from bringing forth fruit. Instead of “You made a way before it,” Symmachus translated: “You cleared the ground before it.” Then he went on: “and you rooted its roots.” Since the vine described here received such care from God the Word, it naturally filled the land. It overshadowed mountains, covered cedars with its climbing branches, and stretched out its branches as far as the sea and its shoots as far as the rivers. All these things were true of it. And since it had been granted so much, the passage, as if in prayer, rightly reminds the farmer of this and appeals to him with supplication, and [?]

says to him: “You granted the vine we spoke of such providence and care, and you showed it all these things out of love for humankind and out of grace. So who would not be at a loss and fall into perplexity, and ask: Why did you break down its hedge and let anyone who wished trample it?
