Now whoever wants can pick its grapes, and with no one to fence it in, at one time a boar from the forest ravages it, and at another a solitary wild beast feeds on it.” But the farmer answers this question through the prophet Isaiah, as though making his defence, and gives the reason, saying: “Because I waited for it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns; and not righteousness, but a cry.” No one would doubt that these words were spoken about the Jewish people. You will understand how the shadow of the vine covered mountains if you consider the following. The law had a shadow of the good things to come and not the very image of the realities. It was carried out at one time on the mountain at Shiloh, where the tabernacle was first set up, and at another on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem. And its climbing branches covered the cedars of God. What would you say the climbing branches of the vine are, if not the prophetic souls and those among the former people who were lifted up to a height [?] and lived in a way worthy of God? These also rested on the cedars of God, that is, on the invisible and divine powers. For the souls that stood out among the former people reached as far as these powers, so that they even shared in the Holy Spirit and extended their fruits as far as the angelic power. The branches of the vine, which are something other than the shadow and the climbing branches, stretched out as far as the sea. Instead of “the branches,” Symmachus says: “it stretched out its locks as far as the sea.” The locks and tresses, like countless hairs, or the multiplying branches in the image of the vine, would be the great number of the Jewish nation. This number did indeed reach as far as the sea and filled the whole of human life. That is why the prophet Hosea says: “And the number of the children of Israel was like the sand of the sea, which shall not be measured or counted.” Certain other shoots, younger and newly sprung, which are distinct from the branches, stretched out as far as the river. These are the heralds of the New Covenant, by which I mean the apostles and the disciples of our Saviour. They had their growth and origin from the vine we spoke of, and became like shoots of it. Yet they did not advance as far as the sea, as the locks and the branches did, but as far as the river, because of the mystery of rebirth in Christ that is granted through them. This is why Psalm 71 says of the Saviour himself: “And he shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the inhabited world.” For he began from his baptism at the river Jordan and filled the whole world. Four orders of the vine we spoke of

are described by the present passage: its shadow covering mountains; its climbing branches raised so high that they cover not simply cedars but the cedars of God; besides these, branches stretching as far as the sea; and after all these, shoots reaching to the river. We have interpreted their meaning according to the grace given us. We took the shadow as the figurative and shadowy worship that was carried out on visible, physical mountains. We took the climbing branches as the prophetic souls, which were supported on the cedars of God, the angelic and divine powers. We took the branches, or locks, or tresses as the whole multitude of the Jews, which stretches as far as the sea because human life is unstable and tossed by waves. Finally, we took the shoots as the apostles of our Saviour, who are joined to the river of which it is said: “The rushing streams of the river gladden the city of God.” God the Word, who once watched over the vine described here, had granted it so much. So the passage next and fittingly raises the question as if to the very one who had given so much, saying: “Why have you broken down its hedge?” And he answers: “Because I waited for it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns”; and again: “I waited for it to produce justice, but it produced lawlessness, and not righteousness, but a cry.” In Jeremiah too the same one rebukes the vine, for it was a rational vine, saying: “But I planted a fruitful vine, wholly true. How have you turned to bitterness, you foreign vine?” And through Isaiah he adds: “I will take away its hedge, and it will be plundered; I will break down its wall, and it will be trampled. I will abandon my vineyard, and it will be neither dug nor pruned. Thorns will come up on it as on barren ground, and I will command the clouds not to rain on it.” Once the hedge was taken away, that is, the power that guarded and fenced them in, it was natural that all their enemies from then on, invisible and unseen and more savage than wild beasts, should ravage them, namely those whom the passage accuses. A first unclean boar, the Assyrian, broke in by force and ruined the vine described here, so that he even carried off the multitude captive to Assyria. Then a second enemy, Nebuchadnezzar, came in and devoured what the first had left; he also set the temple on fire and razed it to the ground. That is why Symmachus also says: “A boar from the forest devoured it, and a [?] solitary beast grazed it down.” Instead of “and a solitary wild beast,” Aquila translated “and every kind of country.” According to another interpretation, the vine referred to was ravaged first by the Babylonian, who was also the first to lay Jerusalem waste by siege. Then after him the Roman army, which came after the coming of our Saviour, devoured it. Asaph prophesies all these things. He lived in the time of David, before the building of [?] Jerusalem,

and foretold to it what would happen in the times indicated. Through the present psalm, then, he seems to prophesy both the first siege, carried out by the Babylonians, and the second, carried out by the Romans. Through the psalm before this he prophesies the events under Antiochus Epiphanes, and through Psalm 73 only the events of the final siege, carried out by the Romans, as has been shown in what was said on Psalm 73. “O God of hosts, turn now, look down from heaven and see, and visit this vine, and restore the one your right hand planted, and upon the son of man whom you strengthened for yourself. Burned with fire and dug up, they shall perish at the rebuke of your face.” As one would with a good farmer, he has reminded him of his great care for the vine and of the desolation that afterward befell it. Next, and consistently, he begs him to turn back, since he had turned away and by turning away had handed the vine over to all its enemies. He begs him to visit it and to look down from heaven above. He begs him to remember that this vine was in fact his own planting, cultivated by his own right hand. And having remembered, he begs him to visit it, since it was once planted by his right hand but is now burned with fire and dug up, and has perished at the rebuke of his face. He asks him to restore it, taking it up and recovering it like a saviour and physician, and to do this through the Son whom he strengthened for himself. Through these words the passage clearly teaches [?] that before the burning carried out by the Romans he asked for the Saviour's appearance as God to take place, which has now already happened. It was fitting, after the first disasters that befell the place, to entreat and beg the Redeemer to come. When he came, they did not accept the grace he announced to them first, and so they naturally suffered the final desolation. He himself pronounced it against them when he said: “How often I wanted to gather your children together, as a bird gathers its chicks under its wings, and you were not willing! Look, your house is left to you desolate.” Then also, as the Apostle says, the wrath came upon them [?]

“Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the son of man whom you strengthened for yourself. And we will not turn away from you; you will give us life.” The Holy Spirit teaches a single cure for everything mentioned before: the coming of the Christ of God among human beings. Therefore, after the prophecies about the desolation of the vineyard and the burning that came upon it, he offers the present supplication, so that they may look for a redeemer: the man of God's right hand, the son of man strengthened by God. This was God's beloved. He teaches his readers to know him and to pray for his coming. In this way those who are taught these things in advance would recognize him, believe in him, and hope to obtain through him the cure of their ills. Therefore, speaking for those who need a cure, he says: “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and

upon the son of man whom you strengthened for yourself. And we will not [?] turn away from you.” The force of the passage has this meaning: “Now at last let your unseen and invisible hand shine upon the man who serves your right hand, and upon the one who is to be called Son of Man. You prepared him for yourself and strengthened him as an instrument of your power, raising him up like an image of your own divinity. For when he appears, we will no longer worship idols, nor be enslaved to the error of many gods, nor turn away from you from then on. Instead, given life through him and obtaining the salvation that comes from you, we will call on your name. We will no longer be named after any human being. We will not be called Israelites after Israel, nor Jews after Judah, but we will be called Christians after [?] the name of Christ.” That is why Symmachus translates: “You will give us life, and we shall be called by your name.” It is astonishing that the children of the Jews read these words and study them from their earliest years, and yet do not ask who the man of God's right hand was, nor recognize the one called Son of Man. That is why they remain in their misfortune. For if they had recognized him and learned about him, they would also have known God the Word who dwelt in him, the one whom the present prayer called upon. But we know that he existed beforehand and has cared for human beings from the beginning. “For he was in the world, and the world came into being through him, and the world did not [know] him.” [?] [we know] him who came to his own. Then his hand, that is, his active power, came upon the man of his right hand, who in the Gospels is called Son of Man. He formed this man for himself, fashioning him from the Holy Spirit. Knowing him, we shall from now on never turn away, since we are given life through him and are called by his name. We, then, who looked for the Son of Man and have hung our hopes on him, say these things about ourselves. But on behalf of our members we send up the rest of the supplication, saying: “O God of hosts, turn [?] us, and [?] show your face, and we shall be saved.” We make these words a shared prayer on behalf of those who have not yet turned and have not recognized his appearing, and who therefore have not yet obtained the salvation that is with God.

[?] of God, and the many altars in them. He indeed presented these when he said: “How lovely are your dwellings, Lord of hosts”; and again: “My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord”; and then: “Your altars, Lord of hosts.” The present psalm, however, urges others to rejoice and shout and sing, while it presents the rejection of the Jewish nation and its cause. In this it follows very closely on the prophecies in the earlier psalms. In the psalm before this he asked: “Why have you broken down its hedge, so that all who pass along the road pick its grapes?” Now he answers that question in the present psalm, saying: “If my people had listened to me, if Israel had walked in my ways, I would have humbled their enemies in no time.” And he adds: “But my people did not listen to my voice, and Israel paid no attention to me. So I sent them away according to the devices of their hearts; they will walk in their own devices.” Since he presents their refusal to listen and their disobedience, he naturally changes the subject. The Holy Spirit announces the good news of the calling of the nations, addressing all people and saying: “Rejoice in God our helper.” He says this in the person of the prophetic choir. In Psalm 8 he said, “O Lord, our Lord,” where the speakers claim God as their own, because God belonged to them first. In the same way here the same speakers call to those who were estranged and foreign and say: “All of you, leave behind those you wrongly believed to be gods. Come quickly to our God, and rejoice in him who has always been the helper of us who are devoted to him.” Next they show who he was, saying: “Shout aloud to the God of Jacob.” That is: Come and shout aloud to the God who appeared long ago to our forefather. This agrees with what is said in Psalm [?]: “Shout aloud to God, all the earth.” He makes clear what “all the earth” was when he says: “Clap your hands, all you nations; shout aloud to God with a voice of rejoicing.” So in the present psalm too the choir of prophets calls to these same people and says: “Rejoice in God our helper; shout aloud to the God of Jacob.” By the God of Jacob he means the Saviour, who appeared to Jacob in human form. That was when Jacob named the place where God appeared to him “Form of God,” adding: “For I have seen God face to face, and my soul was saved.” So he commands them to shout aloud to him, since he is our king, and to send up a victory hymn [?]. He himself teaches how the Father appoints him king, saying: “But I was appointed king by him on Zion, his holy mountain.” He wants those who have been called not only to shout aloud to the God of Jacob, but also to take up a psalm and give the drum, and a pleasant psaltery with the cithara. In Aquila's version he says: “Lift up

a melody, and give the drum, a fine cithara with the harp.” In Symmachus's version: “Take up a song, and give the drum, a sweet lyre with the harp.” So he commands them to take one thing and to give another. They are to take a melody, according to Aquila, or a song, according to Symmachus. In return they are to give the drum, or the sweet lyre with the harp. By this the passage commands us to receive the teaching of the words with our ears, and to give in return the action we perform through the body. For song and melody are delivered to the ears in words. That is why he says, according to Aquila and Symmachus, “Take a song and a melody.” Having received these, you are to give in return a pleasant psaltery with the cithara, or a sweet lyre with the harp. The drum is an instrument made from the hide of a body, and the psaltery is a kind of cithara made in much the same way [?] with strings. By these he hinted at our body. He wants them, then, to carry out in actual works and deeds the commands given in words. The passage gives these commands to those who gather in the churches of God throughout the whole world. That is why the psalm has the headings “For the end” and “On the winepresses.” By winepresses, understand nothing other than the churches of God. In them we gather together and bring our fruits into one place, and so make one blend for the glory and joy of the Word of God. It is remarkable that the psalm before this one showed the burning and the complete desolation and destruction of the vine transplanted out of Egypt, while the present psalm sets up several winepresses, as though another vine and another vineyard had come into being, or rather several vineyards. It also announces glad news to those who are called to them. For the former people he introduced one vineyard, one winepress and one vine, when he said: “My beloved had a vineyard on a hill, in a rich place.” And then he says: “And I dug a winepress in it, and planted a vine of Sorek.” In the psalm before this he also pointed to one vine, saying: “You brought a vine out of Egypt.” But in the psalms headed “On the winepresses” he points to several winepresses, and so clearly to several vineyards. If you wish to know the new vine, which sprang up among human beings after the destruction of the former one, learn it from God the Word, who teaches this about himself: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that bears fruit he prunes, so that it may bear more fruit. You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it abides in the vine, neither can you unless you abide in me. I am the vine, you are the branches. Whoever abides in me, and I in him, bears much fruit; for apart from me you can bear nothing.” So the psalm before this described the end of the former vine. But what kind of planter and farmer the true vine has, and what kind of branches and what kind of clusters, the [?]

[?] …the saving teaching sets forth. From its branches, then, spread throughout the whole inhabited world, vineyards were planted; and their fruits, gathered together in the churches throughout the whole world, produced a great multitude of winepresses. It is because of these that the psalms "For the Winepresses" were uttered prophetically through the Holy Spirit. "Blow the trumpet at the new moon, on the notable day of your feast." At its opening the psalm called them to exultation, and commanded them to shout aloud, that is, to send up a hymn of victory to the God of Jacob who had been named. Then, having received words of teaching, they were to fulfil them in deeds; and having carried out the deeds, they were now at last to proclaim and trumpet to all people, to sound out the Gospel and make it heard by all, just as the Savior commanded when he said to his disciples: "What you hear in the ear, proclaim on the housetops." That is why it is said to those who have accomplished the first things: "Blow the trumpet." And how does he want them to trumpet, if not as those trumpeted long ago who carried out the images, the symbols and types of the true realities? They trumpeted at the new moon and on the notable day of the feast. They did this in the seventh month, when they came together and celebrated the Feast of Trumpets, doing it once a year. The text of the law says: "In the seventh month, on the first day of the month, you shall have a rest, a memorial of trumpets; it shall be a holy convocation for you." So just as they trumpeted at the new moon then, he wants those who have been called to trumpet now as well. That day of the Feast of Trumpets was a notable day; Moses says of it: "You shall do no laborious work. It shall be a day of signal for you." That is why it is said here too: "On the notable day of your feast." It was a notable day, and a feast of nothing else but trumpets; hence it was called the Feast of Trumpets. There were three feasts in that same month: first the Feast of Trumpets, held at the new moon; another, the Day of Atonement, on the tenth day of the month; and a third, the Feast of Tabernacles. Yet he commands them to imitate only the Feast of Trumpets, saying: "Blow the trumpet at the new moon." Put more plainly, he might have said: "Just as at the new moon they once trumpeted, running about everywhere to announce the feast, so you too, whom the word commands, blow the trumpet." He wants the heralds to the nations not to attend to the other Jewish observances, but to use the proclamation alone, and to trumpet the saving word of the Gospel to all people. For Moses made the symbols of these very things, and this was a command specially laid down by law for Israel: that they must blow the trumpet, and by the trumpet signal to everyone the feast of the season. This command was given by judgment, by the will and judgment of the God of Jacob. For he who long ago appeared to Jacob as God in the form and shape of a man was the one who ordained, through Moses, that the people should do these things in figure. That "trumpeting" is used in place of crying aloud and proclaiming to all, the Savior teaches when he says: "When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you."

"He appointed it as a testimony in Joseph, when he went out from the land of Egypt; he heard a language that he did not know." The command about trumpets mentioned above, he says, he appointed as a testimony in Joseph; or, in Symmachus' version, "He ordained it as a testimony through Joseph." He gave the testimony as though solemnly bearing witness, and it was a sign of something else; for it hinted at certain trumpets whose work the apostles of our Savior and the heralds of the Gospel word fulfilled in part, trumpeting to the whole earth and proclaiming to all nations the feast of the saving manifestation of God. But the fulfilment of the more hidden things will come about through angels, as he teaches who said: "For the trumpet will sound, and the dead in Christ will rise first"; and again: "In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet"; and again: "The Lord himself will descend with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God." The Savior too initiated his disciples into these mysteries, saying: "And they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. And he will send out his angels with a great trumpet, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of the heavens to the other." The resurrection of the dead, then, will one day come about through Gospel trumpets announcing the arrival of the kingdom of the Son of God; but already, at his first coming, the apostles used trumpets, the mighty voices of the Holy Spirit, and summoned all who were dead in soul to life in God. Moses handed down the symbols of these things when he legislated the feast of trumpets. That is why it is said: "He appointed it as a testimony in Joseph." And what was this command? The one about the trumpets. By the single tribe of Joseph he denoted the whole nation. And why does he call the whole nation Joseph here? Because it was on account of Joseph that they had all gone down into Egypt. And when did he appoint the law about trumpets as a testimony for the people, if not at the time when he brought them out of the land of Egypt, when "he heard a language that he did not know"? For while they were living in the desert, they were counted worthy to hear the voice of God, as he audibly gave them the Ten Commandments. At that same time they were also set free from slavery and hardship among the Egyptians. That is why it is said: "He removed his back from burdens; his hands served in the basket"; or, in Symmachus' version: "I took his shoulder from the load; his hands were released from the basket." For when they were slaves to Pharaoh, toiling at clay and brickmaking and building cities for him, their hands were worn out by baskets and their shoulders by loads. But they were set free from all of this when God visited them. That is why he says: "He removed his back from burdens." And who removed it,

if not God, who set them free? He granted them this because they called upon him in their affliction. The Scripture of Moses also shows this, saying: "And the sons of Israel groaned, and cried out to the Lord, and their cry went up to God." In agreement with this the present oracle says: "In affliction you called upon me, and I rescued you; I heard you in the hidden place of the storm; I tested you at the water of contradiction." In place of "I heard you in the hidden place of the storm," Aquila has: "I will answer you in the hidden place of thunder," and the fifth edition likewise. Then he adds: "I tested you at the water of contradiction." This too the Scripture of Moses clearly sets out, saying: "There was no water for the people to drink; and the people railed at Moses, saying: Give us water to drink. And he said: Why do you rail at me, or why do you test the Lord?" And further on: "Moses cried out to the Lord, saying: What shall I do with this people? A little more, and they will stone me." Then the Lord says to him: "Behold, I stand there before you, on the rock in Horeb. And I will strike the rock, and water will come out, and the people will drink. And Moses did so. And he called the name of that place Testing and Railing, because of the railing of the sons of Israel, and because they tested the Lord, saying: Is the Lord among us or not?" The prophecy before us teaches all this to the people from the nations, so that they may learn what kind of things the first people received and to what kind of end they came, and may be brought to their senses by the example. That is why it necessarily joins to what was said before the words that follow: "Hear, my people, and I will testify to you: Israel, if you will hear me, there shall be no new god among you, nor shall you worship a foreign god. For I am the Lord your God, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt; open wide your mouth, and I will fill it. But my people did not hear my voice, and Israel paid no heed to me. So I sent them away according to the devices of their hearts; they will walk in their own devices." What I gave to the people, he says, was such as the passage has described; but what they gave me in return was not like it, nor worthy of what they had received from [me]. For I, the provider of so many good things for them, commanded them this one thing, the very sum of the laws: I mean, not to worship idols, but to acknowledge me alone as God. I urged exactly this, saying: "Hear, my people, and I will testify to you: Israel, if you will hear me, there shall be no new god among you, nor shall you worship a foreign god; for I am the Lord your God, who brought you up out of Egypt." This is what I urged; this is what my mind intended. And a promise of good things was joined to the commands, in which I said: "Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it." For if you keep these things,

you will have your food in abundance without toil, whether the food of the body or that supplied to the soul through divine teachings. So I urged and promised these things; but they did not hear my voice, and Israel, though counted worthy of such great benefits, paid no heed to me. Therefore I rightly sent them away according to the devices of their hearts. Symmachus rendered this as: "But my people did not obey my voice, and Israel was not persuaded by me. So I left them to the pleasure of their heart, to walk in their own counsels." From this the divine Apostle teaches about certain people, saying: "Therefore God gave them up in the desires of their hearts." In place of "There shall be no new god among you," Aquila has: "There shall be no foreign mighty one among you," and Symmachus rendered: "Let there be no strange god among you." A strange, foreign and new god is what he calls the one mistakenly believed in among the nations, thereby dismissing polytheistic idolatry. To this he adds: "For I am the Lord your God," showing that he himself is a God neither strange, nor foreign, nor new. For it was one and the same Word of God who long ago spoke to the ancients in various ways, who was called the God of Jacob, and who at the consummation of the ages appeared on earth. For he was in the world even before his manifestation, and the world came into being through him. That is why he exhorts them, saying: "For I am the Lord your God, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt. If my people had heard me, if Israel had walked in my ways, I would have humbled their enemies in no time, and laid my hand on those who afflict them." He has made a sufficient defense, showing that the wrath of God came upon the Jewish nation neither without judgment nor by chance. And it seems to me that here the answer has been given to the questions raised earlier in "Why, O God, have you rejected us forever? Why has your anger been kindled against the sheep of your pasture?" and again: "Why have you broken down its hedge, so that all who pass along the way pluck its fruit?" For why they suffered such things he teaches, saying: "Because my people did not hear my voice, and Israel paid no heed to me"; and: "If my people had heard me, if Israel had walked in my ways, I would have humbled their enemies in no time." Symmachus rendered this: "In a very short time I would have defeated their enemies, and turned my hand against their adversaries." I would have done these things, he says, against the enemies of the people, if I had had them obedient, and if they had walked in the ways I laid down for them. But as it is, having become deaf and disobedient, they have made themselves enemies of God. Then, since the Holy Spirit, out of overflowing kindness, had called the disobedient and deaf his people, he teaches that no one who disobeys God could be his people. That is why he adds: "The enemies of the Lord lied to him"; or, in Symmachus' version: "Haters of the Lord, who lied to him." And he goes on: "And their time will be forever." For even though they have dared such things, they will nevertheless have the present age. And this is their time, in

which, even after so many offences, he fed them with the fat of wheat and satisfied them with honey from the rock. In this he fulfilled it, counting them worthy of his own food, not only bodily but also heavenly and spiritual: when the Christ of God first came to dwell among them, he gave them himself as food, the heavenly bread. More than that, he fed them wondrously from five loaves in the desert, as long ago he gave them the manna through Moses. Further, he satisfied them with honey from the rock; and the rock was he himself, supplying them with teachings sweeter than every pleasure and all honey, of which one could say: "How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth!" Long ago, too, through Moses he gave them drink from the rock. But the honey from the rock here must be taken in no other way than according to the sense, since Moses himself gives the same testimony, saying in the great Song: "They sucked honey from the rock, and oil from the solid rock." These things did not happen according to the bare letter, but are to be understood allegorically, in their sense alone. For Christ himself is the rock, providing all these things to them through his teaching, not only at the time when he dwelt among them but even before his coming in the flesh, so that they are wholly without excuse, and the judgment of God, which after so much brought about their rejection, is just. But the word teaches these things to us from the nations, who through the first people have been called to godly exultation, putting us on our guard so that we ourselves may never fall into the same things. "God stood in the assembly of gods; in their midst he judges between gods." The preceding psalm accuses the whole Jewish people, God saying plainly: "My people did not hear my voice, and Israel paid no heed to me. So I sent them away according to the devices of their heart"; and again: "If my people had heard me, if Israel had walked in my ways, I would have humbled their enemies in no time." The psalm before us, following on from that, accuses the leaders of the people. It addresses them as rulers and judges, saying: "How long will you judge unjustly and show favor to the persons of sinners? Judge the poor and lowly; vindicate the orphan and the needy." Then he adds: I commanded these things, "but they did not know nor understand; they walk about in darkness." He calls them gods either because of the honor the people paid them, approaching them with the greatest fear and honor, as if they were God himself; or because they held the place of God, having taken on the office of judging, punishing and chastising wrongdoers according to their law; or because they had been honored by God with the name of adoption, so that it was said of them: "I have begotten sons

and raised them up"; or because they were made according to the image and likeness of God, through the intellectual and rational being that is in human beings. Indeed, further on in this same psalm, the word says to those accused: "I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High. But you die like men, and fall like one of the rulers." It is when God the Word examines the leaders of the people, that is, the priests and high priests and the other rulers, that he goes through what is before us. That is why it is said: "God stood in the assembly of gods; in their midst he judges between gods"; or, in Aquila's version: "God stood in the assembly of the mighty; in the inmost part the Lord judges"; or, in Symmachus' version: "God took his stand in the council of God; in the midst, God judging." This God who judges, namely the Word of God, also judges between those of the so-called assembly of gods, and brings reproofs against those on trial. And since "the mighty will be mightily tested," he rightly sets apart the rank of the gods just mentioned and judges them separately, having already gone through the reproof of the mass of the people in the preceding psalm. And he judges between them, deciding who are worthy of salvation and who are not. He does not judge arrogantly or tyrannically, seated on high, but stoops down to those being judged and stands in their midst, made like them in the human form he assumed. And from this point on he addresses them in advance, correcting those who are to be judged and guarding them so that they may not fall into the punishment of judgment, but may first set themselves right and take precautions in response to the reproofs brought against them. That is why he says: "How long will you judge unjustly and show favor to the persons of sinners? Judge for the poor and the orphan." The prophetic Spirit cried out similar things through Isaiah, saying: "Learn to do good, seek justice, judge for the orphan and vindicate the widow; and come, let us reason together, says the Lord. And though your sins are like scarlet, I will make them white as snow." Such are the warnings the word gives beforehand; but those who had been honored with the title of gods, and counted worthy of such great teaching, did not know nor understand; they walk about in darkness. These words might also be referred to the time of our Savior's first coming, when he went into the synagogues of the Jewish nation and, passing into the midst of the rulers, held his discussions with them, brought reproofs against them, [?] bearing witness…

…having received from the Father, how is it not entirely just to exalt him with the venerable honor due to God? The Savior himself put this to the very rulers of the Jews as a rebuke, using these very words. For when they said: "We are not stoning you for a good work, but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God," Jesus answered them: "Is it not written in your law, I said, You are gods? If he called them gods to whom the word of God came, and Scripture cannot be broken, do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, You are blaspheming, because I said, I am the Son of God?" If the Savior says, "Is it not written in the law?", do not be surprised; for he teaches us to receive every word of God, not only that of Moses but also what was spoken through the prophets, as a kind of royal law, so that one might reasonably call what was commanded through the prophets laws of God too, and likewise what was given in the psalms. So the Word of God himself, taking the form of a servant and being found in appearance as a man, stood in the assembly of gods, and, being in the midst of those who among men were called gods, judged them when he said to them: "The word that I have spoken to you, that will judge you." It is more fitting to understand the present Scripture in this way than to think that the God who is beyond all things, the Father himself, is presented here as standing among other gods. For it is not right to suppose that any beings share equal honor with him, nor to bring him so low as to imagine him present and standing in the midst of human beings. But all these things would fit the Christ of God, who in saying "How long will you judge unjustly and show favor to the persons of sinners?" would be saying it not only to those with whom he spoke in person but to all who have received authority to judge others. He rightly blames those who defer to the persons of the rich while oppressing the poor, when they ought to judge by the scale of justice, remembering the law that says: "You shall not show partiality in judgment." But as it is, we too are often harsh judges when the poor commit some small fault, and unrelenting in our sentences against them; yet when the rich commit the gravest sins and then come into the Church of God, we show them partiality. So the words "How long will you judge unjustly and show favor to the persons of sinners?" apply to us as well. In saying "how long," he reminds them of their departure from this life. For how much time, he says, will you have in which to go on like this? After that, the judgment of God will overtake you. That is why he adds: "Judge the poor and the orphan; vindicate the lowly and the needy. Rescue the needy, and deliver the poor from the hand of the sinner." If, then, we listen to these words and are instructed by them, and keep their commands, we shall gain the benefit of the words. Otherwise it will be said of us too: "They did not know nor understand; they walk about in darkness." But what … not [?]

…knew nor understood, or that very soon they themselves will stand before the judgment seat of God to give an account of the cases they judged unjustly. But those who have not set God's judgment before their eyes walk on in darkness, having filled the eyes of their soul with the darkness of ignorance. So those who are enlightened by the light of the Word ought either not to judge at all, remembering the one who said, "Do not judge, so that you may not be judged"; or, if judging is ever necessary, to do it as justly as possible and to reprove those who sin, even if they must die for the truth. They should be firmly convinced that there will be a consummation and transformation of all things at God's universal judgment, which he will carry out through his Christ. The present passage also points to this judgment when it goes on to say: "All the foundations of the earth shall be shaken. I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High; but you die like men, and fall like one of the rulers." To the gods already mentioned, that is, the leaders and rulers of the people, the God who came to be in their midst also addresses these words. He teaches that, imitating the Father's generosity, he did not begrudge sharing his own divinity with all of them. So he proclaimed them gods and called them all sons of the Most High, a title that belonged to him alone. But they treated this grace with contempt. You will understand how those who received their authority from God came to hold the honour of gods among those they ruled if you consider what was said to Moses: "See, I have made you today a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet." Moses was a man of God, and because he received this honour from God he was proclaimed a god to Pharaoh. In the same way, all whom God honours have taken the place of gods among those placed under them. That is why their subjects approach them with reverence and fear, not because of any military bodyguard, nor because of wealth and power, but because of the honour with which God has surrounded them. So too Moses' face was glorified. So too were the faces of our Saviour's apostles and of God's prophets of old, and of all the true servants of God, who remained without renown and lived in poverty, yet were honoured among the God-fearing because of the grace God had given them. "I, then," he says, "both willed it and said, You are gods. I wanted you to become sons of the Most High, like me, the God who stands in your midst. But you rejected the grace. So you die in human vices and in your own sins. For the soul that sins shall die. That is why you die like men, and fall like one of the rulers." The devil was once counted worthy of honour with God and was one of the ruling angels in heaven. Then, by making a wicked choice, he fell from his place, so that it was said of him: "How has the Morning Star, who rose at dawn, fallen from heaven!" In the same way you too have

become something of that kind. You were not evil by nature, but you made a choice that was not good. What came from me called you to the honour of God; but you imitated the ruler of the fall, and so you yourselves also fall like one of the rulers. "Arise, O God, judge the earth, for you shall inherit among all the nations." This follows very fittingly. In the psalm before this one the passage accused the whole Jewish nation, and in the psalm at hand it likewise brought an accusation against the rulers of the people. Now it asks for reconciliation and prays that an appearing may come, no longer to the Jewish nation alone but to all the nations. So it adds: "Arise, O God, judge the earth, for you shall inherit among all the nations." Do not ask who it is that inherits among all the nations. Examine the matter itself, and you will find that it is none other than the Christ of God, to whom the Father said: "You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession." So the present passage rouses this God who stood in the midst of the gods and refuted those mentioned before, and it asks him at last to fulfil the promise made to him, saying: "Arise, O God, judge the earth, for you shall inherit among all the nations." It means: "Those who were accused before became evil judges and walked in darkness. But it belongs to you to judge justly, for the Father has given judgment to the Son alone. So now at last arise yourself, and through your own resurrection bring about the common resurrection of all people. And judge the earth, that is, all the people who live on the earth. It is fitting for you to judge all people, since you shall inherit among all the nations." The present psalm spoke of an assembly of gods and of God standing in their midst and judging between gods. All of its teaching concerned judgment, and at the end it added: "Arise, O God, judge the earth." The Holy Spirit uttered all these things through the prophet Asaph. But we have found that Psalm 49 is also inscribed "Of Asaph" and treats judgment just as these psalms do. So we have reasonably concluded that it follows on from this one: it too belongs to Asaph and introduces the same subject. In it we read: "The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting." See how the end of the psalm at hand says, "Arise, O God, judge the earth," while Psalm 49 begins, "The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and summoned the earth." Here it says, "For you shall inherit among all the nations"; there, "from the rising of the sun to its setting." Again, Psalm 49 says, "God will come openly, our God, and will not keep silent." What he will do when he comes is taught by the psalm at hand: "God stood in the assembly of gods; in their midst he judges between gods." And how he judges, Psalm 49 makes clear: "Fire will blaze before him, and around him a mighty storm.

He will summon the heaven above and the earth to judge his people." For these reasons, then, we have reasonably concluded that Psalm 49 follows the psalm at hand. This too should be noted: like the psalms of Asaph grouped together here, it contains the rejection of the Jewish nation and the reasons for it. Psalm 49, which belongs to the same prophet, introduces the overthrow of the law of Moses by rejecting the sacrifices. So in this respect too the connection in the thought of these psalms is shown. Why Psalm 49 has been moved out of its connection with these psalms and placed before the confession in Psalm 50 we have already explained in our observations on it.

A SONG: A PSALM OF ASAPH. PSALM 82. "O God, who shall be likened to you? Do not keep silent, and do not be still, O God." Psalm 79 foretold the destruction of the vineyard, the fall of the Jewish nation, and the burning and desolation of the place they honoured. The two psalms that follow it taught why they suffered these things. The present psalm, joined to those, makes supplication and entreaty on behalf of the people. After such gloomy things it was necessary to bring a kind of remedy for what had been said, since the psalms of Asaph [?] were to conclude with this one. That is also why the present passage is inscribed "A Song: A Psalm": it prays for good things for the people. This psalm is the eleventh of those inscribed "Of Asaph," of which Psalm 72 was the first. If Psalm 49 is counted with them, because it too belongs to Asaph, there are twelve in all. In this psalm the Prophet says in his supplication to God: "O God, who shall be likened to you? Do not keep silent, and do not be still, O God." He means: "No one is like God, who is long-suffering and forbearing and therefore bears with everyone. Who else could endure, as you do, the blasphemies and arrogance of godless and impious men? So no one shall be likened to you, O God. But I, as a man overcome by my own weakness, dare to entreat you, God, and to say to you in supplication: Do not keep silent, and do not be still, O God." God is said to be silent when godless and impious men exalt themselves and he seems to take no notice: he does not bring his wrath upon them at once, nor does he punish them. That is why the same Asaph, in Psalm 49, presents God saying to sinners: "These things you did, and I kept silent; in your lawlessness you supposed that I would be like you." The Apostle teaches the reasons for God's silence, forbearance and long-suffering when he writes: "Or do you despise the riches of his kindness and forbearance and long-suffering, not knowing that God's kindness leads you to repentance?" The Prophet continues: "But you, as God, bear with all things and endure everyone

gently. Even when people commit impious and godless sins and blaspheme against you, God, you keep silent. But I cannot bear to see these things. I beg and entreat to be pardoned for not being able to endure them as you, God, do; for who shall be likened to you? So as a man with zeal for reverence toward you, I dare to bring you a supplication: that you cease from your unspeakable long-suffering and your forbearing silence, and now at last be moved against those who have dared to do things beyond remedy. That is why I say: Do not keep silent, and do not be still." Here Aquila has "Do not keep quiet," and Symmachus "Do not rest." He then adds: "For see, your enemies have made an uproar, and those who hate you have lifted up their head." Aquila has: "For see, your enemies have gathered in a mob, and those who make themselves haters of you have lifted up their head." Symmachus has: "For see, your enemies roar together, and those who hate you lift up the head." The enemies of God make an uproar and gather in a mob when they no longer mutter their blasphemies against God secretly or with restraint. Instead they all openly and together hurl godless words against God, as they dare to do in times of persecution. Then also [?] and snorting with pride they lift up their head, especially when God's silence brings about their ruin. When they lift up their head, the people of God are worn down and humbled. Conversely, when the enemies of God are humbled, the heads of holy and God-loving men are lifted up. That is why it is said somewhere in their person: "And now he has lifted up my head over my enemies."

"Against your people they have craftily devised a plan, and they have plotted against your holy ones. They said: Come, let us wipe them out as a nation, and the name of Israel shall be remembered no more." The Prophet, in the Holy Spirit, presses God by reminding him that it was his people who had suffered so much. Then he also recalls God's holy ones who shone among the people long before. He begs and pleads that God remember not the impious and lawless among them but only his holy ones, and for their sake have mercy on the whole nation. The enemies of God, true to their character, make war on his people, using craft and deceit to overthrow it and turn it away from reverence for God. That is why it is said: "Against your people they have craftily devised a plan, and they have plotted against your holy ones." With care and deliberation they patch together secret schemes against God's people and contrive plots against his holy ones. They have set before themselves a single aim, and they say: "Come, let us wipe them out as a nation, and the name of Israel shall be remembered no more." Those who fight against God do not want a nation of God to exist among men; they are eager that even the name of Israel be blotted out. But God is always forming a nation for himself on earth. After the fall of the former people he established the Church from the nations,

the new and young nation that has come into being throughout the whole world from those chosen out of the nations. So the name of Israel and the memory of all God-loving men are celebrated all the more, and the achievements of godliness shine out. "For they have conspired with one accord; against you they have made a covenant: the tents of the Edomites and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagrites, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek, foreigners with those who dwell in Tyre. For Assyria too came with them; they became a support to the sons of Lot. Interlude." In his supplication for the people the Prophet says "against you," as though rousing and provoking God. He means: "The enemies of your people have dared all this not against the people but against you and against your covenant." Next he recounts what was done when the Assyrians attacked the Jewish nation. He prophesies these things after first going through the reasons why they were handed over to their enemies. In the psalm before this one he refuted the rulers of the people, saying, "How long will you judge unjustly?" and again, "They have not known nor understood; they walk on in darkness." In the psalm before that he accused the whole nation, saying, "And my people did not hear my voice, and Israel paid no heed to me." And in Psalm 77 he went through a long list of their transgressions. So it follows that he now prophesies what happened to them long afterwards for the reasons already given. They were besieged at different times: first by the Babylonians, second by Antiochus king of Syria, and last of all by the Romans, after their outrage against our Saviour. So it is fitting that the same prophet, through the Spirit's foreknowledge, foretells these three sieges. In Psalm 73 he points to the last, as we showed in the proper place. In Psalm 78 he points to the siege under Antiochus the Syrian, as has been demonstrated. In the psalm at hand he mentions the first, I mean the Assyrian siege, which Psalm 79 also foretold when it pointed to the burning of the vineyard and its desolation. One can also learn from history how many nations [?] together against the Jewish people in the first Assyrian attack. The prophecy at hand also lists them, naming first the Edomites, then the Ishmaelites, third the Moabites, fourth the Hagrites, then the Gebalites, the Ammonites and the Amalekites. Besides these it says: "foreigners with those who dwell in Tyre." For "foreigners" Aquila and Symmachus have "Philistia"; it is customary to call those who live in Gaza, Ascalon and the coastal region by this name. He means: "These coastal foreigners, together with the inhabitants of Tyre, attacked your people. Above all came the Assyrian, the very head of these evils, who set out with them

and drew up his forces using them as allies." And all those mentioned together became a support to the sons of Lot. Here Aquila has "They became an arm to the sons of Lot," and Symmachus "They became allies to the sons of Lot." The sons of Lot were the Ammonites and Moabites, for Lot had two sons, Moab and Ammon. History clearly shows that these things were fulfilled at no other time than in the time of the Assyrians. At that time all the neighbouring nations envied Jerusalem and the temple of God raised up (1) in it, and thirsted for the destruction of the whole Jewish nation. So they attacked the Jews together, as allies of the Babylonian power. At that time, then, many nations allied with the Assyrians were gathered against them. But neither under Antiochus nor in the last siege do the nations listed appear as allies of the Romans when the Romans undertook the war against the Jews. "Do to them as to Midian and to Sisera, as to Jabin at the torrent of Kishon. They were destroyed at Endor; they became like dung on the ground. Make their rulers like Oreb and Zeeb and Zebah and Zalmunna." The Prophet declares that the nations mentioned will suffer what once befell Midian and Sisera and Jabin at the torrent of Kishon: they were all destroyed together at Endor and became like dung on the ground. He also asks that the rulers of these nations suffer what Oreb and Zeeb and Zebah and Zalmunna suffered. You will find the story of all of them in the book of Judges, where Scripture sets out what Sisera, Jabin and the others named devised against Israel and what they suffered. We refer anyone who wants to know about them to that book, since the account is rather long. He entreats that these enemies suffer the same things as those, because they spoke just as those did: "Let us take for ourselves the sanctuary of God as an inheritance." Sisera, Jabin and the others whom the passage [?] word for word (2) said this about the tabernacle and the ark of God. These were the sanctuary of God, since Jerusalem had not yet been established. The Prophet prayed for these things against those named, and not long afterwards his prayer was fulfilled. Immediately after the siege of the Jews, the Assyrian power was destroyed. It had lasted for [?] periods of time, and it endured only until they dared such things against Jerusalem. Not long afterwards Cyrus took control of the Persian kingdom and overthrew the empire of the Assyrians. The other nations named one by one also suffered the things the passage foretold. So one might reasonably say that in these words the Prophet is not cursing those named but prophesying what would happen to them. By a certain habit of Scripture he uses the imperative mood instead of the predictive, so that we should understand the words. (1) Read: "raised up."

"Do to them" as meaning "You will do to them as to Midian and to Sisera." These things are prophesied about the end of the Assyrians and of those listed with them. Nothing of the kind, however, was said about those who carried out the last siege after the coming of our Saviour. That is why the Romans suffered nothing of the sort after their attack on the nation. "My God, make them like a wheel, like stubble before the wind." It is not without reason that the Prophet, or rather the Holy Spirit in him, [calls upon] God in the present account by saying "my God." He says not "our God" but "my God," as if at the time of the Assyrian siege only one rare person worthy of God was left. Since the whole people had fallen away and had been handed over to the besiegers because of their sins, he does not make the invocation shared but speaks it in his own person alone: "My God, make them like a wheel." A wheel by nature turns and does not stay in one place. The whole life of the godless is like that: at one time it is raised on high, then it turns to the opposite, just like a wheel. So first he says, "Make them like a wheel"; then, "like stubble before the wind"; then, "like fire that will burn through a forest"; and besides these, "like a flame that will burn up mountains." Through these words he foretells that they would rise up against one another and bring upon themselves the punishment for what they had dared, saying: [?] them. Compare "like stubble before the wind" with what is said elsewhere: "Not so the ungodly, not so; but like chaff that the wind drives from the face of the earth." The words "like fire that will burn through a forest" show that they themselves are the fire and they themselves are the forest, so that they will be burned by themselves. This agrees with the oracle that says: "Walk by the light of your fire and by the flame that you have kindled." The words "like a flame that will burn up mountains" show how great their wickedness is: their own flame will burn up their pride and their heights as if they were mountains. To these he adds: "So you will pursue them." Elsewhere it is also said: "Fire and brimstone and a scorching wind are the portion of their cup." By these words the passage taught that the storm and wrath of God are not passions in God. They are a kind of judgment through which these people rose up against themselves and received from themselves the punishment for what they had done. He entreats, or rather prophesies, that all these things will come upon the enemies of God, so that even in this way they might at some point be helped. The greatest help is to know God and to come to seek his name, and he teaches that this will happen to them after the things already mentioned, saying: "And they will seek your name, O Lord. Let them be put to shame and troubled for ever and ever; let them be confounded and perish. And let them know that your name is Lord; you alone are Most High over all the earth." He teaches that the end of God's enemies will come about in two ways

…he prophesies, one in which he holds out good hopes for them, if indeed the knowledge of God is a good thing, and the grasp of his name, and that those who did not know God before should be taught that he alone is Most High over all the earth. For it is likely that those who confess these things have forgotten their own former error of many gods and have put away the vain and deceitful falsehood about gods. The other way is the one in which he foretells shame and confusion and disgrace, and on top of all these destruction, for those who deserve them. To those who change for the better through turning to God he teaches that the knowledge of God will come; but to those who grow old in their own wickedness he threatens ruin and destruction. So concerning the worse it has been said: “Let them be put to shame and troubled forever and ever, and let them be disgraced and perish.” But concerning those who will be changed for the better: “And let them know that your name is Lord; you alone are Most High over all the earth.” Yet the whole could also be said of the same people, namely the enemies of God. At the time when they suffer what was foretold, they will be disgraced and put to shame and handed over to destruction. Then, by experience itself, they will come to know and confess that the one and only God is the Most High over all the earth, the one who also punished them with just judgment for what they had dared

FOR THE END, CONCERNING THE WINEPRESSES, FOR THE SONS OF KORAH. A PSALM. [?]

“How beloved are your dwellings, Lord of hosts!” Now that the psalms inscribed to Asaph have come to an end, of which the first was the 72nd and the last the 82nd, the present 83rd follows. It is inscribed to the sons of Korah, about whom we set out our views in the introductory discussions. It must be observed that the psalms of Asaph number twelve in all, and those inscribed to the sons of Korah are equal to them in number. Of the sons of Korah, eight were joined together in sequence, beginning from the 41st psalm; the remaining four are placed here, beginning from the 83rd and set immediately after those inscribed to Asaph. Likewise eleven of Asaph's are joined together, from the 72nd to the 82nd, and the twelfth is placed immediately after the first eight of the sons of Korah. It is as if an exchange had been made, because the insights contained in the prophecies of each group are shared with the other. The first psalms of the sons of Korah, then, were eight in number, beginning with the 41st and ending with the 48th. To put it in summary, they contained weeping, lament and mourning over the people of the circumcision, and also the coming of Christ and the calling of the nations. Such was the subject of those eight. Of the four now before us, also inscribed to the sons of Korah, the last two take in his birth and death, as though the Word had deliberately held back until the end of all of them to reveal the predictions about

these things. There was much said, at any rate, about his birth, which he hinted at in veiled terms in the 86th psalm; and fuller and deeper was what was said about his death, which he took upon himself for the sake of humankind. This is contained in the last of all those inscribed to the sons of Korah, I mean the 87th. The two psalms that precede these, the one in hand and the one after it, prophesy his coming among humankind and the achievements that followed from it. The present psalm is inscribed “For the end, concerning the winepresses.” Of the three that bear such an inscription, this is one; the 8th is inscribed in the same way, and so is the 80th. But two of these were called psalms, the 8th and the present one, and for this reason they contain announcements of good things. The 80th was “concerning the winepresses” but was not also called a psalm, because it contains some gloomy things against Israel. The three “concerning the winepresses” are assigned to three persons: the 8th to David, the 80th to Asaph, and the one in hand to the sons of Korah. And in agreement all three are inscribed “For the end,” I think because of the prophecies in them, which were fulfilled at the end of the times and at the consummation of the age. Long ago, then, since there was one vineyard, of which it was said, “For the vineyard of the Lord of Sabaoth is the house of Israel,” there was, so to speak, one winepress in it. Isaiah mentions it, speaking in the person of the Lord: “And I built a tower, and dug a wine vat in it.” By the tower he meant the temple in Jerusalem, and by the wine vat the altar beside the temple. He fittingly called it not a winepress but a “fore-press,” since bodily things came before spiritual ones, and before the New Covenant the Old preserved among the Jews symbols and images of the true things. That is why the altar among them was called not a winepress but a fore-press. As there was one vineyard, there was of old one winepress, and one temple's altar. But the three psalms now in view mention not one but many winepresses, and in this way they point to the churches of our Saviour throughout the whole world. Right away in the present psalm the heading says “concerning the winepresses,” and next is added: “How beloved are your dwellings, Lord of hosts!” The word all but plainly [?]

indicates the altars, dwellings and courts throughout the whole inhabited world of humankind. “Others love other things,” he says, “and set great store by them; but to me, O Lord, your dwellings are dear and beloved, in which you yourself deigned to dwell, having spent your life among human beings, as you said: ‘Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst.’ These things are so dear and beloved to me that, through the excess of my longing for them, I confess my soul faints, overcome by yearning for them, and I prefer time spent in your courts to life itself. And not only does my soul faint, but my heart as well, and besides my heart my very body and the flesh I am clothed in. For these too are filled with joy and gladness at the memory of the life with you, so that I speak the truth when I say: ‘My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God.’” For our God is living. He alone possesses life as his own and by nature in himself; or rather, since he is himself the source of all life, he gives a share of it to all who draw near. Therefore even my flesh, mortal and corruptible by nature, rejoices and shares in the joy, since through him it will partake of eternal life and receive the grace of God. The prophet says these things to show what love and longing he had for the things he prophesied. That is why our Saviour said: “Many prophets and righteous men longed to see what you see, and did not see it.” He says that the flesh together with the heart rejoices in the living God, hinting, I think, at the Saviour's resurrection from the dead as well. For the supposed gods of the nations are dead and lifeless: “For the idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands,” and these were what people worshipped in those days. “But I,” he says, “foresee no such god, but a living God, and I am glad in my heart. And this very flesh of mine has rejoiced in this God, as in a God who truly lives and gives life to the dead, who will also give life to my very flesh through his own resurrection. Therefore, besides my soul, my flesh too has rejoiced.” “For the sparrow has found itself a house, and the turtledove a nest for herself, where she will lay her young: your altars, Lord of hosts.” “And how is it not right,” he says, “to confess that your dwellings are dear and beloved, O Lord, when they have become a refuge for everyone who can say, ‘Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters,’ and again for the one who says, ‘In the Lord I have put my trust; how can you say to my soul, “Flee to the mountains like a sparrow”? For see, the sinners have bent the bow, they have made ready arrows in the quiver’?” Many were trying to bring down the God-loving soul with snares and to hunt it as with nets, while it flitted here and there and wandered everywhere, having no rest in this mortal life. For such a soul, God's dwellings alone became a refuge. So it was said, “For the sparrow has found itself a house,” but

also “the turtledove a nest.” The soul that practises dignity and chastity in this present life (for such the bird is said to be), weeping and lamenting the wickedness among humankind, has itself also found refuge in the altars set up throughout the whole world through the teaching of your Christ. There, as in nests and nesting places, she will lay the newborn and newly hatched of her offspring, having found a safe dwelling for her chicks, free from any plot. So your altars are a house for the sparrow and a nest for the turtledove. For these birds, I mean the sparrow and the turtledove, had no refuge in former times, before the altars were established everywhere on earth. They wandered for long periods, during which they were driven off and pursued by the hunters. That is why the one driven like a sparrow said, “In the Lord I have put my trust; how can you say to my soul, ‘Flee to the mountains like a sparrow’?” And once rescued from the hand of their enemies, they too confessed, saying, “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters.” The hunters, then, hidden and invisible, plotting against the souls that pursue the heavenly and exalted life, set nets and snares and prepared every kind of trap to catch them. This was shown in the preceding psalm, where it was said: “For see, your enemies have made an uproar, and those who hate you have lifted up their head. Against your people they have laid crafty plans; they have plotted against your holy ones.” In these times of persecution, when the enemies of God were waging war on his people and driving them out, the people of God fled here and there like sparrows. At last they were counted worthy of peace and found God's dwellings, his courts and his altars, a refuge and a rest for themselves. You might say that those who travel light and have chosen the solitary life are the sparrow, while those who have taken on the care of raising children and of managing other affairs are the turtledove. He says the turtledove must offer her own chicks to God and dedicate them at his altars, as in a nest. “My King and my God, blessed are all who dwell in your house; they will praise you forever and ever. Pause.” Why are your dwellings dear and beloved to me? For what reason does my soul faint for them? And in what have my heart and my [?] rejoiced? Because the sparrow has found itself a house and the turtledove a nest: your altars, Lord of hosts. At these altars, those who do not stay briefly but dwell there continually and remain there permanently are thrice blessed. In saying this he set aside all the legal observances of Moses. For he did not call blessed the circumcised, nor those who keep the Sabbaths, nor those who observe the sacrifices prescribed by Moses and the other commandments of the bodily law, nor even the descendants of Abraham, nor Israel,

nor the nation of the Jews. He called blessed, quite simply, all who dwell in the house of God. For what could truly be more blessed than to claim God as one's own King, and the Lord of hosts, and to dwell continually in his house, which provides immortality from God and eternal life? This at any rate is what the word presents when it says, “Forever and ever those who dwell in your house will praise you.” How else could anyone praise God forever and ever, except by living forever himself, having gained everlasting and immortal life? “Blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has set ascents in his heart, in the valley of weeping, in the place which he has appointed.” Having completed the sequence and train of thought, he changes the direction of his words after the pause. So, having called blessed above, in the plural, those who dwell in God's house, here he singles out one person as especially blessed. Who is this, if not the one counted worthy of help from God in the valley of weeping, the one who has also had ascents of God in his heart? It is this man he now calls blessed, and not the one who keeps the bodily commandments of Moses. Such is everyone who weeps for himself in this mortal, human life and is weighed down by this earthly existence, which the word calls the valley of weeping. It is so called because things here deserve weeping, and people on earth do things that deserve weeping, and because God's saints weep in the present life, groaning and weighed down, as the Apostle says. Everyone, then, who receives help from God in the valley of weeping, that is, in mortal life, would truly be blessed, especially when ascents of God arise in his heart. For other people are dragged down by mortal thoughts into every kind of sin, and are tripped up as well by the assaults of demons and the promptings of evil spirits. But the one who is not caught by these, and by God's grace gains good ascents and thoughts sent from God in his heart, is truly blessed. He also dwells always in God's house and, like a priest, devotes himself solely to the worship of God. He is blessed because, first, he has God as his helper, who aids him and supports him in all his actions; and then because he possesses ascents of God in his heart. The ascents signify good thoughts and good reflections which, in keeping with God's will, rise up and run up into the mind of the one who is called blessed. You will understand this if you set beside it the saying: “When they persecute you and bring you before councils, do not be anxious about how or what you are to say; for the word will be given you when you open your mouth. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father in heaven who speaks in you.” The one in whom the Spirit of God speaks has ascents of God arising in his heart. That is why he is fittingly called blessed. And this same man, in the place of weeping, that is, in the [?] place, has set forth [?], championing the covenant of God and his oracles. (Matt. 10:19–20; Eph. 6:19.)

Instead of “He has set in the valley of weeping,” Symmachus says, “Passing through the valley, he wept.” We have said that in these words the valley of weeping signifies human life. The blessed man passes along and runs through it like a sojourner and a stranger, longing for his heavenly homeland, and he weeps [?] the weeping that makes one blessed, according to the saying “Blessed are those who weep.” Such was Paul, who says: “We who are in this tent groan, being weighed down.” Instead of “in the place which he has appointed,” Aquila says, “They will make it a spring,” and Symmachus, “A spring will be appointed.” What will they make a spring, he asks, if not clearly the valley of weeping? Aquila, at any rate, rendered the whole verse this way: “Passing through the valley of weeping, they will make it a spring.” By this he shows that the sojourners and strangers in this life will make the valley of humankind a spring, or appoint a spring, as Symmachus has it, and in this way he names the divine teaching. For a spring of life and a drink of immortality have been laid down in the valley of weeping, which is human life, by the people of God. They did this through the life-giving and godly teaching which they themselves followed and have left behind for others in their writings. To these very people, he says, their lawgiver will give blessings as a reward for their weeping and as its worthy fruit. To whom will he give the blessings, if not clearly to those who weep in this valley and have set up a spring in it? Instead of “the lawgiver,” Aquila used the word “the early rain,” Symmachus “the one who shows,” the fifth edition “the one who enlightens,” and yet another, sixth edition besides these, “the one who teaches.” So from all of them we are to understand the saving Word. For he is the one who gives the law; he is also the one who enlightens and the one who teaches; he is the early rain, and he is the one who shows. He uses these titles according to each aspect of the powers in him. From him those who weep in the valley receive blessings, and they will go on, completing their journey and being strengthened day by day, so as always to progress and advance from lesser power to greater power, and from glory to glory. As the divine Apostle says, “being transformed into the same image from glory to glory.” That is why Symmachus rendered it, “They will journey from strength to strength.” “The God of gods will be seen in Zion. Lord God of hosts, hear my prayer; give ear, O God of Jacob.” Having said, “The lawgiver will give blessings,” he goes on to teach how he will give the blessings to those in the valley. How then will he give them, he asks, if not by deigning to be seen on earth? And very consistently, having prophesied that there would be a great many winepresses of God throughout the whole world, and a great many dwellings, more courts and a great many altars, the word adds the cause through which all these things were to be established on earth. He teaches what that cause was when he says, “The God of gods will be seen in Zion,” clearly teaching the coming of God among humankind and his manifestation.

The Word of God is named God of gods, and by gods we understand the blessed and God-loving men to whom the word of God came. To them it was also said, “I said, You are gods,” and “God stood in the assembly of gods,” and “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and called the earth.” For in these passages too, none other is proclaimed God of gods but only the Word who was in the beginning with God. It was he who made them gods, through his own gift and through their sharing in his Spirit. For he says that those to whom the Word of God came are gods. Next he also mentions Christ by name, saying in prayer, “And look upon the face of your Christ.” Instead of “The God of gods will be seen in Zion,” Aquila says, “The mighty God will be seen in Zion.” Who this might be, who was to become visible and be seen with the eyes, he teaches as he goes on, saying, “Give ear, O God of Jacob.” For this was that same Word of God who long ago appeared to Jacob in human form and said to him: “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name; for you have prevailed with God, and are mighty with men.” Whereupon the God-loving man, perceiving God speaking with him, says: “I have seen God face to face, and my soul was saved.” That very God, then, who appeared to Jacob will be seen again, he says, in Zion; and in this way the manifestation of God the Word to humankind is expressly signified. Calling upon this very God of Jacob, then, he begs him to hasten his coming. “O God our protector, behold.” Whom does he ask him to behold, if not those who toil in the valley of weeping? Next he adds, “And look upon the face of your Christ,” praying that the coming of God the Word into his Christ, whom he put on from the seed of David, might be hastened. Hence Aquila says, “Our shield, see, O God, and turn toward the face of your anointed one,” and Symmachus, “Our protector, see, O God, and look upon the face of your Christ.” These things are prayed by those who speak the whole psalm. These were the prophets of God, who had been saved from their spiritual enemies and had passed from war to peace. By the divine Spirit they foresaw God's dwellings that were to come, and they longed for his courts and altars. They also entreat the Word of God, who had been their protector in the time of wars, to look upon the face of his Christ. They pray that when he has appeared and has taken up the Christ who is from the seed of David according to the flesh, all may be released from their former evils, and the human race may receive good things in their place through Christ. “For one day in your courts is better than thousands.” The one who speaks the present psalm considers the one day of God's coming, the day of the resurrection from the dead, far better than thousands and more to be prized. I think that by the thousands he hints at the period during which Jerusalem stood. For in all

…the temple stood in it for a thousand years. That is the length of time from Solomon's building of the temple to the coming of our Savior. I think this is shown again by Psalm 89, which is titled "A Prayer of Moses" and says further on, "For a thousand years in your eyes are like yesterday, which has gone by, and like a watch in the night." So for the one who has come to long for it, the one day of our Savior's resurrection from the dead is to be preferred to that thousand and valued more highly. That is why he prays for his coming to be hastened, saying, "Behold, O God, and look upon the face of your Christ, for one day in your courts is better than thousands." "Thousands" should not necessarily be taken as a plural, for among the Hebrews this word means a single thousand, as anyone who looks into it will see. The one day in the courts established throughout the whole world by the theophany of the God who is prophesied is preferable to the thousand. That is why he also said above, "My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord." And again, he said above, "Blessed are those who dwell in your house; they will praise you forever and ever." Believing this, and fully convinced that the word is true, he says in effect, "For this reason I say: I have chosen to be cast aside in the house of my God rather…", so that by being in the house of God I may be able to praise God forever and ever. Or rather, just as I chose the one day above the thousand, so I have chosen the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth, rather than to dwell in the many tents of sinners. For sinners too have built themselves imitations of the tabernacles of God. But God's tabernacles are lovely, while those of sinners deserve hatred. "For the Lord God loves mercy and truth; the Lord will give grace and glory." In place of "For the Lord loves mercy and truth," Aquila says, "For the Lord God is a sun [?] and a shield."
