The fifth edition has "For the Lord God is a sun and a protector," and Symmachus, in agreement with these, called him "sun" (1). That, he says, is why that one day is better than thousands: the Lord himself, the Word of God, is the sun of that day. The prophet also hinted at this sun when he said, "But for those who fear me the sun of righteousness will rise, with healing in its wings." The one who said, "And the sun will set upon the prophets who lead my people astray," pointed to the same sun. Isaiah says it more plainly: "The sun will not be your light by day, but the Lord will be your everlasting light, and God your glory." Since the Lord is such a sun, he will give grace and glory, and a still greater and better good, one that cannot be spoken or uttered, to those who walk in innocence [?]. Or, as Symmachus has it, "to those who journey in

perfection." Therefore, believing what has been said, and having convinced myself that the words about these things are true, I say as the conclusion of the whole discourse: "O Lord of hosts, blessed is the man who hopes in you." Anyone whom most people call blessed on other grounds is called blessed in error. To tell the truth, the only one who is blessed, as being full of all good things for the reasons already given, is the one who has made himself depend on you alone and has placed all his hopes in your promises. This is now the third time in the present psalm that the text has called blessed the people it speaks of. Yet it nowhere mentioned the Jewish nation or Israel, nor did it call blessed those who carry out the law of Moses through works. First it spoke in general of those who dwell in the house of God. Second, it spoke of every man whose help comes from the Lord. And at the end of the whole discourse it spoke without limit and universally of every person who hopes in the Lord. For since the appearing of God and the coming of Christ to humanity were being proclaimed, the blessings that come from God had to be announced not to Jews only but to all people.

For the end. For the sons of Korah. A psalm. 84.

"You have been pleased, Lord, with your land; you have turned back the captivity of Jacob." This psalm follows on from the previous one. After the theophany foretold there, the present psalm prophesies deliverance from evils, redemption from captivity, and pardon and forgiveness of sins. These things followed the coming of God to humanity and the other things shown in the previous psalm. That psalm foretold that very many tabernacles, courts and altars of God would be established on earth. The cause of these was to be God appearing on earth, and the one looked upon was called by name Christ. At any rate it said, "The God of gods will be seen in Zion," and again, "Shine upon the face of your Christ." So it is fitting that the present psalm should proclaim in advance what was to happen throughout the whole inhabited world of humanity. These things were fulfilled at the coming of our Savior. At that time God was pleased with the earth and counted it worthy to be trodden by his Christ. Long ago it had been said to the first-formed man, "Earth you are, and to earth you will return," and, "Cursed is the ground in your labors." Another of the prophets said, "Cursing and murder and lying, theft and adultery have spread over the land, and they mingle blood with blood." But when the Son of God came to dwell on earth and took up a body formed from earth, the former evils were reversed. The whole element of earth received God's blessing in place of the former curse, and churches and houses of prayer to God were established throughout the whole world. That is why it is said here, "You have been pleased, Lord, with your land," and elsewhere, "The Lord has become king; let the earth rejoice," and again, "Sing to the Lord, all the earth." So it is fitting that the earth is called the Lord's own, as in "You have been pleased, Lord, with your land." For the reasons given, it has become not only his creation and his work but also his possession.

You will understand the meaning of "You have turned back the captivity of Jacob" from the Savior's own words. He read the prophecy of Isaiah that says, "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the poor, to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind." Then he added, "Today this prophecy has been fulfilled in your hearing," teaching that the oracle was fulfilled in himself. For he was indeed the Savior and redeemer of human souls. He set them free from the bitter slavery of polytheistic error and the working of demons, and loosed the cords of their sins. The present psalm presents this very thing when it says, "You have forgiven the iniquities of your people; you have covered all their sins." Elsewhere too Scripture knows of iniquities that are forgiven and covered, when it says, "Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered." By these words the Spirit signifies the forgiveness of former sins that the Savior granted to those redeemed from the spiritual captivity of souls. If they sin again after being forgiven, he no longer grants them a second forgiveness, but a covering of their sins. For he has allowed them to cover their earlier sins with later good deeds. The God of the universe gave all these things to the land of humanity, that is, to those who dwell in it, through the Savior's coming. He put an end to the wrath and anger that the earth's inhabitants had formerly deserved, since they were his enemies because of their excessive impieties. But God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them. Therefore it is said: "You have put an end to all your wrath; you have turned from the fury of your anger. Turn us, O God of our salvation, and turn your anger away from us. Will you be angry with us forever? Or will you prolong your anger from generation to generation? O God, you will turn and give us life, and your people will rejoice in you." The earlier verses prophesied what would happen over the whole earth, and these things were fulfilled through the coming of our Savior, in line with the interpretation given above. The present verses, however, contain a prayer for the people of the circumcision. Through the divine Spirit the prophet foresaw the Jewish nation's disobedience toward Christ, and the wrath that would overtake them because of what they would dare to do. So it is fitting that he offers the present prayer on their behalf. This means the psalm should not be thought to contradict itself, as if it first foretold favorable things for the whole earth and then prayed in these verses as though nothing good had been done. The first verses, then, prophesied the benefits our Savior would bring to human life. In the second, the prophet prays for his own people. He begs that the wrath against them may cease, and that they too may be counted worthy of God's turning toward them and of the joy that is in God's Christ. Isa. 61:1. Luke 4:18. Ps. 31:1.

"Show us your mercy, Lord, and grant us your salvation." The prophet prays for these things too. He begs that he himself may be counted worthy to see with his own eyes what would come about through God's mercy, which was prophesied above. When he says, "And grant us your salvation," he also asks to share in the light of Christ shining on humanity. Simeon clearly taught in the Gospels that this salvation is Christ himself. Taking Jesus, still an infant, into his arms, he said, "Now, Master, you are dismissing your servant in peace, according to your word, for my eyes have seen your salvation." This is what the prophet too prays to see. That is why the Savior says, "Many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see, and did not see it." "I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me, for he will speak peace to his people, and to his holy ones, and to those who turn their hearts to him." Having prayed, the prophet gives himself over to silence, trusting that he will be heard. Then, expecting an answer, he says to himself: "This is what I have prayed. Now it is time to listen to the Holy Spirit and learn from him what he will declare about the peace of his people and about those who are to turn to him through his Christ." Then, after keeping silent for a little while, he is filled with the divine Spirit and goes on to prophesy, saying something like this: "Surely his salvation is near to those who fear him, so that glory may dwell in our land." By these words he shows that God's salvation was just about to come to humanity. He had prayed for it above, saying, "Show us your mercy, Lord, and grant us your salvation." He says, then, that this very Salvation is very near, already close to those who fear him. It is the reason glory will dwell in our land and tabernacles will be established there. We have often shown with many examples that it is the custom of divine Scripture to call the Christ of God "salvation." The text now prophesies this too. It teaches that in place of the former dishonor of idolatry that prevailed on earth, glory will dwell there, and tabernacles will be established everywhere on earth for the glory that will be offered to God through the teaching of the gospel. Next he explains how the promises were to be fulfilled, saying: "Mercy and truth have met; righteousness and peace have kissed." By this he says that two pairs have met each other: the first is mercy and truth, the second righteousness and peace. They met each other, he says, and embraced as friends. Truth and mercy together kissed righteousness and peace. He goes on to teach where they came from when they met, saying: "Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked

down from heaven." So they met each other as if after a great distance, and embraced and kissed. Righteousness looked down from heaven above onto the earth, and truth sprang up from the earth below. Following on from this, we will set beside these verses the opening of the psalm, where it said: "You have been pleased, Lord, with your land; you have turned back the captivity of Jacob. You have forgiven the iniquity of your people; you have covered all their sins." For it was prophesied that all these things would come about when God's salvation appeared on earth. Along with the Salvation, truth sprang up from the earth. Righteousness looked down from heaven and met it, and spread God's grace to all people equally and with perfect justice. These words clearly present the theophany of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Through him alone truth sprang up from the earth, since he himself was the truth. The word of his gospel teaching was no longer handed down in types and symbols as in the past, but through truth itself. That is why it is said, "The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ." All his actions too were truth: his birth, his passion and the rest. The godless heretics supposed that these happened only in appearance and imagination. If every man is a liar, it is fitting that he alone, being truth, should have sprung up from the earth. The earth yielded something foreign to it, a good such as it had never before produced. On him the righteousness that looked down from heaven came to rest. What could the righteousness that rested on the truth be, if not God the Word himself? Of him it is said, "who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption." He came down from heaven and rested on the truth that sprang up from the earth. He was united with it and embraced it as a friend. Mercy accompanied the truth that sprang up from the earth, running ahead of it, for the whole dispensation of the truth came about because of God's mercy. Peace followed the righteousness that came down from heaven. So the people who dwell on earth were to enjoy not only God's mercy and truth, but also the righteousness from heaven, and with it peace, its friend. In the past heaven was the dwelling place of righteousness and peace. Now the earth is too, since God's mercy has come to be on earth. Mercy was the cause of everything that followed: because of God's mercy all the rest came after it. After mercy came truth, then righteousness, and finally peace. Scripture clearly says of our Savior, "For he is our peace, who has made both one," and, "having made peace through him for the things in heaven and the things on earth," and again, "He came and proclaimed peace to those who were far off and to those who were near." For these reasons it is fitting that the psalm says, "Surely his salvation is near to those who fear him, so that glory may dwell in our land." For great and abundant glory came to dwell in our

land, by which I mean the inhabited world of humanity, through the fulfillment of what was prophesied. How could glory not dwell in our land, when God's Salvation, his Christ himself, the righteousness from heaven, deigned to set foot on it? The prophet heard all these things, which God had foreordained and spoken in advance concerning his people. So after his prayer he prophesies, saying, "I will hear what the Lord God will speak," and then he adds, "For he will speak peace to his people." This peace came to the people when mercy and truth met, and righteousness and peace kissed. Since this is so, both what the prophet prayed for and what was said before the prayer have been fulfilled. The Lord was pleased with his land, counting it worthy of mercy and truth and the rest. He also turned back the captivity of human souls. He ended all war, granted peace, and broke the bonds and collars that came from sin. That is why "You have turned back the captivity of Jacob" is joined to "You have forgiven the iniquities of your people" and "You have covered all their sins." For the turning back of the captivity was accomplished in no other way than through the forgiveness of sins. The Savior himself taught in the Gospels that these things too were fulfilled through his appearing. He took the book of Isaiah and read, "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the poor, to proclaim release to captives," and so on. Then he added, "Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing." If one thinks about it, one would say that long ago the human race was dragged into captivity by invisible enemies, the true enemies of God, into idolatry and every shameful and lawless deed. One would not hesitate to call this a terrible captivity of souls. Our Savior and Lord delivered us from it and set us free. Through the washing of regeneration he granted forgiveness of old offenses and release from former impieties. So he became for us the reason for the thanksgiving in the psalm, and we too can say: "You have been pleased, Lord, with your land; you have turned back the captivity of Jacob. You have forgiven the iniquities of your people; you have covered all their sins." "For the Lord will give goodness, and our land will yield its fruit." Long ago, when the earth was under a curse, it produced thorns and thistles, as it is said: "Cursed is the ground in your labors; it will bring forth thorns and thistles for you." But now that such good things have come to it, the earth is said in turn to yield fitting fruit, since it has received goodness from the Lord. Fruit worthy of God is not thorns and thistles, but surely the things through which the earth is counted worthy of blessing from God. "Land that drinks the rain that often falls on it, and produces crops useful to those for whom it is farmed, receives a blessing from God." Fittingly, then,

the earth is commanded to sing the new songs, since it has been counted worthy of the things just described. The Holy Spirit calls out to it, saying, "Sing to the Lord, all the earth; sing to the Lord a new song," and, "The Lord has become king; let the earth rejoice," and other words like these. "Righteousness will go before him, and will set his steps on the way." The other translators have expressed the sense of this more clearly, especially Symmachus, who says, "The righteousness of each one will go before him, and will set his feet on the way." After the good things granted to the earth, each of the earth's inhabitants shares in the righteousness that looked down from heaven and acquires a righteousness of his own. He will have it leading him onto the road that goes upward and ordering his steps. So, having traveled the road that leads to heaven, supported and led by the hand by his own righteousness going before him, he may obtain the heavenly promises. Our Savior and Lord proclaimed these to all people, saying, "The kingdom of heaven has come near," and, "Blessed are those who are such, for theirs is the kingdom of

"Incline your ear, O Lord, and hear me, for I am poor and needy." In this part of the Psalter there are four psalms in a row titled "of the sons of Korah": first 83, then 84, third 86, and last 87. One might reasonably ask why David's prayer has been placed in the middle of them, out of place, as one might say. I think the present prayer has been mingled with the prophecies about Christ not without reason, but very fittingly. The first of the psalms titled "of the sons of Korah," namely 83 and 84, prophesied promises of good things and forgiveness of sins, the coming of God to humanity, and the arrival of Christ as redeemer and Savior of humanity. The ones that follow, also ascribed to the sons of Korah, proclaimed the calling of the nations, the birth of Christ, and his death for humanity. So I think it was necessary for David's prayer to be inserted in the middle of the prophecy about these things. In it he begs that he too may obtain the good things the Savior provides for all people. Then he too, having a share in what was prophesied, might obtain forgiveness of sins and enjoy the gift of salvation proclaimed to all the nations. In his prayer, at any rate, David mentions the grace of God poured out on the nations. He marvels at this grace and is amazed by it when he says, "There is none like you among the gods, O Lord, and there are no works like yours. All the nations you have made will come and worship before you." Since he too prayed to obtain the same good things, it is fitting that he places his own prayer in the middle of the gospel psalms. These things, then, concerning the

…let that suffice regarding the proposition stated. We should also be aware that several other psalms are headed "A Prayer." This one, however, is so called with the addition "of David." Another is headed "A Prayer of Moses, the man of God," and another "A Prayer of the poor man, when he is weary and pours out his petition before the Lord." But our Savior's apostles, as men who had risen above the prayers in the Old Scripture, came and asked him to teach them to pray. And he teaches them, handing on a prayer suited to them alone and to those like them. That is why he says to them: "Pray then like this: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name," and so on. So let each person examine himself, whether he is worthy, as one who has already become a son of God, to call upon the Father in heaven and to say "Our Father in heaven" and the rest. If he has not reached that stage, let him take pains to gather for himself, from the book of Psalms and from the words of the prophets, the prayer that fits his own condition. The present prayer, at any rate, is David's; for that is how Aquila and Symmachus rendered it, saying "of David" instead of "to David." David seems, by the divine Spirit, not to have been ignorant of the blessing pronounced by our Savior on the poor. That is why he confesses that he is poor and needy, even though he was a king and overflowing with great wealth. But since he was such in spirit, in keeping with "Blessed are the poor in spirit," it is fitting that in his prayer he puts forward his poverty and need as his virtues and achievements. You might also put it another way: just as Moses, on hearing the voice of God, confessed that he was weak of voice, saying this in comparison with the divine voice, so too David, though great and rich and wise when compared with other people, nevertheless, when he lifted up his eyes to God, saw himself as nothing. And since he was not yet able to name God as Father, he calls him Lord, indicating that he holds the place of a servant. Then, as though he himself remained somewhere below, in the depths, while God is on high, he begs God to incline his ear, since because of his own weakness he cannot cry out so loudly as to send his voice up on high and stretch it out to God. That is why he asks God to incline his ear, and asks that the divine hearing condescend to his own lowliness. "Preserve my soul, for I am holy; save your servant, O God, who hopes in you." He asks to be preserved by God in the state he was in, so that his soul might not be robbed of the virtues it had acquired. These he made known, first by saying "For I am poor and needy," and second by saying "For I am holy." That is why he also says elsewhere: "Let not the foot of pride come against me." And since he was conscious that he was not yet a son, he rightly confesses himself a servant and says: "Save your servant, O God, who hopes in you." Now a servant of God is one who is not a slave to sin, nor subject to any passion, but is subject to the Word of God alone, and

who hopes in no one else but in God alone. "Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I will cry to you all the day long. Gladden the soul of your servant, for to you, O Lord, [I have lifted up] my soul." "Even if I am holy," he says, "even if I am poor and needy in spirit, still I do not send up my prayer trusting in myself. Rather I ask and beg to obtain mercy from you, and this is my unceasing prayer." Indeed, instead of "all the day long," Symmachus rendered: "for I cry to you every day." For we must not devote ourselves to prayer for a single day, but through the whole of our lives. And since he took no great joy in any human affairs, he asked through prayer that joy be granted him by God; and this meant that his own soul be counted worthy of the gladness that is with God himself. For he knew that his body and his flesh rejoiced in bodily things. That is why he declines these and asks only for the gladness that comes from God, laying claim to the delight of the soul. And knowing that not everyone is able to obtain this, but only those who distance themselves from mortal life and bodily desires and draw near to God alone with their mind and thoughts, he rightly adds: "For to you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul." "For you, O Lord, are kind and gentle, and abounding in mercy to all who call upon you." Instead of "and gentle," Aquila and Theodotion said "and propitious," and Symmachus "and forgiving." These words too were usefully spoken by David, to remedy what might have been thought a presumptuous statement, namely "to you I have lifted up my soul," and, earlier, "for I am holy." "For these things too," he says, "were not procured by my own power but by your grace. For you led me to them, since you are kind and forgive sins, not only for me but for all who call upon you; for you abound in mercy." And by making his words general with "to all who call upon you," he urges all of us to pray and to hope as he did. "Give ear, O Lord, to my prayer, and attend to the voice of my supplication. In the day of my affliction I cried to you, for you heard me." Here too it is evident that the psalm is a prayer, as the heading also shows. Since [?] "I cried" and "you heard" are spoken in the past tense, note that Aquila says: "I will call upon you, for you will hear me." So what is sent up in the prayer refers to the future, asking God for help, so that if ever a time of trouble should come and affliction should come upon him, he might, calling on the Lord in his afflictions, find him ready to listen. And it is good, before affliction and before gloomy times, not to grow complacent in our desires or to grow careless about our prayers to the Lord, but to prepare ourselves in advance for the time to come. "There is none like you among the gods, O Lord, and there are no works like yours. All the nations you have made will come and worship before you, O Lord, and will glorify your name. For great

are you, and you do wonders; you alone are God." All the prayers of God's saints are beneficial and necessary. Yet I think not all of them were written down, but only those in which, as they prayed, they were moved by the divine Spirit, so that they uttered prophetic words. I believe, then, that David too sent up many prayers to God, none of which was thought worthy of being written down, except those that share in predictive and prophetic power. That is why the present prayer was taken into the book of Psalms and inserted in the midst of the prophecies about Christ, since it is mingled with prophetic words and contains the calling of the nations. Indeed, the calling of the nations is plainly foretold in these words too. For since he had prayed for many things concerning himself alone, saying "Hear me," and "Preserve my soul," and "Save your servant, O my God," and "Have mercy on me," and "Gladden the soul of your servant"—since, then, he had prayed for so much concerning himself, the rich and bountiful God shows him that he will grant the things asked in the prayer not to him alone, but that the divine grace will spread out to all the nations as well, so that they too would enjoy the things David asked to obtain. Hence, enlightened by the Holy Spirit and beholding what was to come, he is utterly astonished at the bounty of God's grace and says the words quoted above. As for the "gods" spoken of here, one person will take them to be the righteous and God-loving men among human beings, because of the saying "I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High"; another will take them to be the divine powers in heaven, because the Apostle says: "For even if there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth (as indeed there are many gods and many lords), yet for us there is one God, the Father." Since, then, neither any of the angels nor any of the prophets brought about the calling of the nations, I think it fitting that "There is none like you among the gods, O Lord" is spoken as addressed to Christ. Someone else will say that since many people falsely and mistakenly think there are gods, and among all the nations one being is deified here and another there, while only our Savior and Lord has been proclaimed God throughout the whole world and has won for himself peoples from all the nations, for this reason these declarations about God are uttered prophetically as addressed to him. Then, since many prophets before our Savior performed extraordinary works, but no one is ever recorded to have done such things as are related of our Savior in the Gospels, and such as have been shown through the conversion of all the nations, for this reason "there are no works like yours" is also said. And what works these are he teaches when he says next: "All the nations you have made will come and worship before you." And if "You alone are God" follows, you will apply this too to the Savior, setting it beside "There is none like you among the gods, O Lord." For just as, in comparison with the gods mentioned, there is none like you, so, when set beside those same gods, you are God

alone. For our Savior and Lord alone was in the beginning, and was the Word of God, and was with God, and was God. That is why there is none like him among the gods, and he alone, as it were among the gods, would be God, since none of the many so-called gods can be styled God when set beside him. But another, because "You alone are God" is added to all this, might say that everything set out here is sent up in the prayer to the Father and God of the universe. For it was by his gift and grace that the calling of the nations came about through his Son. He was the creator, maker and author of the universe, having established all things through the Son, both those in heaven and those on earth. And he was the one who worked all the wonders through the Son, both those related in the Old Testament and those recorded in the New. That is why it says, "There are no works like yours," and "Great are you, and you do wonders; you alone are God." The word "alone" was also spoken by our Savior to the Father in "that they may know you, the only true God." But since the Son shares in the Father's divinity and partakes of the same kingdom, being the only-begotten Son, the Word of God and the Wisdom of God, he too might fittingly be included in this present declaration about God, which teaches that among the many so-called gods there is none like the God who is over all. For the likeness of the Father is preserved in one alone, his only-begotten Word. That is why he is called the image of God, and "the Word was God," so that the likeness of the Father is preserved in him alone, and no longer in the many gods. "Guide me, O Lord, in your way, and I will walk in your truth; let my heart rejoice to fear your name." To keep from straying from God's truth, we need a guide. So Aquila says: "Enlighten me, O Lord, in your way; I will walk in your truth"; and Symmachus: "Show me, O Lord, your way, so that I may journey in your truth." And again, instead of "Let my heart rejoice to fear your name," Aquila says: "Make my heart single to fear your name"; and Symmachus: "Unite my heart in the fear of your name." "I will confess to you, O Lord my God, with my whole heart, and I will glorify your name forever." Having spoken of many good things above, he necessarily recalls to memory the confession of the sin he had committed, so that he might not seem, because of the pardon granted him and the blessings that came to him afterward, to grow slack and live more carelessly. So he turns himself back and calls his sin to mind, so that his thanksgiving to God may be greater. That is why he says, "I will confess to you," and adds: "You have rescued my soul from the lowest Hades." For the sin unto death is of this kind: it drags one down into the lowest Hades. For since sins are many, some seem to carry one to the upper regions of Hades, others to the lowest, and, so to speak, to its very

bottom, of which it is said: "There are ways that seem right to a man, but their end looks to the bottom of Hades." "But from there," he says, "you rescued me, since your mercy toward me has become great." For having prayed in Psalm 50 to obtain great mercy, where he said, "Have mercy on me according to your great mercy," here he confesses that he has obtained what he prayed for. That is why he confesses not in a casual way, but with his whole heart. "O God, lawless men have risen up against me, and an assembly of the mighty has sought my soul, and they have not set you before them. But you, O Lord God, are compassionate and merciful, long-suffering, abounding in mercy, and true." Having passed from prayer to confession and acknowledged to God the grace by which he rescued his soul from the lowest Hades, he makes his defense, declaring the cause through which he sinned. He says that he suffered this through the plotting of many invisible enemies who envied his progress in the things of God. That is why he says, "O God, lawless men have risen up against me." All the other translators said "the arrogant," hinting at the invisible and arrogant powers. And he teaches what violence David's soul suffered, not from one power but from many, when he says, "and an assembly of the mighty"; or, as Aquila has it, "and an assembly of those who prevail by force"; or, as Symmachus has it, "and an assembly of the irresistible has sought my soul." "The assembly of my enemies sought my soul, since they did not set God before their eyes. But you, O Lord," he says, "granted and bestowed what they did not expect, rescuing my soul from the lowest Hades. And you did this as one who is compassionate and merciful, long-suffering and abounding in mercy, and true in all these things." "Look upon me and have mercy on me; give your strength to your servant, and save the son of your handmaid." "Seeing me," he says, "have mercy on me." David shows his own lowliness and the affliction of his soul, which he also set forth at the beginning of the prayer when he said, "I am poor and needy." Instead of "Give your strength to your servant," Symmachus translated more clearly, saying: "Give strength from you to your servant." "So that I may not grow weak and slip, I ask, along with the other things you have provided, to be made strong, so that I may not again be overthrown by the assembly of the mighty. And having made me strong in this way, you will save me as one who has become your servant, and the son of your handmaid"—that is, of your Church, or else of the mother who brought him up in godly discipline. "Work with me a sign for good, and let those who hate me see it and be put to shame, because you, O Lord, have helped me and comforted me." Just as God set on Cain a sign that made his wickedness known, a sign which kept those who saw it from killing him, because God had decreed that he should groan and tremble on the earth, so too he gives his perfect ones a sign for good. Seeing it, their

friends rejoice, while their enemies and those who hate them are put to shame, having learned from the sign that the person has been helped and comforted in what befell him. And perhaps in Cain's case the hostile powers, seeing the sign placed on him by God, gloated over him, since they delight in evil, while God's angels groaned over him, recognizing through the sign the wrath from God that hung over him. In the case of the God-loving soul it is the opposite: the hostile powers are put to shame when they see the good sign placed on it, while the divine and good angels rejoice and are glad with it. This is what the Savior taught when he said that there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.

TO THE SONS OF KORAH. A PSALM OF A SONG. "His foundations are on the holy mountains. The Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob. Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God. I will make mention of Rahab and Babylon to those who know me." Instead of "To the sons of Korah," Aquila and Symmachus rendered "Of the sons of Korah," as though the psalm had been composed by them, or had been uttered and spoken through them, not only with the psaltery but also with song. I have asked myself why the psalms headed "Of the sons of Korah" were not all joined together in one place, but are arranged thus: first, as a separate group, those from Psalm 41 on; then again, set apart on their own, two, the 83rd and the 84th; and again another two, the one at hand and the one after it, while between these is inserted the 85th, headed "A Prayer of David." What occurred to me on considering the last of these has already been explained in what was said earlier. But one might also put it another way: all the words contained in the book of Psalms, spoken by different men in the prophetic Spirit, were separate pieces, since they were neither spoken at one time nor prophesied by the same persons. For instance, one is headed "of Moses," others "of Asaph," others again "of David," another "of Solomon," and again one "of Ethan the Ezrahite"; and very many others besides these are transmitted without a title, so that we cannot know whose they might be. Since they were spoken at different times, in ancient times they were preserved here and there among those devoted to such things. Then, later, the 150 were gathered into one book. Perhaps, then, the compiler—whether this was Ezra, as the children of the Hebrews say, or someone else—placed first in the book those that first came into his hands. For since he did not find them all together at one time, he had to attach those that came to hand to the ones he already had. That is why he probably arranged the first eight "Of the sons of Korah" at the time when they were all found together at once, and after them attached those that came to him afterward. Then, after many others had been found in the meantime and taken into the book of Psalms after the 48th [?] psalm, another two "Of the

sons of Korah" were found, which he attached in sequence and placed as the 83rd and the 84th. Then, the Prayer of David having been found in the meantime, he inserted it too after the 84th. And again, after the Prayer of David had been placed in the 85th position, another two "Of the sons of Korah" were found, the one at hand and the one following it; and these too had of necessity to be attached to the Prayer of David. The same person might say that the same reasoning applies to the arrangement of the rest of the psalms as well. What has been said will be confirmed by evidence from the prophets. For in the prophetic books one can often find things foretold earlier in time placed second in order, and things prophesied later placed before those that precede them in time. Jeremiah, for example, begins to prophesy under Josiah and continues until Zedekiah and the captivity; and Zedekiah was the fourth king from Josiah. For after Josiah, his son Jehoiakim succeeded to the throne second; after him, third, Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim; after him, fourth, Zedekiah, Jehoiakim's brother. Although Jeremiah prophesied under all of these, the book that bears his name begins with Josiah; then, as it proceeds, it mentions Jeconiah, the third from Josiah; then it prophesies the events under Zedekiah, who was fourth from Josiah; after these it places the prophecies made in the fourth year under Jehoiakim, who was second after Josiah. Then next it brings in those from the beginning of the same Jehoiakim's reign; then those under Zedekiah, and again those under Jehoiakim. Then it mentions the captivity to Babylon, and how after Zedekiah Gedaliah was appointed leader of those left behind, and how Ishmael killed Gedaliah, after whom Johanan son of Kareah takes the lead. And after all these it next brings in the prophecies spoken in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, and again those spoken at the beginning of Zedekiah's reign. You would find much the same in Ezekiel. For in his book too the prophecies are not arranged in chronological order: those of the twenty-seventh year of the captivity are placed before what was spoken in the eleventh year; for after those of the twenty-seventh year come those spoken in the eleventh year of the captivity; and again after those of the eleventh year come others spoken in the tenth year, and next those of the twenty-fifth year. One might say that the reason for all this is none other than the one already given. For, as is likely, the prophecies delivered piecemeal at various times and under each king were in ancient times preserved here and there among those devoted to them; and either Ezra or some others, gathering into a single collection what each of the prophets had said at different times, placed first the words that were found first, and then attached next those found afterward, even if they were earlier in time. The same reasoning holds for the order of the Psalms: of all of them in general, and in particular of those we are now examining—unless perhaps some deeper understanding, hidden from us, will offer other reasons for what we have been inquiring into. At any rate, what has occurred to us concerning the order of the psalms "Of the sons of Korah," and concerning the Prayer of David that comes before the one at hand,

…of the psalm being so placed, and set in the middle of those headed “Of the sons of Korah,” is laid out for anyone who wishes to read what we said earlier. Let this much serve as our preliminary discussion. Now, since the text of the psalm begins without saying whose they are, “His foundations are in the holy mountains,” one might reasonably ask: whose foundations? Someone might readily answer that God is meant, since next comes “the city of God.” But I paid attention to the sequence of the psalm and found next the words: “Mother Zion shall say: A man, and a man was born in her, and he himself founded her.” In place of this Aquila has: “And to Zion it shall be said: A man and a man was born in her, and he himself will establish her.” Symmachus has: “And concerning Zion it shall be said: Each man was born [?] …” [?] To suppose that the words “The Lord loves the gates of Zion” are spoken of the [?] city, which is now deserted and obliterated; and likewise “Glorious things were spoken of you, O city of God”; and again elsewhere, “The rushing streams of the river gladden the city of God”; and again, “Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised in the city of our God, on his holy mountain” — to suppose that all these are said of a city now inhabited by Greeks, foreigners and idolaters seems to me the mark of a very low and petty mind. But if one understands how the divine and prophetic words habitually call a godly commonwealth the city of God, one will see how our Savior and Lord Jesus, the Christ of God, founded and established this God-loving and godly commonwealth and city throughout the whole world. That is why the prophets proclaim it in various ways in the passages that speak of him, including this one: “He shall build my city.” For the city of God, that is, the way of life that accords with God and the godly commonwealth throughout the whole inhabited world, he alone, born in her, set up and made firm through his catholic Church, which stands in every place and in every country and city. Of the Church we must be convinced that these words are spoken: “Glorious things were spoken of you, O city of God,” and “The rushing streams of the river gladden the city of God,” and all the other such things found in the divine Scriptures.

Of this greatest of cities, a city worthy of God — I mean the Church of God and the godly commonwealth seen in her — the foundations are in the holy mountains. The Apostle explains the saying when he says: “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the cornerstone.” In another sense, too, its foundations are not here below among us, but somewhere above, in what are called the holy mountains. That is why it is said: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains.” These mountains would be the heavens of the heavens, where the great commonwealth of the heavenly Zion, the truly great city of God, has its being. This is not my own idea; it belongs to the Apostle himself, who said: “But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother,” and: “You have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels in festal gathering, and to the Church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven.” The Church of God on earth, then, would be an image of this great city of God. Its supports and foundations stand in the holy mountains we have identified, while the entrances and first elements of that heavenly city are found here among us. The text has called these entrances and ways into the godly commonwealth “the gates of Zion,” saying: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob.” By the dwellings of Jacob I think it here means the Jewish traditions and the bodily forms of worship under Moses. Above these God values the gates of Zion, that is, the entrances and ways into the heavenly kingdom that have been set up in the Church. For in her alone is the kingdom of heaven proclaimed, and the whole aim of the saving Gospel looks toward it. The saving promises, the preaching of the Gospel, and every hope of the life lived according to Christ look to the kingdom of heaven. It is written, at any rate, that the Savior preached, saying: “The kingdom of heaven has come near.” He pronounced those worthy of his beatitudes blessed, promising them the kingdom of heaven; and he also taught his disciples to pray and to ask for the kingdom of heaven, saying in their prayer: “Your will be done, your kingdom come.” Fittingly, then, all such things have been called gates of the kingdom of heaven, since they are entrances and ways into the journey toward it. So the Lord loves these gates of the heavenly Zion more than the synagogues of the Law and of the Jews, which he called the dwellings of Jacob. Among the Jews, after all, nothing is said of the heavenly city of God, nor do they have any aim concerning the kingdom of heaven; bent entirely downward, they place their hopes on earth and fit the promises to things somewhere here below. That is why God values more highly than the dwellings of Jacob the

gates of the heavenly Zion that we have already described, whose foundations are not somewhere here below on earth but in the holy mountains we considered earlier. “I will make mention of Rahab and Babylon to those who know me. And behold, foreigners and Tyre and the people of the Ethiopians — these were born there.” In place of “I will make mention of Rahab and Babylon,” Aquila says, “I will call to mind arrogance and Babylon,” and Symmachus, “I will call to mind pride and Babylon.” I take it that by Babylon and Tyre and Rahab, and by the foreigners and the people of the Ethiopians, the text hints at the calling of the Gentiles, who changed and turned from their former way of life and were counted worthy of rebirth in the city of God. The Word wants to remind them of the stock they came from. For when it says that foreigners and Tyre and peoples of the Ethiopians were born there, what else does it mean but the rebirth of the foreign nations in the city of God? [?] says: “Philistia and Tyre with Ethiopia — this one was born there.” Symmachus rendered it similarly: “Behold, the Philistines and Tyre with Ethiopia — this one was born there.” And where does it say the foreigners were born, if not in the city of God, or in its gates as we have understood them? The sequence of the passage suggests this reading. Having first said, “Glorious things were spoken of you, O city of God,” it adds directly that such and such foreigners were born there, and the people of the Ethiopians was born there: plainly in the city of God just mentioned, or in its gates as we have interpreted them. These things, fulfilled in actual events, confirm the truth of the words, since saving grace regenerates Babylonians and Tyrians and all who are foreign and alien to the race of Israel, through the washing of rebirth and the mysteries of the New Covenant, in the city of God we have described. “Mother(1) Zion shall say: Men, and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her.” The versions of the other translators set out the sense of these words more clearly. Symmachus rendered it this way: “And concerning Zion it shall be said of each one: This man was born there; the Most High himself established her. The Lord will count, as he registers the peoples: this one was born there.” And Theodotion says: “And to Zion it shall be said: Man and man was born in her, and he himself founded her, and the Most High prepared her. The Lord will recount in the register of peoples: this one was born in her.” Notice how, just as was said of the foreigners, “Foreigners and Tyre and the people of the Ethiopians — these were born there,” so here too it says, “It shall be said: Man and man was born there”; and again next, “The Lord, registering peoples: this one was born.” First it speaks of the people of the foreigners; second, of the man who is said to have been born there; and third, of the Lord himself. For the Lord, it says, he who decrees these things and registers peoples, this one was born there. (1) Above: “μὴ τῇ.”

[?] …by saying that he was born there, he presents the indwelling of God the Word in the man. For just as Zion, being the city of God, is the place of the man born in her, so the man himself becomes the place and receptacle of God the Word, who was born in him and dwelt in him as in a holy shrine and temple, or rather as in an image and receptacle of his own divinity. The Word had to teach this so that we might know how foreigners and Tyre and the people of the Ethiopians came to be born in the city of God and became sons of God through the rebirth he gives. For he showed how, and in what manner, so great a grace was poured out toward heaven, by telling of the man who was born there and of the Lord who in turn was born in the man. After all this he adds: “How joyful are all who dwell in you!” In place of this Aquila says, “And singing like dancers, all the springs in you,” and Symmachus, “And they will give praise as with flutes, all the springs in you.” I think that this too signifies the gathering together of all the faithful who will be counted worthy of the holy city of God, and their restoration into a single choir. For by the words “in you” I take it to mean, once again, the place of the city of God, whose foundations were in the holy mountains, while its gates and entrances are somewhere below among us; and in the midst of her, it is prophesied, all will dwell, gathered with joy as in a dance and a divine harmony. But see how the present psalm, while foretelling the birth of God, concealed the mystery in the reading of the Septuagint translation. For “The Lord will count, as he registers the peoples: this one was born there,” as Symmachus has it; or, as Aquila, “The Lord will recount in registering peoples: this one was born there”; or, as Theodotion, “The Lord will recount in the register of peoples: this one was born there” — this is not how the Seventy translated it. Instead they said: “The Lord will recount in a register of peoples and of rulers, of these who have been born in her.” The translators concealed the sense, I think, because the Scripture was to be published for foreign nations in the time of Ptolemy, when our Savior had not yet shone upon the world. The whole psalm, indeed, is highly enigmatic and obscurely expressed. It speaks of “his foundations” without saying whose; it names holy mountains, and gates of Zion which the Lord values above the dwellings of Jacob, and a city of God of which glorious things are spoken; and above all it names as born in the city not Israel, nor the Jewish nation, but Rahab, once a harlot, and Babylon, Tyrians and Ethiopians and foreigners. For what reason all these would be born in the city of God, no one could say, except the birth of the man born in her, and of the Lord born there — that is, in the man just mentioned. On account of these things, at the end of the psalm, it foretells universal joy, dances, songs and praises, and springs of divine and sacred words. And when it says that all this will take place “in a register of peoples,” I think it signifies

the time of the census of the nations, which took place at the birth of our Savior Jesus Christ. For at that time a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be registered, when Quirinius, governing Judea, was conducting the census. The evangelist notes this, at any rate, saying, “This was the first census,” so that the very time is precisely indicated by the present psalm. Perhaps this is also why the psalm has been set apart and placed at a distance from the others headed “Of the sons of Korah”: the Word wished to conceal the mysteries it reveals about the Lord’s birth. So this would be another reason for the question we raised at the start of our discussion. You could say the same of Psalm 87, which follows it and is likewise headed “Of the sons of Korah”; for it too prophesies the death of our Savior, in sequence with the present psalm, which contains his birth. [A song] of a psalm [?] for the sons of Korah, for the end, for Maeleth, for answering; of understanding, for Heman the Ezrahite (1). 87. “O Lord, God of my salvation, by day I cried out, and by night before you.” This psalm too, like the one before it, is “Of the sons of Korah.” But the one before it hinted at the birth of Christ, saying, “And to Zion it shall be said: Man and man was born in her, and he himself will establish her,” as Aquila translated. And going on, it indicated the time of the birth of the man spoken of, for it said, “In registering peoples, this one was born there.” The fifth version gave the sense of this more clearly, where it says, “In the census of peoples, this one will be born there.” It quite clearly mentioned the census during which our Savior and Lord was born, as the evangelist shows when he says: “In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be registered. This was the first census, taken when Quirinius was governor of Syria.” That psalm, then, indicated his birth; the present one, his death. Symmachus translated “for Maeleth” as “through a choir,” and Aquila as “for dancing.” I think this hints at the people of Christ and the choir of the Church, in which the death of our Savior is celebrated in hymns. And since his birth too is sung by this choir, the psalm before this one, having foretold his birth, fittingly went on to say, “And singing like dancers, all the springs in you,” pointing to the choirs in the Church of Christ that sing and hymn his mysteries. As for Heman the Ezrahite, as he is called, they say he was one of the sons of Zerah the son of Judah, and that among the Hebrews he was called by his father’s name, the Zarahite; that there were five sons in all; and that the first book of Chronicles

bears witness to this, as follows: “The sons of Judah: Perez and Zerah. And the sons of Zerah: Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Darda — five in all.” The Hebrew said that these prophesied in Egypt, living before Moses, and that the psalms headed with their names are theirs: the present psalm, for instance, and the one after it, which is likewise headed “For Ethan the Ezrahite.” He also said that they are spoken of in the third book of Kingdoms: “And Solomon was wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, and Calcol, and Darda.” Let this be said as regards the history. Whether the meanings of these names contribute anything to the interpretation of the psalm, you can consider for yourself. The present psalm, being the last of those headed “Of the sons of Korah,” covers our Savior’s descent into Hades, as though the Word had deliberately held back the mystery of his death to hand it down at the end of the whole series. And it seems to me that these four psalms “Of the sons of Korah” — I mean the eighty-third, the eighty-fourth, the eighty-sixth and the eighty-seventh — follow on from one another in a certain sequence. The eighty-third clearly contained God’s coming among human beings and a prophecy of Christ by name; the one after it prayed that what had been foretold might come quickly; the one before the present psalm hinted at his birth in the flesh; and following on from all these, the present psalm proclaims in advance the death he accepted on behalf of humankind. “O Lord, God of my salvation, by day I cried out, and by night before you. Let my prayer come before you; incline your ear to my petition.” In Psalm 21, which also refers to Christ and clearly prophesies his passion — as the text shows from its very opening, “O God, my God, attend to me; why have you forsaken me?”, words our Savior is recorded to have spoken verbatim during his passion — after the opening it goes on: “My God, I will cry out by day, and you will not hear, and by night, and it is not counted folly in me.” And the present psalm says: “By day I cried out, and by night before you.” It seems to me that the saying sketches the life our Savior lived as man, devoted to God not only all day but all night as well. The Gospels too record how he gave himself to prayer continually. Here he entreats the Father and asks him to incline his ear to his petition, that is, to grant his requests. He prays this as one about to offer himself to the Father as a sacrifice on behalf of all the nations. Since he is about to relate [?] a great deal about his own death, and sees the salvation that will follow him after death, he fittingly dedicates the opening of the psalm in advance to his own salvation. That is why he says, “O Lord, God of my salvation.” “For my soul is filled with evils, and my life has drawn near to Hades; I was counted among those who go down into the pit.” Here he clearly presents his descent into Hades, and the evils with which he said his soul was filled.

By “evils” he means either his afflictions, the word “evils” being taken in a more general sense, or else the wickedness of human beings, with which he said his soul was filled; but also our sins, which he took upon himself, and on account of which he became a curse for us, as the Apostle says: “The Lord died for us, becoming a curse for us, for it is written: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.” That is why, as the psalm puts it, his soul was filled with evils, and his life drew near to Hades — which itself clearly shows his descent into death. Hence Aquila rendered it, “And my life has reached Hades,” and Symmachus, “And my life touched Hades.” And just as it is said elsewhere, “He was counted among the lawless,” so here too he says, “I was counted among those who go down into the pit.” In place of this Symmachus rendered, “I was counted among those who are brought down into the pit.” For all human beings are dragged down and brought down into the place of death, which is here likened to a pit; and they go down there because of their own sins, having been judged deserving of that place. “And I too was counted among them,” he says, “not because I deserved it, but because I became obedient to the Father to the point of death.” Here, then, he says, “My life has drawn near to Hades,” and, “I was counted among those who go down into the pit.” But in another psalm, recalling these same things, he indicates his ascent from there, saying: “O Lord, you brought up my soul from Hades; you saved me from among those who go down into the pit.” And again elsewhere: “I waited patiently for the Lord, and he attended to me; and he heard my petition, and brought me up out of the pit of misery, and set my feet upon a rock.” And in Psalm 15 it is said: “You will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor let your holy one see corruption.” “I became like a man without help, free among the dead; like the slain who sleep in the grave, whom you remember no more, and they have been thrust away from your hand.” Those who are truly without help, mastered by death, are led down and carried off by it. But our Savior and Lord alone emptied himself and humbled himself to the point of death; and just as he came in the likeness of sinful flesh, so he became like one of those men who are without help. Yet since he was not truly one of the many, he alone was free among the dead, remaining unenslaved to death. In place of “free among the dead,” Aquila rendered “free among those who have died,” and Symmachus, “among the dead, released free.” You may also read the verse with a slight pause, setting apart on its own “I became like a man without help among the dead”; then, putting a comma after “among the dead,” you will add “free” as a declaration. The sense would then be: “I, who am free and alone truly Lord of all, became like a man without help among the dead — not truly without help, but like one without help.” That these words fit no one else to say except the one who touched death and went down into Hades, yet was not enslaved

…to him, it is plain to everyone, I think, that what is said in the psalm cannot be applied to any other man, but only to our Savior. And just as he became like a man without help, so also he became like the slain who sleep in the grave, whom you remember no more. These words also point to his burial, which the divine Apostle mentions too when he writes to the Corinthians: For I handed on to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried. Isaiah also mentions his burial, saying: His burial is in peace; he has been taken from the midst. In place of “like the slain,” Aquila says, “like those who have been killed,” and Symmachus, “like one wounded.” This too was fulfilled quite plainly when the soldier wounded his side with a spear. That he was wounded and was laid in the grave is clearly shown. Only, he says that he became like one wounded and like those who sleep in the grave, but he does not stop there. Join the whole together and you will see the meaning of the saying. For he says: I became like the slain, whom you remember no more. The others, once they were laid in their graves after death, were left behind and remained earth and dust, since God no longer remembered them after death. But I became like one of them without being like them. For after I was wounded, after I died, and after I was laid in the grave, you remembered me, and afterwards you counted me worthy of life and of the salvation that comes from you. That is why, at the beginning, he also sent up a hymn of thanksgiving, saying: O Lord, God of my salvation, by day I cried out, and by night before you. Such, then, was my own case. Nevertheless, I became like the many who have been laid in the grave and are no longer counted worthy of your remembrance, because they have been thrust away from your hand. For in place of “whom you remember no more, and they were thrust away from your hand,” Aquila rendered, “whom you remember no more, and they were cut off from your hand,” and Symmachus says, “whom you will remember no more, who were cut off by your hand.” They laid me in the lowest pit, in dark places and in the shadow of death. In place of “they laid me,” Aquila rendered “you laid me,” and Symmachus “you appointed me.” By this he shows that it was by the will and counsel of the Father that he went down, not simply into death, nor only into Hades and what is called the pit, but into the deepest, the lowest and, so to speak, the outermost of the places there. He himself shows this too in the Gospels when he says: The Son of Man must spend three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. In place of “in dark places and in the shadow of death,” Aquila says, “in dark places and in depths”; Symmachus, “in dark places, covered over”; and the fifth edition, “in dark places, in sunken places.” I have

pointed this out of necessity, so that no one might suppose that he was not really in death because the Seventy say “in dark places and in the shadow of death.” For it has been shown that he was in the darkened places, the depths and the sunken places of death itself. That is why neither the Hebrew nor the other translators rendered it “shadow of death.” For Scripture often calls the present life and our existence here a shadow of death. But here the Savior, having entered death itself, describes his whole saving dispensation. Your wrath has pressed hard upon me, and you have brought all your billows over me. Interlude. You have put my acquaintances far from me; they have made me an abomination to themselves. I was handed over, and I could not go out. Christ died for us, according to the Apostle, and became a curse for us, for it is written, Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree. And, according to the same Apostle, God made him who knew no sin to be sin for us. So it was fitting that he should draw upon himself the wrath of God that lay upon us, who were once ungodly and sinners, and God's anger against us, and that, out of his surpassing love for humankind, he should take upon himself the punishment and chastisement that were ours. This is why he utters the words before us, since he became the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. That is why the prophet says of him: He bears our sins and suffers pain for us; by his bruise we were healed, and the Lord handed him over for our sins. This, then, he himself shows through the psalm when he says: Your wrath has pressed hard upon me, and you have brought all your billows over me. In place of this Symmachus says: Your wrath weighed heavily on me, and with your tempests you afflicted me. He is like a loving father who, in a time of storm or war, shields his own true sons. He covers them, hiding and sheltering them in his arms, and exposes himself in place of them all to the tempests and the missiles. He exchanges his own death for his children's safety and turns upon himself the anger aimed at them. For this reason he became a curse, though he himself is the blessing of God, and he became sin, though he is righteousness. He drew upon himself the wrath of God that weighed upon humanity, and he scattered it away from himself, so that it harmed neither him nor anyone else, and he made [?] gracious to the human race. There is no need to say how all the disciples abandoned him at the time of his passion, and some even denied him, since the four evangelists agree in teaching the same things. It is these very things that he foretells, prophesying the future through the words before us, which Symmachus translated as follows: You made my acquaintances far from me; you appointed me abhorrent to them, kept under guard and not going out. And it was indeed then that the disciples denied him, when he was being kept under guard in the house of Caiaphas the high

priest. My eyes grew weak from poverty. I cried to you, O Lord, all day long; I spread out my hands to you. Symmachus rendered this too more clearly, saying: My eye streamed with tears from affliction; I called upon you every day; I spread out my hands to you. For he was always weeping over the miseries of humankind and wearing out his eyes, mourning with tears the destruction of those who did not receive him. And just as he wept over Jerusalem, so it was natural that he, the loving Son of an all-good Father, should weep over the fall of the apostle who betrayed him, the rejection of the whole Jewish nation and the ruin of everyone else who was perishing. For this reason he stretched out his hands and sent up his cries, calling aloud in his prayers to the Father and interceding with the Father with groanings too deep for words. In another sense, you would not be wrong to say that his eye, or the eyes that grew weak, are the apostles, if indeed all his people are his body, as the one who said, You are the body of Christ, and individually members of it, taught. And his hands, that is, the deeds he performed for the glory of the Father, he spread out, displaying them to the only one able to behold them. But in his constant prayers too, and in his passion, he spread out his hands on behalf of the world, taking away its sin and propitiating the Father. As he goes on, he teaches in these words what he prayed for with his hands spread out to the Father, and what he cried out to his Father on that day referred to here: Will you work wonders for the dead, or will physicians raise them up, and will they give you thanks? Interlude. Will anyone recount your mercy in the grave, and your truth in destruction? Will your wonders be known in the darkness, and your righteousness in a land of forgetfulness? In place of “Will you work wonders among the dead?” Symmachus says, “Will you then work marvels for the dead?” And throughout what follows, where it says, “Will anyone recount in the grave?” and again, “Will they be known in the darkness?” Symmachus rendered, “Or will anyone recount, or will they be known?” For he did not utter these words on that day, that is, the day of his passion, out of despair about what is said. Rather, being persuaded that these things are possible for the Father alone, he was teaching the reasons for his descent into death, saying: Will you then work marvels for the dead? For otherwise, O Father, you would not have willed that I go this far, that I enter death and the lowest pit, unless you surely meant to display wonders among the dead as well, so that your power might accomplish what physicians cannot. That is, you meant that those who are in death should rise and give you thanks. For it was not for physicians to be able to do these things, but for your divine and mighty working. Was it, then, for these reasons that you willed me to undergo death: so that in the graves your mercy might be recounted, in destruction your truth

made known, in the darkness your wonders proclaimed, and in the land of forgetfulness your righteousness remembered? If anyone turns his attention to the wonders that have been accomplished in our own day at the tomb and the Martyrium of our Savior, he will truly know how the things foretold have been fulfilled in deed. See how in these words he describes the region of death in various ways. First he plainly calls them the dead; second, those in the grave; third, those in destruction; fourth, those in darkness; fifth, those in the land of forgetfulness. All these describe the same people, to whom the loving and good God was going to show and grant wonders, and who would recount his mercy, and the truth and the righteousness of God. We can recognize how all these things, I mean God's wonders, his mercy, his truth and his righteousness, reached those who had long been dead, in the graves, in destruction, in darkness and in the land of forgetfulness, if we consider how many good things our Savior and Lord brought about for those who had long been in death. It was for their sake that he went down into those places, so that he might be Lord not only of the living but also of the dead. For in the words before us he has made the reasons for his descent into death shine out clearly. And these were fulfilled, according to the evangelists, when many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised and entered with the Savior himself into the holy city of God, that is, the heavenly city. And I have cried to you, and in the morning my prayer will come before you. In the twenty-first psalm, which is plainly spoken in the person of our Savior, the superscription says, “For the help at dawn,” and there the text hints at our Savior's resurrection, which took place at the hour of dawn. So too here, I think, the same thing is meant by “In the morning my prayer will come before you.” The text shows that the Savior's prayer came to fulfillment at no other time than at dawn and in the morning, when, as is attested, the resurrection from the dead also took place. That is why he says that my prayer will come before you not in the evening, nor at midday, nor at any other time, but in the morning. Why, O Lord, do you cast off my soul and turn your face away from me? In the twenty-first psalm too he said, “O God, my God, attend to me; why have you forsaken me?” [?] testimony of the Savior [?]

so that he might become the Lamb of God and a sheep offered in sacrifice for the salvation of the world. That is why the prophet also said: And the Lord handed him over for our sins. And: He bears our sins and suffers pain for us. And: He was wounded for our sins and made weak for our iniquities; by his bruise we were healed. In the twenty-first psalm he goes on to say: O God, I will cry by day, and you will not hear, and by night, and it is not counted folly in me. And in the words before us: You turn your face away from me. I think these are like what was fulfilled in deed in the Gospel, where he withdrew from the disciples and fell on his face, praying and saying: Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; yet not as I will, but as you will. And again: Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done. I am poor and in toils from my youth; but having been lifted up I was humbled and brought to despair. Your wrath passed over me; your terrors troubled me. They surrounded me like water all day long; they encompassed me together. You have put friend and neighbor far from me, and my acquaintances because of misery. Symmachus rendered this too somewhat more clearly, saying: Being poor and failing from youth, I took up your fear. Moreover, your wrath passed by through me; your terrors silenced me. They came around me like waters; all day long they encircled me. And Aquila says: Your wrath passed over me. He himself teaches in the Gospels how he was poor and in toils from his youth, when he says of himself: Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart. And the Apostle says: Who, though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself. So it is clear in what sense the Seventy's words, I am poor and in toils from my youth, were spoken. In his youth, moreover, being brought up under Joseph, his supposed father, and his mother according to the flesh, he was poor among the poor. And in the rest of his life too, though he was rich, he became poor for our sake, so that we might become rich through his poverty. But later, when he worked marvels and performed the mighty works of God, he was lifted up; and having been lifted up through his passion, he was humbled. That is why he said: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up. And again: When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he. And in the passage before us: But having been lifted up I was humbled and brought to despair. Then there are the words “your wrath passed by through me” in Symmachus, “your wrath passed over me” in Aquila, and “your wrath went through me” in the Seventy. They clearly show that the wrath did not strike him but passed through him, and that it did not remain but went on through. And “they troubled me,” in the Seventy, is like what is said in the [?]

Gospels: Now my soul is troubled; and, My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. The rest was fulfilled as the history records, when the apostles abandoned him and went away, and Peter denied him three times. In another sense, too, he spoke all the words before us making the evils of others his own. I mean the destruction of Judas the traitor and the fall of the whole Jewish nation. Out of his surpassing compassion and love for humankind, he took these things upon his own person and lamented over them, as over wicked sons perishing through their own wickedness. You will understand this if you pay attention to the prophet who says: He bears our sins and suffers pain for us. So, suffering pain on their behalf, he cried out, saying: Your wrath passed over me; your terrors troubled me. For he saw the wrath that would soon come upon them, which wiped out all their sacred things at a single stroke. The Holy of Holies and the altar were destroyed from their foundations. Their kings, who had continued by succession from their ancestors up to that time, were brought to an end. The self-government under which they had lived for a long age was extinguished, and so was their worship according to the law, along with the priesthood itself and the rest of their rulers and leaders, so that not even a trace of them remains to this day. They suffered all these things from the wrath of God, which, not long after his passion, overtook their whole nation because of what they had dared to do against him. He made this plain when he said: Your wrath passed over me, as if he were saying “because of me,” or, as Symmachus has it, “through me,” since in very truth they suffered all these things because of him. And, foreseeing their ruin, he said: Your terrors troubled me. Through their dullness, the terrors of God threatened against them through the prophets did not trouble them in the least. But as for me, he says, who see how your fearful words will come to pass, your terrors troubled me. In this way, then, he entreated the Father for them because of their impieties, grieving exceedingly in his soul and troubled on their account, and he was very sorrowful even to death. For the wrath of God pressed so heavily upon them that the prayers he sent up for them were not granted. In these prayers, as the Gospels tell, he entreated and pleaded, fell down, and, lying prostrate on his face, cried out: Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. Then, seeing that the Father's will refused, he added: Yet not as I will, but as you will. And going away a second time, he falls on his face and prays, saying: Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done. And going a third time he spoke the same words. So, to signify these things, he also said in the words before us: Why, O Lord, do you cast off my soul and turn your face away from me? and: Your wrath passed over me; your

terrors troubled me. He saw those for whom he was praying falling far away from God's salvation, though they were very dear to him and beloved for the sake of their fathers, and so he said: You have put friend and neighbor far from me, and my acquaintances because of misery. He means those in the nation who had formerly been his acquaintances and friends, since they were his portion and inheritance. But they truly were put far from him through their own unbelief. Once his friends, they made themselves his enemies; though known to him, they did not recognize him when he came, nor did they receive him. For all these reasons they were also put far from God, on account of their own misery. And so they have fallen away from God, as the oracle says: For those who put themselves far from you shall perish. With this the psalms inscribed “of the sons of Korah” come to an end.

Of understanding; for Ethan the Ezrahite. Psalm 88. I will sing of the mercies of the Lord forever. To generation upon generation I will proclaim your truth with my mouth. A little further on he is going to say: Where are your ancient mercies, O Lord, which you swore to David in your truth? So, through the words before us, he prepares the way in advance for what he is going to say. In effect he is saying this: Human affairs throw my soul into perplexity and trouble it, and they make me dizzy and bewildered about your judgments, O Lord. A little later I will even venture to speak boldly and be at a loss over the promises that you, the God who does not lie, made to David, since things have turned out contrary to your promises. That is why I am going to say, Where are your ancient mercies, O Lord? Nevertheless, I am persuaded that your promise will not prove false and that the truth of your word will not fail. So I anticipate the words I am going to speak out of human weakness and secure my own faith and the piety of my mind in advance. That is why I say: Your mercies, O Lord, I will sing forever. For I will sing of the mercies of the Lord not only now, as I speak and utter these words, but also in gloomier times, even in those very times that will make me say, Where are your ancient mercies, O Lord? For then too, and in the time after, and through all the ages, I will not cease to hymn your mercies, O Lord. I know well that you, who promised the prophecies in the psalm, will not prove false, since you are the true God. That is why I will not only sing your mercies, O Lord, forever, but will also proclaim your truth in every generation. For even if things happen in the meantime that seem to run contrary to your promises to David, I have still believed, and have truly persuaded myself, that the truth of your words, O Lord, will never fail. So for all the time of my life I will not cease to proclaim your truth with my mouth. What is more, I will commit it to writing and leave it to those who come after, so that they too, in every generation, may be taught and may learn, as I have, to carry your truth on their

[?] and to be convinced that your promises can never fail. The whole psalm foretells Christ's birth from the seed of David, and his kingdom.
