The preceding psalms had prophesied his birth among human beings, as was shown in Psalm 86. But besides his birth we also needed to learn where he would come from, and the present Scripture necessarily teaches this, since it contains God's promise to David that the Christ would come forth from his seed. So this psalm too follows in sequence from the psalms placed before it. It alone is titled "of understanding"; it is called neither a psalm nor a hymn. It would be a prophetic song that calls for understanding in God's way. That is why it says, "I will sing forever, and to generation after generation I will proclaim your truth." From "I will sing forever" one might reasonably call it a song; from "I will proclaim your truth to generation after generation," and from what follows, a prophecy. It is spoken by Ethan the Ezrahite, about whom we said what seemed fitting in our introductory discussion of the Psalms. "For you said: Mercy will be built up forever; in the heavens your truth will be prepared." In place of "For you said," Aquila translated "For I said"; Symmachus, "For I said"; Theodotion likewise, "For I said"; and the fifth edition, "For I said"; as though the words were spoken in the person of the Prophet. This was Ethan the Ezrahite, as the title shows. Some such thought [?] that there seems to be irregularity in human life. But since the promises God made to David are divine and heavenly, and not earthly and bodily, as the children of the Jews might suppose, the Prophet rightly makes it clear beforehand that the truth of God's promises will be prepared not on earth but in the heavens. Symmachus therefore translated more clearly, saying, "In the heavens your truth will be established." "I made a covenant with my chosen ones; I swore to David my servant: Forever I will prepare your seed, and I will build your throne to generation after generation. Interlude. The heavens will confess your wonders, O Lord, and

indeed your truth in the assembly of the saints." These words are clearly spoken in the person of God. So it seems to me that in the Seventy the earlier words, "For you said: Mercy will be built up forever; in the heavens your truth will be prepared," were joined to "I made a covenant with my chosen ones," so that, read with a transposition, the sense of the passage is this: "Since you yourself, O Lord, said in your promises concerning David, 'My mercy toward David' (or else toward all people) 'will be built up forever,' and you added, 'I made a covenant with my chosen ones' (or rather, with my chosen one), and 'I swore to David my servant,' and what follows, I am convinced that your promises will never prove false but remain true and unfailing. Yet they are not to be realized on earth, for they are not earthly and perceptible, nor mortal and short-lived like human life, but immortal and eternal and befitting your divinity. Therefore the truth of your promises to David will be prepared not on earth but in the heavens." In place of "I made a covenant with my chosen ones," all the other translators have "with my chosen one." This rendering suits the sense better, for the passage is not about many people but about David alone. To him, he says, I also swore, since he was my servant and my chosen one. It was not enough simply to make a covenant with him, as I made one with Noah, and after him with Abraham, and again after Abraham with the sons of Israel in the desert through Moses. With them I did so without an oath; but with my chosen one, my attendant and servant David, I made the covenant and added an oath. For I swore to him that I would prepare his seed forever and build his throne, and not for one generation but to generation after generation. On God's swearing, the holy Apostle says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: "so that through two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have strong encouragement." God adopted an oath as well, to strengthen the assurance still further. By what the oath was sworn, he teaches as he goes on: "Once I swore by my holy one." Here you should also consider who this holy one of God was, by whom he swears as by

his only-begotten Son, so that the terms of the promise might be confirmed in every way. Even the demons in the Gospels confessed the Holy One. Unable to bear his divine power, which punished and drove them out, they cried out, "Ah, what have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? We know who you are, the Holy One of God." By him, then, God swore, as a father swears by his only-begotten and beloved son, when he made the promise to David. He teaches this himself when he says, "Once I swore by my holy one that I will not lie to David." As I searched for the reason why God made the promise about his seed by oath to David alone and to none of the other saints,

I think I have found it: I noticed that David himself had sworn an oath before God made his promise to him. The divine Spirit teaches that he swore in Psalm 131, saying: "Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness: how he swore to the Lord and vowed to the God of Jacob, 'I will not enter the dwelling of my house, I will not go up onto the bed where I lie, I will not give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob.'" David had vowed and promised such things and had sworn an oath upon them, and God, giving him an equal return, swears in turn himself and makes a promise in return, giving like for like and repaying oath with oath. That is why the same Psalm 131, in which David is said to have sworn, goes on to add the testimony of the Holy Spirit, which runs something like this: "The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not set it aside: Of the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne." So David swore first, and then God, repaying him, swore an oath to him in return. David first, moved by pious reasoning, promised something to God; then God in turn, as though giving him grace for grace, himself made a promise in return, in keeping with the words of our Savior: "With the measure you measure, it will be measured back to you. Good measure, shaken down, pressed together, running over, they will pour into your lap." With the very measure David used, then, when he made under oath a promise befitting good and godly reasoning, it was measured back to him, and he receives his recompense: God's promises sworn on oath. Now it is time to consider what David's sworn promise means. He saw the nations of the whole inhabited world enslaved to demonic and polytheistic error. Everywhere on earth temples, sacred precincts and shrines had been raised to wicked demons; in cities, countryside and villages, on mountains and hills, the wicked, hostile power was honored by all people, while God, the maker and creator of all, was nowhere remembered by anyone. Stung to the soul by this, and zealous with a good zeal, like the one who said, "I have been very zealous for the Lord," he vowed a vow and promised a promise and bound it with an oath: that he would truly be the first to build on earth a temple and holy sanctuary for God the King of all, where he would lay up and give rest to the tent of witness and the ark of the covenant, which Moses had made in the desert at God's command. Until David's time it had been carried about here and there, moved from place to place: now in Gilgal, now in Mizpah, now in Shiloh, at another time among the Philistines, from there to Beth-shemesh, from there to Kiriath-jearim, then to the house of Abinadab, from there to the house of Obed-edom, and from there David brought it to the city of Zion. Seeing this happen, he resolved to raise a holy house and build a temple

and to set up the ark of God there. It was about this that David swore to the Lord and vowed to the God of Jacob, saying: "I will not enter the dwelling of my house, I will not go up onto the bed where I lie, I will not give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob." When he had resolved this, God accepted his pious intention but did not allow the house to be built. For God, being God, has no need of a perceptible house, still less of one built from lifeless stones. If God was indeed to dwell on earth, then from David's own seed would come the one who would receive his divinity, who would also build for God a worthy holy house and a holy temple, and whose throne would endure for all eternity. He was thus pointing to his Christ, who would be born of David's seed according to the flesh, and to the Church that would be established through him throughout the whole world. That this is so, the Scripture of Kingdoms teaches as follows: "And it came to pass, when David sat in his house and the Lord had given him possession all around, free of all his enemies, that the king said to Nathan the prophet, 'See now, I live in a house of cedar, while the ark of God sits in the middle of the tent'" (or "in the middle of a hide," as the Hebrew word means). "And Nathan said to the king, 'Whatever is in your heart, go and do it, for the Lord is with you.' And that night the word of the Lord came to Nathan, saying, 'Go to my servant David and say: Thus says the Lord: You shall not build me a house for me to dwell in. For I have not dwelt in a house from the day I brought the sons of Israel up out of Egypt until this day, but I have been going about in a lodging and in a tent. Wherever I went among all Israel, did I ever speak a word to a single tribe of Israel that I commanded to shepherd my people Israel, saying, Why have you not built me a house of cedar? Now then, this is what you shall say to my servant David: Thus says the Lord Almighty: I took you from the sheepfold, from following the sheep, to be leader over Israel. I was with you wherever you went, I destroyed all your enemies before you, and I made you renowned like the name of the great ones on the earth. I will appoint a place for my people Israel and plant them there, and they will dwell on their own and no longer be anxious; the son of wickedness will no longer oppress them as he did from the beginning, from the days when I appointed judges over my people Israel. I will give you rest from all your enemies, and the Lord will tell you that you will build him a house. And when your days are fulfilled and you sleep with

your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, who will come from your own body, and I will prepare his kingdom. He shall build me a house for my name, and I will set up his throne forever. I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me. If he commits wrong, I will rebuke him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of men. But my mercy I will not take away from him, as I took it away from those whom I removed from my presence. His house and his kingdom shall be made sure before me forever, and his throne shall stand firm forever.' In accordance with all these words and all this vision, so Nathan spoke to David." I have quoted all this because I wanted to show that, since David first promised to prepare a house for the ark of God, God, accepting his piety, promises in return to raise up his seed and through it to prepare a house for himself; and that, since David first swore to do nothing else until he had found a place for God, God in his turn swears through the promise, condescending to speak in rather human terms. Countless other things too are said of God in divine Scripture in human terms, to convey some meaning to be grasped by contemplation. Now that this has been shown, it is time to examine the wording of the psalm. What, then, does God's promise mean? It foretells two things: first, that he will keep David's seed forever; second, that he will build his throne to generation after generation. Then, since these things were not to be realized perceptibly on earth or in a human kingdom, he next refers the fulfillment of the promises to the heavens. So, just as he said above, "In heaven your truth will be prepared," now too, after God's promise, he adds, "The heavens will confess your wonders, O Lord." For people on earth, he says, will not be able to understand what meaning the promises have, O Lord, or what the fulfillment of the prophetic words is; only the heavens themselves can, that is, the divine powers in heaven. So it is fitting for the heavens to recount and interpret your wonders contained in the promises. Likewise, again, your truth, glorified in the promises to David, belongs to none but the heavens and the angels in the heavens to hymn and recount. [?]

other than that David was named God's chosen one, that from him came a seed that would hold an eternal throne, and that God made an eternal covenant with him, or that a compact was made with him? For so Aquila and Symmachus translated, saying "compact" instead of "covenant." It was a wonder, too, that God swore to a human being and said to him, "Forever I will prepare your seed," as Symmachus has it, "and I will build your throne for every generation," as the same translator has it. But the greatest wonder of all was that God, in promising such things, sealed them with an oath; and most wonderful of all, that after the divine oath God's words seemed not to have been fulfilled, but the very opposite of what was sworn came to pass. He goes on, then, to show that things contrary to God's promises had happened. This is what most astonishes and amazes the Prophet, and so he goes on to complain, saying, "Where are your mercies of old, O Lord, which you swore to David in your truth?" But he relieves his own perplexity, having said above, "In the heavens your truth will be prepared," and in what follows, "The heavens will confess your wonders, and indeed your truth in the assembly of the saints. For who in the clouds will be equal to the Lord, or be likened to the Lord among the sons of God?" In place of "in the clouds," Symmachus says, "For who in the ether?" He has joined these words very aptly to what he said before. Your truth and your wonders, he says, even if human beings cannot understand them (which is why I am about to say a little later, "Where are your mercies of old, O Lord, which you swore to David?"), the heavens will nevertheless recount, and the assembly of the saints will testify, that nothing you swore to David will fail and your promises will not prove false, for it is impossible for you to lie. Who will be your equal in truth, or who will be like you in speaking and making good your promises? No one can withstand your counsel so as to overturn what you have once determined, much less what you have promised on oath. So even if the truth of your promises is not yet known to us, this much we know for certain: that you are mighty, O Lord, and your truth is all around you. Whatever you have willed, then, you are able to do, and the truth of your words spoken beforehand about David surrounds you, so that it is known to all who are near you and attend your divinity as your bodyguard, but unknown to those who stand far off from you. It seems to me that in these words the Prophet, carried along by God through the Holy Spirit, with the eyes of his soul lit up by spiritual light, saw the glory of the Only-begotten of God standing in the midst of the assembly of the saints and escorted by the saints in his kingdom. Having mentioned the heavens, then, and gazing by the divine Spirit on the assembly of the saints, he seems to have seen the Son of God in their midst; then, after contemplating him, to have turned his eyes to the surrounding holy angels and archangels and the

choir of divine spirits and powers; to have marveled at their divine nature, yet to have been utterly overwhelmed by the one who is beyond them all and above them all, the Only-begotten of God; and then, out of wonder, to have cried out, "For who in the clouds will be equal to the Lord?" or, as Symmachus has it, "For who in the ether will be set beside the Lord among the sons of God?" These words, said of the Only-begotten of God, would preserve a pious sense, but not if said of the Father and God of all, for that comparison would be unfitting and impious. To set the cause of all things beside the sons of God, and to dare to compare the God who is beyond all things with others, would be the most unholy thing of all. But there is no danger in a statement that compares the only-begotten Son of God with the sons of God, and that signifies, through the words "Who in the clouds will be equal to the Lord?" (meaning "no one"), that he is beyond comparison with all and cannot be set beside anyone, surpassing them beyond measure. For even if many saints and myriads of angels, the assembly of the firstborn, principalities and authorities, thrones and dominions, holy spirits and divine powers dwell as citizens among the hosts of heaven and make up the heavenly assembly, still, he says, who in the ether beyond the firmament will be equal to the Lord? And even if there are many sons of God and gods, according to the words "God stood in the assembly of gods," and "The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken," and "I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High," still, "who will be likened to the Lord among the sons of God?" Though there are countless sons, no one, he says, will be like him or equal to him, since he is the chosen one, the only-begotten and the firstborn of all creation, the Word and Wisdom and Power and Wisdom of God. It seems to me that he points to the knowledge of these things in the words above, where he said, "The heavens will confess your wonders." For this too was one of the wonders: what he was about to say next about the Only-begotten of God. And necessarily so: since he was about to point, through the prophecy, to the one who would be born of David's seed, he first contemplates the divinity of the one who would dwell in him, so that we might learn at the same time what power was to dwell in him, and that the one was son of David, while the one who would dwell in him was the Son of God. "God, glorified in the council of the saints, great and fearsome over all who are around him." The one who has no comparison, no equal, and no likeness among any of the so-called sons of God, he now shows what kind of being he is, saying: This is the God who is glorified in the council of the saints. By "council of the saints" he means the assembly of the saints mentioned above. He seems to have called the assembly of the firstborn enrolled in heaven a "council" by analogy with the council chambers of particular places. In this council of the saints the one who has no comparison or likeness among the so-called sons of God is glorified; and he is not only glorified in the council of the saints, but is also fearsome over all who are around him. Who would those around him be, other than the sons

…of God, and are themselves called gods, about whom it has been said, “God stood in the assembly of gods”? For “In the council of the holy ones,” and “In the assembly of the firstborn,” and “In the assembly of gods” seem to me to be one and the same. Standing, then, in the midst of these, with them as his escort, the Son of God is said to be glorified, and great and fearful. Symmachus rendered the passage this way: “O God, invincible in the great company of the holy ones, and terrible over all who are around you.” Aquila says: “Mighty One, prevailing in the secret council of the holy ones, a multitude, a multitude, and fearsome over all who are around him.” The sense of the passage shows how it follows on. For since you are mighty, Lord, he says, and your truth is round about you, it is fitting that you are great and fearful, and glorified in the council of the holy ones and among those who encircle your divinity. They see the truth of your promises, and in wonder at your divinity they send up the thanksgiving that befits it. That is why they said a little earlier: “The heavens will confess your wonders, and your truth in the assembly of the holy ones. O Lord God of hosts, who is like you? You are mighty, Lord, and your truth is round about you. You rule the might of the sea, and you calm the tossing of its waves. You humbled the proud like one who is wounded; with the arm of your power you scattered your enemies.” Here too he allows none of the things that have come into being to be like the Son of God, who is here spoken of as God. For he is the Mighty One, and the God of the mighty, and Lord of the powers themselves, so that no one can gainsay him or resist his will. Therefore he says and does all things, since he alone is mighty. For here too “Who is like you?” is meant not in the sense of “few” but of “none.” He says, then, that none is like the one who is properly called Lord, and he compares with him the sons of God mentioned above. For the present words keep to the same sense as the earlier ones, where it was said: “For who in the clouds shall be equal to the Lord, shall be likened to the Lord among the sons of God?” And now he says, “Who is like you?” because you are mighty, and the truth of your words and your promises are around you and with you. For your truth is with you, with those who encircle you. If any stand near you and round about you, they themselves know your truth. But we on earth, who are still far from you, see your mighty works in what your providence brings about at sea, and so we confess that you are mighty and that your truth is round about you. For you alone rule the sea and so vast a basin of waters, and you alone calm the tossing of its waves. You set bars and gates about it and fixed bounds for it, so that it should not overstep them and flood the world where human beings live. This indeed is itself one

of the greatest proofs of your power. For like a slave serving its master, so great a mass of moving water arches up to a height and rears itself, then cowers and crashes back upon itself, shut in within its own bounds. And just as you bridled the waves and threats of the sea by your command and calmed its heights, its surges and its rages, so too with the invisible powers. If any were ever hostile and opposed to the purpose of your providence, these too you scattered, since you alone are most mighty and above all. Their ruler and tyrant, a braggart and proud, the ruler of this age, you humbled by your own power and made one of the wounded. You struck him with the great and fearful sword, in keeping with the prophecy that says: “The Lord will bring the great and strong sword upon the dragon, the crooked, fleeing serpent, and he will slay the dragon that is in the sea.” And another prophet taught that this wounded dragon makes his haunts in the sea, saying: “This is the sea, great and wide; there are creeping things without number. This is the dragon that you formed to make sport of him.” Since this is so, consider whether the present passage too was hinting at this very sea when it said, “You rule the might of the sea, and you calm the tossing of its waves.” At any rate, he joined to these words, “You humbled the proud like one who is wounded; with the arm of your power you scattered your enemies.” For he seems to call the domain of the opposing powers, the demons and evil spirits, “the sea.” That is why he followed what he said about the sea with what concerns the wounded one and the enemies of God, plainly signifying the opposing powers and their ruler. In another psalm too it is said: “You crushed the heads of the dragons upon the water. You crushed the head of the dragon; you gave him as food to the peoples, the Ethiopians.” And in Job: “You will draw the dragon with a hook, and put a halter round his nose, and pierce his lip with a ring. He will speak to you softly, with petition and supplication, and you will take him as a slave for ever.” And next it adds: “He is king of all that are in the waters.” In the same way it is said about the same dragon, in the person of the Lord, to Job: “Do you not fear, because he has been made ready for me [?]?” In the present passage, then, the divine Spirit had good reason to mention these things, for it is teaching that the Only-begotten of God descended even to the sea we have described. Having first spoken of him as God, and having told of his first dwelling among the holy ones, who he is, and with whom and among whom he goes forth, he next shows that this same one will rule over the sea we have described, will humble the wounded one in it, and with the arm of his might will scatter all his

enemies. He has good reason to say this. Having said before, “You are mighty, Lord, and your truth is round about you,” he shows by the deeds themselves how mighty the Lord is, to confirm his truth and prove true the promises made to David. “Yours are the heavens, and yours is the earth; you founded the world and all that fills it; you created the north and the sea. Tabor and Hermon will rejoice in your name.” The sense of the passage is something like this: You made promises to David, O Lord, concerning his seed and his throne, which would endure for ever, and you swore to David that you would fulfil them. But we human beings see that they are not being fulfilled, as far as what can be perceived and seen is concerned. That is why we say, “Where are your mercies of old, Lord?” Nevertheless we are persuaded that you are wholly truthful, because you are mighty and your truth is round about you. And all who are around you are witnesses of your truth. The heavenly powers, at any rate, will confess your wonders, and your truth in the assembly of the holy ones. And it is fitting that the heavenly powers should confess your truth, since “in heaven your truth will be made ready.” So we must no longer suppose that your promises to David are earthly and bodily, for in heaven your truth will be made ready. Having learned this myself from the Holy Spirit, I say: “I will sing of your mercies for ever; from generation to generation I will proclaim your truth with my mouth.” And one must be persuaded that you speak the truth, since you are God and Lord of all, for nothing is like your power. You are Lord even of the bodiless and divine powers, and you alone are mighty and above all, so that your truth is made sure. And if among all that exists there is one who is proud, the one called the devil, who always opposes and makes war on your truth, you have humbled him. And if there are other hostile and opposing powers besides him, these too you have scattered. You always prevail, and you rule the substance of the universe, since you are also the maker of all things. For this very sea, so great an element of liquid substance, is your work and claims you as its lord. And if certain heavens are understood to lie higher than the firmament, dwellings of divine spirits and holy powers, of the angels and archangels who encircle your divinity, these too are yours, together with all who dwell in them. And another element, no small one, the dry substance, the earth that lies beneath the heavens, is also yours. Since, then, all things serve at your nod, and you prevail over all, being Lord and King and God of all, who will resist you? Or what will prevent you from making good your promises to your chosen David, which you made to him with an oath? Very fittingly, then, and in keeping with what was said before, he went on in this passage: “Yours are the heavens, and yours is the earth; you founded the world and all that fills it.” For you founded not only heaven, he says, and the powers in it, but the earth too. This agrees with the saying in

Proverbs: “God founded the earth by wisdom, and he prepared the heavens by understanding.” Here he has used the word “world” in a special sense for the inhabited part of the earth, distinguishing it from the desert and uninhabited land. He also added “all that fills the world,” signifying in this way the human race, which fills the world. But you would not be wrong to give another meaning to “all that fills the world” and take it as the Church of the Savior, which the Word of God himself founded upon the rock. That is why it is said elsewhere: “The Lord has become king; he has clothed himself with majesty. For he has established the world, and it shall not be moved.” How he founded the world, he says next: “You created the north and the sea [?].” The fifth edition has: “You created north and south.” It seems to me that by the two sides and extremities of the world he indicates the whole universe, which the power of our Savior has filled. And see how these words show that the eastern part is the face of the whole universe, the northern part is its left, and the southern part, toward the noonday sun, is its right. For by saying, “You created the north and the right,” he taught that the northern side is the left, if indeed the southern side is the right. So if we stand with the south on our right hand and the north on our left, we will be facing the east, with the west behind our back. These things are said, then, as a kind of natural philosophy, setting out the position of the whole universe. These points too must be noted, to show that the teaching of the divine Scriptures has not left out even this kind of knowledge. For you created all things, he says, both the right-hand parts of the world and the left. But he named the right explicitly, while he took care not to use the word “left.” Hence Symmachus has, “You created the north and the right,” and Aquila, “You created north and right.” The fifth edition translated more clearly what “the right” is, saying: “You created north and south.” The left is passed over in silence by them all, because it is thought to be sinister and the opposite of the right. But nothing in the universe is sinister, nor is anything opposed to the good. You created all things, then, he says. But two mountains, Tabor and Hermon, are singled out above all the rest, for these will rejoice in your name. Aquila has, “Tabor and Hermon will give praise in your name”; Symmachus, “Tabor and Hermon will speak well of your name.” The history of the Old Testament mentions these mountains in various ways, and I think that the marvellous transfigurations of our Savior took place on these mountains, as did most of his sojourning when he lived among human beings. Whether the meaning of the names also contributes something to the sense of the passage, you will consider for yourself. “Yours is the arm, with might; let your hand be made strong, let your right hand be lifted high. Righteousness

and judgment are the preparation of your throne. Mercy and truth will go before your face.” These words too are taken up to glorify the Only-begotten of God, as Aquila translated more clearly, rendering it this way: “Yours is the arm, with might; invincible is your hand, lofty your right hand; righteousness and judgment are the base of your throne.” He had good reason to include these virtues that befit God in his account of the divine, because of God's promises to David. For nothing, he says, will withstand your will; with the will to act you also have the power, as God and Master of all. For you have a great arm, and might, and rule over all things, a strong hand and a right hand lifted most high. And just as the thrones of those who reign on earth are made of precious materials, so this throne of your kingdom too has been built of what befits you as God. Virtues worthy of God, righteousness and judgment, adorn your throne. Since you, God, have such powers, the truth of your promises runs before you smoothly and without hindrance, and no one can obstruct your decrees. These you swore to David when, out of mercy and grace, you made him the promises set out above. Instead of “Righteousness and judgment are the preparation of your throne,” Aquila has, “Righteousness and judgment are the foundation of his throne,” and Symmachus says that righteousness and judgment are the base itself. And when righteousness, and judgment joined with righteousness, go forth, mercy and truth run on ahead. By mixing mercy with his righteousness, he makes his threats against sinners milder; otherwise no human being could endure his righteousness undiluted. “Blessed is the people that knows the shout of joy. Lord, they will walk in the light of your face, and they will rejoice in your name all the day long, and they will be exalted in your righteousness. For you are the boast of their strength, and in your good pleasure our horn will be exalted. For our help is from the Lord, and from the Holy One of Israel, our king.” You may also understand the shout in another way, from soldiers who raise a shout in time of war and strike fear into the enemy by the loudness of their cry and their shouting together as one. But the divine Apostle teaches that prayers in the Holy Spirit, which are sent up not with an audible cry but in the power of the Spirit, are of this kind, when he says: “The Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words.” So great and rare a thing is the shout so often named in the divine Scriptures that whoever understands it is called blessed, just like those who are called blessed for their other godly achievements. That is why it is said here: “Blessed is the people that knows the shout of joy.” Elsewhere the divine word teaches that such a shout is a sacrifice, saying: “I went around and offered in his tent a sacrifice of shouting.”

It seems to me, then, that here the divine Spirit is plainly calling the people of Christ blessed. For this people has come to know our Savior's victory over his foes, and it shouts against the enemy, raising the shout on behalf of its own king. Moreover, this people alone is accustomed to offer to God the bloodless and spiritual sacrifice with a shout of joy, sending up thanksgiving to God with one voice in the spiritual sacred rites and in the worship we perform under the New Covenant, the bloodless, immaterial and spiritual sacrifices. Instead of “that knows the shout of joy,” Symmachus rendered “that knows the signal.” Why, then, is this people of Christ that understands this shout blessed? Is it not because it recognizes the divinity of the Savior, which has been called his face, and, lit by the light of his face, goes on its way saying, “The light of your face has been set as a sign upon us, Lord,” and, “In your light we shall see light”? For this reason, then, this people is blessed. And third, because it is not content with being enlightened through the knowledge of Christ, but also takes pride in his name and is called Christian after him, it rejoices and exults all the day long, or rather every day, for that is how Symmachus rendered it; and for this reason too it is blessed. And fourth, because it has grown to greatness and height and is exalted by the righteousness of God. For God has judged it just to raise to the heights and to great glory the people that understands this shout, that is enlightened by the face of the Savior, that exults in his name, and that boasts, but not in its own achievements. The passage had good reason to mention what has been described, for it is foretelling what Christ's coming among human beings would accomplish. It was about to teach the birth of the one who would come forth from the seed of David, and to foretell the overthrow of what the Jews held sacred, which is why it asks in perplexity, “Where are your mercies of old, Lord?” So it had good reason to give the teaching set out above, that God's promises to David would in every way prove true. But since we had to learn beforehand for which people the grace of the Savior's kindness was being stored up, he went on to mention not Israel, nor the nation of the Jews, but the people that knows the shout of joy. And rightly he called this people blessed and promised it a great many good things. Because they know the shout of joy, first, they will walk in the light of God's face; next, they will rejoice in his name every day; third, they will be exalted in his righteousness; and fourth, the Lord himself will be the boast of their strength. For since this people is strong and mighty, being built upon the rock, so that not even the gates of Hades can prevail against it, it will rightly boast, though not in its own strength, but in the Lord who founded it upon the rock. For all these reasons, blessed is the people that

knows the shout of joy. And the horn of us ourselves, the prophets who foretell these things through the Spirit, will be exalted. What horn is this, if not the one that was to come forth from the seed of David according to your promise, O Lord? For this horn of ours, with which we shall gore our enemies, will be exalted in your good pleasure, while you, the Holy One of Israel, our king, take charge of the birth of this horn. These would be the voices of the prophets, speaking these words in their own person and confessing that their horn is the Christ of God, who would appear in the flesh. “Then you spoke in a vision to your sons and said: I have laid help upon one who is mighty; I have exalted one chosen out of my people. I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him. For my hand will support him, and my arm will strengthen him. No enemy shall get the better of him, and no son of lawlessness shall harm him. I will cut down his enemies before his face, and put to flight those who hate him. My truth and my mercy shall be with him, and in my name his horn shall be exalted.” Since the passage has already mentioned the horn in the preceding words, where it said, “In your good pleasure our horn will be exalted,” it has good reason, as it goes on, to teach what this horn was, where it would come from, and how it would be exalted. That is why it says: “For the help is from the Lord,” that is, the help of the horn. And from what Lord, if not the Holy One of Israel, our king? For the Lord himself, the Holy One of Israel, the king, the Word of God, will be the help of our horn, according to the promises he made when he speaks through the prophets about the one who was to come forth from the seed of David. For when, it says, you spoke in a vision to your holy ones, you, O God, made the promises set out here through your own sons, the prophets, to whom you revealed visions of what was to come. Through them you made your promises to David, using these words: “I have laid help upon one who is mighty; I have exalted one chosen out of my people.” For these words Symmachus gave this rendering: “I have laid help of men [?]; I have exalted one chosen from my people. I have found David my servant,” and the rest is close to the Seventy. Their sense is this: After searching long among human beings to find one worthy of me, I found at last, and barely, my servant David. Out of surpassing piety, he alone of all since time began resolved to build me a house of prayer on earth. Therefore, to reward him for his good and pious resolve, in return for the house he resolved to build, I myself will build for myself an all-holy temple from his seed. For the man born of David's seed was the temple of God the Word, who dwelt in him. The Savior himself taught this about his own body, when he said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”

And God made his return to David in a way that answered very fittingly to David's own promise. "Since, then," he says, "I found David fit for my promises and worthy of them, I counted him worthy of my help. I declared him chosen and raised him above all the people. And further, since after searching long I found him alone worthy of my promises, once I had found him I counted him worthy of anointing with my holy oil, by which I also made him an anointed one, a christ. And I promise to give him these things: My right hand will be with him steadfastly, and my arm will make him strong. The enemy will not deceive him, nor will the son of injustice harm him. I will cut down before him those who hate him, and I will strike those who do him harm. My steadfastness and my grace will be with him." All these things will be his according to Symmachus's translation. According to the Seventy, however, he says: "My hand will help him, and my arm will strengthen him. The enemy will gain no advantage over him, and the son of lawlessness will not harm him. I will cut down his enemies from before his face, and I will put to flight those who hate him. My truth and my mercy are with him." And finally, after all this: "In my name his horn will be exalted." This horn of his is the one that was to come forth from him, the temple that was to be built for me from his seed. This horn of his will be exalted in my name, for it will be counted worthy of my name and my title. So it too will bear my own designations, and through my titles it will be exalted among all. That is why it was said earlier, "And in your good pleasure our horn will be exalted." But there the choir of the prophets cried out to God, saying, "And in your good pleasure our horn will be exalted"; now God himself, in making his promises about David, adds as a seal on them all, "In my name his horn will be exalted." By this he points to the Christ who was to come forth from him, who is called the horn not only of the prophets but of David himself. Of him he goes on to say: "And I will set his hand on the sea, and his right hand on the rivers. He will call upon me: You are my Father, my God, and the helper of my salvation. And I will make him firstborn, high among the kings of the earth. I will keep my mercy for him forever, and my covenant will be faithful to him." If anyone pays careful attention to the sense of these words, he will find that they are prophesied not of David but of the horn that was to come forth from him. For after saying, "And in my name his horn will be exalted," the text goes on to speak of the horn and says, "I will set his hand on the sea" (clearly the horn's hand), and so on. From this point on, then, the words are properly referred to the Christ who was to be born of David's seed. If anyone does not take them this way but refers the passage to David, his interpretation will not hold together. How did God set David's hand on the sea and his right hand on the rivers? Let anyone who wishes

explain that. For David never ruled the coastal lands. Or how could it be said of David, "He will call upon me: You are my Father," and "I will make him firstborn"? Why should David be thought the firstborn of God rather than Abraham, or Isaac, or Israel, or Moses, or Elijah, or the other righteous men and prophets? And how would God be speaking truly when he says of him, "I will make him high among the kings of the earth"? When, pray, was David ever [?] among the Persians, or the Scythians, the Indians, the Ethiopians, the Moors, the Spaniards, the Britons, or the kings of the other nations? But if you take these words of the one born of his seed, you will find that they fit him most firmly and most properly. The Gospel also bears witness to the fulfillment of the prophecy. In Luke's account, Zechariah, the father of John, himself called him a horn by prophetic power. The evangelist says: "And Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying: Blessed be the God of Israel, for he has visited his people and brought about their redemption. He has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David, as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old." The Christ of God is properly named a horn. That is also why he is called a unicorn, according to the Scripture that says, "And the beloved one like the son of unicorns." For through him every power opposed and hostile to God was routed, gored by the horn and shattered. Of all those who became David's successors, Jesus Christ our Savior and Lord alone, coming forth from his seed, truly overturned and destroyed all the error of demons and idols by the horn of the Godhead within him. That is why the sacred words fittingly call him both horn and unicorn. His hand, his right hand and no one else's, has become master of the whole world, of rivers and seas. For his teaching has filled even the islands of the nations, and everywhere on earth every race of men proclaims him Lord and God and King. What is said here, "I will set his hand on the sea, and his right hand on the rivers," resembles what is said of him again in Psalm 71: "And he will rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the world." Beginning from his baptism in the river Jordan to preach the kingdom of God, the Savior filled the whole world. And in the prophet Zechariah it is said: "Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion. Behold, your king comes to you, gentle and riding on a beast of burden, a young colt. And he will rule from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the outlets of the earth." In place of this the Hebrew reads, "and from the rivers to the ends of the earth." But one could also take these words in another, more hidden sense. His right hand is said to be on the rivers because all who stand at his right are cleansed through the washing of regeneration and are counted worthy of the divine rebirth

through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. We have been taught to understand those at his right as the ones to whom he made the promise: "Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me something to eat," and so on. He promised to set at his right hand these, whom he called his sheep. So in a deeper and more hidden sense his right hand is said to be on the rivers. His peoples are also called rivers, as in, "The rivers will clap their hands together," and again, "The rivers have lifted up, O Lord, the rivers have lifted up their voice; the rivers will lift up their pounding waves." On these rivers of his, then, he promises to set his right hand. His other hand, which he has left us to understand as the left, he says he will set on the sea, on the salt waves of this life. That is where the dragon makes his haunts, as in, "There is the sea, great and wide; there are creeping things without number. This is the dragon you formed to make sport of him." It is not the right hand but the other hand, the one beside the right, that will be laid on these dragons and on the sea understood in this way, to punish and chastise the enemies and to humble them. And the one indicated here (plainly the horn of David), the one who would be born of David's seed, will call God Father. For he has been counted worthy to have the only-begotten Son of God dwell in him, and to be joined and united with him. That is why God the Word himself, the Firstborn of all creation, who promised beforehand, "In my name his horn will be exalted," will make him firstborn. He gives a share of his own name and his own dignity to the one who would come forth from David's seed, so that he too, born of David's seed according to the flesh, may be styled Son of God and be named Firstborn because he is joined to the Only-begotten of God. These were the things through which he promised that he would be exalted when he said, "In my name his horn will be exalted." For the only-begotten Son of God bestowed his own name on the son of David according to the flesh, and proclaimed him too Firstborn and Son of God. He also promised to make him high among the kings of the earth, or in Symmachus's version, "highest of the kings of the earth." He has proved higher and stronger than all who were to make war on him. He shatters the uprisings and persecutions against his Church, and he glorifies and strengthens the word of his teaching. He also says he will keep his mercy for him forever and make his covenant faithful to him. This surely means the New Covenant, which he proclaimed to all the nations throughout the whole world when he gave the Gospel in place of the covenant given through Moses. This covenant he promised to keep faithful and to confirm. "And I will establish his seed forever and ever, and his throne as the days of heaven. If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments,

if they profane my ordinances and do not keep my commandments, I will punish their lawless deeds with a rod and their wrongdoing with scourges. But I will not scatter my mercy from him, nor will I deal unjustly in my truth. Nor will I profane my covenant, and I will not set aside what goes out through my lips." What was said about the horn has been completed in the preceding verses, and the horn was shown to be none other than the Christ born of David's seed according to the flesh. Now, following on from the oracles about him, he uses these verses to show what kind of succession he will have. He says, in effect: "I will establish the seed of the horn I have described not simply for one age, the present one, but also for the age of ages to come. I will keep his throne not for a few days or for short cycles of years, but I will make it last as long as the days of heaven." Symmachus translated it in the same way: "And I will make his seed perpetual, and his throne as long as the days of heaven." What should we understand by the seed of Christ but the churches he has established throughout the whole world, and the peoples born again to him among all the nations? His throne is the one set up in his Church throughout the whole world through the bishops who succeed one another from him. He says this throne will last as the days of heaven. It is not like the royal throne of the Jews, which lasted only a short time and then was extinguished, having been preserved for only about four hundred years, from David to the captivity in Babylon. This present throne of the Church's bishops, foretold in these verses, will endure and be preserved like the days of heaven. And if it should ever happen that the people and the sons of the one prophesied, by which I mean his successors, go astray, he says they will undergo correction through persecutions. Yet they will never fall from their thrones or be deprived of God's mercy. For if his sons (clearly Christ's sons) do such and such things, he says this will happen to them: "I will punish their lawless deeds with a rod" (that is, the deeds of the sons) "and their wrongdoing with scourges; but I will not scatter my mercy from him." Notice that it does not say "from them" but "from him," clearly meaning the one prophesied, even though the preceding words were in the plural: "I will punish their lawless deeds with a rod and their wrongdoing with scourges." Whose deeds are these, if not plainly those of the horn's sons? But the words "I will not scatter my mercy from him" are said of one only, either the throne or the horn that is prophesied. Next he adds, "Nor will I profane my covenant," clearly the new covenant, the one of which he said above, "And my covenant will be faithful to him." Then he again seals the truth of his word, saying, "I will not set aside what goes out through my lips." He means: "I will make what I have promised faithful and true, adding deeds to my words through the actual outcomes."

So much, then, for the promises to David about the horn and his throne, about those who would come from him, and about his New Covenant. But such promises were not to be thought of as put forward in a simple, bare word. So he takes up the word again and repeats it, sealing what he has said with an oath to confirm the promises. That is why he says: "Once for all I have sworn by my Holy One that I will not lie to David. His seed will remain forever, and his throne will be like the sun before me, and like the moon established forever. And the witness in heaven is faithful." Pause. God does not lie, and his promise needs no oath. But since he was speaking as to human beings, he had to accommodate himself to them, like people who swear honest oaths and call on God as witness to confirm their words. So he too says that he has sworn and will not break his oaths, "so that through two unchangeable things," as the divine Apostle says, "in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have strong encouragement." Another reason has also been given for why God is presented as swearing: it was in return for David's promise made with an oath. God swears by his Holy One, as a father who swears honestly by the welfare of his true-born and beloved son. "In the same way," he says, "I too have sworn by my Holy One, that is, upon my Holy One, that I will not lie to David." What did the oath contain? "His seed," he says, "will remain forever." This comes first, and it is the first promise, the one about the seed. Of this it was said above, "And I will establish his seed forever and ever," which pointed to the succession of Christ. The second promise is about the throne already mentioned, so he adds, "And his throne will be like the sun before me, and like the moon established forever." He says, then, that the seed, meaning the word of Christ sown far and wide, or his people and Church, will never be destroyed or fail, and that his throne will last forever. Or in Symmachus's version: "Like the moon it will remain firmly established forever." So too will Christ's throne in the Church be. But perhaps the text, by first saying "Once for all I have sworn by my Holy One" and then adding "His seed will remain forever," foretells that the seed of his Holy One will prevail forever. In that case the seed of God's Holy One, that is, of God's Only-begotten, is the teaching he sowed on earth, having himself become its sower, according to the parable he told, in which it is said, "The sower went out to sow," and so on. "And these things," he says, "will be so; they will come to pass and be confirmed. For their faithful witness is God, who dwells in heaven." What has actually been accomplished proves the truth of the word. For we see with our own eyes the seed and succession of David's horn, that is, of our Savior Jesus Christ. [Editor's note: For "will not break" (diapseusasthai), perhaps read diapseusesthai.]

We also see the heavenly seed of the gospel teaching, sown [?] on earth by the Holy One of God, his only-begotten Word, enduring through the ages. More than that, throughout the whole inhabited world, among all nations, in cities, villages, and lands, we see the throne set up in his Church filling the entire world. But suppose someone takes the throne not in this sense but in a Jewish way, thinking it means David's bodily kingdom. Then the prophecies will be shown to be false. For after the Jewish nation was carried captive to Babylon, no one sat on David's throne. From then until now it is about a thousand years since David's throne was dissolved, when his kingdom was overthrown and his line of succession came to an end. That is why the following verses of the psalm lament these very things. They plainly signify the overthrow of the bodily throne and show that, as far as the visible throne and the bodily succession of David's kingdom are concerned, the opposite of the promises came about. These things also had to be included in the prophecy about Christ rather than passed over in silence, so that we might learn this: when the time of the things prophesied arrived, the visible things the Jews held to would be wholly done away with, and God's promise would be fulfilled in other outcomes, understood in a way worthy of God. "But you have rejected and scorned him; you have put off your anointed one. You have overturned the covenant of your servant; you have profaned his sanctuary to the ground. You have torn down all his walls; you have turned his strongholds into terror. All who passed along the road plundered him; he has become a reproach to his neighbors. You have raised the right hand of his oppressors; you have made all his enemies rejoice. You have turned back the help of his sword, and you have not supported him in battle. You have stripped him of his purity; you have hurled his throne to the ground. You have cut short the days of his time; you have poured shame over him." Pause. These words have been shown to apply to David's more bodily line of succession and to his bodily kingdom, which was overthrown at the time when the Jewish people were taken captive to Babylon. From then on the anointed one, that is, the visible king of David's line, has been lacking. The throne of his kingdom was hurled down, and everything else foretold was fulfilled. Over all this the text laments in the person of the Jewish nation, as though God had promised one thing and something else had happened. We ought to pay attention to this point. Since God does not lie, his words must prove true. And if they do not prove true of David's visible kingdom, it is time to understand the promises in another way. What that way is, the divine Spirit itself taught in the earlier verses, where it said: "Your truth will be prepared in heaven"; and again, "The heavens will praise your wonders, O Lord, and your truth in the assembly of the saints"; and again, "You are mighty, O Lord, and your truth is all around you"; and again, "Mercy and truth will go before your face." For all these

[?]…serve to show that God's promises do not prove false but are fulfilled, for reasons that he knows. For "in the heavens [?]," it says, "your truth will be prepared," clearly showing that God's promises are heavenly and divine. And the outcome of these words has been shown fulfilled through our Savior Jesus Christ, who came from the seed of David. For his kingdom and throne were not human, nor of this world. That is why he said before Pilate, "My kingdom is not of this world." And when Pilate asked him whether he was a king, he answered, "For this I was born." So if he was born for this, he will remain in it. The angel Gabriel, who announced his birth to the Virgin, bears witness to this word when he says to her: "And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus. He will be great, and will be called Son of the Most High. And God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end." He was born for this, then, yet his kingdom was not of this world. The kingdom of this world cannot last forever. It is not endless, and it does not stretch on without limit. But the kingdom promised to the seed of David was eternal and immortal: "And his throne," it says, "will be like the sun before me, and like the moon established forever, and the witness in heaven is faithful." The promises made to the Virgin about the one who would be born of her are of the same kind. In his message to her the angel promised, saying, "And God will give him the throne of David his father." What this throne was, and of what sort, he goes on to explain when he says, "And he will reign forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end." Such was the one promised to David by God with an oath. Making this plain, the angel interpreted his own oracle. First he said, "And God will give him the throne of David his father," and then he went on to add, "And he will reign forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end." These things were fulfilled in deed in our Savior Jesus, the Christ of God. Born of the seed of David, he holds power, gives laws and reigns over the whole inhabited world of humankind, not in a human way but by divine power. And his seed truly remains forever. This seed is either his succession, which fills the whole world through his apostles and disciples, or the rational seed of his heavenly teaching. And his throne shines like the sun, illuminating and lighting up the souls of [?]. All these things have reached their fulfillment and are still being fulfilled even now, in keeping with what God swore to David. But the promises were not fulfilled in a human way in David's successors, nor in the manner usual for human kings. Nor did they reach a bodily fulfillment even in our Savior himself, since his kingdom was not of this world and he did not sit on the visible throne of David. On the contrary, the opposite came about because of the suffering

that befell him. So it was fitting that the divine and prophetic Spirit should set forth these very things as well, rousing us to search out the outcome of God's oracles. Therefore it says: "But now you have rejected and scorned, O Lord, you have cast off your Christ; you have overturned the covenant of your servant," and what follows. With these words, which name the Christ explicitly, the passage shows that nothing escaped it, either of what would befall David's succession and his bodily kingdom or of what happened to the Christ of God in his passion. So it taught us to expect these things concerning his succession, his kingdom and the one who would come forth from the seed of David. In the verses above, a great many glorious things had been said about him. He would be exalted and would stretch out his hand over the sea and over the rivers. He would call upon God as Father and would in turn be proclaimed Firstborn by him. He would be the highest of kings and would have a faithful covenant, a seed that endures forever and ever, and a throne that lasts as the days of heaven, like the sun and the moon. Yet the divine Spirit also foretells that these gloomy things will befall him. It must prophesy and teach these things in advance as well, so that when events turn out as the words said, concerning both the Christ of God and David's succession, those who had long ago received from their forebears that these things would happen might not be troubled. They would know well that both the gloomy and the happier things had been prophesied concerning him. Indeed, the same passage foretells opposite things concerning one and the same person, and we have received these things in the events themselves. At the time of our Savior's passion the gloomier things were fulfilled in him, while in the time that followed, the promises of better things were in turn brought to completion in him in deed. What befell him in the passion was precisely shown by the words, "But you have rejected and scorned, you have cast off your Christ." Instead of this Aquila says, "You have broken faith with your anointed," and Symmachus, "You were enraged against your Christ." At that time the terms of his covenant with the apostles were also scattered, when they even denied him. And his sanctuary, that is, the body taken from the holy Virgin, was profaned to the ground. Then God also took away all his hedges, namely the angels who fenced him round, guarding and attending him like a bodyguard. He took away his strongholds as well. These were his apostles and disciples, who fell into such cowardice that they denied him, abandoned him and fled. Then too he became a reproach to his neighbors, and the right hand of those who afflicted him was exalted. All the rest was also fulfilled at that time in the one from the seed of David. Otherwise one could not apply these words to David himself, or show that the present passage was fulfilled in him, any more than one could do so with the more solemn and happier things contained in God's promises. David's throne did not light up the whole inhabited world, shining on it like the sun. It did not endure like the moon, nor was it preserved forever and ever. Nor is there any reason

why that David should have been called God's Firstborn, since countless men better than he lived both before and after him. Nor does David appear to have stretched out his right hand over rivers and his left over the sea, or to have ruled from [?] to sea, or to have gained a kingdom that reached to the ends of the world. Nor can all this be applied to Solomon his son. He too is not recorded as ruling more than Judea, just like his father. He did not reign for more than forty years, just like his father. Nor did he live a blameless life. In fact his conduct was such that he was charged with a mania for women and with idolatry, and on that account God is said to have sent a Satan against him. Nor can the promises be referred to any of the others of David's seed and succession who reigned over the Jewish nation after Solomon. Rather, all of them together, the happier and the gloomy alike, are shown to have been fulfilled in one alone who is said to be of the seed of David, Jesus Christ our Savior. The divine Spirit foresaw this. It set out the inspired promises first, and then taught that we must expect the gloomier things to befall one and the same person. It did so especially because it foresaw the visible throne of the kingdom of David's whole succession being overthrown. Those of David's seed who reigned lasted only until the people were taken captive to Babylon. They did not reign over the whole Jewish nation, but only over three tribes, and not even over all of these. The whole period of their rule comes to about four hundred years only. After that, Jeconiah being the last of David's succession, no other king of the Jews from the seed of David is recorded. In this way too, then, the oracles of the divine Spirit before us were fulfilled, in which it is said: "But now you have rejected and scorned, and have cast off your Christ. You have overturned the covenant of your servant, you have profaned his sanctuary to the ground," and the words that follow. Some of God's promises to David outlined good and great hopes for David's seed, while what befell his succession was entirely the opposite, and the throne of his human kingdom had been dissolved and had ceased from the time of Jeconiah. Since this was so, the prophetic Spirit, having foreseen these things, fittingly urges us to search for the truth of God's words. It teaches us to seek and learn from God himself, asking him and saying: "Where are your ancient mercies, O Lord, which you swore to David?" For the succession of his visible and human kingdom had been dissolved, overthrown long before. And Jesus the Christ, who was born of his seed and was expected to be the heir of the promises made to David, did not acquire a visible or human kingdom. On the contrary, he suffered everything opposite to what people had expected, enduring all things, even to death [?]. These are the things

that the divine Spirit proclaimed by its power of foreknowledge. For this reason it fittingly teaches us to ask and inquire, saying, "Where are your ancient mercies, O Lord," and what follows. After this it adds: "How long, O Lord, will you turn away? Forever? Will your anger burn like fire? Remember what my substance is. Surely you did not create all the sons of men in vain? Who is the man who will live and not see death, who will rescue his soul from the hand of Hades? Interlude." Instead of "will you turn away," Aquila says, "How long, O Lord, will you hide yourself unto victory?" and Symmachus, "Until when, O Lord, will you hide yourself forever?" It seems to me that the passage hints at the unspeakable wrath that came upon David's more bodily kingdom and upon the whole Jewish nation. For since events turned out contrary to the promises, at least as far as the obvious expectation went, the God who had made the good promises to David was being publicly called into question [?]. Therefore the passage entreats him not to prolong the anger that had come upon them, but to let the gloomy things pass quickly and the promises of God come to pass. Then it speaks in the person of human weakness: "Remember what my substance is," and so on. The prophetic word teaches the people to say this so that they may entreat God and implore him to end his anger against the nation, to stop hiding himself, and to deign at last to grant to men what was promised to David. "Human nature," it says, "is weak and poor, yet it has been counted worthy of the highest honor with you. For you did not create the sons of men in vain; you fashioned them after your own image. So that your creature and your image may not perish through the wrath that has come and the postponement of what was promised, hasten to restore what has turned gloomy and to heal what has fallen sick by fulfilling the good promises. If men had been created in vain, like the irrational animals on earth, there would have been no need to promise them anything great. But since the oaths sworn to David announce such good news to men in advance, they make it plain to everyone that you did not create the sons of men in vain. Since, then, human nature has been counted worthy of such honor with you, I rightly say, 'Remember what my substance is'; and remember that you did not create the sons of men in vain. I ask you to remember this as well: there is no man who does not taste death. No one is able to rescue his own soul from death, nor does he even obtain this benefit. Those of the Jewish nation may have sinned so greatly that the promises made to David were turned into their opposite against them, and the succession from his seed was dissolved together with the throne of the kingdom. Your Christ himself may have suffered at their hands the things your words prophesied in advance would happen to him. Even so, we ask you not to turn away forever, and not to let your anger burn like fire.

Remember what my substance is, mine who intercede for them, and how weak men are, who have been given a mortal nature enslaved to death. Remember yourself as well, for you did not create the sons of men in vain but for the great hopes that are with you. Now that these things have been called to mind, we entreat you at last to send down to us the one who rescues even from death and calls back from Hades. Stop turning yourself away from us. Put an end to the anger that has come like fire upon your people, and accomplish in deed the promises you swore to David." "Where are your ancient mercies, O Lord, which you swore to David in your truth?" "Since you did not create all the sons of men in vain," it says, "but they are honored by you, and yet they cannot rescue themselves from death, I beg and implore you to make haste and show us the outcome of your good promises, brought to pass in your Christ even after the overthrow of David's kingdom. I ask you to hasten before the human race suffers utter collapse. For who among men is able to rescue himself from the hand of Hades, except the one alone who rescued first himself and then all who have believed in him from the gates of death? Even if he is to suffer the things the prophecy set out in the words beginning 'But now you have rejected and scorned, you have cast off your Christ,' he will still obtain your promises to David. For your mercies, O Lord, and your truth endure forever, and not one word of your promises will fail. Now that I have called to mind the gloomy things that are to happen, I say, 'Where are your ancient mercies, O Lord, which you swore to David in your truth?' Yet I am not unaware that you swore in truth. That is why, at the very beginning of the whole psalm, I looked toward the happy end and said: 'I will sing of the mercies of the Lord forever; from generation to generation I will proclaim your truth with my mouth.' And again I said: 'Mercy will be built up forever; in heaven your truth will be prepared.' So I ask to learn where those very mercies of yours are, O Lord, where they lie hidden and when they will come. Indeed, I entreat you, let them hasten now and come, and take hold of our weakness. For if you do not show your ancient mercies, which you did not merely promise but swore to David in your truth, no hope of salvation remains for men." So just as the word proved true in the gloomy things, and they all happened and came to pass, it follows that the better promises will not prove false either. Through them the word announced to us the good news of David's eternal seed and of his throne shining like the light of the sun over the whole inhabited world of men. For the ancients, then, these things were the object of prayer, awaited by those who had studied the prophetic utterances. But we see them fulfilled in actual deeds, in what has been accomplished in our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ.

"Remember, O Lord, the reproach of your servants, the reproach of many nations which I bore in my bosom, with which your enemies reproached, O Lord, with which they reproached the exchange of your Christ. Blessed be the Lord forever. So be it, so be it." It seems to me that the sense changes after the interlude just mentioned. In the preceding verses the divine Spirit prayed for the people. With the words "Where are your ancient mercies, O Lord?" it calls forth God's promises, and asks that the happier things which God swore to David in his truth should at last come to pass. Then it entreats him to remember the reproach of his servants. Here it is left unsaid that the gloomy things foretold have already been carried out in deed, and that many enemies and nations are pressing upon God's servants and reproaching them because of what has happened. So it sends up its prayer for them, saying, "Remember, O Lord, the reproach of your servants." Instead of "which I bore in my bosom, of many nations," Aquila rendered it more clearly: "as I carry in my bosom all the injustices of the peoples." Symmachus has "I carried in my bosom all the nations." Those reproached, then, are God's servants, and so he said, "Remember, O Lord, the reproach of your servants." Those who reproach are God's enemies, and so he goes on to add, "with which your enemies reproached, O Lord, with which they reproached the exchange of your Christ." The one who says this to God would be the saving Word, who carries the injustices of the peoples in his own bosom. You will understand what is meant by "the exchange of Christ" from Symmachus's rendering, which reads, "with which they reproached the footsteps of your Christ." In this way the passage hinted at the journey of the Christ of God, his road through the passion, and the footsteps of the dispensation of his human life. For these are the things God's enemies are accustomed to reproach us with. But the speaker trusts that he has been heard and will obtain what he prays for, and he hopes that God's promises to David will soon be fulfilled [?]. So he seals the end of the whole psalm with thanksgiving and blessing, saying, "Blessed be the Lord forever." He teaches us to respond with "So be it, so be it," which is the Hebrew expression "Amen, amen." As for the interlude, which is inserted several times in the psalm, the following should be said. God's first promise, spoken at the beginning, contained "I have made a covenant" and "I have sworn to David" and what follows. Then the interlude was placed, and the passage changes the speaker and adds: "The heavens will praise your wonders." Again, a promise was spoken in the person of God, from "I have laid help upon one who is mighty" up to "and the witness in heaven is faithful." Then the interlude is inserted once more, and the passage changes its sense and says: "But you have rejected and scorned, you have cast off your Christ." Then, having gone through the gloomier things,

Again it inserts the diapsalma (the pause) and changes the teaching, saying, “How long, Lord, will you turn away to the end?” And after sending up the prayer, it again uses the diapsalma in between and adds, “Where are your mercies of old, Lord?” Here it changes its train of thought and recalls God’s first promises, those spoken in the beginning. So the diapsalmata have a meaning too: they signal a change of thought or a change of speaker. You can say this of all the psalms in which the diapsalma occurs. It marks either a change of speaker or a change of thought, and sometimes also a change in the Hebrew melody. Aquila, however, never uses diapsalma. In every place he regularly translates it instead as “always.” We ought to be aware of this. The seal on the whole discourse is “Blessed be the Lord forever. So be it, so be it.” Where it says “So be it, so be it,” Aquila has “Faithfully, faithfully,” while Symmachus, following the Hebrew, has “Amen and amen.”

A PRAYER OF MOSES. PSALM 89. “Lord, you have become our refuge in generation after generation. Before the mountains were established and the earth and the world were formed, from everlasting to everlasting you are, O God.” The passage teaches a doctrine. It teaches that the divine is enduring and eternal. For the one who said, “I am God, the One who is,” always is and is always the same. He abides into the infinite ages and never changes his own nature. We, however, pass into life at our appointed times and flow away like a torrent. As Solomon says, “A generation goes, and a generation comes,” and human affairs never stay the same but change, now one way and now another. But the Lord, who endures through every generation, becomes the refuge of those who hope in him. Before the flood Enoch, and anyone else of that generation, had him as a refuge. When the human race was being destroyed in the flood, Noah in turn took him as his refuge and no one else. After that came Lot, out of the generation of the Sodomites, and Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, each in his own generation. So too did Joseph in his generation, and Moses in yet another. In short, in every generation those who have hoped in him have had the ever-existing Lord as their refuge. By these words the passage urges us to hope in no one other than God. We should flee to him for refuge at every season, every day and every hour, in each thing we do, and above all in times of crisis. Those caught in a storm need shelter. Those tossed by the waves at sea need a harbor. Those pursued by enemies and foes, or even by wild beasts, need a wall to take refuge behind. In this present life the man of God wrestles with all of these. So he must be taught to regard his own Lord as his refuge and his wall and his harbor of safety. Then, whether we are driven out by enemies in times of persecution, or are attacked by invisible foes, or are plotted against by those trying to

entrap us, we may soberly flee for refuge to our Lord and God, who in generation after generation becomes the champion and the shield of those who call on him. Instead of “in generation after generation,” Symmachus translated more clearly, “in each generation.” And for “Before the mountains came to be and the earth and the world were formed,” Aquila and Symmachus say together, in agreement, “Before mountains were born and the earth and the world were brought forth in labor.” It seems to me that the Hebrew wording gives an account of nature. It teaches by these words that the mountains in the earth did not exist alongside it from the beginning but sprang up like things being born. That is why it says, “Before the mountains came to be,” or, “Before mountains were born.” Perhaps, when the mountains were born and thrust out from the earth like infants, they did not at once take on the size they have now. Rather, when they had just been born and brought forth, they were small and tiny like newborn babies, and over a long age they gained growth and size. In fact, some natural philosophers say that the mountains are growing even to this day, and that rocks become larger than they were through very small additions over long periods, which escape our notice. And the translators, following the Hebrew, have said that the earth and the world were brought forth in labor. Perhaps, then, we should understand something about the earth similar to what we said of the mountains. Did it come forth from another element, first being in labor like pregnant women who endure birth pangs as they give birth? Some natural philosophers hold that water came into being as the first element, and that the remaining elements then came into being from water and the moist substance.
