If their account holds, one might say that this too is signified in the present Scripture. It shows that there was a time when the earth was inside another element and could not be seen, because it was being conceived and carried in the womb within the nature of the moist substance. That is why the account of the world’s making says, “The earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss.” Later, though, as if it had been born, it came forth from the substance of the waters. This did not happen without divine power and a higher necessity laid upon it, and that necessity was the will of the Creator. With pregnant women, force and necessity come upon them, and what is in the womb is brought forth when the appointed time of delivery arrives, at which they give birth in labor. In the same way, by the power and wisdom of the Creator of all things, the waters brought forth the earth and the inhabited world of humankind. This was fulfilled when God said, “Let the water under heaven be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear. And it was so.” Picture in your mind the earth long ago, hidden within the waters, dissolved like mud and mixed into the mass of the waters, so that it could not be seen and was invisible. That is why it is said, “The earth was invisible and unformed.” Then later, by the will of God, it was gathered together, first compressed and solidified, and after that suddenly thrust up

so that it came forth into the light and rose up into the clear air. See how, at that moment, it seemed no different from things born from the womb. When it was thrust out and emerged from the waters, it was like something being born and brought forth. But before the birth, while it was being compacted and solidified within the waters, settling and sinking down under its own weight like mud, it was at that time being conceived. Later, as though after labor, it was born and became the dwelling place of the living creatures on earth. “But before these things happened in this way, and before the world was constituted at all, you yourself are, O God,” it says. It rightly says not “you were” but “you are.” For the same one was, and is, and will be. Or rather, you are the same and always exist, and you yourself are, as the theological saying puts it: “But you are the same, and your years will not fail.” It is not right to say of him “you were,” or “he was,” or “he will be.” Some of these indicate past time and others future time, and none of them fits the divine name. Only “always being” fits it. That is why it is said here so very precisely, “From everlasting to everlasting you are, O God,” and elsewhere, “But you are the same, and your years will not fail.” Note that in “Lord, you have become our refuge,” the word “Lord” is not written among the Hebrews with the four-letter name. It is written with the common, ordinary letters that are also used in addressing human beings, as when we call a human master “lord.” Accordingly, here too “Adonai” has been translated “Lord.” The four-letter name, which signifies the ineffable divinity of God, does not appear in the present text. Instead the word for “master” is used, and very fittingly, to show that he cares and takes thought for his own servants, whose refuge he also is. Consider too whether the present teaching may refer to God the Word. The wording here, “Before the mountains came to be and the earth and the world were formed, you are, O God,” is not far from what is said in Solomon in the person of Wisdom: “Before the mountains were established, before all the hills, he begets me.” These words seem to hint at the incorporeal and angelic powers. The Word of God and the Wisdom of God exists before them, as this Wisdom herself teaches. “Do not turn man back to humiliation. And you said, ‘Turn back, you children of men.’ For a thousand years in your eyes are like yesterday, which has gone by, and like a watch in the night. Things of nought shall their years be. In the morning may it pass away like grass. In the morning may it flower and pass away. In the evening may it fall, be hardened and withered. For we have failed in your anger, and in your wrath we have been troubled.” The title teaches that these words are Moses’. So, as I try to fit them to the person of Moses, I ask whether through them the passage may be handing down a hidden prophecy of Moses. For I do not think it is a psalm. Rather, as the title teaches, it is a prayer of

Moses. I ask, then, at what time Moses used this prayer. Is it suited to himself, or rather to the people? And should it be applied to the generation of his own time and the people who were with him, or to those who came after them? I think everyone would agree that the present words should not be referred to Moses himself. How could Moses, the man of God, say about himself, “For we have failed in your anger,” or, as Symmachus has it, “For we were consumed in your anger, and in your wrath we have been troubled. You have set our iniquities before you”? Or again, “Our days have failed in your anger”? Or again, “Who knows the might of your anger, and your wrath, out of fear of you?” That these words could not be referred to Moses is clear not only because everything is said about the anger of God, but also because the words are in the plural. Someone might reasonably refer them, then, to the people who were with him in the wilderness. But the passage does not allow us to understand that either. For what does it say? “In the morning may it pass away like grass. In the morning may it flower and pass away. In the evening may it fall, be hardened and withered. For we have failed in your anger.” So it does not say that they failed in the morning. It says, “In the morning may it pass away like grass.” Again, it does not say, “In the morning may it fall,” or, “In the morning may it be hardened and withered.” Rather, the passage says, “May it flower in the morning and pass away.” The falling, hardening and withering, it says, will happen in the evening, for it says, “In the evening may it fall, be hardened and withered.” And “For we have failed in your anger” is said of what will happen in the evening. It is then, it says, that we failed. For in the morning there was flowering, grass and a passing kind of beauty. But in the evening the grass was hardened and the flower withered and failed. Such is the wording of the present prayer. But its meaning does not allow us to tie what is said to the times of Moses and his generation. For it was not evening then, nor the last days of the people of the circumcision. It was their beginning, and the light from God had then dawned on them for the first time. That is why the state of affairs at that time, and God’s visitation of them, was called “morning.” Evening came upon them at the consummation of the age, when the Word who had dawned on them back then set for them. At that earlier time he had dawned and made morning for them, when their affairs were flourishing. But it did not abide in the truth. Having flowered, it passed away and ran by like a shadow. That is why it says, “In the morning may it pass away like grass.” After the death of Moses, in the times that followed, they advanced again to growth and greater stature. Even so, they did not last but passed away. That is why it says a second time, “In the morning may it flower and pass away.” Their final state after these things is signified by this: “In the evening may it fall, and be hardened and withered.” For what

is growing old and aging is close to vanishing away. This is what happened to them when the Sun of righteousness set upon them, as the prophecy says: “And the sun will set upon the prophets who lead my people astray.” Of the righteous it was said, “The Sun of righteousness will rise for those who fear him.” In the same way it is said of the ungodly, “The sun will set upon these.” And again elsewhere: “And the sun will set at noon, and the moon will not give its light.” So it was at the consummation of the age, after the coming of our Savior, when evening came upon them and the light of truth had truly set for them. Then their falling away and rejection reached their end, and the present oracle was fulfilled, which said, “In the evening may it fall, be hardened and withered. For we have failed in your anger, and in your wrath we have been troubled.” It seems to me that in these words Moses composed a prayer suited to the condition of the people after the coming of our Savior. Being a prophet, he foresaw by divine foreknowledge the outcome of their rejection and their final falling away, and he prescribed for them a saving and healing remedy. He handed down the present prayer in secret, it seems, apart from the rest of his writings, to those able to keep secret things among themselves. Among them, it seems, it was guarded privately and unnoticed for a long time. Later, however, it had to be included in the book of Psalms, so that over the long course of time it would not perish, unknown to most people and neglected. So that it might be preserved and remain known to all, it was inserted into the book of Psalms, though it is not a psalm. In fact it contains nothing of a psalm, since a psalm belongs to gladness. The present prayer instead speaks of the anger and wrath of God and of other gloomy things. It seeks to appease God on behalf of those who have fallen away. Through this prayer Moses teaches the people who fell away from God after the coming of our Savior to say these words of appeasement. And it seems to me that it is not without purpose that the present prayer of Moses has been placed after Psalm 88, with its prophecies about the seed of David and the throne promised to him. The passage is hinting, through a deeper contemplation, that the Jewish nation would fall away and be rejected after the coming of the one who was to come forth from the seed of David. The outcome of events has indeed confirmed this. Yet Moses hands down a prayer to them, fitting the words of the prayer by prophetic power to the person of the people who fell away and were cast off. So when it says, “Do not turn man back to humiliation. And you said, ‘Turn back, you children of men,’” it seems to me to teach them to pray in this sense: “O Lord, you have been our refuge through the ages and in each generation. First, when we were in Egypt and oppressed by Pharaoh and the Egyptians, you became our refuge. Again, in the wilderness, when we were attacked, now by Amalek and now by the Canaanite, we had you as our refuge. And after we entered the land of promise and came under foreigners, and many times afterward under our kings, and finally in the captivity in Babylon, we had you

as our refuge. So now too we beg to receive the same from you and to have you as our refuge. That is why we pray, ‘Do not turn man back to humiliation’—that is, do not turn us back to utter downfall and humiliation. For in your love for humankind you said, and sent out a proclamation to all people, ‘Turn back, you children of men.’ Your love for humankind has called all the nations and all the children of men in advance. You command those who long ago turned away from you and were enslaved to demons and evil spirits to turn back to you. If so, do not turn away from us either. Do not leave those who long ago became your own to fall into utter desolation. We flowered for a little while, then rushed past like a torrent. Our thousand years, in which we flourished, have passed away like yesterday, which has gone by.” Having reached this point, I ask in what sense these thousand years are spoken of. If it is said to glorify God and to depict his eternal life, I think the statement contains nothing magnificent. For I consider that not even the whole age, nor the whole time stretching from the first creation of the world to the consummation, amounts to so much as an instant—I do not say of a day, but even of the briefest hour—compared with the life of God, which has no beginning and is unbegotten. He exists before all ages and before every reckoning that can be conceived and stretched out to infinity, and he endures beyond the boundless and endless ages that follow. So the present prayer seems to me to suggest another meaning, when it teaches the people to say, “For a thousand years in your eyes are like yesterday, which has gone by, and like a watch in the night.” The thousand years, then, were the glories of Jerusalem, when their whole nation flourished and bloomed as in daytime and in the light. For the worship bound to that place stood and lasted for only a thousand years, which are counted in this way. From the first building of the temple in the times of Solomon until the siege by the Babylonians, 436 [?] years are reckoned. After this, when the place had been reduced to desolation, Jeshua and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel restored the house in the second year of Darius the Persian. From then until the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, [?] years are reckoned, so that the total is [?]. After they plotted against our Savior, the city remained storm-tossed and unsettled for another 40 years. After that, utter destruction overtook them in the final siege, carried out by the Romans under the emperors Titus and Vespasian. These, then, were the thousand years of which it is said, “like yesterday, which has gone by.” Those who seek to appease God through this prayer lament these years as gone by and no longer existing. They also say that these thousand years have passed away like a watch in the night. For the law of Moses was a lamp shining for them in the night, and the prophets after Moses were lamps, or stars, shining in the night, for the light

of the sun, that is, of the saving Word, had not yet shone its own day and noon on all the nations. A “watch of the night” is the name for a period of the night. You will understand this from the Gospel, where it says, “In the fourth watch of the night Jesus came walking on the sea,” and again, “If the master of the house had known in what watch the thief was coming.” So the thousand years are shown to be not only like a day that has gone by and no longer exists, but also like a brief portion of the night. We should not think of a whole night, but of some part of it, during which they kept the watch of the law’s bodily worship. Next after these words it says, “Things of nought shall their years be.” I think the meaning of these words too is something like this: their years will be things of nought. For their years will no longer be honored, nor earnest and necessary. They will be despised and reckoned as nothing. How their years will come to be reckoned as nothing, he makes clear by saying next, “In the morning may it pass away like grass. In the morning may it flower and pass away. In the evening may it fall, be hardened and withered. For we have failed in your anger.” Long ago, it says, when our affairs had their beginnings and we were in the morning, we became like grass. But when that generation passed away, the grass passed away. After that we flowered and had something greater and more than grass, so that a flower too was found in us. And this flower too passed away. But in the last times, when the light had set for us entirely and evening overtook us, we fell, hardened and withered. We have suffered these things “because we have failed in your anger, and in your wrath we have been troubled.” The wording can also be read in another sense, as giving an account of nature. Human nature sprouts like tender grass in youth, and afterward flowers in the prime of life. Then later, on the threshold of old age, it falls, and it does so only by first hardening in old age and then withering completely. On this reading, “evening” signifies the last part of human life. “You have set our iniquities before you, our age in the light of your face. For all our days have failed, and in your anger we have failed.” Symmachus has: “You have placed our iniquities right in front of you, our negligences to be seen by your face. For all our days have fled away; in your wrath we have been consumed.” It is fitting for the people of the circumcision to say these things in their present condition. For now all their former days have truly failed, since evening has overtaken them and they have failed in the anger of God. Long ago he passed over and overlooked their iniquities. But after the plot against the Savior, this word was fulfilled against them: “I will no longer forgive your sins.” That is why it says, “You have set our iniquities before you,” and, “our age in the light of your face.” In place of this, more clearly

[?] Symmachus rendered it, saying: "Our negligences appear before your face." "Our years were spent in study like a spider. The days of our years—in them are seventy years; and if in strength, eighty years, and the greater part of them is toil and pain." Here it is fitting to set alongside this the prophecy of Isaiah, in which he says: "They have broken asps' eggs, and they weave a spider's web." The prophet foretold these things with reference to the condition of the people after the coming of our Saviour. At that time their rulers, like a bird laying eggs, bring forth offspring of such a kind that they resemble the brood of an asp, because of the venom of blasphemy against our Saviour which they inject, and of their other unbelief toward him. Long ago, then, they wove tunics for the high priest and holy vestments. But now the prophetic word has likened all their weaving to a spider's web, including the teaching built up by speech which they put forth by intertwining and weaving together the divine Scriptures. That is why it says: "They weave a spider's web." And the present psalm, which contains the confession made in their person, says: "Our years were spent in study like a spider." For it has plainly likened to the works of a spider their studies of the Scriptures, in which they wear themselves out, and their secondary traditions, by which they suppose they produce fabrics of teaching. They also say that their only life is this temporary one, which is completed in seventy or eighty years. And they say this because they despair of the eternal life to come that is promised to those who love God. "For meekness has come upon us, and we shall be chastened. Who knows the might of your wrath, and out of fear of you to number your anger? So make known your right hand, and those instructed in heart in wisdom." In place of "For meekness has come upon us, and we shall be chastened," Symmachus says: "For cut off suddenly, we fly away." The present passage also keeps to the sense indicated before. For our years, it says, the years of this temporary life, extend to the number of seventy and eighty; and this is our hope, and after it no other will await us. For when we are cut off suddenly at our end, we fly away; and what will await us after that, who knows? For who can interpret, or even know accurately and declare, what kind of wrath it is that will afterward overtake sinners? Therefore it says: "Who knows the might of your wrath, and out of fear of you your anger?" And who is able to number your right hand? "But you, O God, make known your right hand to us even now, so that we may be able both to understand it and to count up its powers." The sacred words have often taught that the right hand of God is his Christ. So those indicated here are taught, after their confession, to pray to be counted worthy, first, of the meekness of God, so that they may be chastened by it; and then of his right hand, that is, of the knowledge of his Christ

and of his marvellous powers, so that they may become better through knowing these things, and so that, once their minds are instructed, they may share in the wisdom of God. For Christ is the power of God and [?] of God

"Return, O Lord—how long?—and be comforted concerning your servants. We were filled in the morning with your mercy, and we rejoiced and were glad in all our days. We were glad in return for the days in which you humbled us, the years in which we saw evils. And look upon your servants and upon your works, and guide their sons. And let the brightness of the Lord our God be upon us; and direct the works of our hands upon us, and direct the work of our hands." After the confession conveyed in the preceding verses, Moses fittingly goes on to teach a prayer to those of Israel who fell away after the coming of our Saviour, so that in their prayer they may say these words together with those already given. Symmachus has expressed their meaning more clearly, rendering them in this way: "Turn back, Lord—how long? Be comforted on behalf of your servants. Satisfy us with your early-morning mercy, so that we may sing praise [?] and be glad in all our days. Gladden us for all the days in which you afflicted us, the years in which we saw evils. Let your works appear to your servants, and your majesty upon our children; and let the beauty of the Lord our God be above us. Make the works of our hands firm for us, and bring the doing of our hands to completion." Through these words he teaches them to ask to obtain the early-morning mercy, so that they may be counted worthy of the dawning of the Saviour. For the morning mercy is the mercy of Christ, which has dawned upon all people. For just as long ago morning came to the former people at the visitation they were granted while they lived in Egypt, so in the last days the morning mercy shone forth upon all the nations through the saving dawn. Those indicated are taught to ask in prayer to be counted worthy of this dawn, and also to say with the rest: "And let the brightness of the Lord our God be upon us," and "Let your works appear to your servants, and the beauty of the Lord our God." In this way they too may be counted worthy of the saving appearance of God, and of his divine glory, and of the beauty of which it is said, "Fair in beauty beyond the sons of men," and of all the other good things that are conceived in the Christ of God. "He who dwells in the help of the Most High will lodge in the shelter of the God of heaven." The psalm has no title. But perhaps it is not [?] either, but rather a prophecy containing deeper words about Christ and those who are perfected in him? The present words are very much at odds in their sequence with the psalm above. For that psalm foretold, through the prayer of Moses, the final rejection of the Jewish nation,

while the present one contains the contests and trials of one who is being perfected according to the Lord. It also prophesies the temptation of our Saviour himself in the wilderness, when he was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil, and his victory over all. What, then, does the prophetic word say? The former people, lamenting through the preceding prayer of Moses, confesses, saying, "For we have failed in your wrath," and the rest that was made clear by the words given there. But the people that was to be established for God through Christ after them, trusting in the help of the Most High and always dwelling in it, remains untroubled and unshaken. Lodging under God's shelter, it will pay heed to none of its temptations, but at each one it will say to the Lord: "You are my helper and my refuge, my God; I will hope in him." In place of "He who dwells in the help of the Most High," Symmachus rendered "He who dwells under the shelter of the Most High," while Aquila and the fifth edition gave "He who sits in the secret place of the Most High." The phrase signifies the steady and fearless mind of the one who contends according to God in Christ, and it signifies that the Most High himself, as his helper, dwells within him and is seated as it were in the secret place of his soul. Again, in place of "He will lodge in the shelter of the God of heaven," Aquila said "He will lodge in the shelter of the Sufficient One," and Symmachus "spending the night under the shadow of the Sufficient One." The Holy Spirit spoke these words as a kind of prelude. What follows it addresses to him, directing the whole discourse to his person. This is either the one who contends for Christ and conquers, or else the human being understood in the Saviour, whom the pre-existent Word of God used like an instrument. For he too dwelt in the help of the Most High and lodged under the shelter of the Word of God who dwelt in him and overshadowed him with his divinity. He had as his helper and refuge and hope the power of the Word of God that filled him. And just as his human instrument was called the body of Christ, so his people too has been called the body of Christ by the holy Apostle, who says: "Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually." It is fitting, therefore, that what is said in the present passage, since it concerns the body of Christ, may be referred both to the humanity of our Saviour and to the one who is perfected in him. After saying these things, the word goes on to describe all that God will provide for the one who dwells in the help of the Most High and lodges under God's shelter, and who says to the Lord: "You are my helper and my refuge, my God, and I will hope in him." It lists in the following verses what will happen to him: "For he will rescue me from the snare of hunters, from a troubling word. With his shoulders he will overshadow you, and under his wings

you will hope. His truth will surround you with a shield. You will not fear the terror by night, the arrow that flies by day, the thing that walks about in darkness, mishap and the noonday demon. A thousand will fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand, but it will not come near you. Only with your eyes will you observe, and you will see the recompense of sinners. For you are my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge." The word foretells that many attacks will rise up against the one who is prophesied. This was a rare and wonderful person, sitting in the secret place of the Most High, lodging under the shadow of the Sufficient One, and saying to the Lord: "My helper and my refuge, my God, and I will hope in him"; or, according to Aquila, "My God, I will trust in him"; or, according to Symmachus, "My God, and I will take courage in him." Against this man, then, devoted to the help of God in the way described, there rose up plots and schemes of countless foes campaigning against him. They were called snares of hunters, and troubling words, and terror by night, and the arrow flying by day, and the thing walking about in darkness, and the mishap of the noonday demon. Besides all these there were thousands and ten thousands, the thousands occupying his left side and the ten thousands his right. For these plotted against his right side, as being the stronger and mightier part. But none of all these touches the one of whom the word prophesies. Moreover, besides these things, he is said to tread not only upon snakes and scorpions, for these were small things, but upon the asp and the basilisk, and to trample the lion and the dragon, which are the most kingly and princely of beasts and reptiles. I think, then, that these signify the rulers of this age and the invisible ruling powers. Yet the one who is prophesied is said to trample all of them at once. "For you will tread," it says, "upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon." Who, then, could be such a person that these things can fit him? Against his right side ten thousands of enemies campaign, and thousands against the other side, yet they dare not touch him but fall down before him. Come, let us consider. I say that in one sense these things refer to the man perfected in Christ, such as Paul was when he said, "I know a man in Christ," and to everyone who is able to say as he did: "Who will separate us from the love of God? Will tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword?" and again: "For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus." And whoever is able to add, "But in all these things we are more than conquerors," would be worthy to have the present words

spoken of him as well. For such a person, dwelling in the help of the Most High and lodging in God's shelter, will say to the Lord: "You are my helper and my refuge, O God, and I will hope in him." When he has said this with a perfect disposition, the divine Spirit declares to him that he has chosen a secure guardian and gained a good refuge in the Lord. For with such a helper, champion and protector, he will fear none of his enemies, since the Lord himself rescues him from them all. He will deliver him from the snare of hunters and from a troubling word, and he will overshadow him with his shoulders. All that is listed next will be referred to every man who is perfect in Christ, and also to the body of Christ, that is, to the choir of martyrs made up of perfect souls, or to his perfect Church, which he presented to himself without spot or wrinkle or any such thing. He who promised to build his Church upon the rock, so that the gates of Hades would not prevail against it, will himself be its guardian and sentinel, fencing it about [?] and making it secure, so that the gates of Hades do not prevail against it. Therefore to such a Church, and to such a choir of Christ's martyrs, which has no dwelling at all on earth but is able to say, "But our citizenship is in heaven," it will be said: "He who dwells in the help of the Most High will lodge in the shelter of the God of heaven." Then he himself will say to the Lord under whose shelter he chose to dwell: "You are my helper and my refuge, my God, and I will hope in him." When he has gained such a guardian and has enrolled himself under such a saviour and helper, the divine Spirit will tell him that he has found for himself a good portion, a strong wall and invincible armour: his own Lord. For with him he will live in safety and free from care, since he dwells in the help of the Most High and lodges in the shelter of the Sufficient One. "If ever, then," it says, "the hunters of human souls, unseen and invisible powers, secretly hide snares as is their custom and try to set them against you, they will gain nothing. For the Lord himself will rescue you from the snare of hunters: 'The snare was broken, and we were rescued.' And if they try to throw you into confusion with words, releasing the venom of their impiety through their tongues, the Lord will again keep his own man unharmed from these too." So that the blaze of human life and the scorching heat of wickedness may not flare up further and kindle evils against the athlete of piety, the word prophesies to him, saying: "With his shoulders he will overshadow you, and under his wings you will hope." And if hostile troops hurl fiery and deadly darts of false words opposed to the truth at the one described, he himself will keep quiet, obeying the divine law that says: "The Lord will fight for you, and you shall keep silent." [Phil. 3:20; [?]]

[?] And at the right moment it will be said to him: "His truth will surround you with a shield." For this truth of Christ's doctrines has great power and will fence in the one who has it, encircling him and clothing him with its own armour. So he will not fear when night comes on or darkness overtakes him, nor will he be troubled by fears or worry about the arrows sent by day. By night and darkness he means times of adversity, in which, he says, the one fenced about by the armour of truth will fear nothing. By day he means times of calm, fair weather and peace, in which our enemies are accustomed to send flying arrows against us from afar, namely their blasphemous and impious words. For in times of persecution they do not stand far off and shoot arrows. Instead they rush at us from close by and try to swallow us whole, as friends of the death that once prevailed and swallowed. But we, guarded by the armour described, will say: "If it had not been the Lord who was among us when men rose up against us, then they would have swallowed us alive." So neither by day nor by night will our enemies be able to do anything against us, because of the Lord who fights on our behalf. That is why it has been said: "You will not fear the terror by night, the arrow flying by day, the thing walking about in darkness." Nor shall we fear mishap and the noonday demon. And if thousands and ten thousands of enemies and foes, invisible or even visible, rise up against the people of Christ and against his Church, his power will bring all of them down together in a single moment, so that we see the vengeance with our very eyes. That is why it has been said: "Only with your eyes will you observe, and you will see the recompense of sinners." We ourselves have received the truth of this word from the interpretation itself [?], as from time to time we have observed the end of those who made war on the Church of God, and who were themselves warred down by God, immediately and before long. All these things, and those said after them, will be referred to the man in Christ and to everyone who is able to say: "I can do all things in Christ Jesus who strengthens me." This would be the choir of Christ, made up of the holy and perfect martyrs of God, who contend for the truth to the point of shedding blood and carry off the prizes of victory in God over their adversaries. The words will also fit the man of Christ, and the very sequence of the passage shows this. For the word says to a single person, "For he will rescue you from the snare of hunters and from a troubling word," and "With his shoulders he will overshadow you, and under his wings you will hope." To the same person it adds, "His truth will surround you with a shield," and "You will not fear the terror by night," and "A thousand will fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand, but it will not come near you." And to these it adds, "Only with your eyes will you observe, and you will see the recompense of sinners."

Having said all these things in the singular, as to one person, it then continues: "For you, Lord, are my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge." This shows most clearly that it was the Lord to whom all these things were said. For there was no change of person in between, so the word joined everything together in one sense, as addressed to one person. And it made clear who this was by explaining next: "For you, Lord, are my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge." For since you, O Lord, it says, in whom I have hoped, have made the Most High your refuge—that is, the supreme God, your own Father—for this reason neither a thousand nor ten thousand will approach you, nor the snares of hunters, nor anything else that has been listed. And since you, O Lord, are the hope of me who say these things, "you have made the Most High your refuge." That is why at the beginning I said of you, "He who dwells in the help of the Most High," or "He who sits in the secret place of the Most High." For in ineffable and secret places the Most High made you his assessor and the sharer of his throne, saying to you: "Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet." In these words "Most High" is to be understood as the supreme God of the universe, and "Lord" as the Son of God, who made the Most High his refuge. So it was fitting that Moses too, inspired by the same divine Spirit, taught in the Great Song: "When the Most High divided the nations, when he scattered the sons of Adam, he set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God. And his people Jacob became the Lord's portion, Israel the measured lot of his inheritance." In these words Moses too clearly called the unbegotten God "Most High," as the one who distributes the nations on earth among his own angels, and called the Son of God "Lord," as the one who received Israel from the Father. This same Lord, then, was also said in the present passage to dwell in the help of the Most High and to have made the Most High, that is, his own Father, his refuge. That is why it has been said to him: "For you, Lord, are my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge." Aquila and Symmachus, however, have set out their translations in a rather Jewish manner, because they were suspicious of the doctrine handed down to us concerning the Most High and the Lord. Aquila translated: "For you, Lord, are my hope; I have made your dwelling-place most high." Symmachus translated: "For you, O God, are my fearlessness; you have made your dwelling most high." Against them it should be observed, first, that the fifth edition agrees with the Seventy, for it too says: "For you, Lord, are my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge." Second, the Hebrew word, which contains Elion, means "the Most High." We find, for example, in Psalm 56 the words "I will cry to God the Most High," and there, in place of "the Most High," the Hebrew has Elion, just as in the present passage. So one must not force the truth and distort it. And indeed, if according to Aquila it was said to the Lord himself, "For you, Lord, are my hope; I have made your dwelling-place most high," or according to

…Symmachus: “For you, O Lord, are my freedom from fear; you have made your dwelling most high.” And if the passage is referred, as the children of the Jews might suppose, to the God of the universe, how is it that there follows next, according to Aquila: “Evil will not be brought to you, and plague will not come near in your shelter; for he will command his angels to guard you in all your ways. On their palms they will lift you, lest your foot stumble on a stone”; and how, according to Symmachus, after “You, O Lord, are my freedom from fear; you have made your dwelling most high,” is it added: “Evil will not prevail against you, nor will plague come near your tent. For he will give command to the angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways. On their hands they will bear you, so that you do not strike your foot against a stone”? For how would it not be the most impious thing of all for these words to be addressed to the God of the universe? Who is it that commands his angels concerning the God of the universe, that they should guard him in all his ways? Or how will they bear the God who is over all upon their hands, so that his foot may not strike against a stone? But you see that the passage does not allow these things to be referred to the person of the God who is over all, just as it does not allow this of the earlier words either, beginning from “For he will rescue you from the snare of the hunters, from a troubling word. With his shoulders he will overshadow you, and under his wings you will hope,” and what follows them. But if anyone takes these words of the Christ of God, who is here named Lord, as he is also named elsewhere, he would not miss the truth. For the Apostle too says, “One God, from whom are all things, and one Lord, through whom are all things”; and again, “One Lord,” he says, “one faith, one baptism; one God, who is over all and through all and in all.” And two Lords were plainly named by David as well, in the words, “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet.” Moses too, when he says, “The Lord rained sulfur and fire from the Lord on Sodom and Gomorrah,” would be of the same opinion; as also in the words where he said, “When the Most High divided the nations, … the Lord’s portion [?] became his people Jacob.”

…as many nights as days. For as he was about to go forward to the Gospel of the kingdom of God, before beginning his preaching and before his kindness toward human beings, he was led up against the powers that are hostile to the human race and at war with it, so that, having first fought them down and overthrown them, he might then go forward to the redemption and freedom of those who had long been oppressed. For it was necessary first of all to subdue and cast down from their tyranny those very beings who had been held to be gods among all the nations, and who had snatched human souls away as captives from the knowledge and worship of the God of the universe; and only then to deliver the Gospel of the kingdom of God to all people. That is why, before any recorded deed of his, he was led up into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil; and he was with the wild beasts, as the evangelist says, calling the savage and beastlike evil powers “wild beasts.” These very things, then, the present psalm necessarily foretells by the prophetic Spirit. For having been taught by the preceding psalms about the coming among human beings of the one who is prophesied, about his birth in the flesh and about his death, and how he had been proclaimed beforehand as one who would come forth from the seed of David, we must next learn of the contest he undertook against the opposing powers. These things, then, the present prophecy sets before us, foretelling all that he endured in the wilderness for forty whole days and as many nights while he was tempted by the devil. For invisible powers were around him as hunters, preparing snares for him. Some tried to disturb him with troubling words, others to frighten him by night; others again sent spiritual arrows against him by day; and still others, which cannot be named by us nor spoken of to mortal ears, busied themselves with tempting him. This is what the passage indicates when it says, “From the thing that walks about in darkness.” In its place Aquila rendered, “From the word that walks in the dark of the moon,” and Symmachus, “Nor the pestilence that travels in gloom.” And by now even the most shameless and ruling demons, those that dare to show themselves at midday itself, in the full blaze of the sun’s light, were coming against him. For while the others pursue the darkness proper to them and are accustomed to produce their apparitions only at night, the most shameless dare to appear even by day and in the midst of the sun’s rays. Such were those that assailed the Saviour too: by day certain such things came against him, and by night others. That is why it is said next: “You will not be afraid of terror by night, nor of the thing that walks about in darkness.” And seeing his invincible and unconquerable power, the multitudes of opposing powers gathered together again and came against him in throngs. And it seems to me that those who were formerly held to be gods among men, and the opposing spirits, beholding in the man of our Saviour a strange nature and a power able to destroy them all, gathered together from every side, came on in a mass, and wished to dash themselves against him. And

at first the devil attempted to tempt him through other, particular spirits; that is why it is said, “And he was with the wild beasts.” And what sort of wild beasts? The passage before us shows, going on next to say, “You will tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon.” For certain evil powers flying through the region of the air, taking on, as is likely, such shapes and forms (principalities and authorities, the world-rulers of this darkness and the spiritual forces of wickedness), named allegorically asps and basilisks and dragons and lions, or compared to these because their wickedness resembles them, stirred up every temptation against him. At the end of all, when the devil saw that he had trodden upon asp and basilisk and trampled all the powers working under him, he himself at last came in person, humbled and somewhat afraid, and put to him the questions recorded in the Gospels, tempting him and saying, “If you are the Son of God, say this, and do that.” So the present prophecy sets forth the massed onset of the evil spirits and their defeat, teaching that they gathered together, yet could do nothing and had no strength, but fell to the ground as they drew near him. That is why it is said, “A thousand will fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.” Instead of “at your side,” Aquila and Symmachus have rendered “at your flank.” In this way the divine Scripture names the left side of the Saviour, perhaps because there is nothing in him that is sinister or on the left. However, it is of all the opposing powers together that it is said, “But they will not come near you,” and, “Only with your eyes will you observe, and you will see the recompense of sinners.” And all these things, he says, will be around you, since “you, O Lord, are my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge.” I think that these invisible and opposing powers, all those under the whole heaven, gathered together in a mass against him, troubled by the voice that was borne to him when the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove, and the voice from above was heard saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Having heard this voice, then, and seeing that the man pointed out by the Holy Spirit through the dove was named Son of God, they could neither disbelieve the voice nor, seeing the man clothed in flesh, believe that he was the beloved of God. Therefore, beholding something strange and a new human nature, they expected that their own workings would be overthrown by a superior power. That is why they came against him, while he very willingly gave himself up to all the temptations he had taken upon himself for the salvation of mankind. For since he was about, as I said, to proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, according to the prophecy about him, and to draw the souls of men away

from those who had long held them captive, and to set them free from idolatrous error, he necessarily made war first of all against those very beings who had tyrannized over them for a long age. And when he had defeated them by enduring every temptation (hence Luke says, “And when the devil had finished every temptation, he departed from him”), after this he went on to the healing of human beings. Hence the demons also shuddered at him and confessed that they knew who he was, crying out and saying, “Ah, what have we to do with you, Son of God? We know who you are, the Holy One of God.” For they had learned who he was from the voice that was borne to him; and from what he did at the time of the temptation they also knew his power. “No evils will come to you, and no scourge will come near your dwelling. For he will command his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways. On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.” These words might fittingly be said of the man made perfect in Christ, of the choir of Christ’s martyrs, of his holy Church, and indeed of the very body of Christ. For if “the angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him and will deliver them,” then for those who have passed beyond fear and are in a perfect state of virtue of soul, such as is he who “dwells in the help of the Most High and lodges under the shadow of the Mighty One,” for such people, then, not one angel but several encampments are appointed as guards, as many as there are of those who plot against the one who is perfect in God’s sight. So indeed a multitude of angelic bodyguards surrounded the prophet Elisha. Hence it is said that nothing harmful will come upon the one prophesied through the psalm, nor will a scourge touch his dwelling in the body. By “scourge” we do not understand the scourge in the more common sense, for with that countless holy martyrs of God were scourged, and the bodily dwelling of our Saviour himself, his flesh, was tormented with scourges at the time of his passion, in accordance with the prophecy that says of him, “I gave my back to scourges, and my cheeks to blows.” We must therefore take “scourge” here to mean the stroke that comes from the working of demons, such as the Saviour himself is said to have healed and cured among men: the scourges of unclean demons. Such a scourge, then, the present passage says will not come near the dwelling of the one prophesied, because he is guarded by the angels appointed to keep watch over him, who are also said to lift him up on their hands, so that he does not strike his foot against a stone. In one sense you will say that his dwelling is his Church, according to the words, “Until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob.” So too the word knows of many dwellings, the churches throughout

the whole earth, when it says, “How beloved are your dwellings, O Lord of hosts!” In another sense, the bodily instrument in which the Word of God dwelt might be called his dwelling. Now the chief and greater achievements of the one indicated by the prophecy were accomplished through a greater cooperation. For he who “dwells in the help of the Most High,” understood by us according to the flesh as the one born of the seed of David, having himself made the Most High his refuge, was rightly guarded by the Most High. That is why he also said to him, “You are my helper and my refuge, my God, and I will hope in him.” For he himself rescued him from the snare of the hunters and overshadowed him with his shoulders; and he also surrounded him, encompassing him with the shield of truth. And all these things the Most High provided for him, so that he might not be troubled by terror by night, nor by the arrow that flies by day, nor by the thing that walks about in darkness, nor by mishap and the demon of noonday. And besides these, the Most High himself, working together with the one the passage is about, overthrew all the powers of his enemies and foes and cast them under his feet. That is why it was said, “A thousand will fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand, but it will not come near you.” The great and complete achievements, then, as I said, the Most High himself accomplished, working together with the one indicated; but the slight, so to speak, and more bodily matters he ordered to be ministered by angels. These were the matters concerning his dwelling, that is, his bodily instrument, and concerning the flesh itself. Being small and paltry in comparison with those named before, they were handed over to ministering angels to guard, so that nothing harmful might come upon his body and no scourge might approach, not him, but his dwelling; for neither thousands nor ten thousands of evil powers dared to come near him himself. So angels ministered to the flesh and body of the one prophesied, down to the smallest and most trivial matter. This the passage shows when it says, “So that you do not strike your foot against a stone.” For by this, I think, it signifies that angels ministered to him even in whatever chance and very slight thing usually happens to the body. And you have this testimony in the Gospels too about the Saviour himself. For Mark recorded, at the time of the Saviour’s temptation, that he was with the wild beasts, and the angels ministered to him; and Matthew, marking the same time, says, “Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and ministered to him.” But while the evangelists showed that angels ministered to him, they did not mention what kind of ministry they gave him. The present prophecy, however, has taught that it was ministry in bodily and small matters. For they guarded his dwelling so that no scourge might come near him, and they watched over his feet as well, so that they might not stumble, even in the smallest and most trivial thing.

So much for the literal wording. As for the deeper meaning, the dwelling of our Saviour has been shown to be his Church; and his people are also his body, according to the Apostle who said, “Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually.” Of the members, some would be the eyes of Christ’s body, others the ears, others the hands; accordingly, then, others will be his feet, of whom it is said, “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of good things!” For these feet, then, so that none of them may strike against a stone or be tripped up in the race, but may run the course of the Gospel smoothly and unhindered, angels are appointed as guards, keeping watch over the dwelling just described. Again, other angels have been entrusted with the churches of Christ founded throughout the earth. But the devil did not understand these things (for how, or from where, could he understand the utterances of the divine Spirit?) when, tempting the Saviour, he brought him up to the pinnacle of the temple and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down. For it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you, and on their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’” For he had perceived that the prophecy in the preceding verses had been fulfilled in very deed in the Saviour, and he saw a strange spectacle in human nature: all his army destroyed and all his powers conquered by the one who had appeared, thousands in a mass and ten thousands falling before him, while he himself, unshaken and unimpeded, trod upon asp and basilisk and trampled lion and dragon, that is, the devil’s ruling powers. So he tried to learn this as well: whether, if he threw himself from the pinnacle, angels would come and bear him up. To this surmise of his, which was mistaken, the Saviour answered, saying, “It is written: You shall not tempt the Lord your God.” For to hurl and cast oneself down from the greatest height, and to do so in order to learn whether one will obtain help through the angels or not, would be the act of one tempting God; and this is just what the tempter wished to tempt him to do. For it was in keeping with his character that, while tempting the Saviour, he should dare to tempt God as well. But the Saviour did not put God to the test, for he knew well and was fully persuaded of the power of the Father working together with him. That is why he gave the devil a command, saying, “You shall not tempt the Lord your God,” setting a passage of divine Scripture from the Law against the words of the present Scripture, which the devil had brought forward to him without understanding it. He did not perceive that the Saviour had no need of the help of angels, even if, supposing it, he had willed of his own choice to let himself down; for at his ascension into heaven too, which was a greater thing than a descent through the air from the pinnacle of the temple to the earth, he had no need of an angelic hand. And notice how the devil, after quoting “On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone,” did not add the words that are joined

immediately after them, namely, “You will tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon,” which plainly set forth the Saviour’s victory over the devil himself and his angels. For he did not wish to put forward the proof against himself. But if he had had any understanding [?], he ought to have reasoned that it was not for the same person to be able to tread upon and trample such ruling powers and yet to stumble with his foot against a stone, so as to need the guard and help of angels. He, then, without understanding, made use of the words of the present prophecy, because he had seen the rest fulfilled in him. The Saviour, for his part, does not deny that the oracle was spoken about him; but since the devil did not understand it, he lets it pass, using an answer suited to him. As for how we, by the grace of our Saviour himself, have contemplated these passages, it is left to readers to judge from what has been said. “You will tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon. Because he hoped in me, I will rescue him; I will shelter him, because he knew my name. He will cry to me, and I will hear him; I am with him in affliction; I will deliver him and glorify him. With length of days I will fill him, and I will show him my salvation.” The matters concerning the dwelling he committed to angels, as was explained before, so that angels might tend and guard the dwelling of the man made perfect in Christ, or of his Church, or of the flesh which he used like an instrument for the salvation of mankind. For these things, being lesser and more trivial, were entrusted to angels. And I think that, just as one might entrust to servants the care of one’s sandals or the service of some other more trivial things, so for all the small and bodily things accomplished through the flesh of our Saviour, angels were appointed as servants and ministered to him. To this the Gospel scripture also testifies, saying, “Angels came and ministered to him.” But the more important, greater and loftier things it no longer ascribes to angels, but to the Saviour himself. What these were has been shown in what came before; among them was “A thousand will fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.” And the end of all, the final victory of our Saviour over all, is set forth through the words, “You will tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the dragon and the lion.” By these, I think, are meant principalities and authorities and world-rulers, and the spiritual forces of wickedness. Treading upon these, then, …

After “You will tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the dragon and the lion,” the reason is again added. It refers the victory not to angels but to the Most High himself, in whose person the words are spoken: “Because he hoped in me, I will also deliver him.” The passage had already taught how he hoped in him, when it said, “He who dwells in the help of the Most High,” and, “He will say to the Lord, You are my protector and my refuge, my God, and I will hope in him.” So the victorious and final act, which comes after all the acts of our Savior listed before, is set out in the words “You will tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the dragon and the lion.” This act may belong to our Savior, or to the man perfected in him, or to his perfect body, the Church. In every case it ascribes the whole matter, and the cause of the victory, to the Most High. That is why it is said: “Because he hoped in me, I will also deliver him; because he knew my name. I am with him in affliction; I will rescue him and glorify him.” Read in another sense, the prophecy seems to me to foretell the whole course of our Savior's life as a man. I mean the first temptation, the temptation at the Passion, and the assault on the opposing powers after the body was laid aside. Take the first part of the psalm. To speak more generally, let us say that the present prophecy hints at the temptation in the desert, where the Gospels show him being tempted by the devil. The second part, where the passage shows angels ministering to his body, points to his time spent in human life. The third part, where he is said to have trodden upon the asp and the basilisk and trampled the dragon and the lion, points to his victory over the ruling spirits after death. After all this the psalm adds: “I will rescue him and glorify him; I will fill him with length of days, and show him my salvation.” These words set before us his salvation from the dead after death, his long-enduring and immortal life, his divine glory, and his honor and kingdom with the Father. A PSALM OF A SONG, FOR THE SABBATH DAY. It is good to confess to the Lord, and to sing praise to your name, O Most High; to declare your mercy in the morning, and your truth by night, on a ten-stringed psaltery, with song on the lyre. The righteous and God-loving men who lived before Moses neither knew the Sabbath days nor kept them. Abraham himself did not, nor did Isaac, nor Jacob, nor Jacob's sons. Even those who lived still earlier do not appear to have known a Sabbath day. Those of the circumcision think they achieve something great by keeping the Sabbaths, though they do not even keep them as the law intends. We must therefore set these facts before them. The Sabbath means rest, for it is written: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works which he had made, and sanctified

[?] …you will say that we ought to understand the rest of God, and take the true Sabbath in a way worthy of God. For he says that the ungodly will not enter his rest. In the Psalms he says: “They always go astray in their heart, and they did not know my ways. So I swore in my wrath: they shall not enter my rest.” We must therefore take the Sabbaths of God in a spiritual sense, and understand a rest fitting for God. The ungodly are not counted worthy of this rest; only the righteous and the friends of God are. In this sense we may say that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob knew and kept the Sabbaths of God, and entered his rest. So did all who loved God before them and after them. We must therefore consider what the Sabbath means. Scripture shows it to be the rest of God, and introduces it after the making of the visible world. What else could God's rest be than his dwelling among intelligible things above the world? When he watches over the things of sense and busies himself with the works of his providence for the world, he is said to work. This is how we should understand our Savior's words: “My Father is working until now, and I am working.” But when he is among the bodiless things above the world, on his own high lookout, so to speak, he is then understood to keep rest and to celebrate his own Sabbath. The men of God do the same. They are set free from the works that weary the soul, which are all bodily works and the things dear to earthly flesh. Then they give themselves wholly to God, to leisure in divine and intelligible things and to contemplating them. At that point they keep the Sabbaths that are dear to God, and a rest for the Lord God. Scripture teaches about such Sabbaths when it says: “So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God,” and again, “Let us therefore strive to enter that rest.” The perfect Sabbath, the perfect and thrice-blessed rest, is found in the kingdom of God. It lies beyond the six days of creation and outside all things of sense, among the bodiless things above the world, where pain and grief and sighing have fled away. There we will be released from this mortal and perishable life. We will rest with the God-pleasing and blessed rest, set free from bodily activities and from slavery to the flesh. We will be with God himself and beside him, and there we will keep Sabbath and rest. That is why the Apostle says: “Let us therefore strive to enter that rest.” On earth the men of God bore an image of that Sabbath and of that perfect, thrice-blessed rest. They kept leisure and rest from the things that draw us far from God. They gave themselves wholly to contemplating divine things, and they persevered day and night in meditating on the sacred words. So they kept holy Sabbaths at that time and a rest dear to God, resting and keeping Sabbath. For this reason the

law of Moses, which handed down shadows and symbols of these things, rightly set apart a particular day for the people. On that day at least they were to abstain from their usual work and give their time to meditating on the divine law. The present psalm teaches plainly what the Sabbath leisure and the rest from unprofitable things are for. They are for coming together in the same place and doing the things the psalm sets out. First, to confess to the Lord. Second, to sing praise to his name with musical instruments. Third, to declare his mercy in the morning hours. Fourth, to tell of his truth in the night seasons. And all this is to be done not only with lips and voice, but also by playing musical instruments: “on a ten-stringed psaltery,” it says, “and with song on the lyre.” You see how many things the present passage urges us to do on the day of the resurrection. The psalm, at any rate, is entitled “For the Sabbath day.” The priests in the temple also did a great many other things on the Sabbath, as the law required. So the law does not command complete idleness. Nor was the Sabbath day laid down for the priests. It was laid down only for those who could not devote the whole time of their lives, and all their days, to the worship of God and to works dear to God. For these the law ordered that such things be done at intervals. But some give themselves up on the Sabbath day to a full belly, to drunkenness and to every kind of disorder. Through the prophet God threatens them, saying: “You who lay hold of false Sabbaths,” and again, “Your new moons and Sabbaths and great day I cannot endure.” Since those observances were rejected, the Word through the New Covenant moved the feast of the Sabbath and transferred it to the rising of the light. He handed down to us an image of the true rest: the saving day, the Lord's Day, the first day of light. On that day the Savior of the world, after all his deeds among men, won the victory over death and passed through the gates of heaven. He rose beyond the six days of the world's creation and received the Sabbath fitting for God, the thrice-blessed rest. Then the Father said to him: “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet.” This is the day of light, the first day, the day of the true Sun. On it we too come together after an interval of six days. We are those from the nations, redeemed through him throughout the whole world, and we celebrate holy and spiritual Sabbaths. On it we carry out, according to the spiritual law, what the law laid down for the priests to do on the Sabbath. We offer spiritual sacrifices and offerings, those called sacrifices of praise and sacrifices of jubilation. We send up the fragrant incense, of which it is said: “Let my prayer be set forth as incense before you.” We also offer the loaves of presentation, rekindling the saving memorial. And we offer the blood of sprinkling of the Lamb of God, who took away

the sin of the world, as a cleansing for our souls. We kindle the lights of knowledge before the face of God. On the same day we also strive eagerly to carry out what is in the psalm before us. We confess to the Lord in deeds and in words, and sing praise to the name of the Most High. At dawn, at the very rising of our Light, we proclaim the mercy of God that has come upon us. By night we show forth his truth through a sober and pure way of life. Everything else that had to be done on the Sabbath we have transferred to the Lord's Day, since it has more authority. It is the leading day, the first day, and more honorable than the Jewish Sabbath. On this day, at the creation of the world, God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. On this day too the Sun of righteousness has risen on our souls. That is why the tradition handed down to us is to come together on this day. We too are commanded to carry out what the psalm enjoins. The first of these is to confess. The beginning of good things is release from our former evils, which comes about through genuine repentance and confession, and which leads to the good end, God himself. If no one is good except God, then confession is a good beginning of the good journey that leads to God. That is why it says: “It is good to confess to the Lord.” For our confession should be displayed not to men but to the Lord himself, who searches hearts. But, as we have often said, “confession” is also used of thanksgiving. So it is fitting that on the Lord's Day we also render our thanksgivings to the Lord, coming together in his churches throughout the world. Having made progress through confession, we are next told to sing praise, since we have advanced to a better state of soul. When we have grown further and become better than we were, we are commanded to proclaim the Lord's mercies to others as well, and to teach those near us. We are to do this in the morning hours, dedicating the firstfruits of the day's activities to teaching about the mercy of God. The passage urges us to do these things at dawn. By then, of course, we will have kept our souls and bodies holy through the hours of night, pure of all defilement. And we will have received the truth of piety by remembering the service of God even in the night hours. In former times those of the circumcision worshiped through symbols and types. It was then not unfitting for some to send up hymns to God with psalteries and lyres, and to do so on Sabbath days. In doing so they were, of course, breaking the rest and transgressing the law about the Sabbath. But we keep the Jew who is one inwardly, as the Apostle says: “For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is outward in the flesh. He is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter.” So we render our hymn on a living psaltery and an ensouled lyre, and in spiritual songs. More pleasing to God than any musical instrument is the harmony of the

peoples of Christ. In all the churches of God we send up a single melody in our singing of psalms, with like-minded souls and one disposition, with one accord and with the same belief in faith and piety. It is such psalmody and such spiritual lyres that we are accustomed to use, since the Apostle teaches this too when he says, “with psalms and songs and spiritual hymns.” In another sense, the lyre may be the whole body. Through its movements and actions the soul renders the hymn that befits God. The ten-stringed psaltery may be the worship of the Holy Spirit, performed through the five senses of the body and the same number of powers of the soul. The same Apostle points to this somewhere when he says: “I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind also; I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind also.” The mind has its own movements, by which the body is played like an instrument. The spirit in turn has movements of its own, by which it sets the soul to work. For you have gladdened me, Lord, in what you have made, and in the works of your hands I will exult. Scripture says, “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and be glad in it.” Whoever has understood that day, made by God, will say, “For you have gladdened me, Lord, in what you have made.” But the present psalm has the heading “For the Sabbath day.” So you will ask how it can say that on the Sabbath day he was gladdened, and not by God's rest. Nor does it say he was gladdened by God's ceasing from work, as the Jews might suppose, because on that day God rested from all the works he had made. If the things set out in the psalm referred to the Jewish Sabbath, it should have said that he was gladdened by God's leisure, by his rest and ceasing, as they would put it. But it does not say this. It says, “You have gladdened me, Lord, in what you have made, and in the works of your hands I will exult.” This shows plainly that what God has made is to be understood in one way, and the works of his hands in another. It is these that the psalmist confesses have gladdened him, not God's ceasing from work. In one sense, what God has made may be this very day, of which it is said, “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and be glad in it.” This means the day of the resurrection, the Lord's Day. We have shown this by proof elsewhere, setting out the account of the world's creation. There Moses says, “In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth,” and adds, “Let there be light, and there was light; and God called the light day.” You see that nothing else was created on this day except the day itself. So the oracle that says, “This is the day which the Lord has made,” fits it. He made nothing else but the day itself, and this was the first Lord's Day. It is of this day that “For you have gladdened me, Lord, in what you have made” is now said. The works of his hands are the things recorded as made on the days that followed. In another sense, what God has made may mean the intelligible, rational and bodiless creatures of

God. In this sense Scripture records that the soul, created in the image of God, was made. The works of his hands are his visible and bodily creations, of which it is said: “For I will behold the heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have established.” This scripture, then, speaks of a leisure for divine exercises, of keeping free and resting from bodily and mortal works, which the passage calls a Sabbath and a rest. It teaches those who in that leisure give their time to contemplating God's works, both the intelligible and the visible, to say: “For you have gladdened me, Lord, in what you have made, and in the works of your hands I will exult.” “For from the greatness and beauty of created things their Maker is correspondingly perceived.” And, as the holy Apostle says, his invisible things, the intelligible, bodiless and supramundane, are understood through the things he has made, and are clearly seen from the creation of the world. How great are your works, Lord! Your thoughts are very deep. A senseless man will not know, and a fool will not understand these things. He says: You have gladdened me, Lord, in what you have made and in the works of your hands. But not every man has the same disposition as I do. Many are senseless and foolish. They do not know or understand the very things in which I confess that I am glad and exult. The man who is truly senseless and foolish denies that the universe is held together by the providence and reason of God. He attributes God's mighty creations to fate and necessity, to irrational motion and chance. And because he is foolish, he stumbles at the government of the universe, since he thinks he sees many irregularities in this mortal life. So the senseless and foolish man, when he is troubled, turns at once to blasphemous and ungodly reasoning. He claims that godlessness, the absence of providence, randomness and chance are the causes of these things. But I have been taught to be reverent even about the hidden matters just mentioned. I am persuaded that the reasons for your judgment and government are beyond my littleness. That is why I say: “How great are your works, Lord! Your thoughts are exalted exceedingly.” How could mortal reasoning search out the depths of God, and know his thoughts as he governs human affairs? “For no one knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him. So too no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God,” nor is anyone able to tell them. “But we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit of God,” of whom it is said: [⁵ Pyth. 1, 90.]

When the sinners sprang up like grass, and all who work lawlessness peered forth, it was so that they might be destroyed forever and ever. The senseless and foolish man sees the ungodly prospering, and the righteous and godly suffering. He does not understand the reasons of Providence, but turns at once to ungodly thoughts and falls into atheism. But I look into what you have made and into the works of your hands. Among other things I have seen that the end of the ungodly who prosper in this life holds ruin and destruction. So I am all the more amazed at the reasons of the divine judgment. Grass and the flowers of the earth look lovely for a little while. They charm the eye and all the senses. But no sooner do they change and turn than they wither very easily and perish. In the same way the sinners whom the many admire spring up, and blossom for a little while, and peer forth. They show who they really are and what kind of choices they have made. Then before long a ruin overtakes them that is no longer brief and temporary, but destruction without end. For your righteous judgment presides over human affairs. That is the chief reason, I think, why sinners and those who work lawlessness are allowed to spring up and peer forth. In this way their choice is exposed, since it has not used the gifts of God rightly. Therefore an avenging, eternal ruin will follow them. But you, Lord, are Most High forever. For behold, your enemies, Lord, for behold, your enemies will perish, and all who work lawlessness will be scattered. And my horn will be exalted like that of a unicorn, and my old age will be in rich oil. And my eye has looked upon my enemies, and my ear will hear of the evildoers who rise up against me. He says: You, O Lord, are always the same and unchanging, and you will remain Most High in the heights for all ages. You do not change, you are not brought low, you are not altered. You do not become greater than yourself, nor are you made like the lowly things on earth. You neither think nor do anything small or lowly, but remain like yourself without end. But we are lowly and far removed from your power, and we are carried now one way and now another, and we change. Your enemies, O Lord, have made themselves strangers to the life that is with you. They have chosen enmity instead of friendship toward you, who alone are good. So they will perish, and they themselves are the cause of their destruction. For they would not remain with you and be made your friends, but took up enmity against you, their Maker and Savior. So even if they gather countless riches in this life, wealth and treasures, all of it will be scattered together with their very souls and bodies. But I have embraced the knowledge and friendship of you, and have become a stranger to your enemies. I trust in your righteous judgment, and I am persuaded that I will obtain a change for the better. So even if in this present life I seem to the many to be without honor and lowly,

[?] at the end of all things I shall be exalted — or rather, my horn shall be exalted, that is, the hope of the kingdom that I await from you, which will be exalted as high as the horn of the unicorn. For if among intelligible realities there is a unicorn, a single horn, who claims you as his own Father, I know well that I too shall be exalted like him. For since we have been called heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, I am persuaded, he says, that I shall enjoy the same kingdom as your Christ, when my old age, that is, the last part of my life, is exalted in rich oil. For even if the youth and prime of my soul are humbled as much as can be, being trained as in a contest in this present life, yet its last part, the old age of the soul itself, that is, its perfection, will attain the change for the better, as it lives in oil that is abundant, plentiful and rich, in your presence, O merciful God. Then, yes then, my eye, which now wastes away over sinners and weeps over this mortal life, will look upon my enemies, seeing those who are now glorified by the many paying the penalty they deserve, whose end will be given over to scattering. And then not only my eye but also the very ear of my soul will hear of the end of those who today rise up against me and do evil. Because of all these things, then, marveling exceedingly at the reasons of your providence and at the just judgment laid up by you for all, I rejoice exceedingly and exult in the works of your hands; but every senseless and foolish man does not understand these things. Therefore I say: How magnified are your works, O Lord! And your thoughts are not simply deep but very deep — the thoughts by which you govern the universe ineffably and profoundly, permitting and allowing the ungodly to be lifted up and exalted for the present time, and the godly to be humbled, whose ends bear witness to your marvelous and all-wise governance.
