Perceiving this, the divine Apostle too cried out: O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are your judgments, and untraceable the ways

The righteous will flourish like a palm tree; he will be multiplied like the cedar in Lebanon. The sinners were said to spring up like grass and, in keeping with the image of grass, to perish before long; for no sooner has the grass sprung up than it withers and its flower falls, and so it is with the life and glory of sinners. But the righteous will flourish not like grass but like a palm, bearing its roots somewhere on high, and its fronds not lying on the ground but stretching toward heaven. For these reasons, then, the righteous might be compared to a palm, but not to the palm's single trunk; for he is multiplied in the branches that are saved together with him and through him. For this reason he must be compared to the cedar itself — not simply any cedar, but the one in Lebanon; and this grows in abundance and on a grand scale, since it grows on a most fertile mountain that bears

saved through him, in this respect he would resemble the cedar, and the palm in the other respects already shown. But the ungodly were not like this; they spring up like grass and vanish at once. Planted in the house of God, they will flourish in the courts of our God. [?] The one who is supremely perfect, who is also called righteous, has been compared to the palm and the cedar; but since not all are such, one should know that even for the less perfect, provided they have been counted worthy of being planted in the house of God, there is a good end: at any rate they will flourish in the courts of our God. You will understand this too if you take the great house of the Lord to mean his Church on earth, according to the Apostle who said: That you may know how one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God; and if you take those planted in it to be those who have received from it the beginnings of progress in godliness, such as those whom Paul planted, on whose account he also said: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. These, then, who are planted in God's Church on earth will yield a flower that is fragrant and fruitful and bears perfect fruits, when they have been transplanted into the courts of our God, that is, into the heavenly dwellings — since there are many with the Father — where those now planted in the house of God, assigned according to their worth, will flourish at the proper time. They will still be multiplied in rich old age, and will be at ease, to proclaim that the Lord our God is upright, and there is no unrighteousness in him. He says not only that those planted today in his house will flourish in the courts of God, but that they too will be multiplied, as above the cedar in Lebanon was multiplied. And when will this be for them, if not in rich old age? Be assured that old age here means the perfection of the soul; when they reach it, those now planted in the house of the Lord will be at ease. For even if during the present time, in which they are planted in the house of the Lord, they continue in hardship, enduring the first labors of cultivation, yet when they are counted worthy of rich old age they will be at ease, resting from their toils and receiving the prizes of their contests. And they will confess that the Lord our God is upright, and there is no unrighteousness in him. For if the good things just listed were not going to await those devoted to God, and if the ruinous end did not await the ungodly and those who work lawlessness, one might perhaps charge God's providence with injustice. But since such ends have been prepared for the righteous — which we too pray to attain — and such punishments have been threatened for the ungodly — from which may we be delivered — how would it not follow that we should confess that the Lord our God is upright, and there is no unrighteousness in him?

But the senseless man will not know these things, nor will the fool understand them, because he is darkened by his own folly. But I, who know and understand them because I have been enlightened by the divine Spirit, and because I see how very deep are the thoughts of God [?], rightly rejoice and exult in the divine governance, and bear the present nobly because of the hope of what is to come. For this reason, dedicating all my leisure, and my rest from evil, to God, I try to keep the delightful and holy Sabbaths by confessing and singing psalms and declaring in the morning the mercy of God and his truth by night. For the truth of a God-fearing soul is shown most of all when, finding itself in darkness and gloom, it displays the genuineness and sincerity of its conscience as if in the brightest light and the clearest day. Such too is the psalm spoken with song for the day of the Sabbath, that is, for the time of leisure and rest according to God, in which it befits us too, as we devote our leisure to the study of divine teachings, to send up to God the thankful words of the present song. [?] Praise of a song, for David. [?] The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with majesty. According to the Apostle, death reigned from Adam to Moses, that is, from the first origin of humankind until the bodily worship according to Moses, which was carried on long ago in the earthly Jerusalem until the coming of our Savior Jesus Christ. Naturally, then, when death reigned and he who had the power of death, that is, the devil, held sway, it was not the Lord who reigned over humankind at that time, but a polytheistic and demonic error. The same Apostle teaches about our Savior, saying: Since therefore the children share in blood and flesh, he himself likewise partook of the same sufferings, that through death he might destroy him who has the power of death, that is, the devil. Fittingly, then, the pre-existent Word of God, who is himself life, took up the human body as a mortal instrument for the destruction of death; he handed it over to death to demonstrate its own nature, and then took it out of death to display his divine power. So he dissolves the power of death, and dissolves too the devil's tyranny over humankind; he also extinguishes the activity of the evil demons and unclean spirits that long held sway over the human race, and, overthrowing every power opposed and hostile to God, he secures for God the Father's kingdom among all the nations through the preaching of the gospel. Therefore, since the dominion of death has been dissolved and he who had the power of death, that is, the devil, has been abolished, and the Lord now reigns from this time on over all the nations on earth, with life according to God reigning over humankind together with him, the divine Spirit, rightly dancing at this achievement and

gathering all of us into the dance, cries out and says: The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with majesty. And the Lord, who is himself life and himself the Word of God, reigns over every soul that is not gripped by irrationality and folly, over which sin does not reign, which the devil does not hold, and which death does not overpower, wounding and destroying it with its own stings. The Apostle teaches that the sting of death is sin, through which the soul is destroyed, according to the prophecy that says: The soul that sins, it shall die. Therefore we must strive that neither irrationality nor sin nor the devil nor death, through sin, should rule over us, but that only the Word and the life, that is, the Lord, should be master over us, reigning through every virtue over those who have been deemed worthy of his

And since the Word of God, who is himself the Lord, was going to reign not only over the living but also over the dead, and not only over those in heaven but also over those on earth, as he himself teaches when he says, All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, that is, the mortal body and the human instrument; for this was the form of the servant. At that time, when he was doing these things, he put on unsightliness, so that it was said of him: We saw him, and he had no form or beauty; but his form was without honor and fell short of the sons of men. But when he received back the glory that he had before with the Father, he transformed the form of the servant into something better, according to the apostolic testimony which says: who will transform the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of Christ's glory. Then he clothed himself with majesty; then too he established the Father's kingdom and his dominion over all, not only over those in heaven but also over the nations throughout the whole world, overthrowing all polytheistic error. Therefore it has been said: The Lord has reigned, he has clothed himself with majesty. The phrase "he has clothed himself" is said of one who for a time had put off his majesty. And when he was enduring the things of the passion, he was crucified, says the Apostle, out of weakness; but when, having conquered death, he received the kingdom over all, he in turn fulfilled the words: The Lord has clothed himself with power and girded himself. For Christ was the power of God and the wisdom of God. Then, having clothed himself with his own power and girded himself with it, he gives himself to a great achievement. What this was the text teaches next, saying: For he has established the world, which shall not be shaken. For when the whole world had all but been carried down into the abyss, at the time when demonic activity prevailed over all, he raised it up and set it right, overturning all the hostile and demonic power and the polytheistic error. So, then, he established the world, so that it should no longer be sha- ³⁸ 2 Cor 13:4. ³¹ 1 Cor 1:24.

-ken from godliness toward God. And by "the world" the text also signifies his Church, founded on the rock, against which the gates of Hades shall not prevail, and it says that this has truly been established, and that it shall not be shaken. For the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it, because it has been founded on the rock. Your throne is prepared from of old; you are from everlasting. The rivers have lifted up, O Lord, the rivers have lifted up their voice. Your throne, he says, O Lord, was not prepared for you only now, for the first time, when after becoming human you ascended into heaven; but long ago, from of old, and before all ages it was yours, and was always and continually prepared for you, since you yourself are from everlasting, or rather exist before all ages, as you yourself taught, saying: The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works. Before the age he founded me, and before the mountains were settled; before all the hills he begets me. Your throne, then, was yours even before all ages; and yet when you emptied yourself and took up the form of a servant, it was still kept ready for you, since to you alone, and to no other, your Father said: Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet. Thus, then, your throne was ready, on which the Father who begot you bade you sit with him. And it was ready from of old, from everlasting, since you yourself are from everlasting. Not "you were," he says, but "you are." For to him alone is it fitting that "you are" be said. Hence it is said elsewhere too: But you are the same, and your years will not fail. The divine Spirit also signifies this throne in another place, saying: Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; a scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions. Your throne, then, was ready from of old, that is, from when you were with the Father, since you yourself are from everlasting. But now too the rivers have lifted up, O Lord. What they lifted up he shows by repeating the phrase next, saying: The rivers have lifted up their voice. For these things, hidden long before, have now become audible to all those counted worthy of the divine Spirit — prophets, apostles and evangelists — and to the peoples of countless thousands throughout the whole world who announce the saving kingdom in the churches; these too have lifted up their voice, proclaiming with a loud voice the grace of God poured out upon all. But I think that the divine powers and the multitude of angels in heaven are also now called rivers. They too lifted up their voice when they beheld the Savior ascending into heaven from his sojourn among men, clothing himself with the majesty of his divinity, girded with the Father's power, and receiving back his own throne of the kingdom. And

their voice uttered those words with which they cried out, saying: Lift up the gates, you rulers, and be lifted up, you everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall come in. Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle; and again: The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory. And the multitudes of our Savior's churches among men can also be called rivers, for those of the nations who have believed are always flowing together into them like rivers, and they lift up their voice in prayers to God and in doxologies of hymns and psalms; for our Lord himself compares to rivers those who would draw from his divine teaching and drink of the Holy Spirit, saying: Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him, rivers of living water will flow from his belly, springing up to eternal life. The rivers will lift away their surge at the sound of many waters. Wonderful are the swellings of the sea; wonderful on high is the Lord. If we have understood the rivers that lift up their voice at the glory of the Lord's kingdom, let us by contrast understand other rivers, surging and rising up against the knowledge of God, and disposed contrary to those who lift up their voice to God. These opposing rivers, then, he says, will lift away their surge, that is, they will put away all elation, all conceit, and all surging; and they will do this at the sound of the holy waters. You will understand what is said if you consider that long ago there was often among men a profession of the wisdom of this age and the surge of human philosophy, at which the wise of this age were lifted up, puffed up and surging under the mind of their flesh, as though they were pursuing great and wise teachings. But when churches of God were established throughout the whole earth among Greeks and barbarians, pursuing the true wisdom and sending up like rivers the doxologies and hymns befitting God with a louder and bolder cry, and giving out as it were a sound of many waters because of the multitude of worshippers, then the conceit of those long reputed wise was brought down, and all their surge was humbled, their wisdom being counted as nothing. And if anyone has ever marveled at the swellings of the sea — namely the great waves and billows of mortal life that rise up against the knowledge of God — let him know that the Lord on high is wonderful above all, so that those who trust in the Lord need no longer reasonably fear the swellings of the sea. It is likely that the swellings of the sea are the persecutions that rise up against the Church of God, which the dragon who dwells in the sea is accustomed to stir up, raising its waves, booming, roaring and churning, and all but threatening to flood the Church of God and wipe it out entirely. You might also explain these words otherwise, according to the letter, and say that the rivers — these very rivers that we perceive — lift up their voice to God, the Creator who made

them and brought them into being, displaying his glory. For as the Maker is perceived from the greatness and beauty of created things, in the same way the wonder of God's mighty works is presented through the parts of the world to those able to see. If then someone were to reason with himself: where does so great a flow of rivers come from? Whence such magnitudes and quantities of liquid substance? Whence the springs that have never failed since the beginning of time, gushing forth the ever-flowing and immense rivers? From what depths do they start, and from what source do they flow through all the ages? — if someone considers these things, he will see that the mighty work of the Creator and Maker of all, displayed through these very rivers, all but gives out a voice, bearing witness to his divinity. So too someone who sees the swellings of the sea — how its waves arch and are lifted on high, and how they collapse again and break upon themselves, and how they cannot and dare not overstep the boundary and law appointed for them — will see through these too the power of God's majesty. For he said to it: Thus far you shall come, and within you your waves shall be broken; and he set a boundary for it, and it shall not pass over it, nor turn back to cover the earth. And in yet another way besides what has been said, one might say that the swellings of the sea were wonderful when the disciples came and said to him, Lord, save us, we are perishing — when he rebuked it, and there was a great calm. And again at another time, when, divided at the Lord's command, it parted and drew back within itself, and provided a passage for the sons of Israel to go through it as through dry land. For then too its swellings became wonderful. Moreover, the rivers also lifted up their voice in another way: when the ark crossed the Jordan and the waters drew back and stood still, proclaiming the glory of God through deeds; and when, as the Savior himself was baptized in that same river, the heavenly voice proclaimed him to the hearing of all as the beloved Son. Your testimonies have been made very sure; holiness befits your house, O Lord, for length of days. Before the outcome of events, the prophecies about the future, which also contained the testimonies about the Lord's kingdom, did not yet allow the trustworthiness of the words to be seen. But after the outcome and the fulfillment in deeds, the testimonies of God were made sure. For long ago the things concerning God's kingdom over all the nations had been spoken and foretold and long expected; but this testimony that spoke of it has been confirmed now, when the oracle is seen fulfilled in deeds. And long ago it was said of the Lord that he clothed himself with majesty; but now, since the word is confirmed by the deeds themselves, the truth of the prediction has appeared: when he had put off the form of God and put on that of the servant, and had gone as far as an unsightly death, after this he laid aside this unsightliness and clothed himself with the ma-

[?]…majesty, having crowned himself with kingship over all things, both those in heaven and those on earth. Again, the prophetic testimonies declared that the Lord, having clothed himself with power, established the world, which shall not be shaken. These too were confirmed when, after the passion, he took back his own power and established his Church throughout the whole inhabited world of men, so that the souls of men would no longer be shaken this way and that, wandering in godless superstition. Again, the testimonies given through the prophets foretold that the rivers would lift up their voice, and other rivers would take up their pounding. These testimonies too were confirmed when, in all the Churches of God and throughout the whole world, the multitudes who worship God according to the Gospel lift up voices of thanksgiving, sent up to God in prayers and hymns. By these the wise men of this age, long since worn down, have been brought to nothing, and the rivers have carried away their pounding, so that all their philosophy has been extinguished. In the same way, as you go through the remaining predictions of the prophecies, you will apply to each one the words: "Your testimonies have been made very sure." The testimonies of the divine Scriptures, then, have gained great credibility through the truth seen in their fulfillment. But for your house, that is, your Church, nothing is so fitting for preserving it to length of days as holiness. For just as truth and faithfulness belong to your testimonies, so holiness befits your house; guarded by it, the house remains and will remain to length of days. For if it should ever happen that something unseemly were found in your house, and that instead of holiness there were profane, unclean and abominable conduct, it could no longer endure to length of days. For God, who dwells in it, being holy and resting among the holy, would say, if (God forbid) something unseemly and foreign to holiness were ever found in his house: "Behold, your house is left to you desolate." Therefore, when we enter the house of God, we must care for sanctification and self-control before all else and above all else. A PSALM OF DAVID, FOR THE FOURTH DAY OF THE WEEK. The Lord is a God of vengeance; the God of vengeance has spoken openly. Among the Hebrews the psalm has no title, but it contains exhortation and consolation for those who in the present life are persecuted and oppressed for the sake of piety, and further on he also sets down their prayer. He places the exhortation and consolation before the prayer, anticipating the petition of the persecuted and tending their sufferings in advance, and so showing in deed that the words "While you are still speaking I will say, Here I am" are fulfilled in their case. Take courage, then, you people, he says: for the Lord in whom you have hoped, just as he is God the Maker, God the Creator, God the Savior, God the Benefactor, God the Judge, God the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, long-suffering

and abounding in mercy and relenting over sins, and bearing countless other divine titles, is also a God of vengeance. For he cares about what is done in the heavens, so as to exact the due penalty from wrongdoers, to judge justly, to punish those who must be punished, and to render to each according to his works. Take courage, then, now that you have learned that you have a God of vengeance. For your God is by nature a God of vengeance, and since he acts boldly as the avenger of the wronged, he proclaims this expressly and openly through his prophets. In this way the doctrine of his providence is also established, by which he governs all things justly and wisely. For the time being, in the present life, he makes his sun rise on the just and the unjust and sends rain on the wicked and the good, granting his good things to all alike; but at the proper time he becomes a God of vengeance, when he will exact the fitting penalty from those who have not used his benefits well. Be exalted, you who judge the earth; render recompense to the proud. How long shall sinners, O Lord, how long shall sinners boast? They will utter and speak unrighteousness; all who work unrighteousness will speak. The divine Spirit prophetically gave the answer to the prayer as well, anticipating what would be said after the prayer, because he foreknew what the prayer would contain. That is why the two verses containing the Holy Spirit's answer, the answer suited to the prayer, were placed first. The supplication to God itself begins with "Be exalted, you who judge the earth." The Word, then, says: From the time human life first began, sinners began to prevail over the righteous: Cain over Abel, the giants at the time of the flood over those among them [?], Esau over Jacob, and Joseph's brothers over Joseph. And so, going forward through the ages, you would find sinners rising up against the righteous in every generation. How long, then, O Lord, will this go on? How long will sinners carry their oppression so far as even to boast of their impieties, not even keeping silent about what they do or hiding their wickedness, but uttering their injustices aloud for all to hear? How long, then, will they prosper in doing these things? Now at last, ascend the lofty throne of your just judgment: Be exalted, you who judge the earth, and render recompense to the proud, paying them the punishment they deserve. For now they have despised you yourself, as though you had nothing lofty about you and neither saw nor judged the earth. That is why they have supposed that the affairs of their life go unjudged and unwatched by providence. But I, praying to be a stranger to their impiety, am persuaded that you are a God of vengeance and that you are the one who judges all the earth. For even if you humble yourself, showing kindness, forbearance and long-suffering, and hold back your wrath against the ungodly, still I believe that

nothing will go unjudged while you oversee all things, and I entreat and beg you to be exalted and to show everyone your own greatness and the height of your divinity, so that sinners may at last stop priding themselves and boasting of all they do in defiance of the law. They have humbled your people, O Lord, and afflicted your heritage. They have killed the widow and the stranger, and murdered orphans. And they said, The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand. It was not enough for the sinners, he says, to sin against themselves; now they have also risen up against your people and your Church, humbling some, afflicting others and destroying others utterly. They have dared to do these things against your people, O Lord, and against your heritage, all but thinking impious and blasphemous thoughts about you. For they reasoned impiously within themselves and said: "The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand." So, as though you neither oversaw nor understood, they set about doing so much against your people and your heritage, against widows, strangers and orphans, who in human terms have no protection and no help. Yet they did these things not so much against them as against you, O Lord. For those who were oppressed were your people and your heritage, and those who oppressed them, blaspheming and acting impiously against you, reasoned as though you did not exist, did not oversee, did not understand, and did not avenge what was done. That is why I rightly said in my prayer, "How long shall sinners, O Lord," how long will they go on doing these things? By the people and heritage of God we must understand, in former times, the Jewish nation, since "Jacob his people became the Lord's portion, Israel the lot of his inheritance." But after their rejection, which a prophetic word presents when it says, "I have forsaken my house, I have abandoned my heritage," another prophecy accordingly brings in a new people from the Gentiles in their place, speaking in the person of Christ: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your heritage, and the ends of the earth for your possession." Understand, you senseless among the people; you fools, when will you be wise? He who planted the ear, shall he not hear? Or he who formed the eye, does he not perceive? He who disciplines nations, shall he not rebuke, he who teaches man knowledge? The Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain. The Prophet complained and lamented, as a man would, over the outrages the ungodly dared to commit, and prayed, saying, "Be exalted, you who judge the earth; render recompense to the proud." Then, as though he had stirred God and roused him by saying, "They have afflicted and humbled your people and your heritage, and said, The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand," he is filled with the power of the Holy Spirit, and to those who had said,

"The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand," he answers: How, you who are truly blind in mind, can he who supplied these faculties to those who lacked them fail to see and hear? For surely whoever imparts something to others first possesses himself what he imparts. The statement is made in the form of a syllogism and establishes the doctrine of providence. It is especially fitting to attend to passages of this kind in the divine Scriptures, as proof that they do not set before us an irrational faith, but supply the testimonies for their doctrines with clear reasoning and logical demonstration. Countless such passages are scattered throughout the sacred books. He argues, then, against the ungodly and the atheists who say that God does not oversee human affairs. Tell me, you people, he says: did the nature of living creatures come into being of itself, or did it arise from some cause? To say that lifeless, soulless and mindless matter produced, at random, by chance, irrationally and spontaneously, so many living creatures, the particular structure of each kind of creature, their shapes and forms, so intricate an arrangement of parts and limbs, such variety of beauty and so many differences, is utterly foolish and silly, and belongs to men whose souls are truly dead. For how could what has no share in life give life to another? How could what is soulless bring a soul into being? How could what is irrational fashion anything rational? How will what is by its own nature immobile be set in motion in the first place, or how will it move anything else? And such is the element of earth, from which all kinds of living creatures came forth, with eyes and ears and the other sense organs, sharing in life, motion and impulse. Man surpasses even these, being of a rational nature and capable of mind and knowledge. Did all these things, then, come into being from an irrational and soulless element? No: the evidence overcomes even the man unwilling to admit it, and natural reason is forced to speak the truth, that neither soulless matter nor dry, irrational substance is the cause of these things, but that there is a divine and creative mind, the Word of God, the maker of the world, himself the maker of all things, who gave to all the other creatures, and to man himself, the senses of the body and the reasoning of the soul, and mind besides, so as to grasp the nature of things: to behold visible things with the eyes, to hear audible things with the ears, and to understand intelligible things with reason. How then is it possible that he who has given the power of sight to others, who do not have it of themselves, should not see himself? And how is it possible that he who bored hearing and an ear into the earthy vessel of clay, so that voiceless and deaf matter hears in its ears [?] the voices from outside, should not, before all, apprehend the thoughts of men far better and more fully? And if whole nations on earth, barbarian and Greek, moved by the natural notions they have received from God, have framed laws and ordinances for themselves, how shall God, who granted them this understanding, not rebuke those who dare to act contrary to nature and contrary to right notions?

Where does men's [?] knowledge of anything whatever come from? Where do the arts come from? Where the theories of the sciences? Where the [?] of learning? Do they not come from him who sowed in them the power to grasp these things? Why, then, would he who bestowed such a nature on man be himself deprived of knowledge, so as not even to know the very things he gives? So stop [?], you vain men; be persuaded by true reason and know that he who planted the ear in men will himself, long before them, hear what is spoken among men; and not only will he see what is done [?], but he who formed [?] in men will also understand their intentions while they are still hidden in the mind. For this is the power of God, who knows and discerns the thoughts of men, that they are vain. Truly, all that men consider truth, and all their wisdom, which they put forward from their own reasonings and mortal thoughts, must be vain. For all that is wise and true is found with him alone, and from him it is given only to the worthy. Blessed is the man whom you discipline, O Lord, and teach out of your law, to give him calm from evil days, until a pit is dug for the sinner. Persuaded by what has been said and believing it, and believing that the thoughts of men are vain, I rightly consider that man alone blessed, O Lord, who draws from your wisdom and discipline as from a spring. [?] …someone who has been made a disciple of your discipline or of your law? For this reason too [?] written laws of [?], so that those who are taught by them might share in your instruction. And through them we are taught that the painful things that befall the righteous happen for their benefit, as they are trained and tested like God's athletes and proved through toils and blows by their endurance. Therefore we must not grieve or be distressed over those who suffer affliction in the present life, but rather call them blessed, since they are being disciplined by God. For "blessed is the man whom you discipline, O Lord, and teach out of your law." For whoever is disciplined and taught by you is calmed in evil days. In the very times of trial he is healed, receiving the consolations of your law and being taught to endure and be patient until a pit is dug for the sinner; for that is the end awaiting the sinner, as your law teaches. So the righteous man, learning these things in times of trial, is calmed and healed, looking to how things will turn out, and setting before his eyes both the pit into which the sinner who oppresses him will fall and his own good hopes with God [?]. For the Lord will not cast off his people, nor will he forsake his heritage, until righteousness returns to judgment, and all the upright in heart hold fast to it. Accordingly, after the pit laid up for the

sinner, he describes the good end of those who are afflicted for God's sake. For since it was said above, "They have humbled your people, O Lord, and afflicted your heritage," he now rightly sets out what becomes of the humbled people and the afflicted heritage, saying: The Lord will not cast off his people, nor will he forsake his heritage. For even if for a short time he permits the ungodly, by his forbearance, to humble and afflict his people, he will not cast off his people forever, nor abandon his heritage. Which people and which heritage, we have learned from the voice spoken in the person of Christ: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your heritage, and the ends of the earth for your possession." The prophet Zechariah also foretells this same people, the people drawn from the Gentiles, saying: "Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; proclaim it, daughter of Jerusalem: for behold, I am coming, and I will dwell in your midst, says the Lord. And many nations shall take refuge in the Lord, and they shall be my people, and I will be their God." This people of his, then, the Lord will not cast off, nor will he forsake his heritage, until righteousness returns to judgment. For he will guard his people and his heritage until the righteousness of God returns to give the prizes for their labors to those who have contended well. Those who hold fast to the righteousness of God will stand near him, ranked at the King's right hand, since they have become straight and upright in heart, have let nothing crooked or twisted into their soul, and have walked only the straight and royal road. Who will rise up for me against evildoers, or who will stand with me against those who work lawlessness? Had the Lord not helped me, my soul would very soon have dwelt in Hades. If I said, My foot has slipped, your mercy, O Lord, helped me. The break marked by the diapsalma has also brought about a very great change in the thought. For as though the earlier discourse were complete, he says, making a fresh start: "Who will rise up for me against evildoers?" For we have learned, he says, from the teaching of the divine Spirit, that the Lord is a God of vengeance, that he will render recompense to the proud, that a pit will be dug for the sinner, and that he will not cast off his people nor abandon his heritage; but that at the end of things, when the people return to judgment, he will render to each according to his works; and that all the upright in heart will stand, as those on the right, near his righteousness, spending their days with the Lord himself in the kingdom of heaven and presenting their whole life to him. These things, then, I have believed, and in believing I have been comforted. But meanwhile, in the present time, who will stand up for me against the evildoers? Or who will stand by me as an avenger against those who work lawlessness? Indeed I would say,

confessing the truth, that I will find no helper among men, but that I have one ally only, the Lord. Had he not helped me, I would long ago have been overcome by the evildoers and those who work lawlessness and would be dwelling in Hades, with my very soul, the rational substance made in the image of God, allotted death and Hades for its dwelling. This, then, is what I would have suffered had the Lord himself not stood by me and helped me. So whenever, tested in the contests, I became aware of my own weakness, so that the feet of my soul were in danger of being shaken, I confess that I at once felt your mercy, O Lord, and was helped by you. Had that mercy not been with me, holding up my feet, I would long ago have slipped and fallen from my place before you. But now your mercy, O Lord, gives me the boldness to say: You set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps. According to the multitude of the sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul. Your mercy not only gave my feet strength so that they would not be shaken, and your help not only held my soul fast so that it would not dwell in Hades; your consolations also healed the sorrows I carried in my heart, as the ineffable power of your goodness comforted my soul and filled it with gladness. For there was not just one consolation, or a second, but more, as many as the sorrows in my heart. You matched my sorrows with consolations from you, one for each sorrow, applying your consolation like a saving remedy, and as for many wounds, applying many treatments. It was such consolations that the divine Apostle laid hold of when he said: "Blessed be God, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those in any affliction with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God. For just as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our comfort also abounds." And one could add to this, adapting the words "The sufferings of the present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us": "The multitude of the sorrows in my heart is not worth comparing with your consolations, O Lord, with which you have gladdened my soul." And if at each sorrow a person is comforted by God and is counted worthy of the gladness that comes from God, would he not pray to endure more sorrows for God's sake, so as to receive more consolations and more of the gladness that comes with them? Shall the throne of lawlessness have fellowship with you, which frames trouble by decree? Rightly, he says, according to the multitude of the sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul, since

…the throne of iniquity has no part with you, since you are God, just and good; for you govern all things with just judgment and right law. Therefore you frame toil into a commandment; that is, your commandment produces toils and labors, because of the rewards that will follow the toils for those who have contended well and endured the toil eagerly and vigorously. "They will hunt after the soul of the righteous, and condemn innocent blood. But the Lord became my refuge, and my God the helper of my hope. And he will repay them their iniquity, and according to their wickedness the Lord our God will destroy them." The ungodly, he says, will hunt the soul of the righteous so relentlessly, surrounding it with snares and nets, that they drive it even to death, condemning innocent blood. For they are not content with losses of property, nor with blows and torments against the bodies of the righteous, but they also pass the sentence of death against them. Such are they. But I, having learned to despise even such things and to stand courageously even unto death, know that I have the Lord as my refuge, and my God as the helper of my hope. He will help me, becoming my refuge; but to those who hunt the soul of the righteous and condemn innocent blood he will repay their iniquity upon their own head, and turn their wickedness against them at the time of righteous judgment, when the Lord our God will also destroy them. That is why he was called "God of vengeance" at the beginning of the psalm. "Come, let us rejoice in the Lord; let us shout aloud to God our Savior." The superscription is not found among the Hebrews, and rightly so; for it would not have been reasonable to entitle as a psalm, or a hymn, or a song, a piece that calls the people of the Jews to rejoicing but threatens them with wrath and brings its exhortations to a gloomy close. Note whether "come" is said anywhere else in Scripture, and in what manner he calls those who have stood apart and gone far away to draw near to him; you will also observe that he always makes the call for good, as in "Come, children, listen to me," and "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord," and "Come to me, all you who labor," and "Come, you blessed of my Father." And in the psalm at hand he clearly urges them to come to rejoicing. Note, therefore, that those who think the yoke of godliness gloomy and grievous are mistaken; for he makes the call to good and joyful things. Set beside these "Depart into the eternal fire" and similar sayings, addressed to sinners as the opposite of "come." And since in times of war the victors are accustomed to raise a shout and cry aloud against the enemy, he fittingly commands not only to rejoice and exult but also to shout aloud over the saving victory. And who would our Savior and our God be, if not the Word of God, who said, "Take

courage, I have overcome the world"? He also rescued us from the demonic power that long held sway over us, and his name, Jesus, means "salvation" in the Hebrew tongue. Whom the word calls to rejoicing in the first place you would find by attending to what follows, where it is said, "As in the day of testing in the wilderness, where your fathers tested me." For by these words he clearly indicates the sons of those who provoked God in the wilderness, plainly those of the circumcision. These, then, he summons, saying, "Come, let us rejoice in the Lord." But he foretells that they will not obey the call; at any rate he says at the end: "They always go astray in heart. And they did not know my ways, as I swore in my wrath: they shall not enter into my rest." Since, then, they always go astray in heart, the psalm that follows fittingly calls all the nations to the new song and to rejoicing in God. "Let us come before his face with confession, and shout aloud to him with psalms." At his first coming the Word of God hid his divine face and put on the form of a servant; therefore it is said: "A man in affliction, and knowing how to bear infirmity; for his face was turned away, he was dishonored and not esteemed." But at his second coming he will appear with unveiled face and with power and great glory. Therefore the word, having first set out in the earlier verses what had to be done at his first coming, next and in due order reminds us of his second and glorious appearing, urging us to anticipate what is to come and to come before his face with confession. For it is good to anticipate and to forestall, and, before his face appears in glory, to obtain for ourselves through confession a cleansing for the sins we have committed. And the confession would be genuine if we shout aloud to him with psalms, that is, through the instruments of the soul, which are our bodies. Through these it is fitting to perform the shout spoken of, displaying the harmony of the divine Spirit and the holy rhythm by a temperate life and virtuous conduct. These things are said primarily to the people of the Jews, the word summoning them to the knowledge of our Savior; yet they could also be usefully applied to all of us. "For the Lord is a great God, and a great King over all the gods." What was enjoined above must be carried out in our Lord and Savior, that is, in the Word of God, both for other reasons and because, being by nature a great God, he is also a great King, as the only-begotten Word of God. And he is a great King over all the gods, or, according to Symmachus, "above all the gods": either the gods mistakenly believed in among the nations; or those like Moses, to whom it was said, "I have made you a god to Pharaoh"; or the gods of whom it was said,

[?Who will be likened] to the Lord among the sons of God?" "For in his hand are the ends of the earth, and the heights of the mountains are his." For this reason, too, let us rejoice and shout aloud to God: not only because he is Lord and God and a great King over all the gods, but because he has also brought the ends of the earth under his rule and made them subject to himself. For he asked this of the Father and received it, according to the words: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession." And if there were any heights of mountains, whether those honored in divine Scripture, such as Sinai, Horeb, Tabor, Mount Zion, the Mount of Olives, and any other like them, or their opposites, those long held by demons, on which the nations sacrificed to wicked demons as to gods, we have been taught that all these too belong to our Lord and Savior; for he was their maker. But perhaps the ends of the earth are in his hand because earthly things are governed under his hand, whereas the heavenly things, figuratively called heights of mountains, have something superior to the things on earth, since they are, as it were, his own possession and the dwelling place of his kingdom? "For the sea is his, and he made it, and his hands formed the dry land." Do not wonder, he says, if the ends of the earth are his, and if the heights of the mountains are his. Rather, learn that the whole element of watery substance, on which the earth is established, is his work: it is not only his possession but also his making. The sea, then, by which the whole element of watery substance is meant, he made; but the dry land his hands formed, perhaps because it is said, "God took dust from the earth and formed man," and again, "God formed from the earth all the wild beasts." It seems that the element of earth, being spherical, as they say, or shaped in some other way, likewise received its formation by the Word of God. That is why it is said precisely, and in accordance with natural reason: "And his hands formed the dry land." "Come, let us worship and fall down, and weep before the Lord who made us." Having set forth the divine power of the Lord through the preceding teaching, and having said above, "Let us come before his face with confession," the word now necessarily explains the manner of confession. Beginning the psalm very persuasively, he did not start from the gloomier things but from the more cheerful ones, so that those called would not turn away on hearing "let us fall down and weep" right at the beginning. Or perhaps he indicates two orders by these words: one the better, which

he calls first to praise and rejoicing; the second, the one that needs healing. That is why "Come, let us rejoice" is said first; then, after what has been said of the Lord's divinity and after the call of the first order, he passes on to the second and teaches them to use weeping and confession for their former sins, in place of water and sprinklings. And persuasively, after "let us weep before the Lord," by adding "who made us" he held out good hopes, teaching that we are not strangers to him but his work and his making; so it is fitting to expect kindlier things, since he cares for his own creation. Further, through "Let us fall down and weep before the Lord," he teaches us not to do this before men or for men's sake, but in secret, according to the saying, "Your Father who sees in secret will reward you." In general, then, what has been enjoined fits everyone; but properly and primarily the Word calls the people of the Jews to repentance for what they dared to do. "For he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand." He is not only our Lord, as a master of servants, nor only our maker, as our creator, but he is also our God, and a God who is good and merciful. Therefore he will spare us and have mercy on us, since we are not only his making but also his possession. The more rational are his people, while those still imperfect and less rational are the sheep of his hand; so that if we confess to him, and worship and fall down and weep before him, we shall certainly be saved, some as his people, others as the sheep of his hand. Indeed he is called the good shepherd, and we are taught to say, "The Lord is my shepherd, and I shall lack nothing." "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the provocation." Once before, he says, you hardened your hearts after hearing his voice in the wilderness; see, then, that you do not do the same a second time, if you hear his voice again when he has come among men today. The word is spoken primarily to those of the circumcision, and is uttered in the person of the choir of the prophets. At the beginning they said everything in the plural, counting themselves among those called; for they said, "Come, let us rejoice, and shout aloud, and come before him," and again, "Come, let us worship and fall down and weep." But here, speaking to others, they exhort them not to refuse the call, nor to disbelieve the voice that was to speak to them today. The Apostle took "today" to mean the whole span of our life, according to the words "as long as it is called today." And the word urges us, too, to begin from this point on what has been enjoined. For even if there has been much negligence in the time past, yet at least from the day called

today, and from the present time, let us be eager to attend to what has been said. Let us not emulate that people who, having heard God's voice at the vision in the wilderness, were hardened in heart at the time of the provocation, when their bodies were all strewn in the wilderness because they disobeyed the voice of God. He necessarily reminds us of them, so that we too, hearing God's commands on this day, today, and disobeying them, may not provoke him by hardening our hearts and refusing to obey the saving commands, and so make him a bitter and severe judge for ourselves. The command, then, fits all of us, as I said; but in the primary sense these things are said to the people of the circumcision, with this meaning: "Once already, long ago in the wilderness, having heard God's voice, you provoked him by hardening your hearts in the time of Moses. But since the same Word of God is about to speak to men a second time, appearing in this life, and to teach among you yourselves the mysteries of the New Covenant, see that you do not harden yourselves again as you hardened yourselves before, nor provoke him again if you hear his voice once more, nor imitate your fathers in this, so that you may not deprive yourselves of the true sabbath rest and of his rest. In that rest the Word of God himself will rest, having received his own kingdom and resting in it; and he will receive into the same rest all who receive him, and will grant his holy and true Sabbath to those who are worthy of rest beside him and with him." "As in the day of testing in the wilderness, where your fathers tested me; they put me to the proof and saw my works. For forty years I was angered with that generation, and I said: They always go astray in heart. And they did not know my ways, as I swore in my wrath: they shall not enter into my rest." How the fathers tested God in the wilderness (the fathers not only of the Jews of old, as one might suppose, but also of those who even today hear the voice of God yet are hardened) is set down in Moses, and is told many times in the seventy-seventh psalm and in the hundred and fifth, which you will find by searching for yourself. Since, then, for these reasons God swore that those who provoked him would not enter his rest, which the word has briefly set forth, we too must take forethought and [?]…

[?] …but our life with him after our departure from the present life, in which we shall rest in his kingdom, freed from every way of life that consists in action, and devoting ourselves solely to the contemplation of divine and heavenly things? Then pain and grief and sighing shall flee away, and idleness and release from evils, leisure and repose, and the true Sabbath will receive us. In a true Sabbath the Word of God himself will also rest. [?] In the sense that concerns the sensible world, he addresses the contents of the psalm to the people of the Jews, and exhorts them, if they should be counted worthy a second time, as first in the wilderness, to hear the voice of the Word of God, which was to speak to them again at his incarnation, not to emulate their fathers nor to provoke God again as before. In making such exhortations he seems to me to foretell and hint at their future unbelief in Christ, since he was not ignorant of what was to come. At any rate, he next adds, in the person of God, and says: "And I said: They always go astray in heart"; and again: "As I swore in my wrath: they shall not enter into my rest." For if the divine mouth does not lie, and it pronounced a decree and declared that they always go astray, and confirmed with an oath that they would not enter his rest, then it clearly foretold the future. Hence it appears that, as first under Moses, so a second time under the Lord, they went astray in heart and for this reason were deprived of the promise. Therefore, fittingly, after the present psalm the next one calls all the nations to the promise of God, since the former people did not obey. [Psalm title:] Of David, when the house was being built after the captivity. 95. "Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth. Sing to the Lord, bless his name." In the preceding psalm the word said about the people of the Jews, "They always go astray in heart," and "As I swore in my wrath: they shall not enter into my rest." Since it called them first to rejoicing in God and found them disobedient, it now passes on to the calling of the nations. And it addresses these words to the apostles and disciples of the Savior, as is clear from "Proclaim the good news of his salvation from day to day," said next, and "Declare his wonders among the nations"; for these words were put into effect through none other than the apostles of our Savior. Hence it fits that these words be addressed to them alone, because of the New Covenant and the new song of the gospel, which was preached to all the nations through them. These, then, are commanded to sing to the Lord a new song in all the earth; and this they fulfilled in deed, when their sound went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. The new song was the saving Gospel, which contained not the old ordinances of Moses but the precepts of Christ, suited to all the Greeks

alike; for those of Moses were not of this kind. In the first place, then, he commands them to sing the new song to the Lord himself. But since not all the earth was able to understand who the Lord was, nor to know the deeper teachings about the Lord, he necessarily adds next, in the second place, "Sing to the Lord, bless his name," with this meaning: even if the nations throughout the whole earth cannot understand who the creator of the whole world is, and who is the Lord and master of all things, and even if they cannot perceive how, being the creative Word of God, he directs and steers all things by an unseen and invisible power, yet it is enough for them, as an introduction, to bless his name. For the very name of the Lord, his bare title, when praised and blessed, is enough to bring the greatest benefit to those who bless it, more than to those who blessed Abraham, to whom it was said, "Those who bless you shall be blessed." Let those who have been counted worthy of the new world sing the new song after the captivity throughout the whole world. That is why the superscription of the psalm says, "When the house was being built after the captivity." When, then, the great house of God, his Church, was to be built among all the nations after the captivity of souls by the great and wise master builder, our Lord and Savior, of whom the prophet says, "He shall build my city and turn back the captivity of my people," then the Savior himself, about to fulfill in deed what had been foretold through the prophets, took in hand and read through the passage of Isaiah spoken in his own person: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach good news to the poor, to proclaim release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind." And folding up the book after the reading, he said, "Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing." He was teaching that he himself was the one anointed, not with bodily ointment like those anointed in a bodily way, but with the Spirit of the Father's divinity, and for this reason was proclaimed Christ; and that through him the Gospel was proclaimed to those held captive in their souls, in accordance with the prophecy. The prophets of the Jewish nation did not sing such things, nor did they proclaim good news to the people of their own time. They sang rather such things as Moses says to the people in the great song: "Blemished children, a crooked and perverse generation, is this how you repay the Lord? So foolish a people, and not wise"; and what follows, among which is also: "They provoked me with strange gods; with their abominations they embittered me. They sacrificed to demons and not to God"; and "They made me jealous with what is no god; they provoked me to anger with their idols." And Isaiah, singing a song in keeping with these, said: "Let me sing now to my beloved a song of my beloved concerning his vine[yard] [?]…

[?] …my vineyard. To these he adds: “What shall I do for my vineyard? For I waited for it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns. I will tear down its hedge, and it will be plundered; I will tear down its tower, and it will be trampled; and I will abandon my vineyard,” and what follows. Jeremiah too sang lamentations over the people of the Jews, and the other prophets likewise, bewailing their fall, sang songs suited to them. But the new song proclaimed to the nations was not like those; it contained promises of new and fresh blessings, addressed not to the people of the Jews but to all the earth. Very precisely the superscription says that the new song would be proclaimed to all the nations “when the house was being built after the captivity.” For in another sense too, after the captivity of the Jews and after their falling away and the wrath from God that came upon them, which the psalm before this one foretold when it said, “They always go astray in their heart, and they did not know my ways; so I swore in my wrath, they shall not enter my rest,” the people who inhabit the whole earth, barbarians and Greeks alike, when the house of God, namely his Church, was established among them, were taught to sing the new song, having put off the old song of demonic and polytheistic error. From then on they also proclaim the salvation of God, making use of the readings of the holy Gospels throughout the whole world. “Proclaim his salvation from day to day; declare his glory among the nations, his wonders among all the peoples.” And to whom should we think these commands are properly addressed, if not to those who later fulfilled them in deed, namely those who proclaimed the salvation of God to all the nations? For the divine Spirit was urging them from above, and long beforehand, to do this. To the same people he also addresses what follows, as to those who would declare the Lord's glory among all the nations and would herald his wonders among all the peoples. Who, then, were those who accomplished these things in deed? If it were possible to point to others, whether in the times of Cyrus or in those of Darius [?] … the commands set forth here are given to the disciples of Jesus, who hear: “Go and make disciples of all nations.” For the Holy Spirit wants them to accomplish the work of the gospel with intense and unceasing zeal; this is what “from day to day” indicates: that they should continually proclaim the salvation of which it was said, “This is truly the Savior of the world.” “Bring to the Lord, O families of the nations, bring to the Lord glory and honor; bring to the Lord the glory due to his name.” Not in vain did he command at the opening of the psalm that a new song be sung; rather, since the calling in this psalm is something new, the preaching is new. For the nations, as you see, who are called (sic), are required to sacrifice not calves or lambs, nor any external

offering of imperfect things (for everything irrational is deficient), but to sacrifice themselves, and they are commanded to bring glory and honor as to God. And since one must not only speak of God in words and correct doctrines but also offer sacrifices, he adds: “Take up sacrifices and enter his courts; worship the Lord in his holy court. Let all the earth be shaken before him; say among the nations, The Lord has become King,” and what follows. By sacrifices he means the rational and spiritual ones, which we see continually offered on behalf of the faithful and performed by the priests; and the virtues too are sacrifices of this kind. By courts he means the churches, in which the sacrifices of the New Covenant are offered: spiritual acts of worship, the bearing of fruit in good works, offerings of thanksgiving. Moreover, he did not give these commands to the Jews, so that no one might suspect he meant the sacrifices of the Law, but to the families of the nations, about whom God speaks through another prophet when addressing the Jews: “I take no pleasure in you, and I will accept no sacrifice from your hands; for from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice.” And it is well said, “Take up sacrifices,” that is, raise up your understanding of sacrifices: do not grovel on the ground slaughtering oxen and killing other animals, but understand loftily what these things signify, the spiritual and heavenly sacrifices, of which the sacrifices offered in a visible way were patterns and shadows. What sacrifices the psalm requires, blessed Paul reminds us when he says: “Present your bodies as a pure and living sacrifice, pleasing to God, which is your rational worship.” “And enter,” he says. By what path are we to come? Clearly through faith, for faith is the entrance to salvation. “Let the heavens rejoice and let the earth exult; let the sea be shaken, and all that fills it. The fields shall rejoice, and everything in them.” Instead of “Let the sea be shaken,” Aquila has “shall thunder,” and Symmachus “shall resound.” By these words Scripture signifies that the preaching of the gospel would pass through the open seas and the islands in the sea, and to the people who dwell on them, who are called “all that fills it.” And this too has come to pass. Indeed, churches of Christ now fill all the islands, and the saving teaching grows and advances daily, reaching as far as those who dwell by the Ocean. “[?] …of the forest before the face of the Lord, for he comes, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world in righteousness, and the peoples in his truth.”

“…let many islands be glad.” Since the superscription is found in the Septuagint translation, we shall say this: David often met with misfortunes, at one time when he was hunted by Saul, wandered in the deserts and lived among the foreigners, at another when he was occupied with wars. He sang the present psalm, I think, at the time when his land was settled, when both his mind and his kingdom had come to rest in calm, peace and tranquility after the destruction of all his enemies. Then, being in a state of peace, the prophet was moved by the divine Spirit to the teaching set forth here. But since among the Hebrews it is headed neither “song” nor “psalm,” you might say that what is set forth here is prophecy and plain teaching about the second and glorious coming of our Savior. Daniel too mentions this coming when he says: “I watched, and behold, on the clouds of heaven one like a Son of Man was coming, and he reached the Ancient of Days. And to him was given dominion and honor and the kingdom, and all peoples, tribes and tongues shall serve him. His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and his authority shall never be taken away.” Then, he says, “let all the earth exult,” that is, the new creation, and all the people of God who have dwelt on the earth from the beginning; or else those who are to inherit the heavenly land, according to the saying, “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.” For when bodily substance is changed into incorruption according to the principles of the resurrection, the earth will exult, since it too will be counted worthy of the kingdom of heaven. “Let many islands be glad”: many, not all, because of those who hold false beliefs, for the impious must not rejoice. For holy Scripture sometimes calls the churches islands, since they lie, as it were, in the sea of this world, surrounded by the bitter waters of its troubles and battered by persecutions as by the most violent waves, yet firmly fixed without falling, standing up high and not submerged by afflictions. For the churches are unshakable because of Christ, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against them. So if someone wishes to understand the islands as the churches from the nations, he will not stray from the proper aim. At any rate, they are renewed for [?] … newly established, rising up out of the brine of unbelief, and they gain a solid footing for God. So here too he rightly calls islands the souls of those who show steadfastness and immovability in times of trial: the brine of wickedness surrounds them on every side, yet when it strikes it has not strength enough to set the firm ground of virtue tossing. “Cloud and darkness are around him; righteousness and judgment are the foundation of his throne.” A cloud

is a very fine fabric of [?] air [?]; darkness is a murky [?] gloom. By both, Scripture magnifies the invisibility of the divine nature. For just as it is impossible to see what is covered by a cloud and by darkness, so it is altogether impossible to behold the divine nature. It also signifies the Lord's hidden descent among humans, when he was in the form of a servant, so that the flesh he assumed is to be understood as cloud and darkness, since it concealed his divinity, according to the verse: “He made darkness his hiding place; his tent was all around him.” It also reminds us that he is the same one who on Mount Sinai made his own [?] through cloud and darkness, and it teaches that, even if it is impossible to see the divine nature, yet one can behold its power through its activity. For he trained humans in righteousness, and taught those who did everything indiscriminately to live with right judgment. These things his throne and his kingdom accomplished; therefore he adds: “Righteousness and judgment are the foundation of his throne.” This, he says, was the reason for his coming: to judge our case justly, namely the case we had against the wicked and hostile powers. For Christ became our King in order to justify by faith those who were in sin. And he used a judgment befitting God and full of love for the good; for he justified us not by works of righteousness but according to his great mercy, and he saved us also through the holy and mystical water, in which the many-headed dragon was crushed and trampled, or rather perished, together with the evil powers with him. These things the kingdom of Christ accomplished. This is clear from the fact that we were set free from those who had unjustly enslaved us, while they were condemned. For this is a just judgment: to bring down the devil who played the tyrant, and to set free the humans he had tyrannized. Nevertheless, he also requires us to achieve righteousness and judgment. “Fire shall burn before him and set his enemies ablaze all around. His lightnings lit up the world; the earth saw and was shaken. The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord, before the face of the Lord of all the earth. The heavens declared his righteousness, and all the peoples saw his glory. Let all be put to shame who worship carved images, who boast in their idols.” In these words he shows the terrors of the power that repays, through the fire and the flashing lightning at Christ's second coming. He also reveals the illumination of the gospel, calling lightnings the words of the divine preaching that shine out over the whole world. For surely we do not say that he was speaking of the lightning that comes with rain; rather, by the name of lightning he signifies the shining forth of the divine and spiritual light. Or else he calls

the lightnings of Christ those who serve as priests of the divine preaching of the gospel, that is, the apostles and evangelists, who like light illuminated the world. To them Christ himself said: “You are the light of the world.” For he himself, the Son, is the true light that enlightens every rational creature. But since they too have become sharers in the light that comes from him, according to the verse, “Coals were kindled from him,” they are called the light of the world. So these became like lightnings, running everywhere under heaven and sending the divine and spiritual light into the hearts of those being initiated into the mysteries. And when the psalmist speaks of fire, he does not mean this fire perceived by the senses at all, nor the visible flame, but a divine power that is invincible, hard to withstand and hard to escape, devouring like fire those who are hostile to him. Foremost among these were the accursed demons and the master of their herd; him the Savior burned up together with the rest. For there was no other way to rescue those on earth who had fallen under his power, unless he let loose on him, like a fire, the wrath that consumed and destroyed him. In this way he rescued those who had fallen under him, saved those in captivity, delivered those who had gone astray, and called them into the light of truth. Perhaps David mentioned fire and lightning, that is, flame and light, because the action of fire is twofold: it has not only the power to burn but also the power to give light. The light is bestowed on the righteous, while the burning is reserved for the lawless. These too are the prophecies of the second appearing; these Daniel also saw: “A river of fire,” he says, “flowed before him.” And the Lord said that his coming would be like the lightning that reaches from east to west. His fire will go before him because of his enemies; but for the sake of pious and God-loving people, his lightnings, sent forth from his own light, will illuminate the world in place of the sun. For if at that time the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, according to the saving teaching, from where else will the world receive light, if not from him? For the Lord himself is eternal light. “Worship him, all his angels. Zion heard and was glad, and the daughters of Judea rejoiced because of your judgments, O Lord.” We should understand Zion to be the Church of Christ, and the daughters of Judea the apostolic souls who came from the nation of the Jews. They are filled with gladness and exultation as they learn of the Lord's judgments, both the punishments laid up for idolaters and the promises kept for the nations. And they rightly rejoice, since they are dedicated to him and hope to be counted worthy of his glorious coming. “For you are the Lord Most High over all the earth; you are exalted far above all gods. You who love the Lord, hate evil. The Lord guards the souls of his holy ones; from the hand of sinners

he will rescue them.” If, he says, you turn away from evil and become holy, then you will both obtain protection from God and be rescued from the hand of the devil, for he is the sinner in the proper sense. The way to love the Lord, then, is to hate evil; and its reward is to have him as the guardian of one's life and to prove stronger than the enemies who rise up against us. Do you see how great are the benefits we enjoy from loving God? We become holy by being dedicated to him, and we have God as the guardian of our greatest possession, our soul, so that we do not fall under the hand and power of the enemy. “Light has dawned for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart. Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous, and give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness.” A PSALM OF DAVID, 97. “Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done marvelous things.” This psalm too has the same meaning: it foretells both appearings of the Savior, but says more about the second. He rightly commands that a new song be offered to God, since he proclaims a change in the former state of things and foretells a new way of life. For the things done by the God of all for our salvation are extraordinary and astonishing. For the Savior came to dwell in the world, and by the grace of God tasted death for everyone in order to take away the sin of the world; and, as the following verses will show, he has counted us worthy of great and ineffable mysteries. “His right hand and his holy arm have saved for him.” That the Savior is the right hand and the arm of God has been shown in many passages where the right hand and the arm are mentioned. So his right hand saves, for God himself, those who are raised up to blessedness. For not everyone who is saved is saved for the Lord God, but only, and every one, who is set free from evils and passions in accordance with right reason and has received the knowledge of the truth together with godliness. For someone saved from diseases and wounds is by no means saved for God, especially when he does not believe that his health was given him by God. The arm of God is holy, not by receiving holiness through participation, but by being the arm of the Holy Spirit [?]. And perhaps the active power of God, which is none other than God the Word, is called the right hand because it does all things rightly, that is, in a holy, wise, blameless and praiseworthy way; and the arm because of its strength and surpassing might. “The Lord has made known his salvation; in the sight of the nations he has revealed his righteousness. He remembered his mercy to Jacob and his truth to the house of Israel. All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.” Having long ago promised Abraham that the nations would be blessed in his seed, he confirmed the truth of his words by the outcome of events; and the mercy he had promised on oath to grant, this he showed fulfilled in deed. These things closely resemble the prophecies of Isaiah, through whom the Father said to the Only-begotten: “I have given you as a covenant to the race, as a light to the nations, so that

you may be salvation to the end of the earth.” For since the God of all had promised the marvelous patriarchs and David that he would raise up Christ from their seed according to the flesh, and through him grant salvation to all people, he called the promise made to the fathers a covenant. And he called Israel his race, since Christ is from the Jews according to the flesh. “I have given you, then, as a covenant to the race,” that is, so as to fulfill the agreements made with the Jews; but as a light no longer to the Jews but to the nations. For the nations gained a share in salvation through faith, while the Jews loved the gloom of unbelief. David said the same thing here too: “He remembered his mercy to Jacob,” that is, to Israel; in other words, he fulfilled the promises made to them and brought them to effect. Therefore “all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.” For when the Gospel had been preached in all the world under heaven and throughout the inhabited earth as a testimony to all the nations, as Christ had foretold, all the ends of the earth saw Christ, the Salvation

“Shout to God, all the earth; sing, exult and make music. Make music to the Lord with the lyre, with the lyre and the sound of a psalm, with hammered trumpets and the sound of the horn trumpet. Shout before the King, the Lord,” and what follows. According to the letter, he says: join instruments of psalmody to your hymns. But according to the higher sense, the lyre is the active life and the sound of a psalm is contemplation. Glorify the Lord, then, he says, through action and contemplation; and alongside the psalm struck on the instrument, that is, the bodily activities that accord with virtue, let a voice also sing, namely contemplation of what ought to be done. By the lyre he means the harmony of the body with the soul. And one can see this law continually fulfilled in the churches, for on the spiritual lyre we strike up the divine melody. We too make our mouths into rational lyres, using our teeth in place of strings and our lips in place of bronze. The tongue, moving more swiftly than any plectrum, produces the harmonious sound of the notes, and the mind moves the tongue like a musician who skillfully guides its movements. This lyre is more pleasing to God than the lifeless one. He himself is witness to this, crying out through the prophet: “Take away from me the noise of your songs; I will not listen to the sound of your instruments.” “With hammered trumpets and the sound of the horn trumpet.” The words of the apostles of our Savior are called hammered trumpets because their faith was tested and refined by fire, and horn trumpets because of their active life. For horn trumpets are made from oxen, and the ox is a working animal. Paul too says of the apostles: “Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Surely he says it for our sake.” So the voices of the holy apostles of the Savior were at once hammered trumpets and horn trumpets. [?]

…the lyre: in another sense, do not hesitate to call the whole people of Christ a lyre, tuned together from different souls as from many strings and sending up one prayer and thanksgiving to God.

A PSALM OF DAVID. 98.

“The Lord has become king; let the peoples be angry. He who sits upon the cherubim, let the earth be shaken.” Among the Hebrews this psalm has no title. It too is one of the psalms that proclaim the good news of Christ’s kingdom. No one would say that anyone is angered because the God of the universe reigns over all things. But the present passage says that the peoples are angry at the kingdom of Christ, meaning those of the circumcision and those of the Gentiles who do not believe in him. Who this Lord is, he makes clear when he goes on to say: “He who sits above the cherubim.” The unbelievers are stung and grieved by jealousy over the salvation of the Gentiles, for they did not understand the prophetic words about his kingdom. “Let the earth be shaken.” The demons, who once had great power, were so weakened that all their powers were shaken and their workings ceased.
