And the people who dwell on the earth changed their minds, recognized how ruinous their ancestral error was, and enrolled God the Word as their Lord. Even those who did not believe in him were greatly shaken, stirred and astonished at the power of his teaching. He said “sits” because he was speaking to human beings, for the incorporeal nature cannot be contained or circumscribed. “The Lord is great in Zion, and he is high above all the peoples.” Zion means “watchtower.” Divine Scripture customarily uses this name for the whole godly commonwealth, and in this way it refers to those who look toward heavenly things, as the Apostle did when he said, “We look not at the things on earth but at the things in heaven.” Among these, then, the Lord is great. “Let them confess your great name, for it is fearsome and holy.” For now the peoples are angry at the kingdom of our Savior. But a time will come when they too will confess his great name, “when every knee shall bow, of things in heaven and on earth, and every tongue shall confess that Jesus is Lord, to the glory of the Father.” “And the honor of the king loves judgment.” The honor and virtue of the king are rightly joined with judgment, and so they make his name fearsome to some and holy to others. Those who transgress his law dishonor him by the very act of transgressing. In the same way, those who fulfill the divine law honor the King who gave it by the very act of keeping it. They love the judgment that comes from him, knowing that his judgment is just and that they will obtain divine rewards in keeping with his will, because they have lived piously and justly. “You have prepared uprightness; you have worked judgment and righteousness in Jacob. Exalt the Lord our God,” and so on. “Let no one suppose,” he says,

“that the Lord glorified here is someone other than the God who gave the law in the wilderness.” “For you, Lord,” he says, “whose kingdom we proclaim, are yourself the one who ordained judgment and righteousness for the people of the circumcision, through the legislation given to them, which contains ordinances and judgments. And you yourself have also prepared uprightness, to be given at the time of recompense to those who keep judgment and righteousness.” “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name. They called upon the Lord, and he heard them; he spoke to them in a pillar of cloud. They kept his testimonies and the commands that he gave them.” These verses carry the same meaning as the saying, “If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me.” He means that Moses, Aaron and Samuel, and any others, whether prophets or priests, called upon this very Lord who is here spoken of as God, and no other. This was the Word of God himself. He is now high above all the peoples and glorified among all the nations, and he is the one who heard them and spoke to them in a pillar of cloud. The men named here obtained such great honor for no other reason than that they kept his testimonies and the command he had given them. In the same way he has given us, through the New Testament, commands, precepts and testimonies. If we keep them, we too will be counted worthy of the same honor. “O Lord our God, you heard them; you were gracious to them, and yet you took vengeance on all their deeds.” “You,” he says, “our Lord and God, the King of the nations whom we proclaim, were the very one who listened to Moses and Aaron and those with them. You granted them such great freedom of speech when they sought to appease you on behalf of the people who provoked you, and you counted them worthy of great favor. Even if they fell into certain weaknesses, as human beings do, as Moses did through his unbelief about the water and Aaron through making the calf, you, as the all-good Son of an all-good Father, were gracious to them and granted pardon to mortal weakness.” “And you took vengeance on their deeds.” “Even if they seemed to sin in some way, as human beings,” he says, “you disciplined them where they needed discipline.” For Aaron was rebuked for his sin over the calf, and Moses over the water of [?]

“Exalt the Lord our God, and worship at his holy mountain, for the Lord our God is holy.” “Think nothing lowly or merely human about the Lord,” he says. “Exalt him by holding exalted views about him, and offer him the reverence that is his due.” In the past Zion was called the holy mountain, but now the holy mountain is the height of the knowledge of God. This is what Isaiah and Micah prophesied: “In the last days the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest”; [Notes: John 5:46; Isa. 2:2; Mic. 4:1 [?]]

that is, the knowledge of God will become plain to all. The Apostle also knows of a spiritual Mount Zion: “For you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.” So we have been commanded, according to the [?] (tradition?) given us by God, to offer worship to him who is our Lord, since we are his servants, and our God, since he is our Maker. Let us, then, understand the psalm in this more spiritual way.

A PSALM FOR CONFESSION. 99.

“Shout to the Lord, all the earth,” that is, all the nations on earth. With these words they are called to confess their former sins, in which they wallowed when they gave heed to the error of idolatry. That is why the psalm is entitled “For confession.” “Serve the Lord with gladness,” submitting yourselves to his yoke. To serve him is the same as serving light, serving life and truth, and serving righteousness and holiness, for the Lord is all of these. “Come in before him with rejoicing.” If anyone does not serve him with gladness, let him not dare to come in before him and enter his Church with unwashed feet. “Know that the Lord, he is God. He made us, and not we ourselves; we are his people and the sheep of his pasture.” For when we know that he is God, that he is the Lord, then by that very knowing we have come in before him, and we will also confess him as our Maker. That we do not make ourselves, even if we seem to be the cause of the birth of our children, is clear from this: Job and David were both born of a father and a mother, yet each of them says, “Your hands made me and fashioned me.” And God himself says to Jeremiah, “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you.” Again, when a woman spoke wrongly to her husband, saying, “Give me children, or else kill me,” the man, being wise, rebuked her with sound teaching: “Am I in the place of God, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?” Even if fathers seem to make their children, it is God who makes them. He is the cause, and they are co-causes, serving the command he gave in the beginning. That is why many who long to have children cannot. Symmachus renders it: “He made us when we did not exist; and we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand.” By these words he made known not only his lordship but also his care. He is not only our master but also our shepherd, who provides us with good pasture. We are his people, as of a king, and his sheep, as of a shepherd. The “people” are the better and more rational. The “sheep” are those of lower standing, who occupy a less rational rank and are not experienced in the divine oracles, as in the saying, “I went astray like a lost sheep.” Yet since he is the God and Maker of all, he calls all and makes all his own. “For God saves both men and beasts”: the former as his people, the latter as the sheep of his hand.

(COMMENTARY ON THE PSALMS.)

“Enter his gates with confession, his courts with hymns.” “Remember,” he says, “the evils in which you were first found, when you were far from the Lord and were led about by other, wicked masters. So, using the confession of your former impieties as a basin of sprinkling water, enter his gates with confidence. After the gates, that is, after the beginnings and first entrances into the service of God, you will pass into the innermost places and the courts. There you will no longer need confession, but from then on you will devote yourselves to hymns to him.” Just as one must first enter the gates and then the courts, so one must first confess one’s sins and then sing hymns to God, so that once the tongue has been cleansed by confession, a pure hymn may be offered. “Confess to him. Praise [?] his name, for the Lord is good; his mercy endures forever, and his truth from generation to generation.” “It is right,” he says, “to give thanks and sing hymns to him who shows unspeakable love for humankind and brings his good promises to fulfillment.” What he promised in the generation of our forefathers he has fulfilled in ours, and the salvation he announced he has truly bestowed. The kindness he has shown us will never cease, and that kindness is truth, as in the verse, “He remembered his covenant forever.” Or “Confess” may mean: lay bare the wounds of your soul through confession, as to a physician. Do this with confidence, since you have learned a true teaching about him: that he is good, abundant in mercy and true, and that in every generation his words are full of truth.

A PSALM OF DAVID. 100.

“Of mercy and judgment I will sing to you, O Lord; I will sing psalms and understand in a blameless way. When will you come to me?” That is: I will sing of your mercy and your judgment, describing how it is your way not first to judge and then to show mercy, but first to show mercy and then to judge, and to pronounce your sentences with love for humankind and with mercy. Or: “Since I myself practice mercy and judgment toward my neighbors, I take courage to come forward to sing and make music to you. Understanding how this must be done, I keep my ways blameless and irreproachable, convinced that this is how to make music to you pleasingly, through good works. So come to me now, O Lord, and you will find a dwelling ready with me, since all good things have been prepared, as I wait for the time when you will come to me.” “I walked in the innocence of my heart in the midst of my house. I set no lawless thing before my eyes; I hated those who commit transgressions.” Most people put on a show in the marketplaces and appear dignified and reasonable. But in their own houses they no longer hide their character, and they are exposed as worthless. “But I,” he says, “walked in the innocence of my heart in the midst of my house, with no evil thoughts coming out from within my heart. So I never sinned by deliberate choice;

and if I fell into some human failing, it did not happen by my intention.” “A crooked heart did not cling to me.” The counsels of the devil are crooked and perverse, since there is nothing straight in them. “I never received them into my heart,” he says. “And knowing that whoever clings to a righteous man will be righteous, I refused to let any perverse man join himself to me and cling to me.” For the straight cannot be joined to the crooked, since they do not fit together. “When the wicked one turned away from me, I did not know it.” The perfect man has no crooked heart in which the wicked one can work, and he is filled with God, so the wicked one finds no place in him and turns away from him. “And when he turned away,” he says, “I did not know it,” because I had no awareness of his presence: “I had no thought or deed of his within me.” You may also understand this of a wicked man: “I was not aware of him either when he approached or when he withdrew. That is how little account I took of such pests. I pretended to know nothing of them, for I did not think it fitting to be their friend.” Was this, then, out of pride? “Not at all,” he says. “But knowing that bad company corrupts good morals, I did not associate with the wicked.” “The one who secretly slandered his neighbor, him I drove out.” “Whether it was a man,” he says, “or a thought suggesting to me something evil against someone, I cast it out of my heart like a dog that bites by stealth.” The earnest person loves to be open in everything. Just as he rejects things done in secret, because they deserve shame, so he cannot bear to speak or hear anything against someone covertly. Such a thing belongs to a malicious and ignoble character, and danger hangs over the practice, as Scripture says: “Do not love to slander, lest you be cut off,” and, “Do not speak against one another, brothers, lest you fall under judgment.” We should set out, in outline, what slander is. Speaking about someone in just any way, even in secret, is not slander. We often speak badly of someone who is absent, not because we want to slander him, but because we are grieved that he is perhaps a bad man, and we try to talk about him with people who care about him as we do and are concerned for him out of friendship. Whoever speaks against an absent person in this way is not a slanderer. The slanderer, by contrast, is eager to speak against him and does so with pleasure. He is not grieved that the other has done such things; he even rejoices. He tells what he knows about the man to those who hate him and who are able to spread it abroad to many others. But what does the added word “secretly” mean, when it is obvious that all slander happens in secret? Either it simply states the fact, or we must draw a distinction. Of those who speak against others, some abuse them to their face, when they are present, and these are usually called revilers and insolent people, though by speaking against someone they too would be slanderers. Others speak against the people they accuse secretly, while they are absent. The one who belongs to this second class,

then, is the one the saint says he drove out, not those who heap abuse on someone to his face. For the person against whom the abuse is directed is present and will either defend himself or, if he is shown to be such a man, will be put to shame. Secret slander may also be distinguished from accusation before judges. Such accusation is slander of a kind too, but it is not done in secret. To reject the wicked, then, is the fruit of a holy mind. But to slander a brother, and to do so secretly rather than to his face so that the accused cannot be present to defend himself, is proof of the utmost wickedness. Whoever slanders another in our presence will not refrain from slandering us in front of others. So such a person should rightly be banished as a common enemy, since he imitates the serpent in paradise, who deceived Eve by slandering God. As for us, let us neither speak ill of others nor lend our ears to those who do. “Do not receive an idle report,” Scripture says. It did not say “Do not believe it,” but “Do not receive it.” That is why the Prophet too says, “I drove out the slanderer.” He did not say, “I did not believe him,” or “I did not accept what he said,” but that he actually drove him away as an enemy. Say to the slanderer: “If you have someone to praise, I open my ears to receive the perfume. If you want to speak ill, I block the entrance against your words, for I will not put up with taking in dung and filth.” Muzzle the slanderer when he speaks in your hearing, so that you do not commit a double sin along with him, both training yourself in a deadly passion and failing to stop him from babbling against his neighbor. Do not give your ear to the slanderer’s tongue, nor your tongue to the ear of the fault-finder, by gladly speaking or listening against your neighbor. Otherwise you will fall away from love and be found a stranger to eternal life. Condemning, despising and slandering are different things. To slander is to say something against someone, for example, “So-and-so lied,” or “got angry,” or “committed fornication,” or something of the kind, for such a person has spoken with passion about his brother’s sin. To condemn is to say, “So-and-so is a liar, a fornicator, an angry man.” Here he has condemned the very disposition of the man’s soul and passed judgment on his whole life, saying that this is what he is. It is one thing to say, “He got angry,” and another to say, “He is an angry man.” To despise is, as it were, to loathe one’s neighbor and to be disgusted by him as by something repulsive, and this is even more deadly than condemning. “He who acts proudly did not dwell in the midst of my house.” Above he spoke of a proud friend; here he speaks of a servant: “I chose to have no arrogant person living with me. Such a one was not given the first place or freedom of speech in my house, as someone in the midst of the house would have boldness and liberty, for such a one is always in his master’s sight.” To act proudly is to act with boastfulness. He might also mean, “No thought suggesting pride dwelt in my heart.” “He who speaks unjust things did not prosper before my eyes.” In
short: “I turned away from all injustice and did not tolerate it even in words. Whoever spoke unjust things achieved nothing; he did not prosper before me; he did not succeed [?]

“In the mornings I killed all the sinners of the land, to destroy from the city of the Lord all who work injustice.” He shows how exact, unerring and sober his justice was. “Neither anger nor drunkenness prompted me to kill,” he says. “Even if anger had provoked me the day before, it was softened over the long night. And even if I had drunk heavily in the evening, sleep had thinned it out well enough. So I armed myself against those who sin against God with clean hands and a clean mind, and my reasoning was not thrown off by a judgment formed under wine or under anger.” And he killed the sinners, not of the whole earth without qualification, but of the land under his rule; and not all at once, but now this one, now that one. Or rather, it is surely clear to everyone that this is said in a veiled way, as a riddle. The passage does not mean, “At the beginning of each day I stained my hands with human blood.” Besides being abominable, that would also be implausible. How could he, every morning, kill with his own hand all the sinners of the land? One man cannot overpower everyone, since sinners are presumably many. And if he had overcome them in war, he would have killed them all in a single morning, not killed them with his own hand every morning. What, then, does it mean? Let us listen to these words with more understanding, so that we do not accuse the prophetic oracles of falsehood, which would be wrong. The city of the Lord is the constitution of the human being. The sinners of the land are those of whom the Savior says: “From within, out of the heart, come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies. These are what defile a person.” These sinners of the earth, that is, those that come from the earthly flesh, are the ones that a person who purifies himself destroys from his own constitution with every thought of God. Morning and dawn come in the soul at each rising of saving teaching, and at that time all the thoughts that work lawlessness must be destroyed. For unless the first movements of the soul toward wickedness are cut out, our thoughts will inevitably go on to action. For example, the thought that suggests adultery is a sinner of the land; it is what brings about looking at a woman so as to desire her. Suppose this thought is not killed out of the soul, as with a sword, by the cutting word that destroys the passions, and suppose this does not happen in the morning, that is, as soon as it is brought out into the open (for everything that is made manifest is [light]). Then, after the adultery of the heart, it will lead the person on to a greater sin than this, to the one committed through [?]

…calling himself out to the activity of the body. This, then, is what David says: "I chastised the sinful and passionate thoughts that spring from the earthly body with morning prayers and with constant attendance on God. By the light of knowledge and by the disclosure that comes through confession, I sifted out and utterly destroyed the passions of the body and the lawless thoughts from my heart." For this is the city of the Lord, as the house of the Holy Spirit, according to the words: "Its foundations are on the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob. Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God." Since, then, the prosperity of vice is truly a blow against the virtues, it is good for those who have emulated the prophetic word to make morning for themselves, in order to kill all the sinners of the land and to destroy from the city of the Lord all the thoughts that work lawlessness. The city is the soul, and the destruction of these thoughts becomes the life of the better ones, according to the words: "I will kill and I will make alive; I will strike, and I will heal, and there is none who will deliver out of my hands." For when the members that are on earth are put to death, and the body is buffeted and brought into subjection, the occasions of sin that arise from the flesh can no longer stir up thoughts in the soul that hurry to commit lawlessness for the enjoyment of pleasure. From then on the better things live. We must therefore not only slay the passions of the body but also destroy the passionate thoughts of the soul. For the "sinners of the land" are the passions of the body, while those who "work lawlessness" and are destroyed from the city of the Lord are the lawless thoughts of the soul. In the literal sense he says, "I killed the sinners," in order to destroy the transgressors, so that lawlessness, seeing the severity of the punishment, might shrink back and vanish. The "morning" indicates zeal for speed, and what is lawful is the removal of the wicked; for "Remove," it says, "the wicked one from among you." [?] [A prayer of the poor man, when he is weary, and before the Lord] pours out [his supplication] [?]

"Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you. Do not turn your face away from me," and so on. Since the title reads, "A prayer of the poor man, when he is weary, and pours out his supplication before the Lord," you will understand the poor man spoken of here by comparing him with the one who is called blessed, according to the words: "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." The words "Blessed are those who weep and mourn, for they will be comforted" would also fit the weary poor man. Everyone, then, who is devoted to God, poor in the affairs of this life but rich toward God, is gripped by weariness when he grieves, or by despondency, as Symmachus renders it, at the wickedness and ruin of the many. Such was the one who said: "Woe is me, for the godly man has perished from the earth,

and there is none among men who does right; all go to law for blood; each one oppresses his neighbor with oppression." Such too was the one who said: "There is none who does good." In these circumstances, however, the poor man, weary and despondent, devises for himself a remedy to heal his suffering. This was prayer to God, which was his only consolation. Through it he spreads out his soul and brings [?] all his thoughts before God, and so he is said to pour out his supplication before the Lord, or, as Symmachus has it, his words. But the one who is poor according to God, that is, the choir of the prophets, filled with grief at the overthrow of the former people, also prays to the Lord, sending up supplications for the people with fasting and tears, so that the people too might be pitied. "On whatever day I am afflicted, incline your ear to me." Here let the saying of Isaiah be quoted: "Lord, in affliction we remembered you; in slight affliction your chastening was upon us." One ought, however, to give oneself to supplication even before being afflicted, and not only in times of crisis. Yet the saint prays not that he may escape affliction, for that is impossible, but that when afflicted he may not be overcome, and that, rejoicing in hope, he may endure his afflictions and even boast in them. For affliction produces hope through endurance and proven character. "Hear me, then," he says, "on whatever day I am afflicted, inclining your loving ear to me." God is said to incline his ear because human strength and human crying cannot reach up to the height of his Godhead. Therefore he himself, stooping down from his majesty, inclines his hearing to those who are counted worthy to be heard. The words "On whatever day I am afflicted" mean: not only now, but throughout my whole life, and above all in afflictions, for that is when help is most needed. Or perhaps it is said not of a future affliction but of a present one. For he means: since this is the day whose weight cannot be borne, bend down and give swift help. "On whatever day I call upon you, hear me speedily." And what is the urgency? What is the reason for the speed, and what kind of reason is it? "For my days have vanished like smoke." By the smoke he shows how brief and insubstantial they are. "And my bones have been parched like kindling. I was struck down like grass, and my heart withered, because I forgot to eat my bread. Because of the sound of my groaning my bone has cleaved to my flesh." The prophetic choir, or else David, makes its own what befell the people. It shows that all their strength, by which the worship prescribed by the Law had been upheld, was destroyed and lost. This strength was the high priesthood, the temple, the sacrifices of animals, and the self-rule of the nation. On a higher level, the one who is poor according to God teaches as his first achievement that the days of his transient life have vanished like smoke, since he spends them without glory and unnoticed. You will understand this from what Job says: "When

the lamp shone above my head; when I was very wealthy." The lamp shone for him then, while he was prospering. But when all his possessions had fallen away, he too might have said: "For my days have vanished like smoke." Such is the one who is poor according to God: he spends the days of his transient life without glory and unnoticed. Then, subjecting himself to fasting and hardship, he wears himself down and parches himself with hunger and thirst. And since "all flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass," he says, as he withers his own flesh, "I was struck down like grass." True groaning, which also has a voice that God hears, wastes the body and brings about the deadening of the flesh, so that the inner man is renewed. You may also take it this way. The smoke of a fire that is being put out vanishes; it lasts only as long as the fire that it accompanies is burning. "So that my days, then," he says, "may not vanish as well, take away my afflictions. It will not be for my good if the light that makes my days is put out in me. If my afflictions persist, they will cause my days to vanish; and if they remain, they will parch my bones still more," that is, the vigorous and most steadfast powers of the soul, which are parched by the burning of the soul's passions. He says that his heart has withered because it has nothing cheerful and nothing in which to take delight. For he has been so hard pressed by his present troubles that he can no longer be nourished with the bread that suits and befits his more precious substance. One can partake of this bread only when one is not dragged about or troubled by external things. He says that he had gone so long without being nourished by this bread that he had even forgotten ever having tasted it. "Groaning greatly because of my present troubles, I let out so intense and continuous a groan that, through my voice raised in wailing, my bone has cleaved to my flesh and in a way become one with it. In my great dryness, all the moisture spread through my body has been drained away by the affliction that has come upon me. For when I still had this moisture, it fattened the bone and kept it apart from the flesh, filling the space between flesh and bones." "I have become like a pelican of the wilderness": that is, fleeing the pastimes of the crowd, I lived alone and withdrew from human company. For this creature, the pelican, is said to love solitude. He also depicts the desolation of the nation, at the time when only one or two here and there, and a few others, were to be found, such as Jeremiah or Baruch, or another of those left behind at that time, in whose person these words are spoken. The Lord too is likened to a pelican of the wilderness because of this bird's most wonderful tenderness toward its young. This creature builds its nests beside sheer rocks, and so ensures that its chicks are not easily destroyed by any of their enemies. But when their father has flown away, the serpent, since it cannot get near the nest, pours upon them from afar

its venom. It watches where the wind is blowing from, and from there it breathes its venom on the chicks, and they die. But the parent flies back to them, and since it knows of the plot by natural instinct, it also knows how they will be brought back to life. It looks for a cloud and flies up high, and from above it gently flutters its wings over them. Then, beating its sides hard with its wings on either side, it lets drops of blood fall on them. These drops, dripping down through the cloud, put a life-giving power into the dead chicks, and they rise. The pelican, then, is taken to mean the Lord, the chicks the first-formed humans, the nest [?] paradise, and the serpent the apostate devil. Through disobedience the devil breathed upon the first-formed humans who had been placed in paradise, and he put death into them. But Christ, out of his love for us, was lifted up high on the cross and pierced in his side. From there he let fall his life-giving blood, and through the cloud of the Holy Spirit he brought us back to life when we had been put to death. "I have become like a night raven in a ruined house." The night raven is timid. So it flees from everywhere, lodges in the ruins of houses, and cries out at night out of fear. By the pelican, then, he signified the utter desolation of the people. By the night raven he shows the darkness that had seized the people: the light that shone on them had been put out, so they were as if in darkness and night, without knowledge of God. Perhaps, too, the saint rightly compares himself to the night raven because he cried out all night long in prayer. "I kept watch, and became like a sparrow alone on a housetop. All day long my enemies reproached me, and those who praised me swore against me." I became a laughingstock to my foes. I, who was once envied and renowned, have now become an oath to those who once admired me; for they swear by my misfortunes: "May I not suffer what So-and-so has suffered." "And those who praised me swore against me," as though I did not have God as my helper. It was not only the enemies of God who did this; even those who loved me swore against me, that is, those of the same nation and race. They at any rate refused to believe the very same prophecies. They disparaged the consolations and the promises of things to come, and swore against me that they would not believe what I had prophesied. "For I ate ashes like bread, and mingled my drink with weeping." Similar to these are the words in Psalm 79: "You will feed us with the bread of tears, and give us tears to drink in full measure." By these words he shows how extreme his pain was. For if the time of eating was full of pain, what other time could be free of it? "I am overwhelmed by these evils," he says, "since you, Master, have stirred up your anger against me." The Prophet says this as he makes the people's misfortune his own and laments the destruction of so great a multitude: "Because of your anger and your wrath; for you lifted me up and dashed me down." He makes his own what befell the people and the place, teaching that

the people had been raised to great glory, so that they were called the people of God, and this house was named the house of God because of the sanctuary within it. God lifted them up and honored them to match the glory to which they had been raised. Then, bringing them to the opposite state, he dashed them down, handing the place over to siege and utter desolation and the people to captivity. "My days have declined like a shadow, and I have withered like grass." For all flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass. Again, sharing in what is said of the people, he adds: "And I have withered like grass." "But you, Lord, endure forever, and your remembrance from generation to generation." "Mortal and human things," he says, "are such as has been shown: changeable and uneven, never staying in the same state. They are lifted up and dashed down, exalted and humbled, and they undergo every kind of turn and change because of the wickedness that dwells among human beings. But you, Lord, have nothing mortal or perishable. You endure forever, always the same and unchanging, since you are eternal and unalterable. What you have once decreed and ordained by promise remains as an everlasting memorial, if not for the present generation, then for the one to come, as the psalm says. This above all ought to move you, Master: that my nature is so perishable and short-lived, and I have been yoked to such great misfortunes, while you are eternal and immortal. So you could easily grant me some change in my present evils." This is what he adds: "You will arise and have pity on Zion, for it is time to have pity on her, for the time has come." "Grant," he says, "a change for the better in our misfortune. The time calls for mercy, for the period of our wretchedness has been completed." By these words he hints at the end of the punishment and captivity that had been limited to seventy years. So too the wonderful Daniel, having counted the years of the captivity, offers his supplication, and the words of the spiritual song agree with these. And Zechariah said in prayer: "Lord Almighty, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, which you have disregarded? This is the seventieth year." I think that the appearing of Christ among human beings is also prophesied here, which would be the cause of Zion's rebuilding, that is, of the opening up of the commonwealth of godliness. And what is the much-prayed-for and deeply longed-for time in which the things promised to Zion are said to be fulfilled? It is the time of your resurrection, Lord. For you came to take away the sin of the world, and it was not fitting for one so great to come and suffer for a few sinners. So when the time came of which it is said, "All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God," then you tasted death for all.

"For your servants have taken pleasure in her stones, and they will pity her dust. And the nations will fear your name, Lord, and all the kings your glory." Fittingly, alongside the delight taken in the stones of the former people, he adds the calling of the nations, and he shows more clearly that one day they will take up the fear that brings salvation and will worship God. By "kings" he means kingdoms. For there is no nation and no kingdom that does not worship the glory of Christ, either wholly or in part. "For the Lord will build up Zion, and he will be seen in his glory." In another sense the Lord will build Zion, that is, the Church. By building I mean that by which the nations were created through faith, and then he will be glorified in them. "He has looked upon the prayer of the lowly, and has not despised their petition. Let this be written for another generation, and a people that is being created will praise the Lord. For he has looked down from his holy height; the Lord looked from heaven upon the earth, to hear the groaning of the prisoners, to set free the sons of those put to death, to proclaim the name of the Lord in Zion and his praise in Jerusalem, when peoples are gathered together, and kings, to serve the Lord. He answered him in the way of his strength: They declared to me the fewness of my days. Do not take me away in the midst of my days." On a higher level, it seems to me that by these words the prophetic choir signifies the calling of the nations through our Savior, and laments that they themselves did not share in it. For in the presence of the good things to come, the nations and their kings will worship no longer their ancestral demons but the Lord. "At that very time," he says, "the Lord weakened my strength and cut short my days, so that I would not live to see that time." It is the prophetic choir, then, that answers, or rather asks, and says to God what our life will be like. For it prayed to learn whether its life would last until those days in which the Only-begotten, having become man, was to appear on earth. He calls his coming on earth "the way of his strength," for he came to bind the strong man. And the "midst" of his days, or of his course of life [?], is the period until he comes to behold the appearing. He prayed, then, that his whole time would be completed and his life somehow extended, so that he might be counted worthy of the actual outcome of events; for in this way his whole life would be fulfilled. "For the time being," he says, "at present, as I prophesy these things and foresee what is to come, I seem to be in part of God's day. But I lack the sight, with my own eyes, of the outcome of what is prophesied. If I obtain it, I shall receive my life complete. But if my prayer fails, I am like those who lay down their life incomplete and untimely in the midst of their days." And it seems to me that it was because of such prayers of the prophets that our Savior said: "Many prophets and

righteous men longed to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it." In the historical sense he says: "Seeing myself feeble and weighed down, I suppose that little time of life remains to me. May I not depart from the body halfway through my days, with them unfinished." "Your years are throughout the generation of generations." He has had to say beforehand, "Do not take me away in the midst of my days," and has prayed that his life be extended until the outcome of what was prophesied. Then he sees that this is impossible because of the weakness and brevity of mortal nature, and so he says: "Your years alone, Lord, stretch from generation to generation. You will come to that generation and to that people, of whom it was said above, 'Let this be written for another generation,'" and so on. "In the beginning you, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain." "If you had not been there in the beginning, O Lord," he says, "and if the heavens were not the works of your hands, it would not be possible for them to be changed or to undergo alteration. For if they were uncreated, they would also have remained without end. But as it is, since you are their maker, you are also able to make them pass away when you will. For they are of a corruptible and perishing nature, since they did not exist before and came into being by your will and power. Only one thing remains forever and can never cease to be: you yourself, the sole maker of all things." "And they will all grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will roll them up, and they will be rolled up." Even the heavens, though they are a great and exceptional creation, will nevertheless themselves be subjected to corruption. But this corruption will become their renewal, and you will draw them together as easily as one rolls up a cloak. They will be rolled up as they are changed into a better form; they will be changed and will undergo a good transformation, from oldness to renewal and incorruption. "But you are the same, and your years will not fail. The sons of your servants will dwell secure, and their seed will be directed forever." When they have been made new and refashioned for the better, their seed too, that is, the seed of your servants, will be directed forever. "Bless the Lord, O my soul." Perhaps it is because the soul is left in between the body and the spirit. The body drags it down to its own desires and slavish pleasures, as though casting it down from a height above. But the spirit draws it back up to itself, leading it upward toward God, and urges it to remember the Lord, to bless him, and to keep him always before its eyes. Or else he commands himself to rouse himself to the hymn and to bless God, setting before himself the blessing of God as a fine remedy for his salvation. "And all that is within me, his holy name." He commands what is within him to bless the name of the Lord, that is, by the nature of the things that come forth from within…

…of thoughts, of which there are two classes: some are wicked, such as murders, adulteries and thefts; others are noble and saving, such as love for others, self-control and fellowship. So whoever has set everything within him in order, ready to bless the holy name of God, does well to bring his inner disposition into his thanksgiving to God. He consecrates everything within him and all the powers of the soul, and he stirs every thought to the divine hymn. For by “what is within” he meant the thoughts and reflections, all the movements of the soul and its various powers: the intellect, the reasoning faculty, sight, impulse, imagination, memory and the rest. There are many powers and various movements in the soul. Through them we sometimes think about something serious, sometimes desire, sometimes are desired (1), and sometimes judge. At times we reach for certain things, and at other times we turn away from them. Again, at times we are driven forward, and at other times we shrink back. Sometimes we are in a sorrowful state, and at other times we are kindly, cheerful and at ease. So the divine Spirit urges all these powers of the soul together to bless the Lord. Someone might wish to take the saying in a more bodily sense. He could say that all the inward parts of our body, the entrails and organs, have been made by the deepest wisdom of God, so that nothing in us is useless, and the concord and harmony of all of them with one another contributes to glorifying and blessing God. In that case these too are rightly called to bless God. If, however, the text gives the soul itself a bodily shape and wraps bodily parts around what has no parts, we will understand the parts given to the partless soul in another way. We will fittingly take the head as the mind, and the neck as opinion, since it stands between the rational and the irrational. The breast will be anger, and the belly desire, and we will use the names of the parts as symbols of the powers. “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget his recompenses: he is merciful to all your iniquities, heals all your diseases, redeems your life from corruption, and crowns you with mercy and compassion.” These are God’s recompenses toward us. First, he made atonement for our sins, which we committed in error and idolatry. He was merciful to each of them, anticipating every plea and granting forgiveness through his atonement, which is Christ. Second, even after forgiveness, O soul, you happened to fall sick, having slipped into human passions. The Saviour healed these diseases too, with the rational and saving remedies laid down in his divine Scriptures. Third, besides these, your life was about to pass into corruption and be swallowed up by death, according to the saying, “The soul that sins shall die.” Acting in keeping with his (1) “We desire … we are desired”: one or the other.

mercy, he redeemed it, giving the blood of the Only-begotten to death as a ransom for you. Fourth, since no one is justified by works, he used his own love for humanity, mercy and compassion and crowned you with the gift of adoption. In short, it is he who has granted you forgiveness of sins and healing of the passions, the hope of resurrection and the pledge of the Spirit. He has clothed you in the tunic of incorruption and saved you by grace, for the crown is a gift of grace and love for humanity. All these are the bridegroom’s wedding gifts and presents, for the bride brought nothing but faith. Not only that, but he has also filled you with spiritual goods and satisfied your desire with good things. He forbids [?] the cold [?] soul, but gives good things to those who ask him. If you want to see sufferings and sins undone at the same moment, you have the paralytic, who enjoyed this double grace. He heard, “Your sins are forgiven you,” and, “Take up your bed.” In the same way the sinful woman obtained forgiveness, and so did the thief and the tax collectors, and in short all who believed. “He fills your desire with good things; your youth will be renewed like an eagle’s.” So the soul is renewed when it has put off the old man and put on the new, which is being renewed to the knowledge of the one who created it. “In this way,” he says, “your youth will be renewed, so that it no longer grows old or passes into corruption again, but always remains young in incorruptible life.” The eagle is the most kingly of birds and flies the highest. It alone among living creatures can face the blaze of the sun’s light and look at it steadily. So he rightly compared to the eagle’s nature the soul’s renewal, its flight from earth to heaven, and the life it will live in the highest light. “The Lord performs acts of mercy, and justice for all who are wronged. He made his ways known to Moses, his wishes to the children of Israel.” From that same Scripture of Moses you will learn what justice he gave to the wronged. With just judgment he went after the Egyptians and punished them with God-sent plagues on behalf of the children of Israel, whom they had wronged. “The Lord is compassionate and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in mercy. He will not be angry to the end, nor keep his wrath for ever. He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities. For as high as heaven is above the earth, so has the Lord made his mercy strong toward those who fear him. As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our iniquities from us. As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him, for he knows how we are formed. Remember that we are dust. As for man, his days are like grass; like a flower of the field, so will he bloom.

For a wind passes over it, and it will be gone, and its place will know it no more.” He brought us across from the darkness of ignorance that comes from sin to the light of knowing him. He did this as a good father does: such a father feels compassion for sons who have lost their minds and shows even greater pity to children in a bad way. In the same way he too had compassion on us, turning us from godless people without fear of him into devout people who fear him. “But the mercy of the Lord is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him, and his righteousness on their children’s children: on those who keep his covenant and remember his commandments, to do them.” The saying “showing mercy to those who love me” is similar. The mercy of the Lord, together with its partner righteousness, reaches through every generation to those who fear him and to their children. These children are those who imitate their works. They do not merely remember his commandments; they add deeds to words and shape their own lives by them. The commandments are not given so that we may simply remember and know them. We are to remember them in order to do them. The Saviour shows this too when he says, “Whoever has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me.” The reward is for doing them, not just for remembering them, and it is not the hearers but the doers of the law who will be justified. God’s law is rightly called a covenant, that is, a testament, so that we who keep it may hope to receive an inheritance from it. Our nature is perishable, yet God’s love for humanity keeps the reward owed to the ancestors for their righteousness and pays it even to their descendants. You could find countless proofs of this. Because of the righteousness of Abraham, and of Isaac and Jacob, God later judged the people descended from them worthy of his calling and his own care. He kept the kingdom for Jehu’s house to the fourth generation, though Jehu had not attained perfect piety and had only shown zeal at the beginning of his reign. For the divine David he kept the spark of his line from going out, even though many impious men arose among his descendants. “The Lord has prepared his throne in heaven, and his kingdom will rule over all.” The wording is precise: “will rule over all,” not “rules over all,” since not everyone is worthy of his kingdom. That is why the Saviour promised the kingdom of heaven to those who succeed in living the gospel life. Yet in another sense he does rule over all, for as Lord of all he has power even over those unworthy of his kingdom. “Bless the Lord, all you his angels, mighty in strength, who do his word, hearing the voice of his words.” Earlier the divine Spirit called the human soul to thanksgiving and to blessing God, saying, “Bless the Lord, O my soul.” But now, since he has mentioned the throne of God

and the heavenly dwellings that God has prepared for the worthy, he quite naturally bids the heavenly powers rejoice with the soul at its salvation. This agrees with the Saviour’s saying that there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents. He also leads the human soul and the heavenly powers to the same goal, since he gives the same work of blessing to both. “Mighty in strength, who do his word, hearing the voice of his words.” “Your own powers, O soul,” he says, “are too weak to praise God as he deserves. Still, do it in part. Know [?] that his angels bless him fittingly and worthily, for they are mighty in strength and do his word [?] unfailingly, and they are worthy to hear his voice and his words.” There may also be some among human beings who pursue a life equal to the angels. They bear the image of the heavenly one, and they too are able to do his word and capable of obeying his voice. They can say with the one who said, “I can do all things in him who strengthens me.” Let these too, being equal to the angels, bless him. But let none of those who break his word and refuse to listen to his voice rashly dare to do this. “Bless the Lord, all his powers, his ministers who do his will.” Since there are also hostile powers, David very necessarily adds, “his ministers who do his will.” In this way he shows which powers he wants to bless God, and what kind. He does not mean all of them, nor the opposing ones, but only the worthy ones, which serve him in their various ranks, that is, which do his will. The ministers of God are powers that serve him in whatever he wants to do through them for the benefit and help of all. That is why they are said to do his will. “Bless the Lord, all his works, in every place of his dominion. Bless the Lord, O my soul.” The order of these verses seems to suggest this meaning. “If only angels, divine powers and heavenly ministers of God were to bless him,” he says, “you would do well, O soul, to hold back and leave the blessing to your betters. But the divine word commands all his works to bless the Lord, for the whole creation ought to offer God the hymn that suits it, as far as it is able. So why do you delay, O soul? You too are no contemptible work of God, but were made in his image. Will you not rouse yourself to speak of God and bless him?” As was said, his dominion rules over all things, in heaven, on earth and under the earth. It follows that all his works, as things under his dominion, should bless him as things he has made, for, it says, “all things are your servants.” And how do creatures without reason or [?] life bless him? In the way that “the heavens declare the glory of God”: they surely use their appearance instead of a voice to

show the divine power. From them I take my reasons for singing praise, and I am moved to praise the Creator. Besides, the prophets often bring creatures without reason into the praise of God too, as if rational creatures were not enough. The youths in the furnace did this as well. However, singing in every place does not suit the Jews. When their captors ordered them to sing one of the songs of Zion in Babylon, they answered as the law required: “How shall I sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” But the divine Apostle urges us to lift up holy hands in prayer in every place. Christ the Master said the same to the Samaritan woman. He did away with worship bound to a place and taught worship in Spirit and truth.

“Bless the Lord, O my soul. O Lord my God, you have been made very great. You have clothed yourself with praise and majesty, wrapping yourself in light as in a garment.” The magnificence, providence and variety of created things teach the soul both to rejoice and to take courage. It takes pride in claiming the maker of such great things as its own Lord and God, and makes him its own when it says with feeling, “My God.” “You have clothed yourself with praise and majesty, wrapping yourself in light as in a garment.” Someone wrapped in a visible garment is covered on every side. In the same way, the fact that no one can see through the light around God shows that his essence cannot be grasped. But what are you saying, David? The evangelist says that he is “the true light, which enlightens every person coming into the world.” Paul says that he “dwells in unapproachable light.” Do you say that he is wrapped in light as in a garment? You see that no one can grasp the matter clearly, whether prophet, evangelist or apostle. Instead, they climb up little by little from the names we use and offer some dim idea of that unspeakable glory. Since they do not know what its essence actually is, they try hard to take hold of it through the bright things we know.

“He stretches out the heaven like a skin and roofs his upper rooms with water. He makes the clouds his chariot and walks on the wings of the winds. He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flaming fire.” So it is fitting that the word “seraphim,” translated into Greek, means “those who burn” or “burners.” “Seraphim” is said to mean burning. That is why it is said about the angelic power, “He makes his angels spirits and his ministers
“He set the earth on its firm foundation; it will not be shaken for ever and ever. The deep is his covering, like a garment; the waters will stand above the mountains. At your rebuke

they will flee; at the sound of your thunder they will be afraid. Mountains rise up and plains sink down to the place you established for them. You set a boundary they will not cross, and they will not return to cover the earth. He sends out springs into the ravines; the waters will flow between the mountains. They will give drink to all the wild animals of the field; wild donkeys will wait for them to quench their thirst. The birds of the sky will nest beside them and sing from among the rocks. He waters the mountains from his upper rooms.” At the beginning he said, “He roofs his upper rooms with water,” and now he says, “He waters the mountains from your upper rooms.” Unless one prefers to take God’s upper rooms as the air, which he made and wrapped in clouds. So God waters the mountains, the plains between them and all the rest of the earth. He does not do this from the springs in the ravines or from the rivers that flow over the earth. He does it from his upper rooms, supplying enough rain, in due measure, from on high. He calls the air God’s upper rooms, as if the whole world were a single house. The mountains are the men who bear the Spirit. They are watered from the upper rooms of God himself, since they are filled with the gifts of the Spirit: the word of wisdom and the gifts listed after it. God’s upper rooms, from which he waters the mountains, are the pure and surpassing contemplations of the truth. They are called upper rooms because nothing rises above them. “The earth will be satisfied with the fruit of your works.” For he himself said, “Let the earth bring forth green grass, and fruit trees bearing fruit,” and so on. The whole earth is satisfied by the works Jesus did in the divine plan of salvation, which bear much fruit. It shares in the wonderful things Jesus did, for this is the fruit of his works. The account of the works of his creation and providence, once it is understood, also satisfies [?] the people, I mean, who live on the earth. “He makes grass grow for the cattle and green plants for the service of men, to bring bread out of the earth; and wine gladdens the human heart,” and so on. He has said that the earth gets its fill from the rain, since God draws the waters up from the sea. Then he points out the benefit that results. Enriched by its supply of water, the earth produces suitable food for all who live on it. For man, a noble creature honoured by God, it produces a special food set apart for him: bread, wine and oil. Bread strengthens and empowers the heart, wine gladdens the soul, and oil makes the body shine and softens it, refreshing it after harsh toil. In this way God, like a father, gave man a rich table of many foods to enjoy. Yet he did not neglect to care for the other animals. He also took thought for their survival and

gave them suitable food as well, making grass grow for the cattle and green plants for the service of men. The prophet has drawn a very precise distinction among the animals. By “cattle” he means in general every animal that eats grass. By “the service of men” he means the tame and, as it were, civilized animals set apart to serve human beings. Some of them plough the land as man’s helpers, like the ox. Some carry burdens, like the donkey. Others provide some other use to the mortal race. He has fittingly and aptly named these “the service of men.” He says that the green plants are given to them, that is, the plants that people sow and cultivate. To the other cattle he gives the grass that grows by itself. But it may also be that both the green plants and the grass are given to the cattle and to the service of men alike. He did not mention wild beasts or reptiles here, because they live on other food. The beasts eat meat, while the reptiles feed on the earth itself. See how the discourse goes around in a circle. It passes over the clearer matters and lingers on those that many dispute. It does not leave the creatures without reason, their usefulness and their service. It does this for two reasons. First, it wants to silence, with more than enough proof, the shameless people who say that some things in the world are superfluous and useless. Second, it wants to show how much God cares for human beings, since he takes such account of the things made for their sake. What could equal this care? He feeds even the creatures that serve us so well, and he does not let us toil over everything. He did not abandon man, nor does he weigh him down with labours, but he provides for his survival in many different ways. Here it is fitting to say to the man who enslaves his own kind: “The creatures without reason are the only service meant for human beings, but you disdain them. So you have split nature into slavery and lordship, and made it [?] serve itself and lord it over itself.” Who could sell one who is in the likeness of God and ruler of the whole earth? Who could buy him? Only God could do this. Or rather, not even God himself could, for his gifts are irrevocable. And if God does not enslave what is free, who sets his own power above God’s? Still, let it be enough that service is given to the free, and that the difference goes no further than this: out of the same dust, one rules and the other is ruled. But let the yoke not be heavy, nor the penalty of our first sin. In these supernatural and most lofty words of his, which are mountains, he makes grass grow, which the less rational can take as food. The grass on these mountains is the teaching about the things of the senses and the letter of Scripture. It is also the more moral teaching, which even the many will be able to share. Each of these says, “The Lord is my shepherd, and I shall lack nothing. He made me dwell in a place of green pasture; he nourished me beside the water of rest.” But when they one day rise above this state, they are no longer the service of men but have become men. Then each will say in turn, “You have prepared a table before me in the presence of those who afflict

…those who afflict me. You anointed my head with oil, and my cup intoxicates like the finest wine. And your mercy will follow after me all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days. To bring forth bread from the earth, and wine gladdens the heart of man; to make the face cheerful with oil, and bread will strengthen the heart of man. Here it is worth asking why David, after saying, “He who makes grass spring up for the cattle,” went on, “To bring forth bread from the earth,” meaning, of course, the bread made from wheat. What is it that he wishes to hint at? That the same seed becomes common food for both irrational animals and humans, though not in the same way. This too belongs to the wisdom of God. Consider: wheat is sown, and for the time being it is food for humans only; but when it sprouts, it comes up carrying the food of the irrational animals as well. For just as the animals received their very existence for our sake, so too their food takes its origin from our food. The green blade came about first of all for this purpose, to protect the grain. You see, then, that not only do the irrational animals serve us, but the food of the irrational animals also serves our food, and in its order it imitates this same thing. For just as the irrational animals came first and then man, since the irrational animals exist for man's sake, so in the growing plant the green blade comes first and then the grain, since the blade exists for the grain's sake. And wine gladdens the heart of man. Not every wine, but only that which has its origin from him who said, “I am the true vine.” But since all sensible things are called “earth” because of their material nature, and one may take this to refer to the word that leads us up by a kind of analogy to intelligible things, this word too is bread brought forth from the earth to nourish the inner and hidden man, brought forth from the bodily narratives of Scripture, which are called “earth” because of their historical sense. The bread brought forth is the mystical word. To make the face cheerful with oil, and bread will strengthen the heart of man. The face of the inner man is made cheerful and radiant by the oil that nourishes the divine light and that heals the diseases and pains of the soul; it differs only in concept from the wine already explained. For the Word of God is an olive tree just as he is a vine: “I,” he says, “am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God.” For his teaching, under different aspects, is wine and oil and bread. The trees of the plain will be satisfied, the cedars of Lebanon which you planted; there the sparrows will nest. The heron's house leads them; the high mountains are for the deer, the rock is a refuge for the rock badgers. The Hebrew and the other translators have put “the trees of the Lord.” Having gone through the fruit-bearing trees, he must also mention the unfruitful ones, since they too supply something people need. That is why he called them “of the Lord,” as being self-

grown and not planted by hand, but sprung up by the divine word. The cedars of Lebanon which you planted. He rightly ascribed the planting of the cedars to God, because they grew so great without human care. No grove-keeper planted them; it was the divine Word that made the mountain peaks thickly wooded. And if he himself planted them, they are certainly useful, for all things that God made are very good. By mentioning Lebanon, as a famous mountain, and the cedars on it, he pointed through these to the other mountains and trees as well. There the sparrows will nest. The heron's house leads them. Aquila has it thus: “There the birds will nest. For the heron, the firs are its house.” For the same trees supply one need for humans and another for the birds

He made the moon for seasons; the sun knew its setting. Having gone through everything on earth, shown the creation of the invisible natures, and pointed out the making of the heavens, he now also mentions the luminaries, which came into being on the fourth day. Not without purpose, I think, does the text now, after so much else, take up again what seemed to have been passed over above, when it was speaking of the things in heaven and of the clouds and winds: it does so to teach that these too came into existence for the sake of use. For perhaps, if he had mentioned them first, some pretext would have been left to those who think they ought to be worshipped as divine, as the causes of the existence of the living things and fruits on earth. This, at any rate, is what those who are strangers to true religion supposed, and so they were moved to worship the sun and moon as gods, as though they were the causes of our birth, nourishment and growth. But the divine word does not teach this; rather, it teaches that even apart from these the universal providence of God brought into being not only the things in heaven but also the animals and plants on earth. Wishing to teach this, Moses too first introduced the generation of plants from the earth, and only then the establishment of the luminaries. And now David returns again to providence in the heavens, saying that the moon came into being for no other purpose than the counting and distinguishing of months and days; for this is what “for seasons” means: that is, so that through its phases we may recognize the changes of the seasons and count months and years. The moon's changes make it possible to measure time, for it produces the measure of the month, waxing and waning over so many days; so the moon was created to teach us the seasons. And no ordinary benefit comes from knowing the seasons and preparing for everything accordingly; if this were not so, everything would have perished, since neither the farmer would know when to cut the earth nor the sailor when to cut the sea at the proper time. This knowledge drawn from the seasons is fitting and most useful not only for humans but also for irrational animals. Concerning the luminaries it is also said in Genesis: “Let them be for signs and for seasons, and for days and for years”: for signs

of rain, of drought, of the movement of winds; for seasons, meaning the changes of the weather—winter, spring, summer, autumn—which the ordered motion of the luminaries enables us to pass through in good order; for days, not in order to make days, for day and night are older than the creation of the luminaries, but in order to rule the days; and for years, because the moon, when it has completed its course twelve times, makes a year, while the solar year is the sun's return from a given point to the same point. The sun knew its setting. You appointed darkness, and it became night; in it all the beasts of the forest will roam. Young lions roar to snatch their prey and to seek their food from God. The sun rose, and they will gather together and lie down in their dens. Man will go out to his work and to his labor until evening. How magnified are your works, O Lord! You have made all things in wisdom; the earth is filled with your creation. The sun knew its setting, that is, the setting appointed for it by the One who is greater. For the sun has learned not only to give light—and that not always and without ceasing, but as the ruler of the day—but also by night to give way to the stars that shine then, so as to complete its own course; so that when night has come and darkness has spread over the earth, the tame animals withdraw and retire, while the wild beasts come out for their own food, at their own fitting time, the span of the night. Young lions roar to snatch their prey and to seek their food from God: since the earth did not make grass spring up for them as for the cattle, and green plants for the service of humankind. God, as the guardian of all things and exercising providence for the preservation and life of all, arranged that some creatures should be driven away by the sun's rays and flee the light as an enemy, while he allowed others, as being akin to the light, to go out by day and pass their life in the light: the beasts lie down in their dens, while the rational creature goes out by day and in the light to his work and to his labor until evening. This is the great and wide sea; there are creeping things without number, small creatures with great. In these words he shows that just as the element of earth gives birth to and nourishes many creatures, in the same way the watery substance also nourishes kinds of creatures beyond counting. For God did not make the regions empty, but filled them all with living things—the air, the earth and the sea: the first with birds alone, the second with four-footed and winged creatures, the third with countless fish, some larger and some smaller; the smaller are food for the larger, and yet the species is not used up. This too is a proof of divine care, that the small kinds live alongside the great

ones and are not wholly consumed by them; for the stronger feed on the weaker, yet they are not exhausted, since the increase outstrips the consumption. Those people who swallow up the weaker resemble these. But there, what happens is no crime, for it is a matter of nature; you, however, will have no defense at all, you who have been honored with reason and law and yet lead yourself into the confusion of the irrational beasts. He calls the fish “creeping things” because, having no feet, they drag themselves along, as it were, through the water, as creeping things do on the earth. There the ships pass through—in the sea, that is. Having said how great a brood the sea nourishes, and that neither its creatures can be counted nor the sea itself measured, he also says how useful it is to people. For by the art of shipbuilding and the science of navigation we carry to one another what is lacking: we supply others with the produce that grows among us, and receive what is produced among them, so that what is surplus is not without profit and what is lacking is not left unsupplied. In a higher sense he likens the Church to a ship, and human life to the sea, because of the instability and ceaseless motion of the affairs in it. And by the innumerable race of creeping things he means the varied and, as it were, many-faced multitude of human beings, the difference being understood with reference to the variety of their dispositions. For nature is the same in all, and the manner of birth is no different, but the mind in us is divided many ways and the heart holds many opinions. Knowing this, someone said: “As faces are not like faces, so neither are the thoughts of men.” And we say that the ships which, as it is written, pass through this intelligible sea too are the holy Churches of our Savior, which are in the world yet above the world, just as indeed one can see merchant ships, which are in the water yet above the waters. The churches, then, like ships [?], sailing across the intelligible sea, take on board those who believe, and carry them, as to some other land or country, to the kingdom of heaven, to the hope that is in Christ, to the sanctification that comes through the Spirit, and to the homeland of the saints, which is virtue. For being, as it is written, sojourners and strangers on the earth, they have no lasting city here, but hasten toward that city whose craftsman and builder is God. So if this world of ours is understood under the figure of the sea, the Church will be understood as a vessel or ship, with the sanctified as her sailors, who through accepting the faith have Christ always with them, spreading a gentle calm [?]. In another sense he calls “ships” those who in their bodies are tossed about in the salty surge of this life. And the ships that are praised are those that cross the sea and do not stay in it, nor are swamped by the waves. For those who are in the flesh but do not wage war according to the flesh, trampling on the surge of life

and rising above it, do business on many waters, going down with others in order to win some of those who have sunk. Further, signifying to us elegantly the distractions of this life and the bitter flood and confusion of its affairs, the psalmist says: This is the sea; there are creeping things without number, small creatures with great. For those may very well be likened to fish who sometimes dart this way and that for no necessary benefit, and gather only such things as make them carnal and lead them to endure pointless toil. So we swim like fish through this broad and wide sea, that is, the world; for each person's life is in some way different. This is the dragon which you formed to play with it. All things look to you to give them their food in due season. When you give it to them, they will gather it; when you open your hand, all things will be filled with goodness. See whether you can draw a general doctrine from this: that all created things are poor, lacking, and in need of the supply that comes from God, and by sharing in it they are empowered and made strong, as though kept alive by food. All things look to you to give them their food in due season. By saying “all things,” the text has included together the intelligible and holy powers as well as sensible beings and those in mortal bodies. For in this way his goodness shines out all the more, in that he grants a share of his kindness to the worthy and the unworthy alike. You will take away their breath and they will fail, and return to their dust. You will send forth your spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth. The text is speaking about human beings, and I think these words point to the end of the present age and the renewal of the age to come, so that no one may suppose that the present order of the world extends without end, but that we may have hope in that new age and in the resurrection. This the text sets forth when, after saying, “They return to their dust,” it adds: “You will send forth your” life-giving “spirit, and they will be created,” rising from the earth, “and you will renew the face of the earth,” the beauty of the earth, that is, the human beings formed from the earth. Here he has clearly proclaimed to us in advance both the resurrection and the return to life through the all-holy Spirit, and the re-forming of human bodies in the last times of the age and their being brought into existence once again. And he shows that he himself is master of both death and life. For he does not wish to dwell on gloomy things; having said just enough to cause fear, he brings the discourse back again to good things. What is said elsewhere, that he is Lord of both death and life, he shows here, saying that those who have returned to the dust are created by the Spirit and that the human race is renewed; for the resurrection is a restoration to the original state. By the “sending” of the Spirit he means its condescending to act, not a passing from place to place,

since the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and by him the face of the earth is renewed. For this is the beauty of the world: the animals in it, the plants, the human race. And for these to exist there is need of the breath and life he gives, which he can easily both give and take away, and all things swiftly and with ease. This above all shows his power. You see the resurrection rehearsed even in the present life—in seeds, in plants, and in the human race itself. For both animals and plants have their existence through a last echo of life; when that is taken away, as the oracle says, all life fails, and what has failed through its weakness in sharing in life, turning back again toward it [?], becomes alive again. But the most divine thing is that he has promised to transfer us wholly—I mean our souls and the bodies yoked to them—to perfect life and immortality: a thing which perhaps seemed contrary to nature in former times, but which in truth is divine and above our nature, though not above the all-powerful nature; for to that nature no life is contrary to nature or above nature. So let the arguments of Simon's drunken raving against these things be driven away. Some understand the verses this way: “You will send your Spirit,” who comes upon us through holy baptism, “and they will be created” into a new creation, into a new people; so that the first interpretation is understood of the resurrection from the dead, when the earth too will be renewed and set free from corruption, and the second of the regeneration that comes from baptism. Let the glory of the Lord endure for ever; the Lord will rejoice in his works. He looks on the earth and makes it tremble; he touches the mountains and they smoke. I will sing to the Lord in my life; I will sing psalms to my God as long as I exist. Since I have been taught these things, he says, I will therefore spend my whole life in a hymn to the Creator; and as long as I live and exist in this life, I will render to my God the psalm I owe him. The addition shows great affection and intimacy toward God. For he did not say, “I will sing psalms to God,” but “to my God.” He seems to be saying: to him who created me and nourished me and has become for me the cause of all good things. By “song” here he means not only the song of words but also the song of deeds. For since he found himself indebted to God for much and unable to pay back any worthy return, he offers what he has: to sing hymns without ceasing, to spend his whole life on this. Let those hear this who rot all day long in business and trade and never once turn to prayer, and learn how much they are indebted to God. This is the profit of life, to bless God; for this it is worth even living. Fittingly he added “in my life,” and “as long as I exist I will sing psalms to my God.” For in death there is no one who remembers him, and in Hades who will give thanks? So it was that the door of the bridal chamber was shut against the foolish virgins, who spent the time of the torch-

procession buying oil. May my discourse be sweet to him; and I will rejoice in the Lord. May it be, he says, that I sing and chant such things that my fruit, my discourse, may be sweet to him: that is, my conversation, my talk, my praise; for whoever sings psalms converses with God. What does “May my discourse be sweet to him” mean? May it be well received, may it be accepted so as to please, may it seem most sweet and delightful to God. So prayer is nothing other than conversation with God. Consider, then, that psalmody holds its reward within itself. For what could equal conversing with God? Such a soul is set free from turmoil, is carried up to heaven, is loosed from the bonds of the body, takes wing, becomes lighter, lays aside its passions, strips off its sicknesses. For if someone who converses with an intelligent and sensible person comes away having gained something from the conversation, consider how much virtue the one who converses with God will reap. A hymn, then, is this: conversation with God. And how might it become sweet to God? If the life is pure, if the soul pursues true wisdom. For when you spend the whole day praying while your conduct works against it, you will not easily be heard—and not only you yourself, but not even if someone else does this on your behalf.
