I say this not so that we should stop praying or stop singing psalms, but so that along with singing psalms we should also take care of our life and conduct. You may also understand the verse this way. Many people hastily and perversely deliver their judgments before the understanding that comes from sufficient reasoning and further inquiry has arisen, rashly throwing out their assent to every doctrine without testing it. Now the nature of dialectic is above all trusted to be able to supply this: to divide precisely the natures of things, to recognize what is alike, and to distinguish what belongs to each. Therefore David, conscious that he possessed the divine dialectic, said, “May my discourse be sweet to you.” For the dialectic of those who approach matters contentiously and quarrelsomely is not sweet but embittering. That speech which looks toward what is right is sweet to God he himself says in the Song: “Your lips drip honeycomb, my sister, my bride; honey and milk are under your tongue.” And that whoever is used to frigid talk is unlovely, the Psalms show: “Their throat,” it says, “is an open grave.” And I will rejoice in the Lord. I pray, he says, that this hymn and discourse of mine may seem most sweet to God. For if this happens, I will reap the cheerfulness that comes from it, and I will rejoice in the Lord, that is, in his worship, in adoring him and in his commandments, in having such a Master. For the visible things are beautiful too: the heaven delights, the sun gladdens, and the earth sends up seeds and plants; but more than all these I rejoice in the One who made them. This is my luxury, this my gladness, this my pleasure, this ten thousand good things.

"Let sinners and the lawless vanish from the earth, so that they are no more." This plainly refers to that time when they will hear: "Depart from me, you who are cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you gave me nothing to eat; I was thirsty and you gave me nothing to drink; I was a stranger and you did not take me in; naked and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison and you did not visit me." And they will have no share with those who [fear?] God. But perhaps someone will say: "Does the blessed Prophet, then, pray against those who are living in sin? Does he want them all to perish and be wiped out? Surely, as a holy man who bore the Spirit, he ought rather to have interceded for the weak." Listen, then, for I will put it briefly. Before the Savior came, we were all in sin. Satan ruled everything under heaven. There was no one who did good, not even one. All had turned aside and together become worthless. The Greeks who worshiped idols did not know the ways of decency or understand the road to a good life. Worse, they did not know at all the very Maker of all things and Savior, Christ. The Jews, for their part, had the law as their tutor, but no one could be justified by the law. So we were all in sin, and the earth was full of lawlessness. But when the only-begotten Word of God appeared and became man, the sinners vanished, and those living in lawlessness ceased to be. How did this happen? He justified everyone, released them from their offenses, and made them free and washed clean. So those in sin have become few, and those who have been justified are very many. Here, then, the Psalmist does not pray for human nature itself to be wiped out, or for people to be handed over to utter destruction. He prays against wickedness: let the sinner vanish, so that he is no longer a sinner but has been changed; let the lawless man cease to exist, so that he is transformed. For such are the souls of the saints: they offer their prayers not for themselves alone but for the whole world. So now David, having explored the divine beauty in its unspeakable richness as far as human nature could, longed for all people to share in the same knowledge, and he prayed that the band of sinners might vanish altogether. He was not asking for them to perish but begging for them to be changed. He was pleading for their crowd to come to an end, once they had changed sides and learned divine things anew. So it is in vain that the contentious cite such sayings in defense of their own bitterness. They point to David longing for the sinner to vanish and praying for shame and disgrace upon his enemies. They point to Jeremiah wanting to see God's vengeance on his opponents, and to Hosea asking that his enemies be given a childless womb and dry breasts. They collect many such passages scattered through the divine Scriptures, [insisting?] that we ought to pray against our opponents, and they make God's [?] an accomplice in their own bitterness.

But none of the truly holy, whose sayings were recorded by divine providence to admonish those who came after, will be found eager for anything evil. The whole aim of their words looks to correcting the vice that has settled in our nature. Someone who prays that there be no sick and no poor desires not that people be done away with but that sickness and poverty disappear. In the same way each of the saints prays that what is hostile to our nature may disappear. When the Psalmist says, "Let sinners and the lawless vanish from the earth, so that they are no more," he is praying that sin and lawlessness may vanish. For human beings are not enemies of one another by nature. It is the will's movement toward evil that has turned one who is our kin by nature into an enemy. So he prays that evil may vanish, and a human being is not evil. How could the likeness of the Good be evil? Likewise, even when he prays for shame and disgrace upon his enemies, he is showing you the host of adversaries who make war on human life from the unseen world. The form of the prayer shows that he is praying not against human beings but against demons: "Let them be put to shame," he says, "who seek my soul to take it away. Let those who wish me evil be turned back and disgraced. Let those who say to me, 'Aha, aha!' at once receive their shame. Let all who seek you, Lord, rejoice and be glad in you, and let those who love your salvation say continually, 'May the Lord be magnified.'" Only the demons plot against the soul, and the plot against the soul is its estrangement from God through a disposition ruled by passion. So that he might not suffer this, he prays that those wrestling against him may be put to shame. This is nothing other than praying for his own victory over his enemies, and the enemies are the passions. In the same way Jeremiah, zealous for true worship when king and people were worshiping idols, is not indulging some private passion. He brings his petition to God for the common good of humanity, asking that the blow struck against the ungodly may bring the whole human race to its senses. Hosea, too, condemns to childlessness the vice that was then multiplying its offspring among the Israelites, and wants the bitter teats of sin to dry up, so that evil might neither be born among people nor be nourished. And if any other saying of this kind, with a show of anger, is found among the saints, it surely looks to this same meaning: it banishes the evil without crushing the person. But if someone wants to understand David's words differently, as though the Prophet were cursing those who live in ungodliness, even so he will find the prophecy in agreement with the apostolic teaching. For Paul, writing to the Corinthians, put this at the very end: "If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be accursed." It is characteristic of those who love fervently to hate those who hate the one they love. Perhaps, too,

David is pointing by these words to the state of things after the resurrection, when, as he says, the Lord rejoices in his works and sinners have vanished from the earth. How could anyone be named for sin when sin no longer exists? Pray for such things yourself: "Open, Lord, your rich hand to supply spiritual blessing, so that my most bitter and harsh soul may be filled with kindness. Send your Holy Spirit and renew my ruined earth, so that I may then rejoice in your works, once the tricks of the demons have vanished from my heart." "Bless the Lord, O my soul." Here, having brought the whole psalm to a close in praise of God, he ends it in blessing with the same verse with which it began. He sets a secure roof on his discourse to match the [foundation?], and makes the ending resemble the opening. "You, O soul," he says, "must constantly sing hymns to your Creator and Savior. For he will remove you from the lot of the wicked and make you worthy of the lot of the saints. Make the blessing of him both the beginning and the end of what you say. For continual blessing of God shapes our [life?] into a good life."

ALLELUIA. PSALM 104. "Give thanks to the Lord and call upon his name; proclaim his works among the nations. Sing to him and sing psalms to him; tell of all his wonders." The present psalm is the first of those headed "Alleluia." "Alleluia" is a mystical summons that rouses the ear to sing hymns to God. Its meaning is "Praise the Lord." In those places of holy Scripture where the words "Praise the Lord" appear, the Hebrew expresses this with "Alleluia." "Allelu" is understood as praise directed to God, and "Ia" is one of the names that express the divine nature. Taken together, "Alleluia" is rendered "Praise of God." Since this word is written at the head of the psalm, we should understand that its contents must by all means lead to the glorification of God. Many such headings are likewise found especially in the last psalms of the book. From this we may gather that praising God belongs to those who have already reached the perfection of the virtuous life and have been purified through the earlier sections of the Psalter, according to the spiritual meaning discerned in them. It is fitting for them to be occupied with the very things in which the angelic nature is believed to be engaged. We have learned of no other occupation of the angels besides praising God, and those who are perfect in virtue strive for nothing else than to make their own life a praise of God. Since the psalms headed "Alleluia" are almost all found in the last section of the Psalter, it is clear that this last section, in which most of the content is praise of God or a summons to praise God, stands at the summit of the whole lofty ascent through the psalms.

In the psalm before us the Holy Spirit commands the holy apostles to make known to the people from the nations all the wonders the Lord performed at his coming. He also commands them to make known all the benefits he bestowed on the people of old, and how he repaid what they did. The psalm also recalls the promises God made to the patriarchs and the good things he gave to their descendants for the patriarchs' sake. The memory of these is enough to spur those who enjoyed so many benefits to emulate the virtue of their forefathers. At the same time it also teaches the new people, that is, those from the nations, that he was not unjust in stripping that ungrateful people of his care. In this way they may learn the justice of the sentence passed against them, and, seeing the wages of ingratitude, may not walk the same road as the Jews but travel the straight way. "Give thanks to the Lord and call upon his name." In the usage of Scripture the word for "confession" has a double meaning: sometimes it signifies acknowledging one's sins, sometimes giving thanks. Here we are led toward the virtuous life in both senses. Acknowledging our sins separates and estranges us from evil, and in those who receive benefits with a grateful heart, eagerness to give thanks grows, together with gratitude toward the benefactor. So the passage urges us to offer a hymn of thanksgiving and to tell of God's benefits. Symmachus translated "call upon" as "proclaim." Another translator says, "And call upon in his name," hinting at something great. "If you confess," he says, "and lay aside your sins, you will be able to call on his name with confidence and accomplish great good." It is not for nothing that he wants us first to confess and then to call upon him. It is so that, made clean through confession, we may offer the hymn from a clean instrument. "Proclaim his works among the nations." The hymn before us summarizes the history from Abraham to the exodus of the children of Israel from Egypt. The divine Spirit urges that this history be proclaimed to the nations as well. This makes it plain that he is working for the benefit not only of the Jews but also of those from the nations, since the Spirit rouses the heralds of the nations to seek the Lord and proclaim the accounts of him. And this is to be done with hymns, for he says, "Sing to him and sing psalms to him; tell of all his wonders." He wants the nations, who did not know and had not yet learned, to be told what benefits God bestowed long ago on his former people. They are to hear how that people, after receiving countless good things from God, transgressed and turned to ungodliness, and how through their lawlessness they fell from God's care. He also commands them to become interpreters and expounders of the mysteries in the divine oracles, which would be "his wonders." In short, they are to repay him with hymns and teach those who do not know them the wonders he has done.

"Be praised in his holy name; let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice. Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face continually." Praise and glory belong to those who tell of God's excellence. In place of "be praised," Aquila put "boast." The passage urges the apostles and their successors not to take pride in wealth, strength, or power, but in the knowledge and providence of the true God and in being called Christians. The divine Apostle gave the same charge: "Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord. For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends." Jeremiah and the most wise Hannah say the same: "Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the strong man boast in his strength, and let not the rich man boast in his riches. Let the one who boasts boast in this: that he understands and knows that I am the Lord who shows mercy and justice on the earth." "Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice," that is, of those who call on him for help, or who travel toward him by way of virtue and so find him. He teaches how great a benefit comes from confession. "What you sought," he says, "this will come to you: gladness of mind. For this is the fruit of hope in God." Notice how he began with confession and ended with gladness. Confession is the beginning of progress toward God, and gladness in God is its end, with a great many things in between. So we must first confess to the Lord through genuine repentance and fruits worthy of confession. Then, having improved, we may take courage and call on his name. Calling on him in this way after confession, we are counted worthy of God's gifts. Having received them, we help others by proclaiming to all the works of his we have learned. Then, as though [?] with godly delight, we sing to him and sing psalms. After this we become expounders of the mysteries in the divine oracles. Then, having achieved so much, we are praised in his name. And finally, after all this, we rejoice in the mind, which is called the heart. Let the heart that seeks the Lord enjoy gladness in God from the very seeking and from the finding that follows it. I think that all this is addressed by the Holy Spirit to the apostles. For "Proclaim his works among the nations" fits no one but them. The outcome bears witness to the word, for they alone proclaimed God's works among the nations, who through them came to know the God of all. Earlier he called these nations a new generation and a people being created. So whoever means to seek the Lord must first confess through sincere repentance and its fruits. Such a person is able to seek, and in seeking, to

COMMENTARY ON THE PSALMS. find. If precious stones call for experts, and divers need great skill, how much more is this so with God! For many things keep us from finding him: the crowd of affairs, the rebellions of the flesh, the diseases of the soul, the plots of the demons, and the sluggishness of the will. If we are rid of all these, we will quickly find him, strip off vice, and take up virtue. This is the road that leads there. What, then, is seeking? It is to think of him and reflect on him constantly, for one who seeks keeps the object of his search in mind. "Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face continually." What does it mean to seek the Lord? It means to set one's mind on what is his, to reflect on him always, to keep him always in mind, and never to stop conversing with him through prayer and good deeds. Those who seek will be unbeatable and invincible. Having urged the heralds of the nations to seek the Lord eagerly, the passage strengthens them still further, saying, "Be strengthened," that is, do not grow slack in seeking him. He says this to them because they needed might and power to carry out what they had been commanded, namely to preach to the nations, to Greeks and barbarians alike, as it is written: "The Lord will give a word to those who proclaim good news with great power." He goes on to teach how one must seek: not once or twice, but throughout one's whole life one should seek help from above and reap its benefit. So he added, "Seek his face continually." That is, not by appearing before him three times a year, as in the law given through Moses, but throughout one's whole life. Here "face" means his manifestation, his oversight, providence, care, help, and protection, and our thought of him. For no one will see the face of his essence and live. The Son, too, is his face. "Remember the wonders he has done, his portents and the judgments of his mouth," whether those in the Old Scripture or those in the Gospels. You heralds of the nations will have to pass these on to all the nations, since they have not learned them before from anyone else. So join together all that the Word did when he became man with the things of old, and remember to hand them on to the nations. Here he seems to me to show the way by which it is possible both to seek and to find God. What is that way? To keep his marvelous works, his laws, and his commandments constantly in memory. That is why he adds, "his portents and the judgments of his mouth." By "portents" he means divine signs. By "judgments" he means decrees and commandments, or else the wonders God performed justly and with righteous judgment. Which portents, you ask? Those in Egypt, those after Egypt, those before Egypt, and those after his own coming. For all these

are marvelous and extraordinary deeds that surpass the ordinary course of human affairs. Or perhaps "portents" are the miracles he performed, such as walking on the sea, raising the dead, and the like, while "the judgments of his mouth" are the words he spoke when driving unclean demons out of people, or else the commandments of the New Covenant. But I think that here he rather means by "judgments" the laws in heaven, on earth, and in the sea. For it was not human beings alone who received a law, but all visible things. The sea was given the law not to cross its shores; the mountains, to stand firm; the earth, to stay in place; the sun, to run its course; the moon, its proper order. So too the [varied?] chorus of the stars, and the nature of bodies, of plants, of animals without reason, and of everything else: all are governed by their own laws. All of these came into being by his commands, and that is what "mouth" indicates. So join together whatever his mouth has judged, whether through the Old Covenant or the New, and charge the nations to keep his judgments as royal laws. You may also take "judgments" to mean the wonders worked by his just sentence. Since he is about to recount the events in Egypt, he first teaches that the punishment of the Egyptians was just. All people on earth, being subject to his judgments, needed to know both his works and his judgments. By these judgments he judged worthy of his calling not only the Jewish nation but all people on earth. "Seed of Abraham, his servants; sons of Jacob, his chosen ones. He is the Lord our God." Not all who are descended from Israel are Israel, and not all are children because they are Abraham's seed. So our Savior rightly said to the Jews who boasted of being Abraham's seed, "I know that you are Abraham's seed," and again, "If you were Abraham's children, you would do the works of Abraham." Some, then, are children of Abraham by imitation, and these are also called chosen. Others are merely his seed, and so are not chosen. For it is not the seed that is called chosen but the sons, while the seed are "his servants." The Savior's disciples, who became heralds of the nations, had both titles, since they were both servants and chosen. That is why it is said to them, "Seed of Abraham, his servants; sons of Jacob, his chosen ones." Beside "his chosen ones" you may set "Jesus chose these twelve and named them apostles," and "Did I not choose you, the twelve?" We will understand how special the chosen are from "Many are called, but few are chosen." "He is the Lord our God; his judgments are in all the earth." "We must not fail to recognize," he says, "that he is the Lord our God, who by his providence governs the whole world with divine judgments, so that nothing happens without judgment or apart from God's providence." "He has remembered his covenant forever, the word he commanded for a thousand generations, which he made

to Abraham, and of his oath to Isaac. And he established it for Jacob as an ordinance, and for Israel as an everlasting covenant, saying, "To you I will give the land of Canaan as the portion of your inheritance," when they were few in number, very few, and strangers in it. And they went from nation to nation, and from one kingdom to another people. He let no one wrong them, and he rebuked kings for their sake: "Do not touch my anointed ones, and do my prophets no harm." If you consider carefully what the word was that he commanded, reaching to many generations, you will find that it was spoken to Abraham like this: "And in you all the nations of the earth shall be blessed." And: "In your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed," and, "I will surely multiply your seed." (The phrase does not point to a number of years but to perpetuity and multitude, as "seven times" does in "The barren woman has borne seven," that is, many, and in "The righteous man will fall seven times and rise again.") You would find similar things promised and sworn to Isaac as well, concerning both the land and the multiplying of his seed. These promises were fulfilled after a great many generations through the appearing of Christ, who came from the seed of Abraham and became our Savior. And even now the promise is still at work and remains in force, until the full number of the Gentiles comes in. So after a long age and after a very great many generations (for he has used "thousands" in place of "many"), he was fulfilling these promises to the patriarchs, having granted the blessing of Abraham to all the nations through our Savior Jesus and through his teaching. "And he called a famine upon the land; he broke every staff of bread." In these words the text teaches something else as well, which escapes most people. It sets out why the famine was "called" upon the land as though it were a living creature (I mean the active power of the famine), and why every staff of bread was broken: so that even if bread appeared somewhere, it would not sustain those who ate their fill of it, in keeping with the saying "Bread strengthens the heart of man." For this is what happens above all in famines that come about through God's wrath: even those who eat are not sustained. "He sent a man before them; Joseph was sold as a slave. They humbled his feet with fetters; his soul passed through iron, until his word came." He endured all this until his word came. This was the word he had seen in his visions and told to his father and his brothers, when he said that he had seen sheaves, with his brothers gathering theirs likewise, and that their sheaves then bowed down to his own sheaf; and likewise that the sun, the moon and the eleven stars bowed down to him. "Until his word came. The word of the Lord tried him in the fire." The phrase "The word of the Lord tried him in the fire" is like the saying "Is not

the interpretation of them through God?" For he would not have solved Pharaoh's dreams if God had not given him the ability to understand them. "The king sent and released him, the ruler of the people, and set him free. He made him lord of his house and ruler of all his possessions, to instruct his princes as he would himself, and to teach his elders wisdom." When Joseph had been sufficiently tried in the fire by his trials, God prompted Pharaoh, whom the text here calls both king and ruler. Then Joseph was released from his bonds and appointed ruler of the king's house and of all his possessions. Most people would say that Pharaoh brought him out in order to gather the produce of the years of plenty and store it up for the time of famine. But the present passage teaches that he was raised to power not so much to store the crops as for the spiritual benefit of those who were to be made wise and instructed by him. These were Pharaoh's princes and elders; and since they were benefited, it was likely that all their subjects too would share in the improvement that came from them. "And Israel came into Egypt, and Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham. And he increased his people greatly, and made them stronger than their enemies." Who came in but Israel? And who sojourned in the land of Ham but Jacob? These words refer both to the father himself and to his sons. Jacob did not come in alone; seventy souls came with him, as it says, "With seventy souls Israel went down into Egypt." That is why the words above refer to both the sons and the father. "And he increased his people greatly, and made them stronger than their enemies." They would not have increased or grown strong if they had not had Joseph as their protector, and the honor [?] among the Egyptians that was given to them through Joseph. "He turned their heart to hate his people, to deal craftily with his servants. He sent Moses his servant, and Aaron, whom he had chosen for himself. He set among them the words of his signs and of his wonders in the land of Ham. He sent darkness and made it dark, because they embittered his words. He turned their waters into blood and killed their fish. Their land swarmed with frogs, even in the chambers of their kings. He spoke, and there came the dog-fly, and gnats throughout all their borders. He gave them hail for rain, flaming fire in their land. And he struck their vines and their fig trees, and shattered every tree within their borders. He spoke, and the locust came, and the caterpillar without number, and they devoured all the grass in their land and devoured all the fruit of their land. And he struck every firstborn in their land, the firstfruits of all their labor." Just as

he first allowed Joseph to be a slave and to be humbled with fetters and iron, and then, once Joseph had given proof of his own virtue, raised him to royal power, so now too, wishing to count the people worthy of his visitation, he first hands them over to trials. He does this so that afterward it might be said: "And the children of Israel groaned and cried out to the Lord their God, and their cry went up to God from their labors. And God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob. And God looked upon the children of Israel and made himself known to them." Since it is said that "he turned their heart," that is, the Egyptians' heart, "to hate his people," you will say that God acted justly. For after the Israelites had come into great ease, freedom and honor among the Egyptians, they forgot the God of their fathers and gave themselves over to the idolatries of the Egyptians. Because they trusted in themselves and made light of God, he justly raised the Egyptians up against them. He did this so that, being oppressed by the Egyptians, they would learn not to pay attention to them or to their superstition with its many gods, and would turn back to the God of their fathers. "And he brought them out with silver and gold, and there was no one feeble among their tribes. Egypt was glad when they departed, for fear of them had fallen upon them." Through Moses, God commands the people to plunder the Egyptians as a conquered enemy, and to exact from them wages for the long slavery to which the Egyptians had subjected them. "And there was no one feeble among their tribes." This was far more astonishing: after all their toil and brickmaking, after such great hardship and the scourges, not one of them was feeble, and that although so many plagues had come down on Egypt. This went beyond even the ordinary course of nature. "He spread out a cloud as a covering for them, and fire to give them light at night." Having gone through the scourges against the Egyptians, he moves on in due order to the benefits done for Israel. In this way he urges us too to flee the Egyptian way of life, so that we do not fall into the same punishments, and to pray to be among God's portion, [?] the benefits that come from him. At the same time he recalls the wonders of God that those of the circumcision were counted worthy to receive. He does so to rebuke their way of life and to vindicate their later [?]

"They asked [?], and the quail came, and he filled them with bread from heaven. He split the rock and waters flowed; rivers ran in dry places. For he remembered his holy word to Abraham his servant." Moses too says to them in Deuteronomy: "Do not say, 'It was because of my righteousness that the Lord brought me out of the land of Egypt'; it was because of the oath that the Lord swore to your fathers. And you shall know today

that it is not because of your righteousness that the Lord your God is giving you this good land to inherit, for you are a stiff-necked people." "And he brought out his people with exultation, and his chosen ones with gladness." Each of the things that happened was a very great wonder and held much that was extraordinary: they were set free with joy from those who were driving them hard, they had every kind of abundance, and they were in perfect health. "And he gave them the lands of the nations, and they inherited the labors of the peoples." For he not only freed them from their former troubles but also gave them what belonged to others, nowhere letting them toil, "so that they might keep his ordinances and seek out his law." He promised these things because they kept his ordinances. For such is God, "showing mercy to thousands of those who love him." To these, the descendants of those people, he provided and granted so many good things, urging and spurring them on to keep his ordinances and to seek out his law. But although they had been counted worthy of so much, they did not keep what had been commanded. Then grace was taken away from them. Not only did they lose the land; they have also fallen away from God and have become slaves of the nations and of their enemies. "Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever. Who will tell of the mighty deeds of the Lord, or make all his praises heard? Blessed are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at all times. Remember us, Lord, in your favor toward your people; visit us with your salvation, so that we may see the goodness of your chosen ones, so that we may rejoice in the gladness of your people, so that we may be praised together with your inheritance." The present psalm, too, contains praise and a hymn to God. That is why it is entitled "Alleluia," which means "Praise the Lord." Right at the beginning he commands those who are setting out from their sins to come to the healing Son of God as to a physician and savior, and to lay bare the wounds of their soul to him by confessing their own sins. Whoever does this sincerely, weeping over the sins he committed before, and does it not in words alone but in his disposition and in his very deeds, receives instruction [?] from [?]. He eagerly urges them to confession by announcing "that the Lord is good, that his mercy endures forever." "For this reason," he says, "confess eagerly, because he himself is ready to show kindness, knowing that the affairs of this present age, being mortal and perishable, are in need of mercy." "We have sinned with our fathers; we have acted lawlessly, we have done wrong." "We are not the only ones who have sinned," he says. "If anyone examined our history from the earliest times, he would find that our race has always and in every way been given to sin." For although so many wonders were performed through Moses, they did not understand. Even after they had obtained salvation and had been freed from slavery under the Egyptians,
they did not recognize that it was not because of their righteousness, nor because they were worthy of God's visitation, but because of the greatness of his mercy that these things [?]

"Our fathers in Egypt did not understand your wonders; they did not remember the greatness of your mercy. And they provoked him as they went up at the Red Sea." The psalm before this one covered these events, and it also summed up the marvels in the wilderness without bringing any charge against the people. The present psalm, however, takes up the story again and goes through all the people's impieties. The whole discourse is an indictment of the Jewish people. "And they provoked him as they went up at the Red Sea." They did this by coming to Moses and saying, "Would that we had died in the land of Egypt, or in this wilderness!" and, "Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you brought us out to die in the wilderness? What is this you have done to us by bringing us out of Egypt? Is this not what we told you in Egypt, when we said, 'Leave us alone, so that we may serve the Egyptians'? For it is better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in this wilderness." As far as it lay with them, they made God bitter toward them instead of kind. But the good God, rich in mercy and love for humankind, saved them again for his name's sake, to make his power known, so that the ungodly might not say, "Where is their God?" For this reason he gave them salvation then too, driving them together from every side toward their own salvation. And they, won over, believed his words for a short while, after they had crossed the Red Sea. "And he rebuked the Red Sea, and it dried up, and he led them through the deep as through a desert." The one who rebuked the Red Sea is acknowledged by all to be God. So if Jesus too gives orders to the sea when it is tossing, so that calm comes after the heavy swell and the surge, he is acknowledged by all to be God. He, being God, is the very one who rebuked the Red Sea and dried it up so that it could be crossed. This was the sea that of old was also called "the deep" because of the abundance of its waters. "And he saved them from the hand of the one who hated them, and redeemed them from the hand of the enemy. The water covered those who oppressed them; not one of them was left." Someone might ask about the mixed multitude of Egyptians who crossed the sea and went into the wilderness together with the people. We will answer him that they were not among those who oppressed Israel. The words "Not one of them was left" were said about the oppressors. The mixed multitude was Egyptian, but because they believed the words of Moses, they obtained salvation. "And they believed his word and sang his praise. They quickly forgot his works; they did not wait for his counsel." Although they had sung the song at the exodus with Moses and Aaron [?], they changed straightaway and at once: "they quickly forgot his works."

"And they gave way to craving in the wilderness and put God to the test in a waterless place. And he gave them what they asked for; he sent fullness into their souls. And they provoked Moses in the camp, and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord." When they put God to the test in the waterless place, he could not be tempted and bore no grudge, so he did not repay them but gave them what they asked for. Even when they provoked him as they went up at the Red Sea, he made his power known to them then too. But when they angered Moses and Aaron in the camp, then the earth opened and swallowed them, for his servants were not to be treated with contempt. Moreover, since he shows both kindness and severity, he first offered them the gifts of his kindness. When they did not benefit from it, he then pursued them with a suitable, punishing remedy. "The earth opened and swallowed Dathan, and covered over the head of Abiram. And fire was kindled in their congregation; a flame burned up the sinners." Dathan and Abiram's party angered Moses by saying, "Has God spoken to Moses alone? Has he not spoken to us as well?" [?] Aaron, on the other hand, was angered by Korah and his company, who dared to offer strange fire and sacrifices to God in the place of the priests. Those who spoke against Moses met this end: the earth opened and swallowed Dathan with his whole family, and it covered over the company of Abiram. As for Korah and those with him who were about to offer their censers, a flame came out from the tabernacle and burned them up. "And they made a calf at Horeb and worshiped the carved image, and they exchanged their glory for the likeness of a calf that eats grass. They forgot God, who saved them, who did great things in Egypt, wonders in the land of Ham, fearful things at the Red Sea. And he said he would destroy them, had not Moses his chosen one stood in the breach before him to turn away his wrath, so that he would not destroy them. And they scorned the desirable land; they did not believe his word, and they grumbled in their tents; they did not listen to the voice of the Lord. And he lifted up his hand against them, to strike them down in the wilderness, to cast down their seed among the nations and to scatter them throughout the lands. And they were initiated into the rites of Baal of Peor and ate sacrifices offered to the dead. And they provoked him with their practices, and destruction multiplied among them. And Phinehas stood up and made atonement, and the plague ceased; and it was counted to him as righteousness from generation to generation forever." The story is found in Numbers: Phinehas took a spear and pierced the Midianite woman together with the man who had committed fornication with her, and with that deed the wrath against them ceased at once. The passage shows how much the righteousness of one man can do before God. Because of Phinehas's zeal for God, the wrath ceased and the destruction coming upon the sinners was driven back.

"And they angered him at the Water of Contradiction, and Moses suffered on their account, because they embittered his spirit, and he spoke rashly with his lips. They did not destroy the nations as the Lord had told them. And they mingled with the nations and learned their works, and served their carved images, and this became a stumbling block to them. And they sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons. And they shed innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters, whom they sacrificed to the carved images of Canaan. And the land was polluted with bloodshed, and it was defiled by their works, and they prostituted themselves in their practices. And the Lord was furious with his people." Because of all this he abhorred his inheritance. How, then, was it said above, "So that we may see the goodness of your chosen ones, so that we may rejoice in the gladness of your nation, so that we may be praised together with your inheritance"? But see whether the text does not clearly present the abhorred inheritance as belonging to the former people, while it prophesies about another inheritance, just as it speaks of another people with whom it teaches us to pray to be counted. "And he handed them over into the hands of their enemies, and those who hated them ruled over them." The Lord does not hand over his people unless he first abhors them, and he abhors them because of the deeds described above. And once the Lord hands them over, who is not able to rule over his people? "And their enemies oppressed them, and they were humbled under their hands. Many times he rescued them, but they embittered him with their schemes and were brought low by their iniquities." He himself, he says, kept rescuing them, being kind and showing himself gentle to them; but they embittered him, making him bitter toward themselves. And again he saved them, as a savior would; but they kept perishing, impaling themselves on deeds that led to destruction. This happened many times, until they had humbled themselves by their own iniquities. "And the Lord looked on them when they were in distress, when he heard their prayer. And he remembered his covenant and relented, according to the greatness of his mercy. And he made them objects of compassion before all who had taken them captive." This was fulfilled when God put it into the heart of King Cyrus, and after him of Darius and Artaxerxes, to treat the Jewish nation kindly, as is recorded in the book of Ezra. Even now, while they are subject to Roman rule, they meet with compassion. God has granted them this, not because they were worthy, but once again because of the greatness of his mercy. "And he relented, according to the greatness of his mercy." He calls the ending of discipline "relenting." For God is not subject to the emotion of regret, nor is he pleased with some people at one moment and with others at the next. Rather, he orders all things wisely [?], and he brings on both discipline and kindness [?].

Save us, O Lord our God, and gather us from among the nations, so that we may give thanks to your holy name and glory in your praise. Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. And all the people will say, So be it, so be it. They are taught to pray that they may obtain the gathering from among the nations, so that, released at last from the dispersion, they may be gathered together in one place. The Jews imagine that this will happen in the present life, when their Anointed comes to them. But we, now that our Saviour has shone upon humankind, see the multitude of souls from all the nations being gathered day by day under the Son of God, and being prepared from here for the [?] gathering of the kingdom of heaven, which [?] truly promises. Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. And all the people will say, So be it, so be it. In keeping with the Apostle, who said, "In everything give thanks," the word now teaches us too to bless the Lord always: for the mercy he shows, for the discipline he gives, and for the salvation he brings.

ALLELUIA. Psalm 106. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever. Let those redeemed by the Lord say so, whom he redeemed from the hand of their enemies and gathered out of the lands, from east and west, from north and sea. They wandered in the desert, in a waterless place. We must give thanks to the Lord in both senses of the word: by confessing our own offenses to him as to a physician, and by thanking him for his benefits toward us, since we have the pledge of his healing. For he is not only good, but he also extends his mercy through the whole of the present age. Let those redeemed by the Lord say so, whom he redeemed from the hand of their enemies and gathered out of the lands. Fittingly, here too the calling of the nations, which was carried into effect through our Saviour, is prophesied after the rejection of the Jewish nation [?] made known in the preceding psalm. There, after the long catalogue of their impieties, it was said: "And the Lord was angry with his people, and he abhorred his inheritance." Whom he redeemed from the hand of their enemies: those long enslaved by the enemies and foes of humankind, that is, by the devil. And he gathered them out of the lands, from east and west, from north and sea. He gathers them into his Church from every nation, for he indicated the whole inhabited world by its four regions. Out of these a common nation and an inheritance of God was formed [?]. Now someone might suppose that the present psalm describes the gathering of the Jews from among the nations, as though the Jews throughout the whole world were going to be separated from the nations and released from their sojourn in foreign lands

and gathered into the land of Judea. The children of the Jews imagine such things even now. But these things are not seen to have actually happened to them, for nearly a thousand years have passed since their captivity in Babylon without anything of the kind being done for them. So it is time to fit the words to the outcome of events and to refer the prophecy to the calling of the nations. They wandered in the desert and a waterless place; they did not find the way to a city to dwell in. Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them. This was us. Before we came to the religion of our Saviour, we had long wandered in a fruitless, waterless and barren life, when we were Gentiles without reason, led away to dumb idols. We never found the way to a city to dwell in, when we were aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, having no hope and without God in the world. We were once hated, and our souls fainted in hunger and thirst, because we were deprived of rational and heavenly food and of spiritual drink, as it is said: "I will send out not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord. And the waters will be shaken from sea to sea, and from north to east they will run about seeking the word of the Lord, and they will not find it." So we wandered in a desert, empty of virtues, with no guide or leader to follow. Following such a one, we might have found at the end of the road a city well ordered by sacred law, in which we could dwell and never leave; and this city is virtue and the wisdom of God. And they cried to the Lord in their affliction, and he delivered them from their distresses. When all the nations were wandering in a desert and waterless land, and their soul was fainting for lack of the nourishment of saving words, they cried out to God in supplication that a Saviour common to all might be sent down. And they cried to the Lord in their affliction. Those to whom they had been entrusted suffered and grieved deeply on their behalf, as they thirsted and their souls were already fainting for lack of food. These themselves shouted and cried out to the Lord, each interceding on behalf of his own. And he led them on a straight way, to go to a city to dwell in. Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders to the children of men. For they wandered in a desert and waterless land: this was the first sickness they suffered, the sickness of wandering. Falling into a second evil, they did not find the way to a city to dwell in. And a third evil also gripped them, since they were hungry and thirsty, so that their soul fainted within them. But God, who loves humankind, the good Saviour, first led them on a straight way, and then showed them how they must walk the road that leads to the city of habitation. And what would the straight way be but the saving word of the gospel, which alone leads us to the heavenly city? Once we arrive there, we shall find our dwelling place. Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies [?]

[?] and for his wonders to the children of men. [?] proclaiming to all the children of men, so that all, having learned of the grace that has come to us and of the mercies of God, may [?] to their own salvation. For he satisfied the empty soul, and filled the hungry soul with good things: those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, bound fast in poverty and iron. For they embittered the words of the Lord and provoked the counsel of the Most High. You would not be wrong to call idolatry and the deeds of godlessness the shadow of death, for these are what separate us from the true life. In these [?] we [?] formerly, because we embittered God and provoked the counsel of the Most High. For we ought [?] to have contemplated the Maker of all things from the greatness and beauty of his creatures, and to have perceived his eternal power and divinity from the creation of the world. Instead, like blind men living in darkness and the shadow of death, fettered and maimed in the rational powers of the soul, we exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds and four-footed beasts and reptiles. And their heart was brought low with toils; they grew weak, and there was no one to help. For this great achievement was reserved for the Word of God alone, of whom it is said next: He sent his Word and healed them, and redeemed them from their corruptions. And they cried to the Lord

[in their affliction, and out of their distr]esses he saved them. And he brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and broke their bonds apart. For how were we not in distress, enslaved as we were to evil demons and unclean spirits? But God, who loves humankind and is merciful, heard the prayers of his holy prophets and of God-loving men crying to him on our behalf. He not only brought us out of these things, but also broke their bonds. This signifies the complete [?] forgiveness of sinners, of which the grace of our Saviour Jesus Christ has counted us worthy. Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders to the children of men; for he shattered gates of bronze and crushed bars of iron. He took hold of them out of the way of their lawlessness, for because of their lawless deeds they were brought low. Now the same thing is said in connection with his second benefits. I think these words show that human souls had fallen even as far as death, and for their sake the Redeemer and Saviour of all had to descend even as far as death. When the Christ of God came there, he alone of all who have ever lived shattered the gates that had been bound with iron from eternity and never opened to any mortal, and had therefore become bronze; and he broke their unbreakable bars. Their soul abhorred all food, and they drew near to the gates of death. Because of the [?] of those who turned away from all rational and

saving food of souls, it was fitting that the only-begotten Son of God, when he was sent, should reach as far as the gates of death. He was made flesh and became man, and he stretched out a hand of salvation even to those who had fallen so far and had cried out to him. And they cried to the Lord in their affliction, and out of their distresses he saved them. He sent his word and healed them, and rescued them from their corruptions. Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders to the children of men. And let them offer him a sacrifice of praise, and declare his works with rejoicing. Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing business on many waters. Having mentioned the coming of the Redeemer and Saviour, through whom everything foretold has been accomplished, the word next adds the prophecy concerning his apostles. For they were the ones who went down to the sea in ships, plainly and literally, as the divine Scripture of the Gospels testifies. So the present prophecy very consistently joined the remembrance of the apostles and those with them to the coming of the Word of God among men. It was to these very men, then, that it gave the command to perform the new mysteries of the New Covenant, saying: And let them offer a sacrifice of praise, and declare his works with rejoicing. He spoke, and a stormy wind arose, and its waves were lifted high. They mount up to the heavens and go down to the depths; their soul melted away in troubles. They were troubled, they staggered like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up. And they cried to the Lord in their affliction, and he brought them out of their distresses. And he struck the storm, and it settled into a breeze, and its waves fell silent. These things, foretold in prophecy, were fulfilled plainly and literally. For when the disciples of our Saviour were sailing with him, "a great storm," it says, "arose on the sea, so that the boat was being covered by the waves. And they fell before him and said to him, 'Lord, save us, we are perishing.' And he said to them, 'Why are you afraid, you of little faith?' Then he rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm." And they were glad because the sea grew quiet, and he guided them to the haven of his will. Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders to the children of men. Let them exalt him in the assembly of the people, and praise him in the seat of the elders. They were guided to the haven of his will. Because of this the word necessarily commands for the fourth time that they give thanks to the Lord and keep his mercies on their lips, and it urges them to proclaim his wonders to all the children of men. He turned rivers into a desert, and springs of water into thirst, a fruitful land into a salt waste, because of the wickedness of those who dwelt in it.

He turned the desert into pools of water, a waterless land into springs of water. And he settled the hungry there, and they founded cities to dwell in. And they sowed fields and planted vineyards, and produced a fruitful harvest. And he blessed them and they multiplied greatly, and he did not let their cattle decrease. And they became few and were afflicted by the pressure of evils and pain. Contempt was poured out on their rulers, and he made them wander in a trackless place, where there was no road. For the multitude of the Jewish nation was driven to such a scarcity of good things that few were found among them who were approved by God. The whole nation underwent what this prediction foretold. And their rulers—certain patriarchs, high priests and teachers of the law, Sadducees, scribes and Pharisees—were covered with shame and handed over to contempt, since they had been called to the straight way and refused it. And he helped the poor man out of poverty. Here too Symmachus, as usual, rendered it: "And he will strengthen the poor man out of affliction." For those others, he says, will suffer what was foretold, but he will strengthen the poor people—that is, the people gathered from the nations. Our Saviour and Lord Jesus Christ called them blessed, saying: "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." And he made families like sheep. Aquila says, "And he will place kindreds like a flock"; Symmachus says, "And he will arrange kindreds like a flock." These are the Churches in every city and every region, formed out of different kindreds. The upright will see and be glad, and all lawlessness will stop its mouth. What will they see but the change from worse to better? This is why the Saviour said to those who beheld the fulfillment of the prophecies: "Blessed are your eyes, for they see"; and, "Many prophets longed to see what you see, and did not see it." And all injustice will stop its mouth: it rages and bursts with envy, yet it can do nothing, because of God who willed these things. And we can see this clearly. The lawlessness of unbelieving and idolatrous men raged against the Church of Christ and often went mad against it, but in the end, able to do nothing, it stopped its own mouth, muzzled by the divine Word. In the times of persecution he said to it too: "Be silent, be muzzled." By lawlessness you should understand the devil and everyone who acts in accordance with it, as in the saying: "The mouth of those who speak unjust things was stopped." Who is wise, and will keep these things? And they will understand the mercies of the Lord.

A Song of a Psalm of David. Psalm 107. My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make music in my glory. Awake, my glory; awake, harp and lyre; I will awake at dawn. I will give thanks to you among the peoples, O Lord; I will sing to you among the nations. For your mercy is great above the heavens, and your truth reaches to the clouds. He who [?]

has become worthy of the beatitude in which it is said, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God," could say with confidence: My heart is ready, O God. So the Prophet, having done through virtuous deeds the things that are dear and akin to the Holy Spirit, sends up this prayer to God, the giver of such gifts. I will sing and make music in my glory: that is, having received my own glory, which is the grace of prophecy. Awake, my glory; awake, harp and lyre; I will awake at dawn. Perhaps he is rousing the powers of his own soul and body because of the inspiration of the divine Spirit that was about to come upon him. In the spiritual sense, we take [?] to mean the members and sense organs of the body, through which the mind strikes up its music whenever it wishes, and the harp to mean the incorporeal and rational powers of the soul. He prepares these to receive the Spirit when he says: Awake, harp and lyre. Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth, so that your beloved may be delivered. Save with your right hand, and hear me. God has spoken in his holy one: I will be exalted, and I will divide Shechem, and measure out the valley of tents. I beseech and entreat that grace may come quickly, and that you, the Most High God, who are hymned in the heavens, may be made known and may make your glory manifest over all the earth. For when this happens, your beloved will be delivered from the bitter slavery and captivity they have suffered since they fell into subjection. Save with your right hand, and hear me. God has spoken in his holy one. Who was his holy one but the only-begotten Child, who is truly holy and beloved? Through him God made his answer to the prayer they had offered. To the prayer that said, Be exalted above the heavens, O God, he answers, I will be exalted. And to the words And your glory over all the earth, he again answers with what follows, beginning from I will be exalted, and I will divide Shechem, and measure out the valley of tents. This valley, then, he says—that is, the whole inhabited world of men—I will measure out into tents, as though surveying the land and registering them. I will measure it out into tents in every city, region and village; and again, I will measure out and survey tents for myself, that is, the Churches everywhere. Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine, and Ephraim is the support of my head. Judah is my king, Moab is the basin of my hope. Ephraim and Manasseh were sons of Joseph, and their descendants occupied the land called Gilead, as well as Shechem and Samaria, where the kingdom of Israel was established. For this reason he says that these too are his. Ephraim in particular, because of the kingdom that arose from him, he calls the strength of his own head. Judah is my king, Moab is the basin of my hope. He says that Judah is his king. And it is evident that, as the Apostle says, our Saviour

and Lord Jesus Christ has sprung from Judah, from whom the royal line arose. In these words the word brings Ephraim and Judah together, because in ancient times the whole Jewish nation was divided into two kingdoms. It prophesies that this division would no longer exist, and that the whole nation would be united. These things too were fulfilled at the appearing of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. In those times, at any rate, the whole nation of the Jews was united and no longer divided into two kingdoms. This is why the Saviour proclaimed the gospel of the kingdom to all alike, and sent out his disciples to all their tribes. Judah is my king, Moab is the basin of my hope. When these, he says, have been received first, at the beginning of the calling, not even the worst of the foreigners will be made strangers to me. I will take to myself and receive even Moab himself, who was forbidden to enter the assembly of the Lord. For this is what I hope. Moab is the basin of my hope. Aquila and the fifth edition rendered the meaning more plainly and clearly. In them it reads, "Moab is the basin of my washing," that is, the vessel for my washing. Symmachus says, "Moab will be the basin of my freedom from care." I know that I once heard an account of these passages handed down in secret by a certain Hebrew. He said that these words mystically signify that the birth of Christ according to the flesh drew on the race of Moab, through Ruth the Moabitess. From her came King David, of whose seed the Christ of God was born according to the flesh—the same Christ who also came to the baptism of John and the washing in the Jordan. Moab is the basin of my hope. It seems to me that through these words God also promises Moab the grace of the calling, and that in no other way than through the regeneration of the washing. And since he promises such things to Moab, he leaves us to understand the same about the other nations. For when the prophecy admits the Moabites, who were formerly forbidden, it is clear that through them it also sketches good hopes for the rest of the nations. Over Idumea I will cast my shoe; foreigners have been subjected to me. Who will bring me into a fortified city, or who will lead me as far as Idumea? Is it not you, O God, who rejected us? And will you not go out, O God, with our armies? Give us help out of affliction, for the salvation of man is vain. In God we shall do valiantly, and he will bring to nothing those who afflict us. That is: I will set foot upon the nations and walk among them. For the Idumeans were descended from Esau, the hated one, of whom it is said: "Was not Esau Jacob's brother? says the Lord"; and, "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated." I will cast my shoe, then, he says, no longer on Israel, nor on the land of Judea, nor on Jerusalem alone, but on the very land of the hated one. So I will set foot upon the former enemies and place them in the ranks of friends. Foreigners have been subjected to me. Instead of [?]

Aquila, for his part, says, “Over the Philistines I will make an alliance”; the fifth edition, “Over the foreigners I will be honored”; and the fifty-ninth psalm, “Foreigners were made subject to me.” That those who were formerly unsubdued, strangers to God and in the grip of evil demons, have been made subject to him is a sign of knowledge of God, of friendship, of fellowship and of love.

TO THE END. A PSALM OF DAVID. 108. “O God, do not pass over my praise in silence; for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful have been opened against me. They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue, and surrounded me with words of hatred, and fought against me without cause.” As usual, here too, in place of “to the end,” Aquila has rendered “for the one who gives victory,” and Symmachus has said “a song of victory”; it is almost as though the Holy Spirit were teaching us that these present words also ought to be counted among the victory songs of our Savior and his trophies over death, since in them his human life and his endurance of sufferings are set forth. “O God, do not pass over my praise in silence; for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful have been opened against me. They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue, and surrounded me with words of hatred, and fought against me without cause.” The present psalm refers to the person of Christ, containing [?] of his. The book of the Acts of the Apostles bears witness to this statement, where Peter, recalling the fall of the traitor Judas and urging that another must be taken into the number of the twelve apostles, made use of the prophetic testimony in the present psalm, which says, “Let his homestead become desolate, and let there be no one to live in it,” and, “Let another take his office.” So, according to Peter’s teaching, this very utterance was spoken about Judas, and so were the others found in the psalm. The Savior, then, beginning with these words in a human manner, as one who had become man while remaining God, which he was, entreats his own Father not to let those who were plotting against his zeal succeed. And his whole zeal was to extinguish all idolatry from among human beings and to establish praise to [?] on earth, as he teaches elsewhere when he says, “I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the assembly I will sing your praise.” But those who were plotting his death were zealous to silence and suppress this very praise. “But you, O Father,” he says, “do not allow my praise to be silenced, which is zealously pursued for your honor and glory.” “For the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful have been opened against me.” The mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful was, above all, that of the whole body of the Pharisees and scribes, who hypocritically called him Teacher and Rabbi, and especially that of Judas, who betrayed his own Savior and Lord with a kiss. “They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue, and surrounded me with words of hatred, and fought against me without cause. Instead of loving me, they slandered me;

but I kept praying.” For they ought to have loved him as a benefactor and as a physician not only of bodies but also of souls; yet they stitched together slanders against him. “Instead of loving me, they slandered me; but I kept praying. And they laid against me evil for good, and hatred for my love.” In this he is all but teaching his disciples by his own deed what sort of people they too should be, if ever they meet with similar treatment. Since the words “But I kept praying” are said without qualification, and what he prayed for, even on their behalf, is not stated, one might reasonably say that he prayed for them the things that agreed with his own teachings, in which he said, “Pray for those who abuse and persecute you.” “And they laid against me evil for good, and hatred for my love.” About these things there is no need to say anything, since the history in the Gospels contains the multitude of benefits he bestowed on them when he became man, healing every disease and every infirmity among them. “Set a sinner over him, and let the devil stand at his right hand.” The devil also tripped him up, stripping away everything he had previously seemed to possess on the right hand of his soul. “When he is judged, may he go out condemned, and may his prayer become sin. May his days be few, and may another take his office. May his sons become orphans and his wife a widow; may his sons be driven about and wander, and beg; may they be cast out of their homesteads.” It is likely that all these things were fulfilled expressly, according to the bare letter, against the traitor after he hanged himself: his children became orphans, his wife was left in widowhood, and all the things listed after these came to pass word for word, so that our Savior’s prediction through the psalm that these things would happen proved true. You will also understand these things as having been fulfilled literally upon the people of the Jewish nation after the plot against Christ. For when a few years had passed after the cross, the whole nation was thrown into turmoil; some were killed, and their wives together with their children were sold into slavery. “Let the creditor search out all that he has, and let strangers plunder their wealth. Let him have no helper, nor let there be anyone to pity his orphans. Let his children be given over to destruction; in a single generation may his name be blotted out.” Symmachus renders it thus: “Let the exactor shatter all his possessions.” And the Roman emperors are also exactors, collecting the tribute imposed. These plundered the property of the Jews, searching everything so thoroughly as to find and seize even what had been hidden. When these things had happened, and the enemies were dividing up what belonged to them, there would be no one to help them, nor would their children be thought worthy of mercy. Then, after not many [?] years had passed, the Jewish people suffered total destruction.

“May the iniquity of his fathers be remembered before the Lord, and may the sin of his mother not be blotted out. May they be before the Lord continually, and may their memory be destroyed from the earth, because he did not remember to show mercy.” The virtue of fathers has often benefited even children who went astray, as the faith of Abraham benefited the Jews, and as the piety of David benefited Solomon; but the wickedness of fathers increases the punishment of children who are like them, for no ground for sparing them is found anywhere. “May the iniquity of his fathers be remembered before the Lord.” By their fathers he means those who practiced impiety in the wilderness, those in the time of the judges, those in the period of the kings, and those who lived in lawlessness after the return from Babylon. “And may the sin of his mother not be blotted out.” By mother he means Jerusalem, in which the abomination of the murder of Christ the Master was dared. “May they be before the Lord continually, and may their memory be destroyed from the earth, because he did not remember to show mercy.” “God,” he says, “ever beholding all the lawless deeds they dared to commit, will not deem them worthy of any mercy, but will hand them over to total destruction.” And from this it is plain that he is speaking not of Judas alone but of all the Jews who refused to believe; for he has shifted the discourse from the singular to the plural. He no longer said “his,” but

“And he persecuted a man poor and needy, and pierced to the heart, to put him to death”; that is, stricken because of the lawless deeds he saw among them. That is why he also said to Jerusalem, weeping over her, “If you too had known the things that make for your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes.” He put him to death in that he became the cause of his being handed over to death. “And he loved cursing, and it shall come upon him; and he did not want blessing, and it shall be removed far from him. And he put on cursing like a garment, and it entered like water into his inward parts, and like oil into his bones. Let it be to him like a garment that he wraps about himself, and like a belt with which he is always girded. This is the work of those who slander me before the Lord, and of those who speak evil against my soul.” Since the prophecy says in the person of the Savior, “Those who bless you are blessed, and those who curse you are cursed,” it is plain to all how those throughout the whole world who have come to know God through him and have believed in him are counted worthy of the blessing that comes from God, so that they multiply and increase and fill all things with the Church of Christ; and how the Jews, cursing him and blaspheming him every day, draw down upon themselves the curse that comes from God, is also clear from the fact that they have not lifted up their head or recovered since the time of the plot against our Savior. “And you, O Lord, deal with me for your name’s [?] sake; for your mercy is good. Deliver

me, for I am poor and needy, and my heart is troubled within me. Like a shadow when it declines I have been taken away; I have been shaken off like locusts. My knees have grown weak from fasting, and my flesh has been changed for want of oil.” Anxious over the ruin of their souls—of the traitor himself and of those who had contrived the plot against him with him—and over the casting off and falling away of the whole Jewish nation, he confesses that, as one who loves humankind, he is troubled on their account. That is why he says, “And my heart is troubled within me.” “And I became a reproach to them; they saw me and shook their heads. Help me, O Lord my God, and save me according to your mercy. And let them know that this is your hand, and that you, O Lord, have done it.” In the resurrection from the dead the hand of God became known, that is, his only-begotten Word; and he who until then had been hidden from the many was made manifest, since he himself willingly endured the cross, despising the shame, and he himself raised his own body, being the right hand and power of the Father. “Let them know, then,” he says, “that this is your hand”—the one they reproach and mock—“and that you, O Lord, have made it,” in that you were pleased for it to take up a body. For the hand of God is his power that makes all things, and it is none other than God the Word, through whom all things came into being. “They will curse, but you will bless. Let those who rise up against me be put to shame, but your servant shall rejoice.” To this very day the Jews have persisted in their blasphemies against the Savior; yet while they blaspheme, the proclamation becomes more conspicuous every day. “Let those who slander me be clothed with disgrace, and let them wrap themselves in their shame as in a double cloak.” For the Jews, after the plot against Christ, deprived of God’s care, have wrapped themselves in shame; but our Savior and Lord is still even now filled with gladness, since the Church has been established through his name throughout the whole world. “But your servant shall rejoice.” Not even this phrase will compel us to apply the passage to a different subject; for we hear the inspired Paul too saying that “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant”; and he himself cries out through Isaiah, “Thus says the Lord, who formed me from the womb to be his servant.” “Let those who slander me be clothed with disgrace, and let them wrap themselves in their shame as in a double cloak.” You can learn this too if you consider what thoughts the children of the Jews must have when they see their own venerable and holy things obliterated from their foundations, while, of the one whom they clothed with dishonor and handed over to the cross and to death, the tomb of his death is honored with zeal and lavish munificence, and the churches founded by his power throughout the whole world grow day by day, multiply, and advance still further in glory. For when the children of the Jews see these things with their own eyes, how could they not rightly be clothed with disgrace and shame? “I will give great thanks to the Lord with my mouth, and in the midst of many I will praise him; for

he stood at the right hand of the poor, to save my soul from those who persecute it.” Of many: and who are these, if not all the nations that have believed in him, and the churches throughout the whole world? For he is the one who said, “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.” Therefore, throughout the whole world, in the midst of the churches, the greatest thanksgiving goes forth from the Lord to the Father.

A PSALM OF DAVID. 109. “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.’” Our Savior pointed out a very precise and true word when he said, “If then David in the Spirit calls him Lord, how is he his son?” For apart from the Holy Spirit David could not have said, “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand.’” For where could human reasoning have obtained knowledge of the Father’s conversation with the one he calls his Lord? The throne, then, signifies his royal dignity, and the sitting the firm, settled and unshaken permanence of his reign; and “at the right hand” means that he also shares in the Father’s right-hand gifts. For the Son bestows all things on the right hand—bright, good and saving things—as coming from the Father. By enemies he means those made known through the preceding psalm; and not only them, but also all the opposing powers. For through the present psalm the Father announces that he will put them all under his feet. “The Lord will send forth the rod of power from Zion; and rule in the midst of your enemies.” The rod of power here I take to mean the gospel word. But consider whether perhaps the rod of power spoken of here is meant in a different sense from the one called a rod of iron in the second psalm. The gospel word, which proclaims the power of our Savior and his saving economy, would be the rod that instructs and saves; but the rod that destroys his enemies and the foes of his Church is called iron, and with it he is said to shatter his enemies like a potter’s vessels. Since, then, Christ established his churches in the midst of cities and in the very midst of the nations, among enemies and foes, it is said of necessity, “The Lord will send forth the rod of your power, so that you may rule in the midst of your enemies.”

“With you is the sovereignty in the day of your power, in the splendors of the saints; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” Aquila: “From the womb of the early dawn, yours is the dew of your childhood”; Symmachus: “As at dawn, your youth is to you like dew”; the fifth edition: “From the womb, from the dawn, yours is the dew of your youth.” And it seems that by these words the economy of his birth in the flesh is signified. For from the womb, he says, there will come the early-dawning dew of your childhood; or, from the womb there will

come to you your dew of dawn in your youth. I think what is signified by these words is that his birth in the flesh came about not from the seed of a man but from the Holy Spirit. For just as dew is borne down from heaven above, so in some such way the formation of his flesh took place in the womb of the mother who carried him, in his childhood. In place of “from the belly” or “from the womb,” the Hebrew has “Mariam.” I know [?] having heard from someone that the Hebrew word here makes mention of Mary; for “Mariam” signifies the name of Mary, so that in these words the Mother of God is mentioned by name. “The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind: ‘You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.’ The Lord at your right hand has shattered kings in the day of his wrath. He will judge among the nations, he will fill [?] with corpses, he will shatter heads upon the earth. He will drink from the brook by the way; therefore he will lift up his head.” These words seem to me to be joined in very close sequence with the passage written before them. “For even if you did indeed undergo birth from the womb,” he says, “and were born like dew from the Holy Spirit, taking flesh in your childhood, still you will not end your life as other human beings do; rather, you will remain forever serving as priest to God the Father. For this has been decreed, and declared with the confirmation of an oath by your Father.”

ALLELUIA. 110. “I will give thanks to you, O Lord, with my whole heart, in the council of the upright and in the congregation.” The form of the title of this psalm and of those that follow shows that these words were not spoken to the psaltery, and that they do not occupy the place of an ode, nor of a prayer, nor of any of the other titles, but are hymns of thanksgiving. That is why they are headed “Alleluia,” which, translated into the Greek tongue, means “praise of God.” “I will give thanks to you, O Lord, with my whole heart, in the council of the upright and in the congregation.
