Great are the works of the Lord, sought out in all that he wills. Thanksgiving and majesty are his work, and his righteousness endures forever and ever.” Very fittingly, after the prophecy given concerning our Savior, a hymn of thanksgiving is joined to it in these words, spoken in the person of the Savior himself as he gives thanks to his own Father for the salvation of all human beings. For the word “confession” used here, in the customary usage of Scripture, sometimes signifies the confession of sins, and sometimes denotes thanksgiving. Thus in the Gospels our Savior himself says, “I give thanks to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and have revealed them to infants. Yes, Father, for so it was well-pleasing in your sight. All things have been handed over to me by the Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, and who the Father is except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal

him.” “In the council of the saints and in the congregation. Great are the works of the Lord, sought out in all that he wills.” “No longer in the council of crooked or perverse men, but in that of good and upright souls will I render the hymn of thanksgiving to you, my own Father.” By these words he signifies the Church established by his grace throughout the whole world. By the council of the upright he meant the ranks of the saints in his Church; and the congregation signifies a second rank after the council of the upright, the second assembly of the multitude in his Church. “Thanksgiving and majesty are his work, and his righteousness endures forever and ever. He has made a memorial of his wonders; the Lord is merciful and compassionate; he has given food to those who fear him. He will remember his covenant forever; the strength of his works [?] he has proclaimed to his people, to give them the inheritance of the nations. The works of his hands are truth and judgment. Faithful are all his commandments, established forever and ever, made in truth and uprightness. He sent redemption to his people; he commanded his covenant forever. Holy and fearful is his name; the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” Perhaps, since the one who fears is not yet made perfect, the entry is accomplished through fear, but the goal through love? For perfect love casts out fear. And such a one would be the person who loves the Lord God with all his heart and soul and strength. “And good understanding belongs to all who practice it. His praise endures forever and ever.” Understanding is good only when it is carried out in deeds; that is why he did not call understanding good without qualification, but good to all who practice it. “His praise endures forever and ever.” For the goal of the blessed is to be with God, to stand in his presence, and to devote themselves solely to speaking of God and praising him.

ALLELUIA. 111. “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he will greatly desire his commandments. His seed will be mighty in the land; the generation of the upright will be blessed. Glory and wealth are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever and ever.” It is Scripture’s custom to give this name to everyone from the nations who comes to God. This is shown by the fact that, distinctly after Israel, after the house of Aaron and after the house of Levi, those who fear the Lord are called to the hymn of God, as is said elsewhere. For who could those who fear the Lord be, coming after these, if not the foreigners and those of other races from among the nations? So in the psalm before us the one pronounced blessed would be none other than the people from the nations who have come to God, whom he calls one who fears the Lord. Yet such a person is not yet blessed unless he also does what follows, namely, to desire greatly God’s commandments, and unless he truly possesses that desire, so that he keeps the commandments not under compulsion nor against his will, but willingly, with affection, with all eagerness, and with a genuine love for keeping the commandments of God.

"Light has dawned in darkness for the upright; he is merciful, compassionate and righteous." The one who is called blessed does not cease making his own light rise, though not for all. He gives his teaching to his upright ones, provides the light of knowledge within the generation of the upright, and enlightens the upright. "Good is the man who shows compassion and lends." He does not shut up his compassion, but shares his possessions with those in need, because he keeps the commandment that says: "Who then is the faithful and wise steward, who will give his fellow servants their portion of food at the proper time? Blessed is that servant whom his master will find doing so when he comes. Truly I tell you, he will set him over all his possessions." "He will manage his words with judgment, for he will never be shaken." Such a man, he says, who acts in this way, will neither fall nor be shaken from his stand upon the rock. He will not cower at the threats of rulers, nor at those who try to disturb and trouble him in times of hardship. "The righteous will be remembered forever; he will not be afraid of evil news." Nor will he suffer any harm from false words that claim to be the truth but are raised up against the knowledge of God, since he is founded upon the rock and nothing separates him from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus. "His heart is ready to hope in the Lord; his heart is established; he will not be afraid until he looks upon his enemies." For these reasons, he says, he will not be shaken, nor will he be afraid of evil news, since his heart is ready to hope in the Lord. Symmachus rendered this as: "His heart is steadfast, free of care in the Lord." Therefore he despises such disturbances. He not only has no fear of his foes, but because of his hope in God he even waits patiently for their defeat. "He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever and ever; his horn will be exalted in glory. The sinner will see it and be angry; he will gnash his teeth and melt away; the desire of the sinner will perish." The whole discourse concerns those who are made perfect through faith, and it has been speaking of the people from the nations who worship God according to the divine teaching. So it fittingly goes on to mention also those of the circumcision who are cut to the heart at the progress of those from the nations. This is why it says: "The sinner will see it and be angry; he will gnash his teeth and melt away." The sinner here is the lawless one, who received the law but transgressed it. Such is everyone of the circumcision who gnashes his teeth at our salvation. Yet the unbelievers among the nations suffer the same thing at the progress of those among them who have passed over to the godly way of life. But both groups, cut to the heart against those who are being made perfect in Christ, will melt away, and their desire will perish.

Alleluia. Of Haggai and Zechariah. Psalm 112. "Praise the Lord, you children; praise the name of the Lord. May the name of the Lord be blessed from now and forever." In the previous psalm the word sketched every man who has become blessed through fearing the Lord, and described the life of such people, their godly conduct, and the end that awaits them from God. In the present psalm it teaches who these people are and whom they resemble. It calls them children because their age of soul is young and newly born, and it summons them to the praise of God. Instead of "children," Aquila and Symmachus called them "servants," saying: "Praise the Lord, you servants; hymn the name of the Lord." For children are no different from servants while they are being trained under the fear of servitude. "May the name of the Lord be blessed from now and forever." Since the children do not know how they ought to hymn the Lord, the prophetic Spirit, like a tutor and teacher, hands them the very words. This is a prayer offered on behalf of us ourselves, the children, that the name of the Lord may remain with us forever, not fleeing from us but resting upon our life. "From the rising of the sun to its setting the name of the Lord is to be praised. The Lord is high above all the nations; his glory is above the heavens." And when did this saying find its fulfillment, if not after the appearing of our Savior Jesus Christ? Before that, God was said to be known in Judea alone, and his name was great in Israel alone. The nations outside Judea were enslaved to demons and unclean spirits, and the name of the Lord never even entered the minds of those who clung to idolatry. But when our Lord Jesus Christ himself appeared and sent his disciples out to all the nations, then the [?] handed down to all through these words was fulfilled

"Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high and looks upon the lowly things in heaven and on earth?" Through these words the new people is taught that even though our Lord has been taken up and is at the right hand of the Father, the whole earth is nonetheless full of him and enjoys his oversight. Does this saying not seem great? Yet when you consider of whom it was said, it falls far short. For how can he dwell in the heavens who fills heaven and earth, who is present everywhere, who says, "I am a God near at hand, and not a God far off," who measured the heaven with a span and the earth with a handful, who holds the circle of the earth? But since his words were addressed to Jews, he uses such language for the time being, stooping to their dullness. Then, little by little, he leads their understanding upward, gives wings to their thought and lifts it up, and gently adds "in heaven and on earth," that is, both above and below. He said this because of the

weakness of the Jews, which was infatuated with idols and worshipped gods shut up in places and temples. So by saying "in heaven and on earth" he gives us to understand that he is everywhere, both there and here, and pervades all things. He does not look at the things on earth from afar, like someone shut up in heaven. Rather, he is present everywhere, uncontained and uncircumscribed, and he encompasses all things. Do you see how he gives wings to the understanding of his hearers little by little? For he is not seeking, for the moment, how one might speak worthily of the glory of God, but how it can be grasped by them. Elsewhere too heaven is called God's throne, because the heavenly powers have the glory of God firmly established among them, and the earth is called his footstool, because people on earth can barely grasp even the lowest of the things concerning God. Here David, having raised the hearer up from the earth, turns to another demonstration of God's power, saying: "He raises the poor from the earth and lifts the needy from the dunghill, to seat him with rulers, with the rulers of his people; he settles the barren woman in a home, a mother rejoicing over her children." He is hymning the power of God, which easily changes whatever it wishes. For not only, he says, does he make the needy rich and glorious, but he even seats him beside the rulers of the people and raises him to rule. It is the mark of a great and ineffable power to lift up what is small. The verse can also be applied to the people from the nations, of whom the prophet says: "And for this reason the poor people will bless you, and cities of wronged men will bless you. For you have become a helper to every lowly city, and a shelter to those who lost heart through want; you will rescue them from wicked men; you are a shelter for the thirsty and the breath of wronged men." For he will raise this poor and needy people from base things, from the dishonor of the passions and from the dunghill of pagan abominations, and seat it with the rulers of Israel, which is his people. The rulers of the Hebrew people are the apostles, or else the patriarchs, and with them those from the nations who have believed will dwell. This is what the Lord says: "Many will come from east and west and will recline with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven." The saying, then, is a general one. But if someone wishes to take it in a higher sense, he will see it fulfilled once again at the coming of Christ. For what is poorer than our nature? Yet he raised it up, led up our firstfruits, and seated it in the highest heaven. By "dunghill" he here means what is worthless, together with the sudden change from that state, showing that all things are easy and simple for him. Blessed Hannah said these things too, when she offered her hymn of thanksgiving to God: "The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and he lifts up; he raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dunghill, to seat him with the mighty of the people and to give them a throne of glory as their inheritance." We see

these things being done continually by the God of the universe. Thus he made blessed David, who was a shepherd, a king. Thus he seated Joseph, who had fallen into slavery, upon the royal throne. Thus he made Moses, who had become a shepherd, the leader of the people, and appointed him as a god to Pharaoh. Thus he deemed the nations, which were enslaved to impiety and sat upon the dung of sin and abomination, worthy of the good things that had been given to Israel. Thus he took up human nature, which had fallen to the very bottom of Hades, led it up, and seated it far above every rule and authority and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come.

Alleluia. Psalm 113. "When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarian people, Judea became his sanctuary, Israel his dominion." This too is a hymn. It recounts the benefits God granted to the Jews, tells of God's power, and mocks the weakness of idols. This hymn also suits those from the nations who have believed and been set free from the error of idols, for they learn how great the difference is between the things that are not and the One who is, and that there is one God of the Old and the New Testament. Instead of "from a barbarian people," Aquila rendered "from a people of another tongue," and Symmachus "from a people of foreign speech." "Judea became his sanctuary, Israel his dominion." Long ago, when those of the former people made their journey out of Egypt under Moses, a small portion of land, a quite insignificant corner of the whole world, namely Judea, was chosen for God, together with a single nation, that of the Jews. But when the grace of the saving appearance spread over the whole world, "from the rising of the sun to its setting the name of the Lord is praised," and the Lord has become high not over one nation, Israel, but "high above all the nations." "The sea saw and fled; the Jordan turned back; the mountains skipped like rams, and the hills like lambs of the flock. What ails you, O sea, that you fled, and you, Jordan, that you turned back? You mountains, that you skipped like rams, and you hills, like lambs of the flock? At the presence of the Lord the earth was shaken, at the presence of the God of Jacob, who turned the rock into pools of water and the flint into springs of water." Here again the word seems to me to be prophesying the calling of all the nations. Long ago, he says, at the journey out of Egypt, Judea alone became God's sanctuary, and Israel alone was under his dominion. And long ago only a partial awareness came to the sea, the river, the mountains and the hills. But now let the whole element of the earth be moved and shaken, or rather, as Aquila has it, let it be in labor, so that what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah may be fulfilled: "Who has

heard such things, and who has seen the like? Did the earth travail in one day, and was a nation born all at once?" For since the nations were being called and the grace of God was about to be poured out over the whole inhabited world, it was absolutely necessary that the objects of worship the nations had set up from ages past should be shaken and made to totter, and that the demons in them should flee, so that the people from the nations might be born to God throughout the whole world. "Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory, for the sake of your mercy and your truth, lest the nations should say, 'Where is their God?' But our God is in heaven and on earth; he has done whatever he willed. The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands." Here the Holy Spirit seems to me to be hinting at the rejection of the people of the circumcision. He hands them a prayer of confession and speaks these words in their person, showing that they no longer have the divine power watching over them. Through these words they are taught to pray and entreat, saying: "We are unworthy of the grace that all the nations have been granted. Do not do it for us, Master, but for the sake of your name, which was called upon us from the beginning. Grant it not for our righteous deeds, but for your mercy and your truth. For if you do not have mercy, the nations will say, 'Where is their God?' So that they may never say this, be gracious to us and grant us your mercy. For even if your oversight no longer steers us, we are still persuaded that you are in heaven and do whatever you have willed." "Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory, for the sake of your mercy and your truth, lest the nations should say, 'Where is their God?' But our God is in heaven and on earth; he has done whatever he willed. The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths but will not speak; they have eyes but will not see; they have ears but will not hear; they have noses but will not smell; they have hands but will not feel; they have feet but will not walk; they will make no sound in their throats. May those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them. The house of Israel has hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and protector. The house of Aaron has hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and protector. Those who fear the Lord have hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and protector. The Lord has remembered us and blessed us. He has blessed the house of Israel; he has blessed the house of Aaron; he has blessed those who fear the Lord, the small together with the great. May the Lord add to you, to you and to your children. You are blessed by the Lord, who made heaven and earth. The heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord, but the earth he has given to the children of men. It is not the dead who will praise you, O Lord, nor any of those who go down

to Hades. But we who are alive will bless the Lord from now and forever." In some copies these verses are separated from Psalm 113 and set apart on their own, so that the psalm before us becomes Psalm 114. But when I looked into the Hebrew book itself, I found its letters and words joined together. So I judged it right to follow the Hebrew book and to join these verses to the preceding ones, so that they form part of the 113th hymn. These verses, then, seem to depend on what came before. The children to whom it was said, "Praise the Lord, you children," that is, the new people, are being taught what kind of Lord it is fitting to praise: clearly the very one who worked so many wonders at Israel's exodus from Egypt. Following on from that, the same people are taught not to be ignorant of what sort of things the gods they once believed in really were: that they are lifeless and deprived of all sensation, dead, deaf and blind idols, bearing no likeness, I will not say to the great and wonder-working Maker of the universe, but not even to the least of living creatures, which have a share in sensation. They are simply lifeless matter through and through. Living creatures were formed by the Word of God, but these gods are fabrications of human handiwork.

Alleluia. Psalm 114. "I have loved, because the Lord will hear the voice of my supplication, because he inclined his ear to me, and I will call upon him all my days." The one who once feared the Lord, having now advanced beyond fear and passed over to the love of God, might well say, "I have loved." And whom does he love, if not plainly the Lord God, with all his heart and strength and soul, so that for his sake he contends for the truth even to death, endures every temptation, and eagerly faces every danger out of love for God? "Because he inclined his ear to me, and I will call upon him all my days. The pangs of death encompassed me, the dangers of Hades found me; I found affliction and pain, and I called upon the name of the Lord: 'O Lord, deliver my soul.' The Lord is merciful and righteous, and our God shows mercy. The Lord preserves the little ones; I was brought low, and he saved me. Return, my soul, to your rest, for the Lord has been good to you; for he has rescued my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from stumbling." All these things, he says, I endured for God's sake, and I loved them. Not against my will, nor trying to escape them, but eagerly giving myself up to them all, I embraced them out of love for God, so that I can say: "For your sake we are being put to death all day long." For I loved all these things for the Lord's sake, and having loved, I called upon the name of the Lord. "I will be well-pleasing before the Lord in the land of the living." This world is itself mortal, and it is a place of the dying. For since the constitution of visible things is composite, and everything composite naturally dissolves, we who are in the world and are part of the

world necessarily share in the nature of the whole. But there, there is no alteration, either of body or of soul. There is no straying of reason, no change of mind, and no circumstance takes away the steadiness and calm of one's thoughts. That is the land of those who are still living, in which above all the prophet promises to be well-pleasing to God, since he will be interrupted by nothing from outside. That is a land in which there is no night, no sleep, which is the image of death, no food and no drink, which are the props of our weakness, and none of the hardships that come from outside. It is a land of the living: not of those who die through sin, but of those who live the true life that is in Christ Jesus.

Alleluia. Psalm 115. "I believed, therefore I spoke; but I was greatly humbled. I said in my alarm, 'Every man is a liar.' What shall I give back to the Lord for all that he has given me?" In the Hebrew copy these verses too are joined to those before them, so that their meaning depends on what was said earlier and forms part of it. For he had said, "Return, my soul, to your rest," and again, "I will be well-pleasing before the Lord in the land of the living." Here he continues by saying: "I believed, therefore I spoke." That is: I believed that there is another land of the living besides this human life, and another rest for the soul besides our sojourn on earth. "I believed, therefore I spoke; but I was greatly humbled. I said in my alarm, 'Every man is a liar.'" I humbled myself and afflicted myself greatly; for so Symmachus interpreted it, saying, "I was greatly afflicted." I did this because I knew that every man is a liar. I was anxious and concerned that I too, being a man, might prove a liar in what I had declared about myself when I said, "I will be well-pleasing before the Lord in the land of the living." For that reason I had believed in the life to come, in the rest of the soul and in the land of the living, and because I believed I had spoken these very things. So, lest I should ever fall away from the promise and be cheated of my hope, I humbled myself greatly. "I said in my alarm, 'Every man is a liar.'" For the reasonings of men are timid, and our designs are unsure. For a perishable body weighs down the soul, and this earthly tent burdens the mind with many cares; we can hardly guess at the things on earth, and what lies at hand we find only with toil. But who has traced out the things in heaven? Yet I did not speak as a man, for then I would indeed have lied. Rather, I believed the words of God and the promises of God. "What shall I give back to the Lord for all that he has given me? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord. I will pay my vows to the Lord in the presence of all his people. Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones. O Lord, I am your servant; I

your servant and the son of your handmaid. You have broken my bonds. He calls himself the son [?] of the handmaid, meaning the Church. By “bonds” he means the cords of his own sins, which had held him tight. “Freed from sin and made the son of your handmaid, the Church, I have been released from my former sins through your grace.” To you I will offer a sacrifice of praise, and I will call on the name of the Lord. I will pay my vows to the Lord in the presence of all his people, in the courts of the house of the Lord, in your midst, O Jerusalem. This shows the progress of the one who speaks these words, by whom I mean the people from the nations. By “To you I will offer a sacrifice of praise” he means: “I will partake of the body and the blood. As I partake of them I will call on your name, and I will pay my vows of thanksgiving to you, the Lord, inside, in the midst of the true Jerusalem, before all the people, and [I will keep] the promises I once made.” ALLELUIA. Psalm 116. Praise the Lord, all you nations; extol him, all you peoples. For his mercy has been made strong over us, and the truth of the Lord endures for ever. So the word summons all the foreign and alien nations to the hymn of God. Then it distinguishes the peoples from the nations and adds: Let all the peoples extol him. You will understand the difference if you consider the prophecy in Zechariah that says: Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion; for behold, I am coming and will dwell in your midst, says the Lord. And many nations will flee for refuge to the Lord, and they will be a people to him, and I will be their God. As long as they were nations, they were not yet his people. But when they turned from their former life and shared in the mysteries of God through rebirth and the washing of regeneration, they became his peoples. This is being fulfilled even now throughout the whole inhabited world. Peoples of countless thousands stand as if in choirs and sing hymns to the God of the Hebrew prophets, and they are taught the same readings, lessons and doctrines. These things, which we see with our own eyes, came about throughout the whole world of the nations by no other means than the saving power alone.

ALLELUIA. Psalm 117. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures for ever. Let the house of Israel now say that he is good, that his mercy endures for ever. Let the house of Aaron now say that he is good, that his mercy endures for ever. Let all who fear the Lord now say that he is good, that his mercy endures for ever. Here too the grace of the Gospel has been poured out on all the nations. The people of the circumcision was one part of these nations, and indeed the very first part. So the word fittingly calls them to thanksgiving first, and after them those from the nations who have come to the Gospel, according to the saying: To the Jew first and also to the Greek. But if

anyone examines the matter closely, the Jews above all ought to give thanks for the very coming of Christ. Even if they suffered the opposite, it was not because of the one who came but because of their own ingratitude. He came to them himself and said again and again: I came only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. If they proved unworthy of the benefit, let them put it down to their own transgressions and their boundless ingratitude. Out of affliction I called on the Lord, and he heard me and set me in a broad place. The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what man can do to me. The Lord is my helper, and I shall look upon my enemies. It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man; it is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in rulers. All the nations surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I drove them back. They surrounded me on every side, and in the name of the Lord I drove them back. They surrounded me like bees around a honeycomb, and they blazed up like fire among thorns, and in the name of the Lord I drove them back. I was pushed and overturned so that I would fall, but the Lord took hold of me. The Lord is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation. The voice of rejoicing and salvation is in the tents of the righteous. “I also gained something from taking in [?] with my own eyes the end of the ungodly. For I learned that they blazed up like fire among thorns, or were quenched like a fire of thorns (sic). So I am no longer troubled when I see the ungodly exalted and rising up against the people of God, for I have been taught what end [awaits] them [?]

The right hand of the Lord has done mighty deeds; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me; the right hand of the Lord has done mighty deeds. I shall not die but live, and I shall tell of the works of the Lord. The Lord has disciplined me severely, but he has not handed me over to death. The persecutions were not for nothing. They happened for the benefit and testing of those who were tried, and he teaches this when he says: The Lord has disciplined me severely. “For I came to know my own weakness, and I was not unaware of the power given to me by God. I was taught what the [right hand?] of the Lord was like, which humbled the enemies.” Open to me the gates of righteousness; I will go in through them and give thanks to the [Lord]. This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it. I will give thanks to you, for you heard me and became my salvation. Righteousness, the general name for all the virtues, is placed first. But if one then divides them by kind, one might say in the same way: “Open to me the gates of righteousness, and the gates of prudence, and of the other actions that accord with God.” When someone has passed through all the gates, he finally comes to the end, to the innermost holy place, so to speak. There he will no longer see many gates but a single gate of the Lord himself, through which all the righteous will enter. One might call this the last and

final gate, beyond which no one can go any further. The last gate of the Lord would be the contemplation of him, according to the saying: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. The stone that the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This was the Lord's doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes. This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it. O Lord, save us; O Lord, grant us success. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. He saw the benefit done to the world and the change in its affairs, its transformation for the better. So he rejoices with those who enjoy it and says: O Lord, save us; O Lord, grant us success. That is: “Keep safe those who enjoy these things, so that they may be filled and may show fruits worthy of the grace. Make the way easy for them, so that once they have obtained such good things they may not fall away from them.” We have blessed you from the house of the Lord; the Lord is God, and he has shone upon us. They confess that no one other than the Lord himself appeared to them and [?]. That is why they say: “We have blessed you, because he appeared and showed your salvation.” The prophets prayed, and by the Holy Spirit they foresaw what was to come. So they call blessed those who would one day be found worthy of its fulfilment. Join in the festival with thick boughs, up to the horns of the altar, you who are from the nations, with thick boughs. Aquila translated this as: Bind the festival with fat portions. Symmachus has: Bind together thick boughs in solemn assembly, up to the horns of the altar. Through these words [?] he commands them to fill the house of God with many treasures and to crown it with many offerings at the seasons of the festivals. You are my God, and I will give thanks to you; you are my God, and I will exalt you. The people gathered together in Christ, from Israel, from the house of Aaron, and from those who fear the Lord, is commanded to give thanks and to say in its thanksgiving: You are my God, and I will give thanks to you; you are my God, and I will exalt you. I will give thanks to you, for you heard me and became my salvation. To whom does he say this? To the Lord made known above, who rescued him from affliction, humbled his enemies, exalted the stone rejected by the builders, and granted success and salvation to those who believe in him. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures for ever.

ALLELUIA. Psalm 118. Blessed are those who are blameless in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are those who search out his testimonies; they will seek him with their whole heart. For those who do iniquity have not walked in his ways. You have commanded your commandments

to be kept with great care. O that my ways were directed to keep your ordinances! Then I shall not be put to shame when I look on all your commandments. I will give thanks to you with an upright heart, when I have learned the judgments of your righteousness. I will keep your ordinances; do not utterly forsake me. The blameless would also be those who are perfect in the way. Whoever is at the beginning of divine learning is taught to call them blessed. In this way he will not be [?] or grow puffed up as though he were already blessed, but will know that he falls far short of those who are called blessed. Blessed are those who search out his testimonies; they will seek him with their whole heart. We have already discussed the testimonies. The way [?] of these would be to travel according to their intent, [?] of prudence, as the Prophet says:

How shall a young man make his way straight? By keeping your words. With my whole heart I have sought you; do not thrust me away from your commandments. I have hidden your sayings in my heart, so that I may not sin against you. Blessed are you, O Lord; teach me your ordinances. With my lips I have declared all the judgments of your mouth. I have delighted in the way of your testimonies as in all riches. I will meditate on your commandments and consider your ways. I will ponder your ordinances; I will not forget your words. “When I call to mind the words of your righteous judgment,” he says, “I gain the greatest benefit. But I am afraid that I may somehow forget them. So I have prayed to remember your judgment throughout my whole life and at all times.” Or, to put it another way: “My soul has longed to know the judgments of your providence over all things, O Lord.” Deal bountifully with your servant; I shall live and keep your words. Uncover my eyes, and I shall perceive the wonders of your law. I am a sojourner on the earth; do not hide your commandments from me. My soul has longed to desire your judgments at all times. You have rebuked the proud; cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments. Take reproach and contempt away from me, for I have sought out your testimonies. For princes sat and spoke against me, but your servant pondered your ordinances. For your testimonies are my meditation, and your ordinances are my counsellors. “At times,” he says, “they reproached me, perhaps for old sins. At other times they held me in contempt and belittled me as worth nothing. But I sat alone and devoted myself to the divine words. I had no counsellor and no other comfort, so I used your ordinances in place of counsellors.” My soul has cleaved to the dust; give me life

according to your word. I declared my ways, and you heard me; teach me your ordinances. Make me understand the way of your ordinances, and I shall ponder your wonders. My soul has drowsed from weariness; strengthen me with your words. Remove the way of injustice from me, and by your law have mercy on me. Drowsiness is the beginning of sleep. In the same way the soul is sometimes said to drowse when it is at the beginning of sins: sin drags it down as if into sleep, but it lifts itself up and wakes through the remembrance of better things. “So I must ask to be given understanding and to have my eyes enlightened to understand the laws, so that every way of injustice may depart from me.” Instead of “Remove the way of injustice from me,” Aquila said: “Remove the way of falsehood from me,” and Symmachus: “Take the false way away from me.” This confirms the interpretation given above. For each person prays to be free of every false opinion and every false understanding of the divine Scriptures. I have chosen the way of truth; I have not forgotten your judgments. Only one person will say this verse: the one who despises what is seen as temporary, looks to what is unseen as eternal and alone truly real, and hastens toward it. The way chosen by someone who trades in the wealth of this world and in earthly glory is not the way of truth. So whoever has chosen to walk the way of truth, in the sense we have explained, does so because he does not forget the judgments of God and his recompense. The lover of truth, who never utters a false word with his mouth, might say: I have chosen the way of truth. And the one who always keeps the judgments of God before his eyes and remembers them in every action will say: I have not forgotten your judgments. I have cleaved to your testimonies, O Lord; do not put me to shame. A person has cleaved to the testimonies when he unites himself to the words handed down about heaven and earth, or about anything else written, and never departs from them. Let such a person take courage even if he has done shameful deeds before. Or let him also ask God for forgiveness [?] and say: Lord, do not put me to shame. I ran the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart. “In a short time,” he says, “I ran through the way, not of one commandment but of all your commandments. I carried it out in works and fulfilled by my very deeds what your commandments declare.” This is why Paul, having done just this, says: I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. Lay down for me as law, O Lord, the way of your ordinances, and I will seek it out always. He asks God for some things and promises to contribute the other himself. “You, O Lord,” he says, “lay down for me as law the way of your ordinances, and I will devote the whole time of my life to searching for it.”

Give me understanding, and I shall search out your law and keep it with my whole heart. The prophet wants to search out the law of God because he knows that it is not plain and not to be taken lightly. “So give me understanding, that I may seek it with fitting search and attention, and so gain from it the practice and the understanding of both practical and contemplative matters. In this way I shall be able to keep it with my whole heart, approaching it without hesitation [?].” If he needs understanding merely to search out the law, what must he need in order to find its goal, if not understanding given by God? Lead me in the path of your commandments, for I have desired it. He says this to name the law, that is, the path [?], for there is a path of commandments. A “path” means the well-trodden road that many righteous people before us have walked. Unless someone takes the righteous as his guide, he cannot walk according to the commandments of God. For we must become imitators of Christ, take up [?] the cross, and follow after him. Incline my heart to your testimonies and not to greed. Turn my eyes away from looking at vanity; give me life in your way. Establish your word for your servant, so that he may fear you. Take away my reproach, which I dreaded, for your judgments are good. Behold, I have longed for your commandments; in your righteousness give me life. The saints refer everything to God and so teach us that without God we can do nothing. For he says: Unless you abide in me, you can do nothing. But perhaps someone will say: “If everything is referred to God, where is what depends on me?” Not so [?]: everywhere he has woven what depends on us together with what comes from God. From God: Lay down for me as law, O Lord, the way of your ordinances. What depends on us: And I will seek it out always. Again I ask from God: Give me understanding, and I shall search out your law. And what depends on me: And I will keep it with my whole heart. A third time I ask from God, saying: Lead me in the path of your commandments. What depends on me? For I have desired it, clearly meaning the law mentioned above. So let us ask that what comes from God may be granted to us, while also promising what depends on us, and not lying, so that we may not break our covenants with God. Let your mercy come upon me, O Lord, your salvation according to your word. And I shall have an answer for those who reproach me, for I have hoped in your words. Do not take the word of truth utterly out of my mouth, for I have hoped in your judgments. And I shall keep your law continually, for ever and ever. And I walked in a broad place, for I sought out your commandments. And I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not ashamed. This would fittingly suit someone brought before governors and kings to bear witness

for the name of Christ. And I meditated on your commandments, which I loved very much. And I lifted up my hands to your commandments, which I loved, and I pondered your ordinances. To lift up one's hands to the commandments means to do every action in harmony with the divine commandments. So the Psalmist testifies to both of these about himself. At the same time he lays down a law for us: we must give God's commandments both our fulfilment of them and our constant [?] meditation and contemplation. In this way we ourselves will fulfil them more exactly and will also lead others to fulfil them. Remember your words to your servant, through which you gave me hope. This comforted me in my humiliation, for your saying gave me life. The proud transgressed exceedingly, but I did not turn aside from your law. “While those who held other opinions boasted against the law and slandered it, I clung all the more to keeping it. I did not allow my assent to it to be shaken even a little.” I remembered your judgments of old, O Lord, and I was comforted. Despondency seized me because of the sinners who forsake your law. Your ordinances were songs to me in the place of my sojourning. I remembered your name in the night, O Lord, and I kept your law. This happened to me because I sought out your ordinances. You are my portion, O Lord; I said that I would keep your law. Someone who has renounced the affairs of this life will say: The Lord is my portion. He has no portion on earth and does not even wish for one, but is content with the Lord in place of everything. And it follows that he should say: I said that I would keep your law, meaning the spiritual law, of which Paul says: We know that the law is spiritual, and so on. How could they fail to keep the law or the commandments of the Lord when they have him as their portion, like the Levites, who were commanded to possess nothing in this life? For it is said: The Levites and the priests, the sons of Aaron, have no portion or inheritance among the sons of Israel, because the Lord is their portion. I entreated your face with my whole heart; have mercy on me according to your saying. I considered your ways and turned my feet to your testimonies. I was ready, and I was not troubled, to keep your commandments. The cords of sinners entangled me, but I did not forget your law. At midnight I did not (sic) rise to give thanks to you for the judgments of your righteousness. I am a companion of all who fear you and keep your commandments. The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord; teach me your ordinances. Consider the multitude of those who sin, who act impiously and speak injustice on high. Then see God's patience toward so many sins: how even after all this he makes his sun rise on the evil and the good, and

…sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous, you will say: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord; teach me your statutes.” “You have dealt kindly with your servant, Lord, according to your word. Teach me kindness and discipline and knowledge, for I have believed your commandments.” Instead of “You have dealt kindly,” Symmachus rendered, “You have done good to your servant.” The one schooled in divine things is taught not to be insensible of the benefit that God has done him, but to know that, since God’s kindness has reached him, he has been counted worthy to be called a servant of God, having become one according to his word. “Before I was humbled I went astray; therefore I have kept your word.” “Because of the sins I committed earlier,” he says, “I was handed over [?] by the judgment of God and suffered these things. For this reason, having been handed over to discipline, I ask for teaching, so that I may know that the humbling that befell me came about through kindness and for discipline.” “You are kind, Lord; in your kindness teach me your statutes.” It is the mark of a righteous man, who is content with all that happens and cheerfully accepts what Providence allots him, to say to God even in what are thought to be the more bitter things, “You are kind,” and “I will bless the Lord at all times,” holding to the same resolve. Instead of “You are kind,” the other versions translated, “You are good.” “I know, then,” he says, “and I do not doubt concerning your essence, that it is by nature goodness itself; but I need teaching in your statutes, and I ask you to teach me. For I need teaching in order to understand the words about the proud.” “The injustice of the proud has multiplied against me, but I will search out your commandments with my whole heart.” The more righteous someone is, drawing ever closer to God, and the more the peace of God multiplies in him, the more the injustice of the proud who wish to wrong him multiplies against him, as against a greater athlete, whether they are opposing powers or men. Yet when this happens he does not yield in the least: he goes on searching out the commandments of God with his whole heart, so as also to do them. “Their heart has curdled like milk, but I have meditated on your law. It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I might learn your statutes. The law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver.” For before their pride some were in good condition and tender of heart, and wholesome, so that their heart could be compared to milk, the most nourishing of foods; but when they had all put on pride and become [?], they changed, as it were, from milk into cheese. Instead of “curdled,” Aquila says, “Their heart grew fat like suet,” and Symmachus, “Their heart turned to marrow like fat.” “Nevertheless, even if they were in this state, I did not withdraw from the task set before me, searching out your commandments with my whole heart, and from searching them out hunting for the knowledge of your provi-

-dence and of your governance of all things. Their heart grew fat on the food they had at hand, but I meditated on your law.” “Your hands made me and fashioned me; give me understanding, and I will learn your commandments.” For when he had created heaven and earth and everything in them by a word and a command, on coming to man he said, “Let us make man after our own image and likeness.” To whom else does he say, “Let us make man,” than to his Only-begotten and to the Holy Spirit, whom he here calls “hands”? And in Job too it is written: “Your hands made me and fashioned me; after this you turn and terribly destroy me, renewing your examination of me.” So the hands of God both made and fashioned. Origen and some others say that “made” refers to the soul and “fashioned” to the body. Others say that “made” refers to the first creation, and “fashioned” to the regeneration and refashioning of the washing. “Those who fear you will see me and rejoice, because I have hoped in your words. I know, Lord, that your judgments are righteousness, and in truth you have humbled me. Let your mercy now comfort me, according to your word to your servant. Let your compassions come to me, and I shall live, for your law is my meditation.” If your mercy should come upon me and your compassions reach me, I will not be swallowed up by my humbling, but by persevering with endurance, I know well that I shall live. And I ask to obtain your mercy and your compassions, since I myself never cease to do all that lies with me, and even in my humbling itself I will meditate on your law. “Let the proud be put to shame, for they have unjustly done wrong against me; but I will ponder your commandments. Let those who fear you turn to me, and those who know your testimonies. Let my heart be blameless in your statutes, so that I may not be put to shame.” For every sin deserves shame. As long as the heart is imperfect, there is much worry and anxiety lest it should somehow grow weak and become worse than itself; but once it reaches the summit of perfection and is settled in a habit of virtue, it will be beyond all fear, no longer in doubt lest it should ever be put to shame. “My soul faints for your salvation; I have hoped in your words.” Quite consistently, explaining what the salvation is, he adds next, “I have hoped in your word,” signifying that the salvation is the Son of God. “My eyes have failed for your word, saying, ‘When will you comfort me?’ For I have become like a wineskin in the frost; I have not forgotten your statutes. How many are the days of your servant? When will you execute judgment on those who persecute me? The lawless have told

me idle tales, but not like your law, Lord. All your commandments are truth; they have persecuted me unjustly; help me. They almost made an end of me on the earth, but I did not forsake your commandments. Give me life according to your mercy, and I will keep the testimonies of your mouth.” To live according to God’s word is to live with godliness, not simply this life of the senses. Whoever obtains this will live well, so as to keep the testimonies of God’s mouth, testified and demonstrated by the Word of God, whom I have said is his mouth. “Your word, Lord, abides forever in heaven. Your truth is from generation to generation; you established the earth, and it abides. By your ordinance the day abides, for all things are your servants.” He calls “truth” this promise, which he knows will certainly be fulfilled from generation to generation. For in each generation you send people certain portions of the truth, and all the parts of the world, including the visible ones, are held together by your ordinance, not moving from their bounds nor transgressing the law laid down for them. The cause of the permanence of all these things is that you alone are Lord of all; all else is your servants, and as servants they are subject to you. “Had your law not been my meditation, I would then have perished in my humbling.” It has been said that the time of temptations and adversities is called humbling. It is the mark of a blessed man, then, to be in humbling and not perish. It is as if he said: I have come into the trial of martyrdom; if the law of God was always my meditation before I fell into it, and I practiced it, then when I come into the humbling of the trial of martyrdom, I do not perish. In the same way it is fitting to say this of every temptation, and also of the evil thoughts and the opposing powers that make war on me: I would have perished if your law had not been my support

“I will never forget your statutes, for by them you have given me life.” But I will remember your teachings, which I learned in this life; for through them I have passed from earth to heaven and dwell with angels. A man who has recovered firm and lasting health from a serious illness through certain medical remedies does not, simply because he is healthy and fit, forget the remedies that made him so healthy and strong. In the same way this saint, made alive by God through the statutes he received from him, says that he will not forget them for all eternity, and gives the reason: that God has made him live by them (sic). “I am yours; save me, for I have sought out your statutes. Sinners waited for me to destroy me; I have understood your testimonies. I have seen an end of all perfection; your commandment is exceedingly broad. How I have loved your law, Lord! All the

day long it is my meditation. You have made me wiser than my enemies through your commandment, for it is mine forever. I have understood more than all my teachers, for your testimonies are my meditation. I have understood more than the elders, for I have sought out your commandments.” If the Savior says somewhere, “A disciple is not above his teacher,” and so on, we must reply that the Savior said this after making a further distinction, when he said, “Do not call anyone on earth teacher; for you have one teacher, who is in heaven.” In relation to that teacher, then, no disciple is better. But the many teachers indicated here are of another kind, and the disciple is often better than they are. This comes about through greater and more continual [study] of the divine words

“I have held back my feet from every evil way, so that I may keep your words. I have not turned aside from your judgments, for you have given me the law. How sweet your words are to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth! From your commandments I have gained understanding; therefore I have hated every way of injustice. Your law is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths. I have sworn and confirmed it, to keep the judgments of your righteousness.” Since no one forced him, but by his own impulse and good choice he bound himself by an oath and swore to keep the judgments of God’s righteousness, he prays that his oath may be found worthy of acceptance with God; for the knowledge of God’s judgments also requires much teaching. “I have been humbled exceedingly, Lord; give me life according to your word. Be pleased, Lord, with the freewill offerings of my mouth, and teach me your judgments. My soul is in my hands continually, and I have not forgotten your law. Sinners have laid a snare for me, yet I have not strayed from your commandments.” A person’s soul is in his hands whenever he is in danger, and common usage says, “I had my soul in my hands.” “I, then,” says the righteous man, “die daily; I am always in danger for the sake of your word, for the truth, for reproof, for the kingdom [?]; and because of these things my soul is in my hands continually. For the danger of death did not make me forget your law.” One may also understand the saying in a loftier sense and say that “my soul was in my hands continually” means “in good deeds,” for the hand often stands for deeds. And if it were “in your hands,” let us understand the hands of God to be his creative work [?] continually. “I have inherited your testimonies forever, for they are the joy of my heart. I have inclined my heart to perform your statutes forever, for the reward.”

“I have hated the lawless, but I have loved your law. You are my helper and my protector; I have hoped in your words. Depart from me, you evildoers, and I will search out the commandments of my God. Uphold me according to your mercy and give me life, and do not put me to shame in my expectation.” Having said, “Depart from me, you evildoers,” he consistently calls on God for this too: that by God’s power the evildoers may be driven out of his soul, and that, once he is free of them, he may obtain the life and salvation that come from God and not fall short of his expectation. And again he asks to obtain help so as to be saved: “Help me, and I shall be saved, and I will meditate on your statutes continually. You have despised all who depart from your statutes, for their thought is unjust. I have counted all the sinners of the earth as transgressors; therefore I have loved your testimonies. Pierce my flesh with the fear of you; for of your judgments

“I have done judgment and righteousness; do not [?] me to those who wrong me.” The one who received his first instruction at the beginning, as one who has now advanced far and achieved great things, prays not to fall away from his progress. Then, seeing that many envy the good, and that although they have nothing bad to say about them they weave slanders, he entreats and begs to be rescued from them. Instead of “those who wrong me,” Aquila rendered, “Do not leave me to those who slander me.” “I have done judgment and righteousness; do not hand me over to those who wrong me. Receive your servant for good; let not the proud slander me.” The one who has repented, escaped from the powers that worked within him, and been redeemed from captivity, says: “Receive your servant for good; for these received me for evil. If you do not receive me, your servant, who had fallen into the hands of the enemy, these proud ones, the opposing powers, are going to slander me.” How do they slander? They worked on me and persuaded me to become a sinner, and then they become my accusers, laying the whole blame for the sins on me. He is therefore bound to beg God to become his sponsor, as it were his guarantor, so that God himself may be his guardian, keeping and guarding the pledge for himself, so as to give no handle to the slanderers lying in wait for him. “My eyes have failed for your salvation and for the word of your righteousness. Deal with your servant according to your mercy, and teach me your statutes. I am your servant; give me understanding, and I shall know your testimonies. It is time for the Lord to act; they have scattered your law.” “Looking up to your salvation and your word,” he says, “I have hung all my hopes on these, asking to be rescued from those who begrudge me my salvation.” “Therefore I have loved your commandments more than gold and topaz.” “I have done judgment and righ-

-teousness, and for you, God, there will one day be a time to act, that is, to do judgment and righteousness, because of those who have scattered your law. Knowing this, then, and taking care not to be caught by that time, I have loved your commandments above everything that people consider precious.” “Therefore I was set straight toward all your commandments; I have hated every unjust way.” The human soul, once its reason has come to completion, inevitably comes to be in vice. For as soon as the natural law has come to completion in human beings, it is impossible for sin not to arise. So when vice arises and the soul is twisted, it needs straightening. What, then, are the things that straighten it? One commandment can to some extent [straighten] the twist of the soul that has come from vi-

…but to [straighten] the soul here is impossible without all the commandments. If, however, the soul is taken away while still crooked, it will no longer be straightened by commandments, but by fire or darkness or being cut in two, or by some other of the grimmer measures God applies. If, then, we do not do all the commandments, we are not set straight. Hence it is wonderfully said, “Therefore we were set straight toward all your commandments; we have hated every unjust way.” For the one who has been set straight toward all the commandments of God no longer abstains from injustice while still being pulled about by the desire to do wrong; he abstains because he has come to hate injustice

“Your testimonies are wonderful; therefore my soul has searched them out. The disclosure of your words will give light and give understanding to infants. I opened my mouth and drew in spirit, for I longed for your commandments.” The first knowledge, the teaching of your words handed down at the beginning, will give light and understanding to infants. But your testimonies are wonderful and full of astonishment. “Fittingly, then, I spread open the vessel of my own soul and, as it were, opened my mouth, and so I received the divine Spirit from you, believing the promise that says, ‘Open your mouth, and I will fill it.’ And I did this, drawing into myself the spirit that comes from you, so that I might know your wonderful testimonies and gain the illumination of your words, having received the understanding of them through your Spirit.” “I opened my mouth and drew in spirit, for I longed for your commandments”: the very content of the commandments draws in and attracts the spirit. He is speaking of the mouth of the hidden man; and the mouth of the soul may be its intellectual faculty, which in thinking brings forth the word that is in the mind. It makes no difference whether one says “receive a word” or “draw in spirit,” for the spirit is the same as the divine word. That is why the Savior also said of the word and the sayings he spoke, “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and are life.” “Look upon me and have mercy on me, according to the judgment of those who love your name.” Of those

who receive mercy from God, some obtain it through repentance, as they are just turning away from their sins and confessing them; others experience God’s mercy so that, as they advance, they may hasten to the very goal of virtue. So this man prays to be shown mercy not according to the judgment of those who repent, but of those who love the name of the Lord; for the speaker is one of those who have advanced far in virtue and in the knowledge of the truth. That is why he speaks boldly of being seen by God. “Look upon me,” he says, and my receiving mercy will necessarily follow. “Direct my steps according to your word, and let no lawlessness have dominion over me.” According to God’s word he directs my steps as I pass from vice and ignorance to virtue and the knowledge of the truth. For the guide and leader of such steps is the right

“Redeem me from the slander of men, and I will keep your commandments.” As the reward for the mercy of being redeemed from the slander of men, he promises to give the keeping of the Lord’s commandments; or rather, not a reward but thanksgiving for being redeemed from the slander of men. Joseph and Susanna obtained this request [?]. Figuratively, “men” might be taken to mean the devil and the evil powers ranged with him, from whose slander God alone [can] redeem. “Make your face shine upon your servant, and teach me your statutes.” Longing to see the second shining forth of the Savior, he makes this request concerning it, saying to the Father, “Make your face shine, Lord”; whoever has seen it has seen the Father as well. For he himself says of himself, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” [?] “My eyes have run down in streams of water, because they did not keep your law. You are righteous, Lord, and your judgments are upright. You have commanded your testimonies in righteousness and in great truth. My zeal for you has consumed me, because my enemies have forgotten your words. Your word is thoroughly refined, and your servant has loved it. I am young and despised, yet I have not forgotten your statutes. Your righteousness is an everlasting righteousness, and your law is truth. Tribulations and distresses have found me; your commandments are my meditation.” Symmachus gave a different sense, saying, “Tribulations and weariness have overtaken me, but your commandments delighted me.” This is how it is with every God-fearing person: weighed down and troubled by the affairs of life, and worn out by human wickedness, his only consolation, refreshment and delight is meditating on God’s commandments. “Your testimonies are righteousness forever; give me understanding, and I shall live.” This righteousness, which

…we practise in the present is repaid to us not over a few days but for ever. In all these things the Prophet asks God for understanding, the most necessary of God's gifts, and says: "Give me understanding, and I shall live." For no one foolish or without understanding comes to that blessed life. One must ask for understanding from God, who gives it to all who ask him with their whole soul, so that, having received understanding, we may be able to say: "Give me understanding, and I shall live." "I cried out with my whole heart; hear me, O Lord; I will seek out your statutes. I cried out to you; save me, and I will keep your testimonies. I rose before the dawn and cried out; I have hoped in your words. My eyes were awake before the morning, to meditate on your sayings." Whoever rises in the dead of night and calls on God is set free from the plots of the night. And in his morning, that is, at the rising of the light, since he has risen early, his eyes are already there to meet it, and he meditates on the sayings of God with confidence. For the soul that rejoices most in the law is the one that is conscious within itself of having done what is right. "Hear my voice, O Lord, according to your mercy; according to your judgment give me life. Those who persecute me have drawn near to lawlessness, but they have gone far from your law. You are near, O Lord, and all your ways are truth. From the beginning I have known from your testimonies that you founded them for ever. Look on my humiliation and rescue me, for I have not forgotten your law. Judge my cause and redeem me; give me life for the sake of your word." He asks to be judged against his enemies, those who make war on him secretly or openly, and to be redeemed. For God alone redeems us from both, and he not only delivers us from death, which the demons threaten and bring about, but also gives life through the same word. "Salvation is far from sinners, for they have not sought out your statutes. Your compassions are many, O Lord; according to your judgment give me life." A man's mercy is for his neighbour, but the Lord's mercy is for all flesh, even for one who seems to be most righteous. For when human beings are compared with the exact judgment of God, even the righteous person needs mercy. Everything that seems to have come about through mercy comes about through God's mercy. For what has anyone done that is worthy of eternal blessedness and the kingdom of heaven without being helped by God? "Many are those who persecute and afflict me; I have not turned aside from your testimonies. I saw those without understanding and I wasted away, because they did not keep your sayings. See that I have loved your commandments, O Lord; in your mercy give me life. The beginning of your words is truth, and all the judgments of your righteousness are for ever. Rulers have persecuted me without cause, and my heart has stood in awe of your words. I will rejoice over your sayings like one who finds much spoil. I have hated and abhorred injustice, but

your law I have loved. Seven times a day I have praised you for the judgments of your righteousness." [?] And so, setting about it as one who rises from his bed before the sun, in the words of the one who says, "From the night my spirit rises early to you, O God," and "O God, my God, to you I rise early," he sent up the first hymn. Then, when day had come, at the first hour, as though offering sacrifice to God at dawn, he sent up the second; at the third hour, likewise, the third; again at the sixth hour, the fourth; at the ninth hour, the fifth; and at the twelfth, the sixth. Then in the evening, after caring for the body and when about to turn to his bed, he [?] the seventh hymn, and so he fulfilled the words "Seven times a day."

"Great peace have those who love your law, and for them there is no stumbling block." Those who long for the name of God obtain great peace. This is not so much outward peace, for that is not in our power, but peace in the thoughts, through which one comes to have calm and freedom from the disturbance that comes from passion. Those who have it from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ [?] it together with the grace that goes with it. So, possessing it because of the name of God and being surpassingly perfect, they have no stumbling block within themselves. For having one belongs to the little ones and not to the great, as the Saviour says: "See that you do not cause one of these little ones to stumble." And if there is great peace for those who love the law of God, then such a person has great peace, and war does not touch his soul. For none of the sins inflames his soul, and since he has peace he has become such that he is no longer made to stumble by anything, and he says: "Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will affliction or distress?" and so on. "I have waited for your salvation, O Lord, and I have loved your commandments." Waiting for the true salvation that comes from you, I have not only kept your commandments but also loved them. For once the commandments have been carried out and accomplished with love, the salvation that is waited for will follow at once, and that salvation is nothing other than the salvation of those who are being saved. And if he is also waiting for the Saviour, of whom it is said, "All flesh shall see the salvation of God," then it follows that he loves the commandments of God, whose salvation he has also waited for. In this way he [?] both his practice, purely, and his expectation, contemplatively, always waiting for and contemplating that God the Word has come to seek and save what was lost. "My soul has kept your testimonies and has loved them exceedingly." Not only have I [?] your commandments, but my soul has also loved your testimonies exceedingly and kept them. First, then, he said "I loved" and "I have loved your commandments"; second, "My soul has kept your testimonies"; and in the third verse he brings both together into one and says: "I have kept your commandments and your testimonies, for all my ways are before you, O Lord."

[?] The sinner will not say, "All my ways are before you," for the ways of the sinner are not in the sight of God; only the ways of the righteous are. So, in order that all our ways too may come to be before God, namely the laws, the prophets, and above all the perfect, true and good way, Christ Jesus, who said, "I am the way," let us pray that we may travel on the way to the end and reach the God and Father of all through Christ Jesus. "Let my petition draw near before you, O Lord; according to your saying give me understanding. Let my request come in before you, O Lord; according to your saying deliver me. My lips shall pour forth a hymn when you teach me your statutes; my tongue shall utter your sayings, for all your commandments are righteousness." This follows very fittingly after his prayer about the mind. To be given understanding of the sayings of God was a matter not for the lips or the tongue but for the thinking part of the soul. So, having asked for the primary things, he moves on to the secondary ones and asks that the instruments of the word within him, his lips and his tongue, be consecrated. Then his lips would pour forth a hymn continually, as his mind is taught God's statutes by God himself, and his tongue would utter nothing other than the sayings of God, and would do this because all his ways are righteousness. "Let your hand be there to save me, for I have chosen your commandments." Seeing how great the task before him is, he needs help from God to accomplish what he has just said. But while asking great things of God, he also contributes his own part, saying, "For I have chosen your commandments." That is, whatever lay within my power, I have fulfilled. I have chosen your commandments, having loved them, as I said before.

"I have longed for your salvation, and your law is my meditation." Most people long for salvation, but not God's. What they long for is the salvation of the flesh in this world. But it is a real achievement to long for God's salvation, so as to be saved in God, to rest in him, and to inherit the holy things. For this is God's salvation: eternal life. If you want to take the reasoning higher, God's salvation is Christ, for "Jesus" means "salvation of God." He was sent to us. The way for one who longs for God's salvation is to make the law his meditation, since the law proclaimed in advance his coming here. By "law" he here means the whole of the old and divine…

"My soul shall live and shall praise you, and your judgments shall help me." He confined the life of the soul to the time to come, for "our life is hidden with Christ in God." Then the soul will praise God in the true sense. "And your judgments shall help me." God's judgments are given to help those who are judged. But the help that judgments give the righteous person is of one kind [?],

[?] the kind that comes without torments and toils; the help that judgments give the one who must be led through toils and torments is another way. "I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant, for I have not forgotten your commandments."
